Chapter 1 · Why Rust Feels Different

Why Rust Feels Different

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

Chapter 1 argues that Rust's difficulty is architectural, not syntactic: ownership, mutation authority, fallibility, and thread-safety stop being conventions and become contracts the compiler checks. These exercises ask you to practice that shift in the small before later chapters formalize it. You translate a familiar resource-lifecycle idea into a single-owner Rust design, separate the compile-time structure of an abstraction from the runtime work it still performs, replace a sentinel-value API with explicit Option and Result, and read three compiler diagnostics as ownership feedback rather than obstacles.

The lab grounds all of this in a function you can run. parse_limit is deliberately tiny, but it forces every theme of the chapter into one signature: a missing value modeled as None rather than a magic number, an invalid value modeled as Err rather than a panic, and a return type that makes callers acknowledge failure. Get this function and these exercises right and the rest of the book reads as elaboration rather than novelty.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Translate a familiar lifecycle pattern into Rust

Take RAII from C++ or, equivalently, the using/IDisposable pattern from C#: a resource is acquired in a constructor and released deterministically when the owning scope ends. In Rust this maps directly onto a struct with a single owner and a Drop implementation, with no class hierarchy and no garbage collector involved. Model a LogWriter that owns a file handle and a buffer. There is exactly one owner of that handle at any moment, because ownership in Rust is a single-owner relationship by construction; passing the LogWriter by value transfers that responsibility rather than aliasing it.

The method signatures encode who is allowed to do what. A read-only method such as fn flushed_bytes(&self) -> usize takes &self because it only inspects state and must coexist with other shared readers. A method that appends, fn write_line(&mut self, line: &str), takes &mut self because it mutates the buffer, and &mut is exclusive: while it is held, no other reference to the writer exists, which is precisely why borrowed mutation is data-race-free. A method that finalizes the resource, fn close(self) -> io::Result<()>, consumes self by value, because after closing there must be no way to use the writer again; consuming self makes that a compile-time guarantee rather than a runtime check or a documented rule.

Deterministic cleanup comes from Drop. When the LogWriter goes out of scope, or when the owner is consumed, the compiler inserts a call to drop at a statically known point: the end of the owning scope. That is the key contrast the chapter draws. C# would defer flushing to a finalizer or rely on the developer remembering using; Go would lean on defer plus a runtime garbage collector for the backing memory. Rust ties release to ownership and scope, so cleanup order is predictable, runs without a collector, and needs no base class. If close was not called explicitly, Drop still runs, so the resource cannot leak by forgetfulness.

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, BufWriter, Write};

pub struct LogWriter {
    sink: BufWriter<File>,
    written: usize,
}

impl LogWriter {
    pub fn open(path: &str) -> io::Result<Self> {
        Ok(LogWriter {
            sink: BufWriter::new(File::create(path)?),
            written: 0,
        })
    }

    // Read-only: shared access, no mutation, takes &self.
    pub fn written_lines(&self) -> usize {
        self.written
    }

    // Mutating: exclusive access, takes &mut self.
    pub fn write_line(&mut self, line: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
        writeln!(self.sink, "{}", line)?;
        self.written += 1;
        Ok(())
    }

    // Finalizing: consumes self so the writer cannot be used afterward.
    pub fn close(mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.sink.flush()
    }
}

// Deterministic cleanup even if close() is never called.
impl Drop for LogWriter {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let _ = self.sink.flush();
    }
}

A single-owner LogWriter: &self reads, &mut self mutates, self finalizes, and Drop guarantees the flush.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • There is exactly one owner of the file handle; moving the LogWriter transfers cleanup responsibility rather than aliasing it.
  • write_line takes &mut self because mutation requires exclusive access, while written_lines takes &self because shared reads must not mutate.
  • Cleanup is tied to scope end via Drop and to consuming close(self); no garbage collector and no base class are involved.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the zero-cost part and the real runtime cost

Read critical_count from the chapter (the why_rust_pipeline sample renamed here): readings.iter().copied().filter(|reading| *reading >= threshold).count(). The abstraction structure is everything that describes how the computation is expressed. iter() produces a slice iterator, copied() adapts &i32 to i32, filter takes a closure, and count consumes the chain. Each adapter is a distinct generic type, and the closure is its own anonymous type. When the function is monomorphized and optimized, that layered structure collapses. There is no Box, no heap allocation for the iterator, and no vtable: the compiler can lower the whole chain to a single pass that is essentially the loop you would have written by hand. That collapse is what zero-cost means here.

The runtime cost is the real work that survives optimization. The CPU still walks the slice element by element, which means the loop is bounded by how the readings sit in cache and memory; a cold or strided slice costs more than a hot contiguous one. For each element it evaluates the predicate reading >= threshold, which is a comparison and a conditional, so branch prediction matters when the data is unpredictable. count performs an increment per match. None of these go away because they are the computation itself, not abstraction tax. If you materialized instead of counting, for example .collect::<Vec<i32>>(), you would add a genuine heap allocation and the cost of copying matches into it; the chapter's distinction is that this allocation is a consequence of asking for a Vec, not of using iterators.

Dynamic dispatch is absent by default and only appears when you opt in. If the function returned the chain as a trait object, for example Box<dyn Iterator<Item = i32>>, the concrete adapter type would be erased and each next call would route through a vtable, defeating the inlining that made the pipeline collapse. The same is true if you stored the closure as &dyn Fn or Box<dyn Fn> instead of letting it be a unique generic type. impl Iterator and ordinary generics keep everything static and monomorphized; dyn is the explicit choice that trades that away for type erasure.

fn critical_count(readings: &[i32], threshold: i32) -> usize {
    readings
        .iter()      // structure: slice iterator type
        .copied()    // structure: &i32 -> i32 adapter, no allocation
        .filter(|reading| *reading >= threshold) // structure: closure is a unique type
        .count()     // drives the pass; the actual work happens here
}

// Real runtime work that survives optimization:
//   - walking the slice (cache/memory bound)
//   - the comparison `*reading >= threshold` per element (a branch)
//   - one increment per match inside count()

// Opting INTO dynamic dispatch (vtable per next() call, blocks inlining):
fn critical_iter_dyn<'a>(
    readings: &'a [i32],
    threshold: i32,
) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = i32> + 'a> {
    Box::new(readings.iter().copied().filter(move |r| *r >= threshold))
}

The adapter chain is compile-time structure; the slice walk, the per-element branch, and the count are the surviving runtime cost. Box<dyn Iterator> is where dynamic dispatch would enter.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • iter/copied/filter and impl Iterator are named as monomorphized abstraction structure that does not imply dynamic dispatch by default.
  • The surviving runtime work is named: walking the slice, cache behavior, the per-element comparison and branch, and the allocation that appears only if results are collected.
  • Returning the chain as Box<dyn Iterator> (or storing the closure as dyn Fn) is identified as the explicit opt-in to vtable-based dynamic dispatch.
Exercise 3implementation

Make fallibility explicit instead of implicit

The C-style version of this API would return a usize and reserve 0 or -1 (often cast to a large unsigned value) to mean missing or invalid, leaving the caller free to forget the check. Rust models the two distinct outcomes in the type system instead. Missing input is structurally different from invalid input, so absence is carried by the Option<&str> argument and failure is carried by the Result return. The signature parse_limit(input: Option<&str>) -> Result<usize, &'static str> makes both visible to every caller, and because Result must be inspected to extract the usize, the failure mode cannot be ignored by accident.

Following the hint, handle the Option first. None is not an error here; it means the caller supplied nothing, so it maps to the default Ok(100). Only in the Some branch do you parse. parse::<usize>() already rejects non-numeric and negative input by returning its own Err, so map that to Err("invalid number"). Then enforce the domain rule that the limit must be positive by matching Ok(0) separately and returning Err("limit must be greater than 0"). Any other successful parse is a valid positive integer and returns Ok(limit). There is no panic, no unwrap, and no sentinel: each invalid state is a value of type Err, and the one non-failure default is a value of type Ok.

The payoff is that invalid states are hard to ignore at call sites. A caller cannot use the limit as a number without first destructuring the Result, so the compiler forces an acknowledgement of failure at the boundary rather than allowing a magic number to flow silently into later arithmetic. This is the chapter's point in miniature: making fallibility explicit pushes the decision earlier, to the place where it can be handled, instead of leaving it to a runtime convention.

fn parse_limit(input: Option<&str>) -> Result<usize, &'static str> {
    match input {
        None => Ok(100), // missing input uses the default, not an error
        Some(raw) => match raw.parse::<usize>() {
            Ok(0) => Err("limit must be greater than 0"),
            Ok(limit) => Ok(limit),
            Err(_) => Err("invalid number"), // non-numeric or negative
        },
    }
}

None first, then parse; both failure cases are Err values, the default is Ok(100), and no sentinel or panic is used.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The signature is exactly Result<usize, &'static str>, with no panic, unwrap, or sentinel value.
  • None maps to Ok(100), so missing input becomes the default without producing an error.
  • Zero and non-numeric input each return a distinct Err, so invalid input is a type-system value the caller must inspect, not a magic number.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Interpret three compiler diagnostics and propose repairs

E0382, borrow of moved value: request. The enforced rule is single ownership with move semantics: a non-Copy value has one owner, and using it (passing by value, returning it, assigning it) moves ownership away. The buggy shape is passing request into a function or another binding and then continuing to use the original name, for example let parsed = handle(request); log(request);. The compiler is telling you the ownership protocol is ambiguous: you both gave the value away and tried to keep it. Repairs, in order of preference, are to borrow instead of move when the callee only needs to read or temporarily mutate (handle(&request) or handle(&mut request)); to have the callee return ownership back if it must consume and you still need the value (let request = handle(request)); or, only when you genuinely need two independent owned copies, to clone explicitly (handle(request.clone())). Cloning is the last option because it is a real cost you are choosing, not a default.

E0499, cannot borrow buffer as mutable more than once at a time. The rule is exclusivity of mutable borrows: at most one &mut to a value may exist at a time, and it may not coexist with any shared borrow. The buggy shape is taking two overlapping mutable references, such as let a = &mut buffer; let b = &mut buffer; a.push(1); b.push(2);, or holding a &mut from a method while calling another &mut method, or aliasing two mutable views into the same container. Repairs are to shorten the borrow's scope so the first &mut ends before the second begins (use one, drop it, then take the next, which non-lexical lifetimes often allow automatically), or to redesign the data structure so the two mutations target disjoint parts. split_at_mut, indexing into separate fields, or restructuring so each writer owns its own region all let you mutate in parallel without overlapping borrows.

E0277, Rc<String> cannot be sent between threads safely. The rule is the Send and Sync trait bounds: thread::spawn requires its closure (and everything captured) to be Send, and Rc is deliberately not Send because its reference count is updated with non-atomic operations. Moving an Rc to another thread would let two threads race on that count and corrupt it, so the trait bound rejects it at compile time. The buggy shape is capturing an Rc<String> in a move closure handed to a new thread. The repair is to use the thread-safe sharing type Arc<String>, whose reference count is atomic, so sharing across threads is sound; if the shared data also needs mutation, pair it with a synchronization primitive such as Arc<Mutex<T>>. The distinction the diagnostic is drawing is exactly Rc for single-threaded sharing versus Arc for cross-thread sharing, and the compiler enforces that boundary rather than trusting you to remember it.

// E0382 — moved value reused. Prefer borrowing; clone only when you mean it.
fn handle(req: &Request) { /* read-only */ }
let request = Request::new();
handle(&request);   // borrow, not move
log(&request);      // still usable

// E0499 — two overlapping &mut. Disjoint borrows instead of aliasing.
let (left, right) = buffer.split_at_mut(mid);
left[0] = 1;        // independent &mut regions, no overlap
right[0] = 2;

// E0277 — Rc is not Send. Use Arc for cross-thread sharing.
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;
let shared = Arc::new(String::from("config"));
let worker = Arc::clone(&shared);
thread::spawn(move || {
    println!("{}", worker); // Arc is Send + Sync
})
.join()
.unwrap();

Each diagnostic mapped to its rule and its idiomatic repair: borrow over move, disjoint mutable borrows, and Arc instead of Rc across threads.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • E0382 is explained as ownership transfer via move, with borrowing, returning ownership, and intentional cloning offered as alternatives.
  • E0499 is explained as exclusive mutable access, with scope shortening (non-lexical lifetimes) and disjoint data-structure redesign (split_at_mut) as repairs.
  • E0277 is explained via the Send bound, with Rc identified as single-threaded and Arc (optionally Arc<Mutex<T>>) as the thread-safe sharing approach.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design a worker pipeline with explicit ownership boundaries

Trace the flow socket bytes -> parse -> validate -> route to workers -> emit metrics and place an ownership boundary at each stage rather than reaching for shared mutable state. Bytes arriving on the socket are borrowed, not owned domain values. The receiver reads into a reusable buffer (&mut [u8]) and parsing borrows that buffer to produce an owned domain value, for example a Request struct with owned fields. The boundary where bytes become owned domain values is the parse step: parse(&[u8]) -> Result<Request, ParseError>. This matters because the buffer can be reused for the next frame the instant parsing returns the owned Request, so nothing downstream holds a borrow into transient network memory.

Validation borrows locally and crosses no thread boundary. validate(&Request) -> Result<(), ValidationError> only inspects the already-owned value, so it takes a shared reference and returns a Result; there is no reason for it to own or mutate the request. Routing is the cross-thread boundary, and the types allowed to cross it are owned, Send work items. Use a channel (std::sync::mpsc, or crossbeam for multiple producers) and send the owned Request to a worker: the value moves into the queue and then into the worker thread, so the worker owns exactly what it needs and no lifetime question is left to convention. This is the chapter's rule that queues, threads, and async tasks are ownership boundaries: hand off owned work items when execution may outlive the current scope. I deliberately avoid starting from a single global Arc<Mutex<HashMap<...>>>; routing by message passing of owned values keeps the hot path lock-free and makes the data flow auditable.

Failure and state are explicit. parse and validate return Result with distinct error enums so a malformed frame is rejected at the boundary instead of propagating; the worker's outcome is itself an enum (Processed, Rejected(Reason)) rather than a boolean plus out-of-band logging. Metrics are the one place where shared state is semantically real: many workers must increment the same counters. There I use sharing on purpose, an Arc<Metrics> where Metrics holds AtomicU64 fields, so increments are lock-free and the sharing reflects a genuine shared aggregate rather than mere convenience. The tradeoff is concrete: message passing of owned requests costs a move (and, under bursts, queue memory and backpressure handling) compared to a shared mutable map, but it removes lock contention from the per-request path, confines mutability, and keeps each stage independently testable. I accept that move cost to gain throughput under concurrency and a design reviewers can reason about.

use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

struct Request { /* owned domain fields */ }
enum ParseError { Malformed }
enum ValidationError { OutOfRange }
enum Outcome { Processed, Rejected }

// Boundary 1: borrowed bytes -> owned domain value.
fn parse(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Request, ParseError> { /* ... */ Ok(Request {}) }

// Local borrow only; crosses no thread boundary.
fn validate(req: &Request) -> Result<(), ValidationError> { Ok(()) }

#[derive(Default)]
struct Metrics { processed: AtomicU64, rejected: AtomicU64 }

fn run(bytes: &[u8], metrics: Arc<Metrics>) {
    // Channel carries OWNED, Send work items across the thread boundary.
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel::<Request>();
    let worker = thread::spawn(move || {
        for req in rx { // worker owns each request
            let outcome = match validate(&req) {
                Ok(()) => Outcome::Processed,
                Err(_) => Outcome::Rejected,
            };
            match outcome {
                Outcome::Processed => metrics.processed.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed),
                Outcome::Rejected => metrics.rejected.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed),
            };
        }
    });
    if let Ok(req) = parse(bytes) {
        let _ = tx.send(req); // move owned work item into the queue
    }
    drop(tx);
    worker.join().unwrap();
}

Ownership becomes concrete at parse, validation borrows locally, owned Requests cross the channel, and Arc<Metrics> with atomics is the one deliberately shared aggregate.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The ownership boundary is placed at parse, before the request is queued or sent across threads.
  • A global Arc<Mutex<HashMap<...>>> is explicitly rejected as the first move; routing uses message passing of owned items, with sharing reserved for the metrics aggregate.
  • Failure and state are explicit through Result and enums (ParseError, ValidationError, Outcome) rather than booleans or log-only failure.
  • The move-cost-versus-lock-contention tradeoff is stated and justified in favor of throughput, confined mutability, and reviewability.

Lab solution

The function takes an Option<&str> so the absence of input is a distinct, well-typed state rather than a sentinel. The outer match handles None first by returning Ok(100): a missing limit is not a failure, it is the default, so it is wrapped in Ok. This is why the first line prints default = Ok(100).

In the Some branch, raw.parse::<usize>() does two things at once. It rejects anything that is not a non-negative integer by returning its own Err, which the final arm maps to Err("invalid number"). When parsing succeeds, an extra arm matches Ok(0) specifically and enforces the domain rule that the limit must be positive, returning Err("limit must be greater than 0"); that is why parse_limit(Some("0")) prints the zero line. Any other successful parse falls through to Ok(limit), so parse_limit(Some("25")) yields Ok(25). Because every line uses the {:?} debug formatter on a Result, the output shows the Ok and Err wrappers verbatim, matching the expected output exactly.

The design point is that no path panics, unwraps, or returns a magic number. Each outcome is a value the caller must destructure to use, so fallibility stays explicit in the type system from end to end.

Example 1-S. parse_limit_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn parse_limit(input: Option<&str>) -> Result<usize, &'static str> {
    match input {
        None => Ok(100),
        Some(raw) => match raw.parse::<usize>() {
            Ok(0) => Err("limit must be greater than 0"),
            Ok(limit) => Ok(limit),
            Err(_) => Err("invalid number"),
        },
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("default = {:?}", parse_limit(None));
    println!("zero = {:?}", parse_limit(Some("0")));
    println!("value = {:?}", parse_limit(Some("25")));
}
Output
default = Ok(100)
zero = Err("limit must be greater than 0")
value = Ok(25)

Review question answers

Why does Rust often feel harder at API boundaries than inside small local functions?

Inside a small local function the compiler can often see the entire lifetime of every value, so moves, borrows, and drops are inferred with little friction. At an API boundary you must instead state the ownership protocol explicitly in the signature: whether a parameter is moved, borrowed shared, or borrowed mutably, and whether the return transfers ownership. That forces design decisions that a local scope let you leave implicit, which is why boundaries feel harder even though the rules are the same.

What is the practical difference between a generic function using traits and a trait object?

A generic function with trait bounds is monomorphized: the compiler generates a specialized copy for each concrete type, so calls are statically dispatched and can be inlined, with no vtable and no per-call indirection. A trait object such as Box<dyn Trait> erases the concrete type behind a pointer and a vtable, so dispatch happens at runtime through that vtable. Generics trade larger code size for speed and static dispatch, while trait objects trade a small runtime indirection for type erasure and the ability to store heterogeneous types in one collection.

Name one category of bug Rust usually catches at compile time and one category it cannot remove from runtime reality.

Rust's safe subset reliably catches memory-safety and data-race bugs at compile time: use-after-free, double-free, and concurrent unsynchronized mutation are rejected by the ownership and borrow rules before the program runs. What it cannot remove from runtime reality are logic and resource-exhaustion problems: an incorrect algorithm, a wrong threshold, a deadlock from lock ordering, or running out of memory are all still possible. Compile-time guarantees eliminate whole classes of undefined behavior, not the cost or correctness of the work itself.

Why is 'just clone it' sometimes correct and sometimes a design smell?

Cloning is correct when you genuinely need two independent owned copies of the data, or when the value is small and copying is cheaper than the complexity of threading a borrow through the code. It becomes a design smell when it is used reflexively to silence a borrow-checker error that is really pointing at an unclear ownership protocol, because the clone hides the design question and adds real allocation and copy cost on a hot path. The chapter's framing is that a borrow-checker error is design feedback, so the first response should be to reshape ownership or borrow, and clone only when the second owned copy is semantically real.

How would you explain Send and Sync to a teammate coming from Go or C#?

In Go or C# you can pass almost any value to another goroutine or thread and the runtime trusts you to synchronize access yourself; the language does not check it. In Rust, Send means a value can be safely moved to another thread, and Sync means a value can be safely shared by reference (&T) across threads, and the compiler enforces these as trait bounds at compile time. The practical consequence is that types like Rc, whose reference count is non-atomic, are not Send, so the compiler stops you from sharing them across threads and points you to the thread-safe Arc instead, turning a class of data races into compile errors rather than production incidents.

Chapter 2 · The Rust Mental Model

The Rust Mental Model

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises convert the chapter's mental model into something you can apply during code review and debugging. They ask you to track ownership transfer line by line, to separate inline storage from heap allocation in a composite value, to rewrite imperative mutation as value-producing expressions, to diagnose a lifetime error as an ownership problem rather than an annotation problem, and to plan ownership across a realistic ingest pipeline.

The common thread is naming the owner at every step. Once you can say which binding owns a value, when that owner is dropped, and which references must stay within that window, most of Rust's diagnostics become predictable rather than adversarial. The solutions below answer each exercise directly in those terms.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Predict the ownership timeline

Track ownership one binding at a time. After let service = String::from("payload");, the binding service owns the heap-backed String. After let alias = service;, ownership moves out of service and into alias. String is not Copy, so this assignment transfers ownership rather than duplicating the value; service is now an unusable, moved-from binding. After consume(alias);, ownership moves again, this time out of alias and into the consume function's parameter.

The owned String is dropped at the end of consume's body, because that is where its current owner leaves scope. Nothing in main drops it after the call, because main no longer owns it once the value was moved into consume. This is the chapter's point that owned values live until their owner is dropped, and that drop is deterministic: it happens at a specific, predictable point in the code, not at an unspecified later time.

A line that would fail to compile is any use of a moved-from binding after its value has been transferred, for example println!("{}", service); placed after let alias = service;, or println!("{}", alias); placed after consume(alias);. The compiler rejects these with a use-after-move error because the named binding no longer owns a value. The fix, when you genuinely need the data in two places, is to clone before the move or to pass a reference instead of transferring ownership.

fn consume(value: String) {
    println!("consume owns {}", value);
    // `value` (the owned String) is dropped here, at end of `consume`.
}

fn main() {
    let service = String::from("payload");
    let alias = service; // ownership moves: service -> alias
    // println!("{}", service); // would NOT compile: service was moved out.
    consume(alias); // ownership moves: alias -> consume's parameter
    // println!("{}", alias);   // would NOT compile: alias was moved out.
}

Ownership moves service -> alias -> consume; the String is dropped at the end of consume.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Ownership is shown moving from service to alias, then from alias into consume's parameter.
  • The drop point is identified as the end of consume, where the value's current owner leaves scope.
  • The failing-line example uses a moved-from binding (service or alias) after its value was transferred.
Exercise 2code reading

Map stack and heap storage precisely

Separate the outer struct layout from the storage owned by each field. A Batch that holds a fixed-size array, say [u32; 4], plus a Vec<String> stores both fields inline in the Batch value itself. The array is stored inline in full: all four u32 words sit directly inside the Batch, with no separate allocation. The Vec<String> field is also inline, but only as a small fixed-size handle: three machine words holding a pointer, a length, and a capacity. Wherever the Batch value lives (a local on the stack, or inside another owner), those words travel with it.

The heap allocations are owned indirectly through the Vec. The Vec<String> owns one heap buffer: the element array of String handles, sized by its capacity. That buffer does not live inside the Batch value; the Vec's pointer field points at it. Each String element is itself a three-word handle stored inside that element buffer, and each non-empty String owns a further, separate heap allocation holding its UTF-8 bytes.

Ownership is layered. The Batch value owns the array inline and owns the Vec handle inline. The Vec owns its element buffer on the heap. Each String element owns its own byte allocation on the heap. When the Batch is dropped, drop runs recursively: each String frees its bytes, then the Vec frees its element buffer, and the inline array needs no separate cleanup because it was never separately allocated.

struct Batch {
    counts: [u32; 4],     // inline: 4 * 4 = 16 bytes live inside Batch
    labels: Vec<String>,  // inline handle (ptr,len,cap); owns a heap buffer
}

// Storage map for a Batch value:
//   counts            -> inline in Batch (no allocation)
//   labels handle     -> inline in Batch: ptr/len/cap words
//   labels buffer     -> heap, owned by the Vec (array of String handles)
//   each String handle-> lives in the Vec's heap buffer
//   each String bytes -> separate heap allocation, owned by that String

The array and the Vec handle are inline in Batch; the Vec buffer and each String's bytes are heap allocations.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The fixed-size array is identified as stored inline in the Batch value.
  • The Vec<String> is shown as an inline handle whose element buffer is a separate heap allocation.
  • Each String element is noted as owning its own heap-backed bytes.
Exercise 3implementation

Refactor imperative mutation into expression-oriented Rust

The original classify introduces a wide mutable temporary, let mut scaled = 0;, then mutates it in two branches and threads it into two separate return sites. The mutable binding spans the whole function even though no value of interest exists until a branch is taken, and the 0 initializer is a placeholder that is never the real answer. That widened mutable scope is exactly what the chapter's expression-oriented style removes.

Because if in Rust is an expression, the entire function body can be a single if/else that evaluates to the tuple. Each branch computes the scaled value directly in the tuple position, so there is no separate mut binding to initialize, reassign, and reason about, and there are no early returns. The return type stays exactly (&'static str, usize): the string literals are &'static str, and the arithmetic stays in usize. No heap allocation or cloning is introduced, since both branches return a borrowed static string and a stack usize.

The result is easier to verify at a glance: the two outcomes sit side by side, each branch is total (it always produces the tuple), and there is no intermediate state that could be left stale. This is the refactor the lab uses, and it produces the same output as the imperative version.

fn classify(depth: usize) -> (&'static str, usize) {
    if depth > 1000 {
        ("hot", depth / 2)
    } else {
        ("steady", depth + 50)
    }
}

A single if-expression returns the tuple directly; no wide mut scaled binding and no early returns.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The wide mut scaled binding is removed entirely.
  • The return type is still (&'static str, usize).
  • Control flow is a single value-producing if/else expression rather than early-return-driven mutation.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Explain the lifetime bug instead of fighting the annotation

The function builds a String locally, takes a reference into it (for example text.lines().next()), and tries to return that reference. The rule Rust enforces is that a reference may not outlive the value it points at. The local String named text is owned by the function and is dropped at the end of the function body; any reference into it becomes dangling at that exact point. Returning such a reference would hand the caller a borrow of memory that has already been freed, so the borrow checker rejects it.

Adding a lifetime annotation does not fix this, because lifetimes describe valid borrowing relationships; they do not extend how long a value lives. A signature like fn first_line<'a>(...) -> &'a str is a claim that the returned reference stays valid for some region 'a, but the only data the reference points at is dropped when the function returns. No annotation can make the local String live past its owner's scope. The annotation would just move the contradiction from one error to another, because there is no caller-provided source for 'a to attach to.

There are two valid repairs with different tradeoffs. First, return an owned value: change the return type to String and return text.lines().next().unwrap_or("").to_string(). This transfers ownership to the caller, costs one allocation, and frees the function from any borrowing relationship. Second, borrow from caller-provided input instead of a local: take text: &str as a parameter and return &str derived from it, so the returned reference points at data the caller already owns and that outlives the call. The first repair is simplest and self-contained; the second avoids allocation but ties the output's validity to the caller's input lifetime.

// Broken: returns a reference into a local String that is dropped on return.
// fn first_line() -> &str {
//     let text = String::from("alpha\nbeta");
//     text.lines().next().unwrap_or("") // borrow of `text`, which dies here
// }

// Repair 1: return an owned String (transfer ownership, one allocation).
fn first_line_owned() -> String {
    let text = String::from("alpha\nbeta");
    text.lines().next().unwrap_or("").to_string()
}

// Repair 2: borrow from caller-provided input that outlives the call.
fn first_line_borrowed(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.lines().next().unwrap_or("")
}

Repair 1 returns an owned String; repair 2 borrows from caller-owned input so the reference outlives the call.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The diagnosis is that the returned reference would outlive the local String owner, which is dropped on return.
  • It is stated that lifetimes constrain references and do not extend a value's actual lifetime, so an annotation cannot fix it.
  • Two real repairs are given: return an owned String, or borrow from caller-provided input.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Choose owned versus borrowed data at a queue boundary

Name the owner at each subsystem edge. The inbound &[u8] request bytes are borrowed, owned by whatever buffer received them (a socket read buffer or a pooled allocation). Parsing should stay inside that borrow: header parsing, field slicing, and validation can all work against &[u8] and &str slices that point into the request buffer. None of these intermediate slices should be stored beyond the parse step, because the request buffer can be reused or freed as soon as ingest moves on. Keeping borrows local to parsing avoids copying data that may turn out to be invalid and gets rejected.

The Event is the value that crosses the worker queue, and a queue is an ownership boundary. The worker runs concurrently and outlives the request buffer, so the Event must own everything it needs: owned String fields, owned Vec<u8> payloads, owned numeric and enum fields. The single deliberate ownership transition is at construction of the Event: validated borrowed slices are converted into owned data (to_string(), to_vec()), and from that point the request buffer is free to be recycled. Sending the Event into the queue then moves ownership to the worker.

Cloning is acceptable exactly at this boundary, where converting a validated slice into an owned field is the price of crossing into an independently-lived subsystem; that is an explicit economic choice, not a default. Cloning is a smell when it appears inside parsing to dodge a borrow-checker message, or when the same Event is cloned to hand copies to several stages that could instead share an Arc<Event> or receive a borrow. For cleanup, rely on ordinary scope exit and Drop: the request buffer is released when parsing's scope ends, and the Event's owned String and Vec allocations are freed when the worker finishes with it and drops it, after persist and metrics have run. No manual free, and no slow network or locking logic in any destructor.

// Borrowed during parsing; owned at the Event boundary.
struct Event {
    topic: String,    // owned: outlives the request buffer
    payload: Vec<u8>, // owned: moved into the worker queue
    priority: u8,     // inline Copy
}

fn ingest(request: &[u8], queue: &std::sync::mpsc::Sender<Event>) {
    // Parse against borrowed slices into `request` (no ownership taken).
    let topic_slice: &str = parse_topic(request);   // borrow stays local
    let body_slice: &[u8] = parse_body(request);     // borrow stays local
    let priority = parse_priority(request);

    // Cross the boundary: convert validated borrows into owned data.
    let event = Event {
        topic: topic_slice.to_string(),
        payload: body_slice.to_vec(),
        priority,
    };

    // Move ownership into the worker queue; `request` may now be reused.
    let _ = queue.send(event);
    // No manual cleanup: request buffer drops with its scope; Event drops in the worker.
}

fn parse_topic(_r: &[u8]) -> &str { "ingest" }
fn parse_body<'a>(r: &'a [u8]) -> &'a [u8] { r }
fn parse_priority(_r: &[u8]) -> u8 { 1 }

Parsing works on borrows into the request buffer; the Event owns its data before it crosses the queue boundary.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Borrowed slices into the request buffer stay local to parsing and validation.
  • Data that crosses the queue is converted into owned Event fields before the boundary.
  • Cloning at the boundary is justified as a deliberate cost, while cloning inside parsing or to feed shared readers is named as a smell.
  • Cleanup is described as scope exit and Drop of the buffer and the Event, with no runtime magic or heavy destructor logic.

Lab solution

The lab completes Exercise 3 by replacing the imperative classify with an expression-oriented version. The body is a single if/else expression that evaluates to the (&'static str, usize) tuple, so there is no wide mut scaled temporary and no early return. Each branch is total and produces the result directly: the high-load branch returns ("hot", depth / 2), and the default branch returns ("steady", depth + 50).

The two calls in main exercise both branches. classify(120) takes the else branch because 120 is not greater than 1000, computing 120 + 50 = 170 and yielding ("steady", 170). classify(1200) takes the if branch because 1200 is greater than 1000, computing 1200 / 2 = 600 and yielding ("hot", 600). The two println! calls then print steady 170 and hot 600 on separate lines, matching the expected output exactly. The returned &'static str values are borrows of string literals baked into the binary, so they are valid for the whole program and require no allocation; the usize results are plain stack values.

Example 2-S. classify_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn classify(depth: usize) -> (&'static str, usize) {
    if depth > 1000 {
        ("hot", depth / 2)
    } else {
        ("steady", depth + 50)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let (status_a, value_a) = classify(120);
    let (status_b, value_b) = classify(1200);
    println!("{} {}", status_a, value_a);
    println!("{} {}", status_b, value_b);
}
Output
steady 170
hot 600

Review question answers

What is the difference between a value and a binding in Rust?

A value is the actual data, such as the bytes of a String or an integer's bits, while a binding is a named slot like let x = ... that currently owns or refers to a value. Ownership belongs to bindings: when you move a non-Copy value, the value is unchanged but the owning binding changes, and the old binding becomes unusable. Thinking in terms of which binding owns a value, rather than hidden object identity, is what makes move and drop behavior predictable.

Where do Vec<T> metadata and Vec<T> elements usually live?

The Vec<T> metadata, a pointer, a length, and a capacity, is a small fixed-size handle stored inline wherever the Vec itself lives, for instance on the stack for a local or inside an enclosing struct. The elements live in a separate heap buffer that the Vec owns and points at through its pointer field. Moving the Vec copies only the three-word handle; the heap buffer stays put, which is why moves are cheap and the Vec frees that buffer when it is dropped.

What does a lifetime annotation constrain, and what does it not do?

A lifetime annotation constrains references: it describes the region during which a borrow must stay valid and ties the validity of one reference to the data it points at. It does not extend how long a value lives, allocate anything, or change runtime behavior; it is a compile-time proof about borrowing, erased before code generation. So when a value is dropped, no annotation can keep a reference to it valid, and a lifetime error is a signal to fix ownership rather than to invent annotations.

Why can block expressions reduce mutation pressure in production code?

Because if, match, and { ... } blocks are expressions that produce values, you can compute a result and bind it once as an immutable let, instead of declaring a wide mut placeholder and reassigning it across branches. Any mutation needed to assemble the value can be confined to a short inner block whose last expression becomes the result, so the surrounding bindings stay immutable. Narrower mutable scope means fewer places where state can be left stale, which is easier to review and to reason about under change.

When is Drop useful, and what kinds of logic should usually stay out of it?

Drop is useful for deterministic resource release and invariant maintenance: closing file handles, freeing buffers, releasing locks, or decrementing reference counts at a precise, predictable point when the owner leaves scope. Logic that should stay out of destructors includes slow or fallible network calls, complex lock-acquisition chains, and critical business logic, because destructors run implicitly, are awkward to handle errors in, and execute during unwinding and shutdown where they are hard to reason about. Keep destructors fast and predictable, and put meaningful work on explicit code paths instead.

Chapter 3 · Project Structure and Tooling

Project Structure and Tooling

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter are about decisions you make before any business logic exists: where to draw crate boundaries, how wide to open a module's visibility, when a Cargo feature is the right tool versus when it is a trap, and which dependencies a core crate is allowed to know about. None of these are aesthetic choices. Each one fixes the direction of your dependency graph, the size of your stable API surface, and the reproducibility of your builds for as long as the repository lives.

The through-line is restraint. Start with fewer crates than your C++/C#/Go instincts suggest, keep visibility as narrow as a real caller forces it to be, prefer additive features to mode matrices, and keep the domain crate ignorant of HTTP and SQL. The lab and the feature-matrix exercise both push the same point: a compile-time switch that has to be evaluated once for the whole build graph is the wrong place to encode a per-request or per-environment mode. Get those boundaries right and the rest of the book has somewhere clean to live.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Name the unit before you design it

First fix the four words so they stop being synonyms. A package is what Cargo manages from one Cargo.toml; it is the unit of versioning and publishing. A crate is what the compiler builds in one pass; it is the unit of compilation and the unit of the visibility system (pub means visible outside this crate). A module is a tree of names inside a single crate; it is purely an organizational and visibility device with no separate build or dependency story. A workspace groups packages so they share one Cargo.lock, one target directory, and one top-level command. The nesting is strict: a workspace contains packages, each package produces one or more crates, and each crate contains a module tree.

For the inherited repository, classify by asking what actually needs isolation. The API service, the worker, and the CLI are three binaries with genuinely different dependency sets and different release cadences, so each justifies its own crate (and, in a workspace, its own package). The shared domain models are reused by all three and benefit from a stable, infrastructure-free public surface, so they belong in their own library crate that everyone depends on. That is the boundary justified by dependency and API isolation, not by folder preference: the domain crate must not pull in the API's HTTP stack or the worker's queue client.

Which boundaries are only organizational and should stay modules? Anything inside one of those crates. The API's routing, request validation, and serialization layers are modules within the api crate, not separate crates, because splitting them buys no dependency isolation and only adds Cargo.toml files, version bumps, and slower incremental builds. The CLI's argument parsing and its command handlers are modules within the cli crate for the same reason. A directory boundary is not automatically a crate boundary; reach for a new crate only when it gives you a real seam (dependency isolation, compile-time separation, a stable reusable surface, or a clean public/private split), and reach for a module when the only thing you want is tidier names.

Which boundary belongs at workspace scope rather than crate scope? The shared policy across all of these: the single lockfile that pins one resolved dependency graph for the whole product, the shared target directory, the workspace-level dependency declarations that let every member agree on one version of serde or tokio, and the top-level cargo check --workspace that builds everything at once. Those concerns are about the product as a whole, not about any single crate, so they live in the workspace root Cargo.toml.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Package (one Cargo.toml, versioned), crate (one compilation unit and the visibility boundary), module (names inside a crate), and workspace (shared lock/target/commands) are each given distinct definitions.
  • The domain crate is split out specifically to isolate it from the API's and worker's dependencies, an argument from dependency isolation rather than folder layout.
  • Routing, validation, and CLI command handlers are explicitly kept as modules inside their crates because a separate crate would add cost without buying isolation.
Exercise 2code reading

Read the public surface from a module tree

Start from what a downstream crate can actually see. The only thing that crosses the crate boundary is what is reachable through a pub path from the crate root. Here the root re-exports two names, so a downstream caller imports exactly use your_crate::OrderId; and use your_crate::OrderService;. They do not import your_crate::domain::OrderId or your_crate::service::OrderService, and they cannot reach anything under the internal adapter modules at all, because those modules are not pub from the root. The flat, root-level path is the stable promise; the deep internal path is an implementation detail they never name.

That distinction is exactly what gives you refactoring room. Because callers depend on the re-exported names and not on the internal layout, the module names domain and service may be renamed, merged, or reorganized freely as long as the crate root keeps re-exporting OrderId and OrderService from wherever they now live. You could move OrderId into a types module, split service into two modules, or restructure the adapters entirely, and no downstream code breaks, because none of those internal names were ever part of the public surface. The pub use at the root is the seam: internal modules stay deep and specific while the public API stays small and calm.

This is why pub(crate) is usually the better first choice than pub. A public path is an API promise even when it felt temporary the day you wrote it; once another crate imports it, widening was easy and narrowing is a breaking change. pub(crate) lets an item be used freely throughout your own crate while keeping it invisible across the crate boundary, so you keep full freedom to change it. The maintenance cost of reaching for full pub too early is that you convert an internal helper into a contract you must support, version, and reason about on every future change; you pay that cost forever, often for a type you only needed two modules over. Climb the visibility ladder one rung at a time, and shape the external surface deliberately with pub use rather than by leaving everything pub by default.

// crate root: lib.rs
// The only two names that cross the crate boundary.
pub use domain::OrderId;
pub use service::OrderService;

mod domain {
    #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
    pub struct OrderId(pub u64);
}

mod service {
    use crate::domain::OrderId;

    pub struct OrderService;

    impl OrderService {
        pub fn submit(&self, id: OrderId) {
            // adapters stay internal; callers never name them
            adapters::persist(id);
        }
    }

    // internal: renaming this module breaks no downstream caller
    mod adapters {
        use crate::domain::OrderId;
        pub(super) fn persist(_id: OrderId) {}
    }
}

// Downstream crate sees only:
//   use your_crate::{OrderId, OrderService};

Root re-exports define the public path; mod adapters stays internal and free to change.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The stable import paths are identified as your_crate::OrderId and your_crate::OrderService at the crate root, not the deep module paths.
  • Re-exporting is shown to hide the domain/service/adapters layout so those internal modules can be renamed or reorganized without breaking callers.
  • Widening to pub too early is described as turning an internal helper into a permanent contract, making pub(crate) the safer default.
Exercise 3implementation

Create a workspace layout for a multi-crate product

Use one workspace root whose only job is to list members, pin one Cargo.lock, and centralize shared dependency versions. Underneath it, give each component its own package. The shared business types go in a domain library crate. Infrastructure code goes in an adapters library crate that implements traits the domain defines (a database repository, an HTTP or message-queue client). The two long-running processes, api and worker, are binary crates, and there is a small cli binary for support tasks. The dependency direction is the whole point: api, worker, and cli depend on adapters and domain; adapters depends on domain; domain depends on nothing in the workspace and on no infrastructure crate at all.

Concretely, domain owns the order, account, and policy types plus the trait definitions like OrderRepository, and its Cargo.toml contains only lightweight, semantically neutral dependencies (something like serde for shape, perhaps thiserror for its own error type). It must not list reqwest, sqlx, axum, or a tracing subscriber. The adapters crate is where sqlx, an HTTP client, and the concrete tracing wiring live, because that is the crate allowed to know about wire formats and storage. The api binary depends on axum and on domain and adapters, wires a concrete repository into the domain's services, and serves requests; the worker binary depends on its queue client plus domain and adapters; the cli depends on clap plus domain and adapters. The arrows all point inward toward domain, never outward from it.

Centralize shared versions with [workspace.dependencies] in the root Cargo.toml so every member agrees on one serde and one tokio, and have each crate opt in with serde = { workspace = true }. Commit Cargo.lock at the root so production resolves the exact same graph every build.

The tradeoff to state plainly: splitting into four-plus crates costs you more Cargo.toml ceremony and makes a cross-cutting change touch several crates at once, but it buys two things that matter for a product. First, dependency hygiene: the domain crate physically cannot accumulate infrastructure dependencies, because they are not in its manifest, so the temptation that ruins prototypes is removed by construction. Second, build and API benefits: changing an adapter does not force a recompile of the domain's public types, and the domain's surface stays small and stable enough to reuse. If the product were small, fewer crates with the same internal module boundaries would be cheaper; the multi-crate layout earns its keep precisely when independent dependency sets and release policy diverge.

# Cargo.toml (workspace root)
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["domain", "adapters", "api", "worker", "cli"]

[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
thiserror = "1"

# domain/Cargo.toml  -> library, no infrastructure deps
[package]
name = "domain"
[dependencies]
serde = { workspace = true }
thiserror = { workspace = true }
# NOTE: no sqlx, no reqwest, no axum here. That isolation is the design.

# adapters/Cargo.toml -> implements domain traits over real infra
[package]
name = "adapters"
[dependencies]
domain = { path = "../domain" }
sqlx = "0.7"
reqwest = "0.12"

# api/Cargo.toml -> binary depends inward
[package]
name = "api"
[dependencies]
domain = { path = "../domain" }
adapters = { path = "../adapters" }
axum = "0.7"
tokio = { workspace = true }

Workspace manifests showing the inward dependency direction; domain lists no infrastructure crates.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The layout has a workspace root plus separate domain, adapters, api, worker, and cli packages.
  • The domain crate's manifest lists only neutral dependencies and explicitly excludes sqlx/reqwest/axum, keeping it infrastructure-free.
  • api, worker, and cli depend on adapters and domain while domain depends on nothing in the workspace, so dependencies point inward.
  • The stated tradeoff weighs extra manifest ceremony and cross-crate changes against guaranteed dependency hygiene and smaller recompiles plus a stable domain surface.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a feature flag matrix without turning Cargo into a mode engine

Name the defect precisely. The crate encodes three mutually exclusive operational modes (sqlite, postgres, memory) as Cargo features and assumes exactly one is enabled. This fights the resolver on two fronts. First, Cargo features are additive by design: anything in the dependency graph can turn a feature on, and the resolver unions all requests, so you cannot rely on exactly one being active. If two consumers each enable a different backend, you get both, and your one-of-three assumption silently breaks. Second, a feature is resolved once for the entire build graph before the compiler runs, so it can only answer compile-time questions. The backend a service should use is a deployment question that can differ per environment and even per run, which a single compile-time choice cannot represent.

The fix is to move the mode out of features and into runtime configuration, while keeping compile-time options only for what genuinely affects which code is built. Decide which backends are even compiled into this binary, and then choose among the compiled ones at startup from config. A clean shape is a runtime Backend enum chosen from an environment variable or config file, constructed once and passed inward. Optional dependencies still belong in features: if a deployment never needs Postgres, keep a postgres feature that gates the sqlx Postgres driver so it is not compiled or shipped. That preserves additive capability (turning postgres on adds a capability, it never removes sqlite), which is exactly how features are supposed to compose.

Reject impossible combinations early and explicitly rather than letting them reach a query. Parse the configured backend into the enum at startup; an unknown value, or a backend that was not compiled into this build, is a hard configuration error reported before the service accepts traffic. That is the runtime analogue of the lab: validate the selection up front and return a clear error for anything that is not exactly one valid choice, instead of assuming the environment is well-formed. So: which parts stay compile-time? Only whether a given backend driver is built in at all, expressed as an additive optional dependency. Which parts move to runtime? The actual backend selection, because it varies per environment and the feature resolver cannot express per-deployment choice.

// Runtime selection: the mode the service runs in today is config, not a feature.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Backend {
    Sqlite,
    Postgres,
    Memory,
}

impl Backend {
    // Validate the configured value up front; reject anything not exactly one
    // valid choice. A backend not compiled into this build is also rejected.
    fn from_config(value: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {
        match value {
            "sqlite" => Ok(Backend::Sqlite),
            "memory" => Ok(Backend::Memory),
            #[cfg(feature = "postgres")]
            "postgres" => Ok(Backend::Postgres),
            other => Err(format!("unsupported or unbuilt backend: {other:?}")),
        }
    }
}

// In Cargo.toml, the only compile-time knob is an *additive* optional dep:
//   [features]
//   postgres = ["dep:sqlx-postgres"]
// Turning `postgres` on adds a capability; it never disables sqlite or memory.

fn main() {
    let configured = std::env::var("APP_BACKEND").unwrap_or_else(|_| "memory".into());
    match Backend::from_config(&configured) {
        Ok(backend) => println!("running with backend = {backend:?}"),
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("configuration error: {e}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}

Backend choice moves to a validated runtime enum; only the optional driver stays a Cargo feature.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The answer explains that features are additive and resolved once per build graph, so mutually exclusive modes cannot be guaranteed and cannot vary per environment.
  • Additive capability is preserved by keeping the Postgres driver behind an optional feature that adds, never removes, a backend.
  • Impossible or unbuilt selections are validated at startup via Backend::from_config, which returns an explicit error before the service runs.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Choose a dependency policy for shared crates

The policy in one sentence: the core domain crate knows business concepts first and infrastructure concepts last, so protocol and storage dependencies move outward into adapter crates and only business-meaningful types live inward. The three prototype shortcuts each violate this and each has a specific home. The HTTP status type is a transport detail; it moves out to the API adapter crate, where the HTTP layer already lives. The database error type is a storage detail; it moves out to the persistence adapter crate. The tracing crate dependency, if it brought a subscriber or transport, moves out too; if the domain wants to emit events it can depend on a thin facade rather than a concrete tracing backend, and the wiring to an actual collector lives in an adapter or the binary. The result is that the domain crate's Cargo.toml stops listing reqwest/axum, the database driver, and the tracing subscriber.

Moving the dependencies out is only half the job; you also need translation boundaries so the infrastructure types do not leak inward through return types. The clearest one is errors. The persistence adapter implements a domain-defined trait such as OrderRepository, catches the database error type internally, and converts it into a domain error like RepositoryError::NotFound or RepositoryError::Conflict before returning. The domain never sees the storage error; it sees a business-meaningful failure it can actually reason about. The same translation happens at the API edge: the adapter maps a domain error to an HTTP status, so the status type lives where HTTP lives and never travels inward. These conversions are the seams that let you swap Postgres for something else, or HTTP for a queue, without touching the domain.

On the shared utility crate: allow one only when it removes real duplication behind a stable, narrow surface, and refuse to let it become a junk drawer. A shared crate of genuinely cross-cutting value types (a validated identifier newtype, a money type, a time helper used identically by several crates) is justified because the alternative is copy-paste that drifts. What is not justified is a util crate that accumulates whatever was convenient, because then every member crate depends on everything and you have recreated the coupling you split crates to avoid. The test is concrete: if you cannot describe the shared crate's purpose in one sentence without the word miscellaneous, it should not exist yet. Keep the domain dependency-light, translate infrastructure types at the boundary, and gate shared crates on real, named duplication.

// In the domain crate: business-meaningful errors only. No DB or HTTP types.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum RepositoryError {
    NotFound,
    Conflict,
    Unavailable,
}

pub trait OrderRepository {
    fn load(&self, id: u64) -> Result<Order, RepositoryError>;
}

pub struct Order {
    pub id: u64,
}

// In the persistence ADAPTER crate: the storage error is translated here and
// never leaks inward. (sqlx::Error stands in for the real database error type.)
//
// impl OrderRepository for SqlOrderRepo {
//     fn load(&self, id: u64) -> Result<Order, RepositoryError> {
//         self.query(id).map_err(|e| match e {
//             sqlx::Error::RowNotFound => RepositoryError::NotFound,
//             _ => RepositoryError::Unavailable,
//         })
//     }
// }
//
// In the API adapter crate: domain error -> HTTP status, also at the boundary.
//   RepositoryError::NotFound   => 404
//   RepositoryError::Conflict   => 409
//   RepositoryError::Unavailable => 503

The domain exposes a business error; adapters translate storage and HTTP types at the boundary.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The HTTP status type and database error type are moved out of the domain crate into the API and persistence adapter crates respectively.
  • A concrete translation boundary is given: the persistence adapter converts the database error into a domain RepositoryError so storage types never travel inward.
  • A shared utility crate is permitted only for named, real duplication behind a narrow surface and explicitly rejected as a default catch-all bucket.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Write the CI command pack for the chapter examples

Order the pack from fastest structural feedback to slowest, so a broken build fails before you spend minutes running tests. cargo check --workspace --all-targets gives the fastest signal: it type-checks every crate and every target (lib, bins, tests, examples, benches) without producing final artifacts, catching the bulk of breakage cheaply. cargo fmt --all --check enforces formatting consistency by failing if any file is not formatted, without modifying the tree, so style never becomes a review argument. cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings is the lint gate; the -D warnings flag promotes lint warnings to errors so the job fails on them rather than letting warnings accumulate unnoticed. cargo test --workspace --all-features then runs the actual behavior checks across every crate.

The flags are not decoration, so justify the ones that matter. --workspace runs the command across every member crate, not just the one you happen to be in, which is the whole point of having a workspace command. --all-targets makes check and clippy look at tests, examples, and benches too, so a test file that no longer compiles or a benchmark with a stale signature is caught in CI rather than the next time someone runs it locally. --all-features compiles the union of feature-gated code so an optional integration cannot rot silently while its feature is off in the default build; note this is a deliberate CI choice and can be heavy, so on large graphs you sometimes split it into a separate job.

Benchmarks are conditional on purpose, because not every repository has a benchmark harness and pretending otherwise produces a CI step that fails on a fresh project. Run cargo bench only when benches actually exist, and run it for compilation and regression signal rather than as a correctness gate, since timing on shared CI runners is noisy. A reasonable pattern is to gate the step on the presence of a benches directory (or a Criterion harness) and treat its results as informational, keeping correctness gating in fmt, clippy, and test. The pack below is specific enough to paste into a pipeline.

# CI command pack: fast structural feedback first, slower checks after.

# 1. Fastest signal: type-check every crate and every target.
cargo check --workspace --all-targets

# 2. Formatting consistency, fail without rewriting files.
cargo fmt --all --check

# 3. Lint gate: warnings become hard failures.
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

# 4. Behavior: run tests across the whole workspace.
cargo test --workspace --all-features

# 5. Benchmarks ONLY if a harness exists; informational, not a gate.
if [ -d benches ]; then
    cargo bench --workspace
else
    echo "no benches/ directory; skipping benchmarks"
fi

A paste-ready pipeline ordered from cheapest feedback to slowest, with benches gated on existence.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The pack includes cargo check, cargo test, cargo fmt --check, and cargo clippy.
  • cargo bench is guarded by a check for an existing benches directory rather than assumed to be present.
  • --workspace, --all-targets, and --all-features are each explained: run across all crates, include tests/examples/benches, and compile feature-gated code so it cannot rot.

Lab solution

The starter version checks s3 first, then local, and falls through to a vague "not configured" error. That has two bugs that mirror the feature-matrix problem from the chapter: it silently accepts the both-on case (it returns Ok("s3") and ignores local entirely), and its error message does not describe the real constraint. Treating two independent booleans as if exactly one is set is precisely the bad assumption Cargo features make when used as mutually exclusive modes.

The fix matches on the tuple (s3, local) so every combination is handled explicitly. (true, false) selects s3, (false, true) selects local, and the wildcard arm covers both remaining cases, neither selected and both selected, returning the same explicit error "choose exactly one backend". The match arms are exhaustive over the four boolean combinations, so there is no fall-through ambiguity and no impossible state slips past unvalidated.

Running main calls the function with all four input pairs. (false, false) and (true, true) both hit the wildcard arm and print the error; (true, false) prints Ok("s3") and (false, true) prints Ok("local"). That produces the four lines of expected output exactly, demonstrating the chapter's point at runtime: reject the impossible combinations up front with a clear message rather than assuming the configuration is well-formed.

Example 3-S. feature_matrix_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn selected_backend(s3: bool, local: bool) -> Result<&'static str, &'static str> {
    // Reject impossible combinations explicitly instead of assuming exactly
    // one backend was configured. Both-on and neither-on are equally invalid.
    match (s3, local) {
        (true, false) => Ok("s3"),
        (false, true) => Ok("local"),
        _ => Err("choose exactly one backend"),
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("none = {:?}", selected_backend(false, false));
    println!("s3 = {:?}", selected_backend(true, false));
    println!("local = {:?}", selected_backend(false, true));
    println!("both = {:?}", selected_backend(true, true));
}
Output
none = Err("choose exactly one backend")
s3 = Ok("s3")
local = Ok("local")
both = Err("choose exactly one backend")

Review question answers

What is the operational difference between a package and a crate?

A package is what Cargo manages from a single Cargo.toml; it is the unit of versioning, publishing, and dependency declaration. A crate is what the compiler builds in one compilation pass and is the boundary the visibility system works against, where pub means visible to other crates. One package can produce more than one crate (for example a library crate plus several binary crates), but each crate is a single thing the compiler emits, while the package is the manifest-level grouping Cargo operates on.

When should you create a new crate instead of a new module?

Create a new crate only when it buys a real boundary: dependency isolation (so the new crate can avoid or contain dependencies the rest cannot), compile-time separation, reuse behind a stable public surface, or a clean public/private split enforced by the crate boundary. If the only goal is tidier names or folder organization within the same dependency set, a module is cheaper, because it adds no Cargo.toml, no version bump, and no incremental-build cost. Start with fewer crates than your instincts suggest and split when independent dependencies or release policy actually diverge.

Why is pub(crate) often a better default than pub?

pub(crate) lets an item be used freely throughout your own crate while keeping it invisible across the crate boundary, so it never becomes part of your external API. Full pub is a promise: once another crate imports a path, widening was easy but narrowing it again is a breaking change you must support and version. Visibility is a ladder you should climb only as far as a real caller forces, and starting at pub(crate) preserves the freedom to rename or restructure internals, shaping the public surface deliberately with pub use re-exports instead.

What kinds of choices belong in Cargo features, and what kinds usually belong in runtime configuration?

Cargo features suit additive, compile-time choices: optional integrations, platform-specific plumbing, optional dependencies, and extra instrumentation, all expressed so that enabling a feature adds a capability rather than removing one. They are resolved once for the entire build graph before the compiler runs, so they cannot represent anything that varies per environment or per request. Operational mode questions like which database backend a service uses today belong in runtime configuration (an environment variable or config file parsed into an enum), because that decision differs across deployments and the feature resolver cannot express a per-deployment or mutually-exclusive choice safely.

Why should benchmarking be explicit rather than assumed?

Not every repository has a benchmark harness, so a CI step that runs cargo bench unconditionally will fail on a fresh project that has no benches. Benchmark timing on shared CI runners is also noisy, which makes it a poor correctness gate compared with fmt, clippy, and test. The honest approach is to run benchmarks only when a harness actually exists (gating on a benches directory or a Criterion setup) and to treat the results as informational signal for compilation and regression, rather than pretending every repository already has benchmarks in place.

Chapter 4 · Ownership, Borrowing, and Lifetimes

Ownership, Borrowing, and Lifetimes

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes out of syntax and into design. The order the chapter insists on holds throughout: decide who owns a value first, decide who may temporarily borrow it second, and only then reach for an explicit lifetime when the compiler genuinely needs you to relate one borrow to another. Most real borrow-checker friction is not a rule you broke; it is an ownership decision you have not made yet.

The through-line is a service boundary. Request bytes arrive borrowed, get inspected and normalized while they stay local, and become owned the moment they cross into something that must outlive the request: a queue, a cache, a stored record, an async task. The warm-up trains you to narrate that flow, the implementation and refactoring exercises make you produce it in code, and the design exercise asks you to commit to concrete owners at every subsystem edge. Each solution names the owner, the borrow, and the boundary, because that triple is what the rest of the book builds on.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Tell the ownership story before touching syntax

Walk the four stages and name an owner or a borrower at each one. The original request bytes are owned by whoever received them from the socket: the ingress layer holds the buffer (a Vec<u8> or an equivalent owned region). Everything downstream that only reads those bytes should borrow them as &[u8] rather than take a copy, because no downstream stage needs an independent buffer while it is merely inspecting.

Header validation borrows. It receives &[u8], scans for the fields it needs, and returns a yes/no or a small set of parsed offsets. It never needs to retain the buffer past its own call, so it should take a temporary shared borrow and nothing more. Building the routing key is the transition point. While the key is being derived it can borrow slices of the request buffer, but the key that comes out is a derived, normalized value, and the moment it is going to live past the request it must become owned: a String, or a small owned struct, not a &str pointing back into the buffer.

The worker queue is the boundary that forces ownership. A job placed on a queue can be picked up by another thread, can sit there after the request handler returns, and can outlive the request buffer entirely. A reference into the request buffer would be a dangling promise: the buffer's owner (the ingress layer) may drop it as soon as the handler returns, which is before the worker ever runs. So the queue must receive owned data. This is the chapter's core operational rule made concrete: borrow while local, transfer ownership when the next stage can outlive the current scope.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names an owner for the request bytes: the ingress layer that received them from the socket holds the owned buffer.
  • Separates borrowed inspection (header validation, key derivation read slices via &[u8]) from owned cross-boundary data (the job sent to the queue).
  • Explains the queue boundary as an ownership transfer point because the job can outlive and run after the request buffer's owner drops it.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the unnecessary clone

The helper clones path into path_copy, prints path_copy, then keeps using the original path. Ask the operational question the chapter trains: does any code need an independent, separately-owned copy of the path? Here it does not. Printing only reads the string, and the original path is still valid and still used right after. The clone produces a second owned String that is read once and dropped, which is pure allocation and copy cost with no semantic purpose. It is a borrow-checker reflex, not a duplication the design requires.

The first repair is to borrow. Printing needs read access, and read access is exactly what a shared borrow grants. Pass &path (or just print path directly, since println! borrows its arguments), and delete path_copy entirely. Nothing about the program's meaning changes, and you save an allocation on every call. If the helper's job were instead to produce a value that must outlive the original buffer, the right move would be to return ownership from the helper, not to clone internally and discard, so that the caller decides the lifetime of the result.

A clone is justified when you genuinely need a second value with an independent lifetime: when you must mutate one copy while preserving the original, when an owned value has to be stored or sent somewhere that outlives the source, or when an API you cannot change demands an owned String. None of those apply to a read-and-print. The discipline is not 'never clone'; it is 'clone only when independent ownership is the point, and say why.'

// Before: a clone that only serves a read.
fn log_path_bad(path: String) {
    let path_copy = path.clone(); // allocates a second String...
    println!("handling {}", path_copy); // ...used once, then dropped
    route(&path); // original still valid and used here
}

// After: borrow for the read, no allocation.
fn log_path(path: &str) {
    println!("handling {}", path); // println! borrows; no copy needed
    route(path);
}

fn route(_path: &str) {}

Replacing a read-only clone with a shared borrow removes an allocation without changing meaning.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Distinguishes semantic duplication (a real second owner with its own lifetime) from a borrow-checker work-around (this clone, read once and dropped).
  • Proposes borrowing first: the path is only read, so &str / a shared borrow is sufficient and the clone is deleted.
  • Justifies a remaining clone only when independent ownership is required (mutate-while-preserving, store/send past the source, or an owned-only API).
Exercise 3implementation

Accept borrowed input and return owned output

The signature is the whole point: fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String. The two inputs are borrowed because the function only reads them to assemble the key; it has no reason to take ownership of the caller's strings.
