The output is owned (String) because a cache key is exactly the kind of value that outlives the inputs: it gets inserted into a map, hashed, retained across calls. Returning &str here would be wrong because there is nothing for it to borrow from that outlives the call, the key is newly constructed, so it must be owned.

Use format! to build the result in one allocation: format!("{}:{}", service, route). This reads both borrowed inputs and produces a single owned String. There are no intermediate clones, the only allocation is the final result itself, which is unavoidable because the caller asked for an owned value. The colon separator gives billing:/v1/invoices and search:/ready for the sample inputs.

This is the chapter's strong default for service code in miniature: borrow for inspection and assembly, return owned when the result must be decoupled from the input buffers' lifetimes. The caller can drop service and route immediately after the call and the returned key remains valid, which is precisely the independence a cache key needs.

fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String {
    format!("{}:{}", service, route)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", build_cache_key("billing", "/v1/invoices")); // billing:/v1/invoices
    println!("{}", build_cache_key("search", "/ready"));        // search:/ready
}

Borrowed &str inputs, a single owned String result built with one allocation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Signature is exactly fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String.
  • Output matches billing:/v1/invoices and search:/ready for the sample inputs.
  • Returns owned data: format! builds a new String, so the result does not borrow from the inputs or any temporary.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Annotate lifetimes only where required

first_word(s: &str) -> &str has exactly one input borrow, and the returned slice can only come from that one input. There is no ambiguity for the compiler to resolve, so lifetime elision applies: Rust reads the single input lifetime as the output lifetime automatically. The signature stays as written. Adding an explicit lifetime, fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str, is legal but changes nothing about the model; it documents a relationship that was never in doubt and just adds noise.

pick_longer is different because it returns one of two input borrows. The compiler cannot guess whether the output borrows from left or from right, and the answer is 'it could be either depending on the runtime comparison.' That forces you to name the relationship: fn pick_longer<'a>(left: &'a str, right: &'a str) -> &'a str. Tying both inputs and the output to the same lifetime 'a tells the compiler the returned reference is valid only as long as both inputs are valid, which is the only sound contract for a function that might return either one.

The key conceptual point, and the reason this exercise pairs the two functions, is what the annotation does and does not do. The 'a on pick_longer does not extend how long anything is stored; the underlying strings live exactly as long as they were going to. It documents a constraint: the caller may use the result only within the overlap of the two inputs' lifetimes. Annotation describes a borrowing relationship the compiler must verify; it never grants extra storage. That is why adding 'a to first_word is harmless but pointless, while leaving it off pick_longer is a compile error.

// One input borrow -> elision is sufficient; leave it elided.
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str {
    s.split(' ').next().unwrap_or("")
}

// Returns one of two input borrows -> name the relationship explicitly.
fn pick_longer<'a>(left: &'a str, right: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if left.len() >= right.len() { left } else { right }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", first_word("GET /ready"));       // GET
    println!("{}", pick_longer("job", "request"));  // request
}

Elision where one input borrow exists; one shared lifetime where the output may come from either input.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Keeps fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str elided, since the single input borrow makes the output relationship unambiguous.
  • Annotates pick_longer with one lifetime 'a tying both inputs and the output together, the only sound contract when either input may be returned.
  • Explains the annotation documents a borrowing relationship the compiler must verify, and never extends how long any value is stored.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix a borrow-checker failure without cloning

Name the conflict precisely first, because the chapter is explicit that this is not a rule violation in the abstract. first holds a shared borrow into buffer (first_word(&buffer) returns a &str slice of buffer). buffer.clear() needs a mutable borrow of buffer. Then first is printed, which means the shared borrow must still be live at the clear(). The shared borrow and the exclusive borrow overlap in time, and overlapping shared-plus-exclusive borrows of the same value are the one forbidden state. The defect is borrow duration, not the borrowing rules being wrong.

The cleanest repair is to shorten the shared borrow so it ends before the mutation begins. Move the use of first ahead of buffer.clear(): print first while the borrow is still valid, and only then clear the buffer. Once the println! is done, the slice is no longer used, the borrow ends (non-lexical lifetimes end a borrow at its last use), and clear() is free to take its exclusive borrow. No clone, no allocation, just sequencing: inspect first, mutate second.

Reach for owned data only if the later code genuinely needs the word after the buffer is mutated, for example if you must print first after clear(). Then converting to an owned value, let first = first_word(&buffer).to_string();, is the justified move, because you really do need a value with a lifetime independent of buffer. The justification is concrete (the value must survive the mutation), not a reflex to silence the compiler. Wrapping the borrow in an inner scope is a third option that makes the duration visually obvious, but here simple reordering is enough.

// Conflict: shared borrow `first` overlaps the mutable borrow in `clear()`.
// Repair A (preferred): use the borrow before mutating, so it ends first.
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str {
    s.split(' ').next().unwrap_or("")
}

fn handle(buffer: &mut String) {
    let first = first_word(buffer);
    println!("first = {}", first); // last use of the shared borrow -> borrow ends here
    buffer.clear();                // exclusive borrow now unobstructed
}

// Repair B (only if the word must survive the mutation): own it deliberately.
fn handle_owned(buffer: &mut String) {
    let first = first_word(buffer).to_string(); // independent lifetime, justified need
    buffer.clear();
    println!("first = {}", first); // valid: `first` no longer borrows `buffer`
}

Reordering ends the shared borrow before the mutation; owning is reserved for when the value must outlive the mutation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Repair ends the shared borrow before the mutable clear() by moving the use of first earlier (or converts to owned only for a stated reason).
  • Does not default to cloning; the to_string() path is presented only when the word must survive the mutation, with that need named.
  • Explains the conflict as overlapping borrow duration (shared and exclusive borrows live at the same time), not as a borrowing rule being violated in principle.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose ownership for a long-lived service API

Map owners and borrowers onto the flow socket bytes -> parse route -> normalize key -> store record -> publish async notification, and the line between borrowed and owned falls in a predictable place. The socket bytes are owned by the ingress layer that read them into a buffer. parse_route and normalize_key both accept borrowed input: parse_route(bytes: &[u8]) inspects the buffer and returns the parsed pieces, and normalize_key(raw: &str) -> String reads the parsed route and produces a canonical key. These stages are local, they finish before the request handler returns, and they have no reason to take ownership of the buffer.

Ownership has to appear before storage and before the async notification. The stored record must be an owned struct, AuditRecord { service: String, key: String, received_at: Instant }, with owned fields, because it lives in a database, a write buffer, or an in-memory store long after the request buffer is gone. The async notification is even stricter: a spawned task may run on another thread and after the handler returns, so the notification payload must be 'static-friendly owned data (an owned struct or String), never a reference into the request buffer. Both boundaries are ownership-transfer points for the same reason as the queue in Exercise 1: the next stage can outlive the current owner.

A borrowed-field struct, struct ParsedRoute<'a> { method: &'a str, path: &'a str }, is justified only as a short-lived view used inside parsing and normalization, where it never escapes the scope that owns the buffer. It is the wrong default for the stored record or the notification, because a lifetime parameter on a long-lived struct couples that struct to the request buffer's lifetime and forces the buffer to stay alive for as long as the record does, which defeats the point of storing it. The tradeoff I am accepting is explicit: converting to owned data at the storage and async edges costs allocations (each record and notification allocates its Strings), in exchange for decoupled lifetimes, a simpler API where stored and queued types are plain owned structs with no lifetime parameters, and long-term maintainability, because adding a new consumer of the record never has to reason about the request buffer. For an audit service, where records are durable and notifications are fire-and-forget, that allocation cost is the right thing to pay; the borrowed view stays confined to the hot, local parsing path where it actually saves work.

use std::time::Instant;

// Borrowed view: confined to parsing/normalization, never stored.
struct ParsedRoute<'a> {
    method: &'a str,
    path: &'a str,
}

fn parse_route(bytes: &[u8]) -> ParsedRoute<'_> {
    let text = std::str::from_utf8(bytes).unwrap_or("");
    let mut parts = text.split(' ');
    ParsedRoute { method: parts.next().unwrap_or(""), path: parts.next().unwrap_or("/") }
}

fn normalize_key(route: &ParsedRoute<'_>) -> String {
    format!("{}:{}", route.method, route.path) // owned: crosses into storage
}

// Owned record: no lifetime parameter, safe to store and outlive the buffer.
struct AuditRecord {
    key: String,
    received_at: Instant,
}

fn make_record(key: String) -> AuditRecord {
    AuditRecord { key, received_at: Instant::now() }
}

// Async boundary takes owned data; a borrow here would dangle once the handler returns.
fn publish(notification: String) {
    // e.g. tokio::spawn(async move { sink.send(notification).await; });
    let _ = notification;
}

Borrowed view for local parsing; owned structs at the storage and async edges, with no lifetime parameter escaping into long-lived types.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Keeps borrowed input local: parse_route and normalize_key take borrows, and the borrowed ParsedRoute view never escapes parsing/normalization.
  • Converts to owned form before storage and async: AuditRecord holds Strings and the notification payload is an owned String.
  • Justifies a tradeoff explicitly: paying per-record/notification allocations to get decoupled lifetimes, a simpler lifetime-free API, and maintainability.
  • Does not present borrowed fields in long-lived structs as the default; the borrowed-field struct is scoped to parsing only, with the lifetime-coupling cost named.

Lab solution

The initial code returns route.to_string(), which drops the service entirely and prints only the route. The fix builds the full key from both borrowed inputs: format!("{}:{}", service, route) reads service and route and produces one owned String in a single allocation, with no intermediate clones.

The two inputs stay borrowed as &str because the function only reads them to assemble the key, while the result is owned because a cache key is meant to outlive the inputs: it gets inserted into a map, hashed, or retained across calls. This is the chapter's strong default in one line, borrow for inspection, return owned when the result must be decoupled from the caller's buffers.

main calls the function twice. The first call joins billing and /v1/invoices with a colon to print billing:/v1/invoices; the second joins search and /ready to print search:/ready. Each println! adds its own newline, producing the two expected lines exactly.

Example 4-S. build_cache_key_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String {
    format!("{}:{}", service, route)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", build_cache_key("billing", "/v1/invoices"));
    println!("{}", build_cache_key("search", "/ready"));
}
Output
billing:/v1/invoices
search:/ready

Review question answers

Why is ownership usually the first question and lifetimes the second?

Ownership decides who is responsible for a value, who cleans it up, and whether the next stage merely observes the data or must outlive the current owner. Once that is settled, a lifetime is just the compiler's name for how long a particular borrow stays valid, a detail that only arises after you have already decided to borrow rather than transfer ownership. Asking lifetimes first inverts the model and leads to the common mistake of adding lifetime annotations to paper over what is really an ownership decision. Decide the owner, then borrow, then annotate only if the compiler needs the relationship spelled out.

What is the operational difference between &T and &mut T?

&T is a shared borrow: it grants read-only access, and many &T borrows of the same value may exist at once because no one is mutating through them. &mut T is an exclusive borrow: it grants the ability to mutate, and Rust permits only one at a time with no other borrows alive, because aliasing plus mutation is where memory and concurrency bugs are born. Operationally you reach for &T when the callee only inspects data and &mut T when it must change the value. The borrow checker enforces that a value is, at any moment, either freely shared among readers or held by exactly one writer, never both.

What does a lifetime annotation describe, and what does it never do?

A lifetime annotation describes a relationship between borrows, most often which input a returned reference borrows from, so the compiler can verify the output is never used past the validity of that input. It is a constraint you are documenting for the compiler to check, not a runtime mechanism. It never extends how long a value is stored or keeps anything alive; the underlying data lives exactly as long as it would without the annotation. That is why adding a lifetime to a single-input function changes nothing, while a function returning one of two inputs needs the annotation to state which borrowing relationship must hold.

When is returning String cleaner than returning &str?

Returning String is cleaner whenever the result must outlive or be decoupled from the inputs, when it is newly constructed, normalized, or formatted and there is nothing borrowable that lives long enough to back a &str. A cache key, an audit label, or any value built with format! falls into this category: it has no source to borrow from, so it must own its data. Returning &str only makes sense when the output is a slice of an input that the caller keeps alive, like the first word of a borrowed string. If the result is going to be stored, queued, retried, or returned across a boundary, String frees the caller from the input's lifetime and is the right choice.

Why do queue, cache, and async boundaries often push you toward owned data?

Each of these boundaries lets a value live past the scope that produced it: a queued job runs later, possibly on another thread; a cache entry is retained across calls; an async task may execute after the spawning function returns. A reference into a local buffer would dangle the moment that buffer's owner drops it, which typically happens before the next stage runs. So the next stage must receive owned data with an independent lifetime, making these boundaries natural ownership-transfer points. This is the same rule everywhere: if a later stage can outlive the current scope, it should own its data rather than borrow from that scope.

Chapter 5 · Pointers, References, and Ownership Inside Structs

Pointers, References, and Ownership Inside Structs

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the borrowing and lifetime rules from Chapter 4 and push them into struct design, where they stop being a borrow-checker formality and become a public data-modeling decision. Every struct in a service is implicitly a policy statement: a borrowed field declares "I am a temporary lens over data someone else owns," and an owned field declares "I am a value the rest of the system may keep, move, queue, test, and reason about on its own." The work here is learning to classify each struct into one of those two roles deliberately, and to recognize the contagion that follows when a single reference field forces a lifetime parameter onto everything that touches the type.

The set builds toward a single durable habit: keep borrowed views local to parsing and validation, convert to owned forms at the first storage, queue, retry, or thread boundary, and reach for Box, Rc, and Arc only when the ownership-count and thread questions genuinely call for them. The lab and the owned-buffer exercises drill the most Rust-native pattern in this space — own the buffer once, slice borrowed views from &self on demand — while the pointer and refactoring exercises make you commit to a representation that Rust can move and store without lifetime baggage.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose owned versus borrowed fields for two domain objects

The two structs have different jobs, so they should have different field shapes. RouteMatchView exists only during request parsing, while the request buffer is still alive and pinned in scope. It is a temporary lens over that buffer, so its fields should borrow directly from it: the matched path, the route pattern, and any captured path parameters are all slices into the incoming bytes. Borrowing here is cheap and the upstream owner is obvious and nearby — the buffer the parser is reading from — so the lifetime relationship is local and easy to name. RouteMatchView<'a> never escapes the parse function, so its lifetime parameter never spreads anywhere.

StoredRouteMatch is the opposite. It outlives the parse step on purpose: it goes into a metrics aggregator, a retry queue, and possibly a persistence layer, all of which run after the request buffer has been recycled or dropped. Every field that must survive that boundary has to be owned — the route id and matched path as String (or an interned id), captured parameters as owned Strings, the timestamp and status as plain Copy values. If StoredRouteMatch borrowed from the buffer, it could not sit in a Vec, a channel, or a cache without dragging the buffer's lifetime along, and it would be impossible to hold across an await point or send to another thread.

The concrete reason the two structs should not share field types: a borrowed &'a str ties the holder to the buffer's lifetime, but the stored record's whole reason to exist is to be independent of that buffer. Forcing one struct to serve both jobs means either the view pays for allocations it does not need during the hot parse path, or the stored record inherits a lifetime parameter that contaminates the metrics, retry, and persistence code downstream. The tradeoff is explicit: StoredRouteMatch pays a handful of allocations at the conversion boundary to buy lifetime independence for everything after it. That allocation is almost always worth it, because the alternative is a lifetime-coupled object graph that cannot be queued, retried, or tested in isolation.

// Temporary lens: borrows from the request buffer, never escapes parsing.
struct RouteMatchView<'a> {
    path: &'a str,        // slice into the request bytes
    pattern: &'a str,     // the route template that matched
    params: Vec<(&'a str, &'a str)>, // captured path params, still borrowed
}

// Long-lived record: fully owned, safe to queue, retry, persist, send.
struct StoredRouteMatch {
    route_id: String,     // owned id, independent of the buffer
    path: String,         // owned copy of the matched path
    params: Vec<(String, String)>,
    status: u16,          // Copy
    matched_at_ms: u64,   // Copy
}

impl<'a> RouteMatchView<'a> {
    // The conversion boundary: allocate once, gain lifetime independence.
    fn into_stored(self, route_id: &str, status: u16, now_ms: u64) -> StoredRouteMatch {
        StoredRouteMatch {
            route_id: route_id.to_string(),
            path: self.path.to_string(),
            params: self
                .params
                .into_iter()
                .map(|(k, v)| (k.to_string(), v.to_string()))
                .collect(),
            status,
            matched_at_ms: now_ms,
        }
    }
}

The view borrows from the buffer; into_stored is the single allocation boundary that produces an owned, queueable record.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • RouteMatchView borrows only from the request buffer, whose ownership is obvious and lexically nearby during parsing.
  • StoredRouteMatch owns every field that must survive past the parse step into metrics, retries, and persistence.
  • The stated tradeoff: a few allocations at into_stored buy lifetime independence, versus a lifetime-coupled graph that cannot be queued or tested.
Exercise 2code reading

Explain the lifetime coupling in a borrowed-field struct

In struct HeaderView<'a> { name: &'a str, value: &'a str }, the bytes behind name and value are owned by something outside the struct — typically the request buffer or response buffer the parser is scanning. HeaderView holds no String, no Vec, no heap allocation of its own; both fields are slices that point into memory the struct does not own. The struct is a window onto that memory, not a copy of it.

The struct needs the lifetime parameter <'a> because it stores references, and a reference is only meaningful relative to the validity of the thing it points at. The compiler cannot type-check HeaderView in isolation; it has to connect the references inside the struct to the owner outside it. <'a> is that connection. Operationally it says: a HeaderView<'a> is valid only as long as the borrow 'a is valid, and the compiler will refuse to let any HeaderView outlive the buffer its slices came from. It is a relationship marker between this struct and an external owner.

What <'a> does not say is just as important. It is not a retention policy and it does not extend storage lifetime. Writing HeaderView<'a> does not make the bytes live longer; it only records that the struct depends on bytes that live for at least 'a. The struct constrains reference validity; it does not own or prolong anything. That is why this design is comfortable in parsing code: the buffer is right there on the stack, the views are produced and consumed inside the same function, and 'a stays local and short. It becomes awkward in caches and queues for the mirror-image reason — a cache entry or a queued message is supposed to outlive the request that produced it, but a HeaderView is structurally forbidden from outliving its buffer. To store one, you would have to keep the entire originating buffer alive for as long as the cache entry lives, or thread 'a through the cache type itself, which spreads the lifetime parameter across the whole storage layer. At that point you want an owned Header { name: String, value: String } instead.

struct HeaderView<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    value: &'a str,
}

// Good fit: views live and die inside the parse, alongside the buffer.
fn parse_first_header(buf: &str) -> Option<HeaderView<'_>> {
    let line = buf.lines().next()?;
    let (name, value) = line.split_once(':')?;
    Some(HeaderView { name: name.trim(), value: value.trim() })
}

// Awkward fit: a cache entry must outlive the buffer, but the view cannot.
// This is the point where you switch to owned fields instead:
struct Header {
    name: String,
    value: String,
}

HeaderView is a borrowed lens valid only within the buffer's lifetime; storing it long-term requires the owned Header form.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States that name and value borrow from an external owner (the buffer), so the struct cannot outlive that owner.
  • Explains <'a> constrains reference validity and does not extend or prolong storage lifetime.
  • Names parsing as the good fit and caches/queues as the burdensome case where an owned Header is needed.
Exercise 3implementation

Build a struct that owns a buffer and exposes read-only views safely

AuditLine owns the raw line as a single String field and exposes level(&self) -> &str, which slices the text before the first colon out of that owned buffer on demand. This is the own-the-buffer, borrow-the-view pattern that the chapter's first example demonstrates with LogLine. The struct manages the lifetime of the data; callers receive a cheap, read-only &str that is derived from &self at call time rather than stored.

The key move is that level does not create a new owned String and does not store a second field. It returns a slice whose lifetime is tied to the &self borrow, so the borrow lives and dies with each call. Because nothing inside the struct points back at the raw field, AuditLine has no lifetime parameter, no self-reference, and no aliasing — it is an ordinary movable value. self.raw.split(':').next() yields everything up to the first colon ("WARN" for "WARN: cache miss"), and unwrap_or("UNKNOWN") supplies a fallback for a line with no colon. split alone, not split_whitespace, gives "WARN" with no trailing space because the colon is the delimiter.

The constructor must actually store the data: the starter code's bug is raw: String::new(), which throws the argument away and leaves an empty buffer. Replacing it with raw.to_string() copies the input into the owned field once. After that, the struct can be sliced as many times as needed without any further allocation, which is exactly why this pattern dominates log parsing, protocol headers, and message frames — own once, slice many times.

struct AuditLine {
    raw: String,
}

impl AuditLine {
    fn new(raw: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            raw: raw.to_string(), // own the line once
        }
    }

    fn level(&self) -> &str {
        // borrowed view derived from &self, sliced on demand
        self.raw.split(':').next().unwrap_or("UNKNOWN")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let line = AuditLine::new("WARN: cache miss");
    println!("level = {}", line.level());
    println!("raw = {}", line.raw);
}

raw.to_string() owns the line once; level returns a &str sliced from &self, with no stored self-reference.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • raw is stored as an owned String, copied in via raw.to_string().
  • level returns a borrowed &str sliced from &self, not a stored field and not a new allocation.
  • Running it prints exactly 'level = WARN' then 'raw = WARN: cache miss', matching the required output.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Refactor a self-referential design into stable indices

The shape struct ParsedLine<'a> { raw: String, first: &'a str } is the classic self-referential trap. The intent is for first to point into raw, but the type cannot say that: 'a is supplied by the caller, not by the struct's own raw field, and even if it were, filling first means borrowing self.raw while moving raw into the same value. Those two operations conflict, and there is no safe way to express "borrow from my own field" because moving the struct would invalidate the internal pointer. So the redesign must remove the self-reference entirely.

The practical repair, matching the chapter's stable-indices example, is to store the first token as a byte range — a (start, end) offset pair, or a Range<usize> — instead of a reference. The struct keeps owning raw and adds first: Range<usize> (a plain Copy value with no lifetime). The accessor first(&self) -> &str then reconstructs the borrowed view at call time by slicing &self.raw[self.first.clone()]. The crucial property is that the borrow originates from &self at call time, so its lifetime is the call's borrow, not a stored 'a. The struct itself has no lifetime parameter, moves freely, and can sit in a Vec, a cache, or a channel.

I chose offsets over a typed token id because for recovering a single substring, offsets are the simplest thing that works and they carry no extra machinery. A typed token id makes sense only when you have an interner or token table the id indexes into; here there is none, so an id would just add indirection. The one rule the design must respect is that the stored offsets are only valid as long as raw is not mutated in a way that shifts byte positions. If the buffer can be truncated, spliced, or re-tokenized, the offsets become stale exactly the way a raw pointer would dangle. So either treat raw as immutable after construction, or recompute the offsets whenever the buffer changes — the indexing metadata and the buffer have to be kept in agreement.

use std::ops::Range;

struct ParsedLine {
    raw: String,
    first: Range<usize>, // stable byte offsets into raw; Copy, no lifetime
}

impl ParsedLine {
    fn new(raw: &str) -> Self {
        let raw = raw.to_string();
        // compute the first token's range against the owned buffer
        let end = raw.find(char::is_whitespace).unwrap_or(raw.len());
        ParsedLine { raw, first: 0..end }
    }

    // Reconstruct the borrowed view from &self at call time.
    fn first(&self) -> &str {
        &self.raw[self.first.clone()]
    }
}

fn main() {
    let line = ParsedLine::new("GET /index.html HTTP/1.1");
    println!("first = {}", line.first()); // first = GET
    // No lifetime parameter: ParsedLine moves freely and can be stored.
}

first is a Range<usize>, not a self-reference; the accessor slices it from the owned buffer per call, so the struct stays movable.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The redesign removes the &'a str self-reference completely; ParsedLine has no lifetime parameter.
  • It stores stable metadata — a Range<usize> byte-offset pair — instead of a reference.
  • The accessor first(&self) reconstructs &str by slicing the owned buffer at call time, borrowing from &self.
  • Notes that mutating raw can invalidate the offsets, so the buffer must stay immutable or the ranges must be recomputed.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Choose Box, Rc, or Arc intentionally

Each pointer answers an ownership-count and thread question, not a mutability question, so the right move is to ask "how many owners?" and "which threads?" before naming the type. The recursive AST node owned by one parent is a single-owner case that needs indirection only because a struct cannot contain itself by value — the size would be infinite. Box<T> is exactly the right tool: it provides heap indirection without changing the ownership count. There is one owner, the parent, and Box gives a stable single-owner pointer that breaks the recursive size cycle. No reference counting is involved because nothing is shared.

The read-mostly UI template shared inside one thread has more than one owner — several parts of the UI hold the same template — but they all live on the same thread. Rc<T> fits: it is shared ownership with a non-atomic reference count, cheap to clone because incrementing the count is a plain integer add. Rc is wrong at a thread boundary precisely because its count is non-atomic; two threads cloning or dropping it concurrently would race on that counter and corrupt it, so Rc is !Send and !Sync and the compiler will not let it cross a thread. That is a feature, not a limitation — it makes the cheaper non-atomic count safe to use within one thread.

The schema object shared across worker threads needs Arc<T>. Arc is the same shared-ownership idea as Rc but with an atomic reference count, so cloning and dropping from multiple threads is safe. The extra truth that must hold before Arc is enough: T itself must be thread-safe. Arc<T> is Send and Sync only when T is Sync (and Send), so Arc makes the reference count safe to share, but it does nothing about the interior. If the schema needs to be mutated across threads, Arc alone is not enough — you need Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<RwLock<T>> to make the contents safely shareable. For a read-only schema that is fine as-is, Arc<Schema> is sufficient.

use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::Arc;

// One owner + indirection to break the recursive size cycle.
enum Ast {
    Num(i64),
    Add(Box<Ast>, Box<Ast>),
    Neg(Box<Ast>),
}

// Many owners, one thread: non-atomic shared ownership.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct UiTemplate {
    body: Rc<str>,
}

// Many owners, across threads: atomic count, and T must stay thread-safe.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct SharedSchema {
    version: Arc<str>,
}

fn main() {
    let ast = Ast::Add(Box::new(Ast::Num(1)), Box::new(Ast::Neg(Box::new(Ast::Num(2)))));
    let tmpl = UiTemplate { body: Rc::from("invoice") };
    let _tmpl2 = tmpl.clone(); // same thread only
    let schema = SharedSchema { version: Arc::from("v2") };
    let _for_worker = schema.clone(); // safe to move to another thread
    let _ = ast;
}

Box for single-owner recursion, Rc for same-thread sharing, Arc for cross-thread sharing where the inner type stays thread-safe.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Box<T> is chosen for the recursive single-owner AST node, giving indirection without changing the owner count.
  • Rc<T> is chosen for the same-thread shared UI template, and its non-atomic count is identified as why it cannot cross threads.
  • Arc<T> is chosen for the cross-thread schema, with the explicit note that T must remain thread-safe (and Arc<Mutex<T>> is needed for shared mutation).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design long-lived service structs without over-lifetime-parameterization

The pipeline socket bytes -> parse headers -> build Event -> enqueue -> retry -> persist has exactly one natural region for borrowed views and a clear boundary past which everything must be owned. The types that exist only inside parsing or validation are the view types: a HeaderView<'a> and a RequestLineView<'a> that slice directly into the socket buffer, plus any transient validation result that references those slices. These never leave the parse-and-validate function. Their lifetime parameter stays local because nothing downstream holds them, so the contagion the chapter warns about never starts. Borrowing here is the right call — it is the hot path, the buffer is alive and nearby, and we avoid allocating for data we may reject during validation.

Event becomes fully owned at the enqueue boundary, and that is the single most important decision in the design. The queue is where the data stops being a lens over the socket buffer and becomes a value the system keeps: the buffer will be recycled for the next request long before the retry and persist stages run, and a queued or retried item may also cross an await point or a thread. So the conversion from borrowed views to an owned Event { method: String, path: String, headers: Vec<(String, String)>, body: Vec<u8>, ... } happens right before enqueue. Queues and retries are ownership boundaries; anything that survives past the input buffer should stop borrowing from it. Every type downstream of the queue — the retry envelope, the persistence record — is plain owned data with no lifetime parameter, which is what keeps the bulk of the service from becoming Thing<'a>.

Arc<T> is semantically real in exactly one place here: shared, read-only configuration or schema that the parse, validation, and persistence stages all reference and that may be read from worker threads — for example Arc<Schema> or Arc<RouteTable>. There it encodes genuine many-owner, cross-thread sharing. Arc would merely hide unclear ownership if it were wrapped around the Event itself just to dodge a move or a clone; an Event has one logical owner as it flows through the pipeline, so Arc<Event> would substitute reference counting for a clear handoff and obscure who is responsible for it. The tradeoff I accept explicitly: I pay the allocations to deep-copy the borrowed views into an owned Event at the enqueue boundary. That is real cost on every request, but it buys lifetime independence for the entire post-queue half of the system — retry, persistence, metrics, and tests all operate on a self-contained value with no external lifetime baggage, no Thing<'a> contagion, and no socket buffer pinned alive longer than it should be.

use std::sync::Arc;

// Parsing/validation only: borrowed views, lifetime stays local.
struct HeaderView<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    value: &'a str,
}

// Owned from the enqueue boundary onward: no lifetime parameter.
struct Event {
    method: String,
    path: String,
    headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
    body: Vec<u8>,
}

// Genuinely shared, read-only, possibly cross-thread: Arc is real here.
struct Schema {
    version: String,
}

fn build_event(method: &str, path: &str, headers: &[HeaderView<'_>], body: &[u8]) -> Event {
    // The single conversion boundary, just before enqueue.
    Event {
        method: method.to_string(),
        path: path.to_string(),
        headers: headers
            .iter()
            .map(|h| (h.name.to_string(), h.value.to_string()))
            .collect(),
        body: body.to_vec(),
    }
}

fn enqueue(event: Event, _schema: Arc<Schema>) {
    // event is fully owned: safe to queue, retry, persist, send across threads.
    let _ = event;
}

Borrowed views stay inside parsing; build_event is the one allocation boundary; Arc<Schema> models real shared read-only state, not Event itself.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Borrowed HeaderView/RequestLineView types are confined to parsing and validation, keeping their lifetimes local.
  • Event is converted to fully owned form at the enqueue boundary, before retry and persistence run.
  • Arc is justified only for genuinely shared read-only schema/config, and rejected for Event where it would hide a clear single-owner handoff.
  • The accepted tradeoff is the per-request allocation at build_event, bought in exchange for keeping the post-queue half of the system free of lifetime parameters.

Lab solution

The starter code had two stubs. The constructor stored String::new(), discarding the argument and leaving an empty buffer, and level() returned the hardcoded "UNKNOWN". The fix is the own-the-buffer, borrow-the-view pattern: new copies the input into the owned raw field with raw.to_string(), so AuditLine holds the whole line, and level slices a read-only view out of that owned field on demand.

Inside level, self.raw.split(':') splits "WARN: cache miss" on the colon, and next() takes the first piece, "WARN". The unwrap_or("UNKNOWN") fallback only matters for a line with no colon. The returned &str borrows from &self, so its lifetime is the call's borrow rather than a stored field — there is no self-reference and no lifetime parameter on the struct, which keeps AuditLine an ordinary movable value.

main prints level = WARN from line.level() and raw = WARN: cache miss from line.raw, because the constructor now actually owns the original line. That produces exactly the two expected output lines.

Example 5-S. audit_line_lab.rs — Reference solution

struct AuditLine {
    raw: String,
}

impl AuditLine {
    fn new(raw: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            // Own the line once, inside the struct.
            raw: raw.to_string(),
        }
    }

    fn level(&self) -> &str {
        // Borrowed view derived from &self: the text before the first colon.
        self.raw.split(':').next().unwrap_or("UNKNOWN")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let line = AuditLine::new("WARN: cache miss");
    println!("level = {}", line.level());
    println!("raw = {}", line.raw);
}
Output
level = WARN
raw = WARN: cache miss

Review question answers

When is a borrowed-field struct a strong design, and when is it a maintenance smell?

A borrowed-field struct is a strong design when it is a short-lived lens over data an obvious, nearby owner holds — for example header or request-line views produced and consumed inside a single parse function, where the lifetime stays local and the borrow is cheap. It becomes a maintenance smell when the struct is meant to be stored, queued, retried, cached, sent across threads, or held across an await point, because then it is structurally forbidden from outliving the buffer it borrows from. The tell is the moment you find yourself threading its lifetime parameter through storage types, channels, or test fixtures; at that point the data should own its fields instead.

Why does one borrowed field often force a lifetime parameter onto the whole struct?

A reference is only meaningful relative to the validity of the data it points at, so a struct that stores even one reference must record which external borrow it depends on, and it does that with a lifetime parameter like <'a>. That parameter is not confined to the type definition: it propagates to every function that builds the struct, every struct that contains it as a field, and every return type that hands it back. This is the contagion the chapter warns about — one &'a str field can turn an entire chain of downstream types into Thing<'a>, which is why borrowed fields should be kept local rather than spread through the data model.

What problem does Box<T> solve that plain owned T does not?

Box<T> provides heap indirection while keeping a single owner, which plain owned T cannot do when the type would otherwise need a known, finite size that it does not have. The canonical case is recursion: a struct or enum cannot contain itself by value because its size would be infinite, but boxing the recursive field stores a pointer-sized handle and breaks the cycle. Box also lets you store an unsized or large value behind a fixed-size, movable pointer without involving any reference counting, since there is still exactly one owner.

Why is Arc<T> not a synonym for 'safe to share and mutate however I want'?

Arc<T> makes only the reference count atomic, so it safely answers the question of shared ownership across threads — it does nothing to make the inner value mutable. By itself Arc gives shared read-only access; concurrent mutation through it would be a data race, which the type system prevents by not offering interior mutability. To mutate shared state you must wrap the interior in a synchronization type, such as Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<RwLock<T>>. And Arc<T> is only Send and Sync when T itself is thread-safe, so the inner type still has to uphold its own thread-safety guarantees.

Why do offsets, ranges, or IDs often beat self-references inside owned structs?

A self-reference — a field that borrows from another field of the same struct — cannot be expressed in safe Rust, because moving the struct would invalidate the internal pointer and the borrow conflicts with owning the buffer. Storing stable metadata instead, such as a Range<usize> byte offset or a typed token id, sidesteps the problem entirely: the metadata is plain Copy data with no lifetime, the struct stays movable and storable, and the accessor reconstructs a borrowed &str from &self at call time by slicing the owned buffer. The one obligation is to keep that metadata in sync with the buffer, since mutating the buffer can shift positions and make stored offsets stale, just as a raw pointer would dangle.

Chapter 6 · Pointers, References, and Ownership Inside Vectors

Pointers, References, and Ownership Inside Vectors

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all circle one fact: a vector owns a single resizable buffer, and growth is allowed to move every element it holds. A borrowed element reference such as &workers[0] names a slot in the buffer that exists right now. Anything that may reallocate or reorder that buffer makes the old handle wrong, and Rust refuses to let you carry such a borrow across that change. The work below is about choosing the handle that survives the operations a real system actually performs.

The progression moves from narrating an invalidation event in operational terms, to reading code for hidden shape changes, to refactoring reference-heavy designs into index or ID handles, to mutating safely while iterating, and finally to choosing between Vec<T>, Vec<Box<T>>, and arena-style storage with a concrete requirement in hand. The recurring idea is the distinction between a stable logical handle (an index or ID, which keeps meaning across growth as long as you understand the reordering policy) and a stable memory address (which only some representations provide, and which you should only pay for when the model genuinely needs it).

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Narrate the invalidation event before proposing a fix

The vector owns one resizable heap buffer plus its three-word control block: a pointer to that buffer, a length, and a capacity. The Worker values themselves live in the contiguous heap storage that the pointer addresses. The local binding holds only the small control block; the data lives behind it.

The borrowed reference let first = &workers[0] does not point at the vector and does not point at "worker zero" as a logical identity. It points at the byte range of the slot at offset zero inside the buffer that exists at the moment the borrow is taken. It is an address into the current buffer, valid only as long as that buffer and the aliasing situation around it stay fixed.

push is allowed to reallocate. When the vector reaches capacity, push asks the allocator for a larger buffer, moves every existing element into it, and frees the old buffer. After that, the address inside first refers to memory the vector no longer owns. Reading first.name afterward would be a read into freed or repurposed memory.

This is not the borrow checker merely being strict. The danger is real and identical to what C++ exhibits when a std::vector reallocates and invalidates outstanding iterators and pointers; there the program compiles and then misbehaves at runtime. Rust rejects the code at the push, not because the rule is pedantic, but because it has proven that a later use of first could read invalidated memory. Valid repairs: keep an index (let first = 0;) and reborrow workers[first].name after all pushes are done; finish using first before any push so the borrow has ended; or, if elements must keep a fixed address, change the representation (Vec<Box<Worker>> or an arena) so growth moves handles rather than the pointees.

// Rejected: the borrow into the current buffer outlives a reallocating push.
// let first = &workers[0];
// workers.push(Worker { /* ... */ }); // may reallocate -> first dangles
// println!("{}", first.name);          // would read freed memory

// Repair: hold an index, reborrow only after growth is finished.
struct Worker { name: String }

fn main() {
    let mut workers = Vec::with_capacity(1);
    workers.push(Worker { name: "a".into() });

    let first = 0usize;                  // durable location handle, not an address
    workers.push(Worker { name: "b".into() });
    workers.push(Worker { name: "c".into() });

    println!("{}", workers[first].name); // reborrow now that the shape is fixed
}

An index survives reallocation; a borrowed element reference does not.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States that &workers[0] points into the vector's current heap buffer, at the slot's address, not at a logical identity.
  • Explains that push may reallocate, move the elements, and free the old buffer, which invalidates the old address.
  • Proposes valid repairs: use an index and reborrow later, end the borrow before pushing, or switch to a stable-address representation.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the hidden shape change

Sort the operations into two hazard categories. Relocation hazards may move the whole buffer to a new address: reserve (when it grows capacity), insert (which may grow), push, and any other growth past capacity. After relocation, every previously taken &sessions[i] points into a freed buffer. Position-shift hazards keep the same buffer but move elements between slots: insert shifts later elements up by one, remove shifts later elements down by one, and sort_by_key permutes elements arbitrarily. Note that insert is in both categories: it can reallocate and it shifts positions.

The key reading insight is that these two categories fail in different ways but are both fatal to a borrowed element reference held too long. A relocation makes the reference's address invalid. A position shift leaves the address valid as memory but breaks the assumption that sessions[i] is still the element you cared about; the element you wanted now lives at a different index, and i now names a different element. sort_by_key is the trap here: it may not allocate at all, so the buffer stays put, yet every position-based assumption about which element is where is now wrong.

The more durable handle depends on what you mean by "the same element." If you mean "whatever sits at this position," an index (usize) is durable across reserve but not across insert, remove, or sort. If you mean "this specific session regardless of where it moves," you need a logical identity: store a SessionId field and look it up, or keep an index plus a generation counter, so a sort that reorders the buffer does not silently hand you the wrong session. For a flow that only grows the vector, an index is enough; for a flow that sorts or compacts, only an ID-based handle stays meaningful.

struct Session { id: u64, score: i32 }

// Hazard map for a handle taken as `let s = &sessions[i];`:
//   reserve(n)        -> may RELOCATE buffer        -> address invalid
//   insert(j, x)      -> may RELOCATE and SHIFTS    -> address and/or position invalid
//   remove(j)         -> SHIFTS later elements down  -> position invalid
//   sort_by_key(..)   -> PERMUTES in place          -> position invalid (address may be fine)

fn find_by_id(sessions: &[Session], id: u64) -> Option<usize> {
    sessions.iter().position(|s| s.id == id) // identity survives sort/compaction
}

fn main() {
    let mut sessions = vec![
        Session { id: 7, score: 3 },
        Session { id: 4, score: 9 },
    ];
    let wanted = 7;
    sessions.sort_by_key(|s| s.score); // index would now be wrong; id still works
    if let Some(i) = find_by_id(&sessions, wanted) {
        println!("session {} is now at index {}", wanted, i);
    }
}

An index survives growth; only an ID survives sorting and compaction.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Distinguishes relocation hazards (reserve, insert growth) from position-shift hazards (insert, remove, sort_by_key).
  • Explains that both categories invalidate a long-held element borrow: one by address, the other by changed position.
  • Chooses an index where only growth occurs, and an ID-based lookup where sorting or compaction reorders elements.
Exercise 3implementation

Return an index handle instead of assuming reference stability

The starter version returns tasks.len(), which is the count after the push, not the position of the inserted task. After pushing the first task, len() is 1, but that task lives at index 0, so the returned handle is off by one and points at the next free slot rather than at the task just enqueued. The fix is to return the position the task actually occupies.

The correct index is computed either as tasks.len() captured before the push, or as tasks.len() - 1 immediately after it. Both name the same slot. Capturing the length before the push reads slightly more clearly because it states the intent ("this is where the new task will land") without the off-by-one subtraction, and it is robust against accidentally moving the line below other operations.

The return type stays usize, and the function returns no borrowed reference, so the handle is fully decoupled from the vector's buffer. That is exactly why it survives later growth: subsequent enqueue calls may reallocate the buffer, but an index is a position, not an address. As long as the code only appends (no insert, remove, swap_remove, or sort between enqueueing and use), index 0 keeps naming the billing task. The caller reborrows through tasks[first] only after all pushes are done, when the vector shape is fixed.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    name: String,
}

fn enqueue(tasks: &mut Vec<Task>, name: &str) -> usize {
    let index = tasks.len(); // position the new task will occupy
    tasks.push(Task {
        name: name.to_string(),
    });
    index // not tasks.len(); that would be the next free slot
}

fn main() {
    let mut tasks = Vec::with_capacity(1);
    let first = enqueue(&mut tasks, "billing");
    enqueue(&mut tasks, "search");
    enqueue(&mut tasks, "indexer");

    println!("first = {}", tasks[first].name); // billing, after two reallocs
    println!("total = {}", tasks.len());
}

Return len() before the push (or len() - 1 after) so the handle points at the inserted task.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • enqueue returns the inserted task's index by capturing tasks.len() before the push (equivalently len() - 1 after).
  • The return type stays usize and no borrowed reference is returned.
  • Because an index is a position rather than an address, the handle stays correct after additional pushes reallocate the buffer.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Convert a reference-heavy graph edge into IDs

Storing &Node edges inside other Nodes that all live in the same Vec<Node> cannot work in safe Rust, and for good reason: the vector owning the nodes would have to be borrowed immutably for as long as any edge reference lives, which forbids ever growing or mutating the node list again, and any growth would invalidate the stored references anyway. The design fights both the borrow checker and the runtime reality of reallocation. The fix is to stop storing references and store stable logical handles instead.

The nodes stay in one owning collection, the Graph's Vec<Node> (or a Vec<Box<Node>> if you also need stable pointees). Edges store handles rather than references. Use a typed ID, NodeId(usize), wrapping the index. A typed wrapper is worth the small ceremony in a larger system: it documents intent, prevents accidentally passing an unrelated usize where a node handle is expected, and gives one place to add generation checks later. Each Node holds Vec<NodeId> for its neighbors.

Lookup recovers a borrowed view on demand. The Graph owns the vector, so the Graph is also the natural place to reborrow: a node(&self, id: NodeId) -> &Node method indexes into its own vector and hands back a short-lived borrow scoped to that call. The borrow lives only as long as the immediate use, so it never collides with later growth. This is the central move of the chapter applied to a graph: the owner of the collection is the place where reborrowing happens, edges carry durable identity, and references appear only transiently at the moment of use. Because NodeId is just a wrapped index, this design is robust under appends; if you later add deletion that reuses slots, add a generation field to NodeId and validate it on lookup so stale handles are detected rather than silently aliasing a recycled slot.

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
struct NodeId(usize);

struct Node {
    name: String,
    edges: Vec<NodeId>, // durable handles, not &Node
}

struct Graph {
    nodes: Vec<Node>, // the single owner of all node storage
}

impl Graph {
    fn add_node(&mut self, name: &str) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len());
        self.nodes.push(Node { name: name.into(), edges: Vec::new() });
        id
    }

    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.nodes[from.0].edges.push(to);
    }

    // Reborrow a transient view from the owner, at use time only.
    fn node(&self, id: NodeId) -> &Node {
        &self.nodes[id.0]
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut g = Graph { nodes: Vec::new() };
    let a = g.add_node("a");
    let b = g.add_node("b");
    g.add_edge(a, b); // growth after this point cannot invalidate `a` or `b`

    let first = g.node(a);
    println!("{} -> {}", first.name, g.node(first.edges[0]).name);
}

Edges carry NodeId handles; the owning Graph reborrows a &Node only at use time.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Removes all long-lived &Node references stored inside the node list.
  • Edges store typed NodeId handles (wrapped indices) instead of references.
  • The owning Graph reborrows a transient &Node by handle at use time, with a note on adding generations if slots are later reused.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Implement safe mutation while iterating

The defect is mixing live element borrows with shape-changing edits in a single pass. While a loop holds a borrow into the vector (whether through an iterator or an outstanding &mut element), appending follow-up work or removing expired jobs may reallocate or shift the buffer, which would invalidate the very borrow the loop is using. This is the same hazard as exercises 1 and 2, now inside a loop: inspection produces borrows, and structural edits invalidate them, so the two cannot safely interleave.

Separate the two kinds of work. Field-level edits that do not change the vector's shape (flipping a flag, incrementing attempts, updating a timestamp) can happen in place with iter_mut, because that borrows elements without touching length or capacity. Shape-changing edits (appending follow-up jobs, removing expired ones) must move into a second pass that runs after no element borrow remains active. The clean structure is two phases: first scan and collect plans (the indices or IDs of expired jobs, plus the follow-up jobs to append) into owned local data; then, with the scan's borrows ended, apply the structural edits.

For the structural edits themselves, prefer standard-library patterns over manual index juggling, which is where off-by-one and skip-an-element bugs breed when the length changes mid-loop. retain expresses "drop expired jobs" directly and handles the index bookkeeping internally. extend or a loop of push appends the collected follow-up work. drain is the right tool when you want to consume and move elements out. None of this requires cloning the whole vector; the only owned data you collect is the small plan (indices and the new jobs), not a duplicate of the collection, which is what the acceptance criterion rules out.

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Job {
    name: String,
    failed: bool,
    expired: bool,
    attempts: u32,
}

fn run_scheduler(jobs: &mut Vec<Job>) {
    // Phase 1: inspect. In-place field edits are fine (no shape change),
    // and we collect a plan for the structural edits.
    let mut followups: Vec<Job> = Vec::new();
    for job in jobs.iter_mut() {
        if job.failed {
            job.attempts += 1;
            followups.push(Job {
                name: format!("{}-retry", job.name),
                failed: false,
                expired: false,
                attempts: 0,
            });
        }
    }

    // Phase 2: apply structural edits, now that no element borrow is live.
    jobs.retain(|job| !job.expired); // standard pattern, no manual index math
    jobs.extend(followups);
}

fn main() {
    let mut jobs = vec![
        Job { name: "a".into(), failed: true, expired: false, attempts: 0 },
        Job { name: "b".into(), failed: false, expired: true, attempts: 0 },
    ];
    run_scheduler(&mut jobs);
    println!("{} jobs", jobs.len());
}

Inspect and collect a plan first; then retain/extend once no element borrow is live.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Separates inspection (iter_mut field edits, plan collection) from shape-changing edits in a distinct second pass.
  • Explains that the real problem is holding live element borrows while reshaping the vector in the same pass.
  • Uses retain and extend rather than manual index juggling, and collects only a small plan, never a full clone of the vector.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose Vec<T>, Vec<Box<T>>, or arena-style storage for a registry

Make Vec<Connection> the default and justify deviations against concrete requirements. The accept and route stages mostly scan a contiguous list (count ready connections, find one matching a key, broadcast), and a plain vector gives the best cache locality and the fewest allocations for that work. Most of the pipeline only needs to walk elements, and contiguous storage is exactly what serves that well.

The authenticate, retry, and drop stages need durable handles rather than direct references, because connections come and go and the vector reshapes over the connection's lifetime. The right handle here is a stable logical identity, not a memory address: a typed ConnectionId rather than &Connection. This is the distinction the chapter insists on. A stable logical handle (an ID, optionally with a generation counter) keeps meaning across growth and across deletion that recycles slots; a stable memory address means the bytes never move. Index handles are the cheapest logical handle, but because drop and retry imply deletion and reuse, plain usize indices become ambiguous after compaction or swap_remove. Wrap the handle as ConnectionId with a generation so a stale handle from a dropped connection is detected rather than silently aliasing a recycled slot. That covers accept, authenticate, route, retry, and drop without any stable-address requirement.

Only the plugin boundary may genuinely need stable element addresses: if a plugin is handed a raw pointer or an FFI handle to a Connection and expects it to stay valid while the registry keeps accepting new connections, then the pointee must not move on growth. Plain Vec<Connection> cannot promise that. The narrow fix is Vec<Box<Connection>>: indexing stays simple, scans still walk the vector of boxes, and growing the vector moves the boxes (pointers) while each boxed Connection keeps its heap address. If, beyond stable addresses, you also need efficient slot reuse and an explicit deletion policy across the whole lifecycle, that is the case for an arena or slab store, which provides generation-checked handles and recycling as its core feature.

Tradeoffs to state plainly. Vec<Box<T>> costs one extra allocation per element and one pointer indirection per access, and scans lose some locality because the Connections are scattered across the heap rather than packed; you pay that only to buy stable pointee addresses. An arena adds API surface and a dependency, and ties handle validity to its generation scheme. The discipline the chapter argues for is to start with the simplest owner that meets the semantics: default to Vec<Connection> with generation-checked ConnectionId handles, and escalate to Vec<Box<Connection>> only at the plugin boundary that actually requires stable addresses, and to an arena only when reuse and deletion policy demand it. Do not pay for indirection or a heavier store by reflex.

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct ConnectionId {
    index: u32,
    generation: u32, // distinguishes a live slot from a recycled one
}

struct Connection {
    generation: u32,
    alive: bool,
    // ... peer, auth state, route key ...
}

// Default representation: contiguous scan + generation-checked logical handles.
struct Registry {
    slots: Vec<Connection>,
}

impl Registry {
    fn get(&self, id: ConnectionId) -> Option<&Connection> {
        self.slots
            .get(id.index as usize)
            .filter(|c| c.alive && c.generation == id.generation)
    }
}

// Escalate to Vec<Box<Connection>> ONLY for the plugin/FFI boundary that
// requires each Connection to keep a stable heap address across growth:
//   slots: Vec<Box<Connection>>  // growth moves boxes, not the pointees

Default to Vec<T> with generation-checked IDs; escalate to Vec<Box<T>> only where stable addresses are required.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Justifies Vec<Connection> as the default for contiguous scanning and explains where Vec<Box<T>> or an arena becomes necessary.
  • Separates stable logical handles (generation-checked ConnectionId) from stable memory addresses (boxed pointees).
  • Names tradeoffs: extra allocation and lost cache locality for boxing, added API surface and dependency for an arena.
  • Keeps the plain vector as the default and avoids boxing or arenas without an actual stable-address or reuse requirement.

Lab solution

The starter code returned tasks.len(), the count after the push. For the first task that count is 1, but the task sits at index 0, so the handle was off by one and pointed at the next free slot. The fix captures the length before the push (let index = tasks.len();) and returns that, which is the exact position the new task will occupy. Equivalently you could return tasks.len() - 1 immediately after the push.

The vector starts with capacity 1, so enqueueing "search" and "indexer" forces at least one reallocation that moves the buffer to a new address. The handle first survives this because it is an index (the value 0), a position rather than an address. The code only reborrows through tasks[first] after all three pushes are done, when the vector's shape is fixed, so the borrow never crosses a reallocation.

With first equal to 0, tasks[first].name reads "billing", and tasks.len() is 3 after three pushes, so the program prints first = billing and total = 3.

Example 6-S. task_handle_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    name: String,
}

fn enqueue(tasks: &mut Vec<Task>, name: &str) -> usize {
    // The new task lands at the current length; capture it before the push
    // so the returned handle points at the inserted task, not the next slot.
    let index = tasks.len();
    tasks.push(Task {
        name: name.to_string(),
    });
    index
}

fn main() {
    let mut tasks = Vec::with_capacity(1);
    let first = enqueue(&mut tasks, "billing");
    enqueue(&mut tasks, "search");
    enqueue(&mut tasks, "indexer");

    println!("first = {}", tasks[first].name);
    println!("total = {}", tasks.len());
}
Output
first = billing
total = 3

Review question answers

What exactly does a borrowed element reference from a vector point into?

It points into the vector's current heap buffer, at the address of a specific slot, under the current aliasing rules. It is tied to the buffer that exists at the moment the borrow is taken, not to a logical identity that follows the element around. If that buffer is reallocated by growth, or the element is moved to another slot by insert, remove, or sort, the reference no longer names the thing you wanted, which is why such borrows cannot be held across operations that reshape the vector.

Why are index handles often the default durable handle for Vec<T>?

An index is a position, not an address, so it stays valid across reallocation: you can store the index, grow or mutate the vector, and then reborrow through vec[i] when you actually need the element. It costs nothing extra to store and keeps indexing simple. The caveat is that an index is a location rather than an identity, so it survives appends but not reordering operations like sort, swap_remove, or compaction; when those are in play you wrap the index in a typed ID with a generation check so a stale handle is detected rather than silently aliasing a recycled slot.

What is the difference between stable logical identity and stable memory address?

Stable logical identity means a handle keeps referring to the same element across operations, even if that element moves within the buffer or the buffer is reallocated; an index (as long as you understand the reordering policy) or an ID provides this. A stable memory address means the element's bytes physically never move, so a raw pointer or reference to it stays valid. A plain Vec<T> gives neither across growth, an index gives logical identity cheaply, and only representations like Vec<Box<T>> or an arena give stable addresses; you should require the address guarantee only when something (FFI, an intrusive structure, a self-referential pointee) genuinely depends on the bytes staying put.

When is Vec<Box<T>> a better fit than plain Vec<T>?

When you need each element to keep a stable heap address even as the vector grows, because growing a Vec<Box<T>> moves the boxes (pointers) but never the pointees. This is the right tactical choice at an FFI or plugin boundary that holds a raw pointer to an element, or for an intrusive or self-referential pointee that must not move, while indexing and scanning stay simple. The cost is one extra allocation per element, a pointer indirection on each access, and reduced cache locality because the elements are scattered across the heap, so you pay for it only when stable addressability is an actual requirement rather than a habit.

Why do two-phase loops often produce the clearest vector mutation code?

Because the core hazard is holding live element borrows while changing the vector's shape in the same pass, which Rust forbids and which would be unsafe anyway. Splitting the work into a first phase that only inspects and collects a plan (indices, IDs, or new elements into owned local data) and a second phase that applies the structural edits once no element borrow remains active removes that conflict by construction. It also avoids the off-by-one and skipped-element bugs of manual index juggling when the length changes mid-loop, and it lets you reach for clear standard-library patterns like retain, drain, and extend in the second phase.

Chapter 7 · Copying Data vs Cloning Data

Copying Data vs Cloning Data

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises train one skill: looking at any line that reuses a value and naming exactly what happens to ownership there. A move hands a single value to a new owner. A copy is an implicit bitwise duplicate that small Copy types opt into. A clone is an explicit, possibly expensive duplication you write by hand. And a borrow avoids duplication entirely. The chapter's whole argument is that these are four different events with four different costs, and a reviewer should always be able to tell which one a given call site chose.

The set moves from classification to construction to judgment. You first label each event in a mixed flow and read a service path for its hidden allocation budget. Then you implement Clone by hand and strip clones that only existed to satisfy a too-greedy signature. The last two exercises are design calls: deciding when Copy is mechanically and semantically safe, and lining up receiver choice (self, &self, &mut self) with a deliberate duplication policy at a worker fan-out boundary. The lab closes the loop by making a manual Clone correct so that mutating a clone leaves the original untouched.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Classify each duplication event correctly

Walk each marked line and ask a single question: after this line runs, does the original binding still own its value, and if a duplicate exists, who paid for it and was it implicit or written down. That question separates the four events cleanly.

The move is the line that rebinds a non-Copy owned value, for example let key = route_key; where route_key: String. Ownership transfers to key, and route_key is no longer usable afterward. Nothing was duplicated; the single heap buffer simply changed owners. The implicit copy is the line that rebinds or passes a Copy value, for example let id2 = id; where id: RequestId(u64). Because RequestId is Copy, the eight bytes are duplicated bitwise and id stays valid. There is no .clone() at the call site precisely because the duplication is trivial and the language makes it implicit.

The explicit clone is the line spelled route.clone() on a String, or schema_string.clone() on owned heap data. That call allocates a second independent buffer and copies the bytes, so later mutation of one does not touch the other. It is worth keeping the Arc<Schema> case distinct: Arc::clone(&schema) is also written explicitly, but it does not deep-copy the Schema. It adds a second owning handle to the same allocation and increments the strong count. Both handles see the same Schema; the clone is cheap because only a counter moved, not the payload.

The borrow is the line that takes &value, for example passing &route to a helper that only reads it. No ownership transfers and nothing is duplicated; the helper observes the existing value through a reference and the owner keeps it. That is the case where borrowing removes the need for duplication entirely: if the helper only inspects the route text, a &str argument means no clone and no move ever has to happen.

use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
struct RequestId(u64);

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Schema {
    version: u32,
}

fn log_route(route: &str) {
    println!("route = {route}");
}

fn classify() {
    let id = RequestId(7);
    let id_copy = id;            // implicit COPY: RequestId is Copy, `id` still valid

    let route_key = String::from("/v1/jobs");
    let owner = route_key;       // MOVE: String is non-Copy, `route_key` now invalid

    let route_clone = owner.clone(); // explicit CLONE: second independent heap buffer

    let schema = Arc::new(Schema { version: 1 });
    let worker_schema = Arc::clone(&schema); // shared owner: bumps count, no deep copy

    log_route(&owner);           // BORROW: no duplication, `owner` keeps ownership

    println!("{} {} {} {}", id_copy.0, route_clone, schema.version, worker_schema.version);
}

One flow showing a Copy, a move, an explicit Clone, an Arc share, and a borrow side by side.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each event is named with the precise term move, copy, clone, or borrow rather than a vague 'copy-like' label.
  • Arc::clone is described as adding a shared owner and bumping the strong count, distinct from the deep String clone that allocates a new buffer.
  • The log_route(&owner) borrow is called out as the case where reading through a reference removes any need to move or clone.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the hidden allocation budget

Read the field types first; the cost of each duplication follows the ownership shape of the type, not the spelling of the operation. In a request path that duplicates a RequestId, clones a String route key, and clones an Arc<Schema>, the three operations have three different price tags.

Duplicating the RequestId is almost certainly trivial bitwise duplication. It wraps a u64, so it is Copy, and reusing it copies eight bytes on the stack with no allocation. Operationally, nothing touches the heap and the original RequestId stays valid. Cloning the String route key is the heap-backed operation: String::clone allocates a fresh buffer the size of the route text and memcpys the bytes into it, producing a second independent string. That is the line that actually spends from the allocation budget, and it spends every time the path runs.

Cloning the Arc<Schema> is neither of those. It increments an atomic reference count and returns a second handle pointing at the same Schema allocation. No Schema bytes are copied; the cost is one atomic increment, paid so the allocation lives until the last handle drops. Calling it a deep copy is the classic misread: the worker and the original share one Schema, they do not each own a private one.

The borrowing repair targets the String clone. If the helper that receives the route key only reads it, for example to log it or compare it, change its parameter to &str and pass &route_key instead of route_key.clone(). That removes the allocation entirely: the helper observes the existing buffer through a reference and the path keeps ownership. A cost review for this function should read: the RequestId reuse is a free scalar copy, the Arc::clone is one atomic increment for shared ownership, and the only real allocation is the String clone, which is removable by borrowing because the consumer is read-only.

use std::sync::Arc;

struct Schema {
    version: u32,
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
struct RequestId(u64);

// Before: the helper takes an owned String it only reads, forcing a clone.
fn audit_before(route_key: String) {
    println!("audit {route_key}");
}

// After: borrowing expresses 'I only read this', so callers stop cloning.
fn audit_after(route_key: &str) {
    println!("audit {route_key}");
}

fn handle(id: RequestId, route_key: String, schema: Arc<Schema>) {
    let _id_again = id;                 // free scalar copy, no heap
    let worker_schema = Arc::clone(&schema); // atomic increment, shared owner, no deep copy

    // Heap allocation only happens if we hand owned strings to read-only code:
    audit_before(route_key.clone());    // clones the route bytes (removable)
    audit_after(&route_key);            // borrows instead: zero allocation

    println!("v{} live", worker_schema.version);
}

The route-key clone is the only line that allocates; audit_after shows the borrowing repair.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The RequestId reuse is identified as a trivial scalar Copy with no heap traffic.
  • The String route-key clone is identified as the heap-backed Clone that allocates a fresh buffer each call.
  • Arc::clone is explained as one atomic increment adding a shared owner, not a deep copy of the schema.
  • The proposed repair changes the read-only helper to take &str, removing the route-key allocation entirely.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement Clone manually for a realistic type

A correct manual Clone must produce a fully independent value: after cloning, mutating either the original or the clone must leave the other unchanged. For JobTemplate { service: String, steps: Vec<String>, retries: usize } that means each owned field has to be deep-cloned, and the scalar field is simply copied.

Clone the owned fields explicitly by calling .clone() on them. self.service.clone() allocates a new heap buffer for the service name; self.steps.clone() allocates a new Vec and clones each contained String into it. This is what guarantees independence: the clone's steps vector is a separate allocation, so pushing onto it later does not touch the original's vector. The retries field is a usize, a Copy scalar, so retries: self.retries copies the value directly. Writing self.retries.clone() would compile and behave identically because usize: Clone, but it adds nothing; copying the value is the idiomatic form.

The defect to avoid is exactly the one in the lab's starter code, which returns String::new() and Vec::new() for the owned fields. That is a stub, not a clone: it discards the data and produces an empty value that shares nothing with the original. The test for correctness is the mutation check. Clone, push a new step onto the clone's steps, and confirm the original's steps.len() is unchanged. A real clone passes this; the stub fails it because the original's data was never duplicated.
