Keep the type non-Copy. JobTemplate owns heap memory through String and Vec, so it cannot be Copy mechanically, and even if it could, implicit duplication of a record that allocates would be misleading at call sites. Clone is the right trait here precisely because the cost is real and should be written down with an explicit .clone().

#[derive(Debug)]
struct JobTemplate {
    service: String,
    steps: Vec<String>,
    retries: usize,
}

impl Clone for JobTemplate {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        Self {
            service: self.service.clone(), // new heap buffer for the name
            steps: self.steps.clone(),     // new Vec, each String cloned
            retries: self.retries,         // Copy scalar: plain value copy
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let original = JobTemplate {
        service: String::from("billing"),
        steps: vec![String::from("parse"), String::from("persist")],
        retries: 2,
    };

    let mut cloned = original.clone();
    cloned.steps.push(String::from("notify"));

    // Independence check: the clone grew, the original did not.
    assert_eq!(original.steps.len(), 2);
    assert_eq!(cloned.steps.len(), 3);
}

Owned fields cloned explicitly, scalar copied directly; the assert proves clone independence.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Clone is implemented by hand in an impl block, not via a derive, placeholder, or stub.
  • service and steps are duplicated with .clone(), producing fresh heap allocations.
  • Pushing onto the clone's steps leaves the original's steps.len() at 2, proving independence.
  • The type stays non-Copy because it owns String and Vec heap data, where implicit duplication would mislead.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Remove unnecessary clones from a read-only API

The defect is a signature that takes ownership of data it only reads. fn route_label(route: String) -> String demands an owned String, so every caller that still needs its route afterward is forced to write route_label(route.clone()) just to satisfy the parameter. The clone exists only to feed the signature, not because independent ownership is needed. The helper logs and compares route text; it never stores or mutates it.

The parameter should become &str. A read-only helper that inspects text needs nothing more than a borrowed view, and &str accepts both &String (via deref coercion) and string literals, so it is the most flexible read-only contract. The return type is the second decision. If the helper genuinely produces a new label, returning an owned String is honest. But if it returns the input unchanged in the common case, returning Cow<'a, str> lets the borrowed case avoid allocation and only the transformed case pay, matching the clone-on-write pattern the chapter uses. For a pure log-and-compare helper, the cleanest form often returns nothing or returns &str borrowed from the input, since no new owned string is created at all.

Once the parameter is &str, every route_label(route.clone()) call site drops its .clone() and becomes route_label(&route). The route stays owned by the caller, no allocation happens, and the same call works for literals too. One signature change removes clones at every call site at once, which is why fixing the parameter type is more valuable than patching individual callers.

Borrowing communicates the contract more clearly than taking ownership here. fn route_label(route: String) tells the reader the function might keep or consume the route, which is a lie for a helper that only reads. fn route_label(route: &str) states plainly that the function borrows and returns, makes no ownership claim, and lets the compiler guarantee the caller's value survives the call. The signature now documents the real behavior instead of forcing defensive clones.

use std::borrow::Cow;

// Before: forces owned input, so read-only callers must clone.
fn route_label_before(route: String) -> String {
    println!("route = {route}");
    route
}

// After: borrow for the read-only contract; Cow pays only when it rewrites.
fn route_label(route: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    println!("route = {route}");
    if route.starts_with('/') {
        Cow::Borrowed(route)
    } else {
        Cow::Owned(format!("/{route}"))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let route = String::from("/v1/jobs");

    // Before: the clone existed only to satisfy the signature.
    let _ = route_label_before(route.clone());

    // After: no clone; the caller keeps `route`, literals work too.
    let label = route_label(&route);
    let made = route_label("v2/jobs");
    println!("{label} {made}");
}

Changing the parameter to &str drops the caller's clone; Cow allocates only on the rewrite branch.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The signature is changed to borrow with &str because read-only access is all the helper needs.
  • At least one caller drops its .clone(), passing &route instead.
  • The explanation states that &str documents the read-only, non-owning contract that String falsely implied.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Decide whether a type should implement Copy

Copy has two gates: a mechanical one the compiler enforces, and a semantic one you enforce in review. Mechanically, a type may be Copy only if it has no Drop implementation and every field is itself Copy. Semantically, it should be Copy only when an implicit bitwise duplicate is trivial and unsurprising, leaving both copies independently valid with no hidden cost or shared resource. The checklist is stricter than 'this seems lightweight.'

RequestId(u64) should be Copy. It wraps a single u64, which is Copy, it owns nothing on the heap, and duplicating an ID implicitly is exactly what callers expect. This is the canonical case for deriving Copy, Clone. Span { start: usize, end: usize } should also be Copy. Both fields are Copy scalars, the value is a plain pair of indices with no ownership, and an implicit duplicate of a span is predictable. Two small, trivially duplicable types, both safe.

SessionKey(String) must not be Copy, and the compiler will not allow it anyway because String owns heap memory and is not Copy. Even setting the mechanical rule aside, making session keys implicitly duplicable would hide allocations and blur the question of which copy is authoritative. It should be Clone, so duplication is explicit. SocketOwner(TcpStream) must not be Copy either. A TcpStream owns a file descriptor and has Drop, so the mechanical gate fails outright; semantically, two implicit owners of one socket is a correctness hazard. It should usually be neither Copy nor Clone. Resource ownership deserves a visible, deliberate API, often a move.

SharedSchema(Arc<str>) is the interesting one. Arc<str> is mechanically Clone but not Copy, so the wrapper cannot be Copy regardless. The temptation is that Arc::clone is cheap, so why not make the wrapper Copy to get implicit duplication. The answer: cheap to clone is not the same as trivial to copy. Each Arc clone performs an atomic reference-count increment, which has a real, if small, cost, and silently spawning shared owners on every implicit copy hides that the type participates in shared ownership. Keeping it Clone-only forces an explicit .clone() at each new owner, which is the visible signal shared ownership deserves. So: approve Copy for RequestId and Span; reject it for SessionKey, SharedSchema, and SocketOwner, using Clone for the first two and likely no duplication trait at all for the socket.

use std::sync::Arc;
use std::net::TcpStream;

#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
struct RequestId(u64);            // Copy: single u64, trivial duplicate

#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
struct Span { start: usize, end: usize } // Copy: two Copy scalars, no ownership

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct SessionKey(String);        // Clone only: owns heap; implicit copy would mislead

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct SharedSchema(Arc<str>);    // Clone only: clone is an atomic increment, not free

struct SocketOwner(TcpStream);    // neither: owns an fd and has Drop; move it

fn main() {
    let id = RequestId(1);
    let _again = id;              // implicit copy, `id` still valid
    let span = Span { start: 0, end: 4 };
    let _span2 = span;           // implicit copy

    let key = SessionKey(String::from("sess-9"));
    let _key2 = key.clone();     // explicit, allocation is visible

    let schema = SharedSchema(Arc::from("event.v1"));
    let _shared = schema.clone(); // explicit, signals a new shared owner
}

Copy for the trivial scalar wrappers; Clone for heap and shared owners; no trait for the socket.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Copy is approved only for RequestId and Span, where implicit duplication is trivial and unsurprising.
  • Copy is rejected for SessionKey (heap-owning) and SocketOwner (resource-owning with Drop).
  • The explanation states that Arc being cheap to clone does not justify Copy, because each clone is an atomic increment and shared ownership should be explicit.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose receivers and duplication boundaries together

Receiver choice and duplication policy answer the same underlying question, which is who owns the value after a method runs, so design them together. The aim is that reading a method's receiver tells a reviewer the ownership transition, and every clone has a stated reason.

The builder's finalizer should consume self. fn build(self) -> ServiceConfig takes the builder by value because finalizing ends the builder's life: it converts accumulated state into the finished config and the builder should not be reusable afterward. Consuming self lets build move owned fields straight into the result with no clones, and the compiler enforces that no one keeps using the spent builder. During construction, the setter methods that only configure can take &mut self and return &mut Self for chaining, or take and return self if you prefer a move-based builder; either way they avoid rebuilding from a fresh clone on each step.

On the long-lived ServiceConfig, inspection methods take &self. fn name(&self) -> &str and fn retries(&self) -> usize borrow read-only and hand back a borrowed view or a copied scalar, so callers can query the config repeatedly without moving or cloning it. Mutations take &mut self. fn bump_retries(&mut self) edits in place rather than cloning the whole config, applying a change, and swapping it back, which would allocate a new config on every edit for no reason. The receiver set then reads as a contract: &self views, &mut self mutates in place, self finalizes or transforms ownership.

The publish fan-out is where an explicit clone or share is justified. If each worker needs its own independent, mutable copy of some job data, cloning per worker is legitimate: the clone buys independent ownership so workers do not contend, and you state that reason in review. But if the workers only read shared, immutable configuration, the right model is Arc: build one Arc<ServiceConfig> and hand each worker an Arc::clone, paying one atomic increment per worker instead of deep-copying the config N times. The tradeoff is concrete. Per-worker Clone costs N allocations and N deep copies but gives full independence; Arc costs N atomic increments and shares one allocation but forbids mutation without interior-mutability machinery. Choose Clone when workers must own and mutate, Arc when the data is genuinely read-shared, and avoid the two failure modes of cloning everything (wasted allocation) or forcing everything through Arc (atomic overhead and shared-state complexity where a plain move would do).

use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct ServiceConfig {
    name: String,
    retries: usize,
}

impl ServiceConfig {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name }          // &self: read-only view
    fn retries(&self) -> usize { self.retries }    // &self: returns a Copy scalar
    fn bump_retries(&mut self) { self.retries += 1; } // &mut self: edit in place
}

struct ConfigBuilder { name: String, retries: usize }

impl ConfigBuilder {
    fn retries(mut self, n: usize) -> Self { self.retries = n; self } // move-builder step
    fn build(self) -> ServiceConfig {              // self: finalize, move fields out
        ServiceConfig { name: self.name, retries: self.retries }
    }
}

fn publish(config: ServiceConfig, workers: usize) {
    let shared = Arc::new(config);                  // one allocation, read-shared
    for w in 0..workers {
        let worker_config = Arc::clone(&shared);    // atomic increment per worker
        println!("worker {w} reads {}", worker_config.name());
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut live = ConfigBuilder { name: String::from("ingest"), retries: 0 }
        .retries(1)
        .build();
    live.bump_retries();
    publish(live, 3);
}

build(self) finalizes, &self/&mut self separate reads from edits, Arc shares one read-only config across workers.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • build(self) consumes the builder to finalize, while &self inspects and &mut self mutates, so receivers express ownership transitions.
  • The Arc fan-out is justified economically: one allocation plus N atomic increments instead of N deep clones, chosen because workers only read.
  • The design avoids cloning everything and avoids forcing everything through Arc, picking each based on whether workers must own and mutate.
  • The tradeoff is named explicitly: per-worker Clone costs allocations for independence, Arc costs atomic increments for shared read-only access.

Lab solution

The starter code's manual Clone is a stub: it returns String::new() and Vec::new() for the owned fields, discarding the original's data. The fix is to deep-clone each owned field with self.service.clone() and self.steps.clone(), and to copy the scalar retries directly with self.retries. This is exactly what #[derive(Clone)] would generate; writing it by hand makes the duplication of each field explicit.

Because steps is cloned into a fresh Vec backed by its own allocation, the clone is independent of the original. When main pushes "notify" onto cloned.steps, only the clone's vector grows. The original still owns its two-element vector, untouched.

That independence is what produces the expected output. The first line reads original.service ("billing") and original.steps.len() (still 2), printing 'original = billing 2'. The second reads the clone, whose steps now holds three entries after the push, printing 'cloned = billing 3'. The clone's service is its own "billing" buffer copied from the original. The third line prints the copied scalar, 'retries = 2'.

Example 7-S. manual_clone_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct JobTemplate {
    service: String,
    steps: Vec<String>,
    retries: usize,
}

impl Clone for JobTemplate {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        Self {
            // Deep-clone the owned fields so the clone is fully independent.
            service: self.service.clone(),
            steps: self.steps.clone(),
            // retries is a Copy scalar: copying the value is enough.
            retries: self.retries,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let original = JobTemplate {
        service: String::from("billing"),
        steps: vec![String::from("parse"), String::from("persist")],
        retries: 2,
    };

    let mut cloned = original.clone();
    cloned.steps.push(String::from("notify"));

    println!("original = {} {}", original.service, original.steps.len());
    println!("cloned = {} {}", cloned.service, cloned.steps.len());
    println!("retries = {}", cloned.retries);
}
Output
original = billing 2
cloned = billing 3
retries = 2

Review question answers

What is the practical difference between moving a String, copying a u64, and cloning an Arc<T>?

Moving a String transfers ownership of its single heap buffer to a new binding and invalidates the old one, so no data is duplicated and the original can no longer be used. Copying a u64 is an implicit bitwise duplicate of eight stack bytes that leaves the original valid, because u64 is Copy and the duplication is trivial. Cloning an Arc<T> creates a second owning handle to the same allocation by incrementing an atomic reference count; it does not duplicate the inner T, it adds a shared owner so the value lives until the last handle drops.

Why is Copy intentionally much narrower than 'cheap enough to duplicate'?

Copy makes duplication implicit, so the language will silently duplicate the value on assignment and argument passing while keeping the original valid; that is only safe when the duplicate is a trivial bitwise copy with no hidden cost and no shared resource. Mechanically Rust forbids Copy on any type with a Drop impl or a non-Copy field, which rules out heap owners, file descriptors, and reference-counted handles. Even types that are cheap to clone, like an Arc wrapper, are deliberately excluded, because an Arc clone is an atomic increment that participates in shared ownership and should be written down explicitly rather than happening invisibly.

When is Cow<'a, str> a better API than always returning String?

Cow<'a, str> is better when the common case returns the input unchanged and only some inputs require a rewrite. The borrowed branch (Cow::Borrowed) returns a reference with no allocation, and the owned branch (Cow::Owned) allocates only when the value is actually transformed, so the API pays for an owned String exactly when one is needed. Always returning String forces an allocation on every call even when the input was already in the right form, which wastes work on the hot path of unchanged inputs.

Why is Arc::clone not the same thing as deep-cloning the inner value?

Arc::clone copies only the handle, not the payload: it increments the strong reference count and returns a second Arc pointing at the same allocation, so both handles observe one shared inner value. A deep clone of the inner value would allocate a separate copy that the two owners could mutate independently. With Arc the value is shared, not duplicated, which is what makes the clone cheap (one atomic increment) and also why mistaking it for a deep copy leads to wrong reasoning about how many independent copies exist.

How do receiver choices reduce unnecessary cloning in production APIs?

Choosing &self for read-only methods lets callers inspect a value repeatedly without moving or cloning it, since the method borrows rather than taking ownership. Choosing &mut self lets a method edit a value in place instead of cloning it, mutating a copy, and swapping it back. Reserving self for finalizers and transforms lets those methods move owned fields straight out with no clone. Together these receivers express the real ownership contract, so callers are not pushed into defensive clones just to satisfy a signature that demanded more ownership than the method actually needed.

Chapter 8 · Undefined Behavior and Unsafe Rust

Undefined Behavior and Unsafe Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all circle one discipline: turning vague confidence about a pointer or a chunk of memory into a written list of preconditions, and then placing the unsafe operation behind a boundary that makes those preconditions true before the operation runs. You start by naming invariants in prose, move to spotting where a real routine leaves obligations undocumented, then implement a safe wrapper over an unsafe internal write, repair a MaybeUninit ordering bug, decide honestly whether an API should be safe or unsafe, and finally design an FFI adapter that converts C contracts into Rust types.

The through-line is the containment boundary from the chapter: almost everything is ordinary safe Rust where the compiler proves memory safety, and a small explicit region holds the operations the compiler cannot prove. Your job in every exercise is to keep that region small, attach a precise SAFETY justification, and make sure each check that legitimizes the unsafe step already holds by the time control reaches it.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Name the invariant before the pointer

slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) does not validate anything. It trusts you. So the invariants must be stated as caller obligations, not as runtime checks the function performs.

Pointer validity. The pointer must be non-null. from_raw_parts specifically forbids a null pointer even when len is 0; in that case it still requires a non-null, properly aligned dangling pointer such as NonNull::dangling(). It must be aligned to align_of::<u8>() (trivially 1 for bytes, but for a typed parser returning a wider element type alignment matters). The entire range ptr..ptr.add(len) must point into a single allocated object that is currently live, and all len elements must be initialized and readable. The total size len * size_of::<T>() must not exceed isize::MAX, which is what keeps pointer arithmetic from wrapping.

Lifetime story. from_raw_parts produces &'a [u8] for some lifetime 'a that the caller chooses, and nothing ties that 'a to the real owner of the backing allocation. The invariant is that the backing memory must remain valid and unmoved for the entire span of 'a, and the produced slice must not outlive the packet buffer it was carved from. If the parser's buffer is dropped, reallocated (a Vec growing), or reused while the slice is still reachable, the slice dangles. The honest practice is to bound 'a to the borrow of the owner, for example by writing a function whose signature already ties the output lifetime to an input &Buffer.

Aliasing story. A shared slice &[u8] asserts that for its whole lifetime nothing mutates the bytes it covers. If you also hold a *mut into the same region and write through it, that is a violation even though no &mut exists, because the optimizer is allowed to assume the &[u8] data is immutable. If instead you build &mut [u8] via from_raw_parts_mut, the requirement is stronger: that range must be exclusively yours, with no other live reference or other mutable pointer reading or writing it for the slice's lifetime. Aliasing is the rule that turns a merely-readable pointer into a valid reference.

// The invariants written as a SAFETY contract, then upheld honestly
// by tying the output lifetime to the owner of the bytes.
struct Packet {
    bytes: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Packet {
    /// Returns a view of `len` bytes starting at `offset`.
    fn window(&self, offset: usize, len: usize) -> Option<&[u8]> {
        // The honest, safe version: let the slice API check bounds and
        // tie the lifetime to `&self`. No raw pointer needed.
        self.bytes.get(offset..offset + len)
    }

    /// The raw-pointer form, for comparison. Marked `unsafe` because the
    /// caller, not the function, must uphold the contract.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    /// - `self.bytes` must contain at least `offset + len` elements.
    /// - The returned slice must not outlive `&self`.
    /// - No mutation of `self.bytes` may occur while the slice is alive.
    unsafe fn window_raw(&self, offset: usize, len: usize) -> &[u8] {
        let ptr = self.bytes.as_ptr().add(offset); // non-null, aligned, in-bounds by contract
        std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)
    }
}

The safe form lets the slice API enforce bounds and lifetime; the raw form must spell the same facts out as an unsafe contract.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Pointer validity is named explicitly: non-null even at len 0, aligned, and all len elements live and readable inside one allocation.
  • The lifetime obligation is stated: the slice cannot outlive the owner of the backing buffer, and is upheld by tying 'a to &self.
  • Aliasing is addressed for both cases: a shared slice forbids concurrent mutation, and a mutable slice requires exclusive access to the range.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the UB risks in a raw-pointer copy helper

The function under review looks like a thin memcpy: it takes dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, len: usize, loops with pointer arithmetic, and is exposed as a safe pub fn with no checks. The defect is not that it uses raw pointers; it is that it makes promises it cannot keep. A safe function asserts that no input can cause undefined behavior, but this function can do nothing to make that true, because every fact it depends on lives in the caller.

Undocumented caller obligations. There are several, not one. (1) Non-null: both dst and src must be non-null; the loop dereferences them with no guard. (2) Validity for the range: src must be readable for len bytes and dst must be writable for len bytes, each within a single live allocation. (3) Writability: dst must point to memory the caller is actually allowed to write, not into a read-only mapping or a shorter buffer. (4) Bounds: len must not exceed either allocation; nothing checks this. (5) Aliasing and overlap: if src and dst regions overlap, a byte-by-byte forward copy may corrupt data, which is the classic memcpy-versus-memmove distinction; more fundamentally, holding both a *mut and a *const into overlapping ranges and writing is an aliasing question. (6) Lifetime: both allocations must stay live and unmoved for the whole call. (7) Initialization: src bytes must be initialized, or you propagate uninitialized memory. None of these appear as documentation or as runtime checks.

Should it stay safe? No. A safe public API is wrong precisely because the callee cannot enforce the contract. The function cannot test whether a raw *mut u8 is valid for len writes; that information simply is not recoverable from a bare address at runtime. Marking it safe is a lie that the borrow checker will faithfully propagate, letting safe callers invoke undefined behavior without an unsafe block anywhere in sight. The two honest options are: make it unsafe fn with a written contract enumerating the obligations above, so callers must acknowledge them at the call site; or redesign it around slices so the obligations become statically checked. The slice redesign is strongly preferred for anything that does not cross an FFI boundary, because &[u8] and &mut [u8] carry length, validity, initialization, exclusivity, and lifetime as part of the type, and the standard copy_from_slice already encodes the overlap-safe, length-matched copy.

// BEFORE: a safe signature that cannot honor its promise.
// pub fn copy(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, len: usize) {
//     for i in 0..len {
//         unsafe { *dst.add(i) = *src.add(i); } // null? bounds? overlap? all unchecked
//     }
// }

// OPTION A: keep the raw shape but tell the truth with `unsafe fn`.
/// # Safety
/// - `src` is valid for reads of `len` bytes; `dst` is valid for writes of `len` bytes.
/// - Both point into live allocations that outlive the call.
/// - The `src` and `dst` ranges do not overlap.
/// - `src`'s `len` bytes are initialized.
pub unsafe fn copy_raw(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, len: usize) {
    std::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(src, dst, len);
}

// OPTION B (preferred): redesign around slices so the contract is in the types.
pub fn copy(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8]) {
    // Length, validity, initialization, exclusivity, and lifetime are now
    // all enforced by the borrow checker and the slice API.
    dst.copy_from_slice(src); // panics on length mismatch instead of corrupting memory
}

Option B moves every obligation into the type system; Option A at least relocates the obligation to the caller's unsafe block instead of hiding it.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Multiple distinct obligations are identified: non-null, range validity, writability, bounds, overlap/aliasing, lifetime, and initialization.
  • The safe public signature is explained as wrong because the callee cannot validate a bare raw pointer at runtime, so safety would be asserted falsely.
  • Both remedies are offered: an unsafe fn with a documented SAFETY contract, and a slice-based redesign that makes the obligations static.
Exercise 3implementation

Wrap unsafe internals in a safe public API

This is the canonical shape of a safe abstraction over unsafe internals: validate the precondition first, and only then enter a small unsafe block that inherits an already-proven invariant. The public signature stays safe because the function can fully enforce its own contract. It receives &mut [u8], which carries both the length (so bounds are checkable) and exclusive access (so no aliasing write can race it), and it returns a Result so the one failure mode it cares about is expressed in the type rather than as a panic or silent corruption.

The length check is the load-bearing line. Buffers shorter than four bytes return Err("buffer too small") before any pointer is formed. Once control passes that early return, the four writes at offsets 0..4 are guaranteed in-bounds, so ptr.add(3).write(33) cannot stray outside the allocation. The bytes 82, 83, 84, 33 are the ASCII codes for R, S, T, and !, so a valid buffer reads RST! when interpreted as UTF-8.

Why the unsafe block is justified, in the chapter's terms: the only genuinely unsafe step is pointer arithmetic plus write, and everything around it exists to make that one step legal. The exclusive &mut [u8] borrow supplies the aliasing guarantee, the length check supplies the bounds guarantee, and u8 has no drop glue, so overwriting the existing bytes with .write() does not skip a destructor. Note that for a drop-carrying element type such as String, using .write() over an already-initialized slot would leak the old value's resources, and you would reach for std::ptr::drop_in_place or simple assignment instead. For u8 the write method is exactly right.

fn write_magic(buf: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    // Precondition check first: the unsafe block must inherit a true invariant.
    if buf.len() < 4 {
        return Err("buffer too small");
    }

    let ptr = buf.as_mut_ptr();

    // SAFETY:
    // - The length check above proves at least 4 writable bytes exist,
    //   so offsets 0..=3 are in-bounds.
    // - `buf` is exclusively borrowed as `&mut [u8]`, so no other access aliases it.
    // - `u8` has no drop glue, so overwriting initialized bytes needs no destructor.
    unsafe {
        ptr.add(0).write(82); // 'R'
        ptr.add(1).write(83); // 'S'
        ptr.add(2).write(84); // 'T'
        ptr.add(3).write(33); // '!'
    }

    Ok(())
}

The early return makes the precondition true before the unsafe block runs, so the four raw writes inherit a proven bounds-and-exclusivity invariant.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Buffers shorter than four bytes return Err("buffer too small") via the early return before any pointer is formed.
  • Buffers of length four or more return Ok(()) and contain 82, 83, 84, 33, which decode to RST!.
  • The unsafe region is four writes only, and it executes solely after the length check has established the bounds invariant.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Move assume_init to the only valid place

The inherited code does this: MaybeUninit::<[u32; 4]>::uninit(), then assume_init() immediately, then writes only some elements into the resulting array. The one-sentence explanation for a reviewer: assume_init is called while the storage is still uninitialized, so the program claims a valid [u32; 4] exists and then reads or moves uninitialized memory as if it were a real typed value, which is undefined behavior.

Where writes must occur. Every initialization write must happen through the MaybeUninit storage, before assume_init, not after it. assume_init is not a constructor and performs no work at runtime; it is a promise to the compiler that the bytes already hold a valid T. The correct order is a one-way ratchet: start in the not-yet-valid state, write every element exactly once into the uninitialized storage, and only at the end assert validity. What must be true before the final [u32; 4] exists is that all four u32 slots have been written; only then does every invariant of the type hold and the value legitimately exists.

The repair is about order, not about adding more unsafe. The fix keeps a single small unsafe block, writes all four elements into the MaybeUninit, and moves assume_init to be the last operation, after the loop completes. A common and even safer variant avoids the raw cast entirely by treating the storage as [MaybeUninit<u32>; 4] and writing element by element, then transmuting once everything is initialized; for an array of a Copy type like u32, simply building the value directly without MaybeUninit at all is the most honest option when the elements are known up front. MaybeUninit earns its place only when you genuinely cannot produce all elements before you need typed storage, for example when initializing in place to avoid an extra copy on a hot path.

use std::mem::MaybeUninit;

// BEFORE (UB): asserts a valid array before any element is written.
// let arr = MaybeUninit::<[u32; 4]>::uninit();
// let mut arr = unsafe { arr.assume_init() }; // reads uninitialized memory as [u32; 4]
// arr[0] = 10;
// arr[1] = 20; // only some elements written; the rest were never valid

// AFTER: write every element into the storage first, assume_init last.
fn build() -> [u32; 4] {
    let mut storage = MaybeUninit::<[u32; 4]>::uninit();
    let ptr = storage.as_mut_ptr() as *mut u32;

    // SAFETY:
    // - each of the 4 slots is written exactly once, in-bounds.
    // - no read of `storage` occurs before initialization completes.
    unsafe {
        for i in 0..4 {
            ptr.add(i).write((i as u32 + 1) * 10);
        }
        // Only now is every element a valid u32, so the array is a real value.
        storage.assume_init()
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", build()); // [10, 20, 30, 40]
}

assume_init moves to the final position, after all four slots are written; before that point the storage is not a valid array.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The value stays inside MaybeUninit storage and every element is written through that storage before any assume_init.
  • assume_init is the last operation, executed only once full initialization is complete.
  • The bug is explained as reading uninitialized memory as a valid [u32; 4], which treats invalid bytes as a typed value.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Decide whether the function should be safe or unsafe

The function fn view<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] is unsound as a safe function and should not exist in that form. The fatal flaw is the unconstrained lifetime parameter 'a. Because 'a appears only in the return type and is not tied to any input, the caller may freely choose 'a = 'static, and the function will happily manufacture a 'static slice out of a pointer to a buffer that lives for one stack frame. The callee cannot verify the pointer is valid for an arbitrary 'a, because validity-for-a-lifetime is a fact about the lifetime of the backing allocation, and a bare *const u8 carries no such information. The function is asserting a lifetime it cannot prove.

Is the returned lifetime tied to a real owner? No, and that is the whole problem. A reference's lifetime is supposed to be a conservative under-approximation of how long the referent is valid. Here the lifetime is invented at the call site with no connection to the owner of the bytes, so the type system's central guarantee, that a live reference always points to live memory, is silently broken. This is the lifetime fiction the chapter warns about: raw pointers plus arbitrary returned references are exactly where it becomes dangerous.

The honest redesign. There are three coherent shapes, in order of preference. (1) If a borrowed view is wanted, take the source as &[u8] (or a wrapper that owns the bytes) and return a sub-slice; the borrow checker then ties the output lifetime to a real owner with no unsafe at all. (2) If the bytes truly come from a raw source such as FFI, make it unsafe fn view<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] with a SAFETY contract stating that the caller must guarantee the pointer is valid and initialized for len bytes and that 'a does not exceed the real lifetime of the backing allocation; this relocates the obligation to the caller, who has the context to discharge it. (3) If the data should be owned downstream, return Vec<u8> by copying, eliminating the lifetime question entirely. The distinction throughout is between caller-held obligations, which an unsafe fn makes explicit, and callee-enforced checks, which a safe slice-based signature lets the compiler verify.

// UNSOUND: 'a is unconstrained, so a caller can fabricate a 'static slice
// from a pointer to short-lived memory. Do not ship this as safe.
// fn view<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] {
//     unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) }
// }

// FIX 1 (preferred): borrow a real owner; the lifetime is now honest.
fn view<'a>(src: &'a [u8], offset: usize, len: usize) -> Option<&'a [u8]> {
    src.get(offset..offset + len)
}

// FIX 2: if the source really is raw (FFI), make the obligation explicit.
/// # Safety
/// - `ptr` is non-null, aligned, and valid for reads of `len` initialized bytes.
/// - The chosen `'a` does not outlive the real backing allocation.
unsafe fn view_raw<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] {
    std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)
}

// FIX 3: hand back ownership and drop the lifetime question entirely.
fn view_owned(src: &[u8], offset: usize, len: usize) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
    src.get(offset..offset + len).map(|s| s.to_vec())
}

The unconstrained 'a is the defect; the three fixes either tie the lifetime to an owner, make the obligation an unsafe contract, or remove the lifetime by owning the data.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • It is explained that the callee cannot manufacture an arbitrary valid lifetime, because validity-for-'a is a property of the backing allocation that a raw pointer does not carry.
  • A concrete more-honest API is proposed: a borrowed &[u8] view, an unsafe fn with a SAFETY contract, or an owned Vec<u8> return.
  • Caller-held obligations (made explicit by unsafe fn) are distinguished from callee-enforced checks (provided by a safe slice signature).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Wrap an FFI boundary without exporting C mistakes

The design principle is a single translation layer with one direction of travel. Unsafe lives in exactly one adapter module, not in every caller. Raw C values, *const c_char error strings and *mut Record results, enter that module, are converted into Rust types that carry the guarantee, and from there inward the entire service, the parser, the retry loop, the request handlers, is ordinary safe Rust that never touches a raw pointer. If application code anywhere outside the adapter still manipulates *mut Record, the boundary is too wide and the C mistakes have leaked into the system.

Translating the three C contracts into Rust types. Nullability becomes Option or, more usefully, an early conversion to Result: a returned *mut Record that may be null maps to Option<NonNull<Record>>, and a null result combined with a non-null error string maps to Err. Ownership transfer becomes an owned newtype with a Drop impl. If the C library hands back a *mut Record that the caller must later free with record_free, wrap it in a struct Record(NonNull<ffi::Record>) whose Drop calls record_free exactly once; this makes the resource releasable only through the safe owner and prevents double-free and leak by construction. The borrowed-versus-owned distinction matters: a Record we must free is owned; a *const Record the library still owns and only lends us for the duration of a call is a borrowed view with a lifetime no longer than that call. String validity becomes a checked conversion: a *const c_char is read via CStr::from_ptr inside unsafe (after a null check), then to_str() validates UTF-8 and yields Result, so invalid bytes surface as an error instead of propagating a malformed &str.

Cleanup and unwinding. Ownership of native resources rests with the Rust owner types, and release happens deterministically in their Drop, so the retry loop can drop a failed Record on each attempt without leaking. Two failure modes to call out: an error path that returns a null *const c_char (so the code must treat the error pointer itself as nullable, not assume a message exists), and a cleanup mismatch where a Record allocated by the C allocator is freed by the wrong deallocator, which is undefined behavior, so the Drop impl must call the library's own free function. On unwinding: a Rust panic must never cross back into C, because unwinding through a frame that is not prepared for it is undefined behavior. Any extern "C" callback the library invokes, or any closure run while C holds resources, should either use a panic-catching boundary (std::panic::catch_unwind) or be declared extern "C" so that on the abort-on-panic policy a panic aborts rather than unwinds into foreign frames. Stating that policy explicitly at the boundary is what keeps the unwinding assumptions from staying fuzzy.

use std::ffi::CStr;
use std::os::raw::c_char;
use std::ptr::NonNull;

mod ffi {
    use std::os::raw::c_char;
    #[repr(C)]
    pub struct Record { _private: [u8; 0] }
    extern "C" {
        pub fn parse_record(input: *const c_char, out_err: *mut *const c_char) -> *mut Record;
        pub fn record_free(rec: *mut Record);
    }
}

/// Owned handle to a native Record. The ONLY place that frees it.
pub struct Record(NonNull<ffi::Record>);

impl Drop for Record {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // SAFETY: constructed only from a non-null pointer the C library
        // allocated, freed exactly once here with the matching deallocator.
        unsafe { ffi::record_free(self.0.as_ptr()) }
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum ParseError {
    Null,
    Message(String),
}

/// The single adapter. All unsafe lives here; callers get Result + owned types.
pub fn parse(input: &CStr) -> Result<Record, ParseError> {
    let mut err: *const c_char = std::ptr::null();
    // SAFETY: `input` is a valid NUL-terminated C string for the call;
    // `&mut err` is a valid out-pointer; ownership of the returned Record
    // transfers to us on success.
    let raw = unsafe { ffi::parse_record(input.as_ptr(), &mut err) };

    match NonNull::new(raw) {
        Some(nn) => Ok(Record(nn)), // ownership now lives in a safe Drop type
        None => {
            if err.is_null() {
                return Err(ParseError::Null); // failure path with no message
            }
            // SAFETY: `err` is non-null and points to a NUL-terminated string
            // owned by the library for at least this call.
            let msg = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(err) }
                .to_str()
                .unwrap_or("<invalid utf-8>") // string-validity failure mode
                .to_owned();
            Err(ParseError::Message(msg))
        }
    }
}

One adapter owns all unsafe: null becomes Result, ownership becomes a Drop newtype, and C string validity is checked via CStr::to_str before crossing inward.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • All unsafe is confined to a single adapter module, and the rest of the service uses Result and owned types with no raw pointers.
  • Nullability maps to Option/Result, ownership transfer maps to a Drop-owning newtype, and C string validity maps to a checked CStr conversion.
  • Native resource ownership rests with the Rust Record type and release happens once in its Drop, with borrowed views distinguished from owned handles.
  • At least one failure mode is named: a null error pointer, invalid UTF-8 in the message, a mismatched free, or a panic unwinding across the C boundary.

Lab solution

The initial code is missing the one check that makes the unsafe writes legal: it dereferences four offsets without first confirming the buffer holds four bytes. The completed solution adds the early return if buf.len() < 4, which turns write_magic into a genuinely safe public function. For the three-byte buffer, control reaches the early return and the function yields Err("buffer too small") before any pointer is formed, so the first printed line is short = Err("buffer too small").

For the four-byte buffer, the length check passes, so the unsafe block runs with a proven invariant: offsets 0 through 3 are in-bounds, the &mut [u8] borrow guarantees exclusive access, and u8 carries no drop glue, so the four .write() calls are sound. The function returns Ok(()), giving value = Ok(()). The bytes written are 82, 83, 84, 33, the ASCII codes for R, S, T, and !, so std::str::from_utf8 over the now-filled buffer decodes to RST!, producing buf = RST!.

This is the chapter's safe-abstraction shape in miniature: a small unsafe core wrapped by a check that establishes its precondition, with a safe signature that callers can use without an unsafe block of their own.

Example 8-S. write_magic_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn write_magic(buf: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    // Precondition check first: the unsafe block must inherit a true invariant.
    if buf.len() < 4 {
        return Err("buffer too small");
    }

    let ptr = buf.as_mut_ptr();

    // SAFETY:
    // - The length check above guarantees at least 4 writable bytes exist,
    //   so offsets 0..=3 are in-bounds.
    // - `buf` is exclusively borrowed as `&mut [u8]`, so no other access aliases it.
    // - `u8` has no drop glue, so overwriting initialized bytes needs no destructor.
    unsafe {
        ptr.add(0).write(82);
        ptr.add(1).write(83);
        ptr.add(2).write(84);
        ptr.add(3).write(33);
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    let mut short = vec![0u8; 3];
    let mut ok = vec![0u8; 4];

    println!("short = {:?}", write_magic(&mut short));
    println!("value = {:?}", write_magic(&mut ok));
    println!("buf = {}", std::str::from_utf8(&ok).unwrap());
}
Output
short = Err("buffer too small")
value = Ok(())
buf = RST!

Review question answers

What does an unsafe block let you do, and what does it not excuse?

An unsafe block grants a specific, finite set of capabilities: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions (including FFI), accessing or modifying mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and accessing union fields. It does not disable the borrow checker, type checking, ownership, or any ordinary Rust rule; the surrounding code still obeys them. Above all it does not excuse undefined behavior. unsafe simply means the compiler cannot prove this operation sound, so a human takes on the obligation to guarantee it, ideally recorded in a SAFETY comment.

Why is a data race undefined behavior in Rust rather than merely an unlucky concurrency bug?

Rust's memory model, like C++'s, defines program behavior only for executions free of data races; an unsynchronized conflicting access (at least one a write) to the same location from two threads has no defined meaning at all. Because the behavior is undefined rather than merely nondeterministic, the optimizer is entitled to assume it cannot happen and may reorder, cache, or eliminate accesses in ways that corrupt memory arbitrarily, not just produce a wrong-but-bounded result. Safe Rust prevents this by construction through ownership transfer, the borrowing rules, and the Send/Sync bounds enforced at thread boundaries. Only unsafe code can reintroduce a data race, which is why those accesses must be synchronized with atomics or locks.

What is the difference between a raw pointer and a reference in terms of promises made to the optimizer?

A raw pointer is just an address with no promises attached: it may be null, dangling, misaligned, or aliased, which is exactly why creating one and doing arithmetic on it is always safe while dereferencing it is not. A reference is an address plus a contract the optimizer relies on: &T promises the pointee is valid, aligned, and immutable for the reference's lifetime, and &mut T additionally promises exclusive access with no other live reference to the same data. The optimizer uses those promises to cache loads, reorder, and assume no aliasing. Turning a raw pointer back into a reference reintroduces all of those promises, so the conversion is sound only if they genuinely hold.

Why is MaybeUninit<T> the right model for not-yet-valid storage?

Uninitialized memory is not a valid value of any type, and reading it as a real T is undefined behavior; the same applies to constructing invalid bit patterns for types with invariants such as references, bool, and many enums. MaybeUninit<T> models the not-yet-valid state explicitly: it reserves correctly sized and aligned storage without claiming a valid T lives there, and it suppresses drop glue so a partial value is never destructed. You write every required field or element, then call assume_init exactly once to assert that a valid T now exists. This makes the invalid state visible in the type system instead of hiding it behind a fake placeholder value, which is what keeps the one-way initialization ratchet honest.

When should an API be unsafe fn instead of a safe function with internal unsafe code?

Keep the public API safe and isolate the unsafe internally when the callee can actually enforce the whole contract, for example a slice wrapper or parser that can check bounds, maintain ownership, and guarantee non-aliasing through an exclusive &mut borrow. Mark the function unsafe fn when correctness depends on facts only the caller can establish, such as a raw pointer being valid for a chosen lifetime or a caller-controlled aliasing guarantee that no runtime check can recover. The deciding question is whether the function can validate its preconditions itself; if it cannot, a safe signature would be asserting a guarantee it has no way to uphold, so the obligation must be pushed to the caller and documented precisely with a SAFETY contract.

Chapter 9 · Smart Pointers and Pinning

Smart Pointers and Pinning

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move smart pointers out of the realm of "which type maps to which other language" and into the realm of deliberate ownership design. Each one forces you to read a pointer type as a set of independent statements: how many owners exist, whether they cross a thread boundary, whether the shared value mutates and under which enforcement model, and whether the value's address must stay stable. The composites you build (Rc<RefCell<T>>, Arc<Mutex<T>>, Pin<Box<dyn Future>>) are just those statements layered together.

The lab and the tree-tracing exercises center on the one structural rule that reference counting cannot enforce on its own: owning edges stay strong, observational back-edges become weak. Get that rule right and the cycle problem disappears; get it wrong and you leak. The pinning exercises add the orthogonal concern of address stability, which is a movement question, not an ownership or mutation question.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Read each pointer type as an ownership statement

The point of this exercise is to keep four independent properties separate: owner count, mutation authority, thread sharing, and address stability. A single pointer type usually answers only one or two of these, and the composites answer the rest.

Box<T> provides one owner plus heap indirection. It does NOT provide sharing, reference counting, or interior mutability. Its job is to give a recursive or large type a finite, fixed-size field while keeping single-owner semantics.

Rc<T> provides shared ownership on one thread by incrementing a non-atomic count on clone. It does NOT provide mutation through the shared handle, nor thread safety, because the non-atomic count makes it neither Send nor Sync. Arc<T> provides the same shared ownership but with an atomic count, so it can cross thread boundaries. It does NOT provide arbitrary mutation safety; the atomic count protects only the count, not the data. The single implementation difference between Rc and Arc is atomic versus non-atomic counting, and that difference is exactly what decides single-thread versus cross-thread use.

RefCell<T> provides interior mutability with the borrow rules enforced at runtime: it hands out borrow tokens and panics if you violate the aliasing rule. It does NOT add owners by itself and does NOT provide thread safety. Mutex<T> provides exclusive access only after lock acquisition, moving the aliasing rule's enforcement to lock acquisition rather than the compiler or a runtime panic. It also does NOT add owners by itself; you reach for Arc<Mutex<T>> precisely because Mutex alone gives mutation but not sharing.

Weak<T> is a non-owning edge: it points at an allocation without keeping it alive, so it does not contribute to the strong count. Calling upgrade() returns Option<Rc<T>> (or Option<Arc<T>>), where None means the owner is already gone. Of the listed items, none speak to address stability; that is Pin's exclusive job, which is why the chapter treats it separately.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Box<T> is stated as one owner plus heap indirection, explicitly without sharing, reference counting, or interior mutability.
  • Rc<T> and Arc<T> are both shared ownership, differing only in non-atomic versus atomic counting and therefore single-thread versus cross-thread use.
  • RefCell<T> is named as runtime-checked borrowing that panics on violation, Mutex<T> as exclusive access after lock acquisition; neither is presented as adding owners on its own.
  • Weak<T> is identified as not keeping the allocation alive with upgrade() returning Option<Rc<T>>/Option<Arc<T>>, and Pin is noted as the only address-stability item (not in this list).
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the strong and weak edges in the tree sample

Walk the smart_pointers_tree sample line by line, tracking the counts on each allocation.

After let leaf = Rc::new(...), leaf's allocation has strong count 1 (the leaf binding). After root.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(&leaf)), the children vector now holds a second strong handle to the same allocation, so leaf's strong count rises to 2. Rc::clone never copies the node; it increments the non-atomic count and returns another owner of the one allocation. The children edge is therefore a strong, owning edge.

After *leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&root), root's allocation gains a weak count, not a strong count. Rc::downgrade produces a Weak<Node> that observes root without owning it. So at this point root's strong count is 1 (only the root binding) and its weak count is 1 (the leaf's parent edge). The parent edge is an observational, weak edge.

The call leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade() must return an Option because a Weak does not keep the allocation alive. Between downgrade and upgrade the strong owners could have been dropped, leaving a dangling intent; upgrade() asks "is the allocation still alive?" and answers Some(Rc) if so or None if not. You cannot dereference a Weak directly precisely because that safety question has not yet been answered; upgrade() is the checkpoint that converts an observation into a temporary strong handle.

The program prints root strong = 1. The only strong handle to root is the root binding itself. The leaf-to-root edge is deliberately weak, so it contributes nothing to root's strong count. Because the two edges between the nodes are of different kinds (children strong, parent weak), there is exactly one strong cycle's worth of edges missing, and no cycle forms. That is the whole reason the graph stays acyclic and both nodes can eventually drop.

// Counts as the sample runs:
//
//   let leaf = Rc::new(Node { .. });
//   // leaf:  strong = 1, weak = 0
//
//   root.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(&leaf));
//   // leaf:  strong = 2, weak = 0   (binding + children vec)
//
//   *leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&root);
//   // root:  strong = 1, weak = 1   (binding strong; parent edge weak)
//
//   leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade()   -> Some(Rc<Node>) while root lives
//                                       None once root's strong count hits 0
//
// Printed:  root strong = 1  (only the `root` binding is a strong owner)

Reference-count trace for each line of the tree sample.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States that pushing Rc::clone(&leaf) raises leaf's strong count to 2 and that downgrade adds a weak (not strong) count to root.
  • Explains Rc::strong_count(&root) is 1 because only the leaf-to-root edge is weak and no second strong handle to root exists.
  • Explains upgrade() returns Option because a Weak does not keep the allocation alive, so the owner may already be gone.
  • Identifies the children edge as the owning (strong) edge and the parent edge as the observational (weak) edge, which is why no cycle forms.
Exercise 3implementation

Build a single-thread cache with Rc plus interior mutability

The instinct under shared ownership is Rc<RefCell<T>>, but RefCell hands out interior borrow tokens and adds a runtime panic mode. For a counter you never need an interior reference; you only ever copy the value out, add one, and write it back. That is exactly the Cell<T> contract, so Cell<u32> is the smaller, sufficient tool and avoids the runtime borrow bookkeeping entirely.

The shared ownership lives in the Rc, not in the Cell. Rc<Stats> lets several handles own one allocation; the Cell<u32> inside that single allocation is what they mutate. record_hit takes &Rc<Stats> (a shared, immutable handle) and still mutates the count, because Cell provides interior mutability: get() copies the current value out, and set() replaces it, neither requiring &mut and neither producing an interior reference. snapshot likewise returns the count by value with get(), never borrowing into the cell.

Cloning the Rc with Rc::clone produces a second owner of the same allocation, so both handles read and write the same Cell. Incrementing through one handle is observed through the other, which is the demonstration that there is one shared allocation, not two copies.

The field-design note: Cell is correct here only because whole-value copy/replace is enough. If a field were larger or needed an interior &mut reference handed out (for example, mutating one element of a Vec in place, or calling a method on the inner value through &mut), Cell would not suffice and you would move that field to RefCell<T>, accepting its borrow tokens and its panic-on-violation runtime check.

use std::cell::Cell;
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Stats {
    label: String,
    count: Cell<u32>,
}

fn record_hit(stats: &Rc<Stats>) {
    // No &mut and no interior reference: copy out, add, write back.
    stats.count.set(stats.count.get() + 1);
}

fn snapshot(stats: &Rc<Stats>) -> u32 {
    stats.count.get() // returns the value by copy
}

fn main() {
    let a = Rc::new(Stats {
        label: String::from("cache"),
        count: Cell::new(0),
    });
    let b = Rc::clone(&a); // second owner of the SAME allocation

    record_hit(&a);
    record_hit(&b);
    record_hit(&a);

    // Both handles observe the same Cell inside the one allocation.
    println!("{} via a = {}", a.label, snapshot(&a)); // 3
    println!("{} via b = {}", b.label, snapshot(&b)); // 3
    assert_eq!(snapshot(&a), snapshot(&b));
}

Rc<Stats> shares ownership; Cell<u32> supplies copy-out/replace interior mutability without borrow tokens.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Stats uses Cell<u32> for the count, and record_hit mutates it through &Rc<Stats> with no &mut.
  • snapshot returns the count by value via get() and never borrows an interior reference.
  • Two cloned Rc handles read the same updated count, shown by the assert_eq, demonstrating shared ownership of one allocation.
  • The answer notes Cell is correct because only whole-value copy/replace is needed, and RefCell would be required only if interior references had to be handed out.
Exercise 4implementation

Poll a hand-written future through Pin

This mirrors the smart_pointers_pin_poll sample. The poll contract is fixed by the Future trait: fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>. The receiver is Pin<&mut Self> because the executor must be able to hold an address-sensitive state machine still while it is driven, and the only way to mutate it is through that pinned view.

Inside poll we call self.get_mut() to recover &mut Self. This is permitted because Ticker is a plain struct of Copy fields and therefore implements Unpin automatically. Unpin means "pinning imposes no real constraint on this type because it is freely movable," so Pin::get_mut is sound: there is no address-sensitive invariant to protect. For a !Unpin type (such as a self-referential generated future), get_mut would not be available, and you would need pin-projection or unsafe machinery instead.

The driver builds a no-op Waker via a Wake implementation, wraps it in a Context, and pins the future with Box::pin. Box::pin gives owned, pinned heap storage that can be polled repeatedly; each poll call uses task.as_mut() to produce the temporary Pin<&mut Ticker> the trait demands. We loop, printing each Pending and breaking on Ready.

For remaining = 3: the first poll sees remaining == 3, decrements to 2, returns Pending; the second sees 2, decrements to 1, returns Pending; the third sees 1, decrements to 0, returns Pending; the fourth sees 0 and returns Ready("fired"). That is three Pending results before the single Ready, matching the decrement-then-check structure where zero is only observed on the call after the last decrement.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

struct Ticker {
    remaining: u8,
}

impl Future for Ticker {
    type Output = &'static str;

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        // Sound because Ticker is Unpin (plain Copy fields, freely movable).
        let this = self.get_mut();
        if this.remaining == 0 {
            Poll::Ready("fired")
        } else {
            this.remaining -= 1;
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

struct NoopWake;
impl Wake for NoopWake {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}

fn main() {
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(NoopWake));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut task = Box::pin(Ticker { remaining: 3 });

    let mut pending = 0;
    loop {
        match Future::poll(task.as_mut(), &mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(value) => {
                println!("ready = {}", value);
                break;
            }
            Poll::Pending => {
                pending += 1;
                println!("pending #{}", pending);
            }
        }
    }
    // For remaining = 3, `pending` is 3 here.
    assert_eq!(pending, 3);
}

A hand-written Unpin future driven through Box::pin; three Pending polls precede Ready for remaining = 3.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • poll has the signature taking Pin<&mut Self> and returns Poll::Ready("fired") only when remaining reaches zero.
  • self.get_mut() reaches the fields, with the note that it is sound because Ticker is movable (Unpin).
  • The driver pins with Box::pin and polls task.as_mut() in a loop until Poll::Ready.
  • For remaining = 3 the program reports three Pending polls before the Ready result (asserted).
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Break a reference cycle and fix a misused pointer

There are two independent defects: a memory leak from a strong-strong cycle, and a thread-safety mismatch from moving Rc across a thread boundary.

The leak. With parent: RefCell<Option<Rc<Node>>> and children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>, both directions are strong, owning edges. The parent owns the child (in its children vector) and the child owns the parent (in its parent field). Dropping the external root and leaf bindings lowers each node's strong count, but the mutual edges keep each count at least 1: the parent's allocation is kept alive by the child's parent field, and the child's allocation is kept alive by the parent's children vector. Neither strong count can reach zero, so neither allocation is ever freed. Reference counting cannot collect this on its own.

The fix is the chapter's rule: owning edges stay strong, observational back-edges become weak. Change the parent field to RefCell<Weak<Node>>. Set it with Rc::downgrade(&parent), which adds a weak count rather than a strong one, and read it with upgrade(), which returns Option<Rc<Node>> (None once the parent is gone). Now only the children edge is strong; dropping the root lets its strong count reach zero, the allocation frees, and the leaf's weak parent edge cleanly upgrades to None.

The thread-safety mismatch. Rc<Node> uses a non-atomic reference count, so cloning or dropping it from two threads would race on that count. For that reason Rc is neither Send nor Sync, and the compiler rejects moving Rc<Node> across a thread boundary (the closure passed to thread::spawn requires Send). The minimal change for the cross-thread case is to replace Rc with Arc, whose atomic count makes it Send + Sync (when T is). Note that the inner contents must also satisfy the relevant bounds; RefCell is not Sync, so for the cross-thread version the interior-mutability tool must change too.

Finally: switching to Arc alone does NOT make shared mutation safe. Arc solves ownership count, not mutation authority. Two threads sharing Arc<T> can both read, but if they need to mutate, you must add synchronization, typically Arc<Mutex<T>> (shared ownership plus serialized mutation) or redesign toward message passing. Read the composite literally: Arc is the ownership decision, Mutex is the separate mutation decision.

// Single-thread fix: break the cycle with a weak back-edge.
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Node {
    parent: RefCell<Weak<Node>>,        // was RefCell<Option<Rc<Node>>> (strong -> leak)
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>,   // owning edge stays strong
}

fn attach(parent: &Rc<Node>, child: &Rc<Node>) {
    parent.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(child));   // strong, owns
    *child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent);    // weak, observes
}

fn parent_of(child: &Rc<Node>) -> Option<Rc<Node>> {
    child.parent.borrow().upgrade() // None once the parent has dropped
}

// Cross-thread version: Rc -> Arc, and mutation needs a Mutex.
// use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex, Weak};
// struct SharedNode {
//     parent: Mutex<Weak<SharedNode>>,
//     children: Mutex<Vec<Arc<SharedNode>>>,
// }
// Arc fixes ownership count only; the Mutex supplies synchronized mutation.

Weak parent edge breaks the leak; Arc plus Mutex is the cross-thread shape (Arc for ownership, Mutex for mutation).

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The leak is attributed to a strong-strong cycle in which neither side reaches a strong count of zero.
  • The parent field is changed to RefCell<Weak<Node>>, set via Rc::downgrade and read via upgrade() returning an Option.
  • Rc<Node> is identified as not Send/Sync due to its non-atomic count, with Arc<Node> as the cross-thread replacement.
  • It is made clear that Arc fixes ownership count only and shared mutation across threads still needs a Mutex (or message passing).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose pointer types for a mixed-ownership service

Answer the questions in order for each concern: how many owners, one thread or many, does the shared value mutate, and under which enforcement model. The type then falls out, and each composite reads as a layered statement.

Recursive parser state, single owner. One owner, one thread, no sharing. The only reason a pointer appears at all is recursive shape: a node that contains nodes has no finite size unless the recursive field is behind an indirection. Use Box<T>. It gives one owner plus heap indirection, making the field one pointer wide regardless of depth, with no reference counting or interior mutability implied.

Planning data shared on one thread. Many owners, one thread. If it is read-only after construction, Rc<T> is enough: multiple owners of one allocation, non-atomic count, never crossing threads. If those owners also need to mutate it, the honest type is Rc<RefCell<T>>, read literally as shared ownership plus runtime borrow checking, accepting that borrow violations become runtime panics.

Schema shared read-only across worker threads. Many owners, multiple threads, no mutation. Use Arc<T>. The atomic count makes cloning safe across threads, and because the schema is read-only after construction no further mechanism is needed. The atomic counting is the only cost over Rc.

Retry coordination mutated by several threads. Many owners, multiple threads, mutation required. Use Arc<Mutex<T>>. Read it as two decisions stacked: Arc is shared ownership across threads, Mutex is synchronized mutation where exclusive access is granted only after lock acquisition. Arc alone would give sharing but not safe mutation; the Mutex is the separate enforcement model.

Future stored to be polled later. Use Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ...>>>. A future compiled from async code is a state machine that can hold internal references into its own storage; once polling begins it must not move, or those internal references would dangle. Pin<Box<...>> owns the future on the heap and guarantees its address stays stable across polls. A plain Box<dyn Future> owns it but does not promise address stability, so it cannot satisfy the poll contract for an address-sensitive future.

Operational concerns the Mutex introduces (at least two, and all four matter): lock scope (hold the lock for the shortest critical section so you do not serialize unrelated work); contention (many threads queuing on one lock erodes the parallelism Arc bought you); poisoning (a panic while the lock is held marks it poisoned, so subsequent lock() calls return a PoisonError you must handle); and deadlock risk (acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order, or re-entering a non-reentrant lock, can hang threads permanently).

// Each composite read as a layered statement.
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::future::Future;

// 1. recursive parser state, single owner -> heap indirection only.
enum Ast {
    Leaf(i64),
    Pair(Box<Ast>, Box<Ast>),
}

// 2. planning data shared on one thread (mutated) -> shared + runtime borrow.
type Plan = Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>>;

// 3. schema shared read-only across threads -> shared ownership, atomic count.
type Schema = Arc<SchemaData>;
struct SchemaData;

// 4. retry coordination mutated by several threads -> shared + synchronized.
type RetryState = Arc<Mutex<u32>>; // Arc: who owns; Mutex: how it mutates

// 5. future stored to poll later -> owned heap storage with stable address.
type StoredTask = Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>>;

One pointer type per concern, each chosen by owner count, then thread boundary, then mutation model.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Recursive parser state is Box<T> (one owner, heap indirection for finite size); shared planning data is Rc<T> or Rc<RefCell<T>> on one thread.
  • The cross-thread read-only schema is Arc<T> and the cross-thread mutable retry state is Arc<Mutex<T>>, each justified by owner count, then thread boundary, then mutation model.
  • The stored future is Pin<Box<dyn Future>>, justified by the address-sensitive state machine needing to stay put while polled.
  • At least two operational concerns of the Mutex are named (lock scope, contention, poisoning, deadlock); in fact all four are addressed.

Lab solution

The whole lab turns on attach making the two edges between root and leaf deliberately different kinds. parent.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(child)) puts a strong, owning handle to the child into the parent's children vector, so the parent owns the child. *child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent) stores only a Weak handle in the child's parent field, so the child observes the parent without owning it. RefCell supplies the runtime-checked interior mutability that lets us mutate these fields through the shared Rc handles.

The first two lines print directly from this structure: root has exactly one child, and the leaf's parent edge upgrades successfully (the root is still alive) to yield the name "root". The count lines confirm the shape: root strong = 1 because the only strong owner of root is the root binding itself (the leaf's parent edge is weak and contributes nothing to the strong count), and root weak = 1 because that single weak parent edge is the one weak reference to root.

The last line is the proof that the graph is acyclic. Inside the println block we drop(root), which removes the last strong owner of the root allocation; its strong count reaches zero and the allocation is freed. The leaf's parent field still holds a Weak, but upgrade() now returns None because the allocation is gone, so parent_name falls through to "none". Had the parent edge been strong, the mutual ownership would have pinned both strong counts above zero and leaked, and this line would still print "root".

Example 9-S. weak_parent_edge_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Node {
    name: String,
    parent: RefCell<Weak<Node>>,
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>,
}

impl Node {
    fn new(name: &str) -> Rc<Node> {
        Rc::new(Node {
            name: String::from(name),
            parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()),
            children: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
        })
    }
}

// Parent owns the child with a strong edge; child observes the parent
// with a weak edge, so the two-node graph stays acyclic.
fn attach(parent: &Rc<Node>, child: &Rc<Node>) {
    parent.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(child));
    *child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent);
}

fn parent_name(node: &Rc<Node>) -> String {
    node.parent
        .borrow()
        .upgrade()
        .map(|p| p.name.clone())
        .unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("none"))
}

fn main() {
    let root = Node::new("root");
    let leaf = Node::new("leaf");

    attach(&root, &leaf);

    println!("root children = {}", root.children.borrow().len());
    println!("leaf parent = {}", parent_name(&leaf));
    println!("root strong = {}", Rc::strong_count(&root));
    println!("root weak = {}", Rc::weak_count(&root));
    println!("leaf parent (after root drop) = {}", {
        drop(root);
        parent_name(&leaf)
    });
}
Output
root children = 1
leaf parent = root
root strong = 1
root weak = 1
leaf parent (after root drop) = none

Review question answers

What does Box<T> provide, and which three things that people often associate with smart pointers does it deliberately NOT provide?

Box<T> provides single ownership plus heap indirection: one owner of a heap allocation, accessed through a thin pointer-sized handle. It deliberately does NOT provide shared ownership, reference counting, or interior mutability. It is the right tool when you still want one owner but need recursive shape (a finite-sized field for a self-referential type), a smaller stack footprint, or a fixed-size field for a dynamically sized or trait-object value.

Rc<T> and Arc<T> both give shared ownership; what is the single implementation difference between them, and what consequence does it have for thread boundaries?

The single difference is how the reference count is updated: Rc<T> uses a non-atomic count, while Arc<T> uses an atomic count. Because Rc's count can race when touched from two threads, Rc<T> is neither Send nor Sync and cannot cross a thread boundary; Arc's atomic count makes clone and drop safe across threads, so Arc<T> is the cross-thread sibling. Arc pays a small atomic cost for that safety, which is why you use Rc when everything stays on one thread.

Cell<T> and RefCell<T> are both single-thread interior-mutability tools; when must you choose RefCell<T> instead of Cell<T>, and what failure mode does RefCell add?

Choose RefCell<T> when you need to hand out an interior reference to the value, &T or &mut T, rather than only copying, replacing, or swapping whole values, which is all Cell<T> supports. RefCell tracks borrows at runtime and enforces the aliasing rule dynamically, so the failure mode it adds is a runtime panic: borrowing mutably while any other borrow is active (or two mutable borrows) panics instead of being caught at compile time. Cell avoids that panic entirely precisely because it never produces a borrow token.

Why can reference counting alone never reclaim a cycle, and what edge change turns a cyclic graph back into a collectable acyclic one?

Reference counting frees an allocation only when its strong count reaches zero, but in a cycle each node's strong count is kept above zero by the other node's strong edge, so no count ever drops to zero even after all external handles are gone. The repair is to make the back-edge non-owning: keep owning edges strong (Rc/Arc) and change observational back-edges to Weak. A Weak does not contribute to the strong count, so the owning direction can reach zero and free normally, and the weak side simply upgrades to None afterward.

What invariant does Pin<T> protect, why does Future::poll take Pin<&mut Self>, and why does the distinction not matter for ordinary Unpin types?

Pin<T> protects address stability: once a value is pinned it will not be moved, so any address-sensitive invariant (such as internal references into its own storage) stays valid. Future::poll takes Pin<&mut Self> because a future compiled from async code is a self-referential state machine that must not move between polls; the pinned receiver guarantees that while still allowing mutation of the state. The distinction does not matter for ordinary Unpin types, which are freely movable and have no address-sensitive invariant, so pinning imposes no real constraint and methods like Pin::get_mut hand back a plain &mut T soundly.

Chapter 10 · Arrays, Slices, and Vectors

Arrays, Slices, and Vectors

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises drill the chapter's central decision: pick the narrowest contiguous-storage shape that the workload's semantics actually require. Arrays carry a compile-time length as part of their type; slices borrow a contiguous view without owning the allocation; vectors own a growable heap buffer. The skill being built is reading a workload's ownership, size invariant, mutation pattern, and locality needs, then mapping those to [T; N], &[T], or Vec<T> without resorting to habit or folklore.

The later exercises push the same model into operational territory: reading len versus capacity, writing algorithms against slices so callers keep storage control, measuring whether preallocation matters instead of assuming it, and repairing a borrow that outlived a structural mutation. The lab is the concrete payoff: a single &[u32] function that serves an array subslice and a vector subslice with no allocation and no narrower public signature.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose array, slice, vector, or inline-first storage from the workload

Work from invariants first, performance last. The four cases map cleanly once you separate API shape from storage shape.

The 16-byte protocol header has a compile-time fixed length that is part of the invariant: a header is exactly 16 bytes, not "usually about 16." That is [u8; 16].
