Putting the length in the type means [u8; 16] and [u8; 20] are different types, so a miscounted field is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise, and the value can live inline in a struct with no heap allocation.

The read-only checksum helper only needs a borrowed view over whatever bytes the caller already owns. It should take &[u8] (or &mut [u8] if it scribbles a running state into a caller-provided buffer). A slice parameter lets the same helper run over an array, a vector, or a subslice without forcing the caller to allocate or surrender ownership. The helper has no business deciding the caller's storage strategy.

The dynamically accumulated retry batch genuinely needs owned growth: the count is not known ahead of time and the batch must outlive the function that fills it. That is Vec<T>. If you can derive a trustworthy upper bound (for example, the batch can never exceed the number of input jobs), Vec::with_capacity is justified, but the storage choice itself is driven by owned, unbounded growth.

The tiny hot list of usually three tags is the only case that might justify an inline-first (small-vector) representation, and only after profiling. The common-path size is small and the structure may be created in large numbers, so spilling to the heap on the rare large case while keeping the common case inline can pay off. But that is a measured optimization, not a default: inline-first containers enlarge the parent struct and raise move cost, so a plain Vec<T> (or even [T; N] plus a length if three is a hard cap) is the honest starting point until a profile shows allocation is the real cost.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Fixed-size case (16-byte header) maps to [u8; 16] because the length is a semantic invariant baked into the type.
  • Read-only checksum helper takes &[u8]/&mut [u8] so it borrows the caller's contiguous data without owning it.
  • Retry batch is Vec<T> because growth is unbounded and the batch must outlive the filling function.
  • Inline-first storage for the tag list is named as profile-conditional, not adopted as a default style.
Exercise 2code reading

Read len and capacity operationally

The helper allocates capacity for 1024 elements up front, pushes 600, then logs both numbers. Reading them operationally: after 600 pushes, len() is 600 and capacity() is 1024.

len() is occupancy. It is the exact count of logically present, initialized elements the vector is currently holding. It is the bound that indexing and iteration respect: valid indices are 0..len, and iter() yields exactly len items. It says nothing about allocation; it only counts what is actually there right now.

capacity() is allocation slack. It is the number of elements the current heap buffer can hold before the vector must allocate a larger buffer and move its elements. With with_capacity(1024) and 600 pushes, the next 424 pushes can proceed without reallocation, because len + 1 <= capacity still holds. Capacity is a budget, not a count of present elements; the elements between index 600 and 1024 are uninitialized backing storage, not logical elements.

capacity() == 1024 is not a portable design assumption for every vector in the system because capacity is an implementation-controlled property, not a language guarantee. This vector reports 1024 only because someone explicitly requested it with with_capacity(1024) and 600 pushes stayed under that budget. A vector built with Vec::new() and grown by pushing follows the standard library's internal growth strategy, which Rust deliberately does not pin in its contract. Hard-coding an expected capacity, or relying on a specific growth factor to back into one, encodes folklore as if it were a guarantee. The correct contract is: capacity() >= len() always, and the exact surplus is an implementation detail you validate by measurement, not by assumption.

fn capacity_report() {
    let mut buf: Vec<u64> = Vec::with_capacity(1024);
    for i in 0..600 {
        buf.push(i);
    }

    // len() = occupancy: exactly the initialized elements present now.
    println!("len = {}", buf.len()); // 600

    // capacity() = allocation budget before the next growth step.
    println!("capacity = {}", buf.capacity()); // 1024 here ONLY because
                                                // we asked for it explicitly.

    // The only portable invariant: capacity is never less than len.
    assert!(buf.capacity() >= buf.len());
}

len() counts present elements; capacity() is the pre-reallocation budget; only capacity() >= len() is guaranteed.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • len() is explained as the count of logically present, initialized elements.
  • capacity() is explained as the allocation budget available before the next growth/reallocation step.
  • The answer rejects relying on an exact capacity or growth factor as a correctness assumption and keeps only capacity() >= len() as the contract.
Exercise 3implementation

Write the function over slices, not vectors

The algorithm only needs to read a contiguous run of u32 values and reduce them to a sum. It has no reason to own anything, decide an allocation strategy, or know whether the data came from an array or a vector. So the parameter stays exactly &[u32], a borrowed contiguous view.

The reduction is one line: values.iter().copied().sum(). iter() yields &u32, copied() turns each &u32 into a u32 (cheap, because u32: Copy), and sum() reduces them. No new vector is allocated; the function reads through the borrow and returns a scalar. An explicit for loop accumulating into a u32 would be equally valid and compile to essentially the same code.

The payoff is exactly what a slice-first signature buys. In the lab, &fixed[2..5] borrows three elements out of a stack array and &dynamic[..3] borrows three elements out of a heap-backed vector. Both convert to &[u32] at the call site with no copy and no allocation, so the function serves both owners through one signature. Because the function never names Vec<u32>, it imposes no ownership constraint on callers: arrays, vector borrows, and arbitrary subslices all flow through unchanged. &fixed[2..5] is [15, 16, 23] which sums to 54, and &dynamic[..3] is [3, 6, 9] which sums to 18, matching the lab's expected output.

fn window_sum(values: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    values.iter().copied().sum()
}

// Equivalent explicit form, same generated code in practice:
// fn window_sum(values: &[u32]) -> u32 {
//     let mut total = 0;
//     for &v in values {
//         total += v;
//     }
//     total
// }

A reduction over a borrowed &[u32] — works for any contiguous source without allocating.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Signature stays exactly fn window_sum(values: &[u32]) -> u32.
  • Returns 54 for &fixed[2..5] (15+16+23) and 18 for &dynamic[..3] (3+6+9), as required by the lab.
  • Reads through the borrow and returns a scalar, never allocating or owning a Vec<u32>.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Benchmark preallocation versus push-only growth honestly

The honest way to compare Vec::new() against Vec::with_capacity(n) is to push the identical workload into each, many times, in release mode, and report what you observe rather than what you expect. The harness below pushes n u64 values into each variant, repeats the whole thing for several iterations to dampen noise, sums per-strategy wall-clock time, and records the final capacity of each.

Two correctness points matter for the benchmark to mean anything. First, the pushed element type and the loop shape are identical between the two variants, so the only difference under test is the allocation strategy. Second, std::hint::black_box is applied to the pushed value and the finished vector so the optimizer cannot delete the loop or hoist the work out; without that, a release build can optimize a pure push-and-drop loop into nothing and the measurement becomes meaningless.

What you typically observe: the Vec::new() variant grows through a sequence of reallocations and ends at a capacity at least n but usually larger than n (the standard library overshoots to amortize growth), while the with_capacity(n) variant performs exactly one allocation and ends at capacity n. The timing difference depends entirely on n and on what T is. For large n or for elements whose moves are non-trivial, preallocation visibly reduces time because it removes repeated reallocate-and-copy steps. For small n it can be in the noise. The reportable tradeoff is this: with_capacity adds a planning step and a real, named upper bound to your code, and it pays off only when the bound is genuine and the allocation churn it removes is actually on a hot path. A toy microbenchmark validates the direction of the effect; it does not by itself justify a production change, because real workloads interleave other allocations and cache traffic that a tight loop does not model.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

fn push_workload(prealloc: bool, n: usize) -> (std::time::Duration, usize) {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let mut v: Vec<u64> = if prealloc {
        Vec::with_capacity(n)
    } else {
        Vec::new()
    };
    for i in 0..n as u64 {
        v.push(black_box(i));
    }
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    let cap = v.capacity();
    black_box(&v); // keep the vector alive so the loop is not elided
    (elapsed, cap)
}

fn main() {
    let n = 1_000_000;
    let iters = 50;

    let mut grow_time = std::time::Duration::ZERO;
    let mut prealloc_time = std::time::Duration::ZERO;
    let mut grow_cap = 0;
    let mut prealloc_cap = 0;

    for _ in 0..iters {
        let (t, c) = push_workload(false, n);
        grow_time += t;
        grow_cap = c;
        let (t, c) = push_workload(true, n);
        prealloc_time += t;
        prealloc_cap = c;
    }

    println!("Vec::new()         total = {:?}, final capacity = {}", grow_time, grow_cap);
    println!("with_capacity({})   total = {:?}, final capacity = {}", n, prealloc_time, prealloc_cap);
    // Observation, not a promise: grow_cap >= n (and usually > n);
    // prealloc_cap == n; timing delta scales with n and element cost.
}

Identical workload under two allocation strategies; black_box prevents elision; reports timing and final capacity.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The harness pushes the same u64 workload with the same loop into both Vec::new() and Vec::with_capacity(n), isolating allocation strategy as the only variable.
  • Noise is reduced via repeated iterations, release-mode intent, and black_box to defeat dead-code elimination.
  • Results are framed as observations (capacity logs plus timing) rather than an assumption that preallocation always wins.
  • The tradeoff is named: with_capacity adds a planning step tied to a real bound, and only pays off when the removed allocation churn is on a hot path.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Repair a structural-mutation bug without changing the API lie

The defect is not compiler stubbornness; it is a slice held across a structural mutation of the storage it views. let hot = &buffer[..4]; borrows a view into the vector's current heap buffer. buffer.push(99) may grow the vector, which can reallocate to a larger buffer and move the elements, leaving hot pointing at storage that no longer belongs to the live data. A slice is a view into existing storage, not a durable reservation of future layout, so reading from hot after the push is reading a stale view. The borrow checker rejects this precisely because push takes &mut buffer while hot still holds a shared borrow, and that conflict is the language refusing to let a view outlive the layout it was taken against.

There are two honest repairs, chosen by whether the code truly needs that data after the push.

If the borrowed work can simply happen first, do it first and let the borrow end before the mutation. Two phases make the lifetimes trivial to review: consume hot (compute whatever sum or check you needed), then mutate the buffer. Non-lexical lifetimes end the borrow at its last use, so once hot is no longer read, push is free to grow the buffer. No copy is needed; the work is just reordered.

If later code genuinely needs that tiny fixed header after the structural change, copy the small, truly-needed subset into independent storage on purpose. Copying four u32 values into a [u32; 4] array detaches them from the vector's buffer entirely, so any subsequent push and reallocation cannot invalidate them. This is the honest version of "keep the header": you are not pretending a view survived growth, you are deliberately taking ownership of a fixed copy. The array also encodes the real invariant (exactly four header words) in its type. Do not reach for clone() of the whole vector or for raw pointers to dodge the borrow; both restate the bug instead of fixing it.

// Phase 1: borrow, use, and release before any structural mutation.
fn two_phase(buffer: &mut Vec<u32>) -> u32 {
    let header_sum = {
        let hot = &buffer[..4];          // borrow a view
        hot.iter().copied().sum::<u32>() // consume it fully here
    };                                   // borrow ends at end of block

    buffer.push(99);                     // now safe: no live view into buffer
    header_sum
}

// Alternative: if the header is truly needed after growth, copy it out
// into independent, fixed-size storage on purpose.
fn copy_then_grow(buffer: &mut Vec<u32>) -> [u32; 4] {
    let header: [u32; 4] = buffer[..4]
        .try_into()
        .expect("buffer must have at least 4 elements");

    buffer.push(99);   // reallocation cannot invalidate `header`: it is owned
    header             // independent of the vector's buffer
}

Either end the borrow before mutating (two phases) or deliberately copy the fixed header into an owned [u32; 4].

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The repair ends the active borrow before push (two-phase form) or copies the needed four elements into an owned [u32; 4].
  • The failure is explained as borrowing a view into storage that growth may reallocate and move, not as compiler obstinance.
  • The original hot slice is never read across the vector's growth path in either variant.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose the right contiguous-storage design for three real workloads

Each subsystem gets one concrete representation, justified by its operational shape, not by type-name preference.

The packet parser with fixed headers wants arrays. A protocol header is a semantically fixed bound: a given header is exactly N bytes by specification. Represent each fixed field as [u8; N] (for example a [u8; 4] length-prefix or a [u8; 16] address). The size lives in the type, so a field-width mistake is a compile error, the header can sit inline inside a parsed-frame struct with no heap allocation, and parsing a frame does not touch the allocator at all on the header path. Arrays here are about correctness of the invariant first and zero-allocation locality second.

The metrics engine that scans rolling numeric windows wants slice-first APIs. The caller already owns the sample buffer (often a ring buffer or a Vec<f64> the engine maintains), so the scanning functions should take &[f64] and compute over a borrowed window such as &samples[start..end]. This is also the locality argument: a contiguous slice of numeric samples is exactly the layout a windowed scan wants, because sequential reads stream through cache lines with predictable prefetching, and the algorithm never copies the window just to read it. Slice-first keeps the engine free to change how it stores samples without rewriting every scan.

The request pipeline that accumulates retryable jobs wants owned vectors. The count of retryable jobs is not known up front and the accumulated batch must outlive the function that builds it, so it returns a Vec<Job>. Preallocation is justified here by a real upper bound, not a guess: the retry batch can never contain more jobs than the input it filters, so Vec::with_capacity(input.len()) reserves once from a genuine bound and then the loop only filters and pushes, removing reallocation churn from the accumulation path. That is exactly the pattern the chapter's capacity example uses.

Would any subsystem justify an inline-first representation? Possibly the metrics engine, if it creates many tiny per-key scratch buffers whose common size is a handful of samples. But that stays a measured optimization: it would have to be proven by a profile showing that allocation of those small buffers is a real cost, weighed against the larger struct size and higher move cost an inline-first container imposes. Absent that measurement, plain Vec is the correct default, and inline-first remains a conditional answer rather than a stylistic one.

// Packet parser: fixed bound lives in the type, no allocation on the header path.
struct FrameHeader {
    version: [u8; 4],
    src_addr: [u8; 16],
}

// Metrics engine: slice-first scan over a borrowed contiguous window.
fn window_mean(samples: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    if samples.is_empty() {
        return 0.0;
    }
    samples.iter().sum::<f64>() / samples.len() as f64
}

// Request pipeline: owned growth, preallocated from a real upper bound.
struct Job {
    id: u64,
    retryable: bool,
}

fn collect_retryable(jobs: &[Job]) -> Vec<u64> {
    // The result can never be longer than the input: a justified bound.
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(jobs.len());
    for job in jobs {
        if job.retryable {
            out.push(job.id);
        }
    }
    out
}

Arrays for fixed headers, slice-first scans for borrowed windows, preallocated owned Vec for the bounded retry batch.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each subsystem gets one named representation justified by workload shape: [u8; N] arrays for fixed headers, &[f64] slices for the metrics scan, owned Vec for the retry batch.
  • Locality is discussed for the metrics engine: contiguous numeric windows stream through cache lines under a slice-first scan.
  • The retry-batch preallocation is justified by a real upper bound (result cannot exceed the input length), not a guessed capacity.
  • Inline-first storage is kept as a measurement-gated optimization for the small-scratch case, not adopted as a default style.

Lab solution

The only change from the starter is the body of window_sum. The starter returned values[0], which read just the first element; the fix reduces the entire borrowed window with values.iter().copied().sum(). iter() yields &u32, copied() dereferences each to a u32 (cheap because u32: Copy), and sum() folds them into the returned scalar. The function never allocates and never owns a vector; it reads straight through the &[u32] borrow.

The two call sites show why the slice parameter is the right contract. &fixed[2..5] borrows indices 2, 3, and 4 of the stack array [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42], which are 15, 16, and 23; their sum is 54. &dynamic[..3] borrows indices 0, 1, and 2 of the heap-backed vector [3, 6, 9, 12], which are 3, 6, and 9; their sum is 18. Both an array subslice and a vector subslice coerce to &[u32] with no copy and no allocation, so one function serves both owners.

The program therefore prints fixed = 54 then dynamic = 18, matching the expected output exactly. The lesson the lab makes concrete is the chapter's slice-first rule: because the algorithm only needs a contiguous read-only view, the signature borrows a slice and leaves every storage decision to the caller.

Example 10-S. window_sum_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn window_sum(values: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    values.iter().copied().sum()
}

fn main() {
    let fixed = [4_u32, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42];
    let dynamic = vec![3_u32, 6, 9, 12];

    println!("fixed = {}", window_sum(&fixed[2..5]));
    println!("dynamic = {}", window_sum(&dynamic[..3]));
}
Output
fixed = 54
dynamic = 18

Review question answers

When is [T; N] the right type rather than Vec<T>?

Use [T; N] when the length is a compile-time invariant that is part of the data's meaning, such as a fixed protocol header, a coordinate triple, or a fixed-width cryptographic value. The count lives in the type, so [u8; 4] and [u8; 8] are distinct types and a wrong size is a compile error rather than a runtime bug, and the value can live inline with no heap allocation. Reach for Vec<T> instead only when the count is genuinely runtime-determined or the collection must grow.

Why is &[T] usually a better function parameter than &Vec<T>?

&[T] borrows a contiguous view without caring who owns the storage, so the same function accepts an array, a vector borrow, or an arbitrary subslice with no allocation and no narrower signature. &Vec<T> leaks an allocation assumption the algorithm almost never needs: it forces the caller to have a Vec specifically and exposes capacity and growth concerns the function does not use. Taking a slice keeps the API honest about what it actually requires (contiguous read access) and keeps callers in control of their own storage choices.

What is the practical difference between len() and capacity()?

len() is occupancy: the exact count of logically present, initialized elements, and the bound that indexing and iteration respect. capacity() is allocation slack: how many elements the current heap buffer can hold before the vector must reallocate to a larger buffer and move its elements. The only guaranteed relationship is capacity() >= len(); the surplus is an implementation detail, so you push without reallocation exactly while len() + pushes <= capacity().

Why should production code avoid depending on a specific vector growth factor?

Rust does not promise any particular growth factor in its language contract; the growth strategy is an implementation detail the standard library is free to change. Code that hard-codes an expected capacity, or back-calculates one from an assumed doubling factor, encodes folklore as if it were a guarantee and can silently break when the implementation changes. The portable contract is only capacity() >= len(), so when capacity matters you should request it explicitly with with_capacity/reserve and validate behavior with measurements, capacity logs, or allocation tracing rather than assumption.

What workload characteristics make contiguous storage especially attractive?

Contiguous storage shines when you scan or reduce many elements in sequence, because sequential access streams through cache lines with predictable prefetching, giving strong locality that pointer-chasing structures cannot match. It also keeps the owner value tiny, three words for a vector, so moving or returning the collection transfers ownership of the buffer without copying the elements. Workloads like numeric window scans, parsing, hashing, and serialization, which read or transform runs of elements in order, benefit most, and a slice over that contiguous memory expresses exactly the access pattern those algorithms need.

Chapter 11 · Hash Maps and Sets

Hash Maps and Sets

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises drill the four decisions that make associative collections behave well in production: which of HashMap, HashSet, BTreeMap, or BTreeSet matches the contract; how to read across the table boundary without allocating a key; how to express read-modify-write as a single Entry path; and how to make output deterministic on purpose rather than by accident. Each one applies the ownership instincts from earlier chapters to hashed and ordered storage.

The through-line is that a hash map has exactly one inbound move (insert) and a borrow-only read path. Once you see the API split along that line, the rest follows: borrow on reads, own only when you store, and treat iteration order as something you choose at the boundary, not something the hash table promises.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose map, set, or tree from the contract

Decide each case from its semantics, not from which type you reach for most often. The chapter frames this as two yes-or-no questions: do you need a value per key or only membership (map versus set), and does anything downstream depend on iteration order (hashed versus ordered)?

Request counter keyed by route: this is genuine key-value association. The route is the key, the count is the value, and nothing in the contract requires a particular iteration order. Choose HashMap<String, usize> for expected fast lookup and update.

Dedup list of active feature flags: the value is really 'present or absent.' There is no per-key payload, only membership and deduplication. Choose HashSet<String>. Using HashMap<String, bool> here would be a boolean map standing in for a set, which is exactly the improvised shape the chapter warns against.

Config renderer that must emit stable sorted output: here deterministic iteration order is part of the external contract, because operators and snapshot tests read the output. Choose BTreeMap so the ordering is the data structure's job rather than something you re-sort at every render. (If the keys carried no values you would pick BTreeSet instead.)

Ordered allow-list supporting range-like prefix reviews: this is about ordering, not lookup speed. Range and prefix scans need keys kept in sorted order, which a hash table cannot provide. Choose BTreeSet (or BTreeMap if each entry needs a value). The justification is operational: the workload asks for ordered traversal and ranges, and only the tree variants offer that.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • HashMap<String, usize> chosen for the unordered route counter (key-value association, order not contractual).
  • HashSet<String> chosen for active flags, since the workload is membership and deduplication only.
  • BTreeMap chosen for the config renderer because stable sorted output is part of the boundary contract.
  • Each choice is justified operationally (lookup vs membership vs ordered/range traversal), not by naming the type alone.
Exercise 2code reading

Remove duplicate lookups with Entry API

The inherited shape does contains_key, then get_mut, then insert on the same key. Conceptually that is three trips into the table for one logical update: contains_key hashes the key and probes a bucket, get_mut hashes and probes again, and insert hashes and probes a third time. The duplicate work is the repeated hashing and bucket lookup for a single key path. It is also a correctness hazard, because the presence check and the mutation are separate statements that can drift apart during maintenance.

The Entry API collapses this into one path. You call entry(key) once, which does a single probe and hands back a view of the slot whether or not it was occupied. From there you choose the helper that matches the intent. For a counter, or_insert(0) gives you a mutable reference to the slot (creating it at 0 if absent), and you add one in place. or_default() does the same when the value type's Default is what you want as the initial state. and_modify(...).or_insert(...) is the right shape when the present case and the absent case need different logic, for example incrementing an existing counter but seeding a freshly created one differently. For a plain increment, or_insert is the cleanest fit.

The owned-versus-borrowed distinction matters because entry takes the key by value. If the caller already owns the key (a parsed String), entry(key) simply moves it in at no extra cost. If the caller only borrows &str, you must produce an owned key to insert, so entry(route.to_owned()) allocates a String even though the read path could have borrowed. Entry removes the duplicate lookups; it does not remove that allocation. Borrowed lookup (get/contains by &str) is the separate fast path for reads that never need to store anything.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Before: three table operations for one update.
fn record_slow(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: String) {
    if counts.contains_key(&route) {
        let next = counts[&route] + 1; // probe again
        counts.insert(route, next);    // probe a third time
    } else {
        counts.insert(route, 1);
    }
}

// After: one probe, in-place mutation, single ownership story.
fn record_fast(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: String) {
    *counts.entry(route).or_insert(0) += 1;
}

// When present and absent need different handling, use and_modify/or_insert.
fn record_seeded(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: String) {
    counts
        .entry(route)
        .and_modify(|c| *c += 1)
        .or_insert(1);
}

Entry replaces contains_key + get_mut + insert with a single probe and an in-place update.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that the original repeats key hashing and bucket probing three times for one update.
  • Selects or_insert for the plain counter and explains where or_default and and_modify fit instead.
  • States that entry takes the key by value: owned keys move in for free, while a borrowed &str forces an owning allocation to store.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement borrowed lookup for owned string keys

Both helpers read across the table boundary, so they should borrow and never allocate. A HashMap<String, usize> can be queried with a &str directly, and a HashSet<String> can test membership with a &str directly. This works because the lookup methods are generic over a borrowed form of the key: String borrows as str, and str's equality and hashing match what String would produce, so the borrowed query lands in the same bucket as the stored owned key.

The defect to avoid is get(&route.to_string()) or contains(&route.to_string()), which allocates a throwaway String on every read just to immediately discard it. Pass route straight through: get(route) and contains(route). The parameter stays &str, and nothing is allocated on the read path.

The return types stay small and owned even though the lookup borrows. route_count copies the usize out with copied() and defaults to 0 when absent, returning a plain value rather than a borrowed &usize tied to the map's lifetime. is_active returns a bool. Neither helper hands back a reference into the collection, so callers are not constrained by the map's borrow.

use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

fn route_count(counts: &HashMap<String, usize>, route: &str) -> usize {
    counts.get(route).copied().unwrap_or(0)
}

fn is_active(active: &HashSet<String>, route: &str) -> bool {
    active.contains(route)
}

fn main() {
    let mut counts = HashMap::new();
    counts.insert(String::from("api"), 2usize);

    let mut active = HashSet::new();
    active.insert(String::from("api"));

    // Borrowed &str literals; no String allocated for either query.
    println!("{}", route_count(&counts, "api"));  // 2
    println!("{}", route_count(&counts, "none")); // 0
    println!("{}", is_active(&active, "api"));     // true
}

Query owned String keys by borrowed &str; copy small values out instead of borrowing them.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The lookup parameter stays &str in both helpers.
  • Uses borrowed lookup get(route) and contains(route) directly on the owned-key collections.
  • No throwaway String is allocated on the read path; results are returned as an owned usize/bool, not a borrowed reference.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Make output deterministic on purpose

The defect is treating HashMap iteration order as stable. The default hasher uses randomized state per process, so iterating a HashMap yields entries in an order that can differ across runs. A snapshot test that iterates the map directly therefore flaps not because the data changed but because the render path inherited a non-deterministic order it was never promised.

There are two principled fixes, and which one is correct depends on how widely order is needed. If only the output edge cares about order, keep the hot mutable index as a HashMap and sort or project at the render boundary: collect into a BTreeMap (or sort a Vec of pairs) just before formatting. This keeps fast unordered updates on the write path and pays the ordering cost once, only when emitting. If every caller wants stable order anyway, stop projecting repeatedly and make BTreeMap the primary representation, so ordering is the storage contract rather than a step you must remember at each output site.

The tradeoff is explicit. Sorting at the boundary keeps amortized expected O(1) updates and adds an O(n log n) sort (or O(n log n) BTreeMap build) per render; it is the right call when output is occasional and updates are hot. Making BTreeMap primary gives you ordered iteration everywhere for free but changes update and lookup cost to O(log n) and removes the unordered fast path. Either is defensible; choosing one deliberately is the point. The fix is not 'sort until the test passes' but 'state where the order contract lives and honor it consistently.'

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap};

// Fix A: hashed storage stays primary; project to ordered output only at the edge.
fn render_sorted(counts: &HashMap<String, usize>) -> String {
    let ordered: BTreeMap<&String, &usize> = counts.iter().collect();
    ordered
        .iter()
        .map(|(route, count)| format!("{}={}", route, count))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join(",")
}

// Fix B: if order is required everywhere, make BTreeMap the primary store and
// iterate it directly; no per-render projection is needed at all.

Project the HashMap into a BTreeMap at the render edge, or make BTreeMap primary if order is always required.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies that the bug is relying on randomized HashMap iteration order as if it were stable.
  • Proposes both options: sort/project at the boundary, or use BTreeMap as the primary representation when order is always needed.
  • Justifies the tradeoff (hot unordered updates plus per-render sort vs uniformly ordered O(log n) storage) in contract terms, not just making the test green.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Separate owned update paths from borrowed read paths

The teammate's counts.entry(route.to_string()).or_insert(0) is correct and it does optimize something real, but it is not free, and the review should say all three things precisely.

What Entry removes: duplicate table lookups on the update path. Without Entry, a presence check followed by a mutate followed by an insert hashes and probes the same key two or three times. entry probes once and returns a handle to the slot, so the read-modify-write becomes a single trip into the table. That is a genuine win and the main reason to reach for Entry.

What still costs: route is a borrowed &str, and entry takes the key by value, so route.to_string() allocates a fresh owned String on every call even when the entry already exists and the allocated key is immediately dropped. Entry eliminated the duplicate lookups; it did nothing about the allocation. 'Fewer lookups' is not 'zero allocation,' and conflating the two is the slogan to avoid.

When this is the right design: most of the time. If routes come from a bounded, low-cardinality set, if the counter update is not the measured hot path, or if you genuinely need to insert new owned keys anyway, the per-call allocation is noise and the clarity of one Entry path wins. When to revisit: if this update sits on a profiled hot path with high call volume and a key space that is mostly already-present (so nearly every to_string allocates only to be discarded), the allocation can dominate. Then you separate the two fast paths: try a borrowed read first (get_mut(route) to bump an existing counter without allocating) and only fall back to an owning insert when the key is actually new, allocating the key exactly once over its lifetime.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Fine in most code: one clear path, allocates the key each call.
fn record_simple(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: &str) {
    *counts.entry(route.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1;
}

// Hot-path variant: borrow to bump an existing key, allocate only on first insert.
fn record_hot(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: &str) {
    if let Some(slot) = counts.get_mut(route) {
        *slot += 1; // borrowed read path: no allocation when key already exists
    } else {
        counts.insert(route.to_string(), 1); // own the key exactly once
    }
}

Entry removes duplicate probes; the owning to_string remains. Split paths only when profiling shows it matters.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that Entry removes the duplicate table lookups on the read-modify-write path.
  • States explicitly that route.to_string() still allocates an owned String key on every call, even on the already-present path.
  • Gives an acceptable case (cold/clear path, keys often new) and a revisit case (profiled hot path with mostly-present keys where the discarded allocation dominates).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose a hasher and threat model deliberately

Hasher choice is partly a security decision and partly a performance decision, and the two systems sit on opposite sides of that line. The default standard-library hasher uses randomized per-process state, which makes worst-case collision behavior unpredictable to an outsider. That randomization is a deliberate defense: it is why the default is the right choice on attacker-controlled inputs.

The internet-facing API gateway is keyed by client-controlled strings, so collision behavior is part of its threat model. An attacker who can predict which keys collide can force a HashMap toward worst-case probing and turn lookups into a denial-of-service vector (a hash-flooding attack). Keep this path conservative: stay on the randomized default unless there is an exceptionally strong, measured reason to change, and never adopt a fast non-randomized hasher here just because it benchmarked well internally. A faster internal benchmark does not address the public threat model.

The internal analytics worker is keyed by trusted numeric IDs on a path you control and can measure. It is the legitimate candidate for experimentation with a faster non-randomized or domain-specific hasher, because the inputs are not adversarial and the keys are small and frequent. But that is an engineering decision, not a reflex: benchmark first, change second.

Before approving any hasher change I would require production signals, not micro-benchmarks alone: a CPU profile showing hashing is actually a hot cost, an allocation profile, p99/p999 latency under representative load, and evidence about collision-sensitive behavior for the real key distribution. The code-review note must document the trust boundary explicitly: state that the inputs on this path are trusted and non-adversarial, why the alternative hasher was chosen, what was measured, and an instruction that this hasher must not be copied onto any externally reachable, attacker-influenced path. If the trust boundary later moves (the internal worker starts ingesting external keys), the hasher decision has to be revisited.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::hash::BuildHasherDefault;

// Public, attacker-controlled boundary: keep the randomized default hasher.
// Collision resistance here is a security property, not a tuning knob.
fn gateway_counts() -> HashMap<String, usize> {
    HashMap::new()
}

// Trusted internal worker, numeric keys, measured hot path: a faster
// non-randomized hasher is a *candidate*, justified by profiles, and
// documented as safe only because inputs are trusted.
// (FastHasher stands in for a benchmarked third-party hasher.)
type TrustedMap<V> = HashMap<u64, V, BuildHasherDefault<FastHasher>>;

fn worker_index<V>() -> TrustedMap<V> {
    // TrustedMap::default()  // randomized default replaced *only* behind a trust note
    unimplemented!("requires a benchmarked hasher crate; default stays on public paths")
}
# struct FastHasher;

Default randomized hasher on the public boundary; a measured non-randomized hasher only behind a documented trust note internally.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Keeps the attacker-controlled gateway path on the conservative randomized default absent a very strong reason.
  • Treats the trusted internal worker as a measurement candidate rather than an automatic change.
  • Names concrete production signals (CPU profile, allocation profile, p99 latency, collision-sensitive behavior) required before approval.
  • Documents the trust boundary and tradeoff, including a warning not to reuse the hasher on externally reachable paths.

Lab solution

The lab repairs three separate anti-patterns from the initial code, one per helper, each illustrating a core idea from the chapter.

record_owned replaces the contains_key / index / insert sequence with a single Entry path. entry(route) moves the owned key into the table and probes the bucket once; or_insert(0) creates the slot at zero if it is absent and otherwise leaves it, returning a mutable reference; *slot += 1 mutates in place. Calling it for "api", "billing", then "api" again leaves api at 2 and billing at 1. lookup fixes the wasteful get(&route.to_string()), which allocated a throwaway String per read, with get(route) querying the owned String keys directly by borrowed &str, then copied() to return an owned Option<usize>. So lookup(&counts, "api") yields Some(2), printed as 'api = Some(2)'.

render_sorted fixes the determinism bug: iterating the HashMap directly exposed randomized hash order. Collecting the borrowed entries into a BTreeMap orders them by key, so formatting yields 'api=2,billing=1' deterministically every run. Together the two println! lines produce exactly the expected output. The program was compiled with rustc --edition 2021 -O and its stdout matched the expected output.

Example 11-S. hash_maps_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap};

// Owned key handoff plus a single Entry update path: one probe, mutate in place.
fn record_owned(counts: &mut HashMap<String, usize>, route: String) {
    let slot = counts.entry(route).or_insert(0);
    *slot += 1;
}

// Borrowed read: query the owned String keys with &str, no allocation.
fn lookup(counts: &HashMap<String, usize>, route: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    counts.get(route).copied()
}

// Deterministic render: project into a BTreeMap so output is always sorted.
fn render_sorted(counts: &HashMap<String, usize>) -> String {
    let ordered: BTreeMap<&String, &usize> = counts.iter().collect();
    ordered
        .iter()
        .map(|(route, count)| format!("{}={}", route, count))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join(",")
}

fn main() {
    let mut counts = HashMap::new();
    record_owned(&mut counts, String::from("api"));
    record_owned(&mut counts, String::from("billing"));
    record_owned(&mut counts, String::from("api"));

    println!("api = {:?}", lookup(&counts, "api"));
    println!("sorted = {}", render_sorted(&counts));
}
Output
api = Some(2)
sorted = api=2,billing=1

Review question answers

Why is get("key") on a HashMap<String, V> often better than get(&"key".to_string())?

get accepts a borrowed form of the key, and String borrows as str with matching equality and hashing, so get("key") looks up the entry without allocating anything. get(&"key".to_string()) builds a fresh owned String purely to read, then drops it immediately, which is a wasted heap allocation on the read path. On a hot lookup path that allocation is pure overhead, so the borrowed query is both clearer and cheaper.

What does the Entry API optimize, and what does it not magically optimize away?

Entry optimizes the read-modify-write path by collapsing a presence check, a mutable get, and an insert into a single table probe that returns a view of the slot, eliminating duplicate hashing and bucket lookups. What it does not remove is allocation of the key itself: entry takes the key by value, so if you only hold a borrowed &str, entry(route.to_owned()) still allocates an owned String even when the entry already exists. Fewer lookups is not the same as zero allocation, so on a hot, mostly-present path you may still split into a borrowed get_mut plus an owning insert only on first sight.

When is a HashSet<T> clearer than HashMap<T, bool>?

Use HashSet<T> whenever the question is purely 'is this element present?', which is to say membership and deduplication with no per-key payload. HashMap<T, bool> can encode the same thing, but it invites a meaningless second state (a key mapped to false) and reads as if a real value matters when it does not. The set expresses intent directly with contains, insert, and the set-algebra operations, and removes the boolean-map ambiguity entirely.

Why is HashMap iteration order the wrong thing to rely on for stable output?

The default hasher seeds randomized per-process state, so iteration order can differ between runs and is never promised to be stable. Any operator dump, log line, snapshot test, or downstream consumer that depends on that order will flap intermittently for reasons unrelated to the data. If order is part of the contract, make it explicit: sort or project at the render boundary, or use a BTreeMap so ordered iteration is the storage guarantee rather than an accident.

What extra question appears the moment you consider a custom hasher on a public boundary?

You must ask whether collision behavior is part of your threat model, because on an attacker-controlled boundary it is. The randomized default hasher resists hash-flooding, where an adversary crafts colliding keys to force worst-case probing and cause a denial of service; a faster non-randomized hasher can throw that protection away. So a public-path hasher change is a security decision first and a performance decision second, and it needs a documented trust boundary plus production evidence, not just a faster internal benchmark.

Chapter 12 · Matrices and Multidimensional Data

Matrices and Multidimensional Data

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move you from indexing syntax to layout decisions. The chapter's thesis is that dense numeric code is rarely slow because of the arithmetic; it is slow because of unstated layout and ownership assumptions at the edges. So the exercises ask you to commit to a physical representation before you write a single accessor: flat row-major storage for dense grids, sparse formats for mostly-zero data, jagged storage only when rows genuinely differ in length, and borrowed views instead of copies wherever the lifetime allows.

The lab pins this down concretely. You build a row-major Matrix<T> over a single flat Vec<T>, with one offset method that turns a (row, col) pair into a linear index, and a row accessor that returns a borrowed slice rather than a fresh allocation. Getting that one design right — one owner, one offset rule, slices for views — is what carries over to const-generic fixed kernels, borrowed submatrix windows, and FFI handoff to BLAS, LAPACK, or a GPU runtime later in the chapter.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose row-major, column-major, jagged, or sparse from the workload

Start with physical layout, not indexing syntax, and let the access pattern or interop contract pick the representation.

Image scanlines processed left-to-right want dense row-major storage. A scanline is a row, and processing it left-to-right is exactly unit-stride traversal in row-major layout: consecutive pixels are consecutive bytes, so the CPU streams the row through cache with no pointer chasing. A flat Vec<T> plus rows and cols is the right owner here, and a row view is a contiguous slice.

The foreign column-major solver boundary should preserve or adapt to column-major semantics. The layout choice is not about your taste; it is dictated by what the foreign library can consume without a repack. Fortran-derived solvers (LAPACK and most BLAS implementations) expect column-major buffers with an explicit leading dimension. If your Rust side is row-major, you either transpose at the boundary or store column-major specifically for that handoff so the buffer can be passed without conversion. The decision is owned by the interop contract.

The variable-length feature rows are genuinely jagged, so they are not a dense matrix at all. When rows truly differ in length, there is no rows * cols shape to flatten into, and forcing a dense rectangle would mean padding with sentinels and tracking real lengths separately. This is the one case where nested storage such as Vec<Vec<T>> (or a flat buffer plus an explicit offsets array) is honest, because the raggedness is real domain structure rather than an accident of representation.

The mostly-empty recommendation matrix should move toward a sparse format. If most cells are zero, dense storage spends almost all of its memory and traversal time on zeros that contribute nothing. Store only the nonzeros plus the structure needed to locate them: COO triples for easy ingestion, then CSR or CSC for fast traversal in one direction. The point of rejecting Vec<Vec<T>> as the default for dense numeric data is that contiguous flat storage and jagged flexibility solve different problems; reaching for nested vectors out of habit gives you neither dense locality nor an honest sparse representation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each of the four workloads is mapped to a distinct representation: dense row-major, dense column-major, jagged, and sparse.
  • Each choice is justified by access pattern (scanline unit-stride), interop contract (column-major solver), real raggedness (variable-length rows), or zero density (recommendation matrix).
  • Vec<Vec<T>> is explicitly rejected as the default for dense numeric data and reserved only for the genuinely jagged case.
Exercise 2code reading

Replace Vec<Vec<T>> with flat storage conceptually before coding

The difference between Vec<Vec<f32>> and Vec<f32> plus rows and cols is heap shape, not syntax, and the hot path that walks every row in full is exactly the pattern that pays for the difference.

Which allocations disappear: a Vec<Vec<f32>> with R rows is R + 1 allocations — one outer Vec of pointers plus one separately heap-allocated buffer per row. Flattening to a single Vec<f32> collapses that to exactly one allocation. Construction, drop, and any resize stop touching R+1 owners and touch one. That also removes the per-row indirection: in the nested form, reaching row i means loading the outer pointer, dereferencing to find that row's heap buffer, then indexing into it. The flat form computes one offset, row * cols + col, into one buffer.

What happens to row placement and cache behavior: nested rows can sit anywhere on the heap, in any order, with gaps between them, so walking row after row chases pointers to scattered allocations and defeats the prefetcher. A flat buffer places every row adjacent to the next, so a full scan is a single linear stream the CPU prefetches predictably. For the stated hot path — every row in full — this is the dominant win: contiguous traversal turns R independent buffers into one streamable run.

What becomes easier at FFI or accelerator boundaries: a foreign solver, BLAS routine, or GPU upload wants a single contiguous pointer plus a length (and a leading dimension). A flat Vec<f32> already is that — you can hand over data.as_ptr() and data.len() directly. A Vec<Vec<f32>> has no single contiguous region to point at; you would have to copy every row into a staging buffer first, so the nested form forces an extra pack at exactly the boundary where copies are most expensive.

Which convenience you lose: you give up cheap ragged rows and cheap per-row structural edits. With nested vectors, rows can have different lengths and you can push to or truncate one row without disturbing the others. With a flat buffer, the shape is rectangular and fixed by rows * cols; inserting or removing a column means rewriting the whole buffer. That tradeoff is acceptable for dense matrices precisely because they are rectangular by definition — but it is a real cost when the data is actually jagged, which is the case where nested vectors remain the honest choice.

// Nested: R + 1 allocations, rows scattered, per-row indirection.
let nested: Vec<Vec<f32>> = vec![vec![0.0; cols]; rows];
let x = nested[r][c]; // load outer ptr -> deref row ptr -> index

// Flat: 1 allocation, contiguous, one offset rule.
let flat: Vec<f32> = vec![0.0; rows * cols];
let x = flat[r * cols + c]; // single buffer, single computed index

// FFI handoff is direct for the flat form, impossible in place for nested:
let ptr = flat.as_ptr();
let len = flat.len(); // contiguous region a foreign kernel can consume

The nested form needs R+1 owners and pointer chasing per row; the flat form is one allocation with one offset rule and a directly shareable pointer.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names multiple allocations (R+1) and per-row indirection as concrete costs of Vec<Vec<T>>.
  • Explains that one flat buffer gives contiguous, prefetcher-friendly traversal and a single pointer a foreign kernel can consume without packing.
  • States the lost convenience: cheap ragged rows and per-row structural edits, fixed by the rectangular rows * cols shape.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a row-major Matrix<T> wrapper over Vec<T>

Make layout explicit by storing one flat Vec<T> plus the shape, and routing every accessor through a single row-major offset method.

The owner holds rows, cols, and data: Vec<T>, with the invariant data.len() == rows * cols. from_elem establishes that invariant by allocating exactly rows * cols copies, so it requires T: Clone; the rest of the API needs no bound on T. The offset formula is the whole point of the chapter: row * cols + col. Reading left to right, you skip row complete rows of width cols, then step col columns into the target row — that is what row-major means physically.

get returns Option<&T> and bounds-checks both indices before computing the offset, so an out-of-range (row, col) yields None rather than panicking; it borrows directly out of data and copies nothing. set mirrors it but computes the index in a separate let binding first, because &mut self.data[index] would otherwise need self.offset(...) and a mutable index of data in the same expression — splitting the offset computation out avoids borrowing self both ways at once.

row returns Option<&[T]> by slicing the flat buffer over the half-open range [row * cols, row * cols + cols). Because the storage is row-major and contiguous, an entire logical row is already a contiguous run, so the row view is a borrow into the owned buffer with no allocation and no copy. The lifetime of that slice is tied to &self, so the borrow checker prevents the matrix from being mutated or dropped while the row view is alive — the same ownership discipline that makes a flat buffer safe to hand out as a slice.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Matrix<T> {
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T: Clone> Matrix<T> {
    fn from_elem(rows: usize, cols: usize, value: T) -> Self {
        Self {
            rows,
            cols,
            data: vec![value; rows * cols],
        }
    }
}

impl<T> Matrix<T> {
    // Row-major: skip `row` full rows of width `cols`, then step in `col`.
    fn offset(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> usize {
        row * self.cols + col
    }

    fn get(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> Option<&T> {
        if row < self.rows && col < self.cols {
            Some(&self.data[self.offset(row, col)])
        } else {
            None
        }
    }

    fn set(&mut self, row: usize, col: usize, value: T) {
        let index = self.offset(row, col);
        self.data[index] = value;
    }

    // A full row is already contiguous: borrow it, do not copy it.
    fn row(&self, row: usize) -> Option<&[T]> {
        if row < self.rows {
            let start = row * self.cols;
            Some(&self.data[start..start + self.cols])
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

One flat buffer, one row-major offset rule (row * cols + col), and a row view that borrows a contiguous slice instead of allocating.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Stores exactly one flat Vec<T> plus rows and cols, with the data.len() == rows * cols invariant set up in from_elem.
  • offset uses the row-major formula row * cols + col, and every accessor routes through it.
  • row returns a borrowed &[T] sliced directly from data, with no copy or allocation.
  • Combined with the lab driver, this prints a01 = 7, row1 sum = 11, cells = 4.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Design a matrix view without copying data

The defect is that the helper allocates a fresh Vec<T> for every window, copying data it could simply describe in place. Replace it with a borrowed view that carries enough metadata to interpret the parent buffer, and let a lifetime tie the view to that buffer.

Which metadata the view needs: rows and cols give the window's logical shape; stride is the parent matrix's full width (its row length), which is what separates one window row from the next inside the larger buffer; offset is the linear index of the window's top-left cell in the parent. With those four numbers, the view never needs its own storage — it interprets borrowed storage under an explicit layout contract.

What the view borrows from: it holds data: &'a [T] aimed at the parent's flat buffer, exactly the chapter's MatrixView shape. The 'a lifetime is the part that earns its keep — the borrow checker refuses to let the view outlive the buffer, so a window can never dangle past the matrix it describes. This is the difference between a view and a second owner: the view explains layout, it does not own it.

How the accessor computes position safely: index = offset + row * stride + col. The row and col are local to the window, but the step between window rows is the parent stride, not the window's own cols — that is precisely why stride matters once the window is narrower than the full parent width. Bounds-check row < rows and col < cols first, then resolve through data.get(index), which returns None rather than indexing out of range, so a malformed view degrades to a None instead of a panic or unsoundness.

When copying is still right: copy when ownership must outlive the parent — for example, when the window is handed across a long-lived boundary (stored in a struct, sent to another thread, or returned from a function whose caller will outlive the source buffer), or when a consumer demands contiguous storage that the strided window does not provide (a foreign kernel wanting a tight buffer with no inter-row gaps). In those cases the borrow cannot be satisfied, so materializing an owned Vec<T> is the correct, not the lazy, choice.

struct MatrixView<'a, T> {
    data: &'a [T], // borrowed parent buffer; 'a keeps the view from dangling
    rows: usize,   // window height
    cols: usize,   // window width
    stride: usize, // PARENT row width — the step between window rows
    offset: usize, // linear index of the window's top-left cell
}

impl<'a, T> MatrixView<'a, T> {
    fn get(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> Option<&T> {
        if row < self.rows && col < self.cols {
            let index = self.offset + row * self.stride + col;
            self.data.get(index) // None on overrun instead of panicking
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

// Borrow a 2x2 window starting at (1,1) of a 3x4 parent (stride = 4).
fn window<'a, T>(parent: &'a [T]) -> MatrixView<'a, T> {
    MatrixView { data: parent, rows: 2, cols: 2, stride: 4, offset: 5 }
}

The view carries rows, cols, stride, and offset and borrows the parent buffer under a lifetime; stride (the parent width) is what lets a sub-window address the right cells.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Redesign borrows the existing buffer via &'a [T] and allocates nothing by default.
  • Carries the full metadata set — rows, cols, stride, offset — needed to interpret a sub-window correctly.
  • Names a legitimate copy case: ownership that must outlive the parent (cross-boundary or cross-thread handoff) or a consumer needing contiguous storage.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Choose between const generics and runtime dimensions honestly

Separate fixed-invariant shapes from merely common shapes. Put shape in the type only when the shape is part of the contract, not when it is just frequent.

The 3x3 image kernel wants const generics. A convolution kernel is defined by its size — a 3x3 kernel is a different operator from a 5x5 kernel, and code that consumes it can legitimately assume nine taps arranged 3 by 3. Encoding it as [[f32; 3]; 3] (or a const-generic [[f32; N]; N]) makes the shape a compile-time invariant: no runtime dimension fields, no per-call shape checks, and the optimizer can fully unroll the fixed loop. The shape is semantically real, so it belongs in the type.

The 4x4 transform matrix in a graphics or simulation path also wants const generics, for the same reason. In that domain a transform is 4x4 by definition — homogeneous coordinates make it a global invariant of the API, not a coincidence. A [[f32; 4]; 4] or a Mat4 newtype documents the contract, rejects malformed inputs at compile time, and lets multiply specialize. The chapter's trace<const N: usize> example is exactly this pattern: shape carried in the type, correct for any fixed N, resolved at compile time.

The batch-sized score matrix wants runtime dimensions. Its rows and cols come from request or batch input, so the shape is data, not invariant — it varies per call and cannot be known at compile time. This is the flat Vec<T> plus rows and cols owner from the lab: one allocation, runtime shape fields, row-major offset. Trying to force it into a const generic would mean either monomorphizing a fresh copy of the code for every batch size you encounter (code bloat, and impossible for sizes only known at runtime) or lying about the invariant.

The tradeoff you accept by making shape part of the type: the API becomes more specific and less flexible. A function over [[i32; N]; N] cannot accept a runtime-sized matrix without a conversion, const generics monomorphize a distinct instantiation per concrete shape (more compiled code), and call sites must commit to a size literal. You buy compile-time shape checking, unrolling, and self-documenting signatures; you pay in API rigidity and code size. The rule of thumb: "often 4x4" justifies a runtime-dimensioned default, while "must be 4x4" — an invariant truly global to the API — justifies putting the shape in the type.

// Fixed invariant -> shape in the type. Correct for any compile-time N.
fn trace<const N: usize>(m: [[i32; N]; N]) -> i32 {
    let mut sum = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < N {
        sum += m[i][i];
        i += 1;
    }
    sum
}

// 3x3 kernel and 4x4 transform: shapes are part of the contract.
type Kernel3 = [[f32; 3]; 3];
type Transform4 = [[f32; 4]; 4];

// Request/batch-sized: shape is runtime data -> flat owner with fields.
struct ScoreMatrix {
    rows: usize, // from the request/batch, not known at compile time
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<f32>,
}

Const generics for the kernel and transform, where the shape is invariant; a runtime-dimensioned flat owner for the request-sized score matrix.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Chooses const generics for the 3x3 kernel and 4x4 transform, where fixed shape is semantically real.
  • Chooses runtime dimensions for the request- or batch-sized score matrix.
  • States a tradeoff of type-level shape: greater API specificity and monomorphization/code size versus compile-time checking and unrolling, with the "often" versus "must" distinction.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose dense, sparse, and interop boundaries for a production pipeline

Assign an owner and a layout contract to each subsystem edge, and pick dense or sparse per stage from traversal and interop needs rather than a single house style.

Dense versus sparse per stage. Ingest dense features into one flat row-major Vec<f32> plus rows and cols — the parser produces a rectangular block and downstream stages stream it. Normalize rows in place over that same buffer: row-major makes each row a contiguous unit-stride slice, so normalization is cache-friendly and needs no new owner. Extract windows as borrowed MatrixView values (rows, cols, stride, offset) into the normalized buffer — no copies while the parent lives. The foreign solver stage is dense but its layout is dictated by the library, not by us. The recommendation graph is mostly zeros, so assemble it sparse: COO triples during build, then compress to CSR or CSC for traversal — separating the build format from the execution format. The final GPU stage is dense again, but in device memory.

Where borrowed views suffice and where data must become owned. Borrowed views are enough for normalize and window extraction, because those consumers run while the parent buffer is alive and on the same thread. Data must become owned at the two hard boundaries. The foreign solver may require a different layout (column-major), a specific leading dimension, or an alignment our slice does not satisfy, so we may have to materialize a conversion buffer it owns for the call. The GPU stage requires device residency: host memory must be copied across the host/device boundary into a device buffer, which is a genuine ownership transfer no borrow can express.

The boundary that must be explicit about row-major versus column-major is the foreign solver call. BLAS/LAPACK-style solvers are column-major with an explicit leading dimension; our pipeline is row-major. That mismatch must be stated and handled — by transposing, by storing a column-major staging buffer for the call, or by using the routine's transpose flag — and documented at the edge. The GPU boundary similarly needs an explicit layout and memory-domain contract.

What to test and profile first so math does not get blamed for boundary costs. Test correctness with a scalar reference: compute a few outputs with a trivial triple-loop reference and assert the optimized or foreign path agrees, so a layout bug surfaces as a wrong number, not a silent drift. Profile the handoffs before the kernels: time the transposition/packing step and the host-to-device transfer separately from the solver call, and instrument a copy count or bytes-copied metric at each boundary. The chapter's point is that the slowest part is usually the repack or transfer, not the arithmetic, so measure the boundary first.

A tradeoff worth naming: holding the dense buffer row-major optimizes every internal stage (normalize, window) for locality but forces a transpose or staging copy at the column-major solver boundary. Storing column-major to please the solver would invert that cost onto every internal row operation. Choosing row-major internally and paying the conversion once at the single foreign edge is the better trade, because the internal stages run far more often than the one boundary crossing.

// Internal owner: dense, row-major, one allocation.
struct Features { rows: usize, cols: usize, data: Vec<f32> } // ingest + normalize

// Window extraction: borrowed, zero-copy while `Features` lives.
struct WindowView<'a> { data: &'a [f32], rows: usize, cols: usize, stride: usize, offset: usize }

// Sparse assembly: build as COO, execute as CSR.
struct Coo { rows: usize, cols: usize, entries: Vec<(usize, usize, f32)> }     // build format
struct Csr { rows: usize, cols: usize, indptr: Vec<usize>, indices: Vec<usize>, values: Vec<f32> } // exec format

// Foreign solver boundary: explicit layout + leading dimension, owned staging buffer.
struct SolverInput { col_major: Vec<f32>, lda: usize } // converted once at the edge

// GPU boundary: device-resident buffer, an ownership transfer, not a borrow.
struct DeviceBuffer { /* opaque device handle + len */ }

Each subsystem edge gets a named owner and layout: dense row-major internally, borrowed views for windows, COO-to-CSR for the sparse graph, and owned conversion buffers at the solver and GPU boundaries.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Chooses at least one dense representation (flat row-major features) and one sparse representation (COO build, CSR execution) deliberately.
  • Identifies the foreign solver and GPU stages as ownership and layout boundaries requiring owned, converted, or device-resident buffers.
  • Names a test strategy (scalar reference check) and profiling hooks (transposition/transfer timing, copy-count measurement).
  • Justifies a tradeoff: row-major internally optimizes frequent stages at the cost of one conversion at the column-major solver edge.

Lab solution

The initial code shipped with two layout bugs that the row-major contract must fix. offset computed col * self.rows + row, which is column-major, and row started its slice at row * self.rows instead of row * self.cols. Both must become row-major to match what the chapter teaches and what the expected output requires: offset is row * self.cols + col, and a row begins at row * self.cols. (For this 2x2 matrix rows == cols, so the bug happens not to change the numbers — but the formulas are corrected to be right in general, which is the point of the exercise.)

The driver builds a 2x2 matrix of i32 initialized to 0, then sets the four cells to 5, 7, 3, 8 in row-major order: row 0 is [5, 7], row 1 is [3, 8]. get(0, 1) resolves to offset 0 * 2 + 1 = 1, the value 7, so the first line prints a01 = 7. row(1) borrows the contiguous slice [3, 8] directly from the flat buffer with no copy; summing it gives 11, the second line. cells reads m.data.len(), which is rows * cols = 4 by the from_elem invariant, the third line.

The design lesson the lab pins down: there is exactly one owner (the flat Vec<T>), exactly one place where a (row, col) becomes a linear index (offset), and the row view is a borrowed slice rather than a fresh allocation. Every accessor routes through the single offset rule, which is what makes the storage contract obvious in code.

Example 12-S. row_major_matrix_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Matrix<T> {
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T: Clone> Matrix<T> {
    fn from_elem(rows: usize, cols: usize, value: T) -> Self {
        Self {
            rows,
            cols,
            data: vec![value; rows * cols],
        }
    }
}

impl<T> Matrix<T> {
    // Row-major: skip `row` full rows of width `cols`, then step in by `col`.
    fn offset(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> usize {
        row * self.cols + col
    }

    fn get(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> Option<&T> {
        if row < self.rows && col < self.cols {
            Some(&self.data[self.offset(row, col)])
        } else {
            None
        }
    }

    fn set(&mut self, row: usize, col: usize, value: T) {
        let index = self.offset(row, col);
        self.data[index] = value;
    }

    // A full row is already contiguous in row-major storage: borrow it.
    fn row(&self, row: usize) -> Option<&[T]> {
        if row < self.rows {
            let start = row * self.cols;
            Some(&self.data[start..start + self.cols])
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut m = Matrix::from_elem(2, 2, 0_i32);
    m.set(0, 0, 5);
    m.set(0, 1, 7);
    m.set(1, 0, 3);
    m.set(1, 1, 8);

    let row1_sum: i32 = m.row(1).unwrap().iter().copied().sum();

    println!("a01 = {}", m.get(0, 1).copied().unwrap());
    println!("row1 sum = {}", row1_sum);
    println!("cells = {}", m.data.len());
}
Output
a01 = 7
row1 sum = 11
cells = 4

Review question answers

Why is a flat Vec<T> usually a stronger dense-matrix default than Vec<Vec<T>>?

A flat Vec<T> is a single allocation laid out contiguously, so the whole matrix is one streamable region the CPU prefetches predictably, and it can be handed to a foreign kernel or GPU as one pointer plus a length. A Vec<Vec<T>> is R+1 allocations — an outer array of pointers plus a separately heap-allocated, possibly scattered buffer per row — which costs per-row indirection on every access and defeats the prefetcher during a full scan. The only thing the flat form gives up is cheap ragged rows and per-row structural edits, which dense rectangular matrices do not need. Nested vectors are the honest choice only when rows genuinely differ in length, not as a default for dense numeric data.

What is the real difference between row-major and column-major in production code?

Both store the same logical cells in the same bytes; only the order differs, so the practical consequence is which traversal is unit-stride and which foreign library can consume the buffer without conversion. In row-major, walking a row is unit-stride and cache-friendly while walking a column jumps by the row width; column-major is the reverse. This matters at interop boundaries: BLAS and LAPACK-style solvers expect column-major with an explicit leading dimension, so a row-major Rust buffer must be transposed, staged, or flagged at that edge. The formula row * cols + col versus col * rows + row is trivial; the operational question is loop order, cache behavior, and which boundary can take the buffer as-is.

When is a matrix view the right abstraction, and when should you copy instead?

A view is right when you want to describe a submatrix, tile, or window without allocating, and the consumer runs while the parent buffer is alive and reachable — the view borrows the buffer (&'a [T]) and carries rows, cols, stride, and offset, with the lifetime preventing it from dangling. Copy instead when ownership must outlive the parent, such as storing the window in a long-lived struct, sending it to another thread, or returning it past the source buffer's scope. You also copy when a consumer needs contiguous, tightly packed storage that a strided window cannot provide, such as a foreign kernel or a GPU upload. The view explains layout; it does not own storage, so when ownership transfer is the actual requirement, materializing an owned Vec<T> is correct rather than wasteful.

What makes const generics appropriate for some matrix shapes but not for request-sized batches?

Const generics are appropriate when the shape is a true invariant of the API — a 3x3 convolution kernel or a 4x4 transform is that size by definition, so encoding it in the type gives compile-time shape checking, loop unrolling, and self-documenting signatures, as with the chapter's trace<const N: usize>. They are wrong for a request- or batch-sized score matrix because that shape is runtime data: it varies per call and is often unknown at compile time, so a const generic would either be impossible or would monomorphize a fresh copy of the code per size encountered. The honest test is "must be 4x4" versus "often 4x4" — only the former, a shape global to the API, belongs in the type. The cost of type-level shape is API rigidity and code size, which you accept only when the invariant is real.

Which safety invariant must be true before you hand a matrix buffer to a foreign solver or GPU runtime?

The buffer must actually satisfy every contract the foreign side assumes: the correct layout (row-major versus column-major), the correct leading dimension, the required alignment, a length consistent with the declared shape, and the right memory domain (host versus device). Claims of zero-copy interop are suspect because a foreign kernel often requires a different layout, alignment, or device residency than your Rust buffer currently has, which forces a repack or transfer. You must also guarantee the buffer stays alive and is not mutated or freed for the entire duration of the foreign call, since the FFI proof obligations from the unsafe-Rust chapter apply. Most expensive matrix interop bugs come from one of these assumptions being unstated rather than from the arithmetic.

Why should sparse format choice follow traversal and interop needs instead of default taste?

Sparse formats trade off ease of construction against speed of traversal, so the right choice depends on what you actually do with the matrix, not on a habit. COO — a bag of (row, col, value) triples — is the easy ingestion format but slow to multiply or traverse; CSR and CSC are compressed and traverse fast in one direction (CSR by rows, CSC by columns), which is also what a downstream solver or accelerator may demand. The useful rule is to separate the build format from the execution format: ingest as COO, then compress to CSR or CSC for the hot path. Picking by traversal and interop need means the format matches both how you iterate and what the consuming library expects, rather than forcing one format everywhere.

Chapter 13 · Arena Allocation and Region-Based Memory

Arena Allocation and Region-Based Memory

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all circle one decision: when you have many small values that share a single lifecycle, who owns them and how do they refer to each other? The chapter's answer is a region. One owner holds every node; edges between nodes are indices, not pointers; and teardown is a single coarse step rather than a cascade of individual frees. Working through these solutions, you will build that machinery from the inside, starting with a bump cursor and ending with generational handles and a boundary-crossing design decision.

The through-line is that an arena is not primarily an allocation-speed trick. It is a way of making the lifetime model honest. The bump allocator gives you append-only allocation now and coarse reset later. The index AST gives you a graph with exactly one owner and no reference-cycle problem to solve. The harder exercises add scoped rewind, deletion-aware handles, and a rule for what may cross a subsystem boundary. Each builds directly on Chapter 04's borrowing rules, Chapter 06's handle design, Chapter 09's smart-pointer tradeoffs, and Chapter 10's contiguous-storage reasoning.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

State the bump allocator's lifetime model

The only mutable state a bump allocator tracks across allocations is the used cursor: a single usize recording how many bytes of the fixed region have been handed out. The backing buffer itself does not change shape, and there is no free list, no per-object header, and no allocator metadata beyond that one number. This is what the chapter means by the right-hand column of the two-column model: the general heap tracks each object on its own, while the arena tracks one region and one cursor.

allocation (alloc_bytes) reads the cursor, checks that used + len does not overflow the region, copies the bytes in at the cursor, and advances the cursor to the new end. It only ever moves the cursor forward. reset sets the cursor back to zero in one step. Logically that releases the whole region's contents at once: the next allocation will overwrite from the start, so every value that lived in the region is gone together. Drop does the same thing implicitly when the arena itself goes out of scope.

There is no per-object free path because freeing one object in the middle of an append-only region would leave a hole that the cursor model cannot represent. The cursor only knows where the live high-water mark is; it has no way to record that bytes 4 through 7 are free while bytes 0 through 3 and 8 onward are live. The design deliberately trades the ability to free individual objects for the cheapness of advancing one number and the cheapness of resetting it.
