That is the right trade when most temporary objects share one scope: request-scoped scratch buffers, parser workspaces, the working graph a query service builds and discards per request. It is the wrong trade when individual objects must be freed independently and at different times, because the arena simply has no operation for that, and you would either leak the region until reset or be forced into a different allocator entirely.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names the used cursor as the sole mutable state and states allocation advances it forward.
  • States that reset (or drop) releases the whole region in one step with no individual frees.
  • Ties the fit to request-scoped scratch and parser workspaces where temporaries share one scope.
  • Notes the weakness: poor when objects must be freed independently at different times.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace evaluation through the index-arena AST

alloc pushes onto the nodes vector and returns ExprId(self.nodes.len()) captured before the push, so each id is the slot index the node lands in. The five allocations therefore issue ids in slot order: Number(2) -> ExprId(0) bound to two, Number(3) -> ExprId(1) bound to three, Number(4) -> ExprId(2) bound to four, Add(two, three) -> ExprId(3) bound to sum, and Mul(sum, four) -> ExprId(4) bound to root.

eval(root) looks up slot 4, finds Mul(sum, four), and recurses. eval(sum) looks up slot 3, finds Add(two, three), and recurses again: eval(two) reads slot 0 and returns 2, eval(three) reads slot 1 and returns 3, so the Add yields 2 + 3 = 5. Back in the Mul, eval(four) reads slot 2 and returns 4, so the Mul yields 5 * 4 = 20. Each recursive step reborrows from the arena root through get, because every variant holds ExprId values rather than owned children, so the recursion always indexes back into the one owning vector. The program prints value = 20 and nodes = 5.

If Add held Box<Expr> instead of ExprId, each node would own its children directly: the tree would become a chain of heap allocations, eval would match on owned sub-Exprs without consulting the arena, and len would no longer report a flat node count because there would be no flat table. The ExprId version keeps logical identity into a single owning vector, so an edge is an index, not an owner. That is the distinction the chapter draws: ExprId is identity, not shared ownership, which is exactly why this graph has one owner and no reference-cycle problem to solve.

// Slot indices issued in allocation order:
//   two   = ExprId(0)   Number(2)
//   three = ExprId(1)   Number(3)
//   four  = ExprId(2)   Number(4)
//   sum   = ExprId(3)   Add(two, three)
//   root  = ExprId(4)   Mul(sum, four)
//
// eval(root) expands as:
//   eval(ExprId(4)) -> Mul(sum, four)
//     eval(ExprId(3)) -> Add(two, three)
//       eval(ExprId(0)) -> 2
//       eval(ExprId(1)) -> 3
//       => 2 + 3 = 5
//     eval(ExprId(2)) -> 4
//   => 5 * 4 = 20
//
// Printed output:
//   value = 20
//   nodes = 5

Hand-trace of eval(root) over the five issued ExprId slots.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Maps two->0, three->1, four->2, sum->3, root->4 as the issued ids.
  • Trace shows eval(root) = eval(sum) * eval(four) = (2 + 3) * 4 = 20.
  • Reports value = 20 and nodes = 5 as the printed output.
  • Explains ExprId is logical identity into one owning vector, so edges are indices not owners.
Exercise 3implementation

Add a checkpoint-and-rewind API to the bump allocator

mark and rewind are the same one-cursor idea as reset, generalized from "back to zero" to "back to a saved position." mark takes &self and returns self.used without touching any state; it is just a snapshot of the high-water mark. rewind takes &mut self and sets self.used back to the saved value, so all bytes above that point become available again for the next allocation. No individual allocation is ever freed, and allocation stays append-only above whatever the cursor currently is.

The subtle case is what rewind does when the supplied mark is greater than the current used, which would happen if a caller saved a mark, rewound past it once, and then tried to rewind to the stale higher mark again. Moving the cursor forward to an arbitrary mark would expose stale bytes that were logically released and may have been overwritten or never written, so I treat a forward rewind as a misuse. I guard it with a debug assertion and clamp in release builds so the cursor never moves forward through rewind. This keeps the invariant that rewind only ever reclaims space, matching the chapter's framing that the cursor moves forward only on allocation and backward only on reset or rewind.

The test allocates one value, marks, allocates two more, then rewinds to the mark and confirms used returns to the marked value. A subsequent alloc_bytes then writes over the reclaimed region, demonstrating the bytes were genuinely reused rather than freed.

struct Bump<const N: usize> {
    buf: [u8; N],
    used: usize,
}

impl<const N: usize> Bump<N> {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { buf: [0; N], used: 0 }
    }

    fn alloc_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
        let end = self.used.checked_add(bytes.len())?;
        if end > N {
            return None;
        }
        let start = self.used;
        self.buf[start..end].copy_from_slice(bytes);
        self.used = end;
        Some((start, end))
    }

    fn slice(&self, range: (usize, usize)) -> &[u8] {
        &self.buf[range.0..range.1]
    }

    /// Snapshot the cursor without mutating the arena.
    fn mark(&self) -> usize {
        self.used
    }

    /// Roll the cursor back to a previously returned mark, reclaiming the
    /// bytes above it. Rewinding *forward* (mark > used) would expose stale
    /// bytes, so we treat it as misuse: assert in debug, clamp in release.
    fn rewind(&mut self, mark: usize) {
        debug_assert!(
            mark <= self.used,
            "rewind must not move the cursor forward (mark {mark} > used {})",
            self.used
        );
        self.used = mark.min(self.used);
    }

    fn used(&self) -> usize {
        self.used
    }

    fn reset(&mut self) {
        self.used = 0;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut arena = Bump::<32>::new();

    let base = arena.alloc_bytes(b"keep").unwrap();
    let checkpoint = arena.mark();

    arena.alloc_bytes(b"scratch-one").unwrap();
    arena.alloc_bytes(b"two").unwrap();
    assert!(arena.used() > checkpoint);

    arena.rewind(checkpoint);
    assert_eq!(arena.used(), checkpoint);

    // Reused region: the next allocation overwrites the reclaimed bytes.
    let reused = arena.alloc_bytes(b"fresh").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(reused.0, checkpoint);
    assert_eq!(arena.slice(base), b"keep");
    assert_eq!(arena.slice(reused), b"fresh");
    println!("used = {}", arena.used());
}

mark/rewind reuse the one-cursor model, guarding the unsound forward case.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • mark has signature fn mark(&self) -> usize and returns self.used without mutation.
  • rewind sets self.used to the mark so later allocations reuse the region above it.
  • No individual allocation is freed; allocation stays append-only above the cursor.
  • The test allocates, marks, allocates more, rewinds, and used returns to the marked value.
Exercise 4implementation

Add deletion-aware handles to the AST arena

A plain usize index cannot tell whether the slot it points at still holds the node it was issued for. Once a slot is removed and reused, the old index silently reads the new occupant. The fix is a generational handle: each slot stores a generation counter plus an Option<Expr>, and ExprId carries the (index, generation) pair it was issued for. A read is valid only when the index is in range, the slot is occupied, and the handle's generation equals the slot's current generation.

remove clears the slot's value to None and bumps its generation. That single increment is what invalidates every handle previously issued for that slot, because their stored generation now differs from the slot's current generation. alloc prefers a free slot from a free list; when it reuses a slot it leaves the already-bumped generation in place and stores the new value, so the new handle is issued with the new generation. A stale handle to the old occupant still carries the pre-bump generation, so its get returns None, while a fresh handle to the reused slot matches and returns the new node.

This is the generational arena the chapter describes: the generation counter exists precisely to distinguish a slot's old occupant from its new one. It turns a use-after-free-shaped bug, reading a stale index into a reused slot, into a clean Option::None at the read site, with the cost of one extra usize per slot and one comparison per access. eval is updated to expect a live handle and unwrap through get, since evaluation only ever runs over a tree of currently-live nodes.

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct ExprId {
    index: usize,
    generation: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Expr {
    Number(i64),
    Add(ExprId, ExprId),
    Mul(ExprId, ExprId),
}

struct Slot {
    generation: u32,
    value: Option<Expr>,
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct ExprArena {
    slots: Vec<Slot>,
    free: Vec<usize>,
}

impl ExprArena {
    fn alloc(&mut self, expr: Expr) -> ExprId {
        if let Some(index) = self.free.pop() {
            let slot = &mut self.slots[index];
            slot.value = Some(expr);
            // generation was already bumped at remove time
            ExprId { index, generation: slot.generation }
        } else {
            let index = self.slots.len();
            self.slots.push(Slot { generation: 0, value: Some(expr) });
            ExprId { index, generation: 0 }
        }
    }

    fn remove(&mut self, id: ExprId) -> bool {
        match self.slots.get_mut(id.index) {
            Some(slot) if slot.generation == id.generation && slot.value.is_some() => {
                slot.value = None;
                slot.generation = slot.generation.wrapping_add(1);
                self.free.push(id.index);
                true
            }
            _ => false,
        }
    }

    fn get(&self, id: ExprId) -> Option<&Expr> {
        let slot = self.slots.get(id.index)?;
        if slot.generation != id.generation {
            return None;
        }
        slot.value.as_ref()
    }

    fn eval(&self, id: ExprId) -> i64 {
        match self.get(id).expect("eval on a live handle") {
            Expr::Number(value) => *value,
            Expr::Add(left, right) => self.eval(*left) + self.eval(*right),
            Expr::Mul(left, right) => self.eval(*left) * self.eval(*right),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut arena = ExprArena::default();

    let two = arena.alloc(Expr::Number(2));
    let three = arena.alloc(Expr::Number(3));
    let sum = arena.alloc(Expr::Add(two, three));
    assert_eq!(arena.eval(sum), 5);

    // Remove `two`; the old handle to it is now stale.
    assert!(arena.remove(two));
    assert!(arena.get(two).is_none());

    // Reuse the freed slot for a new node.
    let nine = arena.alloc(Expr::Number(9));
    assert_eq!(nine.index, two.index); // same slot...
    assert_ne!(nine.generation, two.generation); // ...new generation
    assert!(matches!(arena.get(nine), Some(Expr::Number(9))));
    assert!(arena.get(two).is_none()); // stale handle still rejected
    println!("stale-handle protection holds");
}

Generational (index, generation) handles reject access to a reused slot.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • ExprId carries both an index and a generation rather than a bare usize.
  • remove bumps the slot's generation so previously issued handles no longer match.
  • get returns None when the handle's generation differs from the slot's current generation.
  • A reused slot serves new handles correctly while the stale old handle returns None.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Remove the reference cycle from an Rc graph

In the Rc version every edge is an Rc<Node> owner, so each edge contributes a strong count to its target. The back-edge from D to A means A is kept alive by D, and following the forward edges A keeps D alive transitively. That forms a cycle of strong references: A's strong count never falls to zero because D holds it, and D's never falls to zero because the chain from A reaches it. When the external handles go out of scope, the cycle's internal counts remain at least one, so none of the nodes in the cycle are ever dropped. That is the leak. RefCell does not cause it; it only enables the mutation that lets you install the back-edge. The leak is purely the ownership cycle in the strong counts.

The repair the chapter prescribes is structural, not a patch: make one arena own every node in a single vector, and make every edge a NodeId index into that vector instead of an Rc<Node>. Now there is exactly one owner, the arena's nodes vector. Edges own nothing; a NodeId is a plain Copy value that confers no ownership and bumps no count. You build the graph by allocating each node and connecting them by handle, including the D-to-A back-edge, which is now just the index of A stored in D.

The identical back-edge no longer leaks because indices are not owners. A NodeId being stored in D's edge list does not keep A's storage alive; A is kept alive solely by the arena, and exactly as long as the arena. When the arena drops, the whole region drops together in one step, cycles and all, because dropping a Vec<Node> of plain index-bearing nodes never has to chase a pointer or decrement a foreign count. You removed the cycle by construction rather than by retrofitting Weak references after the fact. This is the same one-owner-plus-handles shape the chapter recommends for ASTs, IR, routing graphs, and domain DAGs.

// Before: edges are Rc owners, so D -> A closes a strong-count cycle that leaks.
//
// use std::cell::RefCell;
// use std::rc::Rc;
// struct Node { name: &'static str, edges: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>> }
// let a = Rc::new(Node { name: "A", edges: RefCell::new(vec![]) });
// let d = Rc::new(Node { name: "D", edges: RefCell::new(vec![]) });
// a.edges.borrow_mut().push(d.clone());
// d.edges.borrow_mut().push(a.clone()); // back-edge: A and D never drop

// After: one arena owns every node; edges are NodeId indices that own nothing.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct NodeId(usize);

struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    edges: Vec<NodeId>,
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Graph {
    nodes: Vec<Node>,
}

impl Graph {
    fn add(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len());
        self.nodes.push(Node { name, edges: Vec::new() });
        id
    }

    fn connect(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.nodes[from.0].edges.push(to);
    }

    fn node(&self, id: NodeId) -> &Node {
        &self.nodes[id.0]
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut g = Graph::default();
    let a = g.add("A");
    let b = g.add("B");
    let c = g.add("C");
    let d = g.add("D");

    g.connect(a, b);
    g.connect(b, c);
    g.connect(c, d);
    g.connect(d, a); // identical back-edge, now just an index: no leak

    assert_eq!(g.node(d).edges, vec![a]);
    println!("{} -> {}", g.node(d).name, g.node(g.node(d).edges[0]).name);
    // Graph drops in one step when it goes out of scope; the cycle is harmless.
}

Arena-and-index graph: one owner, indices for edges, back-edge cannot leak.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that Rc edges are owners, so the cycle keeps strong counts above zero and nodes never drop.
  • The refactored graph has exactly one owner: the arena vector of nodes.
  • Every edge stores a NodeId index rather than an Rc or Box, so edges own nothing.
  • States the cycle is removed by construction because indices are not owners and the region drops together.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose between borrowed-reference and index arenas at a boundary

The two arena styles differ in what crosses the boundary back to the caller. A reference arena hands back &'arena T: a borrow chained to the arena's lifetime. An index arena hands back a small owned handle such as ExprId or NodeId that owns nothing and is Copy. That difference is the whole decision, because the borrow checker treats them oppositely at a boundary.

The borrow checker forbids the arena-borrowed reference from outliving the arena. Its lifetime is tied to the arena's, so you cannot store it in a cache that outlives the request, and you cannot move it into an async task whose future may be polled after the request scope ends. The compiler rejects both at the point you try, which is exactly the protection you want, but it means a reference arena cannot serve data that crosses a long-lived boundary. The owned handle has no such tie: it is a plain value, so it travels freely across async tasks, queues, and caches.

For this query service I keep arena-borrowed references for the phase-local synchronous work, name resolution, plan construction, and analysis passes that run entirely within the request and discard the working graph at the end. What crosses to the cache and to the async task is owned data: either fully owned values copied out of the arena (a resolved plan, a result row) or stable handles paired with the arena or table they index into, kept alive for as long as the consumer needs them. The async task that may outlive the request must not hold an arena borrow; it gets owned values or a handle into a structure with an independent, longer lifetime.

The chapter says to ask three questions before picking a style. First, do I want arena-tied references or handles? References are strongest when the phase stays local and synchronous; handles when data must travel. Second, do I need deletion? If slots are removed and reused, a bare index is unsafe and you need a generational handle. Third, does stale-handle protection matter? If a consumer can hold a handle across a removal, you need the generation check to turn stale access into None rather than a silent wrong read. For a boundary-crossing cache, the answers point to stable, generation-checked handles for anything retained, and arena references confined to the synchronous request phase.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States a reference arena returns a borrow tied to the arena's lifetime, forbidden from outliving it.
  • States an index arena returns a small owned handle that can travel across async tasks, queues, and caches.
  • Keeps arena references for phase-local synchronous work and uses owned values or stable handles across boundaries.
  • Lists the three questions: reference vs handle, deletion needed, and stale-handle protection.

Lab solution

alloc_bytes is the whole exercise. It computes end = used + len with checked_add so an absurd length cannot wrap, rejects the request with None when end exceeds the region size N, and otherwise copies the bytes in at the current cursor, advances used to end, and returns the (start, end) range. Allocation only ever moves the cursor forward; it never frees.

In main, the region is Bump::<16>. Allocating b"query" (5 bytes) takes used from 0 to 5 and returns (0, 5). Allocating b"plan" (4 bytes) takes used to 9 and returns (5, 9), so used = 9 prints, and slicing each range back through slice yields query and plan. b"too-many-bytes" is 14 bytes; 9 + 14 = 23 exceeds 16, so alloc_bytes returns None and overflow.is_none() is true. reset sets used back to 0 in one coarse step, releasing the whole region logically, so after reset = 0. The final b"next" allocates from the start of the now-empty region and prints next. The printed lines match the expected output exactly.

The lab's lesson is the lifetime model rather than the arithmetic: append-only allocation now, single overflow guard at the boundary, and one cheap reset that discards everything at once with no per-object free path.

Example 13-S. bump_allocator_lab.rs — Reference solution

struct Bump<const N: usize> {
    buf: [u8; N],
    used: usize,
}

impl<const N: usize> Bump<N> {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { buf: [0; N], used: 0 }
    }

    fn alloc_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
        let end = self.used.checked_add(bytes.len())?;
        if end > N {
            return None;
        }
        let start = self.used;
        self.buf[start..end].copy_from_slice(bytes);
        self.used = end;
        Some((start, end))
    }

    fn slice(&self, range: (usize, usize)) -> &[u8] {
        &self.buf[range.0..range.1]
    }

    fn used(&self) -> usize {
        self.used
    }

    fn reset(&mut self) {
        self.used = 0;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut arena = Bump::<16>::new();

    let a = arena.alloc_bytes(b"query").unwrap();
    let b = arena.alloc_bytes(b"plan").unwrap();
    println!("used = {}", arena.used());
    println!("a = {}", std::str::from_utf8(arena.slice(a)).unwrap());
    println!("b = {}", std::str::from_utf8(arena.slice(b)).unwrap());

    let overflow = arena.alloc_bytes(b"too-many-bytes");
    println!("overflow = {}", overflow.is_none());

    arena.reset();
    println!("after reset = {}", arena.used());

    let c = arena.alloc_bytes(b"next").unwrap();
    println!("c = {}", std::str::from_utf8(arena.slice(c)).unwrap());
}
Output
used = 9
a = query
b = plan
overflow = true
after reset = 0
c = next

Review question answers

What single piece of mutable state does a bump allocator maintain, and what do allocation and reset each do to it?

It maintains a single used cursor: the count of bytes already handed out of the fixed region. Allocation checks for overflow, copies the bytes in at the cursor, and advances the cursor forward by the allocation size. Reset sets the cursor back to zero in one step, logically releasing the whole region's contents at once, with no per-object free path anywhere in the type.

Why does an arena-and-index AST avoid the reference-cycle problem that an Rc<RefCell<Node>> graph can hit?

In an Rc graph every edge is an owner, so a cycle of edges keeps the involved strong counts above zero and those nodes are never dropped. In an arena-and-index AST there is exactly one owner, the arena's vector, and every edge is just an ExprId or NodeId index that owns nothing and changes no reference count. Because indices are not owners, a back-edge cannot keep anything alive, so cycles are removed by construction and the entire region drops together when the arena drops.

What is the difference between what a reference arena and an index arena hand back across a boundary, and which one the borrow checker ties to the arena's lifetime?

A reference arena hands back a borrow that is chained to the arena's lifetime, and the borrow checker forbids that reference from outliving the arena, so it cannot be stored in a longer-lived cache or moved into an async task that may outlive the request. An index arena hands back a small owned handle that owns nothing and is Copy, so it can travel freely across async tasks, queues, and caches. The borrow checker ties only the reference arena's output to the arena's lifetime; the handle carries no such tie.

What problem does a generation counter on an arena handle solve that a plain usize index does not?

A plain usize index keeps pointing at a slot after that slot is removed and reused, so it silently reads whatever new value now occupies the slot, a stale-access bug. A generation counter records, per slot, how many times it has been reused, and the handle stores the generation it was issued for; removing a node bumps the slot's generation. On read, comparing the handle's generation against the slot's current generation returns None for any stale handle, turning a silent wrong read into a clean failure at the access site.

When is the arena model the wrong fit, given that its cheap operation is whole-region reset rather than per-object free?

It is the wrong fit when objects have independent, staggered lifetimes and must be freed individually at different times, because the bump model has no per-object free operation and can only reclaim space by resetting or dropping the whole region. If the workload does not actually share one region lifetime, the arena either forces you to hold memory until reset or pushes you toward a different allocator, and the lifetime mismatch eventually shows. The arena pays off only when most temporaries genuinely share one scope, such as request-scoped scratch or parser workspaces.

Chapter 14 · Interfaces in Rust: Traits

Interfaces in Rust: Traits

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move from reading a trait definition to publishing one as a deliberate API choice. The chapter's mental model is a triangle: the trait names a method set, each concrete type carries its own impl block, and call sites name the trait either as a generic bound or as a dyn object. The exercises drill the three decisions that follow from that model: where dispatch is resolved (compile time versus a vtable), whether to commit an output with an associated type, and whether the trait must remain object-safe so it can live behind Box<dyn Trait>.

The set builds toward a single production judgment. You read the static-dispatch RetryPolicy example to see how an associated type and a where-clause pin an output to bool, extend it with a second policy, then move to the dyn plugin pipeline to see why object safety is what lets unrelated types share one boxed list. The debugging and design exercises close the loop: a generic method silently forecloses dyn, and deciding object safety up front is cheap while retrofitting it later is a breaking change.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Separate the trait, the impl, and the call site

The three corners of the triangle are the trait, the concrete type, and the call site. The trait is a named set of methods with no data of its own (here RetryPolicy with decide, label, and should_log). The concrete type is the data (FixedLimit { max: u32 }). The call site is the code that names the trait, either as a bound on a generic parameter (fn evaluate<P>(... ) where P: RetryPolicy<Decision = bool>) or as a dyn object. The impl block is the third, separate thing that links a type to a trait: impl RetryPolicy for FixedLimit. It is neither part of the struct definition nor part of the trait definition.

Because the link lives in an independent impl block, the same struct can implement Display, Iterator, and RetryPolicy without any of them referencing the others. Each impl is written separately and only the type name ties them together; Display never mentions RetryPolicy, and RetryPolicy never mentions Display. Capability is added in layers, so a type accumulates unrelated behaviors without a class hierarchy declaring them all in one place. That is the concrete meaning of composition over inheritance in this model: you assemble capabilities by adding impls rather than inheriting a fixed bundle from a base class.

The dispatch decision is made at the call site, not at the trait or the impl. The trait only declares the method set and the impl only supplies bodies; neither commits to how the method is reached. The call site chooses: a generic bound monomorphizes into a direct call resolved at compile time, while a dyn object routes the call through a vtable at runtime. The same trait and the same impl serve both, because the choice of dispatch is the caller's.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies the trait as the named method set, the concrete type (FixedLimit's data) as the data, and the call site as where the trait is named as a bound or dyn object.
  • States the impl block is the separate thing linking type to trait, distinct from the type definition.
  • Explains capability is added in independent impl layers, so one struct carries many unrelated impls that do not reference each other.
  • Locates the dispatch choice at the call site (generic bound versus dyn), not at the trait or impl.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the RetryPolicy associated type and where-clause

Self::Decision resolves to bool for FixedLimit. That is declared in the impl block by the line type Decision = bool;. The trait leaves Decision abstract (type Decision; with no body), and each implementer must pick a concrete output; FixedLimit commits to bool. So inside decide, the return type Self::Decision is literally bool, and the body attempts < self.max produces a bool directly.

The where-clause P: RetryPolicy<Decision = bool> on evaluate lets the function assume decide returns exactly bool, not just some opaque Self::Decision. Without that bound, the compiler would only know decide returns an unspecified associated type, which format! could not necessarily display and which the caller could not reason about. With the bound, evaluate can write format!("{} => {}", policy.label(), policy.decide(attempts)) and rely on the bool implementing Display, with no turbofish, no trait import for the output, and no conversion. The associated type plus the equality constraint pin the output so the call site can trust it.

evaluate calls label and decide. FixedLimit overrides label (it returns "fixed-limit" instead of the trait's default "policy"). It does not override should_log, so the default method body return true is inherited unchanged. For FixedLimit { max: 3 } and evaluate(&policy, 2), decide(2) evaluates 2 < 3, which is true, and label returns "fixed-limit", so the first println! prints fixed-limit => true. The second line prints policy.should_log(), which uses the inherited default returning true, so it prints log = true.

// Output of the chapter's traits_bounds_associated_types listing:
// fixed-limit => true
// log = true
//
// Why:
//   type Decision = bool          -> Self::Decision is bool for FixedLimit
//   decide(2) for max 3 is 2 < 3  -> true
//   label overridden              -> "fixed-limit"
//   should_log not overridden     -> inherits default -> true

Predicted output and the reasoning behind each line.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States Self::Decision is bool because the impl declares type Decision = bool.
  • Explains the where-clause guarantees decide returns bool, so format! displays it directly with no turbofish or conversion.
  • Notes label is overridden by FixedLimit while should_log is inherited from the default method.
  • Predicts the output lines fixed-limit => true and log = true.
Exercise 3implementation

Add a second RetryPolicy with a default override

AlwaysRetry implements RetryPolicy with type Decision = bool, which is what lets it be passed to evaluate unchanged: evaluate's bound is RetryPolicy<Decision = bool>, so any implementer that commits its associated type to bool satisfies the signature without any modification to evaluate. The dispatch is still static, monomorphized per concrete type, so adding a new policy costs nothing at the call site.

decide ignores its attempts argument and returns true, expressed by naming the parameter _attempts (or prefixing with an underscore) to signal it is intentionally unused. label is overridden to return "always", replacing the trait default "policy". should_log is overridden to return false, replacing the default that returned true. Overriding a default method simply means writing the method body in the impl block; if you omit it, the trait's default stands, which is exactly why FixedLimit could inherit should_log in the previous exercise.

With these in place, evaluate(&AlwaysRetry, 99) computes label() then decide(99). label returns "always" and decide returns true regardless of the 99, so the formatted string is "always => true". AlwaysRetry.should_log() returns the overridden false. Both results reuse the existing evaluate function and the existing RetryPolicy trait without changing either; the only new code is the struct and its impl block.

struct AlwaysRetry;

impl RetryPolicy for AlwaysRetry {
    type Decision = bool;

    fn decide(&self, _attempts: u32) -> Self::Decision {
        true
    }

    fn label(&self) -> &'static str {
        "always"
    }

    fn should_log(&self) -> bool {
        false
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", evaluate(&AlwaysRetry, 99)); // always => true
    println!("log = {}", AlwaysRetry.should_log()); // log = false
}

AlwaysRetry satisfies the Decision = bool bound and overrides two defaults; evaluate is reused unchanged.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Sets type Decision = bool and compiles against fn evaluate without modifying evaluate.
  • decide returns true for any attempts value, ignoring the argument via _attempts.
  • label returns "always" and should_log returns false, both overriding the trait defaults.
  • evaluate(&AlwaysRetry, 99) yields always => true and AlwaysRetry.should_log() yields false.
Exercise 4implementation

Make a Plugin trait usable both generically and behind dyn

The Plugin trait keeps run(&self, input: &str) -> String and name(&self) -> &'static str, both taking &self with no generic method parameters and no by-value Self. That is what keeps the trait object-safe and therefore usable in Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>. apply_one is the static-dispatch call site: fn apply_one<P: Plugin>(p: &P, input: &str) -> String. The generic bound P: Plugin means the compiler monomorphizes apply_one for each concrete type it is called with, producing a direct call. Its body formats name and run exactly as run_all does for each element, so the two paths produce identical "name => output" strings.

The dyn call site is unchanged from the chapter's listing: a Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> holding Box::new(Uppercase) and Box::new(Prefix { value: "svc-" }) compiles because the trait is object-safe, and run_all iterates that list calling through the vtable. The concrete types are erased behind one element type, Box<dyn Plugin>, while apply_one keeps the concrete type visible and resolved at compile time.

The same trait serves both call sites because it is object-safe: it declares only &self methods with no generics and no by-value Self, which is precisely the property that permits dyn. A generic bound monomorphizes to a direct call; the dyn version dispatches through a vtable; the trait definition is identical for both. apply_one(&Uppercase, "rust") yields "uppercase => RUST" and the same Uppercase inside a Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> yields the same string through run_all.

// Plugin trait stays object-safe: only &self, no generic methods, no by-value Self.
fn apply_one<P: Plugin>(p: &P, input: &str) -> String {
    format!("{} => {}", p.name(), p.run(input))
}

fn main() {
    // Static dispatch: monomorphized, direct call.
    println!("{}", apply_one(&Uppercase, "rust")); // uppercase => RUST

    // Dynamic dispatch: same trait, erased types, vtable calls.
    let plugins: Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> = vec![
        Box::new(Uppercase),
        Box::new(Prefix { value: "svc-" }),
    ];
    for line in run_all(&plugins, "rust") {
        println!("{}", line); // uppercase => RUST, then prefix => svc-rust
    }
}

One generic call site and one dyn call site over the same unchanged, object-safe Plugin trait.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • apply_one has signature fn apply_one<P: Plugin>(p: &P, input: &str) -> String and uses static dispatch via the generic bound.
  • The trait keeps only &self methods with no generic parameters, so Box<dyn Plugin> still compiles.
  • apply_one(&Uppercase, "rust") and the Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> path both produce matching "name => output" strings.
  • The explanation states the trait is object-safe, which is what permits both the generic and the dyn use.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Repair a trait that cannot be boxed

The defect is the added generic method fn run<T: Display>(&self, input: T) -> String. It makes Plugin no longer object-safe, so Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> stops compiling. The object-safety rule it violates is that a trait method may not have its own generic type parameters (other than lifetimes). A dyn Plugin is a fat pointer to data plus a vtable, and the vtable must contain one fixed function-pointer slot per method, decided once when the trait object is created. A method generic over T would need a separate compiled instantiation for every T it is ever called with, so there is no single address to put in the slot; the compiler cannot lay out a finite vtable for an unbounded family of run<T>. At a static call site monomorphization picks the T, but at an indirect call through a vtable there is no concrete type to monomorphize against.

The fix is to remove the generic parameter and give run a concrete signature, for example fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String. That is one fixed function for every implementer, so it occupies exactly one vtable slot, and dyn dispatch works again. If implementers genuinely need to accept varied input types, the object-safe options are to accept a concrete type like &str (callers convert at the boundary) or to take &dyn Display, moving the polymorphism into a second trait object rather than a generic method.

After restoring run(&self, input: &str) -> String, the trait is object-safe again: only &self methods, no generic method parameters, no by-value Self. Box<dyn Plugin> compiles, Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> holds the heterogeneous plugins, and run_all iterates and dispatches through the vtable as before. The boxed pipeline is restored with no change to the call sites.

use std::fmt::Display;

// BROKEN: generic method makes the trait not object-safe.
// trait Plugin {
//     fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
//     fn run<T: Display>(&self, input: T) -> String; // no single vtable slot
// }
//
// error[E0038]: the trait `Plugin` cannot be made into an object
//   because method `run` has generic type parameters

// FIXED: concrete &str parameter -> one fixed vtable slot per method.
trait Plugin {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String;
}

// Need to accept many Display types at a call site? Keep the trait object-safe
// and convert at the boundary, or take a second trait object:
fn run_with(plugin: &dyn Plugin, input: impl Display) -> String {
    plugin.run(&input.to_string())
}

Removing the generic method restores one fixed vtable slot per method, so Box<dyn Plugin> compiles.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Diagnosis names the generic method run<T> as the object-safety violation.
  • Explains a vtable needs one fixed slot per method, which a generic method cannot provide because each T would need its own entry.
  • The refactor removes the generic parameter, giving a concrete &self, input: &str method signature.
  • After the change, Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> and run_all compile again.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Decide static versus dynamic dispatch for a processing stage API

Use Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>. The decisive property is the combination of config-selected, heterogeneous, and runtime-assembled. Operators enable stages by configuration, so the concrete set is not known at compile time; the stages are unrelated types (normalize today; validate, redact, enrich later); and the list is built at runtime from config. A generic bound monomorphizes one homogeneous type per call and cannot hold a mixed list whose membership is decided by a config file at startup. Erasing the concrete types behind Box<dyn Stage> is exactly what lets a heterogeneous, runtime-built list share one element type and one loop.

The cost accepted with dyn is vtable indirection: each describe and run call goes through a function pointer rather than a direct, inlinable, monomorphized call, and there is no per-type specialization or cross-stage inlining. That cost is negligible here because every stage already does meaningful text work (trimming, wrapping, validating, redacting), so one indirect call per stage is lost in the noise of the per-stage processing. The pipeline is not a tight numeric inner loop where the indirection would dominate.

Keep the Stage trait object-safe from the start even though today's stages are few. Object safety is cheap to preserve now (only &self methods, no generic methods, no by-value Self) and expensive to retrofit later, because adding a generic method or a by-value Self return to a published trait is a breaking change that forecloses dyn for every existing implementer and caller. Since the entire design depends on Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>, a later edit that quietly breaks object safety would break the published API. Decide for dyn up front and hold the trait to object-safe signatures so the boxed pipeline keeps working as stages are added.

// Object-safe Stage trait: only &self, no generic methods, no by-value Self.
// This is what keeps Vec<Box<dyn Stage>> valid as stages are added later.
trait Stage {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String;
    fn describe(&self, input: &str) -> String {
        format!("{} => {}", self.name(), self.run(input))
    }
}

// Config-driven, heterogeneous, runtime-assembled => trait objects.
fn build_pipeline(enabled: &[&str]) -> Vec<Box<dyn Stage>> {
    enabled
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|name| match *name {
            "trim" => Some(Box::new(Trim) as Box<dyn Stage>),
            "wrap" => Some(Box::new(Wrap { tag: "b" }) as Box<dyn Stage>),
            _ => None,
        })
        .collect()
}

Trait objects let a config file assemble a heterogeneous stage list at runtime; object safety is preserved up front.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Selects Vec<Box<dyn Stage>> and ties it to config-driven, heterogeneous, runtime-assembled stages.
  • Acknowledges the vtable indirection cost and argues it is negligible relative to per-stage text work.
  • Commits to keeping the trait object-safe from the start to avoid a future retrofit.
  • Identifies that adding a generic method or by-value Self return later would foreclose dyn and break the API.

Lab solution

Two unrelated structs, Trim and Wrap, both implement one object-safe Stage trait, so Box::new(Trim) and Box::new(Wrap { tag: "b" }) can coexist in a single Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>. The trait stays object-safe because every method takes &self with no generic parameters and no by-value Self, which is the precondition for laying out the vtable that Box<dyn Stage> needs.

Trim::run returns input.trim().to_string(), stripping the leading and trailing spaces from " hi " to produce "hi". Wrap::run returns format!("[{}]{}[/{}]", self.tag, input, self.tag), which surrounds the unmodified input with the tag, giving "[b] hi [/b]" (the inner spaces are preserved because Wrap does not trim). Each stage is driven through the trait's default describe method, which calls self.name() and self.run(input) through the vtable and formats them as "name => output". The default method is written once on the trait yet runs for both concrete types via dynamic dispatch.

run_pipeline maps describe over the boxed stages and collects the lines, so the loop prints trim => hi then wrap => [b] hi [/b]. Finally stages.len() is 2, printing stages = 2. The output matches because the default describe method plus the two run implementations compose exactly into the expected three lines.

Example 14-S. stage_pipeline_lab.rs — Reference solution

trait Stage {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String;

    // Default method: reuse name() and run() so every stage prints the same way.
    fn describe(&self, input: &str) -> String {
        format!("{} => {}", self.name(), self.run(input))
    }
}

struct Trim;
struct Wrap {
    tag: &'static str,
}

impl Stage for Trim {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str {
        "trim"
    }
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String {
        input.trim().to_string()
    }
}

impl Stage for Wrap {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str {
        "wrap"
    }
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String {
        format!("[{}]{}[/{}]", self.tag, input, self.tag)
    }
}

fn run_pipeline(stages: &[Box<dyn Stage>], input: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    stages.iter().map(|s| s.describe(input)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let stages: Vec<Box<dyn Stage>> = vec![
        Box::new(Trim),
        Box::new(Wrap { tag: "b" }),
    ];

    for line in run_pipeline(&stages, "  hi  ") {
        println!("{}", line);
    }
    println!("stages = {}", stages.len());
}
Output
trim => hi
wrap => [b]  hi  [/b]
stages = 2

Review question answers

What links a concrete type to a trait in Rust, and why does that separation let one struct implement many unrelated traits?

An impl block links a concrete type to a trait (impl RetryPolicy for FixedLimit); it is a separate item from both the type definition and the trait definition. Because the link lives in its own impl rather than in the type's declaration, you can add as many impls for a type as you like, each for an unrelated trait. The same struct can implement Display, Iterator, and a domain trait because none of those traits references the others; only the shared type name ties the independent impls together, which is composition over inheritance in practice.

How does a generic bound's dispatch differ from a trait object's dispatch, and what runtime cost does each carry?

A generic bound (fn f<P: Trait>(p: &P)) is resolved at compile time by monomorphization: the compiler emits a specialized copy per concrete type with direct, inlinable calls, so the runtime cost is zero indirection at the price of code-size duplication. A trait object (&dyn Trait or Box<dyn Trait>) is resolved at runtime through a vtable: every method call goes through a function pointer, which costs one indirection per call and blocks inlining and per-type specialization. You trade compile-time specialization and speed for the ability to hold heterogeneous types behind one element type at runtime.

When should a trait use an associated type instead of a generic type parameter, and what symptom appears at call sites if you choose wrong?

Use an associated type when each implementing type has exactly one natural output, so the implementer commits to a single answer (type Decision = bool; type Item = u8). Use a generic type parameter when the same type should implement the trait several different ways for several inputs. If you choose an associated type where you needed multiple implementations, you cannot add the second impl. If you choose a generic parameter where one output was correct, the type becomes ambiguous at call sites and callers must disambiguate with turbofish or extra type annotations to tell the compiler which instantiation they mean.

What does object safety require of a trait's methods, and why does each rule exist for a single indirect call through a vtable?

Object safety requires that dispatchable methods take a receiver like &self or &mut self, have no generic type parameters of their own, and do not take or return Self by value; methods that violate these must be bounded by where Self: Sized to be excluded. Each rule exists because a dyn Trait is a fat pointer (data plus vtable) where every method must occupy one fixed function-pointer slot decided once. A generic method would need a different entry per T, so no single slot exists; a by-value Self appears or vanishes through a pointer whose concrete size is unknown, so it cannot be passed or returned across the indirect call. The rules guarantee one fixed, callable layout that works without knowing the concrete type.

Why is deciding up front whether a trait must work behind dyn important, given that adding a generic method or a by-value Self return later is a breaking change?

Object safety is cheap to preserve when you design the trait but expensive to add back later. Adding a generic method or a by-value Self return to a published trait removes object safety, which breaks every existing Box<dyn Trait> and &dyn Trait use across all callers and is therefore a breaking API change. If you know the trait will be used behind dyn (for example a config-assembled plugin pipeline), commit to object-safe signatures from the start so you never have to retrofit; deciding early avoids a forced, breaking refactor of a contract you live behind for a long time.

Chapter 15 · OOP Models in Rust

OOP Models in Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises turn the chapter's central question into practice: for each modeling need, is the set of cases closed and known at compile time, or open and extended later? That one question routes a design to an enum, a struct, a module boundary, or a trait object. The warm-ups make you classify real cases honestly; the implementation and refactoring exercises make you build the closed-set and encapsulation answers; and the design exercise forces you to mix several modeling styles inside one service without pretending one tool is globally best.

The through-line is that Rust separates two concerns a base class used to fuse: reusable data and replaceable behavior. Data reuse comes from owned fields and composition; behavior abstraction comes from traits, with static dispatch by default and trait objects only where one collection must hold heterogeneous implementations. Encapsulation moves from protected members to modules, private fields, and narrow constructors. The lab closes the loop by encoding a document lifecycle as typestate so that invalid states cannot be named at all.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose composition, open polymorphism, or closed polymorphism honestly

Composition with helper structs and no polymorphism: the reusable retry helper shared by three services. There is exactly one retry implementation; the three services do not need to vary its behavior, only to hold it as a field. A RetryPolicy struct owned by each service is the whole answer. Introducing a Retry trait here would be a trait with one implementor, which buys nothing and costs a layer of indirection. The honest model is plain composition: each service has a retry: RetryPolicy field and calls it directly.

Closed polymorphism with an enum: the fixed set of workflow commands. The variant set is closed and known inside one crate, so an enum (enum Command { ... }) plus an exhaustive match is the right shape. The compiler then enforces that every command is handled, and adding a command becomes a compile-time repair rather than a runtime surprise. There is no need to box anything or pay for a vtable.

Open polymorphism with a trait: the payment service with swappable fraud checks. There are several semantically real implementations (a rules-based check, a model-based check, a third-party check), and code wants to ask for the capability without naming one concrete type too early. A FraudCheck trait with a generic bound (fn run<C: FraudCheck>(check: &C, ...)) expresses this with static dispatch where the concrete check is fixed per call site.

Runtime trait objects: the deployment-time plugin registry for exporters. This is the one case that truly needs dyn. The set of exporters is open across time and deployment, and a single registry must hold several concrete exporters at once in one collection, selected from configuration. That requires runtime heterogeneity in a homogeneous container, which is exactly what Vec<Box<dyn Exporter>> provides. The justification is operational, not abstract: exporters are chosen at deployment, registered into one map, and dispatched at run time, so the choice cannot be resolved at compile time.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Open vs closed is drawn explicitly: the command set is closed (enum), the exporter set is open across deployment (dyn).
  • Composition is chosen for the retry helper because no implementation actually varies, so no polymorphism is needed.
  • The exporter-registry choice is justified by runtime and deployment behavior (one registry holds heterogeneous exporters selected from configuration), not by vocabulary.
Exercise 2code reading

Collapse an inheritance tree into Rust pieces

The base class BaseNotifier fused two unrelated concerns: shared state (the metrics fields) and replaceable behavior (the act of sending). Rust wants those split. The shared metrics and configuration belong in a composed component, not in a parent type. Model them as a plain struct such as NotifierMetrics { sent: usize, failed: usize } (and a separate config struct if there is configuration) that any notifier owns as a field. There is no inherited state and no partially initialized parent, so the metrics object is constructed and tested on its own.

The replaceable behavior belongs in a trait: trait Notifier { fn send(&self, msg: &Message) -> Result<(), SendError>; }. EmailNotifier, SlackNotifier, and WebhookNotifier each implement it with their own storage. Crucially the trait carries no data fields, so each implementor chooses its own configuration shape (SMTP host, Slack token, webhook URL) without a shared base forcing a common layout. This is the chapter's point that a trait describes behavior while data reuse comes from ordinary fields.

Notifier selection at the call site depends on the boundary. If a given code path always uses one notifier type fixed at compile time, use a generic bound (fn dispatch<N: Notifier>(n: &N, ...)) for static dispatch and zero indirection. If one registry or sink list must hold several notifier kinds at once selected from configuration, that is genuine runtime heterogeneity and wants Vec<Box<dyn Notifier>>. If instead the full set of notifier kinds is closed and known in this crate and you simply want to dispatch among them, an enum Notifier { Email(..), Slack(..), Webhook(..) } with a match is the calmest choice. Choose from the boundary's needs, not from the habit of one base type.

Encapsulation no longer lives in protected fields. It lives in the module boundary: put the metrics struct and the notifier types in a notify module, keep their fields private, and expose only constructors and methods. The public surface is the contract; the internal layout stays free to change. That gives tighter encapsulation than a protected-member hierarchy because the exported API is narrower and deliberate.

mod notify {
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct Metrics {
        sent: usize,
        failed: usize,
    }

    impl Metrics {
        pub fn record_sent(&mut self) {
            self.sent += 1;
        }
        pub fn record_failed(&mut self) {
            self.failed += 1;
        }
        pub fn sent(&self) -> usize {
            self.sent
        }
    }

    // Behavior is a trait, carrying no shared data fields.
    pub trait Notifier {
        fn send(&self, msg: &str) -> Result<(), String>;
    }

    // Each implementor owns its own configuration shape.
    pub struct EmailNotifier {
        pub host: String,
    }
    pub struct SlackNotifier {
        pub token: String,
    }
    pub struct WebhookNotifier {
        pub url: String,
    }

    impl Notifier for EmailNotifier {
        fn send(&self, msg: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
            Ok(format!("email via {} :: {}", self.host, msg).len() as usize)
                .map(|_| ())
        }
    }
    impl Notifier for SlackNotifier {
        fn send(&self, msg: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
            let _ = (&self.token, msg);
            Ok(())
        }
    }
    impl Notifier for WebhookNotifier {
        fn send(&self, msg: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
            let _ = (&self.url, msg);
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}

use notify::{Metrics, Notifier};

// Shared state is composed, not inherited.
struct NotifyService<N: Notifier> {
    notifier: N,
    metrics: Metrics,
}

impl<N: Notifier> NotifyService<N> {
    fn deliver(&mut self, msg: &str) {
        match self.notifier.send(msg) {
            Ok(()) => self.metrics.record_sent(),
            Err(_) => self.metrics.record_failed(),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut svc = NotifyService {
        notifier: notify::EmailNotifier {
            host: "smtp.example".into(),
        },
        metrics: Metrics::default(),
    };
    svc.deliver("hello");
    println!("sent = {}", svc.metrics.sent());
}

Shared state composed as a Metrics field; replaceable behavior as a Notifier trait; encapsulation via the notify module.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Shared state (Metrics) is separated from shared behavior (the Notifier trait) into distinct types.
  • Traits, composition, modules, and visibility are each used for one job: trait for behavior, fields for state, the notify module and private fields for encapsulation.
  • Dispatch is chosen from the boundary: a generic bound for the fixed call site, with dyn or enum named for the heterogeneous-registry and closed-set cases.
Exercise 3implementation

Model closed polymorphism with an enum

When every variant is known at compile time, the enum is the point. Here a Transport enum lists the closed set of transports, and one dispatch function handles each variant with an exhaustive match. The data for each case lives inline in the variant, so there is no boxing and no pointer chase to reach it, which is the concrete win over a base class plus derived types.

The handler returns a small owned String describing what it did rather than logging from inside each arm. That keeps the function pure and testable, and keeps the variant logic in one place where a reviewer can see every case side by side. Returning a value instead of performing a side effect is also what lets exhaustiveness do real work: the compiler verifies the match covers the full set.

The exhaustiveness guarantee is the design's backbone. There is no wildcard arm, so adding a Transport::Quic variant later does not silently fall through to a default; it produces a compile error at the match, forcing a visible repair at exactly the operation that must handle the new case. That is the difference the chapter draws between an enum and trait objects for a closed set: the gain is not just avoiding a vtable, it is exhaustiveness and simpler review.

enum Transport {
    Http { host: String, port: u16 },
    Grpc { endpoint: String },
    InMemory,
}

fn dispatch(t: &Transport, payload: &str) -> String {
    match t {
        Transport::Http { host, port } => {
            format!("HTTP {host}:{port} <- {payload}")
        }
        Transport::Grpc { endpoint } => {
            format!("gRPC {endpoint} <- {payload}")
        }
        Transport::InMemory => {
            format!("in-memory <- {payload}")
        }
        // No wildcard arm: a new variant breaks compilation here,
        // which is exactly the visible repair we want.
    }
}

fn main() {
    let transports = [
        Transport::Http {
            host: "api.example".into(),
            port: 443,
        },
        Transport::Grpc {
            endpoint: "svc:50051".into(),
        },
        Transport::InMemory,
    ];

    for t in &transports {
        println!("{}", dispatch(t, "ping"));
    }
}

A closed Transport enum with inline data; one exhaustive match handles every variant with no wildcard.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The design uses an enum with inline variant data, not Box<dyn Trait>, for the closed set.
  • dispatch handles every variant with a single exhaustive match.
  • The match has no wildcard arm, so adding Transport::Quic forces a compile-time repair in dispatch.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair encapsulation after a direct OOP port

The defect is that the port made every field pub so downstream code could mutate state the way subclass code once mutated protected members. A public field is an API promise, not a temporary shortcut: every pub field permanently allows outside code to set the value to anything, including states that break the type's invariants. The port effectively published its internal representation as its contract.

The fields that carry invariants must become private immediately. In an Account, the balance, currency, and id should be private to the module. They cannot be exposed for direct mutation because outside code could then set a negative balance or change the currency mid-stream, breaking exactly the invariants the type exists to hold. Their values are still useful, so expose them through read-only accessor methods (balance(), currency()) and a checked constructor (Account::open).

Replace direct field mutation with operations that preserve the invariant. Instead of account.balance = new_value, provide deposit(&mut self, amount) and withdraw(&mut self, amount) -> Result<(), Error> that enforce the rules in one place. The externally useful operations survive; only the unchecked write path disappears. Finally, narrow the module surface: rather than pub mod over internal submodules, keep the submodules private and re-export only the chosen types and functions with pub use, so callers reach a deliberately small API rather than the full internal tree.

This is encapsulation repair, not style cleanup. The change moves representation behind a boundary so the type can keep its invariants and so the internal layout stays free to change without breaking callers. The chapter's framing applies directly: the public surface is the contract, and the internal layout is still allowed to change only because it is no longer part of that contract.

mod accounts {
    mod internal {
        // Internal representation stays private to the submodule.
        pub struct Ledger {
            pub entries: Vec<i64>,
        }
    }

    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub enum AccountError {
        Overdraw,
    }

    pub struct Account {
        // Was pub everywhere; now private so invariants hold.
        id: u64,
        balance_cents: i64,
        currency: &'static str,
    }

    impl Account {
        // Narrow constructor replaces direct field assignment.
        pub fn open(id: u64, currency: &'static str) -> Self {
            Self {
                id,
                balance_cents: 0,
                currency,
            }
        }

        pub fn id(&self) -> u64 {
            self.id
        }
        pub fn balance_cents(&self) -> i64 {
            self.balance_cents
        }
        pub fn currency(&self) -> &'static str {
            self.currency
        }

        // Checked operation replaces `account.balance = x`.
        pub fn deposit(&mut self, cents: i64) {
            self.balance_cents += cents;
        }

        pub fn withdraw(&mut self, cents: i64) -> Result<(), AccountError> {
            if cents > self.balance_cents {
                return Err(AccountError::Overdraw);
            }
            self.balance_cents -= cents;
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}

// Re-export a narrow public API rather than the internal tree.
pub use accounts::{Account, AccountError};

fn main() {
    let mut acct = Account::open(7, "USD");
    acct.deposit(1250);
    let _ = acct.withdraw(2000); // returns Err(Overdraw), invariant held
    println!(
        "id = {} balance = {} {}",
        acct.id(),
        acct.balance_cents(),
        acct.currency()
    );
}

Fields made private, mutation replaced by checked deposit/withdraw, and a narrow public API re-exported.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Representation fields (id, balance, currency) move behind private visibility and a private internal submodule.
  • Useful operations survive as a checked constructor and deposit/withdraw methods instead of public field writes.
  • The change is framed as encapsulation repair: a public field is a permanent API promise, so making it private protects invariants and frees the layout to change.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Refactor a state machine into Rust-native transitions

The defect is a representation that can encode impossible states. With status: String plus approved: bool and published: bool, the type permits combinations the domain forbids: published = true while status = "draft", or approved = false while published = true. The booleans and the string are independent fields, so nothing structurally prevents a contradiction; every consumer must defensively re-check the combination, and a stale write can desynchronize them.

If the value's state varies at run time and the same variable can legitimately be in any state, model it as an enum and let each state carry only the data that state has: enum DocState { Draft, InReview, Approved, Published { slug: String } }. Now published = true while status = draft is simply unrepresentable, because there is no separate published flag; a document is Published or it is not, and the slug exists only inside the Published variant. Transitions become explicit methods that consume one state and return the next, so the only way to reach Published is to call publish on an Approved value.

Typestate is the stronger choice when the transitions are compile-time linear and the API is the thing you are protecting: each phase is a distinct type (DraftPost, ReviewPost, PublishedPost), and a method that needs a published post takes a PublishedPost by type, so a caller cannot even name a draft where a published value is required. The cost is that typestate makes a value's phase part of its type, which is excellent for linear API-facing flows but awkward when something must hold a document of unknown current state in a collection. The chapter's rule decides it: if the same runtime value can be in several states (for example a heterogeneous list of documents in mixed phases), start with an enum; if callers should only ever hold valid phase-specific types across a linear API, prefer typestate.

Either way the redesign prevents the contradiction structurally rather than by validation. The enum prevents it because there is no flag to desynchronize; the slug lives only in Published. Typestate prevents it because a draft and a published post are different types, so published = true while status = draft cannot be constructed at all.

// Runtime state that can vary: enum, with data living only where it is valid.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum DocState {
    Draft,
    InReview,
    Approved,
    Published { slug: String },
}

struct Document {
    title: String,
    state: DocState,
}

impl Document {
    fn new(title: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            title: title.to_string(),
            state: DocState::Draft,
        }
    }

    // One explicit transition: Approved -> Published, deriving the slug.
    fn publish(&mut self) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
        match self.state {
            DocState::Approved => {
                let slug = self.title.to_lowercase().replace(' ', "-");
                self.state = DocState::Published { slug };
                Ok(())
            }
            // Cannot publish a draft: the contradiction is unreachable.
            _ => Err("only an approved document can be published"),
        }
    }

    fn is_published(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.state, DocState::Published { .. })
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut doc = Document::new("Rust OOP");
    // doc is Draft; publishing now is rejected, not silently allowed.
    let early = doc.publish();
    doc.state = DocState::Approved;
    doc.publish().unwrap();
    println!("early = {:?} published = {}", early.is_err(), doc.is_published());
}

DocState enum makes published-while-draft unrepresentable; publish is an explicit Approved -> Published transition.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Impossible flag combinations are eliminated: there is no separate published flag, so published-while-draft cannot be encoded.
  • Enum is chosen for the varying runtime value, with typestate named as the stronger option for linear API-facing flows, each with a reason.
  • The Approved -> Published transition is written explicitly as a method that derives the slug, not as ad hoc field mutation.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose enums, traits, trait objects, and typestate across one service platform

The pipeline ingest -> validate -> enrich -> route -> persist -> export legitimately uses several modeling styles at once. The job of the design is to say which tool fits each boundary.

Closed variant sets, modeled as enums. The fixed set of input commands is closed and known in-crate, so enum Command { ... } with an exhaustive match drives ingest and validate. Routing decisions over a known set of destinations are also enum-shaped (enum Route { Persist, DropInvalid, Quarantine }). The domain justification is that these sets are defined by the system's own contract, not by third parties: a new command is a deliberate change to the platform, and exhaustiveness turns that change into a compile-time repair across every handler rather than a runtime gap. The data for each command lives inline, so there is no boxing on the hot ingest path.

Open plugin seams, modeled as traits and trait objects. Exporters are pluggable and chosen at deployment, and one registry must hold several concrete exporters at once, so the export stage uses trait Exporter with a Vec<Box<dyn Exporter>> registry. This is the runtime-dispatch boundary, and its justification is operational: exporters are registered from configuration at startup, the set differs per deployment, and a single loop must drive all of them, which cannot be resolved at compile time. Where a stage instead has a single implementation fixed per build (for example the enrich enrichment source in a given binary), a trait with a generic bound gives the same abstraction with static dispatch and no vtable.

Plain composition, no polymorphism. The persist stage and the pipeline wiring itself are mostly composition: a Pipeline struct owns a validator, an enricher, a router, a persistence handle, and the exporter registry as named fields. None of those need to vary polymorphically just to be held together; they are dependencies the pipeline owns directly, visible and individually testable. Cross-cutting helpers such as the retry policy and metrics recorder are likewise composed fields, not a base class.

The operator rule workflow (author -> review -> publish) is a closed, linear, API-facing lifecycle, which is the strongest case for typestate: DraftRule, ReviewRule, PublishedRule as distinct types, so a function that activates a rule can require a PublishedRule and a draft cannot be passed where an active rule is expected. If instead operators browse a mixed list of rules in varied phases, an enum state is the better fit because one collection holds values in several states; the deciding question is whether callers hold one rule through a linear flow (typestate) or a heterogeneous set at once (enum).

Observability and testing hooks fall out of these choices. The enum command and route sets get exhaustive state tests, so a new variant fails the build until its handling and its test exist. The Exporter trait gets a plugin contract test that every registered exporter must pass (same input, asserted output shape), since the set is open and only the contract is guaranteed. And because routing and lifecycle transitions are explicit enum or typestate moves, each transition can emit a structured event, giving an event log that renders the document's path through the pipeline for after-the-fact debugging.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Closed set: commands and routes are enums with exhaustive matches.
enum Command {
    Insert(String),
    Delete(u64),
}

enum Route {
    Persist,
    Quarantine,
}

fn validate(cmd: &Command) -> Route {
    match cmd {
        Command::Insert(body) if !body.is_empty() => Route::Persist,
        Command::Insert(_) => Route::Quarantine,
        Command::Delete(_) => Route::Persist,
    }
}

// Open seam: exporters are a trait object registry chosen at deployment.
trait Exporter {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn export(&self, payload: &str) -> String;
}

struct JsonExporter;
impl Exporter for JsonExporter {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "json"
    }
    fn export(&self, payload: &str) -> String {
        format!("{{\"body\":\"{payload}\"}}")
    }
}

// Plain composition: the pipeline owns its dependencies as fields.
struct Pipeline {
    exporters: HashMap<String, Box<dyn Exporter>>,
    persisted: usize,
}

impl Pipeline {
    fn new() -> Self {
        let mut exporters: HashMap<String, Box<dyn Exporter>> = HashMap::new();
        exporters.insert("json".into(), Box::new(JsonExporter));
        Self {
            exporters,
            persisted: 0,
        }
    }

    fn run(&mut self, cmd: Command) -> String {
        match validate(&cmd) {
            Route::Persist => {
                self.persisted += 1;
                let body = match cmd {
                    Command::Insert(b) => b,
                    Command::Delete(id) => format!("delete:{id}"),
                };
                self.exporters["json"].export(&body)
            }
            Route::Quarantine => "quarantined".into(),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut p = Pipeline::new();
    println!("{}", p.run(Command::Insert("hello".into())));
    println!("{}", p.run(Command::Insert(String::new())));
    println!("persisted = {}", p.persisted);
}

Commands and routes as enums, exporters as a dyn-trait registry, and the pipeline as plain composition of owned fields.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Enums own the command and route sets, the Exporter trait object owns the plugin seam, and plain composition owns the pipeline wiring.
  • The exporter registry is justified operationally: heterogeneous exporters registered from configuration at deployment and driven by one loop.
  • The command and route enums are justified in domain terms: a contract-defined closed set whose extension is a deliberate compile-time repair.
  • Observability and testing hooks are named: exhaustive state tests for enums, a plugin contract test for exporters, and per-transition event logging.

Lab solution

The scaffold already encodes the lifecycle as typestate: DraftPost, ReviewPost, and PublishedPost are three separate types, and the only way to move between them is the consuming transition methods request_review and publish. Each method takes self by value, so the previous state is moved out and can no longer be used; a draft cannot be published directly because there is no publish method on DraftPost, only on ReviewPost. That makes invalid orderings unrepresentable at compile time rather than guarded at run time.

The only missing piece is in publish: the original code left the slug empty, which would make published print false. The fix derives the slug exactly where the PublishedPost is constructed, by lowercasing the title and replacing spaces with hyphens, so "Rust OOP" becomes "rust-oop". Because this is the sole construction path for a PublishedPost, the type can never exist with an empty slug, which is the typestate guarantee carried into the data itself.

In main, published = !published.slug().is_empty() is therefore true, and published.slug() is "rust-oop", producing the two expected lines. The let _ = published.title(); line simply reads the retained title so the field is used; the program compiles cleanly with only the standard library.

Example 15-S. typestate_workflow_lab.rs — Reference solution

struct DraftPost {
    title: String,
}

struct ReviewPost {
    title: String,
}

struct PublishedPost {
    title: String,
    slug: String,
}

impl DraftPost {
    fn new(title: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            title: title.to_string(),
        }
    }

    fn request_review(self) -> ReviewPost {
        ReviewPost { title: self.title }
    }
}

impl ReviewPost {
    fn publish(self) -> PublishedPost {
        // Deriving the slug here is the only way to construct a PublishedPost,
        // so a published value can never carry an empty slug.
        let slug = self.title.to_lowercase().replace(' ', "-");
        PublishedPost {
            title: self.title,
            slug,
        }
    }
}

impl PublishedPost {
    fn title(&self) -> &str {
        &self.title
    }

    fn slug(&self) -> &str {
        &self.slug
    }
}

fn main() {
    let draft = DraftPost::new("Rust OOP");
    let review = draft.request_review();
    let published = review.publish();

    let _ = published.title();
    println!("published = {}", !published.slug().is_empty());
    println!("slug = {}", published.slug());
}
Output
published = true
slug = rust-oop

Review question answers

What is the difference between open polymorphism and closed polymorphism in Rust design?

Closed polymorphism means the full set of cases is known at compile time inside one crate, so it is modeled with an enum and an exhaustive match; adding a case becomes a compile-time repair across every match. Open polymorphism means the set of implementations is extended later or across crates and deployments, so it is modeled with traits, using generic bounds for static dispatch or trait objects when one collection must hold several implementations at run time. The deciding question is whether the set of cases is closed and known, or open and extended over time.

Why does composition usually replace inheritance for shared state and shared helpers?

Rust has no class inheritance with shared fields, so a type cannot extend another to inherit state; instead a struct owns the components it needs as named fields. Composition grows data sideways as fields you can name, swap, and test one at a time, rather than downward through a chain of parents with hidden inherited invariants. This removes fragile base classes, partially initialized parent state, and unclear aliasing across broad object graphs, and it keeps every dependency visible, testable, and replaceable, including in tests that substitute one component.

When is dyn Trait the honest runtime model instead of an enum?

Use dyn Trait when the system needs genuine runtime heterogeneity: one collection or registry must hold several concrete implementations at once, and the set of implementations is open across time and deployment rather than fixed in one crate. Typical cases are plugins, strategy registries, sinks, and handlers selected from configuration, where the concrete type cannot be known at compile time. If instead the set of cases is closed and known, an enum is better because it keeps every case in one type, stores data inline without boxing, and gives compiler-checked exhaustiveness.

Why are enums and typestate often better than classical state-pattern objects in Rust?

A lifecycle is a closed set of states with a finite list of legal transitions, which an enum models directly with match arms that the compiler checks for exhaustiveness, so adding a state forces a visible repair everywhere it is handled. Typestate goes further by making each phase a distinct type, so a caller cannot even name a value in the wrong state, eliminating impossible combinations at compile time rather than guarding them at run time. The classical state pattern models each state as a boxed object behind an interface, which is still correct but needlessly dynamic when Rust's enum and typestate alternatives give stronger static guarantees with no boxing.

Where does encapsulation usually live in Rust if not in a base class hierarchy?

Encapsulation lives in modules, private fields, narrow constructors, and focused methods. The module boundary hides the representation, private fields keep invariants enforceable, and the exported API is the contract while the internal layout stays free to change. This often gives tighter encapsulation than a deep protected-member hierarchy because the public surface is narrower and more deliberate, and a module can re-export only the chosen types with pub use rather than exposing its internal submodules.

Chapter 16 · Domain-Driven Design in Rust
