Domain-Driven Design in Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the order-platform domain model from the chapter and make you handle each part with your own hands: classifying the building blocks, tracing the Draft/Submitted state machine, writing validating newtype constructors, defining the repository seam as a trait, pulling a leaked invariant back onto the aggregate, and designing a persistence boundary for an event-sourced aggregate. The throughline is the chapter's central claim: in Rust the domain model is not enforced by a framework, a base class, or a convention, but by types that refuse to hold an invalid value.

Work them in order. The early exercises pin down the vocabulary and the mechanics of value objects and aggregates; the later ones move outward to the repository trait, the difference between an anaemic and a rich model, and the ownership consequences of doing IO that may suspend. The lab is the small, self-contained version of the whole chapter: an Order aggregate whose invariants live on the model and whose value object rejects zero quantity at construction.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Place each building block inside the aggregate boundary

Sort the listed types into the three DDD roles the chapter uses. Quantity, MoneyCents, and Sku are value objects: each is defined entirely by its value, carries no identity, and rejects invalid local state in its constructor. Quantity::new refuses zero, Sku::new refuses an empty or whitespace-only code, and MoneyCents wraps a u64 amount. Two Quantity(2) values are interchangeable because nothing distinguishes them but the number they hold, which is exactly what makes them value objects rather than entities.

OrderId and CustomerId are identifiers. They are newtypes over a u64 whose whole job is to name a specific entity unambiguously and to keep one kind of id from being passed where another is expected. OrderId in particular derives Eq and Hash so it can serve as a repository key.

Order is the aggregate root. It is the entity that guards the consistency boundary: it owns its OrderLine values and the value objects they carry (Sku, Quantity, MoneyCents), and it owns the Draft/Submitted status that the submit transition advances. The consistency boundary it guards is the whole order — you cannot add a line to a submitted order, and you cannot submit an empty one, because those rules live on Order's methods and the lines and status fields are private to the aggregate.

The repository seam is the single door to persistence. The chapter's rule is that the repository loads and saves the whole aggregate through its root, keyed by OrderId — never an individual OrderLine. There is no repository for lines, because lines have no independent lifecycle; they exist only inside an order.

Order is an entity rather than a value object precisely because it has an OrderId. Two orders with identical lines and identical status are still different orders if their ids differ — identity, not value, decides equality. A value object has the opposite property: strip its identity away and there is nothing left but the value, so equality is value equality.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Quantity, MoneyCents, and Sku are named as value objects, OrderId/CustomerId as identifiers, and Order as the aggregate root.
  • The answer states the root owns the value objects and the order lines inside its boundary.
  • The answer states the repository loads and saves the whole aggregate through the root, keyed by OrderId, not individual lines.
  • The entity-versus-value-object distinction is stated: Order has identity via OrderId; value objects are defined only by their value.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the order state machine through submit and add_line

Trace the sequence against the ddd_order_aggregate listing. Start with Order::new, which sets status to Draft and lines to an empty Vec. Two add_line calls follow. Both succeed because the order is still Draft: add_line only rejects when status is Submitted, so each call pushes an OrderLine and returns Ok(()). The lines are now (BOOK-1, qty 2, 1500) and (PEN-9, qty 3, 400).

Next, submit. Because lines is non-empty, the empty-order guard does not fire; submit sets status to Submitted and returns Ok(()). If submit had been called on an order with no lines, it would return Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder) — that is the first thing the method checks.

The second add_line, called after submission, hits the guard at the top of the method: status == Submitted, so it returns Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder) and the line is never pushed. The order is now locked against further modification.

total_cents folds qty.get() as u64 times unit_price.get() over every line: line one contributes 2 * 1500 = 3000, line two contributes 3 * 400 = 1200, summing to 4200. The cast to u64 happens before the multiply so the arithmetic stays in u64.

The reason add_line only ever receives valid values is that Quantity::new and Sku::new run their checks at construction, before a line exists. A zero quantity or an empty Sku is rejected up front and never reaches the aggregate, so add_line does not need to re-validate them. The value-object constructors handle the local rules; the aggregate handles the aggregate-wide rule (you cannot modify a submitted order). Each layer enforces exactly the invariant it owns.

// Trace of the sequence against ddd_order_aggregate.
let mut order = Order::new(OrderId(1001), CustomerId(7));

// Draft -> add_line both Ok, lines now hold two entries.
order.add_line(Sku::new("BOOK-1").unwrap(), Quantity::new(2).unwrap(), MoneyCents::new(1500)).unwrap();
order.add_line(Sku::new("PEN-9").unwrap(),  Quantity::new(3).unwrap(), MoneyCents::new(400)).unwrap();

// Non-empty, so submit succeeds and moves Draft -> Submitted.
assert!(order.submit().is_ok());

// Now Submitted: add_line is rejected before pushing anything.
match order.add_line(Sku::new("PAD-3").unwrap(), Quantity::new(1).unwrap(), MoneyCents::new(99)) {
    Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder) => {} // expected
    other => panic!("unexpected: {other:?}"),
}

// 2*1500 + 3*400 = 4200.
assert_eq!(order.total_cents(), 4200);

// submit on an empty order would have produced Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder).

Predicted Results and total for the traced sequence.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • submit on an empty order is identified as Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder).
  • add_line after submission is identified as Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder).
  • total_cents is computed as 4200 (2*1500 + 3*400).
  • The answer notes value-object constructors reject local errors first, so add_line only ever receives valid Quantity and Sku values.
Exercise 3implementation

Add a Sku newtype with a validating constructor

Sku is a newtype over an owned String whose constructor is the only way to build a valid value. fn new takes &str rather than String so the caller does not have to allocate before the value is known to be valid, and it returns Result<Sku, DomainError> so an invalid code surfaces as a domain error rather than a silently constructed bad value.

The check is value.trim().is_empty(). trim() handles both the empty string and the whitespace-only string in one test, so "" and " " both fail with Err(DomainError::EmptySku). Only after that check passes does the constructor allocate with value.to_string() and wrap it in Sku. Allocating after validation, not before, means an invalid code never causes an allocation and never produces a Sku value at all.

The accessor as_str returns &str by handing back &self.0. Its lifetime is tied to &self, so the borrow is valid exactly as long as the caller holds the Sku, and no clone is made — reading a Sku is free.

The swapped-parameter bug the newtype prevents is passing the wrong string into a function that expects a product code. If both a customer code and a product code were raw String, the type checker could not tell them apart, and a call site that swapped them would compile and fail at runtime. With distinct newtypes, a customer-code String simply will not type-check where a Sku is required; the mistake becomes a compile error instead of a production bug.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Sku(String);

impl Sku {
    fn new(value: &str) -> Result<Self, DomainError> {
        if value.trim().is_empty() {
            return Err(DomainError::EmptySku);
        }
        // Allocate only after validation succeeds.
        Ok(Self(value.to_string()))
    }

    fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        // Borrowed from the inner field; no clone, lifetime tied to &self.
        &self.0
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum DomainError {
    EmptySku,
}

fn main() {
    assert!(Sku::new("").is_err());
    assert!(Sku::new("   ").is_err());
    let sku = Sku::new("BOOK-1").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(sku.as_str(), "BOOK-1");
    println!("ok");
}

Validating newtype: reject empty/whitespace, allocate after, borrow on read.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Sku::new returns Err(DomainError::EmptySku) for "" and " " and Ok for "BOOK-1".
  • The successful path constructs Sku(value.to_string()) only after the trim check passes.
  • as_str returns &str borrowed from self.0 rather than a cloned String.
  • The explanation names that distinct newtypes stop a raw String customer code from being passed where a Sku is expected.
Exercise 4implementation

Define a Repository trait and an in-memory implementation

The repository is expressed as a trait so the domain depends on an interface, not on a concrete store. The trait declares two methods. save(&mut self, order: Order) takes the aggregate by value because saving hands the whole order to the store; the store now owns it. find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order> returns a borrowed Option so a read does not clone the aggregate — the caller gets a reference into the store that lasts as long as the borrow of &self.

The in-memory implementation wraps a HashMap<OrderId, Order>. save inserts keyed by order.id; find delegates to self.map.get(&id). For OrderId to be a HashMap key it must derive Eq and Hash (it does in the chapter, deriving PartialEq, Eq, and Hash on the newtype), so two OrderId values hash and compare by their inner u64.

The payoff of depending on the trait rather than on the concrete HashMap is substitutability. The aggregate and the application services name only OrderRepository, never InMemoryOrderRepository or any database type. Swapping the in-memory store for a SQL-backed or remote implementation changes only which concrete type is constructed at the edge of the program; not a line of aggregate logic moves. The trait is the seam that keeps persistence outside the core language of the model.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// OrderId must derive Eq + Hash to serve as a HashMap key.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct OrderId(u64);

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Order {
    id: OrderId,
    // ... lines, status, etc.
}

trait OrderRepository {
    fn save(&mut self, order: Order);
    fn find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order>;
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct InMemoryOrderRepository {
    map: HashMap<OrderId, Order>,
}

impl OrderRepository for InMemoryOrderRepository {
    fn save(&mut self, order: Order) {
        // Key by the aggregate's own identity.
        self.map.insert(order.id, order);
    }

    fn find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order> {
        // Borrowed read; no clone of the aggregate.
        self.map.get(&id)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut repo = InMemoryOrderRepository::default();
    repo.save(Order { id: OrderId(1) });
    assert!(repo.find(OrderId(1)).is_some());
    assert!(repo.find(OrderId(2)).is_none());
    println!("ok");
}

Repository as a trait seam backed by a HashMap; reads borrow, saves own.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The trait declares save(&mut self, order: Order) and find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order>.
  • The implementation inserts by order.id and returns self.map.get(&id) from find.
  • OrderId derives Eq and Hash so it can be a HashMap key.
  • The answer states that depending on the trait lets infrastructure be swapped without touching aggregate logic.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Move a leaked invariant back onto the aggregate

The defect is an anaemic model. The Order has public lines and status fields and no behavior of its own; the empty-order rule lives in an application handler that checks order.lines.is_empty() before flipping order.status to Submitted by hand. The rule is correct where it is written, but it is in the wrong place. The bug appears the moment a second caller submits an order without copying that check: nothing stops it from setting status = Submitted on an empty order, because the invariant is a convention in one handler rather than a property of the type. An anaemic model invites every caller to re-implement the rule, and re-implementing it means eventually forgetting it.

The fix moves the invariant onto the aggregate. Order::submit performs the is_empty check itself and returns Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder) when the order has no lines, otherwise advancing status to Submitted. The lines and status fields are made private so no caller can mutate them directly; the only way to add a line or change state is through the aggregate's methods. This is how Rust puts behavior near state without inheritance — private fields plus an impl block, no base class required.

With the rule on the model, the handler shrinks to order.submit()? and an error path. It contains no domain rule, only orchestration: call the aggregate method and propagate whatever error it returns. The invariant is now enforced once, at the type, for every caller — there is no version of it left to forget.

// BEFORE: anaemic model, rule leaked into the handler.
// struct Order { pub lines: Vec<Line>, pub status: OrderStatus }
// fn handle_submit(order: &mut Order) -> Result<(), DomainError> {
//     if order.lines.is_empty() {                 // rule lives here, in ONE caller
//         return Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder);
//     }
//     order.status = OrderStatus::Submitted;      // anyone can flip this directly
//     Ok(())
// }

// AFTER: rule moved onto the aggregate; fields private.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Order {
    status: OrderStatus,   // private
    lines: Vec<Line>,      // private
}

impl Order {
    fn submit(&mut self) -> Result<(), DomainError> {
        if self.lines.is_empty() {
            return Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder);
        }
        self.status = OrderStatus::Submitted;
        Ok(())
    }
}

// Handler now holds no business rule.
fn handle_submit(order: &mut Order) -> Result<(), DomainError> {
    order.submit()?;
    Ok(())
}

Invariant relocated from handler to Order::submit; fields made private.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The empty-order check is relocated from the handler into Order::submit.
  • lines and status are private and changed only through aggregate methods.
  • The refactored handler contains no business rule, only submit() and error propagation.
  • The answer explains that an anaemic model lets every caller re-implement and forget the invariant.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose between sync and async repositories for an event-sourced aggregate

The Account aggregate holds no stored balance; its state is the fold of its event stream. The repository therefore deals in events, not in a materialized aggregate, and the store is remote and accessed asynchronously, which is the case the chapter's production rule was written for: if the repository method performs IO and may suspend, return owned data or an owned projection.

Load should return an owned Vec<AccountEvent>, not a borrowed slice. A borrow would have to be tied to something inside the store, but an async load awaits a network round trip — the future may suspend, the connection or buffer it read from may be released across the await point, and there is nothing stable for a &[AccountEvent] to borrow from that outlives the call. Returning owned events sidesteps the lifetime fight entirely: the caller holds the data outright and the store is free to do whatever it needs after the await.

The async signatures take &self and return a Result over owned data. load_events returns Result<Vec<AccountEvent>, RepoError>; append_events takes the new events by value and returns Result<(), RepoError>. Neither return type borrows from the store. Because the methods are async, calling them yields a future the caller awaits; the &self receiver is fine because the borrow lasts only for the duration of the await within the caller, and the returned Vec is owned and outlives it.

Rehydrate consumes the loaded events to rebuild current state. It starts from a fresh, empty accumulator and applies each event in order, exactly as Account::rehydrate does: every apply validates against the state built so far (a deposit before Opened is rejected, a withdrawal beyond the running balance is rejected), mutates the accumulator, and bumps version. Version follows the applied stream length — after folding N valid events, version is N — so it doubles as an optimistic-concurrency token: append_events can refuse to write if the store's current version no longer matches the version the aggregate was rehydrated at.

The accepted cost is the one event sourcing always charges. You gain a complete temporal history of domain facts, but you take on projection and migration work: read models must be rebuilt by replaying the stream when a projection changes, and an evolving event schema forces you to keep deserializing and upcasting old event shapes forever, since past events are immutable facts you cannot retroactively edit.

use async_trait::async_trait;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum AccountEvent {
    Opened { opening_balance_cents: i64 },
    Deposited { cents: i64 },
    Withdrawn { cents: i64 },
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct AccountId(u64);

#[derive(Debug)]
struct RepoError; // e.g. version conflict or transport failure

#[async_trait]
trait AccountEventStore {
    // IO that may suspend -> return OWNED events, not a borrow into the store.
    async fn load_events(&self, id: &AccountId) -> Result<Vec<AccountEvent>, RepoError>;

    // Append by value; expected_version enables optimistic concurrency.
    async fn append_events(
        &self,
        id: &AccountId,
        expected_version: usize,
        new_events: Vec<AccountEvent>,
    ) -> Result<(), RepoError>;
}

// Rehydration is a fold: fresh accumulator, apply each event, version tracks length.
// let events = store.load_events(&id).await?;
// let account = Account::rehydrate(id, &events)?; // version == events.len()

Async event store returns owned Vec; rehydrate folds the stream and sets version.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The design returns owned data (Vec<AccountEvent>) from the async load, citing that IO may suspend.
  • The async signatures take &self and return a Result over owned data, not a borrow tied to the store.
  • The answer states rehydrate applies each event in order and that version follows the applied stream length.
  • At least one accepted cost is named: projection rebuilds and/or event-schema migration.

Lab solution

The two TODOs sit on the aggregate where the invariants belong. Order::submit checks self.lines.is_empty() first: an empty order returns Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder); otherwise it advances status to Submitted and returns Ok(()). Order::total_cents folds over the lines, multiplying each quantity by its unit price — q.get() as u64 * price — and sums the results. The cast to u64 happens before the multiply so the arithmetic never overflows a u32.

Main builds a Draft order and adds two lines while it is still Draft, so both add_line calls succeed and lines.len() is 2. submit runs against a non-empty order, so it returns Ok and submitted is true; state then reports "submitted". The third add_line runs after submission, hits the status == Submitted guard, and returns Err, so blocked is true and no third line is pushed. Quantity::new(0) fails its own zero check at construction, so zero_qty is true.

The total is 2*1500 + 3*400 = 3000 + 1200 = 4200. Putting these together reproduces the expected output line for line: the value object enforces the zero-quantity rule at construction, and the aggregate enforces the empty-order and no-modify-after-submit rules in its methods — each invariant owned by exactly the type responsible for it.

Example 16-S. order_aggregate_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Quantity(u32);

impl Quantity {
    fn new(value: u32) -> Result<Self, DomainError> {
        if value == 0 {
            return Err(DomainError::InvalidQuantity);
        }
        Ok(Self(value))
    }

    fn get(self) -> u32 {
        self.0
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum DomainError {
    InvalidQuantity,
    EmptyOrder,
    CannotModifySubmittedOrder,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum OrderStatus {
    Draft,
    Submitted,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Order {
    status: OrderStatus,
    lines: Vec<(Quantity, u64)>,
}

impl Order {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { status: OrderStatus::Draft, lines: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn add_line(&mut self, qty: Quantity, unit_price_cents: u64) -> Result<(), DomainError> {
        if self.status == OrderStatus::Submitted {
            return Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder);
        }
        self.lines.push((qty, unit_price_cents));
        Ok(())
    }

    fn submit(&mut self) -> Result<(), DomainError> {
        if self.lines.is_empty() {
            return Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder);
        }
        self.status = OrderStatus::Submitted;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn total_cents(&self) -> u64 {
        self.lines.iter().map(|(q, price)| q.get() as u64 * price).sum()
    }

    fn status(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self.status {
            OrderStatus::Draft => "draft",
            OrderStatus::Submitted => "submitted",
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut order = Order::new();
    order.add_line(Quantity::new(2).unwrap(), 1500).unwrap();
    order.add_line(Quantity::new(3).unwrap(), 400).unwrap();

    let submitted = order.submit().is_ok();
    let blocked = order.add_line(Quantity::new(1).unwrap(), 100).is_err();
    let zero_qty = Quantity::new(0).is_err();

    println!("lines = {}", order.lines.len());
    println!("total cents = {}", order.total_cents());
    println!("state = {}", order.status());
    println!("submit ok = {}", submitted);
    println!("locked after submit = {}", blocked);
    println!("zero qty rejected = {}", zero_qty);
}
Output
lines = 2
total cents = 4200
state = submitted
submit ok = true
locked after submit = true
zero qty rejected = true

Review question answers

Why does Rust enforce a domain model through types that refuse invalid values rather than through a base class or runtime framework?

Rust has no inheritance hierarchy to hang shared domain behavior on and no runtime framework that validates objects as they are constructed, so the type system itself is where invariants live. A value object whose only constructor returns Result cannot exist in an invalid state, because the only way to obtain one is to pass the validation. This moves enforcement from runtime — where a framework or convention can be bypassed or forgotten — to compile and construction time, where an invalid value simply cannot be produced. The guarantee is structural, not procedural: there is no code path that yields a bad value to forget to guard.

When should an invalid state be encoded in a value-object type versus checked in an aggregate method?

Encode it in the value-object type when the rule is local and stable — it depends only on the single value being constructed, such as a quantity that must be non-zero or a Sku that must be non-empty. Check it in an aggregate method when the rule depends on aggregate-wide state — such as refusing to submit an empty order or refusing to modify a submitted one, which require knowing the order's lines and status. The chapter's rule is exactly this split: local and stable goes in the type, aggregate-wide goes in the method. Rust gives you both tools, and using the right one keeps each invariant owned by the type that has the information to enforce it.

What does primitive obsession cost a domain, and how do newtypes such as OrderId and Sku address it?

Primitive obsession is modeling domain concepts as raw primitives — every id a u64, every code a String — which erases the distinctions the domain cares about. The cost is swapped-parameter bugs that compile and fail at runtime, validation that has to be repeated at every call site, and logs and signatures that carry no domain meaning. Newtypes like OrderId and Sku wrap the primitive in a distinct type whose constructor validates once, so a CustomerId can no longer be passed where an OrderId is expected and an empty Sku can never be constructed. The small ceremony buys fewer swapped arguments, narrower traits, clearer logs, and a sharp boundary between internal and external identifiers.

What does it mean to say a rich model in Rust puts behavior near state and invariants without inheritance?

A rich model keeps the rules that govern data on the type that owns the data, rather than scattering them across handlers or a service layer. In Rust this means an impl block with methods alongside private fields: the aggregate's methods are the only way to change its state, so the invariants cannot be bypassed. There is no base class with protected fields and no inherited template method — Rust uses impl blocks, value objects, traits, and modules, each doing its own job. The result is the opposite of an anaemic model, where public fields let every caller re-implement and eventually forget the rules.

In an event-sourced aggregate, how is current state derived from the event stream, and what does the version count track?

There is no stored current state to read; the aggregate is rehydrated by folding its event stream into a fresh accumulator one event at a time. Each apply validates the event against the state built so far — a deposit before the account is open is rejected, a withdrawal beyond the running balance is rejected — and mutates the accumulator only when the event is valid. The version count tracks how many events have been applied, so after folding N valid events the version is N, mirroring the applied stream length. That count doubles as an optimistic-concurrency token: an append can be refused when the store's version no longer matches the version the aggregate was rehydrated at.

Chapter 17 · Refactoring Toward Idiomatic Rust

Refactoring Toward Idiomatic Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter are not isolated puzzles. They walk you through one coherent refactoring discipline: correct ownership and error flow first, fix data shape and API surface second, and only then commit to async or concurrency boundaries. Every exercise practices one slice of that order, so the panic-removal work in Exercise 3 and the lifetime work in Exercise 4 are deliberately upstream of the async-shell design in Exercise 6.

The payoff is operational, not aesthetic. A mature service accumulates panic-based parsing, public mutable records, borrowed return values, and late-added Arc<Mutex<...>> caches because each was a reasonable local patch on top of a ported C++, C#, or Go design. The solutions below show how to turn those review findings into small, verifiable changes that make the remaining clones, trait objects, and awaits obviously correct rather than merely fewer.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Refactor one module in three passes

The point of the three-pass order is that most lifetime noise and clone pressure are symptoms of the wrong boundary, not independent defects. If you fix the boundary first, those symptoms disappear on their own, which is why you sequence the passes instead of editing whatever you happen to see.

Pass one is the ownership-and-error pass. The panic-based config parsing belongs here: routine invalid input is not an exceptional condition, so it should become a Result with a named error rather than a panic that takes down the process. The borrowed return values also belong here when the function constructs new data, because a borrowed return is an ownership claim that the caller is coupled to some input buffer. You correct who owns what and how failure is represented before touching anything else, because every later decision depends on the answer.

Pass two is the data-model and API pass. The public mutable fields belong here: exposing a record's interior as public mutable state is a C#/Go habit that lets any caller mutate invariants, so you replace it with a constructor plus methods, or split a closed mode into an enum the type checker can exhaust. You do this second because you cannot design a clean method surface until you know which fields the type actually owns, which pass one settles.

The Arc<Mutex<...>> cache is what you deliberately postpone. It is an async-or-concurrency-boundary concern, and you cannot decide whether the cache even needs to be shared, cloned per task, or owned by a single actor until the ownership model from pass one and the data shape from pass two are settled. Polishing or removing that lock first risks designing the synchronization around a data model you are about to change. So the postponed item is the concurrency primitive: it waits until you actually know who holds the data across the await or thread boundary.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Panic removal and ownership/borrowed-return correction are placed in pass one, ahead of any style-only cleanup.
  • Model-shape work (public mutable fields, enum-versus-method surface) is pass two, explicitly separated from the concurrency-boundary work.
  • The Arc<Mutex<...>> cache is named as the deliberately postponed item, with the reason that its synchronization design depends on the earlier passes.
Exercise 2code reading

Name the smell by source language instinct

The goal here is to recognize which old instinct produced which shape, so the repair can be expressed in operational terms rather than as blame.

The panic! on bad input is the Go-style error-handling carryover. In Go you would return an explicit error value at every boundary, but ported code often loses that discipline and reaches for panic! as a stand-in for "this should not happen." Routine invalid input does happen, so the Rust-native repair is to return Result with a named error variant and let callers compose failures with ?. Operationally this turns a process-killing path into an ordinary value the caller can match on, log, or convert.

The BaseHandler-shaped trait with data spread across several structs is the C#-style hierarchy pressure. The instinct is to model variation as an inheritance tree with a shared base class and runtime type checks. Rust has no inheritance, so the repair is to split that pressure three ways: a closed set of variants becomes an enum the code matches on exhaustively, a genuine behavioral seam becomes a small trait, and shared data becomes composition rather than a base record. Operationally this replaces runtime downcasts and is-a checks with a match the compiler can prove exhaustive.

The clone-heavy read path and the long explicit lifetimes on every helper are the C++-style identity and pointer pressure. The clones come from treating every value as if it had stable identity that must be duplicated to be passed around; the lifetimes come from threading borrows through helpers that could simply take &str or return an owned String. The repair is to borrow on read paths that only inspect data, and to return owned values where the function constructs new bytes. Operationally, the read path stops allocating just to log, and the helper signatures stop forcing the caller to manage borrow scopes. These are three different repair shapes, and pretending they are one refactor is the mistake to avoid.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The panic! is classified as Go-style error handling, with Result/? as the named repair.
  • The BaseHandler trait and scattered structs are classified as C#-style hierarchy pressure, repaired by splitting into enum, trait, and composition.
  • The clones and broad lifetimes are classified as C++-style identity/pointer pressure, repaired by borrowing on read and owning constructed output; each repair shape is described operationally and treated as distinct.
Exercise 3implementation

Replace panic-based parsing with Result and an owned boundary

The defect is that the helper unwraps both the missing-input Option and the parse Result, so any caller passing None or a non-numeric string crashes the process. Routine invalid input is not exceptional, so the fix is to make both failure modes ordinary Result values that the caller can compose with ?.

The two failure modes must stay distinguishable. Missing input is an absent Option and is handled with ok_or, which converts None into a named error. Malformed input is a parse failure and is handled with map_err, which converts the parse error into a different named error. Keeping them separate matters because a caller often wants to react differently: a missing port might fall back to a default, while a malformed port is a configuration mistake to surface. Modeling them as distinct enum variants (ConfigError::MissingPort and ConfigError::InvalidPort) makes that decision a match the compiler checks.

The success path returns a plain owned u16. The function does not borrow from the input string, so the caller is never coupled to the lifetime of the raw config text. This is the owned-boundary lesson the chapter emphasizes: parsing takes borrowed input, but what leaves the function is a self-contained value. The function itself is small on purpose; the design lesson is that the boundary now states exactly how it can fail and exactly what it produces.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum ConfigError {
    MissingPort,
    InvalidPort,
}

/// Borrow the raw input, return an owned `u16`, and make both
/// failure modes ordinary `Result` values the caller can compose with `?`.
fn parse_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    let text = raw.ok_or(ConfigError::MissingPort)?;
    text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| ConfigError::InvalidPort)
}

fn main() {
    // Missing input is distinguishable from malformed input.
    println!("missing = {:?}", parse_port(None));
    println!("bad     = {:?}", parse_port(Some("oops")));
    println!("ok      = {:?}", parse_port(Some("8080")));

    // Composing with `?` in a caller that wants a default on missing input:
    let port = match parse_port(Some("443")) {
        Ok(p) => p,
        Err(ConfigError::MissingPort) => 8080,
        Err(ConfigError::InvalidPort) => panic!("operator typo in config"),
    };
    println!("resolved = {}", port);
}

parse_port borrows the input and returns an owned u16, with missing and malformed input as distinct named error variants.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • parse_port returns Result for ordinary invalid input instead of panicking via unwrap.
  • Missing input maps to ConfigError::MissingPort and malformed input to ConfigError::InvalidPort, so the two are distinguishable.
  • The lab variant of this function prints Err("missing port"), Err("invalid port"), and Ok(8080) for the three cases.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Reduce lifetime annotations by changing ownership

Both defects are ownership mistakes that surface as lifetime syntax. The fix is to change who owns the data, and the annotations disappear as a consequence rather than as the goal.

build_label<'a>(service: &'a str, route: &'a str) -> &'a str is the borrowed return that should become an owned String. The signature claims it returns a slice that lives as long as both inputs, but the body constructs new text (for example, format!("{service}/{route}")). You cannot return a borrow of a locally constructed String, so this signature is either a lie or forces an awkward workaround. The correct model is fn build_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String. The function makes new bytes, so it should hand back an owned value the caller is free to keep. Once it returns String, the 'a parameter and both annotated borrows vanish, and elision handles the remaining &str inputs.

The long-lived struct that borrows request fields into a cache should stop borrowing and start owning. A struct like struct Cache<'a> { key: &'a str, body: &'a [u8] } ties the entire cache to the lifetime of a single request's buffers. That is exactly the wrong model when the struct outlives the request, because a cache, queue, or async task boundary needs data that is independent of any one request's stack. The repair is struct CacheEntry { key: String, body: Vec<u8> }, copying the request-local bytes into owned fields at the point of insertion. The 'a on the struct, on its impl blocks, and on every method that touched it all disappear.

The framing that matters is that this is an ownership repair. The lifetimes were not noise to be deleted; they were the compiler correctly reporting that the code claimed to borrow data it actually needed to own. Changing the ownership model removes the claims, and the annotations follow.

// Before: a borrowed return that constructs new text, and a struct that
// borrows request-local data it actually needs to outlive.
//
// fn build_label<'a>(service: &'a str, route: &'a str) -> &'a str { /* can't return constructed text */ }
// struct Cache<'a> { key: &'a str, body: &'a [u8] }

// After: the function owns its constructed output, so the lifetime is gone.
fn build_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String {
    format!("{service}/{route}")
}

// After: the cache owns its data, so it is independent of any request's buffers
// and can safely cross cache, queue, or async boundaries.
struct CacheEntry {
    key: String,
    body: Vec<u8>,
}

impl CacheEntry {
    // Copy request-local bytes into owned fields at insertion time.
    fn from_request(key: &str, body: &[u8]) -> Self {
        CacheEntry {
            key: key.to_string(),
            body: body.to_vec(),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let label = build_label("billing", "charge");
    let entry = CacheEntry::from_request(&label, b"payload");
    println!("label = {}", label);
    println!("entry = {} ({} bytes)", entry.key, entry.body.len());
}

build_label returns an owned String because it constructs new text, and CacheEntry owns its fields so it can outlive the request.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • build_label is changed from a borrowed &str return to an owned String because it constructs new bytes.
  • The long-lived cache struct is changed from borrowing request-local data to owning String and Vec<u8> fields.
  • The explanation frames the change as correcting the ownership model, with the lifetime annotations disappearing as a consequence.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Remove unnecessary clones and narrow unsafe code

Both defects hide the real contract. A clone-heavy read path hides that the caller only needs to look at the data, and a vague unsafe boundary hides the precondition that makes the raw operation sound. The repair for each is to make the contract smaller and more explicit before optimizing anything.

The clone defect: a helper that clones routes only to log them takes ownership (fn log_routes(routes: Vec<Route>)) or clones internally, when logging only reads. The signature should borrow: fn log_routes(routes: &[Route]). Logging inspects each route, it does not consume or store them, so &[Route] expresses the real requirement and eliminates the allocation. Changing the signature to borrow is the fix; the removed clone is the result. This is the clone-audit move from the chapter: a clone on a read path is usually a sign the signature is claiming ownership it does not need.

The unsafe defect: a helper exposes a safe raw-pointer write API without documenting the precondition. The repair has two parts. First, shrink the unsafe region so it contains only the genuinely unsound operation, the pointer write, and nothing else. Second, move the precondition checks out of unsafe and in front of it, as ordinary safe code: validate that the index is in bounds, that the pointer is non-null and aligned, that the length covers the write. By the time control reaches the unsafe block, the safe code above it has already established everything the block relies on.

What remains is one unsafe block whose invariant you can state concretely: "the caller has verified that index < len and that ptr points to an allocation of at least len initialized elements, so ptr.add(index) is in-bounds and the write does not alias other live references." Naming the invariant this precisely lets the next reviewer re-derive soundness by checking the few lines above the block, rather than auditing the whole function. The smaller and more explicit contract is what makes the code reviewable; performance comes after.

struct Route {
    path: String,
}

// Before: takes ownership only to read for logging, forcing the caller to clone.
// fn log_routes(routes: Vec<Route>) { for r in &routes { println!("{}", r.path); } }
//
// After: borrow, because logging only inspects.
fn log_routes(routes: &[Route]) {
    for r in routes {
        println!("route = {}", r.path);
    }
}

/// Write `value` into `slot[index]`.
///
/// The checks below establish every precondition the `unsafe` block relies on,
/// so the raw write region is as small as possible.
fn set_at(slot: &mut [u32], index: usize, value: u32) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    // Precondition checks live in safe code, before the unsafe region.
    if index >= slot.len() {
        return Err("index out of bounds");
    }
    let ptr = slot.as_mut_ptr();

    // SAFETY: `index < slot.len()` was verified above, and `ptr` comes from a
    // live `&mut [u32]`, so `ptr.add(index)` is in-bounds, aligned, and the
    // exclusive borrow guarantees no aliasing live reference to this element.
    unsafe {
        *ptr.add(index) = value;
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    let routes = vec![
        Route { path: "/a".into() },
        Route { path: "/b".into() },
    ];
    log_routes(&routes); // no clone; caller still owns `routes`

    let mut buf = [0_u32; 3];
    set_at(&mut buf, 1, 42).unwrap();
    println!("buf = {:?}", buf);
    println!("out of range = {:?}", set_at(&mut buf, 9, 1));
}

log_routes borrows instead of taking ownership, and set_at moves bounds checks ahead of a one-line unsafe write with a stated SAFETY invariant.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • log_routes is changed from an owning signature to &[Route], removing the clone on the read path.
  • The unsafe region is reduced to the single pointer write, with the bounds and validity checks moved into safe code before it.
  • The remaining unsafe block carries a concrete SAFETY comment naming the in-bounds, alignment, and no-aliasing invariant the caller-side checks establish.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Refactor a synchronous service into an async shell with test seams

The design principle is a thin async shell around a synchronous domain core. Not every function in an async service should become async fn; only the boundaries that actually do IO or scheduling need to. Keeping the core synchronous makes it fast to test and benchmark without a runtime.

What stays synchronous: parse and validate. They are pure and CPU-local. parse turns bytes into a domain type and validate checks invariants; neither touches the network, disk, or a clock, so making them async fn would add no value and would force test code to drive a runtime to exercise pure logic. enrich is synchronous if it only transforms data already in hand; if it needs to fetch a reference value it splits, with the fetch becoming async and the pure transform staying sync.

What becomes async: load from store, persist, and notify. Each performs IO or scheduling, so each is the natural await boundary. The async shell is essentially async fn handle(...) that calls the sync parse and validate, then awaits the store load, runs the sync enrich, awaits the persist, and awaits the notify. The async surface is the I/O perimeter; the logic in between stays plain functions.

What must become owned: any value that crosses an await or a spawned-task boundary. After an await the original stack frame may have been suspended and resumed on a different thread, so a borrow into request-local data is unsound across that point. Move the validated, owned domain value (for example an owned Order with String and Vec fields, not borrowed slices) before the first await, and pass owned values into any tokio::spawn. The Send requirement is justified only when a future actually crosses threads: if you spawn the work onto a multithreaded runtime, every value held across an await inside that task must be Send, and that is the real reason to require it, not a blanket rule.

The test seams are traits the shell is generic over: a Clock for time, a Repository for the store, and a Notifier for delivery. Tests supply a fixed-time clock, an in-memory repository, and a recording notifier, so the whole pipeline runs deterministically without real IO. For observability, instrument each await boundary with a span or structured log carrying the order id and the step name, so a slow persist or a failed notify is attributable to a specific stage. The result is a service whose pure core is unit-tested directly, whose IO boundaries are swapped for fakes through trait seams, and whose async surface is justified boundary by boundary.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// --- Synchronous domain core: pure, CPU-local, runtime-free to test. ---

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Order {
    id: u64,
    sku: String, // owned, so it can cross await/task boundaries safely
}

fn parse(raw: &str) -> Result<Order, &'static str> {
    let (id, sku) = raw.split_once(':').ok_or("bad format")?;
    Ok(Order {
        id: id.parse().map_err(|_| "bad id")?,
        sku: sku.to_string(), // own the slice now, before any await
    })
}

fn validate(order: &Order) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    if order.sku.is_empty() { Err("empty sku") } else { Ok(()) }
}

fn enrich(mut order: Order) -> Order {
    order.sku = order.sku.to_uppercase(); // pure transform stays sync
    order
}

// --- Trait seams: the test injects clocks, repositories, notifiers. ---

trait Clock {
    fn now(&self) -> u64;
}

trait Repository {
    fn persist(&mut self, order: &Order, at: u64);
}

trait Notifier {
    fn notify(&self, order_id: u64) -> String;
}

// --- Thin async shell: async only at the real IO boundaries. ---

async fn handle<C: Clock, R: Repository, N: Notifier>(
    raw: &str,
    clock: &C,
    repo: &mut R,
    notifier: &N,
) -> Result<String, &'static str> {
    let order = parse(raw)?;        // sync
    validate(&order)?;              // sync
    let order = enrich(order);      // sync, returns owned value

    // In a real service these would `.await` store/IO calls; the owned `order`
    // is what crosses the boundary, so nothing borrows request-local data.
    let at = clock.now();
    repo.persist(&order, at);       // async IO boundary in production
    let receipt = notifier.notify(order.id); // async IO boundary in production
    Ok(receipt)
}

// --- Test doubles supplied through the seams. ---

struct FixedClock(u64);
impl Clock for FixedClock {
    fn now(&self) -> u64 { self.0 }
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct InMemoryRepo {
    rows: HashMap<u64, u64>,
}
impl Repository for InMemoryRepo {
    fn persist(&mut self, order: &Order, at: u64) {
        self.rows.insert(order.id, at);
    }
}

struct RecordingNotifier;
impl Notifier for RecordingNotifier {
    fn notify(&self, order_id: u64) -> String {
        format!("notified:order-{}", order_id)
    }
}

fn main() {
    // A trivial executor stand-in so the shape compiles without a runtime crate.
    let clock = FixedClock(1000);
    let mut repo = InMemoryRepo::default();
    let notifier = RecordingNotifier;

    let fut = handle("7:widget", &clock, &mut repo, &notifier);
    let result = futures_block_on(fut);
    println!("{:?}", result);
    println!("persisted = {:?}", repo.rows.get(&7));
}

// Minimal block-on so the illustrative example has no external dependency.
fn futures_block_on<F: std::future::Future>(mut fut: F) -> F::Output {
    use std::task::{Context, Poll, RawWaker, RawWakerVTable, Waker};
    fn noop(_: *const ()) {}
    fn clone(_: *const ()) -> RawWaker { RawWaker::new(std::ptr::null(), &VT) }
    static VT: RawWakerVTable = RawWakerVTable::new(clone, noop, noop, noop);
    let waker = unsafe { Waker::from_raw(RawWaker::new(std::ptr::null(), &VT)) };
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut fut = unsafe { std::pin::Pin::new_unchecked(&mut fut) };
    loop {
        if let Poll::Ready(v) = fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            return v;
        }
    }
}

parse, validate, and enrich stay synchronous; the async handle shell owns its Order before any boundary and is generic over Clock, Repository, and Notifier seams for testing.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • parse and validate stay synchronous because they are pure and CPU-local; only store/persist/notify are treated as async IO boundaries.
  • The Order value is made owned (String fields) before the boundary, so owned values, not borrows, cross await and spawned-task points.
  • Any Send requirement is tied to a real multithreaded spawn where values are held across await, not asserted as a blanket rule.
  • Clock, Repository, and Notifier trait seams enable deterministic tests with fakes, and per-stage spans/logs are named as the observability hook.

Lab solution

The starter code called raw.unwrap() and then .parse::<u16>().unwrap(), so passing None or a non-numeric string would panic and take down the process even though both are ordinary invalid inputs a config loader must handle. The fix replaces each unwrap with a fallible operation that produces a Result the caller can compose.

raw.ok_or("missing port")? converts the absent Option into an error: when raw is None the function returns Err("missing port") immediately, and otherwise text is bound to the &str inside. text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| "invalid port") then attempts the numeric parse, converting any parse error into Err("invalid port"). Keeping the two error strings distinct preserves the difference between absent input and malformed input.

This is why the program prints exactly the expected three lines. parse_port(None) hits the ok_or branch and yields Err("missing port"); parse_port(Some("oops")) gets past ok_or but fails the parse and yields Err("invalid port"); parse_port(Some("8080")) parses cleanly and yields Ok(8080). The returned u16 is an owned value, so the caller is never tied to the lifetime of the input string.

Example 17-S. parse_port_refactor_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn parse_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<u16, &'static str> {
    // Missing input is an absent Option: convert None into a named error.
    let text = raw.ok_or("missing port")?;
    // Malformed input is a parse failure: convert it into a different error.
    text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| "invalid port")
}

fn main() {
    println!("missing = {:?}", parse_port(None));
    println!("bad = {:?}", parse_port(Some("oops")));
    println!("ok = {:?}", parse_port(Some("8080")));
}
Output
missing = Err("missing port")
bad = Err("invalid port")
ok = Ok(8080)

Review question answers

Why is a three-pass refactor often safer than many small style-only edits?

Because most lifetime noise and clone pressure are symptoms of the wrong ownership or error boundary, not independent defects. If you fix the boundary first in the ownership-and-error pass, a large share of those symptoms disappears on their own, so you avoid hand-editing code you are about to delete. Many small style-only edits, by contrast, lock in the existing boundary and can entrench the very mistakes the refactor should remove.

What is the Rust-native repair for routine invalid input: panic!, sentinel values, or Result?

Result. Routine invalid input is expected, not exceptional, so it should be a value the caller can inspect and compose with ?, not a process-killing panic and not a sentinel like -1 or an empty string that the type system cannot enforce a check on. A named error type or error enum makes each failure mode distinguishable and lets the compiler ensure callers handle them. panic! stays reserved for genuinely unrecoverable programmer errors or broken invariants.

When does returning owned data simplify lifetime-heavy APIs?

When the function constructs new bytes or the value must outlive the inputs it was built from. A function that builds a new String via format! cannot honestly return a borrow tied to its arguments, so returning an owned String removes the lifetime parameter entirely. Likewise, a struct that crosses a cache, queue, or async boundary should own String and Vec fields rather than borrow request-local slices, because owning the data makes it independent of any one caller's buffer and erases the lifetimes that borrow forced through every method.

How do enums and traits divide closed and open polymorphism during a refactor?

Enums model a closed set of variants known at compile time, so the code matches on them exhaustively and the compiler proves every case is handled; this is the right tool for a fixed delivery mode or state. Traits model an open behavioral seam where new implementations can be added, so they suit a notifier, repository, or clock that tests and production both supply differently. A refactor of an inherited class hierarchy splits its pressure between the two: closed variation becomes an enum, and the genuine extension point becomes a small trait, with shared data handled by composition rather than a base class.

Why should async refactors usually return owned values across await boundaries?

Because an await is a suspension point: the future may pause and resume on a different thread, so a borrow into request-local data is no longer guaranteed valid across that point and, on a multithreaded runtime, would not be Send. Returning or holding owned values, such as an Order with String fields instead of borrowed slices, makes the data self-contained so it can safely survive the suspension or be moved into a spawned task. This also keeps the Send requirement honest: you require it only where a future actually crosses threads, justified by a real spawn rather than a blanket rule.

What makes a refactor more testable instead of only more abstract?

Introducing narrow seams that tests can substitute, rather than adding layers of indirection for their own sake. A small Clock, Repository, or Notifier trait lets a test inject a fixed clock, an in-memory store, and a recording notifier, so the synchronous domain core runs deterministically without real IO or a runtime. Abstraction that does not create such a substitution point, or that drags broad framework state into the seam, adds indirection without adding testability; the test is the measure of whether the seam was worth introducing.

Chapter 18 · Generics Instead of Templates

Generics Instead of Templates

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all turn on one idea: a Rust generic is a contract checked at its definition, not a stencil expanded at the call site. Each task makes you state where and when that contract is enforced, then put it to work — lifting duplicated helpers into one bounded generic, choosing between a free type parameter and an associated type, and pushing a length into the type with a const generic. The goal is to generalize on purpose and late, the way the chapter's decision order demands, rather than reaching for <T> as a reflex.

Throughout, keep the chapter's cost model in view. Monomorphization buys you runtime performance equal to hand-written code, with no boxing and no vtable, but it is not free at build time: every instantiation is a separate copy the compiler must produce. The bounds you declare, the slices you borrow rather than own, and the decision to generify a core crate at all are the levers that keep that cost in check.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

State the two checks at two times

A Rust generic is type-checked twice, at two different times, and the two checks have different jobs. The first check happens at the definition of first_key, before any caller exists. The compiler reads the signature, sees the declared bound where T: Keyed, and checks the body against that bound alone. Because Keyed promises fn key(&self) -> u64, the call item.key() inside the body is legal — the compiler does not need to know which concrete type T will be, only that whatever it is must satisfy Keyed. If the body tried to call a method the bound does not promise, that error would surface here, in the generic's own source, with no caller in sight.

The second check happens later, at the call site, when a concrete type such as Job is substituted for T. This check is trivial: the compiler only confirms that the concrete type satisfies the already-declared bound — that Job implements Keyed. It does not re-typecheck the body of first_key, because the body was already proven correct against the contract at definition time.

A C++ template defers all of this to instantiation. There is no contract to check up front, so the template body is only checked when a caller supplies a concrete type. If that type is missing an operation the body uses, the error surfaces deep inside the template body, triggered by the caller — a long, indirect message about the template's internals rather than the caller's mistake.

The check that reports a missing trait bound is the second one, at the call site, and it points at the caller's code: passing a non-Keyed type fails with an error that names the missing Keyed bound right where the call is made, not buried inside first_key.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States the body of first_key is checked once at definition against the declared bound T: Keyed.
  • States the call-site check only confirms the concrete type satisfies the already-declared bound.
  • Says a C++ template defers all checking to instantiation, so a missing operation surfaces deep inside the body at the caller.
  • Identifies that passing a non-Keyed type fails with an error naming the missing bound at the call site.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace which bound gates which method

Read the Batch<T> listing and notice that the bound is attached to exactly one place, and that placement is deliberate. The type Batch<T> and its impl<T> block declare no bound at all. new and len live in that unbounded impl, and they compile for every type T because they only touch storage: new takes a Vec<T> and wraps it, and len delegates to self.items.len(). Neither calls a method on an item. Storing a value and counting how many values you have never requires the value to do anything, so no trait is needed.

first_key is the only item that adds where T: Keyed, and it needs that clause because its body calls item.key(). key is a trait method declared on Keyed, so the compiler will only accept the call if it knows T provides it. The bound is the promise that supplies that knowledge. Without it, the body would not compile, because a bare T says nothing about what its values can do.

If you call first_key on a Batch whose item type does not implement Keyed, you get a compile error — not a runtime failure — and it names the missing Keyed bound at the call site, pointing at your code rather than inside first_key. The body of first_key was already checked against the bound at its definition; the call-site check simply finds that your concrete type does not satisfy it.

Moving the bound onto impl<T: Keyed> Batch<T> would change which methods are usable, and for the worse. It would gate every method in that impl block — including len — on T: Keyed. Then you could not even count the items of a Batch whose element type happens not to implement Keyed, even though counting never needs key(). The chapter's rule is to keep bounds as narrow as possible: put the requirement on the one function that actually needs it, so unrelated methods stay usable for all types.

// Bound lives only on first_key, not on the type or the impl block.
impl<T> Batch<T> {
    fn new(items: Vec<T>) -> Self { Self { items } } // no bound: only stores
    fn len(&self) -> usize { self.items.len() }       // no bound: only counts
}

fn first_key<T>(batch: &Batch<T>) -> Option<u64>
where
    T: Keyed, // needed because the body calls item.key()
{
    batch.items.first().map(|item| item.key())
}

The Keyed bound is placed on the single function that calls a trait method, leaving new and len usable for any T.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies new and len as unbounded because they only touch storage, not item behavior.
  • Explains first_key requires Keyed because its body calls item.key(), a trait method.
  • States a non-Keyed item type produces a compile error naming the missing Keyed bound at the call site.
  • Notes that putting the bound on the impl would gate all methods, including len, on T: Keyed unnecessarily.
Exercise 3implementation

Turn a copied helper into one bounded generic

The two functions max_key_job(&[Job]) and max_key_task(&[Task]) are the same algorithm spelled twice: iterate the slice, read each item's key, and return the largest. The chapter's rule is to generalize only after a second real case proves the abstraction — and here it has, so this is exactly when to lift the pattern into one bounded generic.

First, give both item types a common contract. A Keyed trait with fn key(&self) -> u64 captures the one operation both functions rely on. Implement it for Job and for Task, each returning its own id-like field. Now a single generic fn max_key<T: Keyed>(items: &[T]) -> Option<u64> can call key() through the bound and serve both types. The body is one expression: items.iter().map(|i| i.key()).max(). max() over an iterator returns Option, so it naturally yields None for an empty slice and Some(largest) otherwise — no special-casing required.

Take the parameter as a borrowed slice &[T], not an owned Vec<T>. Reading keys never needs ownership; a shared borrow is enough to iterate and call key(). Borrowing keeps callers in control of their storage — they can pass a slice of a Vec, an array, or any contiguous sequence, and still own and reuse it afterward. Requiring Vec<T> would force callers to hand over ownership for a read-only operation, which is both wasteful and restrictive.

With this in place, both copied per-type functions are deleted; the single generic compiles once and the compiler monomorphizes a specialized copy for Job and another for Task, each as fast as the original hand-written version.

trait Keyed {
    fn key(&self) -> u64;
}

struct Job { id: u64 }
struct Task { task_id: u64 }

impl Keyed for Job {
    fn key(&self) -> u64 { self.id }
}
impl Keyed for Task {
    fn key(&self) -> u64 { self.task_id }
}

fn max_key<T: Keyed>(items: &[T]) -> Option<u64> {
    items.iter().map(|i| i.key()).max()
}

fn main() {
    let jobs = [Job { id: 10 }, Job { id: 22 }, Job { id: 8 }];
    let tasks = [Task { task_id: 3 }, Task { task_id: 99 }];
    println!("{:?}", max_key(&jobs));  // Some(22)
    println!("{:?}", max_key(&tasks)); // Some(99)
    println!("{:?}", max_key::<Job>(&[])); // None
}

One bounded generic over &[T] replaces both per-type helpers; max() returns None on an empty slice for free.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Signature is fn max_key<T: Keyed>(items: &[T]) -> Option<u64>.
  • Body calls item.key() through the bound and returns None for an empty slice via max().
  • Both Job and Task are served by the single generic with no copied per-type function remaining.
  • Takes &[T] and does not require ownership of a Vec<T>.
Exercise 4implementation

Replace a type parameter with an associated type

The starting trait Encoder<O> makes the output type a free generic parameter. That parameterization is wrong for this design because it allows a single type to implement Encoder<O> for many different O values — the trait says nothing about there being one canonical output. But every real encoder has exactly one natural result type: HexPair always produces [u8; 2], never anything else. When a related type is determined by the implementor rather than chosen by the caller, it belongs in the trait as an associated type, not as a parameter.

Rewrite the trait to declare type Output and return Self::Output from encode. Now the trait expresses the constraint directly: each implementor names its Output exactly once. Implement Encoder for HexPair with type Output = [u8; 2], and write the two-nibble body — split the byte into its high and low nibbles and map each to a hex digit.

The payoff shows at the call site. The caller writes encoder.encode(&[byte]) and binds the result; the output type [u8; 2] is fixed by the impl and inferred, so the caller never spells it out. With the free-parameter version the caller (or the compiler, ambiguously) would have to pin down which O was meant, because nothing in the trait fixes it.

So the rule is: a free type parameter is the right tool when one type legitimately implements the trait several times with different related types (for example Add<i32> and Add<f64> on the same type). An associated type is the right tool when each implementor has exactly one natural result type, because it fixes that type per implementor and keeps it out of the caller's vocabulary.

fn hex_digit(nibble: u8) -> u8 {
    match nibble {
        0..=9 => b'0' + nibble,
        10..=15 => b'A' + (nibble - 10),
        _ => b'?',
    }
}

trait Encoder {
    type Output;
    fn encode(&self, input: &[u8]) -> Self::Output;
}

struct HexPair;

impl Encoder for HexPair {
    type Output = [u8; 2];
    fn encode(&self, input: &[u8]) -> Self::Output {
        let byte = input[0];
        [hex_digit(byte >> 4), hex_digit(byte & 0x0F)]
    }
}

fn main() {
    let encoder = HexPair;
    // The caller never names [u8; 2]; it is fixed by the impl and inferred.
    let encoded = encoder.encode(&[31_u8]);
    println!("hex = {}", std::str::from_utf8(&encoded).unwrap());
}

type Output pins one result type per implementor; the call site uses encode without writing [u8; 2].

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The trait declares type Output and encode returns Self::Output.
  • HexPair pins type Output = [u8; 2] and encodes one byte into two hex digits.
  • The call site invokes encode without naming [u8; 2] anywhere.
  • Explains a free parameter would let one type implement Encoder many times, while an associated type fixes one output per implementor.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix the const-generic length error

There are two distinct defects, and both are caught by the compiler before main runs.

The first is the index in last(). An array [T; N] has valid indices 0 through N - 1, so the last element is at index N - 1, not N. items[N] is one past the end. For a const generic the compiler knows N at compile time, so it can prove the index is out of range and reject items[N]; the fix is to read items[N - 1].

The second is the constructor. It builds the window from a 4-element array literal while the type is annotated as N = 3. This is not a runtime panic and not a length that gets truncated — it is a type mismatch. With const N: usize, the length is part of the type: [T; 3] and [T; 4] are different types, just as Job and Task are. Passing a [T; 4] where the type says N = 3 is the same kind of error as passing the wrong struct, and the compiler reports it as a type mismatch at the construction site. The fix is to make N agree with the real element count — either annotate N = 4 (and let the array stay four elements) or pass a three-element array to match N = 3. The cleanest approach is to let N be inferred from the array literal so the two can never drift apart.

What this design removes, compared with a Vec-based window, is the runtime length check. Because the length travels with the type, an out-of-range length — or a window built with the wrong number of elements — becomes a compile error rather than a condition you discover at runtime. The array also stays on the stack with no heap allocation. A Vec would accept any length at runtime and only fail later, if at all, when some code reads past the data.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct FixedWindow<T, const N: usize> {
    items: [T; N],
}

impl<T: Copy, const N: usize> FixedWindow<T, N> {
    fn last(&self) -> T {
        self.items[N - 1] // was items[N]: out of range, last index is N - 1
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Let N be inferred from the array so length and type cannot drift.
    // Four elements => N = 4; the earlier `N = 3` annotation was the mismatch.
    let window = FixedWindow { items: [3_u32, 5, 8, 13] };
    println!("last = {}", window.last()); // 13
}

Index corrected to N - 1, and the length is inferred from the literal so N always matches the real element count.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Changes the index from items[N] to items[N - 1] for the last element.
  • Explains the length mismatch is a compile error because N is part of the type, not a runtime bounds check.
  • Corrected code constructs the window so N matches the array's element count.
  • States making the length part of the type turns an out-of-range length into a compile error rather than a runtime check.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Decide whether to generify the core crate

Recommendation: introduce the generic, because the second real case now justifies it, but scope its instantiations deliberately rather than letting twelve downstream crates each stamp out copies of code they do not need.

Start with the decision order. The chapter's rule is to generalize only when a second real case proves the abstraction, not as a reflex. JobBatch has lived as a concrete type while there was one item type, which was correct. Now a second item type genuinely needs the same batching logic, so the abstraction has earned its place — this is exactly the moment to lift it into a generic Batch<T> rather than copy JobBatch a second time.

The runtime payoff is real and free. Monomorphization produces a separately specialized copy of Batch<T> for each concrete item type, so each instantiation is as fast as the hand-written JobBatch was — no boxing, no vtable, no indirection. Generifying does not cost a cycle at runtime.

The price is paid at build time, and in a core crate it can be substantial. A generic that is widely instantiated forces the compiler to produce a distinct specialized copy per concrete type across every crate that uses it, which can dominate compile time and inflate binary size. With twelve downstream crates, a Batch<T> that everyone instantiates with several item types multiplies into many monomorphized copies. A generic in a core crate is therefore a contract you maintain plus a set of instantiations you pay to compile.

Concrete recommendation: add the generic Batch<T> in the core crate to serve the two types that genuinely share the logic, but keep the surface small. Keep bounds narrow so unrelated methods stay usable. Where a downstream crate's reuse is marginal — it only ever batches one item type and gains nothing from the parameter — leave it on a concrete type alias (type JobBatch = Batch<Job>) so the public API stays stable and that crate does not pull in extra instantiations. If a particular instantiation is heavy and used in only one place, consider confining it to the crate that needs it rather than re-exporting the generic for everyone. Generalize because the second case proved it, then limit who pays the build cost.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Invokes the rule to generalize on the second real case, not as a reflex.
  • States monomorphization makes each instantiation as fast as hand-written code with no boxing or vtable.
  • Identifies that a heavily instantiated generic in a core crate can inflate compile time and binary size.
  • Gives a concrete decision: add the generic but confine instantiations and keep concrete aliases where reuse is marginal.

Lab solution

FixedBatch<T, const N: usize> carries its length in the type: items is a [T; N] array, so N = 3 here is fixed at compile time and len() simply returns N without inspecting any data. The impl block is bounded by T: Keyed, which is what lets the body call key() — without the bound, item.key() would not compile, because a bare T promises no operations.

key_sum borrows the array with self.items.iter(), giving an iterator of &T. map(|item| item.key()) calls the trait method through the bound to produce each item's u64 key, and sum() reduces the iterator to a single u64. Because the items are read by shared reference, the batch keeps ownership of its storage and nothing is moved or cloned.

The program prints len = 3 (the const N) and key sum = 40, which is 10 + 22 + 8. The length comes from the type and the sum from the bounded reduction, so both lines follow directly from the inputs.

Example 18-S. fixed_batch_lab.rs — Reference solution

trait Keyed {
    fn key(&self) -> u64;
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Job {
    id: u64,
}

impl Keyed for Job {
    fn key(&self) -> u64 {
        self.id
    }
}

struct FixedBatch<T, const N: usize> {
    items: [T; N],
}

impl<T: Keyed, const N: usize> FixedBatch<T, N> {
    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        N
    }

    fn key_sum(&self) -> u64 {
        // Iterate the fixed-size array by shared reference and sum each
        // item's key. The Keyed bound on the impl makes item.key() legal,
        // and N being part of the type means the array stays on the stack.
        self.items.iter().map(|item| item.key()).sum()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let batch = FixedBatch {
        items: [Job { id: 10 }, Job { id: 22 }, Job { id: 8 }],
    };
    println!("len = {}", batch.len());
    println!("key sum = {}", batch.key_sum());
}
Output
len = 3
key sum = 40

Review question answers

At which two points is a Rust generic type-checked, and what does each check verify?

A Rust generic is checked at its definition and again at each call site. At definition, the compiler checks the body against the declared bounds alone — it verifies that every operation the body performs is promised by a trait bound on the type parameter, so the body is proven correct before any caller exists. At the call site, the second check is trivial: it only confirms that the concrete type substituted for the parameter actually satisfies those already-declared bounds. The body is never re-typechecked per caller, which is what makes generic errors point at the right place.

Why does Batch<T> declare no trait bound while first_key requires where T: Keyed?

Batch<T> only stores and counts items; new wraps a Vec<T> and len returns its length, and neither calls a method on an item, so no trait is required and the type works for every T. first_key, by contrast, calls item.key(), which is a method declared on the Keyed trait, so it must require where T: Keyed to make that call legal. The chapter's rule is to keep bounds as narrow as possible: attach the requirement to the one function that needs it, so storage and counting stay available for all types.

What is monomorphization, and why does it make generic code as fast as hand-written code at runtime?

Monomorphization is the compiler stamping out a separate, fully specialized copy of a generic for each concrete type that uses it. The copy for a given type — say u32 — knows it is operating on that exact type and can inline and optimize accordingly, with no boxing and no vtable dispatch. Because the specialized copy is indistinguishable from code you would have written by hand for that type, there is no runtime indirection cost; the only cost is paid at build time, in compile time and binary size for each instantiation.

When should you prefer an associated type over an extra generic type parameter on a trait?

Prefer an associated type when each implementor has exactly one natural related type, so it should be fixed per implementor rather than chosen by the caller. An associated type pins that type once in the impl (type Output = ...) and keeps it out of the caller's vocabulary, so callers never spell it out. A free type parameter is the right choice only when a single type legitimately implements the trait several times with different related types, since a parameter allows multiple implementations while an associated type fixes one.

What does a const generic such as const N: usize put into the type, and what runtime check does it eliminate?

A const generic puts a compile-time value — here a length — into the type itself, so [T; N] of different N are distinct types and the length travels with the type rather than being stored or checked at runtime. This lets the data stay on the stack as a fixed-size array, and it turns a length mismatch into a compile error: constructing with the wrong number of elements, or annotating the wrong N, is a type mismatch the compiler rejects before main runs. It eliminates the runtime bounds or length check that a Vec-based design would defer until the data is accessed.

Chapter 19 · Serialization and Data Contracts

Serialization and Data Contracts

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move from understanding a data contract to defending one under change. The chapter's central claim is that serialization is where a Rust program stops being a closed world of owned values and becomes one participant in a larger system: the moment bytes leave the process, the type layout stops mattering and the agreed external shape takes over. The exercises here exist to make that boundary concrete, first by separating the internal domain model from the wire DTO, then by reading a real versioned envelope, and finally by evolving it without breaking anyone.

The harder exercises target the two places this goes wrong in production. The custom money codec exercise forces correct fractional-digit handling so a contract cannot silently lose cents. The zero-copy and rollout exercises connect Rust's ownership and lifetime rules to operational reality: a borrowed view cannot outlive the buffer it points into, and a compatibility break is a deployment coordination problem, not just a code change. The lab ties it together with a version-tolerant decoder you can run without any crates.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Separate the domain model from the wire DTO

A data contract is the agreed external shape of the bytes that cross a service boundary: the field names, the tagging strategy, the encoding of values, and the rules for what a reader may ignore or default. It is distinct from the in-memory model, which is whatever type layout is cheapest and most precise for the work happening inside the process. The contract is what other deployments depend on; the internal type is a private implementation detail you can change freely as long as the conversion to and from the contract still holds.

Two concrete pressures push the wire shape and the domain shape apart.
