The first is evolution cadence and compatibility: the wire contract must stay readable by deployments you do not control and cannot redeploy in lockstep, so it changes slowly and only in additive, tolerant ways, while the internal aggregate can be refactored aggressively on every release. The second is representation: a public JSON API wants human-readable, debuggable text (money as a decimal string, timestamps normalized, legacy booleans preserved), whereas the domain wants money as a cheap, exact integer count of cents. Payload size and consumer mix add further divergence, an internal binary stream optimizes for bytes on the wire while a public API optimizes for clarity.

If a single struct serves both the public API and the internal aggregate, every external compromise becomes permanent core debt. A legacy boolean encoding or a decimal money string that one old API needed gets baked into the domain type, and now the precise internal unit is gone forever. Worse, the contract and the model can no longer evolve independently: a change demanded by an external consumer forces a change to the aggregate, and a refactor of the aggregate risks an accidental, silent contract break. Custom representation logic, decimal money text, compact IDs, legacy booleans, normalized timestamps, belongs at the serialization edge in custom serializers or a dedicated DTO, not in the domain type, so the internal unit stays cheap and exact and the conversion is the one explicit place compatibility work lives.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines a contract as the agreed external shape of the bytes, explicitly contrasted with internal type layout.
  • Names at least two divergent pressures: evolution/compatibility cadence and human readability, plus payload size and consumer mix.
  • States that custom representation (decimal money, legacy booleans) belongs at the serialization edge, not the domain type.
  • Explains that coupling lets one old wire compromise contaminate and permanently degrade the core model.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the versioned event envelope

Serializing the OrderEvent::Created variant with internal tagging produces a JSON object whose discriminant lives in a key inside the same object as the variant's fields. Because the enum is annotated #[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "snake_case")], the variant name Created is rendered as "created" and stored under the "kind" key. The whole envelope serializes to schema_version, event_id, and the nested payload object; trace_id is None and, depending on the format settings, serializes to null. The payload object is: {"kind":"created","order_id":"ord-7","customer_id":"cust-9","total_cents":4200}.

The internal tag lets a reader dispatch on the variant directly rather than guessing it from which fields happen to be present. Without a tag, a reader would have to infer that an object with order_id, customer_id, and total_cents is a Created event and that one with order_id and an optional reason is a Cancelled event, an inference that is fragile the moment two variants share a field set or a new optional field appears. The explicit "kind":"created" key removes that guessing: deserialization reads the tag, selects the variant, and then maps the remaining fields, which is both unambiguous and stable across additive evolution.

The #[serde(default)] on trace_id means a payload that omits the key entirely deserializes successfully, with trace_id taking Option::default(), which is None, instead of producing a missing-field error. That is exactly the forward-compatibility discipline the chapter prescribes: a reader survives an absent optional field by defaulting it. The version and identity information is carried by two distinct fields: schema_version is the explicit version carrier that makes the contract version visible in the data itself, and event_id is the identity carrier that names this specific event. Keeping both in the stable envelope rather than inside the variant payload means version and identity survive regardless of which event variant is nested inside.

// Serializing the Created variant of this envelope:
//
//   EventEnvelope {
//       schema_version: 2,
//       trace_id: None,
//       event_id: "evt-100",
//       payload: OrderEvent::Created {
//           order_id: "ord-7",
//           customer_id: "cust-9",
//           total_cents: 4200,
//       },
//   }
//
// produces (formatted for reading):
//
// {
//   "schema_version": 2,
//   "trace_id": null,
//   "event_id": "evt-100",
//   "payload": {
//     "kind": "created",          // internal tag, snake_case of `Created`
//     "order_id": "ord-7",
//     "customer_id": "cust-9",
//     "total_cents": 4200
//   }
// }
//
// On the round trip, the reader reads payload.kind == "created" and
// dispatches straight to OrderEvent::Created without inspecting which
// fields are present. A payload that omits "trace_id" entirely still
// decodes: #[serde(default)] supplies None.

The internally tagged JSON for OrderEvent::Created, with the "kind" discriminant inside the payload object.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Reconstructed JSON places "kind":"created" inside the payload object alongside order_id, customer_id, and total_cents.
  • States the tag lets the reader dispatch on the variant without inferring it from which fields are present.
  • Explains that a missing trace_id deserializes to None via #[serde(default)] rather than failing.
  • Identifies schema_version as the version carrier and event_id as the identity carrier.
Exercise 3implementation

Add a forward-compatible optional field

The additive, compatible move is to add the new field as Option<String> annotated #[serde(default)]. The Option type means "this value may legitimately be absent," and #[serde(default)] tells the deserializer to supply Option::default() (which is None) when the key is missing from the input, rather than raising a missing-field error. That single attribute is what makes the field invisible to existing readers and tolerable to new ones.

With the field present, a new-format envelope sets source_service to Some("checkout") and round-trips it back intact. An old-format JSON string that never mentions source_service deserializes without error into an envelope whose source_service is None. Because Serde, by default, also ignores keys it does not recognize, the reverse direction holds too: an old reader handed a new-format payload that includes source_service simply skips the unknown key and parses the rest. So the new field is survivable in both directions.

This change is purely additive and compatible in both directions, forward and backward. A new reader can consume an old payload (the absent field defaults to None), and an old reader can consume a new payload (the unknown field is ignored). The compatibility comes entirely from reader discipline plus the default: no producer needs to be redeployed first, which is precisely the property that makes additive optional fields safe to roll out without coordination.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
struct EventEnvelope {
    schema_version: u16,
    #[serde(default)]
    trace_id: Option<String>,
    event_id: String,
    // New, additive, optional field. Old payloads omit it entirely.
    #[serde(default)]
    source_service: Option<String>,
}

fn main() {
    // New-format envelope that sets the field.
    let new_envelope = EventEnvelope {
        schema_version: 2,
        trace_id: None,
        event_id: String::from("evt-100"),
        source_service: Some(String::from("checkout")),
    };
    let json = serde_json::to_string(&new_envelope).unwrap();
    let new_decoded: EventEnvelope = serde_json::from_str(&json).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(new_decoded.source_service.as_deref(), Some("checkout"));

    // Old-format JSON that never mentions source_service.
    let old_json = r#"{"schema_version":1,"event_id":"evt-001"}"#;
    let old_decoded: EventEnvelope = serde_json::from_str(old_json).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(old_decoded.source_service, None); // defaulted, no error

    println!("new source_service = {:?}", new_decoded.source_service);
    println!("old source_service = {:?}", old_decoded.source_service);
}

Adding an optional source_service field with #[serde(default)]; the old-format payload decodes to None without error.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The new field is Option<String> annotated #[serde(default)] so a missing key deserializes successfully.
  • An old-format payload lacking the field decodes into a value with source_service set to None.
  • A new-format payload sets and recovers Some("checkout") correctly via the round trip.
  • The change is classified as additive and compatible in both directions, with the reasoning given.
Exercise 4implementation

Write a money codec that does not lose cents

The serialize side mirrors the chapter's cents_as_decimal: format the integer cents as a decimal string with exactly two fractional digits using format!("{}.{:02}", value / 100, value % 100). The integer division gives the whole units and the modulo gives the cents, and the {:02} format ensures a value like 5 cents renders as "05", not "5", so 1250 cents always serializes to exactly "12.50".

The deserialize side is where the correctness trap lives. The function splits on the dot, then validates that the fractional part is exactly two characters before parsing. This length check is the whole point: the naive version that simply parses the fractional substring and adds it would read "12.5" as twelve units plus five cents, yielding 1205, and "12.500" as twelve units plus five hundred cents, both silently wrong. By requiring cents.len() == 2, inputs like "12.5" (one digit) and "12.500" (three digits) are rejected with a clear error rather than producing a wrong amount. The whole and fractional parts are parsed as u64 and combined as whole * 100 + frac.

Crucially, every failure path surfaces as a deserialization error, not a panic and not a silently wrong value. A missing dot, a wrong fractional length, or a non-numeric component all return Err via serde::de::Error::custom, so the caller's from_str fails cleanly and the bad amount never enters the system. With this discipline, "12.50" deserializes to 1250 cents and re-serializes back to the identical "12.50", a clean round trip that loses no money.

use serde::{de::Error as _, Deserialize, Deserializer, Serialize, Serializer};

fn cents_as_decimal<S>(value: &u64, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
where
    S: Serializer,
{
    // Exactly two fractional digits, always: 1250 -> "12.50", 5 -> "0.05".
    let text = format!("{}.{:02}", value / 100, value % 100);
    serializer.serialize_str(&text)
}

fn decimal_as_cents<'de, D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<u64, D::Error>
where
    D: Deserializer<'de>,
{
    let text = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
    let (units, cents) = text
        .split_once('.')
        .ok_or_else(|| D::Error::custom("expected decimal amount"))?;

    // The validation that prevents silently losing money:
    // "12.5" and "12.500" are rejected, not coerced.
    if cents.len() != 2 {
        return Err(D::Error::custom("expected exactly two fractional digits"));
    }

    let whole = units.parse::<u64>().map_err(D::Error::custom)?;
    let frac = cents.parse::<u64>().map_err(D::Error::custom)?;
    Ok(whole * 100 + frac)
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Payment {
    #[serde(serialize_with = "cents_as_decimal", deserialize_with = "decimal_as_cents")]
    amount_cents: u64,
}

fn main() {
    let p = Payment { amount_cents: 1250 };
    let json = serde_json::to_string(&p).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(json, r#"{"amount_cents":"12.50"}"#); // exactly "12.50"

    let back: Payment = serde_json::from_str(&json).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(back.amount_cents, 1250); // round trip to 1250 cents

    // Wrong fractional length is rejected, not silently mis-scaled.
    assert!(serde_json::from_str::<Payment>(r#"{"amount_cents":"12.5"}"#).is_err());
    assert!(serde_json::from_str::<Payment>(r#"{"amount_cents":"12.500"}"#).is_err());

    println!("serialized = {json}");
    println!("deserialized cents = {}", back.amount_cents);
}

A money codec that serializes 1250 cents as "12.50" and rejects any input whose fractional part is not exactly two digits.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Serialization formats 1250 cents as exactly "12.50" via format!("{}.{:02}", ...).
  • Deserialization rejects a fractional part whose length is not exactly two digits with the cents.len() != 2 check.
  • "12.50" deserializes to 1250 and re-serializes to the identical "12.50" string.
  • All parse failures surface as Err through serde::de::Error::custom, never a panic or a wrong value.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix a borrowed field that escapes its buffer

The compiler error is a lifetime error: a function that parses a locally owned buffer and returns a struct borrowing from it tries to hand back a reference that outlives the data it points into. The borrowed view, a &str or Cow<'de, str> field, is tied by its lifetime to the input bytes. When the function returns, the local buffer is dropped, so the borrow would dangle. The borrow checker rejects this at compile time: the returned struct's lifetime cannot exceed the lifetime of the buffer it was parsed from, and the buffer's lifetime ends at the function boundary. This is the pure-Rust catch the chapter warns about, zero-copy borrowing is free on a hot path but illegal once the value must outlive its input.

The fix is to decide which fields genuinely need zero-copy borrowing and which must own. On the hot path, internal to the parse, borrowing is fine and cheap; the BorrowedAudit<'a> with &str and Cow<'a, str> fields can be produced and consumed within the scope where the buffer is still alive. But the value that crosses the wider subsystem boundary must own its strings. The clean refactor is a paired owned type, an OwnedAudit with String fields, and a conversion that calls into_owned() on each Cow (or to_string()/to_owned() on each &str). A Cow<'a, str> exposes into_owned() precisely for this: it materializes a borrowed view into an owned String, after which the input buffer can be dropped safely.

The operational rule, in one sentence: borrow while parsing if it reduces copying locally, but own the data once the message crosses a wider subsystem boundary, because a borrowed view cannot outlive the buffer it points into. The hot-path parse may still borrow internally, the conversion to owned happens exactly at the boundary where the buffer is about to be dropped, paying one allocation per escaping string in exchange for a value that is safe to return, store, or send onward.

use std::borrow::Cow;
use serde::Deserialize;

// Hot-path view: borrows directly from the input buffer. Cheap, but its
// lifetime is chained to the bytes it was parsed from.
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct BorrowedAudit<'a> {
    #[serde(borrow)]
    request_id: Cow<'a, str>,
    #[serde(borrow)]
    route: Cow<'a, str>,
}

// Boundary-crossing value: owns its strings, no lifetime parameter, safe to
// return after the buffer is dropped.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct OwnedAudit {
    request_id: String,
    route: String,
}

impl From<BorrowedAudit<'_>> for OwnedAudit {
    fn from(b: BorrowedAudit<'_>) -> Self {
        OwnedAudit {
            request_id: b.request_id.into_owned(), // Cow -> String
            route: b.route.into_owned(),
        }
    }
}

// WRONG: returns a borrow into a buffer dropped on return -> lifetime error.
// fn parse_bad(bytes: &[u8]) -> BorrowedAudit<'_> {
//     let text = String::from_utf8(bytes.to_vec()).unwrap(); // local buffer
//     serde_json::from_str(&text).unwrap() // borrows `text`, which is dropped
// }

// RIGHT: borrow internally on the hot path, then own at the boundary.
fn parse(bytes: &[u8]) -> OwnedAudit {
    let text = String::from_utf8(bytes.to_vec()).unwrap();
    let borrowed: BorrowedAudit<'_> = serde_json::from_str(&text).unwrap();
    OwnedAudit::from(borrowed) // converts before `text` is dropped
}

fn main() {
    let raw = br#"{"request_id":"req-7","route":"/checkout"}"#;
    let audit = parse(raw); // owns its data, outlives the buffer
    println!("request = {}", audit.request_id);
    println!("route = {}", audit.route);
}

Borrow on the hot-path parse, then convert to an owned type at the boundary via Cow::into_owned so the buffer can be dropped safely.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Diagnosis names the buffer-outliving issue: the borrow's lifetime cannot exceed the input buffer's, which is dropped on return.
  • The refactor produces an owned type (OwnedAudit with String fields) at the boundary so the buffer can be dropped safely.
  • The hot-path parse still borrows internally (BorrowedAudit with Cow) before converting to owned.
  • The stated rule distinguishes local parsing (borrow) from values crossing a wider boundary (own).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Plan a mixed-version producer-consumer rollout

The rollout order is reader-first, because the safe moves are the ones an old reader can survive without being redeployed. Deploy the tolerant consumers before any producer emits the new shape. A tolerant consumer understands both the old and new field names and defaults the new field when it is absent, so during the window where some producers still emit the old shape and some emit the new one, every consumer can parse every live message. Only after all consumers are upgraded do you begin rolling producers to the new shape. At no instant does a live message reach a reader that cannot parse it, because the readers learned the new vocabulary first. Reversing the order, shipping producers first, guarantees a window where new-shape messages hit old consumers that reject them.

A field rename is made safe by retaining a deprecated alias during the drain window rather than renaming in place. The consumer is taught to read both the new name and the old name (in Serde, #[serde(alias = "old_name")] on the renamed field), so it accepts messages from both old producers, which still emit the old name, and new producers, which emit the new one. The alias stays in place until every old producer has been drained and redeployed; only once no producer emits the old name is it safe to delete the alias. A rename without the alias is an instant break, the new consumer cannot find the field an old producer is still sending.

The version boundary must be made visible in data, tests, and logs before mixed versions meet, because the most expensive serialization bug is silent contract drift that still compiles and deploys. Bump schema_version in the data so a consumer (and a human reading logs) can see which contract a message claims; add tests that decode both an old-shape and a new-shape payload, asserting the alias and the defaulted field both work; and log the observed schema_version distribution so the team can confirm old producers are actually drained before deleting the alias. Finally, route all of this through an explicit DTO-to-domain conversion layer: the wire DTO carries the alias and the optional field, the conversion translates it into the clean domain type, and the domain type never learns about the rename. That separation contains the blast radius, the compatibility shims live in one conversion function, the domain stays clean, and one old wire compromise cannot contaminate the core model.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

// Wire DTO: carries the compatibility shims. The field was renamed from
// `total` to `total_cents`; the alias keeps old producers readable until
// they are drained. `currency` is the new optional field, defaulted.
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct OrderEventDto {
    schema_version: u16,
    order_id: String,
    #[serde(alias = "total")] // deprecated alias, kept during the drain window
    total_cents: u64,
    #[serde(default = "default_currency")]
    currency: String,
}

fn default_currency() -> String {
    String::from("USD")
}

// Clean domain type: never learns about the rename or the alias.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct OrderEvent {
    order_id: String,
    total_cents: u64,
    currency: String,
}

// The single, explicit conversion layer where compatibility work lives.
impl From<OrderEventDto> for OrderEvent {
    fn from(dto: OrderEventDto) -> Self {
        OrderEvent {
            order_id: dto.order_id,
            total_cents: dto.total_cents,
            currency: dto.currency,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Old producer: old field name `total`, no `currency`.
    let old = r#"{"schema_version":1,"order_id":"ord-3","total":999}"#;
    let dto: OrderEventDto = serde_json::from_str(old).unwrap();
    let event: OrderEvent = dto.into();
    assert_eq!(event.total_cents, 999);
    assert_eq!(event.currency, "USD"); // defaulted

    // New producer: renamed field and the new currency field.
    let new = r#"{"schema_version":2,"order_id":"ord-7","total_cents":4200,"currency":"EUR"}"#;
    let dto2: OrderEventDto = serde_json::from_str(new).unwrap();
    let event2: OrderEvent = dto2.into();
    assert_eq!(event2.total_cents, 4200);
    assert_eq!(event2.currency, "EUR");

    println!("old -> {event:?}");
    println!("new -> {event2:?}");
}

A tolerant wire DTO with a deprecated alias and a defaulted new field, converted through one explicit layer into a clean domain type.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The plan deploys tolerant readers before producers emit the new shape, so old and new coexist with no unparseable message.
  • The rename keeps a deprecated alias (#[serde(alias = "total")]) readable until old producers are fully drained.
  • The version boundary is surfaced in data (schema_version), tests (decode both shapes), and logs before rollout.
  • Compatibility work is routed through an explicit DTO-to-domain conversion so the domain type stays clean.

Lab solution

The lab models version-tolerant decoding with no external crates: a payload is a semicolon-separated list of key=value fields, and the decoder is the tolerant reader the chapter prescribes. The completed match arm assigns each recognized key to its field, parsing schema_version and total_cents as numbers and copying the two string fields. The decisive detail is that currency is initialized to a default of "USD" as a mutable binding before the loop, so a payload that omits the currency field leaves the default in place. This is the forward-compatibility rule in plain Rust: a v2 reader supplies a default for a field that v1 writers never emit.

The two backward-compatibility behaviors both fall out of the match. The catch-all arm _ => {} silently ignores any key the reader does not recognize, so the v1 payload's unknown region=eu field is skipped rather than treated as an error. And because the loop only overwrites a field when its key actually appears, an absent field keeps its initialized value. The v2 round trip therefore reconstructs an identical Record (round_trip == v2 is true), proving encode and decode are inverses for a complete payload.

The printed output follows directly. The v2 case sets currency to EUR and round-trips exactly, printing the EUR line and true. The v1 payload sets schema_version to 1 and total_cents to 999, never mentions currency (so it stays USD), and carries an unknown region field that is dropped. The five lines printed are exactly the expected output: a new reader consuming an old payload, defaulting the new field and ignoring the unrecognized one.

Example 19-S. versioned_record_lab.rs — Reference solution

//! Forward/backward-compatible decoding of a versioned record.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Record {
    schema_version: u16,
    order_id: String,
    total_cents: u64,
    // Added in schema version 2. Old (v1) writers do not emit it.
    currency: String,
}

/// Encode a record as a tagged, line-oriented byte payload.
fn encode(rec: &Record) -> Vec<u8> {
    let body = format!(
        "v={};order_id={};total_cents={};currency={}",
        rec.schema_version, rec.order_id, rec.total_cents, rec.currency
    );
    body.into_bytes()
}

/// Decode a payload tolerantly: unknown fields are skipped, and a missing
/// `currency` field defaults so a v2 reader can still consume a v1 payload.
fn decode(bytes: &[u8]) -> Record {
    let text = String::from_utf8(bytes.to_vec()).unwrap();
    let mut schema_version = 0u16;
    let mut order_id = String::new();
    let mut total_cents = 0u64;
    let mut currency = String::from("USD");

    for field in text.split(';') {
        let (key, value) = match field.split_once('=') {
            Some(pair) => pair,
            None => continue,
        };
        match key {
            "v" => schema_version = value.parse().unwrap(),
            "order_id" => order_id = value.to_string(),
            "total_cents" => total_cents = value.parse().unwrap(),
            "currency" => currency = value.to_string(),
            _ => {} // unknown field: tolerated, not an error
        }
    }

    Record { schema_version, order_id, total_cents, currency }
}

fn main() {
    let v2 = Record {
        schema_version: 2,
        order_id: String::from("ord-7"),
        total_cents: 4200,
        currency: String::from("EUR"),
    };
    let round_trip = decode(&encode(&v2));
    println!("v2 currency = {}", round_trip.currency);
    println!("v2 round trip ok = {}", round_trip == v2);

    // A v1 producer omits `currency` and adds a field the reader has not seen.
    let v1_payload = b"v=1;order_id=ord-3;total_cents=999;region=eu";
    let upgraded = decode(v1_payload);
    println!("v1 schema = {}", upgraded.schema_version);
    println!("v1 currency = {}", upgraded.currency);
    println!("v1 total cents = {}", upgraded.total_cents);
}
Output
v2 currency = EUR
v2 round trip ok = true
v1 schema = 1
v1 currency = USD
v1 total cents = 999

Review question answers

Which schema changes are invisible to an existing reader, and which require the reader to be redeployed first?

Additive changes are invisible to an existing reader: adding an optional field with a default, since old readers ignore the new key and new readers default it when absent. Adding fields is safe in general because tolerant readers skip keys they do not recognize. Changes that require the reader to be redeployed first are the breaking ones: renaming or removing a field without a retained alias, changing a field's type or encoding, or tightening a previously optional field into a required one. The rule is that the safe moves are the ones an old reader can survive without being redeployed, so anything an old reader cannot survive must be preceded by deploying a tolerant reader.

What does internal enum tagging (#[serde(tag = "kind")]) give a reader that field-shape inference does not?

Internal tagging stores the variant discriminant explicitly in a key inside the same object, so the reader dispatches on the variant by reading the tag rather than guessing it from which fields happen to be present. Field-shape inference is fragile: it breaks the moment two variants share a field set or a new optional field shifts the apparent shape, and it forces the reader to encode brittle assumptions about presence. The explicit tag makes deserialization unambiguous and stable across additive evolution, the reader selects the variant from the tag and then maps the remaining fields.

Why must a borrowed &str or Cow<'de, str> field not outlive the input buffer it was parsed from?

A borrowed &str or Cow<'de, str> points directly into the input bytes instead of owning a copy, so its lifetime is chained to that buffer. If the value outlived the buffer, the reference would dangle, pointing at freed memory, which Rust's borrow checker forbids at compile time. This is why a function that drops its buffer on return cannot hand back a struct that borrows from it. The operational rule is to borrow while parsing if it reduces copying locally, but call into_owned() or otherwise own the strings before the value crosses a wider subsystem boundary where the buffer is gone.

Why is split-on-dot money parsing a correctness trap, and what validation prevents silently losing cents?

Splitting on the dot and parsing the fractional part without checking its length silently mis-scales the amount: a reader that accepts "12.5" as five cents reads 1205, and "12.500" as five hundred cents, both wrong, and the error is silent because the parse still succeeds. The fix is to validate that the fractional part is exactly two digits (cents.len() == 2) before combining it as whole * 100 + frac, or to scale by its actual length. Inputs with the wrong fractional length must be rejected with a deserialization error rather than coerced, so a malformed amount fails loudly instead of entering the system as a wrong value.

Why is a compatibility break a deployment coordination problem rather than only a code change?

Producers and consumers deploy on independent schedules, so at any instant during a rollout an old producer may send to a new consumer or the reverse, and a single struct edit that compiles cleanly can still break a live message in that mixed window. The break is therefore about ordering deployments and draining old versions, deploy tolerant readers first, keep deprecated aliases until old producers are gone, and make the version boundary visible in data, tests, and logs, not just about writing correct code. The most expensive serialization bug is silent contract drift that still compiles and deploys and only surfaces when mixed versions meet, which is exactly the failure a coordination plan exists to prevent.

Chapter 20 · Metaprogramming

Metaprogramming

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises build a single skill: choosing the smallest abstraction that solves a real duplication problem, and reaching for a macro only when syntax repetition is genuinely the thing being abstracted. The chapter frames the four mechanisms as a ladder you climb one rung at a time. Functions, generics, and traits cover variation in values, types, and behavior. Declarative macros cover small local syntax patterns. Procedural macros cover item-level generation. Build scripts and offline generators cover anything whose source of truth lives outside the crate.

The through-line is ordering. Macro expansion runs near the front of compilation, and every safety check you rely on runs on the output. A macro decides what code exists; it cannot decide what that code is allowed to do. Borrow checking, trait solving, and monomorphization all still happen after expansion. Keep that fact in front of you and most of the design questions answer themselves: if the friction is about ownership or types, a macro will not rescue it, and you have picked the wrong rung.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose function, generic, trait, macro, or build script honestly

The honest way to classify these is to ask what the caller is actually passing: values, types, Rust items, or an external schema file. The answer to that question selects the tool, not habit.

Joining two labels into one string is a normal function. The caller passes two values and gets one value back. There is no repeated syntax to compress and no item to generate, so fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String is the whole job. A macro here would be pure overhead: a larger API surface to keep stable, worse diagnostics on a typo, and no expressive win, because the call already reads exactly like a function call.

Removing repeated route-table item syntax is the macro_rules! case. Here the duplication is in the syntax of the declarations themselves, which is precisely what the chapter's route-table example demonstrates. A declarative macro lets each route stay a compact line that expands to ordinary Route structs in a Vec. This is syntax abstraction: the variation is not in a value or a type but in the literal shape of the source the author has to type repeatedly.

Generating impls from a type annotation wants a derive or attribute procedural macro. The trigger is that code should attach to a type definition and emit trait impls for it. That is item-level generation over syntax the macro inspects at compile time, which is exactly what a proc macro does and a macro_rules! macro cannot do cleanly.

Mapping several concrete types through one algorithm is a generics or trait problem, not a macro problem at all. The variation is in the type, the behavior is identical, and that is the definition of parametric polymorphism. A generic function with a trait bound expresses it directly, gets full type checking, and produces clear error messages; a macro would only obscure that the real abstraction is over types.

Generating a client from an external API schema belongs in a build script or an offline generator. The source of truth is a file outside the crate, so the generation should run where that file can be read at build time and the output reviewed as ordinary Rust. A public macro call site is the wrong fit because the schema is not Rust syntax the caller types, it is external data, and binding generation to a macro invocation would couple the build to that data in a place the type system cannot help you reason about.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The label-joining case is assigned to a normal function, justified because there is no repeated syntax to compress and a macro only enlarges the API surface and degrades diagnostics.
  • Syntax abstraction (route-table repetition, declarative macro) is separated explicitly from type abstraction (mapping concrete types, generics or traits) and behavior abstraction.
  • The external API schema case is identified as a build-script or offline-generator job because the source of truth is an external file, not Rust syntax typed at a macro call site.
Exercise 2code reading

Explain repetition and hygiene in a macro_rules! helper

Read the chapter's sum_values! macro, since it has exactly the shape this exercise describes: a repeated list plus a local accumulator.

The repeated syntax pattern lives in the matcher fragment $($value:expr),* and its mirror in the expansion $( total += $value; )*. The $( ... ),* form on the matcher side says match zero or more comma-separated expressions; the $( ... )* form on the expansion side says emit the body once per matched expression. That repetition operator is part of the pattern grammar itself, not something applied afterward. It is what removes the repeated accumulator code at the call site: the author writes sum_values!(1, 2, 3) instead of three hand-written total += ... lines.

The local accumulator does not casually overwrite a caller variable of the same spelling because of macro hygiene. In operational terms: the identifier total that the macro introduces carries a different syntactic context, a different hygiene mark, from the total the caller wrote in main. The compiler treats those as two distinct names even though they are spelled identically. So when main has let total = 40; and the macro internally does let mut total = 0;, expansion produces two separate bindings that never alias. That is why the chapter's example can print outer total = 40 unchanged after calling the macro. Hygiene is not the compiler vaguely handling it; it is a concrete identity rule that gives macro-introduced identifiers their own scope.

What still goes through normal checking is everything the expansion produces. Macros run near the front of the pipeline, but the Rust they emit is then handed to the same type checker and borrow checker as hand-written code. If $value were a String where total is an integer, the total += $value line would fail type checking after expansion, with the error pointing back through the span. Expansion decides what code exists; it does not exempt that code from type checking, trait solving, or borrow checking.

macro_rules! sum_values {
    // `$( $value:expr ),*` is the repetition matcher: zero or more
    // comma-separated expressions. The trailing `$(,)?` permits an
    // optional final comma so the call site can be list-shaped.
    ($($value:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut total = 0;        // macro-introduced `total`, its own hygiene mark
        $(
            total += $value;      // emitted once per matched `$value`
        )*
        total
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let total = 40;               // caller's `total`, a distinct identity
    println!("sum = {}", sum_values!(1, 2, 3)); // sum = 6
    println!("outer total = {}", total);        // outer total = 40, untouched
}

The $( ),* operator drives the repetition; hygiene keeps the macro's total distinct from the caller's, and the emitted += is still type-checked.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The repetition form is identified concretely as $($value:expr),* on the matcher and $( ... )* on the expansion side, and named as part of the pattern grammar.
  • Hygiene is explained operationally: the macro's total carries a distinct syntactic context or hygiene mark, so it is a different name from the caller's identically spelled total and the two never alias.
  • The answer states that the expanded Rust is handed to the same type checker and borrow checker as hand-written code, with a concrete example of a post-expansion type error.
Exercise 3implementation

Write a macro_rules! helper for repetitive checks

The macro should accept several name => bool pairs and return how many of them are true. The matcher mirrors the chapter's list-shaped macros: a repetition over $name:ident => $status:expr with an optional trailing comma so the call site stays compact and editable.

The body is a single hygienic block. It declares a local accumulator passed, then uses the repetition operator to emit one conditional increment per pair, and finally evaluates to passed. Because the block ends in the accumulator expression, the whole service_checks!(...) invocation is itself an expression that yields the count, which is why the caller can write let passed = service_checks!(...). The $name identifier is kept in the matcher to make the call site read like a labeled check list; the count logic only depends on $status, so the name is bound with stringify! to a discarded value purely for documentation. That keeps real business logic out of the macro: the macro contributes only the repetitive count pattern, not any runtime decision about what each check means.

This is the right scale for macro_rules!. The expansion is ordinary Rust, an integer accumulator and a few if statements, and the call site is plainly more readable than three or four hand-written increments. Nothing here reaches for procedural-macro power, because there is no item to generate and no type to inspect, only local syntax to compress.

macro_rules! service_checks {
    // Repeated `name => bool` pairs, optional trailing comma.
    ($($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut passed = 0;
        $(
            // The name is for readability at the call site; the count
            // depends only on the boolean status.
            let _ = stringify!($name);
            if $status {
                passed += 1;
            }
        )*
        passed
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let passed = service_checks!(
        health => true,
        orders => true,
        billing => false,
    );

    println!("passed = {}", passed); // passed = 2
    println!("total = {}", 3);       // total = 3
}

The macro compresses repeated name => bool checks into one count; the expansion is a plain accumulator that the borrow and type checkers see normally.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The macro accepts repeated name => bool pairs via $($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)?.
  • The expansion counts true cases correctly by incrementing passed only when $status evaluates to true, returning 2 for the lab inputs.
  • Running the lab prints passed = 2 and total = 3, matching the expected output.
  • The call site is a compact labeled list that is easier to read than three hand-written increment lines.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Replace a useless macro with a normal function

Neither macro abstracts any syntax, so both should disappear. The defect is the same in each case: a macro is being used where there is no repeated syntax to compress and no item to generate, which means the metaprogramming buys nothing and costs diagnostics and tooling quality.

route_label!(service, route) should become a normal function. It only expands to format!("{}::{}", service, route), so the call already reads like a function call passing two values. Replacing it with fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String is strictly better: the signature documents the argument types, the IDE can autocomplete and show hover docs, go-to-definition lands on real code instead of a macro arm, and a wrong-type argument produces a precise error at the call site rather than an error inside an expansion. The macro form gave none of that and offered no syntactic win in return.

retry_limit!() should become a constant rather than a function. It only expands to a fixed integer, so it is a named value, not a computation. An associated constant such as const RETRY_LIMIT: u32 = 5; (or RetryPolicy::RETRY_LIMIT) expresses that intent directly: it has a type, it can be used in const contexts like array sizes and match patterns where a function call cannot, and it reads as a value at every use site. A macro that takes no arguments and returns a literal is a constant wearing a costume.

The refactor is justified on call-site honesty and tooling, not taste. A function call should be a function, and a named constant should be a const; making the API say what it actually is gives the reader accurate expectations, gives the compiler better error spans, and gives the editor real symbols to navigate. The trailing ! was advertising metaprogramming that was never happening.

// Before: two macros that abstract no syntax.
// macro_rules! route_label { ($s:expr, $r:expr) => { format!("{}::{}", $s, $r) }; }
// macro_rules! retry_limit { () => { 5 }; }

// After: a normal function and a constant.
fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String {
    format!("{}::{}", service, route)
}

const RETRY_LIMIT: u32 = 5;

fn main() {
    let label = route_label("orders", "create");
    println!("{label}");                 // orders::create
    println!("retry limit = {RETRY_LIMIT}"); // retry limit = 5
}

A two-value transformation becomes a function; a fixed integer becomes a const, recovering typed signatures, const-context usability, and editor navigation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • route_label! is replaced with an ordinary function, justified by typed signature, precise call-site diagnostics, and working go-to-definition and autocomplete.
  • retry_limit!() is identified as clearer expressed as a const (or associated constant), usable in const contexts a function call cannot reach.
  • The justification is framed in terms of call-site honesty, diagnostics, and tooling rather than personal style.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Sketch a derive macro API

Sketch #[derive(TopicKey)] for the event types in a message-driven service. The job is type-local and concrete: given a struct or enum that represents an event, emit the routing key the platform uses to publish and subscribe, so that key derivation cannot drift from the type definition. A good derive does one type-local job well, and this is one.

Input item shape: the derive attaches to a struct or enum definition. For a struct it reads the type name and, optionally, designated fields; for an enum it can produce a per-variant key. The derive does not require any particular field layout, which keeps it usable on existing event types without restructuring them.

Helper attributes: support #[topic(name = "...")] at the type level to override the default key (otherwise the default is derived from the type's name, lowercased and dotted), and #[topic(part)] on individual fields to mark fields whose runtime values are appended to the static prefix to form a fully qualified key. Helper attributes stay optional so the common case needs only the bare derive.

Emitted code: the derive emits an impl TopicKey for T providing const TOPIC_PREFIX: &'static str (the static portion known at compile time) and a fn topic_key(&self) -> String method that concatenates the prefix with any #[topic(part)] field values at runtime. Naming the static prefix as an associated const lets call sites use it in const contexts and lets subscription tables be built without an instance.

Misuse diagnostic: if #[topic(part)] is placed on a field whose type does not implement Display (so it cannot be rendered into the key), the derive should emit a clear compile-time error on that field's span, something like #[topic(part)] requires the field type to implement Display. Reporting on the field span rather than the whole type makes the fix obvious. A second worthwhile diagnostic: reject #[topic(name = ...)] applied to an enum variant when it conflicts with a type-level name, rather than silently picking one.

The implementation lives in a separate proc-macro crate (crate-name-derive, declared with proc-macro = true), parsing the input with syn and emitting tokens with quote. The application crate re-exports the derive alongside the TopicKey trait so users see a single import. Committing to that crate boundary up front is part of the design: it is the cost the derive pays for being able to inspect and generate over the type's syntax.

// In the proc-macro crate (proc-macro = true):
//
// #[proc_macro_derive(TopicKey, attributes(topic))]
// pub fn derive_topic_key(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream { /* syn + quote */ }
//
// Trait the derive implements, in the runtime crate:
pub trait TopicKey {
    const TOPIC_PREFIX: &'static str;
    fn topic_key(&self) -> String;
}

// Intended use after deriving:
//
// #[derive(TopicKey)]
// #[topic(name = "orders.created")]
// struct OrderCreated {
//     #[topic(part)] tenant: String, // appended to the prefix at runtime
//     order_id: u64,
// }
//
// Emitted (sketch):
// impl TopicKey for OrderCreated {
//     const TOPIC_PREFIX: &'static str = "orders.created";
//     fn topic_key(&self) -> String {
//         format!("{}.{}", Self::TOPIC_PREFIX, self.tenant)
//     }
// }

Derive sketch: a type-level prefix as an associated const plus a runtime topic_key, with helper attributes for overrides and field parts.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • A plausible derive name (TopicKey) and target item (event struct or enum) are described.
  • At least one emitted impl is specified concretely: impl TopicKey with a TOPIC_PREFIX associated const and a topic_key method.
  • Supporting helper attributes (#[topic(name = ...)], #[topic(part)]) and a misuse diagnostic (#[topic(part)] on a non-Display field, reported on the field span) are named.
  • The answer acknowledges the implementation lives in a separate proc-macro crate using syn and quote.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose declarative macro, derive, attribute, function-like proc macro, or build script

Each of the five concerns maps to exactly one tool, and the discipline is to give each tool one narrow job rather than forcing a single mechanism everywhere.

Repetitive integration tests want macro_rules!. The duplication is local repeated syntax, a fixed test scaffold instantiated over a list of cases, which is exactly the syntax-compression job declarative macros do best. A test_cases! macro that expands each name => input => expected line into a #[test] fn keeps the cases list-shaped and the emitted code ordinary. There is no item to inspect and no type to query, so reaching past macro_rules! would only enlarge the surface.

Event types that need codec impls want a derive macro. The code should attach directly to each type definition so the codec cannot drift from the fields, and it emits trait impls (encode/decode). That is the textbook derive case: #[derive(Codec)] on the struct, with the generated impl Codec for T living in a separate proc-macro crate.

Handler functions that need registration metadata want an attribute macro. Here an existing item, the handler fn, needs annotation-driven rewriting or registration: #[handler(route = "/orders")] can emit the original function unchanged plus registration glue (for example an inventory or linkme entry, or a generated registry function). An attribute macro is the right form because it receives and can rewrite the annotated item, which a derive cannot do to a free function.

The compact route-table DSL is the borderline case. As a small, fixed grammar it can stay a macro_rules! macro, exactly as the chapter's routes! example shows, expanding to a Vec<Route> of plain structs. If the grammar grows token-level constructs that macro_rules! cannot express cleanly, it graduates to a function-like proc macro such as route_table! { ... }, where token-level parsing is the real API. The honest choice depends on grammar size; the chapter notes that a much larger grammar tips toward a proc macro or an offline generator.

The API client generated from an external schema belongs in a build script or offline generator. The source of truth is a file outside the crate, so generation runs in build.rs (or a checked-in code generator) that reads the schema and writes Rust into OUT_DIR, included with include!. No macro form fits, because the input is external data, not Rust tokens the caller types.

Justifying one proc-macro and one non-macro choice operationally: the #[derive(Codec)] choice is right because the codec must stay attached to the type's field list and regenerate when fields change, which only type-attached generation guarantees; the build-script choice is right because binding schema-driven generation to a macro call site would couple the build to data the type system cannot reason about, whereas build.rs keeps the dependency on the schema file explicit and the output reviewable.

For testing and observability hooks: derive and attribute macros should ship trybuild compile-fail tests that assert the exact diagnostic for misuse (a missing required helper attribute, a wrong item kind), and the generated code should be covered by snapshot tests (for example cargo expand output checked into the repo or a macrotest-style snapshot) so a change in emitted code is reviewable in a diff rather than invisible. The build-script generator's output should likewise be snapshot-reviewed, and cargo expand remains the primary expansion-focused diagnostic when a macro misbehaves.

// macro_rules!  -> repetitive integration tests (local repeated syntax)
macro_rules! test_cases {
    ($($name:ident: $input:expr => $expected:expr),* $(,)?) => {
        $(
            #[test]
            fn $name() { assert_eq!(transform($input), $expected); }
        )*
    };
}

// #[derive(Codec)]   -> event types needing codec impls (attach to the type)
// #[handler(route)]  -> handler fns needing registration (rewrite the item)
// routes! { ... }    -> small fixed DSL via macro_rules!; a token-level grammar
//                       graduates to a function-like proc macro route_table!{...}
// build.rs           -> API client from an external schema (source of truth
//                       outside the crate; write into OUT_DIR, include! it)
//
// Hooks: trybuild compile-fail tests for misuse diagnostics, cargo-expand /
// snapshot tests over generated code, snapshot review of build.rs output.

One narrow job per tool: macro_rules! for repeated test syntax, derive for codec impls, attribute for handler registration, macro_rules!/proc-macro for the DSL, build.rs for schema-driven generation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least four distinct concerns are mapped to the correct tool: repetitive tests to macro_rules!, codec impls to a derive, handler registration to an attribute macro, the DSL to macro_rules! or a function-like proc macro, and the schema client to a build script.
  • One proc-macro choice (derive for codecs, justified by keeping generation attached to the type's fields) and one non-macro choice (build script, justified by an external source of truth) are defended operationally.
  • Testing and observability hooks are named: trybuild compile-fail tests, cargo-expand or snapshot tests over generated code, and expansion-focused diagnostics.

Lab solution

The lab fills in the service_checks! macro so it counts how many name => bool pairs are true. The matcher $($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)? accepts a comma-separated list of pairs with an optional trailing comma, which keeps the call site list-shaped and easy to edit. Each pair binds an identifier $name and a boolean expression $status.

The body is one hygienic block. It declares a local accumulator passed, then the repetition operator $( ... )* emits the conditional increment once per matched pair, so the macro expands to three if checks for the three inputs. The $name is bound to a discarded value via stringify! purely so the call site can read as a labeled check list; only $status drives the count. Because the block ends in passed, the whole service_checks!(...) invocation is an expression that yields the count, which is why let passed = service_checks!(...) works.

For the inputs health => true, orders => true, and billing => false, two statuses are true, so passed is 2. The program prints passed = 2 and then the literal total = 3, matching the expected output exactly. The macro contributes only the repetitive count pattern; the emitted accumulator and conditionals are ordinary Rust that still pass type and borrow checking after expansion.

Example 20-S. service_checks_macro_lab.rs — Reference solution

macro_rules! service_checks {
    // Match repeated `name => bool` pairs with an optional trailing comma.
    // The name is captured for readability at the call site; the count
    // depends only on the boolean status expression.
    ($($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut passed = 0;
        $(
            let _ = stringify!($name);
            if $status {
                passed += 1;
            }
        )*
        passed
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let passed = service_checks!(
        health => true,
        orders => true,
        billing => false,
    );

    println!("passed = {}", passed);
    println!("total = {}", 3);
}
Output
passed = 2
total = 3

Review question answers

What operational difference separates macro_rules! from a procedural macro?

A macro_rules! macro is a declarative pattern-matcher: it matches token patterns in its arms and expands to a substituted template, all expressed in Rust's macro grammar and compiled as part of the same crate. A procedural macro is an actual Rust function that runs at compile time, takes a TokenStream in and returns a TokenStream out, and therefore can run arbitrary logic to inspect and rewrite syntax. The operational consequences follow from that: proc macros must live in a separate crate marked proc-macro = true, add a compile-time dependency and a crate boundary, and can do item-level generation, whereas macro_rules! is lighter weight, stays in-crate, and is limited to template-style expansion of the patterns it can match.

Why do procedural macros operate on TokenStream instead of inferred types?

Because of where they run in the pipeline. Macro expansion happens near the front of compilation, before name resolution, trait solving, and type inference, so there simply are no inferred types or resolved trait impls available to inspect yet. A proc macro therefore receives a TokenStream, a flat sequence of identifiers, literals, punctuation, and grouped sub-streams with spans, and must work purely from that syntax, typically parsing it with a library like syn. A direct consequence is that a macro cannot decide what to generate based on a field's concrete type or whether some trait is implemented, because that information does not exist at expansion time.

When is a derive macro the right fit instead of an attribute macro?

A derive macro is right when the generated code should attach to a type definition and only add to it, typically emitting trait impls or helper methods, without modifying the type itself. An attribute macro is right when an item needs annotation-driven rewriting or registration, that is, when you need to transform or replace the annotated item, or attach behavior to functions, modules, or other items a derive cannot target. So derive fits codec, serialization, or builder impls on a struct or enum; an attribute macro fits decorating a handler function with routing metadata or rewriting a function's body. If you only need to add impls to a type, prefer derive, because it is the narrower and more conventional tool.

Why can a public macro be harder to evolve than a public function?

A public function commits to a typed signature, so the compiler enforces the contract and refactors are guided by precise errors. A public macro instead commits to an input syntax grammar and an expansion, which is a much larger and looser surface: callers can depend on token shapes, on the exact names and items the expansion introduces, and on hygiene behavior, much of which is not captured by any type signature. Changing the grammar or the emitted code can silently break call sites in ways the type system will not flag at the macro boundary, and diagnostics for misuse are harder to keep good. That wider, less-checked contract is why a public macro is a heavier long-term commitment to keep stable than a public function.

What is one concrete signal that a normal function is better than a macro?

The clearest signal is that the macro call already reads like a function call passing values, with no repeated syntax being compressed and no Rust items being generated. The chapter's route_label!(service, route) is the example: it just forwards two values to format!, so it should be fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String. When the only thing a macro does is take value arguments and return a value, a function gives you a typed signature, precise call-site diagnostics, and working editor navigation, while the macro adds API surface and worse errors for nothing in return.

Chapter 21 · Reflection and Type Introspection

Reflection and Type Introspection

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises push you to treat "reflection" in Rust not as one missing feature but as four narrow tools that solve four different problems. Two run at runtime (TypeId plus Any, and the downcast that recovers an erased value), and two run at compile time (derive macros that generate per-type code, and schema generation from DTOs). The work here is mostly about choosing the smallest tool that fits a boundary, then keeping the choice honest: TypeId and Any for process-local, type-keyed storage; ordinary trait methods and explicit metadata structs for plugin facts operators care about; generated schema for public contracts.

The lab anchors the runtime pair: a TypeMap that stores heterogeneous values behind one erased HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>> and recovers each one by concrete type. The design exercises then pull in the opposite direction, asking you to resist downcasting as an architecture and to keep public, persistent, or operator-facing contracts explicit rather than derived from process-local type identity.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Match the need to the Rust tool

Map each need to the smallest tool that satisfies its boundary, not to "reflection" as a blanket answer.

Request extensions want TypeId plus Any. This is the narrow, legitimate case for an erased typemap: values live inside one process for the lifetime of a request, each is keyed by its concrete type, and you recover exactly the type you stored with downcast_ref. There is no public contract and no need to enumerate fields, so type identity is the right and only requirement.

Plugin capabilities want explicit trait metadata rather than downcasting everywhere. The host needs each plugin's name, kind, and capabilities on every plugin, so that data belongs on the trait surface (a metadata() method returning a PluginMetadata struct), not behind a downcast. Downcasting recovers one named concrete type; it cannot answer "what can this plugin do" generically, and reaching for it on the common path is a sign the contract is missing.

Admin docs want compile-time generation rather than runtime inspection. Documentation describes types, and that description should be produced from the source at build time (derive-driven schema or descriptor generation), not by inspecting live values that may not exist yet at doc-generation time.

Human-readable log labels are the one place type_name::<T>() fits: it is a best-effort diagnostic string, fine for a log line a human reads, and explicitly not a stable key.

Public cross-service schema wants a stable, explicit contract. It must not be derived from type_name::<T>() or TypeId, because both are process- and build-local and carry no compatibility guarantee. Define the schema and protocol keys explicitly (or generate them from versioned DTOs) so the contract survives recompilation and refactors.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Any and TypeId are chosen only for request extensions, the narrow erased-storage case.
  • Plugin capabilities and admin docs are handled with explicit trait metadata and compile-time generation, not downcasting.
  • Public cross-service schema and protocol keys stay explicit, never derived from type_name::<T>() or TypeId.
Exercise 2code reading

Explain why Any is not general reflection

The teammate's registry fails for two independent reasons, and it is worth separating them because the second survives even after the first is fixed.

The lifetime problem comes first. View<'a> { route: &'a str } borrows for some lifetime 'a. The Any trait is implemented for T: 'static, so to erase a value into Box<dyn Any> the type must outlive any borrow it could hold; in practice it must own its data or borrow only from 'static. A long-lived registry that outlives the borrowed route would be a dangling reference waiting to happen, and the borrow checker refuses to let a non-'static View enter the erased store at all. This is the ownership model behind the trait bound, not an arbitrary restriction: erasing a type discards the compiler's ability to track the borrow, so Rust requires the borrow not exist in the first place.

The field-enumeration problem is deeper and does not go away if you make the type 'static. Suppose the teammate rewrites it as View { route: String } so it is 'static and stores cleanly. Any still gives them exactly one capability: ask "is the erased value a View?" and, if so, recover a &View by downcast. It does not expose a list of fields, their names, their types, or any methods. Rust monomorphizes generics and resolves calls statically, so the per-type structural metadata a reflective runtime would walk has been compiled away. Any is type identity plus safe recovery, not structural reflection.

Two repairs follow. The ownership repair: own the data (route: String) and keep the borrowed View as a short-lived local view computed on demand from the owned value, never stored erased. The metadata repair: if some path genuinely needs to inspect "fields" of the stored thing, stop trying to discover them and instead attach an explicit descriptor, for example store a small struct that carries the route and whatever named attributes the caller needs, so the data the teammate wanted to enumerate is an ordinary, named API rather than something inferred at runtime.

// Ownership repair: own the data, keep the borrowed view local and short-lived.
struct OwnedView {
    route: String,
}

impl OwnedView {
    // A view is computed on demand, never stored behind `dyn Any`.
    fn view(&self) -> BorrowedView<'_> {
        BorrowedView { route: &self.route }
    }
}

struct BorrowedView<'a> {
    route: &'a str,
}

// Metadata repair: when a path needs to "inspect fields", attach an explicit
// descriptor instead of expecting `Any` to enumerate them.
struct ViewDescriptor {
    route: String,
    attributes: Vec<(&'static str, String)>,
}

Own the data and keep the borrowed view local; attach explicit metadata instead of expecting field enumeration from Any.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that Any requires T: 'static concrete types, so a borrowed View with a wider lifetime claim cannot enter long-lived erased storage.
  • Explains that Any supports recovering one named type, not walking fields or discovering methods, even when the type is 'static.
  • Proposes both an ownership repair (own the data, view locally) and a metadata repair (explicit descriptor).
Exercise 3implementation

Build a tiny TypeId registry

The typemap stores heterogeneous values behind a single erased owner, HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>>, and uses the generic parameter T twice on every operation: once to compute the key with TypeId::of::<T>() and once to drive recovery with downcast_ref::<T>().

insert<T: 'static> boxes the value, erasing its concrete type into Box<dyn Any>, and keys it by TypeId::of::<T>(). The 'static bound is what makes erasure sound: a value with no non-'static borrows can be stored for as long as the map lives. Using the TypeId as the key, rather than a hand-managed string name, means type identity is computed by the compiler and cannot drift or collide with a typo.

get<T: 'static> looks up the same TypeId key and then calls downcast_ref::<T>() on the boxed value. The return type is Option<&T> because recovery legitimately fails when nothing of that type was inserted; the caller must handle the None. Because the key and the downcast both come from the same T, a present entry always downcasts successfully, so the only None case is a genuinely absent type. No string keys are involved anywhere, which is the point: the contract is concrete type identity, not a parallel naming scheme you have to keep correct by hand.

use std::any::{Any, TypeId};
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct TypeMap {
    values: HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>>,
}

impl TypeMap {
    fn insert<T: 'static>(&mut self, value: T) {
        // Erase the concrete type, key it by the compiler-computed TypeId.
        self.values.insert(TypeId::of::<T>(), Box::new(value));
    }

    fn get<T: 'static>(&self) -> Option<&T> {
        // Same key out as in; recovery is type-checked and may fail.
        self.values.get(&TypeId::of::<T>())?.downcast_ref::<T>()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut map = TypeMap::default();
    map.insert::<u16>(8080);
    map.insert::<String>(String::from("billing"));

    println!("port = {}", map.get::<u16>().copied().unwrap_or(0));
    println!("label = {}", map.get::<String>().map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("none"));
    println!("missing bool = {}", map.get::<bool>().is_none());
}

Heterogeneous values behind one erased owner, keyed by TypeId, recovered with downcast_ref.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Stores u16 and String behind a single HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>> erased owner.
  • Lookup is keyed by TypeId::of::<T>(), never by a type-name string.
  • Recovery uses downcast_ref::<T>() and returns Option<&T>, so a missing type yields None.
  • main prints port = 8080, label = billing, and missing bool = true, matching the lab.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a plugin downcast boundary

The defect is not that downcasting fails; it is that the common path was being expressed as a downcast. Facts every plugin has, name, kind, version, and similar, belong on the trait surface or in an explicit PluginMetadata struct returned by a metadata() method. Listing names or reading a kind should never touch Any, because that data lives on the trait every plugin implements and is available generically through dyn Plugin.

The one genuinely concrete-specific query in the scenario, whether a JsonPlugin is configured for pretty output, is the exception path. That fact is meaningful only for one concrete type, so it is the legitimate place for a narrow escape hatch: add as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any to the trait, and in the single specialized site, find_map over the plugins, downcast_ref::<JsonPlugin>(), and read pretty. The escape hatch is present but used once, not threaded through the whole codebase.

Keeping the rest of the codebase from turning every call into a downcast is a contract question, not a willpower question. If callers can get what they need from metadata() and the trait's normal methods, they will, because it is less code and it works for every plugin uniformly. Repeated downcasting is a design smell precisely because it means the trait is under-specified: each downcast site silently assumes a concrete type, breaks when a new plugin is added, and turns a generic collection back into a pile of special cases. The fix is to push any fact that more than one call site wants onto the trait, leaving as_any() for the rare query that is inherently about one named type.

use std::any::Any;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct PluginMetadata {
    name: &'static str,
    kind: &'static str,
}

trait Plugin {
    fn metadata(&self) -> PluginMetadata; // common path: every plugin
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String;
    fn as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any;         // escape hatch: rare concrete query
}

struct JsonPlugin {
    pretty: bool,
}

impl Plugin for JsonPlugin {
    fn metadata(&self) -> PluginMetadata {
        PluginMetadata { name: "json", kind: "formatter" }
    }
    fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String {
        if self.pretty { format!("pretty({input})") } else { format!("compact({input})") }
    }
    fn as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any {
        self
    }
}

fn report(plugins: &[Box<dyn Plugin>]) {
    // Common path: trait methods, no downcast, works for every plugin.
    let names: Vec<_> = plugins.iter().map(|p| p.metadata().name).collect();

    // Exception path: one concrete-specific query, used exactly once.
    let pretty = plugins
        .iter()
        .find_map(|p| p.as_any().downcast_ref::<JsonPlugin>())
        .map(|j| j.pretty)
        .unwrap_or(false);

    println!("plugins = {}", names.join(","));
    println!("json pretty = {pretty}");
}

Common facts on the trait via metadata(); as_any() downcast confined to the single pretty-flag query.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Common facts (name, kind) live in PluginMetadata on the trait surface, reachable without a downcast.
  • as_any() is added as a narrow escape hatch and used only for the one concrete pretty-flag query.
  • Explains that repeated downcasting signals a missing trait contract that breaks as plugins are added.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design explicit metadata for a plugin system

Model the exporter contract so that every fact an operator or the host needs is a plain, declared API, and reserve any downcast for a single optional inspection path.

PluginMetadata carries name, version, kind, config_format, and capabilities. Name and version are stable identifiers; the host reads them at registration time and they appear in startup logs. kind, config_format, and capabilities are facts the host routes on, so they must be available without any downcast at all, returned from a metadata() method that every exporter implements.

The facts that are a fixed, known set should be stronger types than raw strings. kind is a closed enum (Exporter, Formatter, Filter), config_format is an enum (Json, Yaml, Toml, None), and capabilities is a set of enum flags (Streaming, Batch, Compression, Encryption) rather than free text. Enums make exhaustive matching possible in the host, make typos a compile error, and document the valid space in one place. Where a value is genuinely open-ended and human-facing (a description, a vendor label), a string is appropriate; the point is to use the stronger type when the domain is closed.

Everything the host dispatches on lives in metadata() and needs no Any. The single optional specialized path, for example asking whether one concrete exporter has a tuning knob the generic contract does not model, goes through as_any() and is exercised at exactly one site.

Observability and testing hooks make the registry operable. At registration, log each plugin's metadata (name, version, kind, capabilities) so the running configuration is visible in startup logs. Add a registration test that asserts no two plugins share a name and that every declared config_format has a corresponding config schema. Validate each plugin's config against its declared schema at load time, failing fast with a clear message rather than at first use. These hooks are cheap precisely because the metadata is explicit and boring.

use std::any::Any;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum PluginKind { Exporter, Formatter, Filter }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum ConfigFormat { Json, Yaml, Toml, None }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Capability { Streaming, Batch, Compression, Encryption }

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct PluginMetadata {
    name: &'static str,
    version: &'static str,
    kind: PluginKind,
    config_format: ConfigFormat,
    capabilities: Vec<Capability>,
}

trait Exporter {
    fn metadata(&self) -> PluginMetadata; // everything the host routes on
    fn export(&self, input: &str) -> String;
    fn as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any;         // optional specialized inspection
}

// Observability hook: log declared metadata at registration time.
fn register(plugins: &[Box<dyn Exporter>]) {
    for p in plugins {
        let m = p.metadata();
        println!(
            "registered name={} version={} kind={:?} format={:?} caps={:?}",
            m.name, m.version, m.kind, m.config_format, m.capabilities
        );
    }
    // Registration test (sketch): assert unique names, schema per config_format.
    debug_assert!(
        {
            let mut names: Vec<_> = plugins.iter().map(|p| p.metadata().name).collect();
            names.sort_unstable();
            names.windows(2).all(|w| w[0] != w[1])
        },
        "plugin names must be unique"
    );
}

Explicit PluginMetadata with enum kind/format/capabilities, plus a registration hook that logs and asserts uniqueness.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines an explicit PluginMetadata shape (name, version, kind, config_format, capabilities) instead of relying on runtime type names.
  • Uses enums for kind, config_format, and capabilities rather than stringly typed free text.
  • Adds observability and testing hooks: startup metadata logging, a unique-name registration assertion, and per-format config schema checks.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose runtime introspection, macros, schema generation, or no reflection at all

Start from each boundary's contract, not from a preferred mechanism. The four concerns map to four different Rust-native tools.

Request-scoped extensions want a typemap inside one process. They live and die within a single request in a single build, keyed by concrete type, with no external contract. That is the textbook TypeId plus Any case: a HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>> with insert<T> and get<T>. Operationally this is attractive because there is nothing to version and nothing to keep in sync across services; the cost stays inside one process.

The public event schema wants compile-time schema generation from DTOs. The schema is a cross-service, persistent contract, so it must be explicit and stable. Generate it at build time from versioned transport DTOs (derive-driven, for example a schemars-style JSON Schema), so the published artifact is reviewable, diffable, and tied to a DTO version. This is the compile-time approach justified operationally: the contract is produced once at build time, cannot drift from the code that serializes it, and never depends on a live value existing.

The internal admin CLI wants ordinary explicit descriptor structs with no Any at all. Commands, their arguments, and help text are known statically and described best by plain descriptor structs (or a derive that generates them from declarations). There is no erased value to recover, so introducing Any would only add a downcast where a field access suffices.

The browser config form also wants compile-time schema generation from its config DTOs, for the same reason as the event schema: the form is rendered from a description of a type, so generate that description from the DTO at build time rather than inspecting any runtime value.

The concerns that must avoid TypeId and type_name::<T>() are the public event schema and anything persisted: those identifiers are process- and build-local and carry no compatibility guarantee, so a public or stored contract keyed on them would silently break across recompiles. The runtime trick (the typemap) is justified only because it never escapes the process; the compile-time generation is justified because the contract must outlive any single process and stay reviewable.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Maps four concerns to four distinct tools: typemap (extensions), generated schema (event schema and config form), and explicit descriptor structs (admin CLI).
  • Keeps the public event schema and any persisted data away from process-local TypeId and type_name::<T>().
  • Justifies the compile-time approach (build-time schema, no drift, reviewable) and the runtime approach (process-local typemap, nothing to version) in operational terms.

Lab solution

TypeMap erases heterogeneous values into a single HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>>. insert<T: 'static> computes the key with TypeId::of::<T>() and boxes the value as Box<dyn Any>; the 'static bound guarantees the stored value holds no borrow that could dangle for the life of the map. get<T: 'static> uses the same TypeId to find the entry, then calls downcast_ref::<T>() to recover the concrete type, returning Option<&T> because recovery can legitimately fail.

The inserts store a u16 of 8080 and a String of "billing". get::<u16>() finds the u16 entry and downcasts it, so copied().unwrap_or(0) prints port = 8080. get::<String>() recovers the &String, and map(String::as_str) prints label = billing. No bool was ever inserted, so get::<bool>() returns None and is_none() is true, printing missing bool = true.

Because the lookup key and the downcast target are both derived from the same T, a present entry always downcasts successfully; the only way to reach None is a genuinely absent type. This is exactly the narrow, process-local use of TypeId and Any the chapter endorses: type identity plus safe recovery, with no field walking and no public contract leaking out.

Example 21-S. typemap_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::any::{Any, TypeId};
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct TypeMap {
    values: HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>>,
}

impl TypeMap {
    fn insert<T: 'static>(&mut self, value: T) {
        // Store by concrete type id, erasing the value behind Box<dyn Any>.
        self.values.insert(TypeId::of::<T>(), Box::new(value));
    }

    fn get<T: 'static>(&self) -> Option<&T> {
        // Look up by the same TypeId key, then recover the concrete type.
        self.values.get(&TypeId::of::<T>())?.downcast_ref::<T>()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut map = TypeMap::default();
    map.insert::<u16>(8080);
