    map.insert::<String>(String::from("billing"));

    println!("port = {}", map.get::<u16>().copied().unwrap_or(0));
    println!("label = {}", map.get::<String>().map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("none"));
    println!("missing bool = {}", map.get::<bool>().is_none());
}
Output
port = 8080
label = billing
missing bool = true

Review question answers

Why does Rust offer TypeId and Any without offering general field reflection?

Rust specializes generic code by monomorphization and resolves nearly all calls statically, so the per-type structural metadata a reflective runtime would walk (field names, field types, methods) is compiled away and not kept alive at runtime. TypeId plus Any preserve only what is cheap and sound: a copyable token identifying one concrete type and the ability to recover that type safely by downcast. General field reflection would require carrying that discarded metadata for every type, which conflicts with zero-cost abstraction; when you need a field list, you generate it at compile time from the source instead.

What problem does 'static solve in many Any-based designs?

Erasing a value into Box<dyn Any> discards the compiler's ability to track any borrows the value holds, so the value must not hold a borrow that could outlive what it points to. The 'static bound enforces exactly that: the type either owns its data or borrows only from 'static, which makes long-lived erased storage sound and is why Any is implemented for T: 'static. It does not mean the value lives forever; it means the value carries no non-'static borrow, so a registry can hold it safely for as long as the registry lives.

Why is type_name::<T>() useful for diagnostics but weak as a contract key?

type_name::<T>() returns a best-effort, human-readable string that is fine for a log line or a panic message a person reads. It is weak as a contract key because the standard library makes no stability guarantee: the exact string can change between compiler versions and is not promised to be unique or canonical, so two builds may disagree. A persistent or cross-service contract keyed on it could silently break across recompiles, so public and protocol keys should be defined explicitly instead.

How does as_any() differ from ordinary trait methods as a design tool?

Ordinary trait methods express facts and behavior that every implementor shares, so they work generically over dyn Trait without knowing the concrete type. as_any() does the opposite: it deliberately re-exposes the concrete type so a single call site can downcast back to one named type for a query the trait does not model. It is an escape hatch for the rare specialized path, not a general API; if more than a couple of call sites need it, the right fix is to lift that fact onto the trait surface, because pervasive downcasting signals a missing contract.

Why should schema generation usually target DTOs rather than arbitrary live values?

A schema is a description of a type's shape, and DTOs are the types whose shape is the actual wire or storage contract, so generating from them produces a stable, reviewable, versioned artifact tied to the data you serialize. Arbitrary live values may not exist when the schema is built, can carry incidental runtime state that is not part of the contract, and would drift from the published shape. Targeting DTOs with derive-driven generation keeps the schema in sync with the serialization code by construction and lets the contract be diffed and versioned independently of any running instance.

Chapter 22 · Multithreading in Rust

Multithreading in Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises turn the chapter's four primitives, move, share, synchronize, and borrow-in-scope, into design judgment. Each one asks you to read ownership at a thread boundary rather than reach for whatever compiled first. The warm-ups make Send and Sync concrete; the implementation and debugging work force you to put owned data on the correct side of thread::spawn; and the design scenarios make you commit to a concurrency model and name its operational cost.

The throughline is that Rust's thread safety is not a separate subsystem bolted onto the language. It is the same ownership and borrowing model from Chapter 04, extended across an OS-thread boundary by two marker traits. Once you can say where the mutable state lives and who is allowed to touch it, the choice between a channel, an Arc<Mutex<T>>, and a scoped thread stops being a syntax preference and becomes a statement about the design.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Decide whether a type is Send, Sync, both, or neither

Fix the definitions first. Send means a value of the type can be moved to another thread and used there safely as an owned value; ownership transfers across the thread boundary. Sync means it is safe for multiple threads to hold shared references (&T) to the same value at once; equivalently, T: Sync exactly when &T: Send. Both are auto traits: the compiler derives them for a type when all of its fields qualify, and the entire point is that a type which fails to qualify will not compile its way across thread::spawn.

Now classify. String is both Send and Sync: it owns a heap buffer with no shared mutable interior, so moving it to a thread is fine and a &String shared across threads is read-only and safe. Arc<String> is also Send and Sync: Arc uses atomic reference counting, so cloning the handle from several threads cannot corrupt the count, and the inner String is itself immutable through the shared Arc. Mutex<Vec<u8>> is Send and Sync: the lock serializes access, so even though the Vec is mutated, only one thread holds the guard at a time, which is the whole reason Mutex exists.

The two that are not safe to share are instructive. Rc<String> is neither Send nor Sync, because its reference count is a plain non-atomic integer; two threads cloning or dropping the same Rc would race on that counter and could free the allocation twice. RefCell<Vec<u8>> is Send (you can move it) but not Sync, because its borrow flag is a non-atomic cell, so concurrent borrow_mut calls from two threads would not be detected and would alias mutably. That is why Rc<RefCell<T>> is the canonical single-thread sharing tool and never crosses a thread boundary, whereas Arc<Mutex<T>> is its multi-thread counterpart, not a synonym for it.

The raw-pointer wrapper is the case that demands restraint. A struct holding a *mut T is !Send and !Sync by default because the compiler cannot see what the pointer aliases or who else mutates through it. Reaching for unsafe impl Send/unsafe impl Sync is only correct if you can actually prove the hidden aliasing, mutation, and destruction behavior is thread-safe; the keyword is a promise to the compiler, not an escape hatch, and most application code should never write it.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

// String           : Send + Sync  (owned buffer, no shared mutability)
// Arc<String>      : Send + Sync  (atomic refcount, inner is immutable)
// Mutex<Vec<u8>>   : Send + Sync  (lock serializes the mutation)
// Rc<String>       : !Send + !Sync (non-atomic refcount races)
// RefCell<Vec<u8>> : Send + !Sync (non-atomic borrow flag; movable, not shareable)

fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
fn assert_sync<T: Sync>() {}

fn main() {
    assert_send::<String>();
    assert_sync::<String>();
    assert_send::<Arc<String>>();
    assert_sync::<Arc<String>>();
    assert_send::<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>();
    assert_sync::<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>();

    // These lines would FAIL to compile, by design:
    // assert_send::<Rc<String>>();        // Rc is !Send
    // assert_sync::<RefCell<Vec<u8>>>();  // RefCell is !Sync

    // A raw-pointer wrapper is !Send and !Sync until proven otherwise.
    struct Raw(*mut u8);
    // unsafe impl Send for Raw {} // only with a real safety proof
    let _ = Raw(std::ptr::null_mut());

    println!("classifications checked at compile time");
}

Compile-time assertions that pin down which standard types are Send and/or Sync.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Both traits are defined before any example is classified: Send is move-to-thread, Sync is shared-reference-across-threads (&T: Send).
  • Rc<String> is identified as neither Send nor Sync because its refcount is non-atomic, ruling out transfer and sharing.
  • Arc<String> (Send + Sync, immutable inner) is kept distinct from Arc<Mutex<T>> (lock required for mutation).
  • The raw-pointer wrapper is flagged as !Send/!Sync until an explicit safety proof justifies an unsafe auto-trait impl.
Exercise 2code reading

Compare a channel-based design with a shared-state design

Start by asking where the mutable state really lives. In the channel design (the chapter's Example 1), each worker owns its job batch outright: the Vec<Job> is moved into the worker by the move closure, the worker computes a total over data nobody else can touch, and it sends a small owned tuple back over mpsc. The only thread that ever mutates the result map is the main thread, draining rx. Mutation authority is singular and the ownership flow is one-directional. In the shared-state design (Example 2), the mutable state lives behind Arc<Mutex<HashMap<...>>>: Arc makes the one allocation reachable from every thread, and every worker locks, mutates the shared map directly, and unlocks. Mutation authority is shared and arbitrated by the lock at runtime.

Message passing keeps one thread as the owner of mutation. Its operational win is failure visibility and order: results arrive as discrete messages, the aggregation point is explicit and deterministic, and a backed-up consumer shows up as channel backlog rather than as a corrupted structure. Its operational cost is buffering and backpressure, an unbounded channel can grow without limit if producers outrun the consumer, and a bounded channel forces you to decide what happens when it is full (block, drop, or error). It is the calmer model when message order matters, because the receiver sees a defined sequence rather than the interleaving of many concurrent writers.

Shared-state locking makes contention and lock scope the main runtime risk. Its operational win is that it is the honest model when many threads genuinely need to observe and update the same structure: there is exactly one copy of the data, every thread sees the latest committed state, and you avoid copying large structures through messages. Its operational cost is contention, the wider the critical section, the more threads serialize on that one lock, and lock wait time becomes a real, measurable latency source; you also inherit poisoning semantics if a thread panics while holding the guard. It is the calmer model precisely when the data is one shared thing that everyone must read and write, not a stream of results to be folded together.

Neither model is globally superior. The right call follows the workload: a worker-result pipeline where each producer owns its inputs and only the aggregator writes is a natural fit for channels; a hot shared counter table that every request thread must update in place is a natural fit for Arc<Mutex<T>> (or a sharded/atomic variant). The design smell is choosing one because it resembles a pattern from another language rather than because the ownership story actually demands it.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::{mpsc, Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

// Channel design: each worker OWNS its input; only main mutates the result map.
fn channel_design() -> HashMap<&'static str, u32> {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
    for (name, jobs) in [("ingest", vec![2u32, 3]), ("index", vec![4])] {
        let tx = tx.clone();
        thread::spawn(move || {
            let total: u32 = jobs.iter().sum(); // jobs owned by this worker alone
            tx.send((name, total)).unwrap();
        });
    }
    drop(tx); // close the channel so the loop below ends
    rx.into_iter().collect()
}

// Shared-state design: every worker mutates ONE map behind a lock.
fn shared_state_design() -> HashMap<&'static str, u32> {
    let counts = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for route in ["api", "api", "billing"] {
        let counts = Arc::clone(&counts);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let mut map = counts.lock().unwrap(); // contention point
            *map.entry(route).or_insert(0u32) += 1;
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    Arc::try_unwrap(counts).unwrap().into_inner().unwrap()
}

fn main() {
    println!("channel: {:?}", channel_design());
    println!("shared : {:?}", shared_state_design());
}

Two shapes side by side: owned inputs plus channel aggregation versus one locked shared map.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Ownership and mutation authority are stated for both: workers own their inputs in the channel design; the map is shared behind Arc<Mutex> in the other.
  • Message passing gets one win (deterministic, visible aggregation/order) and one cost (channel backlog/backpressure).
  • Shared-state locking gets one win (single source of truth all threads update) and one cost (lock contention and wait time).
  • The answer refuses a global winner and ties each model to the workload that suits it.
Exercise 3implementation

Move owned jobs into worker threads and report totals

The design is the chapter's Example 1 shape: two real OS threads, each the sole owner of its job batch, publishing results back through a channel. The key decisions are all about ownership at the boundary. The worker closure must be a move closure so that the Vec<Job> and the cloned Sender are transferred into the child thread rather than borrowed from the parent stack; if you borrowed instead, the child could outlive the borrowed data and the compiler would reject it. Keeping the input owned, rather than passing a &[Job] slice into thread::spawn, is what lets each worker run independently with no lifetime tie back to main.

Results travel as small owned (&'static str, u32) tuples over mpsc. This is the deliberate channel-first choice: no worker touches a shared result map, so there is no lock, no contention, and no shared mutability to reason about. Each worker computes its own total with jobs.iter().map(|j| j.cost).sum() over data nobody else can see, then sends one message. Because the worker is the sole owner while it runs, this is a clean ownership story end to end.

The caller joins both handles explicitly before treating the result as complete. Joining is where failure from a child thread becomes visible to the parent: a panicked worker surfaces as an Err from join, and joining also guarantees the worker has finished and dropped its Sender clone. Once both senders (the two clones) are dropped, the for (worker, total) in rx loop terminates naturally, because the receiver iterator ends when all senders are gone. The aggregation, summing per-worker totals into a grand total, happens on the single main thread, which keeps the final fold deterministic.

This is exactly the lab. Running it with ingest jobs of cost 2 and 3 and an index job of cost 4 prints ingest = 5, index = 4, grand = 9.

use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Job {
    cost: u32,
}

fn spawn_worker(
    tx: mpsc::Sender<(&'static str, u32)>,
    worker: &'static str,
    jobs: Vec<Job>,
) -> thread::JoinHandle<()> {
    // `move` transfers ownership of `jobs` and `tx` into the child thread.
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let total: u32 = jobs.iter().map(|job| job.cost).sum();
        tx.send((worker, total)).unwrap();
    })
}

fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

    let ingest_jobs = vec![Job { cost: 2 }, Job { cost: 3 }];
    let index_jobs = vec![Job { cost: 4 }];

    let ingest = spawn_worker(tx.clone(), "ingest", ingest_jobs);
    let index = spawn_worker(tx, "index", index_jobs);

    ingest.join().unwrap();
    index.join().unwrap();

    let mut ingest_total = 0;
    let mut index_total = 0;
    let mut grand = 0;

    for (worker, total) in rx {
        grand += total;
        if worker == "ingest" {
            ingest_total = total;
        } else if worker == "index" {
            index_total = total;
        }
    }

    println!("ingest = {}", ingest_total);
    println!("index = {}", index_total);
    println!("grand = {}", grand);
}

Each worker owns its Vec<Job> via a move closure and reports its total through mpsc.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each worker closure owns its input: the Vec<Job> is consumed by a move closure, not borrowed.
  • Results flow through an mpsc channel; no worker writes a shared mutable map directly.
  • The caller joins both handles explicitly before draining the channel.
  • Output is ingest = 5, index = 4, grand = 9, matching the lab's expected ingest/index/grand totals.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a thread boundary that captures the wrong thing

There are two distinct defects, and they want different repairs because their lifetime and ownership stories differ.

Defect one: a function borrows a stack-local slice into thread::spawn. thread::spawn requires its closure to be 'static, because the spawned thread may outlive the current stack frame; a &[T] pointing at a parent local does not satisfy that bound, so the borrow is rejected. There are two correct repairs depending on intent. If the worker genuinely needs to own the data and survive independently, move owned data in: take a Vec<T> (or to_vec() the slice) and capture it with a move closure, the calm default for request-local job data. If, instead, the work is short-lived and finishes before the function returns, the data does not need to be cloned at all: use thread::scope, whose child threads are guaranteed to be joined at the end of the scope, so the compiler permits them to borrow parent-owned data directly. Prefer the scoped repair when the child cannot outlive the parent, it avoids needless allocation and keeps the borrow honest.

Defect two: a function tries to send Rc<RefCell<State>> into a thread. This fails to compile because Rc<T> is !Send (its reference count is non-atomic and would race across threads) and RefCell<T> is !Sync (its borrow flag is non-atomic, so concurrent borrows would alias mutably undetected). The fix is not to paper over it with unsafe; it is to choose the shape that matches what the state actually is. If the state is genuinely shared and mutated by multiple threads, replace it with Arc<Mutex<State>>: Arc gives thread-safe shared ownership via atomic counts, and Mutex serializes mutation so only one thread holds the guard at a time. But justify that on semantics, not on the compiler complaining: if only one thread should really own and mutate the state, the better refactor is message passing, send owned commands to a single owner thread over a channel and let that thread be the sole mutator, which removes the lock entirely and gives one clear owner per mutable subsystem.

use std::sync::{mpsc, Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    hits: u32,
}

// BEFORE (defect 1): borrows a stack slice into a 'static spawn -> rejected.
// fn sum_slice(data: &[u32]) -> u32 {
//     let h = thread::spawn(|| data.iter().sum::<u32>()); // data is not 'static
//     h.join().unwrap()
// }

// AFTER 1a: borrowed data is fine -> use a scoped thread (no clone needed).
fn sum_slice_scoped(data: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    thread::scope(|s| {
        let h = s.spawn(|| data.iter().sum::<u32>()); // scope joins before return
        h.join().unwrap()
    })
}

// AFTER 1b: worker must own and outlive -> move owned data in.
fn sum_owned(data: Vec<u32>) -> u32 {
    thread::spawn(move || data.iter().sum::<u32>()).join().unwrap()
}

// BEFORE (defect 2): Rc<RefCell<State>> into a thread -> !Send / !Sync.
// Repair A (truly shared + mutated): Arc<Mutex<State>>.
fn shared_state() -> u32 {
    let state = Arc::new(Mutex::new(State::default()));
    let mut hs = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..3 {
        let state = Arc::clone(&state);
        hs.push(thread::spawn(move || state.lock().unwrap().hits += 1));
    }
    for h in hs { h.join().unwrap(); }
    state.lock().unwrap().hits
}

// Repair B (one true owner): send owned commands to a single mutator thread.
fn single_owner() -> u32 {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>();
    let owner = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut state = State::default();
        for delta in rx { state.hits += delta; } // sole mutator
        state.hits
    });
    for _ in 0..3 { tx.send(1).unwrap(); }
    drop(tx);
    owner.join().unwrap()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", sum_slice_scoped(&[1, 2, 3]));
    println!("{}", sum_owned(vec![1, 2, 3]));
    println!("{}", shared_state());
    println!("{}", single_owner());
}

Four repairs: scoped borrow, owned move, Arc<Mutex> for real sharing, and channel to a single owner.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one case is repaired by moving owned data into the child via a move closure (sum_owned).
  • At least one case is repaired with thread::scope so borrowed local data needs no clone (sum_slice_scoped).
  • Rc<RefCell<T>> is explained as the wrong cross-thread shape: Rc is !Send (non-atomic count), RefCell is !Sync (non-atomic borrow flag).
  • The Arc<Mutex<T>> repair is justified semantically (state genuinely shared and mutated), with message passing offered when one owner suffices.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Choose channel-based or shared-state concurrency for a service

Map the pipeline accept -> parse -> schedule -> update metrics -> publish completion to the model that makes ownership calmest under load, and let a service use more than one model where each subsystem warrants it.

Channel-based boundaries: the request lifecycle itself moves as owned messages. After accept and parse, each request becomes an owned work item that is sent over a channel into the scheduling stage and on to a worker pool; the CPU-heavy job runs on a worker that owns its input alone. Completion is published the same way, the worker sends an owned completion record back to a publisher thread rather than mutating a shared completion structure. The justification is that these stages have a natural single owner at each step and care about ordering and backpressure: a backed-up worker pool shows up as growing queue depth, a signal you can act on, instead of silent contention. A bounded channel here is deliberate, it lets the service apply backpressure (block or shed load) when producers outrun workers.

Immutable shared state through Arc<T> only: configuration, routing tables, parsing schemas, and any reference data loaded at startup and never mutated should be shared as Arc<Config>. Every thread holds a cheap cloned handle to one allocation, reads are lock-free, and there is no mutation to coordinate. The justification is that this data is read by everyone and written by no one during request handling, which is exactly the case Arc<T> without a lock is for.

Synchronized mutable shared state: the few hot counters and the one central retry table are the honest place for synchronized shared state, but only because they are genuinely shared ownership, not convenience. The retry table must be observed and updated by many request threads (a retry recorded by one thread must be visible to another that picks the work up), so a single shared structure is the correct semantics. For the hot counters, prefer atomics or sharded counters to keep the critical section tiny; for the retry table, an Arc<Mutex<RetryTable>> (or a concurrent map) is defensible, with the lock scope kept as narrow as a single entry update. If a counter could instead be owned by one aggregator thread fed by channel messages, that is often calmer, push the design toward one owner per mutable subsystem.

Observability hooks: monitor queue depth on the work channels (the primary backpressure signal), lock wait time on the retry-table mutex (rising wait time means contention is becoming your latency), and worker panic count from join results (a crashed worker should be counted and replaced, not silently lost). Together these tell you whether the bottleneck is throughput, contention, or failure.

use std::sync::{atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering}, mpsc, Arc, Mutex};
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Config { /* immutable, loaded once */ }

struct Service {
    config: Arc<Config>,                              // shared IMMUTABLE: Arc only
    work_tx: mpsc::SyncSender<Request>,              // owned messages, BOUNDED for backpressure
    requests_done: AtomicU64,                         // hot counter: atomic, no lock
    retry_table: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<u64, u32>>>,      // truly shared + mutated: Arc<Mutex>
}

struct Request { id: u64 }

impl Service {
    fn submit(&self, req: Request) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
        // Bounded send surfaces backpressure as an error instead of unbounded growth.
        self.work_tx.try_send(req).map_err(|_| "queue full: shed or retry")
    }
    fn on_complete(&self, id: u64) {
        self.requests_done.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); // tiny critical section
        // narrow lock scope: one entry, then release
        self.retry_table.lock().unwrap().remove(&id);
    }
}

Each subsystem mapped to its model: bounded channel, Arc-only config, atomic counter, locked retry table.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one channel-based boundary is chosen and justified: request lifecycle moves as owned messages with backpressure as the signal.
  • At least one immutable shared-state boundary uses Arc<T> alone: startup config/routing data read by all, written by none.
  • Mutable shared state (retry table, hot counters) is justified by real shared ownership, with atomics/narrow locks preferred over convenience.
  • Observability hooks are named: queue depth, mutex lock wait time, and worker panic count.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose OS threads, scoped threads, work stealing, async tasks, or distributed workers

The four workloads map to four different execution models, and the discipline is keeping them separate rather than blurring them under the word 'concurrency'.

The request-local slice transform wants scoped OS threads. The data is a slice owned by the parent stack frame, the work is brief, and the child threads will finish before the function returns. thread::scope is built for exactly this: it guarantees its spawned threads are joined at the end of the scope, so they may borrow parent-owned data directly without 'static bounds, cloning, or heap-sharing. Choosing scoped threads here avoids copying the slice just to satisfy thread::spawn's lifetime requirement.

The large CPU-bound collection map wants a work-stealing, data-parallel scheduler (Rayon-style). The chunk sizes may be uneven, so a fixed hand-partitioning into N thread::spawn calls would leave some threads idle while others grind through heavy chunks. A work-stealing pool keeps all cores busy by letting idle workers steal pending chunks from busy ones, and it amortizes thread creation across a fixed pool. This is a scheduler strategy layered over OS threads, not a different kind of thread, the win is load balancing under uneven work, expressed as something close to a parallel iterator.

The network fan-out with many waiting sockets is an async-task problem, not an OS-thread problem. Each connection spends almost all its time waiting on IO, so spawning one OS thread per socket spends real memory and scheduler attention on threads that are merely parked. An async executor multiplexes thousands of waiting tasks onto a small thread pool, suspending each task at its await points instead of blocking a thread. The mistake to avoid is 'solving waiting with more threads', waiting is what async IO is for.

The job that must run on another machine is no longer a multithreading problem at all; it is a distributed-systems problem. Crossing the network boundary changes the ownership and failure model completely: there is no shared address space, no Send to lean on, messages can be lost or duplicated, and the remote worker can fail independently. It belongs behind an RPC or a durable queue with explicit serialization, timeouts, retries, and idempotency, and calling it 'multithreading' hides exactly the failure modes that distinguish it. Keep OS threads, async tasks, and distributed workers in three separate mental buckets.

// Workload -> model (illustrative; rayon/tokio are external crates):
//
// 1) request-local slice transform -> SCOPED OS THREADS
use std::thread;
fn transform(data: &mut [u32]) {
    let mid = data.len() / 2;
    let (a, b) = data.split_at_mut(mid);
    thread::scope(|s| {            // borrows `a`/`b`; joined before return
        s.spawn(|| a.iter_mut().for_each(|x| *x *= 2));
        s.spawn(|| b.iter_mut().for_each(|x| *x *= 2));
    });
}

// 2) large uneven CPU-bound map -> WORK-STEALING POOL (rayon)
//    let out: Vec<_> = items.par_iter().map(expensive).collect();
//    idle workers steal chunks, so uneven costs still balance across cores.

// 3) network fan-out, many waiting sockets -> ASYNC TASKS (tokio)
//    for addr in addrs { tokio::spawn(async move { fetch(addr).await }); }
//    thousands of parked awaits multiplex onto a small thread pool.

// 4) run on another machine -> DISTRIBUTED WORKER (not multithreading)
//    enqueue(SerializedJob { .. }); // RPC/durable queue: timeouts, retries, idempotency

fn main() {
    let mut v = [1u32, 2, 3, 4];
    transform(&mut v);
    println!("{:?}", v);
}

One model per workload: scoped threads, a work-stealing pool, async tasks, and a distributed queue.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • OS threads, async tasks, and distributed workers are kept in three clearly separate categories.
  • Scoped threads are chosen for the borrowed local CPU-bound transform, avoiding needless cloning.
  • A work-stealing/data-parallel model is chosen for the uneven CPU-bound collection map to balance load.
  • Network fan-out is explained as an async-task problem (parked IO waits multiplexed) rather than a thread-per-socket spray, and the cross-machine job is named distributed, not multithreaded.

Lab solution

The starter code had two defects: the worker closure was not a move closure (so it could not own jobs or tx), and it hard-coded let total = 0 instead of summing the job costs. The fix is to make the closure move (transferring ownership of the Vec<Job> and the cloned Sender into the child thread) and to compute the real total with jobs.iter().map(|job| job.cost).sum(). Because each worker owns its batch outright, no lock or shared map is needed; results travel back as small owned (&'static str, u32) tuples over the mpsc channel.

Ownership flows in one direction. main clones the sender once so both workers can publish, then moves each owned job vector into its worker. The ingest worker sums 2 + 3 = 5; the index worker sums 4 = 4. After both workers are joined (which also makes any worker panic visible and guarantees both Sender clones are dropped), the for (worker, total) in rx loop drains the channel; the loop terminates naturally once all senders are gone. The main thread accumulates the grand total 5 + 4 = 9 while recording each per-worker total, then prints ingest = 5, index = 4, grand = 9.

This is the channel-first design from the chapter's Example 1: one owner per mutable piece of state, message passing for results, and a single deterministic aggregation point on the main thread.

Example 22-S. owned_jobs_channel_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Job {
    cost: u32,
}

fn spawn_worker(
    tx: mpsc::Sender<(&'static str, u32)>,
    worker: &'static str,
    jobs: Vec<Job>,
) -> thread::JoinHandle<()> {
    // `move` transfers ownership of `jobs` and the cloned `tx` into the child.
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let total: u32 = jobs.iter().map(|job| job.cost).sum();
        tx.send((worker, total)).unwrap();
    })
}

fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

    let ingest_jobs = vec![Job { cost: 2 }, Job { cost: 3 }];
    let index_jobs = vec![Job { cost: 4 }];

    let ingest = spawn_worker(tx.clone(), "ingest", ingest_jobs);
    let index = spawn_worker(tx, "index", index_jobs);

    ingest.join().unwrap();
    index.join().unwrap();

    let mut ingest_total = 0;
    let mut index_total = 0;
    let mut grand = 0;

    for (worker, total) in rx {
        grand += total;
        if worker == "ingest" {
            ingest_total = total;
        } else if worker == "index" {
            index_total = total;
        }
    }

    println!("ingest = {}", ingest_total);
    println!("index = {}", index_total);
    println!("grand = {}", grand);
}
Output
ingest = 5
index = 4
grand = 9

Review question answers

What does Send mean, and what does Sync mean?

Send means a value of the type can be moved to another thread and safely used there as an owned value, so ownership can cross the thread boundary. Sync means it is safe for multiple threads to hold shared references (&T) to the same value simultaneously; formally, T: Sync exactly when &T: Send. Both are auto traits with no methods that the compiler derives automatically when all of a type's fields qualify, and they are the entire mechanism behind 'data races do not compile'.

Why is a move closure the ordinary shape for thread::spawn?

thread::spawn requires its closure to be 'static, because the spawned thread may outlive the stack frame that created it, so the closure cannot hold short-lived borrows of parent locals. A move closure transfers ownership of the captured non-Copy values (job batches, owned buffers, request-local data) into the child thread, giving the child data that survives independently. That is why move is the calm default: it puts the owned data on the correct side of the boundary instead of leaving the child pointing at a frame that may already be gone.

When is thread::scope a better answer than cloning or heap-sharing more data?

thread::scope is better when the worker only needs to borrow parent-owned data briefly and is guaranteed to finish before the parent continues. The scope joins all of its spawned threads at the end of the block, so the compiler permits them to borrow parent-owned data directly without a 'static bound. That lets you avoid cloning the data or wrapping it in Arc purely to satisfy thread::spawn's lifetime requirement, which is the right call whenever the child cannot outlive the parent.

What is the difference between message passing and shared-state locking as an ownership design?

Message passing keeps one thread as the owner of a piece of mutable state: other threads send it owned commands or results over a channel, and only that one thread mutates, so the aggregation point is explicit and ordering is deterministic. Shared-state locking instead gives many threads access to one allocation (via Arc) and arbitrates their mutations with a lock (Mutex), so authority over the data is shared and serialized at runtime. The first trades buffering and backpressure for a single clear owner; the second trades lock contention for a genuine single source of truth that every thread reads and writes.

Why is work stealing a scheduler strategy rather than a synonym for threads?

Work stealing is how a fixed pool of worker threads is scheduled, not a different kind of thread. Each worker keeps a queue of tasks, and when a worker runs out it steals pending tasks from a busy worker's queue, which keeps all cores busy when chunk sizes are uneven. The threads underneath are ordinary OS threads; work stealing is the load-balancing policy layered on top, which is why a Rayon-style pool is often calmer than hand-rolling many thread::spawn calls for CPU-bound collection work.

Why are async tasks and distributed workers separate from OS-thread design even when all three are 'concurrent'?

OS threads are scheduled by the operating system and cost real memory and scheduler attention, so they suit CPU-bound work. Async tasks are scheduled by an executor and suspend at await points instead of blocking, so they suit IO-bound waiting where thousands of parked tasks can multiplex onto a few threads; solving waiting with more OS threads is the classic mismatch. Distributed workers cross a network boundary, which changes the ownership and failure model entirely, no shared address space, messages that can be lost or duplicated, independent failure, so they belong behind RPC or durable queues with timeouts and retries, not under the label 'multithreading'.

Chapter 23 · Synchronization Primitives

Synchronization Primitives

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all push toward one habit: derive the synchronization primitive from the access pattern, not from instinct or from the primitive you reached for in C++ or Go. A short contended mutation wants a Mutex; a read-mostly snapshot wants an RwLock; a single-word flag or counter wants an atomic; a thread that must wait on a predicate wants a Condvar paired with that predicate's mutex; a phase boundary wants a Barrier; and a subsystem with one logical owner usually wants a channel instead of any shared lock at all. The warm-up and design exercises train the classification step, while the implementation and debugging exercises make you confront the two failure modes that actually ship: misordered locks and condvar waits that trust wakeup instead of re-checking state.

The through-line is that in Rust the lock owns the data. A Mutex<T> hands out a guard, and the guard is a borrow whose lifetime is the critical section; the atomic publication pattern is the same idea expressed without a lock, where a Release store and an Acquire load form the happens-before edge that lets a reader trust everything the writer did beforehand. Keep that ownership-and-visibility framing in view and every exercise below reduces to the same question: who owns this mutation, and who needs to see it.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomic, barrier, or channel from the workload

Work through the six cases by asking the decision-order questions in turn: is the state shared and mutable at all, are readers frequent, is waiting involved, and does the invariant fit in one machine word.

The shared mutable retry map is the only case that is genuinely shared mutable state with no read/write skew worth exploiting: many workers both read and modify it constantly. That is a Mutex<HashMap<...>>. A retry table is mutated on essentially every access, so the read-write distinction buys nothing and a plain mutex is the calmest fit.

The read-mostly config snapshot is a read-mostly state boundary. Every request reads it and only an occasional reload writes it, so an RwLock<Config> lets the many readers proceed in parallel and the rare writer take exclusivity. Even better, if the config is replaced wholesale rather than mutated field by field, an Arc<Config> swapped atomically removes the lock entirely.

The worker waiting for a non-empty queue is a waited-on predicate under one mutex: the predicate is queue.is_empty(), it lives under a Mutex, and the worker uses a Condvar to sleep until it might have changed. The condvar is not the source of truth; the mutex-protected predicate is, which is why the wait belongs in a loop (see Exercise 5).

The hot metrics counter is small enough for atomics: a single AtomicU64 incremented with fetch_add carries the whole invariant in one word, so no lock is needed. The startup start-gun for several workers is a phase boundary, not a state container: a Barrier::new(n) releases all workers at once and holds no data of its own. Finally, the single owner thread receiving commands wants ownership transfer rather than shared mutation: an mpsc channel hands owned commands to the one owner, so there is no shared lock to reason about at all.

The distinction the exercise asks you to keep sharp is condvar-predicate versus channel-handoff. A condvar coordinates threads around state that several of them touch under a shared mutex; a channel moves owned values to a single owner so the state stops being shared. If the queue should belong to exactly one thread, the channel is simpler; if multiple threads must inspect and mutate the same protected queue, the condvar design is the honest one. Atomics are deliberately last on the list for the counter only, because treating atomics as the default answer for every shared-state problem leads straight to memory-ordering bugs that a mutex or channel would have avoided.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each of the six cases is mapped to a primitive (Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomic, Barrier, channel) and justified by the shape of its state and access pattern.
  • The condvar-predicate case (waiting on queue.is_empty() under a mutex) is contrasted explicitly with the channel-handoff case (owned commands to one owner).
  • Atomics are reserved for the single-word counter and explicitly rejected as a default for the map, the config, and the queue.
Exercise 2code reading

Replace a Mutex with RwLock where appropriate

Start from the access pattern, not the type. With Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, Config>>>, every lookup of a route's config calls lock() and serializes against every other lookup, even though lookups never conflict with each other. Reads dominate and writes happen only on occasional reloads, so the lock is serializing operations that are logically read-only.

Under an RwLock<HashMap<String, Config>>, every config lookup becomes config.read(), and only the reload path becomes config.write(). The workload assumption that makes this plausible is exactly the stated one: reads vastly outnumber writes, and a read holds the lock only long enough to clone or copy out the value it needs. Many readers can then hold the lock concurrently, so on a multi-core server the read path stops being a single-lane bottleneck.

An RwLock is not automatically the better choice, and naming a case where it is the wrong upgrade is required. If writes were frequent, the writer would repeatedly have to wait for all readers to drain and then exclude everyone, which can starve and is often slower than a mutex's simple alternation; depending on the implementation, frequent writers can also starve under reader-preferring policies. And if each critical section is tiny, for example a single HashMap lookup that copies out one small Config, the extra bookkeeping an RwLock does to track reader counts can cost more than the contention it removes. In both of those cases a plain Mutex stays calmer and frequently faster. The signal for RwLock is read-mostly access with non-trivial read sections, not a desire to make the code look more concurrent.

Finally, distinguish the primitive change from the ownership-model change. Swapping Mutex for RwLock is a local tactical edit; it keeps the same shared-mutable design. The larger change is to stop sharing mutable state at all. If reloads replace the whole table, store an Arc<HashMap<String, Config>> (or Arc<Config> per route) and publish a new immutable snapshot on reload while readers keep their old Arc until they drop it; readers then take no lock and never block each other or the writer. Alternatively, give the config one owner thread and have it answer requests over a channel. Those are not 'a faster lock'; they remove the lock by changing who owns mutation.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::{Arc, RwLock};

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct Config {
    upstream: &'static str,
}

// Tactical change: reads become read(), the rare reload becomes write().
fn lookup(cache: &Arc<RwLock<HashMap<String, Config>>>, route: &str) -> Option<Config> {
    let guard = cache.read().unwrap(); // many readers proceed in parallel
    guard.get(route).cloned()          // copy out, then release fast
}

fn reload(cache: &Arc<RwLock<HashMap<String, Config>>>, route: String, cfg: Config) {
    let mut guard = cache.write().unwrap(); // occasional exclusive writer
    guard.insert(route, cfg);
}

// Strategic alternative: stop sharing mutable state. Publish an immutable
// snapshot and swap the Arc on reload; readers take no lock at all.
fn snapshot_lookup(current: &Arc<HashMap<String, Config>>, route: &str) -> Option<Config> {
    current.get(route).cloned()
}

RwLock as a read-mostly tactical fit, with an immutable-snapshot alternative that removes the lock by changing ownership.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The lookup path maps to read() and the reload path to write(), and read-mostly access is named as the main signal for considering RwLock.
  • At least one wrong-upgrade case is given: frequent writes (writer starvation) or tiny read sections where RwLock bookkeeping outweighs a Mutex.
  • The local Mutex-to-RwLock swap is distinguished from the larger ownership change of immutable Arc snapshots or a one-owner channel.
Exercise 3implementation

Reason about Acquire and Release in a toy publication protocol

The protocol publishes one payload word through one flag. The writer stores the payload, then stores true into the flag; the reader loads the flag and, only if it is true, loads the payload. The whole correctness argument rests on which atomic operation carries the ordering edge.

Keep the payload word relaxed. A Relaxed store and Relaxed load are still atomic, so the reader never sees a torn value, but Relaxed imposes no ordering on the surrounding memory operations. That is fine here because the payload does not need to order anything on its own; it is the thing being published, not the thing doing the publishing.

Put the ordering on the flag. The writer uses Ordering::Release on the flag store. A Release store guarantees that every write the writer performed before it, in particular the payload store, is visible to any thread that later performs an Acquire load which observes that store. The reader uses Ordering::Acquire on the flag load. When the Acquire load reads true, it establishes a happens-before edge with the writer's Release store, and therefore the reader is guaranteed to also see the payload write that preceded it. This is the canonical release/acquire publication pair.

The key insight the exercise wants you to articulate is why the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge. The flag is the single point both threads agree to synchronize on: the writer's last action and the reader's first decision. The release/acquire relationship is a property of that one pair of operations on the same atomic. The payload load can stay relaxed precisely because the Acquire load of the flag has already fenced everything that happened before the matching Release store. If the consumer has not performed an Acquire load that observed the flag as true, it has no right to trust the payload; loading the payload first, or loading the flag with Relaxed, would break the publication and could legally read a stale zero on a weakly ordered machine. This is exactly the design the runnable lab implements, and it prints ready = true and value = 42.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let value = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let ready = AtomicBool::new(false);

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        // Publisher: relaxed payload, then a Release flag store.
        scope.spawn(|| {
            value.store(42, Ordering::Relaxed);   // payload carries no ordering
            ready.store(true, Ordering::Release); // release edge publishes it
        });

        // Consumer: Acquire load of the flag gates trust in the payload.
        scope.spawn(|| {
            while !ready.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
                thread::yield_now();
            }
            // The Acquire load above observed the Release store, so the
            // relaxed payload load below is guaranteed to see 42.
            println!("ready = {}", true);
            println!("value = {}", value.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
        });
    });
}

Release/Acquire publication: the flag carries the happens-before edge, the payload stays relaxed.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The writer publishes the flag with Ordering::Release.
  • The consumer loads the flag with Ordering::Acquire before it trusts the published state.
  • The payload word stays Relaxed and the runnable lab prints ready = true and value = 42.
  • The explanation states that the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge because release/acquire synchronizes the one shared atomic both threads agree on.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Find and fix a deadlock scenario

The defect is a lock-order inversion that creates a circular wait. Thread A acquires accounts and then tries to acquire audit; Thread B acquires audit and then tries to acquire accounts. The deadlock condition is the moment both threads have taken their first lock and are each blocked waiting on the lock the other holds: A holds accounts and waits for audit, B holds audit and waits for accounts. Neither will release until it makes progress, and neither can make progress, so both wait forever. That this is rare is irrelevant; it is a structural property of the code, not a statistical fluke, and it will eventually be hit in production. All four Coffman conditions hold, but the only one under our control here is the circular wait, so that is the one we break.

The mechanically enforceable repair is a single global lock order that every path obeys: always lock accounts before audit, never the reverse. Once both threads acquire in the same order, the cycle is impossible, because no thread can hold the later lock while requesting the earlier one. This is enforceable rather than a plea to 'be careful' if you funnel both subsystems through one helper that takes the locks in the fixed order, so no call site can get it wrong. The fix is to impose one global ordering that both threads obey.

Lock ordering is the minimal repair, but it is not always the best one, and the exercise asks you to justify the choice. Two stronger options reshape the problem so the second lock disappears. First, make one subsystem the owner: if audit is really a log, give it a single owner thread and send audit records over a channel, so the account path never locks audit at all and there is no second lock to order. Second, reconsider whether the two locks need to be held together. If the only reason both are locked is to keep an account update and its audit entry atomic, you can record the audit event after releasing the accounts lock (accepting a brief window where the update is visible before its audit line), or consolidate the truly-coupled state under one lock so a single critical section covers both. The decision rule: if the two pieces of state are genuinely independent and only incidentally touched together, lock ordering or a channel owner is the clean fix; if they form one invariant, consolidate them under one lock so there is no second lock to invert.

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

// Repair 1: one global lock order. Always accounts, then audit -- everywhere.
// Funnel both paths through one helper so no call site can invert the order.
fn transfer(
    accounts: &Arc<Mutex<i64>>,
    audit: &Arc<Mutex<Vec<&'static str>>>,
    delta: i64,
) {
    let mut acc = accounts.lock().unwrap(); // lock 1: accounts FIRST
    let mut log = audit.lock().unwrap();    // lock 2: audit SECOND
    *acc += delta;
    log.push("transfer");
}

fn main() {
    let accounts = Arc::new(Mutex::new(100));
    let audit = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()));

    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..2)
        .map(|_| {
            let accounts = Arc::clone(&accounts);
            let audit = Arc::clone(&audit);
            thread::spawn(move || transfer(&accounts, &audit, 10))
        })
        .collect();

    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }

    println!("balance = {}", *accounts.lock().unwrap());
    println!("audit_len = {}", audit.lock().unwrap().len());
}

Global lock ordering: both paths acquire accounts before audit through one helper, breaking the circular wait.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The circular-wait condition is stated concretely: A holds accounts and waits for audit while B holds audit and waits for accounts.
  • The proposed repair (one global lock order enforced through a single helper) is mechanically enforceable, not advisory.
  • The answer weighs lock ordering against state reshaping (consolidating the coupled state) and ownership transfer (a channel-owned audit log) and gives a rule for choosing among them.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Repair a condvar wait loop before it flakes under load

The defect is wakeup-as-truth. The worker does if queue.is_empty() { condvar.wait(...) } and then assumes a job is ready as soon as it wakes. An if is the wrong shape because a condvar wakeup does not promise the predicate is now true; it only tells the waiter to re-check. Three things can wake a single if-guarded wait and leave the queue empty: a spurious wakeup (permitted by the platform and the API), a notify_all that wakes several waiters when only one job arrived so all but one find the queue empty again, and a wakeup that races against another consumer that already drained the queue. After any of those, the worker proceeds to pop from an empty queue and panics or misbehaves. Under load these races become frequent rather than theoretical.

The fix is to re-check the predicate in a loop. Replace the if with a while that re-evaluates the predicate every time wait returns, and only leave the loop when the predicate genuinely holds. The predicate that belongs under the mutex is the shared queue state itself, queue.is_empty() (and, in a closeable queue, the closed flag), because that is the real source of truth. The condvar only wakes the worker; the queue state under the mutex remains the real predicate. This is exactly the structure of the chapter's mutex-plus-condvar example, where the worker holds the lock and loops on while state.jobs.is_empty() && !state.closed, calling wait inside the loop so it re-checks after every wakeup.

The notifier side matters too. The notifying thread must update the predicate, in this design push a job or set closed, while it holds the same mutex, and only then call notify. If it notified before updating the state, a waiter could wake, re-check, find nothing, and sleep again, losing the signal. Updating the mutex-protected state first and notifying after guarantees that any waiter that re-acquires the lock observes the change. The mutex-protected state and the condvar are one design, not two independent pieces.

Finally, note when a channel is simpler. If exactly one thread should own and drain the queue, an mpsc channel removes the shared queue, the mutex, and the condvar all at once: producers send owned jobs, and the single consumer's recv blocks until an item arrives and returns it directly, with no predicate to re-check and no spurious-wakeup handling. The condvar design is correct and is the right tool when several threads must coordinate around the same protected queue, but a one-owner channel is the simpler design when the queue has a single natural owner.

use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::sync::{Condvar, Mutex};

struct Queue {
    state: Mutex<(VecDeque<u32>, bool)>, // (jobs, closed)
    ready: Condvar,
}

impl Queue {
    // Consumer: re-check the predicate in a loop, never trust the wakeup.
    fn next(&self) -> Option<u32> {
        let mut guard = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        loop {
            if let Some(job) = guard.0.pop_front() {
                return Some(job); // predicate genuinely held
            }
            if guard.1 {
                return None; // closed and drained
            }
            // wait releases the mutex, sleeps, then re-acquires it; the
            // loop re-evaluates the predicate after every wakeup.
            guard = self.ready.wait(guard).unwrap();
        }
    }

    // Producer: update the protected state FIRST, then notify.
    fn push(&self, job: u32) {
        let mut guard = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        guard.0.push_back(job);
        drop(guard);
        self.ready.notify_one();
    }
}

Predicate-in-a-loop: wait re-checks the mutex-protected queue after each wakeup; the producer updates state before notifying.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The if is replaced with a while loop that re-checks the predicate after each wakeup, replacing wakeup-as-truth with predicate-in-a-loop reasoning.
  • The shared queue state under the mutex is named as the source of truth that remains authoritative after wakeup, with the notifier updating it before calling notify.
  • At least one case is given where a one-owner mpsc channel removes the shared queue, mutex, and condvar entirely.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose the right primitive for a service under load

Walk the pipeline accept -> parse -> route -> update metrics -> consult config -> enqueue work -> wait for completion -> publish result and assign each stage the primitive its access pattern demands, keeping each mutable subsystem with one obvious owner wherever possible.

Immutable shared state with Arc only: the routing table and the parsed request. The routing rules are read on every request and rarely change, so publish them as an Arc<RoutingTable> and swap the Arc on reload; readers clone the Arc and take no lock. The parsed request is owned by the request's own task and never shared mutably, so it needs no synchronization at all.

Mutex or RwLock: the config snapshot is the candidate for RwLock, and only because it is genuinely read-mostly, consulted on every request and rewritten only on occasional reloads, which is the read-mostly pattern that justifies the choice rather than aesthetics. If the config is replaced wholesale rather than edited in place, prefer the immutable Arc<Config> swap and drop the lock entirely. A Mutex is appropriate only for small contended mutable state that is genuinely shared and write-heavy, for example an in-flight or retry table that workers mutate on nearly every access; there the read/write split buys nothing.

Owned commands and results over channels: enqueue work and wait for completion. Submit owned work items to a worker pool over an mpsc (or bounded sync_channel) so the queue has a single owner and there is no shared lock; the bounded variant also gives backpressure. Wait for completion with a per-request oneshot-style channel: the worker sends the owned result back and the request thread blocks on recv until it arrives. Then publish result by sending that owned value onward, again by move, not by shared mutation.

Atomics where a counter or flag is enough: update metrics and the shutdown flag. A request counter or error counter is one word, so an AtomicU64 with fetch_add(1, Relaxed) suffices and needs no lock; a relaxed ordering is fine because counters need no happens-before relationship with other state. A graceful-shutdown flag is an AtomicBool, published with Release and observed with Acquire if it gates other state.

For production measurement before upgrading to a more complex primitive: instrument lock wait time and lock hold time on any Mutex or RwLock, queue depth and enqueue latency on the channels, condvar wakeup rate if a condvar is used, and end-to-end retry latency. Upgrade only when those numbers show a real bottleneck, and keep lock-free structures off the critical path until a measured requirement appears, because they imply unsafe code and a memory-reclamation story that is rarely worth it. One service legitimately uses several primitives at once: Arc snapshots for routing and config, atomics for metrics, a Mutex only for the contended retry table, and channels for the work queue and result handoff. The cleanest version keeps each mutable subsystem under one owner.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::mpsc::{sync_channel, SyncSender};
use std::sync::Arc;

struct Config { upstream: &'static str }
struct RoutingTable { /* rules */ }

struct Service {
    routing: Arc<RoutingTable>,   // immutable snapshot, swapped on reload
    config: Arc<Config>,          // immutable snapshot; RwLock only if edited in place
    requests: AtomicU64,          // hot counter -> one atomic word, Relaxed
    work_tx: SyncSender<Job>,     // bounded channel -> one-owner queue + backpressure
}

struct Job { reply: std::sync::mpsc::Sender<u64> } // per-request result handoff

impl Service {
    fn handle(&self) -> u64 {
        self.requests.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); // metrics: no lock
        let _ = &self.routing;                         // read snapshot, no lock
        let _ = self.config.upstream;                  // read-mostly snapshot

        let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel();
        self.work_tx.send(Job { reply: reply_tx }).unwrap(); // enqueue owned work
        reply_rx.recv().unwrap() // wait for completion: block on owned result
    }
}

One service, several primitives: Arc snapshots for routing/config, an atomic counter for metrics, and bounded channels for the work queue and result handoff.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one subsystem is assigned to channels (work queue and result handoff) and at least one to shared state or atomics (metrics counter, retry table), each with a reason.
  • The RwLock/config choice is justified by a read-mostly access pattern, and the immutable Arc-swap alternative is offered when the config is replaced wholesale.
  • At least one observability hook is named (lock wait time, queue depth, condvar wakeup rate, or retry latency) as the trigger for any upgrade.
  • Lock-free structures are kept off the critical path until a measured requirement appears.

Lab solution

The lab implements the canonical release/acquire publication pattern. publish first stores the payload 42 with Ordering::Relaxed, then stores true into the ready flag with Ordering::Release. The Release store is the publication edge: it guarantees that the preceding relaxed write to value is visible to any thread that later performs an Acquire load which observes the flag as true.

try_consume does the matching half. It loads ready with Ordering::Acquire, and only if that load observes true does it load the payload. The Acquire load pairs with the writer's Release store to establish a happens-before relationship, so the relaxed load of value is guaranteed to see 42 rather than the initial 0. The payload itself stays relaxed deliberately: the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge, which is the whole point the chapter draws out in the atomics-and-ordering section.

In this single-threaded main the writes obviously complete before the reads, so the ordering choice does not change the printed result here; the program prints ready = true then value = 42. The Release/Acquire pairing is what makes the same code correct when publish and try_consume run on different threads, which is the design the chapter's Example 3 demonstrates with thread::scope. The fix over the starter code is precisely upgrading the flag store to Release and the flag loads to Acquire while leaving the payload relaxed.

Example 23-S. acquire_release_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicUsize, Ordering};

fn publish(value: &AtomicUsize, ready: &AtomicBool, next: usize) {
    // The payload write stays relaxed: it carries no ordering of its own.
    value.store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);
    // The flag store is the release edge that publishes the payload write.
    ready.store(true, Ordering::Release);
}

fn try_consume(value: &AtomicUsize, ready: &AtomicBool) -> Option<usize> {
    // The acquire load is what lets us trust the relaxed payload below it.
    if ready.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        Some(value.load(Ordering::Relaxed))
    } else {
        None
    }
}

fn main() {
    let value = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let ready = AtomicBool::new(false);

    publish(&value, &ready, 42);

    println!("ready = {}", ready.load(Ordering::Acquire));
    println!("value = {}", try_consume(&value, &ready).unwrap_or(0));
}
Output
ready = true
value = 42

Review question answers

Why is RwLock not automatically better than Mutex?

An RwLock is a different fairness and contention trade, not a faster mutex. It lets multiple readers hold the lock at once, but a writer must wait for every reader to leave and then excludes everyone, so under frequent writes the writer can stall or starve and throughput can fall below a plain mutex. It also does more bookkeeping to track reader counts, which can cost more than the contention it removes when each critical section is tiny. RwLock pays off only when access is genuinely read-mostly with non-trivial read sections; otherwise a Mutex is calmer and often faster.

Why should a condvar wait happen in a loop instead of a one-shot if?

Because a condvar wakeup does not promise the predicate is now true; it only signals that the waiter should re-check. Spurious wakeups are permitted, a notify_all can wake several waiters when only one item arrived, and another thread may consume the state before the woken thread re-acquires the lock. A while loop re-evaluates the mutex-protected predicate after every wakeup and only exits when the predicate genuinely holds, whereas an if would let the thread proceed on a false wakeup and act on state that is not actually ready. The mutex-protected predicate, not the condvar, is the source of truth.

What does Release on a store and Acquire on a load actually buy you?

Together they create a happens-before edge between two threads through one shared atomic. A Release store guarantees that all writes the writer performed before it become visible to any thread whose Acquire load later observes that store, so the Acquire reader is guaranteed to see everything the writer did beforehand. This is what lets a single flag publish other data: the writer releases the flag, the reader acquires it, and the reader can then trust the relaxed payload writes that preceded the release. Without that pairing the reader has no ordering guarantee and may observe stale values on a weakly ordered machine.

When is a barrier the right tool, and when is it just the wrong primitive for state propagation?

A barrier is the right tool for a phase boundary: it makes n threads all reach a point before any of them proceeds, which is exactly what you want for a startup start-gun or for separating distinct computation phases. It is a synchronization gate, not a data container, and it holds no state of its own. It is the wrong primitive when you actually need to propagate or share a value, because the barrier conveys only the fact that everyone arrived, not any data; for that you still need a lock, an atomic publication, an immutable snapshot, or a channel. Reaching for a barrier to move state confuses 'everyone is here now' with 'everyone can see the new value.'

Why are lock-free structures hard even for experienced engineers?

Lock-free structures replace the simple mutual-exclusion contract of a lock with explicit memory ordering, which means reasoning directly about Acquire, Release, and the visibility of every write across threads on weakly ordered hardware. In real implementations they almost always require unsafe code plus a memory reclamation strategy, since you cannot free a node while another thread might still be reading it, leading to hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or similar machinery. Subtle bugs like the ABA problem and rare orderings that only surface under specific timing make them hard to test and hard to prove correct. That is why 'avoid all locks' is not a mature design principle on its own, and lock-free structures belong off the critical path until a measured requirement justifies the cost.

Chapter 24 · Coroutines, Futures, and Async Rust

Coroutines, Futures, and Async Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the chapter's central claim apart and rebuild it from the bottom: an async function in Rust produces an inert value, and nothing runs until an executor polls that value to completion. The warm-up and code-reading tasks make you say out loud what poll, Poll::Pending, and the executor/reactor split actually do; the implementation tasks have you hand-write the state machine the compiler normally writes for you, so the poll-by-poll mechanics stop being mysterious. By the time you have written a future that yields N times and composed two awaits in one async fn, the enum-shaped state machine model is no longer a metaphor — it is the thing you typed.

The debugging and design exercises then push the model into the situations where it earns its keep: a future that never yields (and therefore wedges the executor), and a real request that fans out to several outbound calls and must be cancelled on a deadline. The through-line is that suspension makes ownership, task lifetime, and cancellation visible in your types. Cancel means drop the future; locals held across an .await become fields of the future; cleanup of partially acquired state is the author's job, not the runtime's. Get those three right and the rest of async Rust is consequence.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Explain what calling an async fn actually does

Calling build_label("billing", "/ready") does not start the work. The call expression evaluates to a value of an opaque future type — the compiler-generated state machine for build_label — and that value is inert. None of the function body has run: no YieldOnce has been constructed, no .await has fired, no String has been formatted. The chapter's one-line summary applies exactly here: calling an async function produces a value and starts nothing.

The only thing that ever advances the future is a call to its poll method, and the component that calls poll is the executor. In this listing the executor is block_on. It pins the future with Box::pin, builds a Context from a Waker, and then loops, calling future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx). Each iteration the future runs forward until it either suspends or finishes.

When poll returns Poll::Pending, no OS thread is blocked. Pending is the future's way of handing control back to the executor and saying "I cannot make progress right now." The executor is then free to do other work — in a real runtime, poll a different ready task. Here block_on simply prints poll = pending and loops again. Crucially, the thread is never parked inside the future's body waiting on a socket; the suspension point is a return out of poll, not a blocking syscall. That is the whole efficiency argument for async: one thread can service many suspended futures because suspension is a return, not a block.

A full runtime splits into two cooperating roles. The executor is the scheduler that decides which ready task to poll next. The reactor (the IO driver) watches the operating system for readiness — a socket becoming readable, a timer firing — and signals the corresponding waker so the executor knows to poll that task again. In this std-only example there is no real IO, so there is no reactor; the NoopWake waker does nothing and block_on just re-polls in a tight loop. block_on is standing in for the executor role: it is the part that turns the future's description into actual progress by repeatedly calling poll.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States that build_label("billing", "/ready") constructs an opaque future value and runs none of the body — no YieldOnce, no .await, no format! yet.
  • Identifies poll as the only advancing operation and block_on (the executor) as the caller of poll in this listing.
  • Explains that Poll::Pending returns control to the executor instead of parking a thread, since suspension is a return out of poll.
  • Distinguishes executor (scheduler) from reactor (IO readiness) and names block_on as the executor here, with no reactor present in the std-only example.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the Handshake state machine by hand

Construct the Handshake from Example 2 with stage = Stage::Start and remaining_polls = 1, then trace the driver loop poll by poll. The match arms are ordered, and the guarded arm Stage::Waiting if self.remaining_polls > 0 fires before the plain Stage::Waiting arm, so order matters.

Poll #1: stage is Start. The Start arm sets stage = Waiting and returns Poll::Pending. State after: stage = Waiting, remaining_polls = 1. The driver prints "pending stage = Waiting" and "pending retries = 1".

Poll #2: stage is Waiting and remaining_polls (1) > 0, so the guarded arm fires: it decrements remaining_polls to 0 and returns Poll::Pending. State after: stage = Waiting, remaining_polls = 0. The driver prints "pending stage = Waiting" and "pending retries = 0".

Poll #3: stage is Waiting but remaining_polls (0) is not > 0, so the guard fails and the plain Stage::Waiting arm fires: it sets stage = Done and returns Poll::Ready("connected"). The driver prints "ready = connected" and breaks.

So poll is called three times before Poll::Ready is produced — two Pending results then one Ready. The sequence of (stage at entry, result) is: (Start, Pending), (Waiting, Pending), (Waiting, Ready).

remaining_polls is the retry budget: it is the number of extra Pending trips the future stays in the Waiting stage after the initial Start-to-Waiting transition. While the counter is above zero each poll decrements it and yields Pending; when it reaches zero the next poll falls through to the unguarded Waiting arm, transitions to Done, and reports Ready. On each Pending the driver loop prints the current stage and the remaining retry count, which is exactly what lets you watch the machine advance: every Pending either changed the stage (Start to Waiting) or lowered remaining_polls (1 to 0), so progress is guaranteed and the loop terminates.

// Poll-by-poll trace for stage = Start, remaining_polls = 1:
//
// poll #  stage at entry  arm taken                       result   state after
// ------  --------------  ------------------------------  -------  ----------------------------
//   1     Start           Start => Waiting                Pending  stage=Waiting  remaining=1
//   2     Waiting         Waiting if remaining>0 (-=1)    Pending  stage=Waiting  remaining=0
//   3     Waiting         Waiting (guard fails) => Done   Ready    stage=Done     remaining=0
//
// Driver output:
//   pending stage = Waiting
//   pending retries = 1
//   pending stage = Waiting
//   pending retries = 0
//   ready = connected
//
// poll called 3 times; 2 Pending results before Ready("connected").

Hand trace: three polls, two Pending, then Ready; the guarded Waiting arm fires before the plain one.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Trace shows Start returning Pending, then Waiting (remaining_polls 1) returning Pending, then Waiting returning Ready, in that order.
  • States poll is called three times before Poll::Ready is returned.
  • Explains remaining_polls is the retry budget keeping the future in Waiting/Pending until it hits zero.
  • Notes each Pending prints the current stage and the remaining retries from the driver loop.
Exercise 3implementation

Write a future that yields N times before completing

Generalize YieldOnce — which flips a single bool — into CountdownYield, which counts an integer down. The struct holds a single field, remaining, recording how many Pending results are still owed. The poll signature is fixed by the exercise: fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str>.

The logic in poll is: if remaining > 0, decrement it and return Poll::Pending; otherwise return Poll::Ready("done"). For n = 3 this returns Pending on the first three polls (remaining going 3 to 2 to 1 to 0) and Ready on the fourth poll, which is exactly three Pending results before completion.

The receiver self: Pin<&mut Self> matters here. To mutate remaining you go through self, the pinned mutable reference — not a separate owned copy of the struct. Because the fields of CountdownYield are plain integers and the type contains no self-referential borrow, the type is Unpin, so you can freely assign self.remaining -= 1 through the pinned reference (this is what mut self: Pin<&mut Self> plus auto-deref gives you). The mutation persists across polls precisely because it writes back into the pinned future the executor owns, not into a temporary. Drive it with the chapter's block_on loop and you will see three poll = pending lines, then label = done.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

struct CountdownYield {
    remaining: u32,
}

impl CountdownYield {
    fn new(n: u32) -> Self {
        Self { remaining: n }
    }
}

impl Future for CountdownYield {
    type Output = &'static str;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str> {
        if self.remaining > 0 {
            self.remaining -= 1; // mutate through the pinned receiver, not a copy
            Poll::Pending
        } else {
            Poll::Ready("done")
        }
    }
}

struct NoopWake;
impl Wake for NoopWake {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}

fn block_on<F: Future>(future: F) -> F::Output {
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(NoopWake));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut future = Box::pin(future);
    loop {
        match future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(value) => return value,
            Poll::Pending => println!("poll = pending"),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let label = block_on(CountdownYield::new(3));
    println!("label = {}", label);
}

// Output:
//   poll = pending
//   poll = pending
//   poll = pending
//   label = done

CountdownYield reports Pending n times (here 3) then Ready("done"), mutating its counter through the pinned receiver.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • poll signature is exactly fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str> (written with mut self so the receiver is mutable).
  • For n = 3 the future returns Poll::Pending three times and then Poll::Ready("done").
  • The counter is mutated via self.remaining through the Pin<&mut Self> receiver, not an owned copy.
  • Driver output shows exactly three poll = pending lines before the ready value, confirmed by the inline expected output.
Exercise 4implementation

Compose two awaits inside one async fn

connect_then_call awaits two YieldOnce subfutures in sequence and then formats the result. The body is: let _ = YieldOnce::new(service).await; let _ = YieldOnce::new(route).await; format!("{}:{}", service, route). The two awaits run one after the other — the second YieldOnce is not even constructed until the first has resolved to Ready.

Each YieldOnce yields exactly one Poll::Pending before becoming Ready, so two of them in sequence produce two Pending results total. Under the chapter's block_on you therefore see two poll = pending lines, then connected = billing:/ready. This is additive precisely because the awaits are sequential, not concurrent: the combined future is suspended once for the first subfuture and once for the second.

The locals service and route must survive across both await points because the final format! uses them after the second suspension. In the compiler's lowering, this is not a runtime accident — it is structural.
