The async fn becomes one enum-shaped state machine, and any local whose value is needed after an .await is stored as a field of that future so it lives as long as the future does. service and route are needed after both suspensions, so they become fields. This is the same mechanism that, later in real code, turns a borrow held across an .await into a lifetime that lasts the whole future.

Relate this to the chapter's model: each .await becomes a distinct variant of the generated state machine. There is roughly a variant for "about to start," a variant for "suspended at the first YieldOnce" (holding service and route), a variant for "suspended at the second YieldOnce" (still holding service and route), and a terminal variant. poll is a match that advances from one variant to the next, returning Pending at each suspension. The hand-written Handshake in Example 2 is exactly this shape spelled out by hand — explicit states, explicit pending, explicit ready — and connect_then_call is the version the compiler writes for you.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

struct YieldOnce {
    value: &'static str,
    yielded: bool,
}
impl YieldOnce {
    fn new(value: &'static str) -> Self {
        Self { value, yielded: false }
    }
}
impl Future for YieldOnce {
    type Output = &'static str;
    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<&'static str> {
        if self.yielded {
            Poll::Ready(self.value)
        } else {
            self.yielded = true;
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

async fn connect_then_call(service: &'static str, route: &'static str) -> String {
    // First suspension: service and route must stay alive past here.
    let _connected = YieldOnce::new(service).await;
    // Second suspension: service and route are still needed below.
    let _called = YieldOnce::new(route).await;
    format!("{}:{}", service, route)
}

struct NoopWake;
impl Wake for NoopWake {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}
fn block_on<F: Future>(future: F) -> F::Output {
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(NoopWake));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut future = Box::pin(future);
    loop {
        match future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(value) => return value,
            Poll::Pending => println!("poll = pending"),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let label = block_on(connect_then_call("billing", "/ready"));
    println!("connected = {}", label);
}

// Output:
//   poll = pending
//   poll = pending
//   connected = billing:/ready

Two sequential awaits produce two Pending results; service and route survive both suspensions as fields of the generated future.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • connect_then_call awaits both YieldOnce values in order and returns the formatted "billing:/ready" String.
  • Predicts two Pending prints, one per sequential YieldOnce, shown in the inline expected output.
  • Explains the awaited locals service and route become fields of the generated future and must outlive each suspension.
  • Connects each .await to a distinct variant of the compiler-generated state machine, tying it to Example 2's hand-written shape.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix a manual future that never yields

There are two defects, and they are opposite failures of the same rule: every Pending must change the future's own state so progress is guaranteed and termination is reachable.

Defect one is the early-Ready arm. The Start arm returns Poll::Ready immediately instead of transitioning to a Waiting stage and returning Pending. This defeats the purpose of the future entirely: it never suspends, so it models no waiting at all. The whole point of a future is to be able to report "not yet" and hand control back; an immediate Ready is just a synchronous function in disguise.

Defect two is the non-advancing Pending arm. A Waiting arm returns Poll::Pending without changing the stage and without decrementing any counter. This is the classic infinite-loop bug: the future returns Pending, the executor polls it again, it is in exactly the same state, so it returns Pending again, forever. block_on would spin without end because the future never changes anything between polls — there is no path to Ready. (In a real runtime it would be even worse: a future that returns Pending without arranging for its waker to fire can hang silently.)

The fix is to make every Pending advance the state. Rewrite the transitions so Start moves to Waiting and yields Pending; Waiting decrements a retry counter and yields Pending while the budget remains; and when the budget is exhausted Waiting moves to Done and returns Ready. Now each poll strictly advances either the stage or the counter, so the future returns Poll::Ready after a finite, predictable number of polls (one for Start, remaining_polls more for the countdown, then the final transition). Tracing it under the driver loop confirms termination: every iteration the printed stage or retry count is different from the last, which is the visible signature of guaranteed progress. This is exactly the invariant Example 2 maintains — every Pending either changes the Stage or lowers remaining_polls.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Stage {
    Start,
    Waiting,
    Done,
}

struct Handshake {
    stage: Stage,
    remaining_polls: u8,
}

impl Future for Handshake {
    type Output = &'static str;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        match self.stage {
            // FIX (defect 1): do not return Ready here; advance to Waiting and yield.
            Stage::Start => {
                self.stage = Stage::Waiting;
                Poll::Pending
            }
            // FIX (defect 2): every Pending must change state — decrement the budget.
            Stage::Waiting if self.remaining_polls > 0 => {
                self.remaining_polls -= 1;
                Poll::Pending
            }
            Stage::Waiting => {
                self.stage = Stage::Done;
                Poll::Ready("connected")
            }
            Stage::Done => Poll::Ready("connected"),
        }
    }
}

struct NoopWake;
impl Wake for NoopWake {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}

fn main() {
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(NoopWake));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut future = Box::pin(Handshake {
        stage: Stage::Start,
        remaining_polls: 1,
    });
    loop {
        match future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Pending => println!(
                "pending stage = {:?} retries = {}",
                future.as_ref().get_ref().stage,
                future.as_ref().get_ref().remaining_polls
            ),
            Poll::Ready(value) => {
                println!("ready = {}", value);
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}

// Terminates after 3 polls: Start->Waiting (Pending),
// Waiting decrements (Pending), Waiting->Done (Ready).

Both defects fixed: Start now yields instead of completing early, and the Waiting arm decrements its budget so every Pending advances state.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Diagnosis names the early-Ready Start arm and the non-advancing Pending Waiting arm as the two defects.
  • Fixed poll advances Stage or decrements remaining_polls on every Pending, guaranteeing progress.
  • Fixed future returns Poll::Ready after a finite, predictable number of polls (three for this construction).
  • Explanation ties the infinite loop to a future returning Pending without changing its own state, contrasting with Example 2's invariant.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design a cancellable fan-out for one request

The request handler parses input, fans out to several outbound RPCs, joins their results, and writes to a database, all under a single overall timeout. The design splits cleanly along the ownership question the runtime forces you to answer.

What stays borrowed versus what must be owned. Values used only inside the handler's own stack frame — the parsed request struct that you read fields from sequentially, a &str slice you only inspect — can stay borrowed, because they never leave the parent's scope. But anything a spawned child task captures must be owned (or '\''static-shared) before the task is spawned. A child task may be moved onto another worker thread and may outlive the exact stack frame that created it, so it cannot hold a plain borrow into the parent's locals. Concretely: if each outbound RPC needs the request id and a target endpoint, clone or move owned copies (String, an Arc of shared config, an owned endpoint) into each child. The discriminator is not "is it cheap to copy" but "does it cross the spawn boundary." If you do not spawn detached tasks and instead keep the children as futures joined in place (join!/a join-set the parent awaits), borrows can survive, because the children never escape the parent future's scope and the borrow checker can see that the parent outlives them.

What cancelling a child actually means. In async Rust a future only advances when it is polled, so cancelling a child means dropping its future — the parent simply stops polling it. There is no signal delivered into the middle of the child and no thread to interrupt; you destroy the state machine and its in-progress work stops at its last suspension point. So the parent triggers cancellation by dropping the child futures (or by dropping the join-set / select! losers), not by calling any cancel() method on the child.

The structured-concurrency rule. The parent owns the entire fan-out and the children cannot outlive it. Implement the timeout as a select between the joined fan-out and a timer: if the timer wins, the parent returns and the joined fan-out future is dropped, which drops every still-pending child. Because the children are owned by the parent's future (not spawned detached), dropping the parent drops them — there are no orphans continuing to run after the request is over. The parent also surfaces the first failure: if one RPC errors, the join can short-circuit and the remaining children are dropped (cancelled) the same way. This is the join-set / request-scoped task-group / parent-owned cancellation-token pattern; the runtime API varies but the ownership rule does not.

Cleanup of partially acquired state. Dropping a future stops it at its last await point, but drop alone does not unwind business-level state. If a child had already, say, taken a distributed lock, written a tentative row, or reserved a quota before it was dropped, that partially acquired state is not rolled back automatically. Cancellation safety has to be designed into the future itself: hold resources in RAII guards whose Drop releases them, defer irreversible side effects until after the last await so a drop before that point leaves nothing to undo, or structure the operation so an interrupted attempt is idempotent or explicitly compensated. The chapter's correction is the load-bearing point: cancel usually means drop the future, and if the future must clean up partially acquired state, that cleanup must be explicit in the future's own design.

// Sketch: parent owns the fan-out; a timeout drops in-flight children.
// (Illustrative; a real version uses a runtime's select!/timeout + join-set.)
//
// async fn handle(req: Request, cfg: Arc<Config>) -> Result<Response, Error> {
//     let parsed = parse(&req)?;          // borrowed locally, never crosses spawn
//     let id = parsed.id.clone();         // OWN it before fanning out
//
//     // Children are owned by THIS future (not detached spawns),
//     // so dropping this future drops them.
//     let fan_out = async {
//         let (a, b, c) = join!(
//             rpc_a(cfg.clone(), id.clone()),
//             rpc_b(cfg.clone(), id.clone()),
//             rpc_c(cfg.clone(), id.clone()),
//         );
//         let a = a?; let b = b?; let c = c?;  // first failure short-circuits
//         db_write(cfg.clone(), id.clone(), combine(a, b, c)).await
//     };
//
//     // Whole-request timeout: if the timer wins, `fan_out` is DROPPED,
//     // which cancels every still-pending child by ceasing to poll it.
//     match timeout(REQUEST_BUDGET, fan_out).await {
//         Ok(result) => result,
//         Err(_elapsed) => Err(Error::Timeout), // children already dropped
//     }
// }
//
// Cancellation safety: rpc_* / db_write must release any acquired
// resource via Drop guards and defer irreversible effects past their
// last .await, because drop does not roll back business state.

Parent-owned fan-out under a timeout: borrowed-locally vs owned-before-spawn, cancel = drop the future, cleanup must be explicit.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Separates values borrowed only within the parent scope from values that must be owned before a task crosses the spawn boundary.
  • States that cancelling a child means dropping its future — the parent stops polling it — with no signal or thread interrupt.
  • Asserts the parent owns the fan-out so children cannot outlive it, and surfaces the first failure via short-circuiting join.
  • Notes that cleanup of partially acquired state must be explicit in the future's own design (Drop guards, deferred side effects), since drop alone does not unwind it.

Lab solution

The Handshake future is a hand-written state machine over three Stage values: Connect, Authenticate, Ready. The poll method advances exactly one stage per call. On the first poll it is in Connect, so it moves the stage to Authenticate and returns Poll::Pending. On the second poll it is in Authenticate, so it moves the stage to Ready and returns Poll::Pending again. On the third poll it is in Ready, the terminal stage, so it returns Poll::Ready("session-open"). Each Pending strictly advances the stage, which is what guarantees the future terminates rather than spinning.

The block_on driver supplies the executor role. It pins the future with Box::pin, builds a Context from a no-op Waker, and loops calling poll. Every time poll returns Poll::Pending it increments a pending counter and prints "poll = pending"; when poll returns Poll::Ready it returns the value together with the pending count. Because the future yields Pending on the Connect and Authenticate stages, block_on prints "poll = pending" twice and the counter ends at 2.

Main constructs the Handshake at Stage::Connect, runs it to completion under block_on, and binds (result, pending_count) = ("session-open", 2). It then prints "result = session-open" and "pending count = 2". The four output lines — two pending prints, the result, and the pending count — are exactly the expected output. The polls field is incremented each poll for instrumentation but is not part of the printed output here.

Example 24-S. handshake_future_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Stage {
    Connect,
    Authenticate,
    Ready,
}

struct Handshake {
    stage: Stage,
    polls: u32,
}

impl Future for Handshake {
    type Output = &'static str;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        self.polls += 1;
        match self.stage {
            Stage::Connect => {
                self.stage = Stage::Authenticate;
                Poll::Pending
            }
            Stage::Authenticate => {
                self.stage = Stage::Ready;
                Poll::Pending
            }
            Stage::Ready => Poll::Ready("session-open"),
        }
    }
}

struct NoopWake;

impl Wake for NoopWake {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}

fn block_on<F: Future>(future: F) -> (F::Output, u32) {
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(NoopWake));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut future = Box::pin(future);
    let mut pending = 0u32;
    loop {
        match future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(value) => return (value, pending),
            Poll::Pending => {
                pending += 1;
                println!("poll = pending");
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let handshake = Handshake {
        stage: Stage::Connect,
        polls: 0,
    };
    let (result, pending_count) = block_on(handshake);
    println!("result = {}", result);
    println!("pending count = {}", pending_count);
}
Output
poll = pending
poll = pending
result = session-open
pending count = 2

Review question answers

Why does calling an async fn in Rust start no work, and what type does the call expression produce?

Calling an async fn produces a value and runs none of the function body — async functions are lazy. The call expression evaluates to an opaque, compiler-generated type that implements the Future trait (the function's state machine), and that value is inert until something polls it. Work begins only when an executor calls Future::poll on it; before the first poll, no locals have been initialized and no .await has run. This laziness is the foundation of the whole model: execution and thread placement are decisions the executor makes, not side effects of the call.

What does the compiler build from an async function, and what determines which locals become fields of that state machine?

The compiler rewrites the async fn into one enum-shaped state machine where each .await is a suspension point, modeled as a variant, and poll is a match that advances from one variant to the next. The locals that become fields of that state machine are exactly those whose values must survive across an .await — that is, any local still needed after a suspension point. Locals used only between two awaits and never read afterward do not need to be stored, while a value (or a borrow) held across an await is kept alive as a field for as long as the future lives. This is why borrows held across awaits turn into lifetimes that last the whole future, and why captured state must outlive each suspension.

Why does Future::poll take a Pin<&mut Self> receiver rather than a plain &mut Self?

Because the generated state machine can be self-referential: a local borrowed across an .await becomes a field that holds a pointer into another field of the same future. Moving such a value in memory would leave that internal pointer dangling, corrupting the future. Pin<&mut Self> is the type-level guarantee that the future will not be moved after polling begins, so those internal references stay valid. Many ordinary futures are movable and implement Unpin, but the poll signature must remain strong enough to handle the general self-referential case at the runtime boundary.

What are the two cooperating parts of an async runtime, and what does each one do?

An async runtime is an executor plus a reactor. The executor is the scheduler: it owns the set of tasks and decides which ready task to poll next, driving futures forward by calling poll. The reactor (the IO driver) watches the operating system for readiness events — a socket becoming readable, a timer firing — and when an event arrives it signals the corresponding task's waker so the executor knows to poll that task again. A future returns Poll::Pending and registers its waker; the reactor later wakes it; the executor re-polls. In the chapter's std-only examples there is no real IO, so block_on plays the executor role and the no-op waker stands in for the reactor.

In async Rust, what does cancelling a future mean operationally, and what is the future author still responsible for?

A future only advances when it is polled, so cancelling it operationally means dropping it: the owner stops polling and destroys the state machine, which halts its in-progress work at its last suspension point. This is what a timeout, a select! that picks another branch, or a dropped join-set does — there is no signal delivered into the future and no thread to interrupt. The author is still responsible for cleanup of any partially acquired state: dropping the future does not unwind business-level effects like a held lock, a tentative write, or a reserved quota. Cancellation safety must be designed into the future itself, typically via RAII Drop guards that release resources and by deferring irreversible side effects until after the last await.

Chapter 25 · Tokio

Tokio

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the chapter's two listings and turn them into a single discipline: decide where each unit of work runs before you write it, then make the queue depth, the cancellation path, and the CPU boundary explicit in the code. The recurring question is not "can Tokio do this" but "which surface does this belong on" — inline on an async worker, on tokio::spawn, or on spawn_blocking — and what the runtime does while that work waits.

The payoff is a service whose capacity is designed rather than discovered. A capacity-one channel makes the producer pace itself; a watch signal raced against accept inside select! gives you a drain instead of a kill; and pushing the only CPU-heavy step behind spawn_blocking keeps the IO workers free to do what they are good at, which is waiting on many things at once. Every solution below is argued in those terms.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Place each stage on the right Tokio surface

Walk the chapter's decision tree once per stage. The tree is short: work that mostly waits stays inline or on tokio::spawn, and work that mostly computes goes to spawn_blocking. The classification follows from whether the stage spends its time parked on an external event or spends it holding the CPU.

Awaiting a TCP read mostly waits. The bytes arrive when the peer and the network deliver them; the task is parked at the await point until the IO driver wakes it. This stays on the async workers — inline in a connection handler, or on tokio::spawn if you want it to run concurrently with other work. It must not go to spawn_blocking, because that would tie up a blocking-pool thread doing nothing but waiting.

Ticking a time::interval also mostly waits, and waits in a specific, cheap way. interval.tick().await registers a deadline with the timer driver and yields; the driver turns the elapsed deadline into a wakeup and feeds the task back to the scheduler. While the interval is idle it consumes no thread at all — it is a registration in the timer wheel, not a background thread and not a busy loop spinning on the clock. That is precisely why a runtime wakeup is the right tool: a dedicated thread would burn an OS thread to sleep, and a busy loop would burn a whole core checking the time.

Summing a batch of u32 values mostly computes. There is no await inside batch.into_iter().sum() — once it starts it runs to completion holding whatever thread it is on. On an IO worker that is a problem: a task that never reaches an await point monopolizes its worker for the entire computation, and the scheduler cannot hand that worker any other ready task in the meantime. So unrelated tasks that are ready to run stall behind a sum that has nothing to do with them. The chapter names putting CPU work on IO workers as the single most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow. The sum belongs on spawn_blocking, which runs it on the dedicated blocking pool and leaves the async workers free.

Reading a filesystem snapshot is blocking work and also belongs on the blocking pool. A synchronous filesystem read can block the calling thread for an unbounded time, and there is no async await point that releases the worker during that block. spawn_blocking isolates it so a slow disk does not freeze an IO worker.

// Stage-by-stage placement, with the reason in each arm.
//
//   TCP read       -> stays on async workers (parked on the IO driver)
//   interval tick  -> stays on async workers (parked on the timer driver)
//   u32 sum        -> spawn_blocking         (CPU-bound, no await point)
//   fs snapshot    -> spawn_blocking         (synchronous blocking IO)

async fn stage_placement(mut stream: tokio::net::TcpStream) -> std::io::Result<u32> {
    use tokio::io::AsyncReadExt;
    use tokio::time::{self, Duration};

    // Mostly waits: parked at the await until bytes arrive. Stays inline.
    let mut buf = vec![0_u8; 16];
    let n = stream.read(&mut buf).await?;
    buf.truncate(n);

    // Mostly waits: a timer-driver wakeup, not a thread and not a busy loop.
    let mut interval = time::interval(Duration::from_millis(10));
    interval.tick().await;

    // Mostly computes: no await inside, so move it off the IO worker.
    let batch: Vec<u32> = buf.iter().map(|&b| b as u32).collect();
    let subtotal = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>())
        .await
        .unwrap();

    Ok(subtotal)
}

Each stage routed to the surface its waiting-vs-computing profile demands.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • TCP read and interval tick are classified as waiting work kept on the async workers, not as blocking work.
  • The u32 sum is sent to spawn_blocking as CPU-heavy work, and the filesystem snapshot is sent to the blocking pool as blocking IO.
  • The answer states that an inline CPU sum monopolizes its IO worker between await points and stalls unrelated ready tasks.
  • The answer explains that time::interval is a timer-driver wakeup that holds no thread while idle.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the accept loop's select! race

Each turn of the loop in Example 2 enters a single tokio::select! with two branches: shutdown_rx.changed() and listener.accept(). select! polls both futures and proceeds with whichever resolves first; the other branch's future is dropped for this turn and re-created on the next turn.

When listener.accept() resolves with Ok((stream, _peer)), the accept branch increments accepted and calls tokio::spawn(handle(stream)). Admission stays in the listener loop — the loop's job is to admit connections and count them — while the actual per-connection work runs in a separate spawned task. The match also has an Err(_e) arm that breaks the loop with the current accepted count, covering a listener that has failed.

The shutdown branch fires when shutdown_rx.changed() resolves, and it checks two conditions because changed() can complete for two different reasons. changed.is_err() is true when every watch sender has been dropped: the receiver can never see another update, so the only sensible interpretation is stop. *shutdown_rx.borrow() re-reads the current value because a watch channel can carry values other than the stop sentinel — it was created with watch::channel(false), and a future design might push intermediate values through it. The branch only treats the channel as a stop signal when the sender is gone or the current value is true, so an unrelated update would not falsely trigger shutdown. In this example the sender sends true exactly once, so on that update *shutdown_rx.borrow() is true and the branch breaks.

The server task breaks with accepted — break accepted; is the value of the loop, which becomes the value the async block returns and therefore what server.await.unwrap() yields. The printed count is the number of connections admitted before the stop signal won the race. Because the outer code sends true only after both clients have read their replies, both connections are admitted first, so the count is 2.

Per-connection work is spawned rather than awaited inline so the loop never blocks on a single client. If the loop awaited handle(stream) directly, it could not return to select! to race the next connection against the stop signal until that one client finished. Spawning keeps admission, draining, and the shutdown race independent of how long any one connection takes.

loop {
    tokio::select! {
        changed = shutdown_rx.changed() => {
            // changed.is_err()  -> all senders dropped: nothing more can arrive, treat as stop.
            // *borrow() == true -> the explicit stop value was sent.
            if changed.is_err() || *shutdown_rx.borrow() {
                break accepted; // becomes the task's return value
            }
            // any other value: not a stop, fall through and loop again
        }
        result = listener.accept() => {
            match result {
                Ok((stream, _peer)) => {
                    accepted += 1;                 // admission counted in the loop
                    tokio::spawn(handle(stream));  // work runs off the loop
                }
                Err(_e) => break accepted,         // listener failed
            }
        }
    }
}

The two select! branches: a stop check that handles both dropped-sender and explicit-stop, and an accept that admits then spawns.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The accept branch is shown to increment accepted and spawn a handler task, keeping admission in the listener loop.
  • A changed() error is explained as all senders dropped, and borrow() re-checks because a watch can carry non-stop values.
  • The loop is shown to break with the accepted count, reflecting connections admitted before the stop signal won.
  • Spawning the handler is justified as keeping the loop free to race the next connection against the stop signal.
Exercise 3implementation

Bound the producer with a capacity-one channel

This rebuilds Example 1's shape directly. Create the channel with mpsc::channel::<Vec<u32>>(1) so its capacity is exactly one buffered item, and move tx into the producer task so the producer owns the sending half. The capacity is the whole point: a bounded mpsc does not error when full — send().await suspends until there is room. With capacity one, the first send buffers the [1,2,3] batch, and the second send([4,5]) cannot complete until the consumer has received the first batch and freed the single slot. The producer paces itself against the consumer rather than racing ahead and buffering without limit.

The consumer drives a time::interval and ticks once per received batch, so consumption is paced on the timer as well as the channel. For each batch, the per-batch sum is offloaded with tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>()) and the JoinHandle is awaited. This keeps the CPU step off the async worker — the worker stays free for the recv().await and the interval.tick().await, which are waiting work.

The recv() loop terminates naturally. When the producer task finishes, tx is dropped, every sender handle is gone, and rx.recv().await returns None, ending the while let loop. The consumer then returns (batches, total). For batches [1,2,3] and [4,5] that is two batches summing to 6 + 9 = 15, so the program prints buffer = 1, batches = 2, total = 15.

use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio::time::{self, Duration};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // Capacity 1: the second send().await cannot complete until the
    // consumer has drained the first batch and freed the single slot.
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Vec<u32>>(1);

    let producer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        tx.send(vec![1_u32, 2, 3]).await.unwrap();
        tx.send(vec![4_u32, 5]).await.unwrap();
        // tx dropped here -> recv() on the consumer side will return None
    });

    let consumer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut interval = time::interval(Duration::from_millis(10));
        let mut batches = 0_u32;
        let mut total = 0_u32;

        while let Some(batch) = rx.recv().await {
            interval.tick().await; // pace one tick per batch

            // CPU step isolated on the blocking pool, result awaited.
            let subtotal = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>())
                .await
                .unwrap();

            total += subtotal;
            batches += 1;
        }

        (batches, total)
    });

    producer.await.unwrap();
    let (batches, total) = consumer.await.unwrap();

    println!("buffer = 1");
    println!("batches = {}", batches);
    println!("total = {}", total);
}

A capacity-one mpsc paces the producer; the sum runs on spawn_blocking; the recv loop ends when tx drops.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The channel is built with capacity 1, so the second send().await blocks until the consumer takes the first batch.
  • The sum runs inside tokio::task::spawn_blocking and its JoinHandle is awaited, off the async worker.
  • The recv() loop ends when the producer drops tx, after which the consumer returns (batches, total).
  • The program prints batches = 2 and total = 15 for [1,2,3] and [4,5].
Exercise 4implementation

Add a watch-based stop signal to an accept loop

Create the signal with watch::channel(false), keep shutdown_tx in the outer code, and move shutdown_rx into the server task along with the bound listener. The server task owns admission: each loop turn is a single tokio::select! racing shutdown_rx.changed() against listener.accept().

The accept branch counts the connection and spawns the handler — tokio::spawn(handle(stream)) — so the loop is free to return to the select! immediately and race the next connection against the stop signal instead of blocking on one client. The shutdown branch breaks the loop, and like Example 2 it treats both forms of stop: changed.is_err() means every sender was dropped, and *shutdown_rx.borrow() being true is the explicit stop value. Breaking with break accepted; makes the accepted count the task's return value, recoverable through the JoinHandle.

The outer code does its client work first, then calls shutdown_tx.send(true) exactly once, then awaits the server handle to recover the count. Sending after the clients finish guarantees both connections are admitted before the stop signal can win the race, so the returned count equals the number of connections admitted before shutdown — here, two.

use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
use tokio::sync::watch;

async fn handle(mut stream: tokio::net::TcpStream) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    stream.write_all(b"pong\n").await?;
    Ok(())
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await?;
    let addr = listener.local_addr()?;
    let (shutdown_tx, mut shutdown_rx) = watch::channel(false);

    let server = tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut accepted = 0_usize;
        loop {
            tokio::select! {
                changed = shutdown_rx.changed() => {
                    if changed.is_err() || *shutdown_rx.borrow() {
                        break accepted;
                    }
                }
                result = listener.accept() => {
                    match result {
                        Ok((stream, _peer)) => {
                            accepted += 1;
                            tokio::spawn(handle(stream));
                        }
                        Err(_e) => break accepted,
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    });

    let client = |addr| async move {
        let mut stream = tokio::net::TcpStream::connect(addr).await.unwrap();
        let mut buf = [0_u8; 5];
        stream.read_exact(&mut buf).await.unwrap();
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf).trim().to_string()
    };
    let a = tokio::spawn(client(addr)).await.unwrap();
    let b = tokio::spawn(client(addr)).await.unwrap();

    // Stop signal sent exactly once, after the clients are done.
    shutdown_tx.send(true).unwrap();
    let accepted = server.await.unwrap();

    println!("accepted = {}", accepted);
    println!("client_a = {}", a);
    println!("client_b = {}", b);
    Ok(())
}

A watch signal raced against accept inside select!; the stop is sent once after clients finish.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The server task owns the listener and watch receiver, and the loop body is a single tokio::select! over the two branches.
  • The shutdown branch breaks on a changed() error or a true borrow(), and the accept branch spawns the handler separately.
  • The outer code sends the stop signal once after its work is done, then awaits the server handle.
  • The returned accepted count equals the connections admitted before the stop signal won the race.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Stop a CPU stage from starving the IO workers

The defect is that batch.into_iter().sum() runs inline on the async worker. The consumer awaits the next item, then computes the sum with no intervening await, then awaits again. During the sum there is no suspension point, so the future never yields control back to the scheduler. The worker thread is held for the full duration of the computation. Individually each operation looks cheap, which is exactly why the slowdown is mysterious: nothing in the code looks blocking, but a task that never reaches an await point monopolizes its worker until it returns.

This interacts badly with the multithread runtime. The scheduler relies on tasks yielding at await points so it can steal and balance work across the pool. A task stuck in a synchronous loop is not stealable — it cannot be migrated mid-computation, and it is not parked, so the worker it sits on is unavailable to every other ready task. Under load, several such sums on several workers leave the pool with fewer threads able to service waiting IO, and the whole service slows even though no single operation is expensive. The chapter calls putting CPU work on IO workers the single most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow.

The fix moves the sum behind tokio::task::spawn_blocking and awaits the JoinHandle. spawn_blocking runs the closure on the dedicated blocking pool, and the await is a real suspension point: the async worker yields while the blocking pool computes, so it is free to service other ready tasks. The totals are identical because the sum is the same computation, just relocated.

tokio::spawn would not fix this. tokio::spawn schedules another async task onto the same IO worker pool — it does not move the work to a different pool. The CPU sum would still run on an IO worker and still hold that worker between await points; you would have moved the problem, not isolated it. Only spawn_blocking changes the pool the computation runs on.

use tokio::sync::mpsc;

// BEFORE: the sum runs inline on the IO worker, holding it with no await.
async fn consume_bad(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<Vec<u32>>) -> u32 {
    let mut total = 0_u32;
    while let Some(batch) = rx.recv().await {
        let subtotal: u32 = batch.into_iter().sum(); // no await: worker is stuck here
        total += subtotal;
    }
    total
}

// AFTER: the sum moves to the blocking pool; the await frees the worker.
async fn consume_good(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<Vec<u32>>) -> u32 {
    let mut total = 0_u32;
    while let Some(batch) = rx.recv().await {
        let subtotal = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>())
            .await
            .unwrap();
        total += subtotal; // same totals, different pool
    }
    total
}

The sum moves from inline (holds the IO worker) to spawn_blocking (runs on the blocking pool), output unchanged.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The diagnosis states the inline sum runs on an IO worker with no intervening await, blocking other ready tasks until it finishes.
  • The fix moves the CPU step to spawn_blocking and awaits its result, keeping the async workers free.
  • The answer explains tokio::spawn keeps the work on the same IO worker pool and does not isolate the CPU cost.
  • The refactored consumer computes the same totals as before.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design backpressure and shutdown for an ingress service

Runtime choice: the multithread runtime. The ingress service handles many independent connections, each producing Send jobs that can run on any worker, and the multithread scheduler can spread those across the pool and steal work to keep workers busy when load is uneven. Work-stealing is the concrete benefit: an idle worker pulls ready tasks from a busier worker's queue, so throughput does not collapse just because connections arrived unevenly. The current-thread runtime would be the right choice only for a small, embedded, or deliberately non-Send service where a single executor thread is sufficient and you want to avoid the synchronization a work-stealing scheduler implies — not the case here.

Queue bounds: every internal queue is a bounded mpsc with an explicitly stated capacity. The queue from the accept/ingress stage to the processing stage is bounded so that when the processing stage falls behind, the channel fills and send().await on the producer side suspends. That is backpressure: a full queue pushes back on the upstream producer instead of silently growing. The capacity is a policy — pick it for the latency and memory budget you can tolerate, and state it, rather than discovering the de facto policy later from a memory graph of an unbounded queue. The chapter's framing applies directly: spawning faster than downstream can finish is not throughput, it is queue growth with nicer syntax, so the bound is what makes capacity an explicit design decision.

Shutdown sequence: a watch stop signal raced against accept inside select!. While running, the accept loop's select! races shutdown_rx.changed() against listener.accept(). On a stop signal — either an explicit true or all senders dropped — the loop stops admitting new connections first. It then drains: in-flight connection tasks, which were spawned separately from the listener loop, are allowed to finish before process exit. Stopping admission before draining is what makes shutdown lossless for accepted work — no new connections are taken, but everything already admitted completes. Awaiting the spawned handles (or a join set / a counted wait) before exit is what realizes the drain.

Blocking and CPU stages: the filesystem-snapshot reads and any CPU-heavy processing (the batch sums) move to spawn_blocking, off the IO workers. Keeping admission and connection ownership separate — the listener owns admission, each connection runs as its own spawned task — keeps admission, draining, and metrics easy to reason about. The closing point is the concurrency-control discipline: spawning more tasks is not a substitute for bounding the queue. Faster spawning without a downstream bound just relocates the backlog from a queue you can see into task memory you cannot, so the bound, not the spawn rate, is the real throughput control.

// Runtime shape sketch for the ingress service.
#[tokio::main(flavor = "multi_thread")] // Send tasks across a work-stealing pool
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    use tokio::sync::{mpsc, watch};

    // Bounded internal queue: a full queue makes send().await suspend (backpressure).
    let (job_tx, mut job_rx) = mpsc::channel::<Vec<u32>>(64); // capacity is explicit policy
    let (shutdown_tx, mut shutdown_rx) = watch::channel(false);

    // Processing stage: CPU work isolated on the blocking pool.
    let processor = tokio::spawn(async move {
        while let Some(batch) = job_rx.recv().await {
            let _subtotal = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>())
                .await
                .unwrap();
        }
    });

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await?;
    let server = tokio::spawn(async move {
        loop {
            tokio::select! {
                changed = shutdown_rx.changed() => {
                    if changed.is_err() || *shutdown_rx.borrow() {
                        break; // stop admitting first
                    }
                }
                result = listener.accept() => {
                    if let Ok((stream, _peer)) = result {
                        let job_tx = job_tx.clone();
                        tokio::spawn(async move {
                            // per-connection work; send().await applies backpressure
                            let _ = job_tx.send(vec![1, 2, 3]).await;
                            let _ = stream; // fs snapshot reads would go to spawn_blocking
                        });
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    });

    // ... do work ...
    shutdown_tx.send(true).unwrap(); // stop admission
    server.await.unwrap();           // drain accepted connections
    processor.await.unwrap();        // drain the processing queue
    Ok(())
}

Multithread runtime, bounded queue for backpressure, watch-driven drain, CPU/fs stages on the blocking pool.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The design chooses the multithread runtime for Send tasks and explains the work-stealing benefit.
  • Internal queues are bounded so a full queue makes send await and pushes backpressure upstream, with capacity stated as explicit policy.
  • Shutdown races a watch stop signal against accept in select!, stops admission first, then drains spawned connection tasks before exit.
  • CPU-heavy and filesystem stages move to the blocking pool, and the design notes that spawning faster than downstream finishes is queue growth, not throughput.

Lab solution

The lab models Example 1's pipeline in plain std so you can see the coupling without a Tokio runtime. A sync_channel with capacity one is the std analogue of the chapter's mpsc::channel(1): it buffers exactly one item, so the producer's second send blocks until the consumer has received the first batch and freed the slot. Producer and consumer speeds are forced to meet — the producer cannot run ahead and buffer without limit, which is the same backpressure the bounded async channel provides.

The only piece to fill in is cpu_subtotal, which stands in for the chapter's spawn_blocking CPU step. In the async version this sum is pushed onto the blocking pool so it never holds an async worker; here it is simply a function the consumer calls. The body is batch.into_iter().sum(), summing the batch into one subtotal.

The consumer loops with while let Ok(batch) = rx.recv(), accumulating batches and total. The loop ends when the producer thread finishes and drops tx: with every sender gone, recv() returns Err and the while let stops. For [1,2,3] and [4,5] that is two batches summing to 6 + 9 = 15, so the program prints buffer = 1, batches = 2, total = 15.

Example 25-S. bounded_queue_backpressure_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel;
use std::thread;

fn cpu_subtotal(batch: Vec<u32>) -> u32 {
    // The CPU-heavy step, isolated from the receive loop just as the
    // chapter pushes it behind spawn_blocking off the async workers.
    batch.into_iter().sum()
}

fn main() {
    // A capacity of one couples producer and consumer: the second
    // send cannot complete until the consumer has taken the first batch.
    let capacity = 1;
    let (tx, rx) = sync_channel::<Vec<u32>>(capacity);

    let producer = thread::spawn(move || {
        tx.send(vec![1_u32, 2, 3]).unwrap();
        tx.send(vec![4_u32, 5]).unwrap();
    });

    let consumer = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut batches = 0_u32;
        let mut total = 0_u32;
        while let Ok(batch) = rx.recv() {
            let subtotal = cpu_subtotal(batch);
            total += subtotal;
            batches += 1;
        }
        (batches, total)
    });

    producer.join().unwrap();
    let (batches, total) = consumer.join().unwrap();

    println!("buffer = {}", capacity);
    println!("batches = {}", batches);
    println!("total = {}", total);
}
Output
buffer = 1
batches = 2
total = 15

Review question answers

What are the four moving parts the #[tokio::main] macro hides, and how do the IO driver and timer driver keep the scheduler from blocking on IO or time?

The macro builds and starts a runtime that wraps four parts: the task scheduler (which runs ready futures), the IO driver (an epoll/kqueue/IOCP reactor for network and file readiness), the timer driver (a timer wheel for deadlines), and the worker threads the scheduler runs on. The key is that the scheduler never blocks waiting for IO or for time. Instead, a task that awaits IO or a timer registers interest and yields; the IO driver and timer driver wait on external readiness and turn each event into a wakeup that feeds the now-ready task back to the scheduler. Genuinely blocking work is kept off this path entirely by routing it to the separate blocking pool.

When should a service use the multithread runtime versus the current-thread runtime, and what does work-stealing buy a Send-task workload?

Use the multithread runtime as the default for a service whose tasks are Send, because it schedules those tasks across a pool of worker threads and can run many of them truly in parallel. Use the current-thread runtime when the application is small, embedded, or deliberately built around non-Send state, where a single executor thread is enough and you want to avoid the synchronization a multi-worker scheduler requires. Work-stealing means an idle worker pulls ready tasks from a busier worker's local queue, so the pool stays balanced even when load arrives unevenly — throughput does not collapse just because tasks piled onto one worker.

Why does a bounded mpsc with an explicit capacity provide backpressure, and what does send().await do when the channel is full?

A bounded mpsc can hold only its stated capacity, so once the consumer falls behind and the buffer fills, the channel itself becomes the signal that the producer must slow down. send().await on a full channel does not error and does not drop the message; it suspends the producer task until the consumer receives an item and frees a slot, then completes. That suspension is the backpressure: it paces the producer to the consumer's rate. Choosing the capacity makes the slowdown policy an explicit design decision rather than something you discover later as unbounded memory growth.

What distinguishes work that belongs on tokio::spawn from work that belongs on spawn_blocking, and what happens when CPU-heavy work runs on an IO worker?

Work that mostly waits — network IO, timers, awaiting other futures — belongs inline or on tokio::spawn, because it parks at await points and returns its worker to the scheduler while it waits. Work that mostly computes, or that calls a synchronous blocking API, belongs on spawn_blocking, which runs it on a dedicated blocking pool. tokio::spawn schedules onto the same IO worker pool, so it does not isolate CPU cost. When CPU-heavy work runs on an IO worker, it executes with no intervening await and so monopolizes that worker for the whole computation; the scheduler cannot hand that worker any other ready task, and unrelated tasks stall — the most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow.

In the graceful-shutdown accept loop, why does the shutdown branch treat both a changed() error and a true watch value as a stop, and why is per-connection work spawned rather than awaited inline?

changed() resolves with an error when every watch sender has been dropped, which means the receiver can never see another update — there is nothing left to wait for, so the only sane interpretation is stop. It also resolves normally when the value changes, and because a watch can in principle carry values other than the stop sentinel, the branch re-reads through borrow() and only stops when the current value is true. Per-connection work is spawned rather than awaited inline so the accept loop never blocks on a single client: spawning lets the loop return immediately to its select! and keep racing the next connection against the stop signal, which keeps admission, draining, and metrics independent of how long any one connection takes.

Chapter 26 · Task Libraries and Parallel Execution

Task Libraries and Parallel Execution

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

Chapter 26 treats Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, and the futures combinators as complementary executors rather than interchangeable concurrency libraries, and these exercises make you commit to the matching every time. The decision order is always the same: first ask whether the dominant cost is waiting or computing, then ask whether the unit you own is a runtime-spawned task, a locally driven future, a thread-pool job, or a channel message. Get that mapping right and the rest is configuration; get it wrong and you put CPU-heavy work on async workers or force a waiting-oriented runtime to schedule dense compute.

The exercises build from classification toward operable design. You sort four workloads onto their primary tool, find CPU-bound work stranded on Tokio workers, implement a bounded worker queue where admission is an explicit policy, repair an async pipeline so cancellation and retry live in one orchestration shell, and finally design pool routing and a public task API that another team can run safely. The lab grounds all of it in one runnable program: a bounded Crossbeam channel feeding a worker that counts accepted jobs, counts one retryable job separately, and observes an explicit shutdown signal when the channel closes.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, or futures utilities from the workload

Apply the chapter's decision order to each case: first name the dominant cost (waiting or CPU), then name the unit of work (a spawned runtime task, a local future, a pool job, or a channel message). The four workloads sort cleanly because each one is built around a different unit.

The TCP accept loop with many idle sockets is waiting-dominated. Almost every socket is parked waiting for bytes, and the runtime makes progress on whichever one becomes ready. This is the canonical Tokio case: each connection is a cheap spawned task that costs almost nothing while idle, and the runtime multiplexes thousands of them onto a few worker threads. Threads-per-connection would waste stacks on sockets that are doing nothing.

The large batch scoring pass over numeric data is CPU-dominated, and the unit is one data set you want to saturate cores with. This is Rayon. A par_iter splits the data across a work-stealing pool and rejoins the result with no manual thread choreography, and crucially it does not borrow an async runtime to do dense arithmetic. Putting this on Tokio workers would monopolize them and starve any concurrent IO.

The thread-based pipeline with bounded handoff between worker stages is coordination-dominated: the unit is a message crossing a queue between OS threads. This is Crossbeam. A crossbeam::channel::bounded gives you the bounded handoff directly, ownership moves with each message, and the bound is the backpressure between stages. You are not waiting on IO here and you are not saturating one data set; you are coordinating threads, which is exactly Crossbeam's model.

The local set of futures you want to poll as they complete without spawning each one is the FuturesUnordered case, because the futures themselves are the unit of composition. You already hold the futures and only need to drive them together inside one task; spawning each one would hand them to the runtime as independent tasks you do not want. FuturesUnordered keeps them local and yields each result as it finishes. The key distinction the chapter draws is spawned tasks (JoinSet, runtime-owned, progress even when you are not awaiting the set) versus locally composed futures (FuturesUnordered, driven only while you poll the set).

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each workload is assigned to one primary tool and justified by scheduling shape: accept loop to Tokio (waiting), batch scoring to Rayon (CPU saturation), thread pipeline to Crossbeam (coordination), local futures to FuturesUnordered (composition unit).
  • Spawned tasks are distinguished from locally composed futures: JoinSet hands work to the runtime, FuturesUnordered keeps futures inside the current task.
  • IO-bound (accept loop) and CPU-bound (batch scoring) workloads are kept on separate tools rather than collapsed onto one library.
Exercise 2code reading

Find CPU-bound work left on Tokio workers

Walk the handler step by step and label each step by whether it parks the worker or pins it. Reading from the socket is a natural async wait: the .await yields the worker while bytes are in flight, so it belongs on the runtime. The database call is the same shape, an async wait that releases the worker until the response returns. Publishing to a queue is typically another await, so it also stays. These steps are async-friendly precisely because they spend their time waiting, and a Tokio worker that is awaiting one connection is free to drive another.

The heavy checksum over the large parsed batch is the defect. It is computed inline in the async function, so it runs on a runtime worker thread and does not yield. While it runs, that worker cannot make progress on any other task. With a small worker pool, a few concurrent requests each computing a heavy checksum can pin every worker at once, and other connections that only need to be polled sit unserviced. This is runtime starvation: async did not make the CPU work parallel, it just put serial CPU work in the wrong place. The parse step sits on the boundary; if it is cheap it can stay, but if it is large it belongs with the checksum.

The fix depends on how much the batch stage dominates. If checksum computation is occasional relative to the IO, tokio::task::spawn_blocking is enough: move the owned parsed batch into the blocking closure so the heavy work runs on Tokio's separate blocking pool and the worker is freed to await the database call. The ownership transfer is what makes this clean, the closure takes the batch by value, so there is no borrow tangling the lifetimes across the await. If the batch stage is the real job of the service and runs on most requests, spawn_blocking is the wrong tool because the blocking pool is sized for occasional bridges, not steady dense compute; a dedicated Rayon pool is more honest, giving CPU work its own budget and work-stealing parallelism instead of overloading the blocking pool.

For observability, the signals are concrete. Runtime task scheduling latency (the delay between a task becoming ready and being polled) climbs when workers are pinned, so a rising poll latency or a Tokio worker that stays busy on compute confirms starvation. For the blocking path, watch the blocking-pool backlog or queue depth: if spawn_blocking jobs queue up because the pool is saturated, that is the signal you have outgrown spawn_blocking and need a real CPU pool.

use tokio::task;

// BEFORE: heavy checksum runs inline on a runtime worker and pins it.
async fn handle_before(conn: Conn) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let raw = conn.read_message().await?;        // async wait: stays on runtime
    let batch = parse_batch(raw);                // cheap-ish: borderline
    let sum = heavy_checksum(&batch);            // CPU-bound: pins the worker
    db_record(sum).await?;                       // async wait: stays on runtime
    publish(sum).await?;                         // async wait: stays on runtime
    Ok(())
}

// AFTER (occasional compute): move owned work off the runtime worker.
async fn handle_after(conn: Conn) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let raw = conn.read_message().await?;
    // Move the owned batch into the blocking closure; the worker is freed to
    // await the database call instead of computing the checksum.
    let sum = task::spawn_blocking(move || {
        let batch = parse_batch(raw);
        heavy_checksum(&batch)
    })
    .await?;
    db_record(sum).await?;
    publish(sum).await?;
    Ok(())
}

// AFTER (batch stage dominates): give CPU work its own Rayon pool budget
// rather than overloading Tokio's blocking pool on every request.

Socket read, DB call, and publish stay async; the dominant cost there is waiting. The checksum moves to spawn_blocking (occasional) or a dedicated CPU pool (when the batch stage dominates).

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Waiting-heavy steps (socket read, database call, publish) are separated from the CPU-heavy checksum step.
  • The checksum is moved to spawn_blocking via an owned-batch closure, with a stated reason (it pins a runtime worker), and a Rayon pool is named for the case where the batch stage dominates.
  • An observability hook is named: runtime scheduling/poll latency for starvation, and blocking-pool backlog or queue depth for blocking-pool overload.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a bounded worker queue

The point of this exercise is that a bounded queue is a policy decision, so the capacity must be visible in code rather than buried in a default. Construct the channel with an explicit capacity, here 2, using either tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(2) for an async service or crossbeam::channel::bounded(2) for a thread-based pipeline. The bound means a fast producer cannot grow memory without limit: once the queue is full, a send blocks (or awaits) until the worker drains an item, which is backpressure pushed back onto the producer instead of silent unbounded buffering.

Work crosses the boundary by ownership transfer, not by sharing mutable state. Each job is an owned value moved into the channel with send, and the worker takes ownership when it recv's. Because the queue owns admission, the producer does not need a broad shared lock to publish, the channel is the synchronization, and the only thing shared is the queue's own internal coordination. This is the chapter's contrast with sharing a mutable buffer behind a lock: here the data moves, so there is no aliasing to reason about and no lock contention on a shared structure.

Count the retryable item separately from accepted normal work so the two outcomes are distinguishable in the accounting, exactly as the orchestration shell in the chapter keeps retry bookkeeping in one place. A job tagged retry increments a retried counter; any other job increments accepted. Finally, add an explicit stop condition: closing the sender (dropping every tx) causes recv to return an error, the worker's loop exits, and the worker records that it observed the shutdown. Wiring the signal in this way once makes adding real mid-flight cancellation later a small change rather than a redesign.

use crossbeam::channel::bounded;

fn main() {
    let capacity = 2;
    let (tx, rx) = bounded::<&'static str>(capacity);

    let worker = std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut accepted = 0;
        let mut retried = 0;
        let mut cancelled = false;

        // recv() returns Err once every sender is dropped: that is the stop signal.
        while let Ok(job) = rx.recv() {
            if job == "retry" {
                retried += 1; // retryable work counted separately
            } else {
                accepted += 1; // normal accepted work
            }
        }
        cancelled = true; // queue closed; the worker observed shutdown
        (accepted, retried, cancelled)
    });

    // Owned items move across the boundary; the bound is the backpressure.
    tx.send("parse").unwrap();
    tx.send("retry").unwrap();
    tx.send("flush").unwrap();
    drop(tx); // close the queue: explicit stop condition

    let (accepted, retried, cancelled) = worker.join().unwrap();
    println!("capacity = {}", capacity);
    println!("accepted = {}", accepted);
    println!("retried = {}", retried);
    println!("cancelled = {}", cancelled);
}

Capacity is explicit at construction, jobs move by ownership through the bounded channel, retries are counted apart from accepted work, and dropping the sender is the visible stop condition.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The channel is constructed with an explicit bounded capacity, not an unbounded default, and the capacity value is visible in code.
  • Each job is an owned value moved through send/recv; no shared mutable buffer or broad lock is used to publish work.
  • Retried items are counted separately from accepted work, and the runnable lab prints capacity 2, accepted 2, retried 1, and cancelled true.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair async orchestration with cancellation and retry

Two defects make this service hard to operate. First, there is no stop signal, so the spawned child tasks have no way to be told to wind down; the only way to stop is to kill the process, which abandons in-flight work. Second, retry is implemented by the task body recursively re-invoking itself on failure. That hides the retry budget inside each task, makes the depth uncapped (a job that always fails recurses forever), and scatters the retry accounting across every handler so no single place knows how many retries are outstanding. The chapter's rule is the opposite: retry budgeting and cancellation belong in one visible orchestration shell, not inside the task body.

For the stop signal, choose by shape. A watch channel is the right primitive when one shutdown flag must be observed by many tasks, because every task can hold a receiver and react to the same change; a oneshot fits a single consumer, and an abort handle (or JoinSet's abort_all) fits forced mid-flight cancellation. The clean design is admission plus draining as one control flow: a watch::channel(false) broadcasts shutdown, the producer stops accepting new work when it sees the flag, and the orchestrator then drains the tasks already in flight rather than dropping them. Stop admitting, then drain, is easier to reason about than abrupt abort.

Replace the recursive retry with a bounded policy in the orchestration shell. Keep the task body small, it just returns Ok(id) or Err(id), and let the shell own the retry counter and backoff. When a result comes back Err, the shell increments a retry counter, checks it against a budget, and only then re-submits the job; when the budget is exhausted it records a terminal failure. This caps retries, makes them observable from one place, and keeps each task trivial.

For centralizing completion, JoinSet is the better fit here because the unit you own is runtime-spawned tasks, and that matches the workload: an IO-heavy service where each job should make progress on the runtime independently. JoinSet::join_next yields results as tasks finish, so the shell can drain, inspect, and re-spawn retries in one loop. FuturesUnordered would be the choice only if you wanted to keep the futures local and drive them inside one task, which is not what a spawned-task service wants. This mirrors the chapter's Tokio orchestration example, where tasks live in a JoinSet that drains results while the bounded channel governs intake and the shutdown flag is observed in one place.

use tokio::sync::{mpsc, watch};
use tokio::task::JoinSet;

const RETRY_BUDGET: u32 = 1;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(2);
    let (shutdown_tx, shutdown_rx) = watch::channel(false);

    let orchestrator = tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut set = JoinSet::new();
        let mut completed = 0_u32;
        let mut retries = 0_u32;
        let mut shutdown_rx = shutdown_rx;

        // Stop admitting when the shutdown flag flips; otherwise admit work.
        loop {
            tokio::select! {
                maybe = rx.recv() => match maybe {
                    Some(id) => { set.spawn(async move { run_job(id) }); }
                    None => break, // producer gone: drain remaining tasks
                },
                _ = shutdown_rx.changed() => {
                    if *shutdown_rx.borrow() { break; } // stop admitting, then drain
                }
            }
        }

        // Retry budget lives here, in one shell, not in the task body.
        while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await {
            match res.unwrap() {
                Ok(_id) => completed += 1,
                Err(id) if retries < RETRY_BUDGET => {
                    retries += 1;
                    set.spawn(async move { Ok::<u32, u32>(id) }); // bounded re-submit
                }
                Err(_id) => { /* budget exhausted: record terminal failure */ }
            }
        }
        (completed, retries)
    });

    tx.send(10).await.unwrap();
    drop(tx);
    shutdown_tx.send(true).unwrap();
    let (_completed, _retries) = orchestrator.await.unwrap();
}

fn run_job(id: u32) -> Result<u32, u32> {
    if id % 2 == 0 { Ok(id) } else { Err(id) }
}

Retry budget and shutdown both live in the orchestration shell: a watch flag gates admission, the loop drains in-flight tasks, and JoinSet centralizes completion. The task body stays a one-liner.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Retry budgeting is moved out of recursive self-calls in the task body into a single bounded policy in the orchestration shell with an explicit RETRY_BUDGET cap.
  • An explicit cancellation path is added via a watch shutdown flag that stops admission and then drains in-flight tasks.
  • Spawned-task orchestration with JoinSet is chosen over FuturesUnordered, justified by an IO-heavy service whose unit is runtime-owned tasks.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Choose thread pools and backpressure for a mixed service

The pipeline accept -> parse -> enrich -> persist -> publish has three distinct work shapes, so it legitimately uses more than one executor. Accept and persist and publish are waiting-dominated (sockets and a datastore), so they stay on Tokio runtime workers, where idle connections cost almost nothing and the runtime multiplexes them. Parse is cheap structural work and can stay inline on the runtime if it is light. Enrich is the CPU-heavy stage, and the central design decision is that it must not run inline on runtime workers, because dense compute there pins the workers and starves the waiting-heavy front and back of the pipeline.

Give the enrich stage a real CPU boundary. Because enrichment is CPU-bound and bursty traffic means many items arrive at once, Rayon is a better fit than a large number of small spawn_blocking tasks: Rayon's work-stealing pool keeps cores saturated and rejoins results without the blocking pool filling up. A flood of small blocking tasks would overload Tokio's blocking pool, which is sized for occasional bridges, not steady compute. So the route is async accept/parse on the runtime, a handoff into a bounded queue feeding a dedicated Rayon pool for enrich, then back to the runtime for persist and publish.

Place backpressure deliberately, and put the budget on the expensive stage, not only the front door. The internal queue feeding enrichment should be bounded so a burst of accepted connections cannot pile up unbounded ahead of the slow CPU stage; when that queue fills, admission slows, which is the backpressure propagating to the accept loop. A concurrency cap (a semaphore) belongs in front of persist if the datastore has a connection limit, so in-flight writes stay within what the store tolerates. The chapter's guidance is explicit here: the budget should follow the expensive stage, so the enrichment intake queue and the persist concurrency cap are where the limits matter most.

For clean rolling shutdown, broadcast a shutdown signal (a watch flag), stop the accept loop from admitting new connections, then drain the bounded queue and let in-flight enrich and persist work finish before exit. Before calling the design production-ready, require at least these metrics: enrichment intake queue depth (rising depth means the CPU stage is the bottleneck), in-flight task count and Rayon pool utilization (to size the pool), blocking-pool backlog if any spawn_blocking remains, and shutdown latency (how long draining takes). Those four let an operator see which stage is saturated and whether shutdown drains cleanly.

// Lanes and budgets for accept -> parse -> enrich -> persist -> publish.
//
//   accept   : Tokio runtime workers      (waiting; cheap idle sockets)
//   parse    : Tokio runtime workers      (light, inline)
//   [BOUNDED QUEUE cap=N]  <- backpressure to the accept loop
//   enrich   : dedicated Rayon pool       (CPU-bound; work-stealing)
//   [SEMAPHORE permits=M]  <- caps in-flight writes to the datastore
//   persist  : Tokio runtime workers      (waiting on datastore)
//   publish  : Tokio runtime workers      (waiting on queue)
//
// Budget follows the expensive stage: the bound sits BEFORE enrich,
// the concurrency cap sits BEFORE persist.
//
// Shutdown: watch(false) -> stop accept -> drain bounded queue -> finish in-flight.
//
// Required metrics before production:
//   - enrich intake queue depth   (CPU-stage saturation)
//   - in-flight task count / Rayon pool utilization
//   - blocking-pool backlog (if spawn_blocking is used anywhere)
//   - shutdown drain latency

A routing sketch: waiting stages on Tokio, enrich on a dedicated Rayon pool, a bounded queue before enrich and a semaphore before persist, with the budget placed on the expensive stage.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one bounded queue (before enrich) and one concurrency cap (semaphore before persist) are placed deliberately.
  • Enrichment is given a real CPU boundary on a dedicated Rayon pool rather than left inline on runtime workers, with Rayon preferred over many small blocking tasks.
  • At least two observability hooks are named: enrich intake queue depth, in-flight task count / Rayon utilization, blocking-pool backlog, and shutdown latency.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design a task API another team can operate safely

The guiding principle is that budgets and outcomes should be first-class in the API, not hidden constants, because another team has to operate this without reading the implementation. Start with ownership at the submission boundary. The submission API should own the work item: callers hand it a value by move (a Job, or a boxed closure plus its owned inputs) so the work can outlive the caller's stack frame and be scheduled freely. The alternative, a spawned-work API that borrows from caller-held data, drags lifetimes through the whole pipeline and forces 'static-or-scoped contortions on callers. The API may borrow caller data only locally during the submit call itself, for example to read configuration, but anything that crosses onto a worker must be owned. This is also what lets the same library run on Tokio for IO-heavy users and on a CPU pool for batch-heavy users: the owned job is portable across both backends.

Make at least one resource budget visible to callers or configuration. Expose queue capacity, a concurrency cap, and a retry budget as constructor or builder parameters (a PoolConfig with queue_capacity, max_in_flight, and retry_budget), with documented defaults rather than buried constants. Callers either set them explicitly or inherit the documented default, but in both cases the budget is discoverable. This follows the chapter's point that a task library is easier to operate when budgets are first-class.

Give callers a clear cancellation path and a structured outcome. For cancellation, return a handle from submit that supports an explicit cancel/abort, and define drop semantics clearly (dropping the handle either detaches or cancels, documented either way); a timeout wrapper can sit on top for time-bounded waits. For the result, return an enum that distinguishes the three real outcomes so a caller cannot confuse them: Outcome::Done(T) for success, Outcome::Retryable(E) for a failure the pipeline already exhausted its retry budget on, and Outcome::Cancelled for work stopped by signal or shutdown. A structured enum beats Result<T, E> here because cancellation is not the same as failure and callers need to branch on it.

Finally, name one testing hook and one observability hook. For testing, make the backend injectable: a trait-object or generic executor so tests can run the same submission API against a deterministic in-line executor instead of a real runtime, making retry and cancellation paths testable without timing flakiness. For observability, expose queue depth and in-flight count (and a shutdown-drain metric) through a metrics handle, so operators can see saturation and confirm clean shutdown.

/// Owned job: nothing borrows from the caller's stack once submitted.
pub struct Job {
    pub id: u64,
    pub payload: Vec<u8>,
}

/// Budgets are first-class and visible, not hidden constants.
pub struct PoolConfig {
    pub queue_capacity: usize, // bounded admission
    pub max_in_flight: usize,  // concurrency cap
    pub retry_budget: u32,     // retries owned by the pool, not the caller
}

impl Default for PoolConfig {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self { queue_capacity: 1024, max_in_flight: 64, retry_budget: 2 }
    }
}

/// Three real outcomes are distinguishable at the type level.
pub enum Outcome<T, E> {
    Done(T),
    Retryable(E), // pipeline exhausted its retry budget
    Cancelled,    // stopped by signal, drop, or shutdown
}

/// Handle gives callers an explicit cancellation path.
pub struct JobHandle<T, E> {
    // await_outcome() -> Outcome<T, E>; cancel() requests abort.
    _marker: std::marker::PhantomData<(T, E)>,
}

pub trait Pool {
    type Output;
    type Error;
    /// Submission OWNS the job; borrows from the caller only during this call.
    fn submit(&self, job: Job) -> JobHandle<Self::Output, Self::Error>;
    /// Observability hook: queue depth and in-flight count for operators.
    fn metrics(&self) -> PoolMetrics;
}

pub struct PoolMetrics {
    pub queue_depth: usize,
    pub in_flight: usize,
}

Owned Job at the boundary, budgets in PoolConfig, a structured Outcome enum, a JobHandle for cancellation, an injectable Pool trait for testing, and a metrics hook for operators.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The submission boundary owns the Job by move rather than borrowing caller data, avoiding a lifetime-heavy spawned-work API while staying portable across Tokio and CPU-pool backends.
  • At least one resource budget (queue_capacity, max_in_flight, retry_budget) is made visible via PoolConfig with documented defaults.
  • Callers get an explicit cancellation path (JobHandle::cancel plus documented drop semantics) and a structured Outcome enum distinguishing Done, Retryable, and Cancelled.
  • A testing hook (injectable Pool trait for a deterministic executor) and an observability hook (PoolMetrics queue depth and in-flight count) are named.

Lab solution

The lab fixes three defects in the starter. The starter wrote retried += 0, which never counts the retry, and it left cancelled initialized to false and never set; it also did not tie the shutdown observation to the queue closing. The solution corrects the retry increment to retried += 1, sets cancelled = true after the loop ends, and uses the drop of the sender as the explicit stop condition.

The flow is straightforward. The bounded channel is built with an explicit capacity of 2, so the queue's admission policy is visible in code and a fast producer cannot buffer without limit. Three owned jobs move across the boundary: "parse" and "flush" are normal work and each increment accepted (giving 2), while "retry" is counted separately and increments retried (giving 1). Work crosses by ownership transfer through send/recv, so no shared mutable buffer or lock is involved.

When the producer calls drop(tx), every sender is gone, so rx.recv() returns Err, the while loop exits, and the worker sets cancelled = true to record that it observed the shutdown signal.
