The thread is joined, its tuple is returned, and the four println! calls emit capacity = 2, accepted = 2, retried = 1, and cancelled = true, which is exactly the expected output. Wiring the stop signal in this way once makes adding real mid-flight cancellation, with select! and an abort path, a small later change rather than a redesign.

Note

This lab depends on an external crate or toolchain (for example tokio, tracing, crossbeam, MPI, or a GPU SDK), so the listing below is a reference solution rather than a standalone rustc-only program.

Example 26-S. bounded_queue_retry_lab.rs — Reference solution

fn main() {
    let capacity = 2;
    let (tx, rx) = crossbeam::channel::bounded::<&'static str>(capacity);

    let worker = std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut accepted = 0;
        let mut retried = 0;
        let mut cancelled = false;

        // recv() returns Err once every sender is dropped: that closing of the
        // queue is the explicit stop condition the worker reacts to.
        while let Ok(job) = rx.recv() {
            if job == "retry" {
                retried += 1; // retryable work counted separately from accepted
            } else {
                accepted += 1; // normal accepted work
            }
        }

        // The queue is closed and drained: the worker observed shutdown.
        cancelled = true;

        (accepted, retried, cancelled)
    });

    // Owned items move across the bounded boundary; the capacity is the budget.
    tx.send("parse").unwrap();
    tx.send("retry").unwrap();
    tx.send("flush").unwrap();
    drop(tx); // close the queue to signal shutdown

    let (accepted, retried, cancelled) = worker.join().unwrap();

    println!("capacity = {}", capacity);
    println!("accepted = {}", accepted);
    println!("retried = {}", retried);
    println!("cancelled = {}", cancelled);
}
Output
capacity = 2
accepted = 2
retried = 1
cancelled = true

Review question answers

What practical signal tells you a workload wants Tokio instead of Rayon?

The deciding signal is that the dominant cost is waiting rather than computing: the work spends most of its time parked on IO (sockets, datastores, timers) with many units idle at once. Tokio multiplexes those waiting units onto a few worker threads cheaply, so thousands of mostly-idle connections cost almost nothing. Rayon is the opposite case, where the job is to saturate cores over a data set; if your work would keep a CPU busy rather than parked, that is the Rayon signal, and putting it on Tokio workers would only pin them and starve the IO.

When is FuturesUnordered calmer than JoinSet, and when is the reverse true?

FuturesUnordered is calmer when you already hold a set of futures and only need to drive them together inside the current task, because it keeps everything local: nothing crosses a task boundary, the futures advance only while you poll the set, and there is no per-task spawn overhead. JoinSet is the calmer choice when the unit you actually own is runtime-spawned tasks, because each future is handed to the runtime as an independent task that makes progress on worker threads even when you are not awaiting the set, and join_next drains completions for you. So the rule is FuturesUnordered for local composition of futures you already have, JoinSet when you want the runtime to own and schedule each unit independently.

Why is a bounded queue already an API and overload decision, not only an implementation detail?

A bound is a policy: it sets the maximum amount of in-flight work the stage will admit, and when it is full it forces backpressure onto the producer instead of silently buffering. That choice determines how the system behaves under overload, whether a fast producer can exhaust memory, whether latency degrades gracefully or the service falls over, so it is visible behavior callers and operators depend on, not a hidden constant. Because it governs admission and overload response, the capacity belongs in the API surface or configuration where it can be seen and tuned, not buried in an unbounded default.

What is the difference between cancellation as task drop, cancellation as explicit signal, and retry as policy?

Cancellation as task drop means stopping work by dropping the future or aborting the task: the work simply stops at its next yield point, which is abrupt and may leave partial state, so it suits forced mid-flight termination. Cancellation as an explicit signal is cooperative: a watch flag or oneshot tells tasks to wind down, so the orchestrator can stop admitting new work and drain in-flight work cleanly, which is easier to reason about and to test. Retry as policy is a separate concern entirely; it is the bounded budget and backoff that decide whether failed work is re-submitted, and the chapter's point is that it belongs in one orchestration shell with an explicit cap rather than hidden as recursion inside the task body.

Why should CPU-heavy work have its own budget even inside an async service?

Async makes IO concurrent, but it does not make CPU work parallel or non-blocking; a heavy compute step run inline on a runtime worker pins that worker and prevents it from polling any other task, so a few such steps can starve the whole runtime. Giving CPU work its own budget, a spawn_blocking allowance for occasional bridges or a dedicated Rayon pool when compute dominates, keeps the runtime workers free to service waiting work and keeps latency predictable. The budget should follow the expensive stage, so the CPU lane is sized and bounded on its own rather than competing with the IO front door for the same worker threads.

Chapter 27 · IO Tricks and Systems Programming Patterns

IO Tricks and Systems Programming Patterns

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

Chapter 27 reduced systems IO to a handful of measurable quantities: how many syscalls you make, how many times bytes are copied, who owns each file descriptor, and whether overload is bounded or hidden. The exercises here drive each of those quantities into concrete decisions. You decide when buffering actually amortizes kernel reads versus when it is noise, who holds close responsibility for a descriptor, how to build a pipeline that batches and applies backpressure, how to make a vectored write complete its logical message, and when memory mapping earns its keep over plain buffered reads.

The throughline is ownership. Buffering, batching, vectored IO, and mmap are all techniques for moving bytes across a boundary efficiently, but every boundary is also an ownership boundary. A buffer has one owner, a handle has one owner with a deterministic close, and a queue or retry path is a place where borrowed bytes must usually become owned. The lab makes the pipeline shape explicit: a bounded channel between a buffered reader and a buffered writer, with a batch size and a trailing-flush that you must not forget.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Compare buffered and unbuffered file reads from the workload

Buffering helps when the underlying source would otherwise see many tiny operations. A BufReader is a userspace staging area that turns a stream of small reads into a smaller number of larger kernel reads. The decision is therefore about where the expensive boundary sits, not about a slogan that buffering is always faster.

The large file read with many tiny line parses is the strong buffering case. Without a buffer, each read_line could turn into a separate underlying read syscall against storage, and the per-syscall overhead would dominate the work. BufReader amortizes that: one large kernel read fills an 8 KiB buffer, and the many subsequent line parses are served from memory. The win here is real and measurable in syscall count.

The small config file read once at startup is the weak buffering case. The file is tiny, so it is likely satisfied by one or two reads regardless, and the operation happens once, so even a large constant factor is irrelevant to steady-state behavior. Wrapping it in a BufReader is harmless but not a meaningful optimization; reaching for it as if it mattered is exactly the folklore the chapter warns against.

The request-local parser over already-memory-resident bytes is not a kernel-read buffering question at all. The bytes are in process memory, so there is no kernel read boundary to amortize. The cost there is in-process parsing CPU and possibly copying, not syscall count. Adding a BufReader over an in-memory slice would only insert a pointless second copy. This is the distinction the exercise is testing: kernel-read amortization is a different axis from in-process parsing cost.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Strong case (large file, many tiny parses) and weak case (tiny startup config) are both identified explicitly.
  • Kernel-read amortization is separated from in-process parsing/copy cost via the memory-resident case.
  • Buffering is treated as a boundary-specific tool, not a universal optimization.
Exercise 2code reading

Identify the ownership responsibilities for a file descriptor

A file descriptor carries a single-owner close invariant: exactly one owning value is responsible for closing it, and that close must happen exactly once, after all use is complete. A File is such an owner; dropping it closes the descriptor. A raw integer (RawFd / RawHandle) is not an owner and proves nothing about lifetime or ownership. It is just a number that happens to index into the kernel's descriptor table right now.

The double-close and use-after-close risk hides in the helper that calls from_raw_fd on the integer while the original File is still alive. from_raw_fd is unsafe precisely because it asserts ownership: the reconstructed File now also believes it owns close responsibility. When that rebuilt File drops, it closes the descriptor; when the original File later drops, it closes the same descriptor again. That second close either fails silently or, worse, closes a descriptor that has since been reused for an unrelated open file, corrupting another part of the program. The reverse ordering gives a use-after-close: the original is used after the rebuilt copy already closed it.

The honest repair is to move the owner. If a helper needs to own the file for the rest of its life, pass it the File by value so ownership transfers and the original variable can no longer be used. If a helper only needs to read or write without taking over close responsibility, pass a borrow (&File or &mut File) or a borrowed BorrowedFd, which lets it operate on the descriptor without claiming ownership. Reconstructing an owner from a raw integer should be reserved for genuine FFI boundaries where ownership is actually being handed across, and even there only one side may keep it.

try_clone is the honest design when two independent owners genuinely need to outlive each other and close on their own schedules. It issues a real dup at the OS level, producing a second descriptor that refers to the same open file description. The semantic cost is that this is duplication, not a free borrow: you now hold two descriptors that share file offset and status flags but each carry their own close obligation, and you consume an additional descriptor slot. Use it when you truly need two owners; do not use it to paper over an ownership mistake that a move or a borrow would solve more cheaply.

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};

// WRONG: rebuilding an owner from a raw integer while the original lives.
// #[cfg(unix)]
// fn broken(file: &File) {
//     use std::os::unix::io::{AsRawFd, FromRawFd};
//     let fd = file.as_raw_fd();
//     let mut dup = unsafe { File::from_raw_fd(fd) }; // claims ownership
//     let _ = dup.write_all(b"x");
//     // dup drops here and closes fd; the caller's `file` will close it AGAIN.
// }

// RIGHT 1: borrow when the helper does not need to own close.
fn write_borrowed(file: &mut File) -> io::Result<()> {
    file.write_all(b"x") // no ownership claimed; caller still owns close
}

// RIGHT 2: move when the helper takes over the file for the rest of its life.
fn drain_owned(mut file: File) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut s = String::new();
    file.read_to_string(&mut s)?; // single owner; closes on drop here
    Ok(s)
}

// RIGHT 3: try_clone when two independent owners are genuinely required.
fn split_into_two(file: &File) -> io::Result<(File, File)> {
    let a = file.try_clone()?; // real dup: a second descriptor, second close
    let b = file.try_clone()?;
    Ok((a, b))
}

Borrow when you do not own close, move when you do, and reach for try_clone only when two real owners are required.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The single-owner, close-exactly-once invariant is stated concretely against the rebuilt-File scenario.
  • The repair moves the owner (or borrows) instead of reconstructing ownership from a raw integer.
  • try_clone is explained as a real dup with its own close obligation, not a free borrow substitute.
Exercise 3implementation

Build a backpressure-aware buffered pipeline

The design has three explicit policy choices that must stay visible in the code: a bounded queue capacity, a batch size, and a buffered output. Each acts on a different part of the pipeline. The bound (sync_channel(1)) applies backpressure so a fast producer cannot outrun a slow consumer; once one item is in flight, send blocks until the consumer takes it. The batch size (2) controls how many logical records each flush covers. The BufWriter controls how often bytes actually cross into the backing store rather than going out one record at a time.

The producer reads lines from the in-memory source, converts each borrowed line buffer into an owned String, and sends it across the bounded channel. Converting to an owned String at the boundary is the load-bearing ownership move: the line buffer is reused on the producer side, so the value crossing the thread boundary must own its bytes. The consumer accumulates received records into a pending Vec, flushes whenever pending reaches the batch size of 2, and counts each completed batch.

The single detail most pipelines get wrong is the trailing partial batch. With three records, the first two form one full batch; the third is left in pending when recv returns Err because the producer hung up and dropped the sender. If you forget to flush that leftover, the last record silently vanishes. The fix is an explicit post-loop check: if pending is non-empty, flush it and count it as a final batch. That is why this run reports batches = 2, not 1.

The byte count is the buffered output measured at the end: 'red\n' is 4 bytes, 'blue\n' is 5, 'green\n' is 6, totaling 15. Because writes go through a BufWriter into a Vec, the count reflects everything that was written and flushed, confirming no record was dropped.

use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, Cursor, Write};
use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let input = Cursor::new("red\nblue\ngreen\n".as_bytes());
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(input);

    // Policy 1: bounded capacity of 1 makes backpressure visible.
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::sync_channel::<String>(1);

    let producer = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut line = String::new();
        while reader.read_line(&mut line).unwrap() != 0 {
            // Own the bytes before they cross the thread boundary.
            tx.send(line.trim_end().to_string()).unwrap();
            line.clear();
        }
    });

    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut received = 0usize;
    let mut batches = 0usize;
    let mut pending: Vec<String> = Vec::with_capacity(2);

    {
        let mut writer = BufWriter::new(&mut out);
        while let Ok(line) = rx.recv() {
            pending.push(line);
            received += 1;

            // Policy 2: logical batch size of 2.
            if pending.len() == 2 {
                for item in pending.drain(..) {
                    writeln!(writer, "{}", item)?;
                }
                batches += 1;
            }
        }

        // The trailing partial batch is the easy thing to forget.
        if !pending.is_empty() {
            for item in pending.drain(..) {
                writeln!(writer, "{}", item)?;
            }
            batches += 1;
        }

        writer.flush()?; // Policy 3: buffered output.
    }

    producer.join().unwrap();
    println!("capacity = {}", 1);
    println!("received = {}", received);
    println!("batches = {}", batches);
    println!("bytes = {}", out.len());
    Ok(())
}

Bounded sync_channel(1), batch size 2, BufWriter output, and an explicit trailing-batch flush.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Uses mpsc::sync_channel(1) as the bounded handoff with visible capacity.
  • Consumer batches two records before writing and flushes the final partial batch explicitly.
  • Output goes through BufWriter rather than one unbatched write per record.
  • Prints capacity = 1, received = 3, batches = 2, bytes = 15.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a scatter/gather write path that assumes too much

The defect is treating one successful write_vectored call as proof that the whole logical response was transmitted. write_vectored promises exactly one write attempt across several buffers; it returns the number of bytes the kernel accepted in that attempt, which may be fewer than the total. On a non-blocking or congested socket the kernel can accept the header and only part of the body, or even just part of the header. The handler that assumes 'the entire header and body are gone forever' will silently truncate the response under exactly the load conditions where correctness matters most. Small demos get away with it because tiny payloads on a quiet loopback usually fit one attempt; production traffic does not grant that luck.

The mechanically correct repair is to loop until the logical message is complete, advancing the slice array by the number of bytes actually written each iteration. The standard library gives you IoSlice::advance_slices, which drops fully written slices and trims the partially written one in place, so the next write_vectored call resumes exactly where the kernel stopped. A return value of 0 means the peer closed before the response finished and must be surfaced as an error, not spun on. This is precisely the write_all_vectored helper the chapter's Example 2 uses, and it belongs near every socket boundary.

Vectored IO is still worth keeping for this workload. The value is that it removes the stitching copy: the header and the body keep their own owners and are never concatenated into a temporary buffer just to issue one write. For a small request-response protocol with a header plus a borrowed body slice, that saved allocation and copy on every response is meaningful. The extra state machine for partial writes is a small, bounded loop you write once and reuse. The tradeoff flips only when the response is already a single contiguous buffer (nothing to gather) or when buffers are so numerous that managing the slice array costs more than it saves; in those cases plain write_all or a BufWriter is simpler. Here, two slices and a short completion loop is the right balance.

use std::io::{self, IoSlice, Write};
use std::net::TcpStream;

// Defect: one call, result ignored, assumed complete.
// fn broken(stream: &mut TcpStream, hdr: &[u8], body: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
//     let parts = [IoSlice::new(hdr), IoSlice::new(body)];
//     stream.write_vectored(&parts)?; // may be partial; truncates silently
//     Ok(())
// }

// Repair: loop until the logical message is fully sent.
fn write_all_vectored(stream: &mut TcpStream, mut parts: &mut [IoSlice<'_>]) -> io::Result<()> {
    while !parts.is_empty() {
        let wrote = stream.write_vectored(parts)?;
        if wrote == 0 {
            return Err(io::Error::new(
                io::ErrorKind::WriteZero,
                "socket closed before full response",
            ));
        }
        // Drop fully written slices, trim the partially written one.
        IoSlice::advance_slices(&mut parts, wrote);
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn send_response(stream: &mut TcpStream, hdr: &[u8], body: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut parts = [IoSlice::new(hdr), IoSlice::new(body)];
    write_all_vectored(stream, &mut parts)?;
    stream.flush()
}

A completion loop with advance_slices turns one hopeful vectored write into a correct full-message send.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names the partial-write risk: write_vectored returns bytes accepted in one attempt, which can be short.
  • Proposes a mechanically correct loop using advance_slices and a WriteZero error on a 0-byte write.
  • Justifies keeping vectored IO because it removes the stitching copy for the header/body workload.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Choose memory mapping, buffered reads, or owned copies honestly

Mmap is an access-pattern tool, not a general performance charm; buffered reads are for streamed one-pass data; and an owned copy is the right move before any long-lived async or retry boundary. Each of the three workloads maps cleanly onto one of these.

The large read-only term index is the good memory-mapping candidate because random access dominates. A search query jumps to scattered offsets in the index rather than sweeping it front to back, so a read-only mmap lets the OS page in only the touched regions and share those pages across processes via the page cache. The caveats must be stated, not waved away: touching an unmapped page triggers a page fault that can block, so tail-latency behavior depends on the OS and the working set; the file must not be truncated underneath the mapping, or accessing the vanished region delivers SIGBUS; and external mutation of the file while it is mapped read-only is undefined from the program's point of view, so the index needs a stable, atomically-replaced-on-disk update protocol. Because Rust's standard library exposes no cross-platform mmap, this is an ecosystem-plus-OS-contract decision, which is exactly why the lifetime story must be clear before adopting it.

The one-pass log replayer wants buffered sequential reading. The data is streamed exactly once front to back, so there is no random access to exploit and no reuse to amortize across queries. A BufReader over the file gives large sequential kernel reads and minimal syscall churn, and when the pass is done the memory is released. Mapping it would add page-fault complexity and a truncation hazard for no benefit, since sequential prefetch already serves this pattern well.

The retry queue wants an owned conversion before the boundary, even if parsing began from borrowed file bytes. A record that will sit in a queue and be processed later by async work cannot hold a borrow tied to a file view or a transient read buffer; that borrow's lifetime ends long before the retry runs, and a mapped view could be invalidated by truncation in the meantime. So at the moment a record enters the queue, copy out exactly the fields you need into owned values (owned String, Vec<u8>, or a small owned struct). The parse can start zero-copy against borrowed bytes for speed, but the handoff into the long-lived retry or async boundary is where you pay for an owned copy and buy correctness.

// Workload 1: read-only term index, random access -> memory map (ecosystem crate).
// let file = File::open("terms.idx")?;
// let map = unsafe { memmap2::Mmap::map(&file)? }; // random offsets, paged on demand
// let entry = lookup(&map[..], term); // borrowed view, valid only while `map` lives

use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader};
use std::fs::File;

// Workload 2: one-pass log replay -> buffered sequential reads, std only.
fn replay(path: &str) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let reader = BufReader::new(File::open(path)?);
    let mut count = 0usize;
    for line in reader.lines() {
        let _record = line?; // streamed once, front to back
        count += 1;
    }
    Ok(count)
}

// Workload 3: retry queue -> own the record at the boundary.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct RetryRecord {
    key: String,   // owned, not a &str into a file view
    body: Vec<u8>, // owned, survives past the read buffer's lifetime
}

fn enqueue(queue: &mut Vec<RetryRecord>, key: &str, borrowed_body: &[u8]) {
    // Parse may have been zero-copy, but the handoff copies into owned values.
    queue.push(RetryRecord { key: key.to_string(), body: borrowed_body.to_vec() });
}

Map the random-access index, buffer the one-pass log, and own the record before the retry boundary.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Deliberately picks the term index as the mapping case and the log replayer as the buffered-read case.
  • Calls out page faults, truncation/SIGBUS, and external-mutation caveats for the mapped case.
  • Chooses an owned conversion before the long-lived retry/async boundary.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Profile and tune an IO-heavy service without folklore

Separate diagnosis from treatment. The pain after a traffic shift could be flush frequency, syscall count, queue backlog, CPU parsing, or blocked runtime workers, and these have different fixes, so the first job is to measure which one moved, not to guess. A strong answer names concrete signals for each candidate.

For flush and syscall behavior, measure bytes per write and writes (or write/writev syscalls) per response; a low bytes-per-write with a high syscall rate points at unbatched or per-record flushing. For the internal queue, measure queue depth over time and time-in-queue; a queue that sits near its bound with rising wait time is the backpressure signal. For CPU, measure per-request parse CPU time and overall CPU utilization; if cores are saturated in the parser, no IO change helps. For the async runtime, measure blocking-pool pressure and worker-thread occupancy (for example, tasks waiting because all workers are parked on blocking calls); high blocking-pool pressure means an IO model or offload problem, not a buffer-size problem. p99 latency is the outcome signal that tells you the symptom is real and lets you attribute improvement to a specific change. Naming bytes per write, queue depth, syscall rate, p99, and blocking-pool pressure already covers the field.

Given bursty small responses, the first experiment I would run is the one that most directly tests the suspected bottleneck: toggle TCP_NODELAY (set_nodelay(true)) and measure p99 and bytes-per-write before and after. Bursty small request-response traffic is the canonical case where Nagle's algorithm coalesces tiny writes and adds a delay before the segment goes out; disabling it trades a little extra packetization for lower per-response latency. It is a single, cheap, reversible socket-option change with a clear hypothesis (latency-sensitive small writes), which is exactly why it goes first rather than a rewrite. If the metrics show the response is already fragmented into many small writes within the application, the alternative first experiment is to batch the header and body through vectored IO or a BufWriter and re-measure syscall rate.

Only after those measurements would I consider the big levers. Memory mapping for the read-mostly config snapshot is justified only if profiling shows config reads are actually hot and random-access (a snapshot read once and cached is not). An async rewrite is justified only if blocking-pool pressure or worker occupancy shows threads parked on IO under the new traffic shape. A larger queue bound is justified only if queue-depth and time-in-queue show legitimate bursty backlog rather than a slow consumer that a bigger queue would merely hide while growing memory. Each of those is a treatment to apply after a metric implicates its specific cause, tied to this workload's shape rather than to generic 'optimize IO' advice.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names at least three concrete signals (bytes per write, queue depth, syscall rate, p99 latency, blocking-pool pressure).
  • Proposes one measured first experiment (toggle TCP_NODELAY and compare p99/bytes-per-write) instead of a rewrite by instinct.
  • Ties diagnosis to the bursty-small-response workload shape and gates mmap/async/queue changes on specific metrics.

Lab solution

The producer thread reads the three records from an in-memory Cursor through a BufReader, one line at a time. For each line it trims the trailing newline and converts the borrowed line buffer into an owned String, then sends that String across a bounded sync_channel(1). The bound is what makes backpressure observable: once one item is in flight, the next send blocks until the consumer has taken the previous one, so a fast reader cannot outrun a slow writer or grow memory without limit.

The consumer accumulates received records in a pending Vec and applies the batch policy of two. When pending reaches two ('red' and 'blue'), it drains them through a BufWriter into the backing Vec and counts one batch. The third record ('green') arrives, is pushed, and then the loop ends because the producer dropped its sender, so recv returns Err. The explicit post-loop check flushes that leftover single-record batch and counts it, which is the detail most pipelines get wrong; without it the last record would be silently dropped. That is why batches is 2, not 1.

The printed values follow directly: capacity is the channel bound (1), received counts all three records, batches counts the two flushes (one full pair plus the trailing single), and bytes is the length of the buffered output. Each written line carries its newline back, so 'red\n' (4) + 'blue\n' (5) + 'green\n' (6) totals 15 bytes. The BufWriter is dropped at the end of its scope before out is read, ensuring all buffered bytes are flushed into the Vec.

Example 27-S. buffered_pipeline_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, Cursor, Write};
use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // Three newline-separated records living entirely in memory.
    let input = Cursor::new("red\nblue\ngreen\n".as_bytes());
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(input);

    // Bounded handoff: capacity 1 makes backpressure visible. A fast
    // producer cannot race ahead of a slow consumer because send blocks
    // once one item is in flight.
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::sync_channel::<String>(1);

    let producer = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut line = String::new();
        while reader.read_line(&mut line).unwrap() != 0 {
            // Hand an owned String across the thread boundary. The
            // borrowed line buffer stays with the producer and is reused.
            let owned = line.trim_end().to_string();
            tx.send(owned).unwrap();
            line.clear();
        }
    });

    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut received = 0usize;
    let mut batches = 0usize;
    let mut pending: Vec<String> = Vec::with_capacity(2);

    {
        // Buffered writer: many small writeln! calls coalesce into the
        // backing Vec rather than going out one record at a time.
        let mut writer = BufWriter::new(&mut out);

        while let Ok(line) = rx.recv() {
            pending.push(line);
            received += 1;

            // Logical batch size of 2: flush a full batch as soon as it forms.
            if pending.len() == 2 {
                for item in pending.drain(..) {
                    writeln!(writer, "{}", item)?;
                }
                batches += 1;
            }
        }

        // The trailing partial batch is the easy thing to forget. With three
        // records the last one is left over after the full batch.
        if !pending.is_empty() {
            for item in pending.drain(..) {
                writeln!(writer, "{}", item)?;
            }
            batches += 1;
        }

        writer.flush()?;
    }

    producer.join().unwrap();

    println!("capacity = {}", 1);
    println!("received = {}", received);
    println!("batches = {}", batches);
    println!("bytes = {}", out.len());
    Ok(())
}
Output
capacity = 1
received = 3
batches = 2
bytes = 15

Review question answers

What does buffered IO change, and what does it not change?

Buffered IO changes how often bytes cross the kernel boundary: it amortizes many small reads or writes into a smaller number of larger syscalls by staging bytes in a userspace buffer. It does not change the total number of bytes transferred, the in-process cost of parsing those bytes, or who owns the underlying handle. It also does nothing useful when the data is already memory-resident or when the file is tiny and accessed rarely, because there is no syscall churn to amortize in those cases.

Why is a borrowed slice not automatically end-to-end zero-copy?

A borrowed slice removes one specific copy (the one you would have made to own the bytes), but zero-copy is a precise claim about which copies remain, not a property of borrowing in general. The bytes may already have been copied from the kernel into the buffer the slice points at, and they will often be copied again on the way out, for example when written to a socket or when the record must be owned to cross a queue or async boundary. End-to-end zero-copy means naming every copy along the path and showing each was eliminated; a single borrow only proves one link is copy-free.

When is moving a handle calmer than duplicating it?

Moving is calmer whenever a single owner should drive the handle, because it transfers the one close responsibility to exactly one place and the compiler then prevents any use of the old binding. Duplicating with try_clone issues a real OS-level dup, producing a second descriptor with its own independent close obligation and a shared file offset and status flags. You only want that duplication when two independent owners genuinely need to outlive each other and close on their own schedules; using it to avoid an ownership decision adds a descriptor and a second close protocol for no benefit.

Why can one vectored write still be only a partial logical response?

write_vectored promises a single write attempt across an array of buffers and returns the number of bytes the kernel actually accepted, which can be fewer than the total when the socket buffer is full or the connection is congested. The header and body keep their own owners and nothing is concatenated, but the kernel is free to take the header and only part of the body in one call. To send the whole logical message you must loop, advancing the slice array by the bytes written each time (IoSlice::advance_slices) and treating a zero-byte write as the peer closing early.

What signals tell you a queue needs a bound or a smaller bound?

Watch queue depth and time-in-queue over time: a queue whose depth grows without bound, or whose occupancy stays high while end-to-end latency climbs, is hiding overload rather than absorbing a burst, which argues for a bound or a tighter one. Rising memory tied to the queue and a producer that consistently outpaces the consumer are the same signal from the other side. A bounded queue converts that hidden backlog into visible backpressure, blocking the producer so the system slows down predictably instead of growing memory until it fails; the right bound is the smallest one that still smooths legitimate bursts without masking a chronically slow consumer.

Why should mmap, async rewrites, and socket tuning all be justified by measured behavior rather than by taste?

Each technique fixes a specific, different bottleneck, so applying one without knowing which cost actually moved is choosing by folklore. Memory mapping only pays off for random access over a reused, stably-managed file and otherwise adds page-fault and truncation hazards; an async rewrite only helps when threads are parked waiting on IO, shown by blocking-pool pressure, not when the parser is CPU-bound; socket tuning like TCP_NODELAY only helps latency-sensitive small writes. Without measuring bytes per write, syscall rate, queue depth, CPU parse time, and p99 latency, you cannot tell which one is implicated, and the fastest-looking optimization is frequently the wrong one for the workload at hand.

Chapter 28 · C++ Integration

C++ Integration

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises turn the chapter's binary-contract discipline into reflexes. Each one forces the same decision the chapter opened with: a type either has a stable, agreed-upon shape that may cross a C ABI seam, or it is a Rust-specific representation whose layout must stay behind it. The warm-up sorts types into those two buckets, the code-reading exercises trace the two runnable listings layer by layer, and the implementation and debugging exercises make you write the guard sequences, ownership shapes, and panic policy by hand.

The through-line is that the compiler checks nothing across the seam. Calling convention, layout, who frees what, how long a pointer stays valid, and what happens on failure are all things you assert and must get right yourself. The design exercise closes the loop by routing a real legacy-C++ integration through the chapter's decision tree, where the tool you pick changes only how much boilerplate is generated, never the ownership, panic, and ABI-stability contract you still owe.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Sort types into what may cross the seam

The decisive question for each type is whether both languages already agree on its in-memory representation. If they do, it may cross unchanged. If the shape is a Rust implementation detail, it must be flattened into pointers, lengths, and integers before it reaches the boundary.

Crossable unchanged: i32 (a fixed-width integer the C ABI already names), *const i32 paired with a usize length (a raw address plus a count, exactly the lowered form of a slice), *mut i64 (a raw writable address, the canonical out-parameter shape), and an opaque handle pointer (a *mut to a type the foreign side never inspects the fields of). These are all addresses and integers with a stable layout.

Must stay behind the seam: &str, Vec<u8>, and Result<u32, MyError>. A &str is a two-word slice (pointer plus length) that additionally carries a lifetime and a UTF-8 validity promise; its layout is not guaranteed across compiler versions and the lifetime has no C expression. Flatten it to *const u8 plus a usize length (and document the encoding). A Vec<u8> is a three-word owning structure (pointer, length, capacity) tied to Rust's allocator; even though it describes contiguous bytes, the foreign side cannot honor the capacity field or the allocator contract, so passing it would invite a mismatched free. Lower it to *const u8 (or *mut u8) plus a usize length, and keep ownership and freeing on one side via an explicit destroy function. A Result<u32, MyError> has no fixed discriminant layout and no agreed-upon error representation, so it becomes an integer status as the return value with the u32 payload delivered through a caller-owned out parameter (*mut u32) on the success path.

The reason &str and Vec<u8> cannot cross even though they are contiguous bytes is layout, not content: a slice or owning vector has no fixed, agreed-upon C representation, and the aliasing, lifetime, and allocator promises they encode cannot be expressed or honored on the C side.

// Behind the seam (Rust-only): rich types.
//   &str, Vec<u8>, Result<u32, MyError>
//
// At the seam (C ABI-safe): flattened shapes.
//   &str         -> *const u8, usize        (pointer + length)
//   Vec<u8>      -> *mut u8,   usize        (pointer + length; one side frees)
//   Result<u32,E>-> i32 status + *mut u32   (status return + out parameter)
//
// Already crossable: i32, *const i32 + usize, *mut i64, *mut OpaqueHandle.

The two buckets: rich Rust types stay behind the seam; flattened pointer/length/integer shapes cross it.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • i32, *const i32 with usize length, *mut i64, and the opaque handle pointer are listed as crossable because each is a fixed-width integer or raw address with a stable layout.
  • &str, Vec<u8>, and Result are identified as Rust-specific representations that may not cross unchanged.
  • &str/Vec<u8> are replaced by a raw pointer plus an explicit length, and Result by an integer status plus out parameters.
  • The stated reason is layout: a slice, owning vector, or Result has no fixed, agreed-upon C representation.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the three layers of the abs wrapper

Example 1 is deliberately split into three layers so the unsafe surface is as small as possible. The foreign symbol is ffi_demo_abs, defined in the c_shim module with extern "C" and no_mangle and reached through an unsafe extern "C" declaration block. The middle layer is the one-line wrapper safe_abs, which performs the actual call inside an unsafe block and documents why it is sound. The top layer is main, which only ever calls safe_abs and never sees a raw call. Only safe_abs holds an unsafe block; the foreign declaration and main both stay safe.

The unsafe extern "C" declaration tells the compiler two things: a symbol named ffi_demo_abs exists somewhere else, and it must be called with the C calling convention rather than Rust's unspecified one. What it does not verify is that the foreign side actually honors that signature. The compiler cannot check that the real ffi_demo_abs takes an i32, returns an i32, has the claimed name, or even exists until link time; asserting the contract is the programmer's job, which is why the call is unsafe.

The seam requires no ownership transfer because the signature is plain i32 -> i32. Both the argument and the result are Copy, fixed-width integers passed by value. Nothing is allocated, nothing is borrowed across the boundary, and nothing needs to be freed afterward, so the only soundness obligation is the calling convention itself. That is exactly what the SAFETY comment records.

If the body used abs instead of wrapping_abs, the input i32::MIN would be a boundary hazard. The absolute value of i32::MIN is 2147483648, which does not fit in i32, so abs panics in debug builds (and the operation is otherwise an overflow). A panic unwinding out of an extern "C" function and across the C ABI boundary is undefined behavior, because the foreign caller's frames were not compiled to be unwound through. wrapping_abs avoids this by defining the result on the whole input range: wrapping_abs on i32::MIN returns i32::MIN, so the function always returns a value and never unwinds. Even a trivial exported function needs a panic policy at the boundary, and this is it.

// Layer 1 - foreign declaration (safe to write, asserts an unchecked contract):
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn ffi_demo_abs(input: i32) -> i32;
}

// Layer 2 - the only unsafe block: the actual call, with a SAFETY note.
fn safe_abs(input: i32) -> i32 {
    unsafe {
        // SAFETY: C ABI; i32 -> i32 by value; no ownership crosses the seam.
        ffi_demo_abs(input)
    }
}

// Layer 3 - main only ever sees the safe wrapper.
fn main() {
    println!("abs({}) = {}", -7_i32, safe_abs(-7));
}

// Boundary panic policy: the exported body uses wrapping_abs, not abs.
// abs(i32::MIN) panics; an unwind crossing the C ABI is undefined behavior.
// wrapping_abs(i32::MIN) == i32::MIN, so the function always returns a value.

Three layers with unsafe isolated to safe_abs; wrapping_abs supplies the boundary's panic policy.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The three layers are named (foreign declaration, unsafe wrapper safe_abs, safe main) with only safe_abs holding unsafe.
  • The declaration is described as asserting the symbol and signature exist elsewhere, which the compiler cannot check on the foreign side.
  • The seam is shown to be plain i32 -> i32 by value, so nothing is allocated or freed across it.
  • abs on i32::MIN is shown to panic and an unwind across the C ABI is undefined behavior, which wrapping_abs avoids.
Exercise 3implementation

Export a length-prefixed buffer reader

This follows the guard-sequence shape of sum_i32s from Example 2: validate the out pointer first, then the input pointer, each returning a distinct nonzero status before any dereference, and only build the slice once both pointers are known non-null. The signature is exactly fn max_i32(ptr: *const i32, len: usize, out_max: *mut i32) -> i32, marked extern "C" with no_mangle so the symbol is exported under a stable, unmangled name.

Order matters. Check out_max first and return status 1 if it is null, because writing the result through a null out parameter would be undefined behavior regardless of the input. Then check ptr and return status 2 if it is null. These checks happen before any raw read or write, so a null from either side is reported as a value the caller can branch on rather than a crash.

The empty-input case is a contract decision, not a free pass. std::slice::from_raw_parts requires a non-null, aligned pointer even when len is 0, and there is no defined maximum of zero elements. Rather than read from an empty slice or write a garbage maximum, the function returns a distinct nonzero status (3) for len == 0 and documents it. The caller now knows that status 3 means "no elements, no maximum produced" and that *out_max was left untouched.

Only after the out pointer is non-null, the input pointer is non-null, and len is at least 1 does the function build the slice inside an unsafe block with a SAFETY comment, compute the maximum (max() on a non-empty slice yields Some, which is safe to unwrap here because emptiness was already ruled out, though using a fold avoids the unwrap entirely), and write it through *out_max on the success path before returning 0. On every failure path *out_max is never written, so the caller's storage is never corrupted by a failed call.

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn max_i32(ptr: *const i32, len: usize, out_max: *mut i32) -> i32 {
    // Guard the out pointer first: writing through null is always UB.
    if out_max.is_null() {
        return 1; // STATUS_NULL_OUT
    }
    // Then the input pointer, before any read.
    if ptr.is_null() {
        return 2; // STATUS_NULL_INPUT
    }
    // Empty input is a defined contract decision, not a read of an empty slice.
    if len == 0 {
        return 3; // STATUS_EMPTY: no maximum exists; *out_max is left untouched.
    }

    let slice = unsafe {
        // SAFETY:
        // - ptr is non-null (checked above) and the caller promises it is
        //   valid for `len` aligned i32 values for the duration of this call.
        // - len >= 1, so the range is non-empty.
        std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)
    };

    // len >= 1, so iter().max() yields Some; fold avoids the unwrap entirely.
    let max = slice.iter().copied().fold(i32::MIN, i32::max);

    unsafe {
        // SAFETY: out_max was checked non-null and the caller promises it
        // points to writable i32 storage. Written only on the success path.
        *out_max = max;
    }

    0 // STATUS_OK
}

Guard out pointer, then input pointer, then empty input; the slice and the write happen only on the validated success path.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The signature is exactly fn max_i32(ptr: *const i32, len: usize, out_max: *mut i32) -> i32 and is marked extern "C".
  • Null out_max returns status 1 and null ptr returns status 2, each a distinct nonzero status checked before any dereference.
  • len == 0 returns a defined nonzero status (3) and leaves *out_max untouched rather than reading an empty slice or writing garbage.
  • The slice is built inside an unsafe block with a SAFETY comment, and *out_max is written only on the success path before returning 0.
Exercise 4implementation

Map ownership across the seam with an opaque handle

Ownership has no syntax in C, so the surface expresses it by choosing fixed pointer shapes. Here Rust owns the allocation; the caller only ever holds an opaque *mut CounterHandle and must call destroy exactly once. The Rust struct behind the handle never appears in any C signature: the four exported functions speak only in the opaque pointer, integers, and out parameters.

create boxes the Rust struct and hands ownership out as a raw pointer with Box::into_raw. This allocates on Rust's heap and deliberately leaks the Box so the allocation outlives the call; the returned pointer is the handle. increment and read each take the raw handle, null-check it, and reconstruct a borrow with unsafe { &mut *handle } or unsafe { &*handle } without taking ownership. They must not reconstruct a Box, because that would free the allocation on return. read uses an out parameter for the value and returns an integer status so its contract matches the rest of the seam.

destroy is the matching reclaim: it null-checks the handle and then calls Box::from_raw exactly once, turning the raw pointer back into an owned Box that is dropped at the end of the function. Box::into_raw and Box::from_raw must be paired one-to-one; calling from_raw twice on the same pointer is a double free, and never calling it leaks the allocation. After destroy returns, the caller's handle is dangling and must not be used again, which is part of the documented contract.

The comment on the surface records the ownership rules so they are readable from the signatures: Rust allocates and owns the counter, the caller holds the handle and may mutate through increment or read through read, and only destroy frees it, exactly once. An opaque handle is just a pointer to a type whose fields the foreign side never sees, which is what keeps the richer Rust model behind the seam.

// Ownership contract (readable from the signatures below):
// - Rust allocates and OWNS the Counter (create -> Box::into_raw).
// - The caller HOLDS the opaque handle and may mutate via increment / read.
// - Only destroy FREES it, exactly once (Box::from_raw). Using the handle
//   after destroy, or calling destroy twice, is undefined behavior.

pub struct CounterHandle {
    value: i64,
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn counter_create() -> *mut CounterHandle {
    Box::into_raw(Box::new(CounterHandle { value: 0 }))
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn counter_increment(handle: *mut CounterHandle) -> i32 {
    if handle.is_null() {
        return 1; // STATUS_NULL_HANDLE
    }
    // SAFETY: handle is non-null and, per contract, points to a live Counter
    // created by counter_create and not yet destroyed. We borrow, never own.
    let counter = unsafe { &mut *handle };
    counter.value += 1;
    0
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn counter_read(handle: *const CounterHandle, out: *mut i64) -> i32 {
    if out.is_null() {
        return 2; // STATUS_NULL_OUT
    }
    if handle.is_null() {
        return 1; // STATUS_NULL_HANDLE
    }
    // SAFETY: both pointers checked non-null; handle borrowed, not owned.
    let counter = unsafe { &*handle };
    unsafe { *out = counter.value };
    0
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn counter_destroy(handle: *mut CounterHandle) -> i32 {
    if handle.is_null() {
        return 1; // STATUS_NULL_HANDLE
    }
    // SAFETY: handle came from counter_create's Box::into_raw and has not been
    // destroyed before. from_raw reclaims ownership; the Box drops here, once.
    let owned = unsafe { Box::from_raw(handle) };
    drop(owned);
    0
}

create/into_raw, borrow-only increment/read, and destroy/from_raw form a one-to-one allocate-and-free pair across the opaque handle.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The four extern "C" functions expose only the opaque *mut CounterHandle, integers, and out parameters, never the Rust struct by value.
  • create uses Box::into_raw and destroy uses Box::from_raw exactly once, dropping the reclaimed Box.
  • increment and read null-check the handle and reconstruct a borrow (&mut */&*) without freeing it.
  • A comment records that Rust owns the allocation, the caller holds the handle, and only destroy frees it.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Stop an unwind from crossing the boundary

The defect is not a wrong value but a path on which the function can unwind out of an extern "C" frame. A Rust panic crossing the C ABI boundary is undefined behavior because the foreign caller's frames were not compiled to be unwound through, and it tends to crash far from the cause. The fix is to remove every panicking operation and report failure as a distinct integer status before control leaves the function.

The panic sources in a body that parses a caller buffer are: indexing such as buf[0] or buf[i] (panics on out-of-bounds), slicing such as &buf[..n] (panics if n exceeds the length), unwrap on the parse Result (panics on malformed input), and raw arithmetic that can overflow (panics in debug builds). Each is a boundary hazard because the panic does not stay inside Rust; it unwinds toward the foreign caller.

The refactor replaces each panicking operation with a checked form that yields a status instead. Indexing becomes buf.get(i), which returns Option and lets a None map to a nonzero status. Slicing becomes get(range) or an explicit length check before slicing. The parse stays as a Result and is matched, never unwrapped, mapping Err to a distinct status. Raw arithmetic becomes checked_add (and friends), mapping the overflow None to a status. Every failure becomes a distinct nonzero return code the caller can branch on, and the successful value is delivered through an out parameter.

Whether to also wrap the body in std::panic::catch_unwind is a judgment call. Once the panicking operations are gone, catch_unwind is a backstop, not the primary fix: it converts any panic that still slips through (for example from a helper you do not control, or a debug-only overflow you missed) into a caught error instead of undefined behavior. It is cheap insurance at the outer edge of the exported function, but it must not be a substitute for removing the panics, because relying on it alone leaves the real hazards in place and obscures the contract. The rule stated plainly: no cross-language unwinding; translate failure to an integer status before control crosses the boundary. With the checked forms in place, every path returns a status and the function cannot unwind.

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn parse_first_u32(ptr: *const u8, len: usize, out: *mut u32) -> i32 {
    if out.is_null() {
        return 1; // null out
    }
    if ptr.is_null() {
        return 2; // null input
    }
    let buf = unsafe {
        // SAFETY: ptr non-null; caller promises `len` valid, readable bytes.
        std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)
    };

    // catch_unwind is a backstop only; the real fix is that nothing below panics.
    let result = std::panic::catch_unwind(|| -> Result<u32, i32> {
        // Was: let head = buf[0];  -> indexing panics out of bounds. Use get.
        let _head = match buf.first() {
            Some(&b) => b,
            None => return Err(3), // empty input
        };
        // Was: &buf[..4] -> slicing panics if too short. Bound-check first.
        let text = match buf.get(..) {
            Some(bytes) => bytes,
            None => return Err(4),
        };
        // Was: std::str::from_utf8(text).unwrap() -> panics on bad UTF-8.
        let s = match std::str::from_utf8(text) {
            Ok(s) => s,
            Err(_) => return Err(5),
        };
        // Was: s.parse::<u32>().unwrap() -> panics on malformed input.
        let value: u32 = match s.trim().parse() {
            Ok(v) => v,
            Err(_) => return Err(6),
        };
        // Was: value + 1 -> raw arithmetic can overflow-panic in debug.
        match value.checked_add(1) {
            Some(v) => Ok(v),
            None => Err(7), // overflow
        }
    });

    match result {
        Ok(Ok(value)) => {
            unsafe { *out = value };
            0 // success
        }
        Ok(Err(status)) => status, // a defined, checked failure
        Err(_) => 8,               // a panic was caught at the backstop
    }
}

Each indexing/slicing/unwrap/arithmetic panic is replaced by a checked form mapped to a status; catch_unwind is only the outer backstop.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Indexing, slicing, unwrap, and overflowing arithmetic are each named and replaced with get, a bound check, a matched Result, and checked_add.
  • Every failure is reported through a distinct nonzero status code, never by panicking.
  • The answer states the rule plainly: no cross-language unwinding; translate failure to a status before control leaves the function.
  • catch_unwind is used as an explicit backstop, with the primary fix being removal of the panics.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose a binding tool for a legacy C++ subsystem

The chapter's decision tree turns on two questions: do you control both sides of the boundary, and how large is the C++ surface you need to reach. For this scenario the answers are: you do not fully control both sides (you own the Rust side but not the historical C++ headers), and the C++ surface is large (a legacy subsystem reached through an existing host process, plugin loader, and native test harness).

Given a large C++ surface you do not control, the recommendation is a deliberate C ABI seam: a hand-written C shim that exposes a narrow, stable extern "C" contract, with bindgen used to generate the Rust declarations for that shim's C header rather than for the raw C++ headers. cxx and autocxx are strongest when you control both sides and want a curated, ongoing C++/Rust bridge that tracks the C++ types directly; here you do not own the historical headers and the requirement is explicitly a narrow ABI contract, not a broad type-level bridge. autocxx attempting to consume a large legacy C++ surface you cannot modify tends to drag in template, exception, and standard-library assumptions you were specifically asked to keep out. The hand-written C shim plus bindgen keeps the contract surface small: layout, pointer validity, ownership, status-code errors, and no cross-language unwinding are all stated explicitly at one thin seam. "C++ integration" here is, correctly, a deliberate C ABI seam around C++ code, which buys a smaller contract and fewer compiler- and standard-library assumptions.

What the tool does not write for you is the contract itself. bindgen generates Rust signatures from the C header, but it does not decide who allocates and who frees, does not establish how long each pointer stays valid, does not convert C++ exceptions or Rust panics into status codes, and does not guarantee the ABI stays stable across compiler versions. Those obligations remain yours: the tool reduces boilerplate, not responsibility. You still author the shim's ownership rules (opaque handles with explicit create/destroy), the status-code error mapping, and the no-unwind policy on both directions of the seam.

To test and sanitize the layer before shipping, exercise the seam under the existing native test harness so it is driven exactly as production drives it, and build that harness with sanitizers: AddressSanitizer to catch use-after-free, double free, and out-of-bounds across the boundary; and where available a leak detector to confirm every create is matched by a destroy and that into_raw/from_raw stay paired. Add targeted tests for each status code and each null path, a round-trip ownership test that creates, mutates, reads, and destroys a handle, and a deliberate fault-injection test that confirms a forced error returns a status rather than unwinding. Miri can validate the Rust-side unsafe blocks in isolation. The combination proves both the values and the contract: that nothing leaks, nothing is freed twice, and no unwind crosses the seam.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The choice is framed around the two decision-tree questions: whether you control both sides (no) and how large the C++ surface is (large).
  • A hand-written C shim plus bindgen is recommended specifically because the C++ surface is large and you do not fully control it, with cxx/autocxx ruled out.
  • The answer states the tool reduces boilerplate but does not change the ownership, panic, and ABI-stability contract you still owe.
  • A concrete plan exercises the seam under the native harness with sanitizer (ASan/leak) builds, plus per-status, null-path, round-trip, and fault-injection tests.

Lab solution

The lab models the exported sum_i32s seam from Example 2 in plain std Rust. The two raw-pointer parameters are stood in by Option<&[i32]> and Option<&mut i64>: a None models a null pointer, and a Some models a validated, borrowed pointer. The caller owns both the input array and the output slot; the function only borrows them for the duration of the call, exactly as the C ABI version borrows the caller's buffer and out storage.

The body is a guard sequence in the chapter's fixed order. It checks the out parameter first, returning STATUS_NULL_OUT (1) if it is None, because there is no defined place to write a result without it. It then checks the input, returning STATUS_NULL_INPUT (2) if it is None. Only once both are present does it do the real work: each i32 is widened to i64 before summing, so the boundary contract cannot overflow i32, and the total is written through the out parameter before STATUS_OK (0) is returned. Failure is reported as a distinct integer status rather than a Result, which is what keeps the seam portable to C.

The expected output follows directly. The first call passes both pointers and the slice [3, 4, 5], so it returns status 0 and writes 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 into total, printing status = 0 and total = 12. The null-input call returns 2 and the null-out call returns 1, matching the two guard branches.

Example 28-S. cpp_integration_status_seam_lab.rs — Reference solution

// Status codes mirror the C ABI seam from the chapter: 0 = success,
// nonzero = a distinct failure the caller can branch on without a Result.
const STATUS_OK: i32 = 0;
const STATUS_NULL_OUT: i32 = 1;
const STATUS_NULL_INPUT: i32 = 2;

// Models the exported `sum_i32s` seam: the caller owns both the input buffer
// and the output storage; this function only borrows them for the call.
// Option<&...> stands in for a possibly-null pointer; &mut i64 is the out slot.
fn sum_i32s(input: Option<&[i32]>, out_total: Option<&mut i64>) -> i32 {
    // Guard the out pointer first, exactly like the chapter's null checks.
    let out = match out_total {
        Some(slot) => slot,
        None => return STATUS_NULL_OUT,
    };
    // Then guard the input pointer before touching the buffer.
    let values = match input {
        Some(slice) => slice,
        None => return STATUS_NULL_INPUT,
    };
    // Widen to i64 before summing so the boundary contract cannot overflow i32.
    *out = values.iter().map(|&v| v as i64).sum::<i64>();
    STATUS_OK
}

fn main() {
    let values = [3_i32, 4, 5];

    let mut total = -1_i64;
    let status = sum_i32s(Some(&values), Some(&mut total));
    println!("status = {}", status);
    println!("total = {}", total);

    let mut ignored = 0_i64;
    println!("null input status = {}", sum_i32s(None, Some(&mut ignored)));
    println!("null out status = {}", sum_i32s(Some(&values), None));
}
Output
status = 0
total = 12
null input status = 2
null out status = 1

Review question answers

What are the four FFI fundamentals the chapter says almost every Rust interop layer is built from?

They are the small set of primitives that turn an internal Rust function into a symbol another language can call without guessing about representation: the C calling convention via extern "C", unmangled exported symbol names via no_mangle, C-friendly layout for any shared data (raw buffers and lengths, or opaque handles, instead of Rust ownership types), and integer status codes with out parameters in place of Result. Together they form the thin, stable contract at the seam. Everything richer stays behind it.

Why must a Rust Result<T, E> be re-expressed as an integer status plus out parameters before crossing a C ABI boundary?

A Result<T, E> is a Rust enum with no fixed, agreed-upon C layout: its discriminant representation is an implementation detail and its E type has no C expression, so the foreign side cannot read it. The conventional lowering is therefore an integer status as the return value, with any successful payload delivered through a caller-owned out parameter on the success path. This keeps the contract portable and lets the caller branch on a status code without ever seeing Rust's Result shape.

What does no_mangle and the extern "C" calling convention each contribute when exporting a Rust function to C or C++?

extern "C" sets the calling convention, so the function is called the way C expects (argument passing, register and stack discipline) rather than with Rust's unspecified convention. no_mangle keeps the symbol's name exactly as written instead of applying Rust's name mangling, so the linker on the C or C++ side can find it by that name. You need both: the right convention so the call works, and a stable, predictable name so the symbol can be resolved.

Why is an in-flight unwind, a Rust panic or a C++ exception, more dangerous to let cross the seam than a bad value?

An unwind crossing into frames the other language did not compile to be unwound through is undefined behavior, not merely a wrong result. The foreign frames have no registered cleanup for that unwinding mechanism, so destructors may not run, invariants are left broken, and the program tends to crash far from the cause, making it hard to diagnose. A bad value can at least be checked and rejected; an in-flight unwind corrupts control flow itself. The conservative, operable rule is no cross-language unwinding: translate failure to an integer status or explicit error object before control crosses the boundary.

Which two questions drive the choice between a hand-written C shim, bindgen, cxx, and autocxx?

Whether you control both sides of the boundary, and how large the C++ surface you need to reach is. When you control both sides and want a curated, type-level C++/Rust bridge, cxx (or autocxx for a larger generated surface) fits; when you do not control the C++ headers and need a narrow, stable contract, a deliberate C ABI seam (a hand-written C shim, with bindgen generating the Rust declarations from its header) keeps the surface small. None of these tools changes the contract you owe; they only change how much of the boilerplate is generated for you.

Chapter 29 · JavaScript and C++ Integration for WASM

JavaScript and C++ Integration for WASM

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises drill the one idea the chapter insists you internalize: the JavaScript host and the WebAssembly module keep separate heaps, and the only thing they share is one linear byte array. Everything richer than a number is encoded and copied across a boundary you design. The warm-ups make you state that two-heaps model precisely; the implementation tasks make you build boundary functions that respect it; the debugging and design tasks make you defend the C-ABI invariants and the cost ladder under pressure.

The through-line is that WebAssembly does not remove the marshalling boundary you knew from other runtimes; it makes the boundary explicit. A copy that used to hide inside a marshaller is now a copy you can see, measure, and design around. Each solution below ties its choice back to ownership (who holds the buffer), borrowing (a &str or &[u8] is copied in and not retained), and the per-crossing cost that decides whether the module is faster than the JavaScript it replaced.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

State the two-heaps model in your own words

The JavaScript host owns its own object graph: strings, arrays, and typed objects that live in the JavaScript engine's garbage-collected heap and that the module cannot reach into. The module owns its stack and its own heap, both carved out of a single contiguous region called its linear memory. The host cannot dereference module objects and the module cannot dereference host objects. The only region both sides can touch directly is that linear memory, exposed to JavaScript as one shared byte array. That asymmetry is the whole model: two private heaps with one shared byte buffer wedged between them.

Because the shared region is just bytes, anything that is not already a plain machine number has to be laid out into those bytes on one side and read back out on the other. For build_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String, the two &str arguments are copied from the host's strings into linear memory so the module can borrow them, and the owned String the function returns is copied back out of linear memory into a fresh host-owned string. After the call the module keeps nothing: the input strings were borrowed for the duration of the call, and the host now owns a separate copy of the result.

A u32 result from sum_bytes is different because a number is not a heap value at all. It rides the WebAssembly function-call interface directly as a native i32/i64-shaped value, so there is no allocation in linear memory and no byte copy to encode or decode. The input slice still has to be copied into linear memory to be summed, but the answer travels back as a bare register-width number with zero marshalling.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States JavaScript holds its own GC heap of objects while the module holds its own stack and heap inside one linear memory.
  • Identifies the shared linear memory (the exposed byte array) as the only region both sides can touch.
  • Explains each &str into build_label is copied into linear memory and the returned String is copied back to a host-owned value.
  • Explains a u32 rides the native call interface directly with no allocation and no copy.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the C ABI crossing in route_score

In the wasm_cpp_ffi_boundary listing, route_score(route: &str) -> u32 is a safe wrapper whose only job is to forward the string's bytes across the C ABI. What actually crosses the inner seam is route.as_ptr() (a *const u8 to the start of the UTF-8 bytes) and route.len() (the byte count). A Rust &str or &[u8] is a fat pointer of (data pointer, length), and the C ABI has no slice type, so you cannot hand the slice over as one value. You decompose it into a raw pointer plus an explicit length, and the shim rebuilds the slice on the other side with std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) for the duration of the call only.

The SAFETY comments name three invariants that together make the unsafe blocks sound. First, valid pointer: route.as_ptr() points at route.len() initialized bytes (the shim also defends against the null-with-len-zero case). Second, correct length: the length passed is exactly the number of bytes the pointer is valid for, so from_raw_parts does not fabricate a slice that runs past the allocation. Third, read-only for the call's duration: the shim only reads the bytes while the call is in progress and does not retain the pointer or mutate through it, so the borrow of route stays valid the whole time and is not aliased mutably.

The unsafe surface is deliberately tiny. cpp_route_score is declared in an unsafe extern "C" block and its body uses an unsafe from_raw_parts; route_score wraps the foreign call in an unsafe block. Everything else, including main and any caller, stays in ordinary safe Rust. For the input "/orders", the shim reconstructs a 7-byte slice (the characters /, o, r, d, e, r, s) and returns bytes.len() as u32 * 10, which is 7 * 10 = 70.

// What crosses the inner C-ABI seam from route_score("/orders"):
//   ptr = route.as_ptr()  -> *const u8 at the first of 7 bytes
//   len = route.len()     -> 7
// The shim rebuilds the slice for the call only and returns len * 10.

fn main() {
    let route = "/orders";
    assert_eq!(route.len(), 7);        // 7 UTF-8 bytes, no multi-byte chars
    assert_eq!(route_score(route), 70); // 7 * 10
}

Confirms the 7-byte length and the resulting score of 70 for "/orders".

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Notes route.as_ptr() and route.len() cross because the C ABI has no slice type.
  • Names the valid-pointer, correct-length, and read-only-for-the-call invariants from the SAFETY comments.
  • Identifies that only the wrapper and the shim are unsafe while the rest stays safe Rust.
  • Computes 7 bytes times 10 = 70 for "/orders".
Exercise 3implementation

Add a byte-returning boundary function

Following the sum_bytes pattern, mask_bytes takes the input as a borrowed &[u8] so the module never takes ownership of the host's buffer; the slice is the copy-in into linear memory, valid only for the call. It returns an owned Vec<u8>, which is the copy-out: the host receives a freshly allocated buffer that it then owns separately from anything the module holds. This mirrors how a real wasm-bindgen export of &[u8] -> Vec<u8> would marshal one copy in and one copy out.

The transform itself is a per-byte XOR with key. Using bytes.iter().map(|&b| b ^ key).collect() reads the borrowed slice without mutating it and builds the owned Vec in a single expression. Nothing aliases or writes through the input pointer, so the borrow stays read-only for the call's duration, exactly the discipline the boundary requires. For [1, 2, 3, 4] with key 1: 1^1=0, 2^1=3, 3^1=2, 4^1=5, giving [0, 3, 2, 5].

/// `bytes` is borrowed (copy-IN to linear memory; not owned by the module).
/// The returned `Vec<u8>` is the copy-OUT the host receives and owns.
fn mask_bytes(bytes: &[u8], key: u8) -> Vec<u8> {
    bytes.iter().map(|&b| b ^ key).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let out = mask_bytes(&[1, 2, 3, 4], 1);
    assert_eq!(out, vec![0, 3, 2, 5]);
    println!("{:?}", out); // [0, 3, 2, 5]
}

XORs each borrowed input byte with key and returns a freshly owned buffer.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Signature is exactly fn mask_bytes(bytes: &[u8], key: u8) -> Vec<u8>.
  • Each output byte is the input byte XORed with key.
  • The input slice is only read, never mutated, and no ownership of the caller's buffer is taken.
  • For [1, 2, 3, 4] with key 1 the result is [0, 3, 2, 5].
Exercise 4implementation

Batch crossings instead of crossing per element

The point of batching is that the boundary crossing, not the arithmetic, is the expensive part. Scoring routes one at a time pays one full host-to-module crossing per route: N routes means N crossings, each with its own copy-in and marshalling overhead. route_scores accepts the whole batch as &[&str], so the entire list is handed across once and the loop runs entirely inside the module.

The implementation reuses route_score per element rather than reimplementing the shim call, keeping the single unsafe C-ABI path in one place: routes.iter().map(|r| route_score(r)).collect(). The result is a Vec<u32> aligned by index with the input, so scores[i] corresponds to routes[i]. Compared with calling once per route, this turns N boundary crossings into exactly one. The per-call boundary overhead you remove scales with N; the inner arithmetic (len * 10 per route) is unchanged because it was never the cost.

fn route_score(route: &str) -> u32 {
    (route.len() as u32) * 10
}

/// One crossing covers the whole batch; reuses route_score per element.
fn route_scores(routes: &[&str]) -> Vec<u32> {
    routes.iter().map(|r| route_score(r)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let scores = route_scores(&["/a", "/bb", "/ccc"]);
    assert_eq!(scores, vec![20, 30, 40]);
    // N routes -> 1 crossing instead of N crossings.
}

Scores every route in one batched call by mapping route_score over the slice.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Signature is exactly fn route_scores(routes: &[&str]) -> Vec<u32>.
  • Result length equals input length and each entry matches route_score for that route.
  • Reuses route_score instead of duplicating the unsafe shim call.
  • States the batch makes one crossing instead of one per route.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix an unsound boundary wrapper

The defect is that score_prefix passes the caller-supplied n straight through to cpp_route_score(route.as_ptr(), n) without checking it against route.len(). The C ABI trusts the length you hand it: inside the shim, from_raw_parts(ptr, n) will fabricate a slice of n bytes starting at route's first byte. If n is greater than route.len(), that slice runs past the borrowed string into memory the pointer is not valid for, violating the correct-length invariant and reading out of bounds. The wrapper is the only place that can enforce a bound, because once the pointer and length cross the seam the shim has no way to know the true size of the allocation.

The fix is to clamp the length to the borrowed region before crossing: n.min(route.len()). That guarantees the length never exceeds the bytes the pointer is valid for, so the pointer-plus-length pair always describes a region inside the string. The pointer stays valid (it is still route.as_ptr()), the length is now correct (at most route.len()), and the shim still only reads for the call's duration, so the read-only borrow invariant holds. With the clamp in place the wrapper is sound for any n the caller passes.

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn cpp_route_score(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> u32;
}

/// Score only the first `n` bytes of `route`, clamped to the string length.
fn score_prefix(route: &str, n: usize) -> u32 {
    let len = n.min(route.len()); // never read past the borrowed bytes
    unsafe {
        // SAFETY:
        // - route.as_ptr() is a valid pointer to route.len() initialized bytes.
        // - len <= route.len(), so the pointer is valid for `len` bytes.
        // - the shim only reads the bytes for the duration of the call.
        cpp_route_score(route.as_ptr(), len)
    }
}

Clamps the length with n.min(route.len()) so the pointer/length pair stays in bounds.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies that n greater than route.len() lets the shim read beyond the borrowed bytes.
  • Clamps the length to at most route.len() with n.min(route.len()) before the call.
  • The corrected wrapper passes a pointer and length that always describe a valid read-only region.
  • A SAFETY comment names the valid-pointer, correct-length, and read-only invariants.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose boundary representations on the cost ladder

Map each workload to one rung of the number / bytes / struct / resident-handle ladder and justify it by copies per crossing plus any encode/decode cost.

Per-frame brightness scalar: send it as a number. It rides the native call interface for free, with no allocation in linear memory and no copy. Doing this per frame is fine because the cost is zero regardless of frame rate.

Parsed config struct sent once at startup: send it as a serialized struct. A struct crossing costs an encode on one side, a copy of the bytes, and a decode on the other. That encode-plus-decode overhead is real, but it is paid exactly once at startup, so the convenience of a structured representation is worth it and the per-frame path never touches it.

Large image buffer processed every frame: cross it as a byte array, one copy per crossing. There is no encode/decode, just the raw byte copy into (or out of) linear memory. The buffer is large, so even one copy per frame is the dominant cost; you minimize it by reusing the same allocation and copying only when the pixels actually change, and by processing the whole frame in a single crossing rather than per-row.
