Parser the host calls thousands of times: keep it resident behind a handle. Instead of copying the parser's state in and out on every call, you construct it once inside the module and return an opaque handle (an integer or a wasm-bindgen object) the host holds. Each subsequent call passes the handle plus only the new input, so per call you pay almost nothing instead of re-marshalling the whole parser. The tradeoff is a managed lifetime: the host must explicitly free or drop the handle, and you own the bookkeeping that the resident state is released.

Where the convenient type loses: encoding the large config struct (or any sizeable structured payload) as JSON and shipping it across on a hot path. JSON adds a serialize on the sending side and a full parse on the receiving side on top of the byte copy. For a struct crossed thousands of times, that encode-plus-decode tax can make the WebAssembly module slower end to end than the plain JavaScript it replaced, even though the arithmetic inside the module is faster. A compact binary layout the host reads directly as a typed array skips the parse entirely and is dramatically cheaper, which is the whole reason the performance discussion is about the boundary and not the math.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Brightness scalar crosses as a number with no copy; image buffer crosses as a byte array with one copy per crossing.
  • The parser called thousands of times is kept resident behind a handle to avoid per-call copies, at the cost of a managed lifetime.
  • Each choice is justified using copies per crossing or encode-plus-decode cost from the ladder.
  • Names a concrete case (a large struct as JSON on a hot path) where the convenient encoding loses to a compact binary layout.

Lab solution

Each helper models one boundary contract in plain std Rust so the crossing logic is testable without a browser. build_label takes two borrowed &str values (the copy-in) and returns an owned String (the copy-out), printing billing::/ready. sum_bytes borrows the slice [1, 2, 3, 4], sums it as u32, and returns 1+2+3+4 = 10 as a bare number with no copy. route_score models the pointer-plus-length C-ABI crossing as len * 10, so "/orders" (7 bytes) yields 70.

The only TODO is route_scores. The batched implementation maps route_score over the borrowed &[&str] and collects into a Vec<u32>: routes.iter().map(|route| route_score(route)).collect(). This scores all three routes inside one call rather than crossing the boundary per element, which is exactly the batching point of the chapter.

Because scores is non-empty after the batched call, the final println! takes the else-free branch of the if and prints batch crossings = 1, signaling that the whole batch crossed in a single call. Every line therefore matches the expected output exactly.

Example 29-S. wasm_boundary_lab.rs — Reference solution

// Models the WebAssembly boundary contracts in plain std Rust.
// Two separate heaps with one shared byte array is simulated here by
// passing borrowed slices in and returning owned values out.

fn build_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String {
    // &str copied in, owned String copied back out.
    format!("{}::{}", service, route)
}

fn sum_bytes(bytes: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    // borrowed slice copied in, u32 rides back with no copy.
    bytes.iter().map(|&value| value as u32).sum()
}

fn route_score(route: &str) -> u32 {
    // Pointer-plus-length C-ABI crossing, modeled: score is len * 10.
    (route.len() as u32) * 10
}

fn route_scores(routes: &[&str]) -> Vec<u32> {
    // Score every route in a single batched crossing, reusing route_score.
    routes.iter().map(|route| route_score(route)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let label = build_label("billing", "/ready");
    let total = sum_bytes(&[1_u8, 2, 3, 4]);
    let score = route_score("/orders");
    let scores = route_scores(&["/a", "/bb", "/ccc"]);

    println!("label = {}", label);
    println!("sum = {}", total);
    println!("score = {}", score);
    println!("batch crossings = {}", if scores.is_empty() { 0 } else { 1 });
}
Output
label = billing::/ready
sum = 10
score = 70
batch crossings = 1

Review question answers

Why does every value richer than a number get copied when it crosses between the JavaScript host and the WebAssembly module?

The host and the module keep two separate heaps and cannot dereference each other's objects; the only memory both sides can touch is the module's linear memory, exposed as one shared byte array. Any value that is not already a plain machine number is a heap value, so it must be laid out into those shared bytes on one side and read back out on the other, which is a copy. A number is the exception because it travels directly on the native function-call interface with no allocation, so it needs no encode-and-copy step.

What role does wasm-bindgen play after a browser-facing crate is compiled as a cdylib?

The cdylib crate type tells the linker to produce a single .wasm artifact. wasm-bindgen then post-processes that artifact to emit the JavaScript glue that knows how to lay out each annotated argument into linear memory and read each return value back out. In other words, it generates the marshalling code that turns the raw WebAssembly imports and exports into callable JavaScript functions with the right copy-in and copy-out behavior for strings, arrays, and structs.

On the cost ladder of boundary representations, how do a number, a byte array, a serialized struct, and a resident handle differ in per-crossing cost?

A number rides the native interface for free, with no allocation and no copy. A string or byte array costs one byte copy per crossing. A serialized struct costs an encode plus a copy plus a decode, since it must be flattened to bytes and rebuilt on the far side. A resident handle costs almost nothing per call because the state stays inside the module and only a small handle plus new inputs cross, but it adds a lifetime the host must manage and eventually release.

How do the outer Rust-to-JavaScript seam and the inner Rust-to-C-shim seam differ in how data and safety are managed?

The outer seam is managed by wasm-bindgen's generated glue: it handles the layout and copying of each value, so the data movement and most of the safety are automatic. The inner seam is the raw C ABI, where data crosses as bare pointers and lengths through an unsafe extern block, and you uphold the pointer, length, and borrow-duration invariants by hand with SAFETY comments. They stack but stay distinct, so a fault should be diagnosed at the correct seam rather than confused between the two.

Why is the WebAssembly performance discussion almost always about the boundary rather than the arithmetic inside the module?

Inside the module WebAssembly computes at near-native speed, so the arithmetic is rarely the bottleneck. The cost that actually varies with your design is the boundary: crossing per element instead of batching, copying a large buffer on every call, or encoding a struct as JSON and parsing it back. A design that mishandles those crossings can be slower than the JavaScript it replaced even though its inner math is faster, which is why the boundary is where the performance work lives.

Chapter 30 · AMQP and Message Brokers

AMQP and Message Brokers

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises build toward one operational truth: a broker decouples services in time, but it does not decouple you from the consistency, idempotency, and observability work that asynchronous handoff requires. You start by pinning down who owns each routing decision, then trace and extend the exact-match exchange, and finally encode the commit-then-ack ordering that keeps acknowledged work from being lost.

The later exercises move from mechanics to policy. You distinguish a transient failure that deserves a bounded retry from a poison message that belongs in a dead-letter queue, you make the handler idempotent so at-least-once delivery becomes harmless, and you design a versioned envelope so a message can outlive the code that produced it. Throughout, the rule is the same one the chapter states plainly: an ack is a promise the work is safely done, and a queue is a place work can pile up invisibly unless you watch it.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Separate routing-key choice from routing policy

When a producer publishes, it controls exactly one thing: the routing key, a stable semantic label such as orders.created that describes what happened, not where it should go. The producer never names a queue. The exchange controls everything else. It owns the binding state, the table that maps routing keys to the set of queues that should receive a copy, and it owns the routing policy, the rule that decides for a given key which bindings match. The producer says what happened; the exchange decides who hears about it.

This split is what lets a new team add a search-indexing queue for orders.created without touching any publisher. They declare a queue and bind it to the routing key orders.created on the existing exchange. The next message published with that key now copies into their queue as well, because routing topology lives in exactly one place, the exchange, and the publisher was never queue-aware to begin with. Nothing about the producer's code, deployment, or contract changes. If routing topology lived in the producer instead, every new consumer would force an edit to and a redeploy of every publisher, which is precisely the coupling the broker exists to remove.

A message whose routing key matches no binding produces zero deliveries. It is not an error and it is not delivered anywhere; the exchange simply finds no matching queues. The chapter's model counts this as an unrouted message rather than silently discarding it because a key with no binding usually means a misconfiguration, a typo in the key, a queue that was never declared, or a binding that was removed by mistake, and a silent drop hides that. A visible unrouted counter turns a routing gap into a metric you can alarm on instead of a message that vanished without a trace.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States the producer chooses only the routing key while the exchange owns binding state and routing policy.
  • Explains a new queue bound to an existing key receives copies with no change to any publisher.
  • States an unbound key yields zero deliveries and is tracked as unrouted rather than delivered or silently dropped.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the idempotent consumer's decision machine

The Consumer in Example 2 runs every delivery through one ordered decision machine in on_delivery. First it checks processed_ids: if the message_id is already present, it counts a duplicate and returns without redoing the work. Otherwise it inspects the order_id. If the order is ord-fail and attempt is below 3, it counts a retry and pushes a clone with attempt incremented onto retry_queue; if ord-fail has reached attempt 3, it pushes the delivery to the dlq. Any other order is treated as success: processed is incremented and the message_id is recorded in processed_ids. Only the success path mutates processed_ids, so only success makes a future copy a duplicate.

msg-1 arrives twice. The first delivery has order_id ord-1, which is not ord-fail, so it takes the success branch: processed becomes 1 and msg-1 is inserted into processed_ids. The second msg-1 now finds its id already in processed_ids, so it takes the duplicate branch: duplicates becomes 1 and it returns without touching the work. This is the idempotency guard absorbing a redelivery exactly as designed.

msg-2 carries order_id ord-fail at attempt 1. Its id is not yet seen, so it falls through to the ord-fail branch; attempt 1 is below 3, so retried becomes 1 and a clone with attempt 2 is queued. The drain loop pops that clone: attempt 2 is still below 3, so retried becomes 2 and a clone with attempt 3 is queued. The drain loop pops that clone: attempt 3 is not below 3, so it takes the dlq branch and dlq now holds 1 entry. Note that ord-fail is never recorded in processed_ids on any path, which is correct, because it never succeeded. Finally msg-3 with order_id ord-3 succeeds, making processed 2. The printed output is therefore processed = 2, duplicates = 1, retried = 2, dlq = 1.

// Hand-trace of the four feeds plus the drain loop:
//
// 1. msg-1 / ord-1  / attempt 1  -> success  : processed=1, ids={msg-1}
// 2. msg-1 / ord-1  / attempt 1  -> duplicate : duplicates=1 (id already seen)
// 3. msg-2 / ord-fail/ attempt 1 -> retry     : retried=1, requeue attempt 2
//    drain: ord-fail / attempt 2 -> retry     : retried=2, requeue attempt 3
//    drain: ord-fail / attempt 3 -> dlq       : dlq.len()=1 (3 is not < 3)
// 4. msg-3 / ord-3  / attempt 1  -> success  : processed=2, ids={msg-1,msg-3}
//
// Final:
// processed = 2
// duplicates = 1
// retried = 2
// dlq = 1

Step-by-step trace of on_delivery showing each branch and the final counter values.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies the second msg-1 as a counted duplicate that returns without redoing work.
  • Shows ord-fail retried at attempts 1 and 2, then moved to the DLQ when attempt reaches 3.
  • Predicts processed = 2, duplicates = 1, retried = 2, dlq = 1.
Exercise 3implementation

Add a wildcard topic match to the exchange

Keep the exact-match path exactly as it is and add wildcard support as a second, separate store. Exact bindings stay in the HashMap keyed by the full routing key, so an exact lookup remains a single O(1) hash probe. Wildcard bindings go in their own collection of (pattern, queue) pairs, because a pattern such as orders.* cannot be looked up by hash; it must be matched segment by segment against the incoming key. Splitting the two stores means the common case, an exact key with no wildcards, pays no scanning cost, and only the wildcard set is iterated.

Matching splits both the binding pattern and the routing key on '.' and compares segment by segment. A '*' segment matches exactly one segment, never zero and never several, so orders.* matches orders.created and orders.cancelled but not orders or orders.created.eu. The pattern matches only when the two segment counts are equal and every segment is either identical or a '*'. This is the single-trailing-wildcard rule the exercise asks for; it deliberately does not implement the multi-segment '#' wildcard, which would match a variable number of segments.

The new route_topic method returns the union of the exact-match queues and the wildcard-match queues with no duplicates. A routing key can legitimately match both an exact binding and a wildcard binding, for example orders.created bound directly to billing and also covered by orders.* bound to audit, and each target queue must appear once. The implementation guards against duplicates by checking membership before pushing (or equivalently by collecting into a set and back into a Vec). A key that matches neither store returns an empty Vec<String>, preserving the chapter's unrouted-versus-routed distinction.

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct DirectExchange {
    // Exact bindings: O(1) lookup, unchanged from Example 1.
    bindings: HashMap<String, Vec<String>>,
    // Wildcard bindings stored as (pattern, queue) pairs.
    wildcards: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl DirectExchange {
    fn bind(&mut self, routing_key: &str, queue: &str) {
        self.bindings
            .entry(routing_key.to_string())
            .or_default()
            .push(queue.to_string());
    }

    fn bind_topic(&mut self, pattern: &str, queue: &str) {
        self.wildcards.push((pattern.to_string(), queue.to_string()));
    }

    // Unchanged exact-match route used by the original example.
    fn route(&self, routing_key: &str) -> Vec<String> {
        self.bindings.get(routing_key).cloned().unwrap_or_default()
    }

    // One '*' segment matches exactly one routing-key segment.
    fn pattern_matches(pattern: &str, routing_key: &str) -> bool {
        let pats: Vec<&str> = pattern.split('.').collect();
        let keys: Vec<&str> = routing_key.split('.').collect();
        if pats.len() != keys.len() {
            return false;
        }
        pats.iter()
            .zip(keys.iter())
            .all(|(p, k)| *p == "*" || p == k)
    }

    fn route_topic(&self, routing_key: &str) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut out: Vec<String> = self.route(routing_key);
        for (pattern, queue) in &self.wildcards {
            if Self::pattern_matches(pattern, routing_key) && !out.contains(queue) {
                out.push(queue.clone());
            }
        }
        out
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ex = DirectExchange::default();
    ex.bind("orders.created", "billing");
    ex.bind_topic("orders.*", "search");
    // orders.created also bound directly to search to test de-duplication:
    ex.bind("orders.created", "search");

    let created = ex.route_topic("orders.created");
    let cancelled = ex.route_topic("orders.cancelled");
    let none = ex.route_topic("payments.settled");

    println!("orders.created -> {}", created.join(","));   // billing,search
    println!("orders.cancelled -> {}", cancelled.join(",")); // search
    println!("payments.settled -> {:?}", none);              // []
}

Exact bindings stay in the hash map; a separate wildcard set is matched segment by segment and unioned without duplicates.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Binding orders.* makes its queue resolve for both orders.created and orders.cancelled via route_topic.
  • The unchanged route method still resolves exact bindings such as orders.created to billing.
  • A key matching both an exact and a wildcard binding lists each queue once via the contains check.
  • A key matching no binding returns an empty Vec<String>.
Exercise 4implementation

Make the consumer ack only after the durable effect

Model the two steps as two distinct operations so their ordering is explicit in the code, not implicit in a single fused call. commit writes the durable effect, here a HashMap standing in for the database keyed by message id. ack appends the message id to an ack list, which stands in for telling the broker it may forget the message. handle calls commit first and ack second, and never the other way around. That ordering is the entire point: the durable effect must be safely recorded before the broker is told the work is done.

The duplicate guard sits at the top of handle. Before writing, it checks whether the message id is already in the durable store. If it is, the message has already been processed, so handle skips the write and only re-acks. This is what makes the handler idempotent under at-least-once delivery: applying the same message twice leaves the store in the same state as applying it once, and the second arrival costs only an ack, not a duplicate write. The guard is also what makes redelivery safe rather than dangerous.

The ordering matters because of what the broker does on a crash. Suppose the consumer commits the durable effect and then crashes before it can ack. The broker never received the ack, so it still holds the message as unacknowledged and redelivers it. On redelivery, the duplicate guard finds the id already in the store, skips the write, and acks. The committed-but-not-acked case becomes a harmless redelivery that the idempotency guard absorbs. The forbidden case is the reverse, acking before committing, which the code structurally prevents: no path in handle ever appends to the ack list for a message whose commit did not run.

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct Consumer {
    store: HashMap<String, String>, // durable effect (stands in for the DB)
    acks: Vec<String>,              // ack list (stands in for the broker)
}

impl Consumer {
    // Step 1: the durable write, on its own.
    fn commit(&mut self, id: &str, payload: &str) {
        self.store.insert(id.to_string(), payload.to_string());
    }

    // Step 2: the ack, on its own.
    fn ack(&mut self, id: &str) {
        self.acks.push(id.to_string());
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, id: &str, payload: &str) {
        // Duplicate guard: already committed -> ack again, never write twice.
        if self.store.contains_key(id) {
            self.ack(id);
            return;
        }
        // commit-then-ack: durable effect strictly before the ack.
        self.commit(id, payload);
        self.ack(id);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut c = Consumer::default();
    c.handle("m1", "order-A");
    c.handle("m1", "order-A"); // redelivery: acked again, no second write
    c.handle("m2", "order-B");

    println!("store entries = {}", c.store.len()); // 2
    println!("acks = {}", c.acks.len());           // 3
}

commit and ack are separate steps; handle always commits before acking and the duplicate guard re-acks without a second write.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • handle calls commit before ack on every write path, so the durable effect precedes the ack.
  • An id already in the store re-acks via the guard without a second commit.
  • Explains a commit-then-crash yields a redelivery the idempotency guard absorbs as a re-ack.
  • No path appends to acks for a message whose commit did not run.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix an ack-before-commit consumer

There are two defects. The first is ordering: the broken consumer acks the broker first and then performs the durable write. An ack is a promise that the work is safely done and that the broker may forget the message. By acking first, the consumer tells the broker to forget the message while the durable effect has not happened yet. If the process crashes in the window between the ack and the write, the broker has already discarded the message and will never redeliver it, so the work is silently lost with no error and no retry. That window is the data-loss bug. The fix is to commit the durable effect first and only then ack, so a crash before the ack leaves the message unacknowledged and the broker redelivers it.

The second defect is unbounded retry of malformed payloads. A malformed or unsupported payload fails the same way on every attempt, so requeuing it forever never makes progress and just blocks the queue behind a message that can never succeed. The fix has two parts. First, classify the failure: a transient failure, such as a temporary database error or a downstream timeout, deserves a bounded retry, while a malformed or unsupported payload is a terminal failure that should go straight to the dead-letter queue without wasting a single retry, because retrying a deterministic failure only delays the inevitable and holds up healthy traffic. Second, make retries counted and capped by an attempt number; once a message exceeds the cap, it too is routed to the DLQ rather than cycling endlessly.

The refactored handle below encodes both fixes. It parses and validates first and sends anything malformed straight to the DLQ. For valid payloads it commits the durable effect and then acks. If the commit fails transiently, it retries while the attempt count is under the cap and dead-letters the message once the cap is reached. The idempotency guard still sits in front, so a redelivery caused by commit-then-crash is absorbed as a re-ack rather than a duplicate write.

use std::collections::HashMap;

const MAX_ATTEMPTS: u8 = 3;

enum Outcome { Acked, Retried, DeadLettered }

#[derive(Default)]
struct Consumer {
    store: HashMap<String, String>,
    acks: Vec<String>,
    dlq: Vec<String>,
}

impl Consumer {
    // Returns Ok on a transient-success commit, Err on a transient failure.
    fn try_commit(&mut self, id: &str, payload: &str) -> Result<(), ()> {
        self.store.insert(id.to_string(), payload.to_string());
        Ok(())
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, id: &str, payload: &str, attempt: u8) -> Outcome {
        // Idempotency guard: already committed -> ack again, never write twice.
        if self.store.contains_key(id) {
            self.acks.push(id.to_string());
            return Outcome::Acked;
        }
        // Terminal failure: malformed/unsupported payloads never succeed,
        // so dead-letter immediately instead of retrying.
        if payload.is_empty() || !payload.starts_with("order-") {
            self.dlq.push(id.to_string());
            return Outcome::DeadLettered;
        }
        // Transient path: commit the durable effect FIRST, then ack.
        match self.try_commit(id, payload) {
            Ok(()) => {
                self.acks.push(id.to_string());
                Outcome::Acked
            }
            Err(()) => {
                if attempt + 1 < MAX_ATTEMPTS {
                    Outcome::Retried // requeue with attempt + 1
                } else {
                    self.dlq.push(id.to_string());
                    Outcome::DeadLettered
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut c = Consumer::default();
    let _ = c.handle("m1", "order-A", 0);  // committed then acked
    let _ = c.handle("m1", "order-A", 0);  // redelivery: re-acked, no rewrite
    let _ = c.handle("m2", "garbage", 0);  // terminal -> DLQ, no retry

    println!("store = {}", c.store.len()); // 1
    println!("acks = {}", c.acks.len());   // 2
    println!("dlq = {}", c.dlq.len());     // 1
}

Commit precedes ack; malformed payloads dead-letter immediately while transient failures retry under a bounded attempt cap.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names ack-before-commit as the cause of silently lost work on a mid-handler crash.
  • Refactor commits the durable effect before sending the ack.
  • Retries are counted and capped, and a message over the cap routes to the DLQ.
  • A malformed or unsupported payload goes straight to the DLQ since it fails identically every time.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design a versioned envelope for mixed deployments

The envelope wraps the payload with metadata that must travel with every message because the message can outlive the code that produced it. The minimum fields are: schema_version, an integer or semantic version identifying the payload contract; message_id, a stable globally unique identifier (a UUID assigned at publish time, never derived from arrival order); message_type, the routing-relevant name such as orders.created; created_at, a timestamp for measuring message age; and payload, the typed body. Optionally a producer field and a trace/correlation id help observability. The decisive point is that the version belongs in the envelope, not in tribal knowledge, so a consumer reading a message weeks later knows exactly which contract it is looking at without guessing.

A consumer reads schema_version before deserializing the payload. If the version is one it understands, it proceeds. If the version is newer or otherwise unrecognized, it must not crash and must not block the queue by requeuing the message indefinitely behind itself; instead it routes the message to a DLQ (or a dedicated parking queue) so the head of the live queue keeps moving, and the message is held for a newer consumer to drain later once that version is deployed. This keeps a single skewed message from stalling an entire partition during a rolling deploy.

The message_id is the idempotency key, which is what makes replay harmless. The consumer records each processed message_id in its durable store and, on seeing an id it has already committed, acks without reprocessing. Because the id is stable across redelivery and replay, a message replayed weeks later, or redelivered after a commit-then-crash, deduplicates to a no-op rather than producing a second side effect. Finally, to keep a pile-up from staying invisible, expose at least these queue-health signals: queue depth (how many messages are waiting), message age (how long the oldest unconsumed message has sat), retry rate (how often deliveries are being requeued), and dead-letter count (how many messages have been parked as terminal). A growing depth with rising age, a climbing retry rate, or a jumping DLQ count each say the system is backed up rather than merely quiet.

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Envelope {
    schema_version: u32,     // explicit contract version, in the envelope
    message_id: String,      // stable UUID -> idempotency key
    message_type: String,    // e.g. "orders.created"
    created_at: u64,         // for message-age health signal
    payload: String,         // typed body (serialized)
}

const SUPPORTED_VERSION: u32 = 2;

#[derive(Default)]
struct Consumer {
    processed: HashMap<String, ()>, // dedup by message_id
    parked: Vec<Envelope>,          // unrecognized versions / terminal
}

impl Consumer {
    fn handle(&mut self, env: Envelope) {
        // Idempotency: a replayed or redelivered id is a no-op re-ack.
        if self.processed.contains_key(&env.message_id) {
            return; // ack only, no second effect
        }
        // Version skew: hold for a newer consumer, do not block the queue.
        if env.schema_version > SUPPORTED_VERSION {
            self.parked.push(env);
            return;
        }
        // ... commit durable effect, then ack ...
        self.processed.insert(env.message_id.clone(), ());
    }
}

// Minimum health signals to expose:
//   queue depth, message age (now - created_at), retry rate, DLQ/parked count.

Envelope carries schema_version, stable message_id, and payload; the consumer dedups by id and parks unrecognized versions instead of blocking.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Envelope carries an explicit schema version, a stable unique message id, and the payload rather than a bare struct.
  • The message id is the idempotency key, so duplicates and replays deduplicate instead of reprocessing.
  • An unrecognized version is parked or dead-lettered for a newer consumer rather than crashing or blocking.
  • Lists queue depth, message age, retry rate, and dead-letter count as the minimum health signals.

Lab solution

The completed route method is the whole point of the lab: it makes the exchange the single owner of routing policy. It looks up the routing key in the bindings map. On a hit it clones and returns the bound queue names; on a miss it increments self.unrouted and returns an empty Vec. The clone is required because route takes &mut self (it must mutate the counter) yet returns owned Vec<String> to the caller, so it cannot hand out a borrow into the map.

In main, orders.created was bound to both billing and search, so route returns both names and the first line prints orders.created -> billing,search. orders.cancelled was bound only to billing, so the second line prints orders.cancelled -> billing. The two keys orders.refunded and orders.archived have no binding, so each takes the miss branch, incrementing unrouted to a final total of 2.

This is the chapter's direct-exchange model in miniature: the producer side names only routing keys, the exchange owns the binding table, and a key that matches nothing is counted as unrouted rather than silently vanishing, which is exactly what makes a routing gap observable instead of invisible.

Example 30-S. direct_exchange_routing_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct DirectExchange {
    bindings: HashMap<String, Vec<String>>,
    unrouted: usize,
}

impl DirectExchange {
    fn bind(&mut self, routing_key: &str, queue: &str) {
        self.bindings
            .entry(routing_key.to_string())
            .or_default()
            .push(queue.to_string());
    }

    fn route(&mut self, routing_key: &str) -> Vec<String> {
        match self.bindings.get(routing_key) {
            Some(queues) => queues.clone(),
            None => {
                self.unrouted += 1;
                Vec::new()
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut exchange = DirectExchange::default();
    exchange.bind("orders.created", "billing");
    exchange.bind("orders.created", "search");
    exchange.bind("orders.cancelled", "billing");

    let created = exchange.route("orders.created");
    let cancelled = exchange.route("orders.cancelled");
    let _ = exchange.route("orders.refunded");
    let _ = exchange.route("orders.archived");

    println!("orders.created -> {}", created.join(","));
    println!("orders.cancelled -> {}", cancelled.join(","));
    println!("unrouted total = {}", exchange.unrouted);
}
Output
orders.created -> billing,search
orders.cancelled -> billing
unrouted total = 2

Review question answers

In the publish path, which decisions belong to the producer and which belong to the exchange, and why does that split let teams change routing topology without editing publishers?

The producer decides only the routing key, a stable semantic label such as orders.created, and never names a queue. The exchange owns the binding table and the routing policy that maps keys to the set of queues that receive a copy. Because routing topology lives in one place, the exchange, a team can declare a new queue and bind it to an existing key to start receiving copies with no change to any publisher. Putting routing in the producer instead would force every new consumer to trigger an edit and redeploy of every publisher.

Why must a consumer commit its durable side effect before sending the ack, and what does the broker do with a message that stays unacknowledged?

An ack is a promise that the work is safely done and that the broker may forget the message, so committing first guarantees the durable effect exists before the broker is told to discard the message. If the consumer acked first and crashed before committing, the message would be gone with the work never done, a silent loss. While a message stays unacknowledged, the broker holds it and redelivers it (to the same or another consumer), so a commit-then-crash before the ack simply becomes a redelivery the idempotency guard absorbs.

Since AMQP delivery is at-least-once, what does it mean for a handler to be idempotent, and how does a recorded message id make replay harmless?

Idempotent means applying the same message twice leaves the system in the same state as applying it once, so a duplicate delivery causes no extra side effect. Because delivery is at-least-once, duplicates are the design center rather than a rare edge case, and idempotency is the only way to make them safe. Recording each completed message id in a durable store lets the handler detect a redelivered or replayed id and ack it again without redoing the work, so a message replayed weeks later deduplicates to a no-op.

When should a failed message be retried versus sent to a dead-letter queue, and what goes wrong if a poison message is requeued forever?

Retry transient failures, such as a temporary database error or a downstream timeout, under a bounded attempt count, because they may succeed on a later attempt. Send terminal failures, such as a malformed or unsupported payload, straight to the dead-letter queue, because they fail identically every time and a message that exceeds the retry cap goes there too. Requeuing a poison message forever never makes progress and blocks the queue behind a message that can never succeed, which the DLQ exists to prevent by moving it aside so healthy traffic keeps flowing.

What does backpressure protect against in a broker-based system, and which signals tell you a queue is piling up rather than merely quiet?

Backpressure protects against unbounded overload: a queue is a shock absorber, but without a limit it just hides the fact that producers are outpacing consumers until the system falls over. It has a broker layer (capping unacknowledged in-flight messages, for example with a prefetch limit) and a consumer layer (bounded local queues), and it lets the system say no gracefully instead of accumulating work invisibly. The signals that distinguish piling up from merely quiet are queue depth, message age, retry rate, and dead-letter count; a growing depth with rising age, a climbing retry rate, or a jumping DLQ count all indicate a backlog rather than an idle but healthy queue.

Chapter 31 · Distributed Task Execution

Distributed Task Execution

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move you from slogans to contracts. The chapter's central claim is that once work crosses a process boundary, the compiler stops protecting you, and the guarantees you actually have are the ones you build: at-least-once delivery, leases with visibility timeouts, classified retries, idempotent completion, and traceable recovery. Each exercise pins one of those guarantees down to a concrete shape in Rust worker and queue code, the same way Examples 1 and 2 in the chapter do.

The through-line is the separation between two layers that beginners conflate. The transport layer decides how many times your handler runs; the application layer decides what a duplicate run means for your durable side effects. Exercises 1 through 3 establish that separation and implement the minimal mechanics. Exercises 4 and 5 centralize the policies (retry, dead-lettering, tracing) that tend to get copy-pasted into every handler. Exercise 6 asks you to assemble the whole control plane for a realistic media pipeline, where a long-running GPU step makes leasing discipline non-negotiable.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Classify delivery semantics and idempotency obligations

The point of this exercise is to keep two questions apart that sound like one. Delivery semantics is a transport property: how many times the queue may hand the same logical task to a handler. Business side-effect semantics is an application property: what happens to durable state when the handler runs twice. A queue can promise at-least-once delivery, but only your code can decide whether a second run is harmless. Claiming "exactly-once" as a queue property by itself is the slogan the chapter warns against; honest exactly-once is something you construct from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent side effects.

Thumbnail regeneration is the workload that can tolerate occasional loss and may accept at-most-once behavior. A dropped regeneration just means a stale or missing thumbnail until the next trigger; nothing is corrupted, and the cost of a lost run is cosmetic. It is also naturally repeat-safe in the other direction, because regenerating writes one deterministic final image and overwrites whatever was there. If you had to pick the workload whose final state is a single deterministic overwrite, this is it.

Billing capture is the workload that must tolerate replay and therefore needs explicit idempotency even under at-least-once delivery. Capturing a payment twice double-charges a customer, so a second delivery of the same task must be suppressed. This is the workload that forces you to define a durable dedupe boundary: an idempotency key (for example the order or invoice ID) recorded in the same durable transaction that performs the charge, so the second attempt sees the key already present and becomes a no-op. The dedupe state has to be durable and co-located with the side effect, not held in a worker's memory.

A cache warmup is loss-tolerant like the thumbnail job (a missed warmup just means a cold cache and a slow first request) and is repeat-safe by overwrite, so it sits comfortably at at-most-once or unguarded at-least-once. A periodic analytics refresh is the more interesting middle case: if it recomputes one deterministic snapshot and overwrites it, replay is harmless; but if it appends or accumulates, a replay double-counts, and then it joins billing in needing an explicit checkpoint or run-ID boundary. The lesson is that you classify from business tolerance and the structure of the side effect, not from the transport label printed on the queue.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Delivery semantics (how many times the handler runs) is kept distinct from business side-effect semantics (what a rerun does to durable state).
  • Thumbnail/cache warmup are identified as naturally repeat-safe overwrites; billing capture is identified as needing explicit durable dedupe state.
  • Exactly-once is treated as constructed from at-least-once delivery plus idempotency, never asserted as a standalone queue guarantee.
Exercise 2code reading

Read a lease timeline like an incident reviewer

Read this timeline the way the chapter reads its lease lifecycle diagram: the duplicate execution is not a bug, it is the recovery mechanism working as designed. The event that makes duplicate execution normal is Worker A's lease expiry. When A claimed task-7 the queue hid it for the visibility-timeout window. A then went quiet past its deadline, so the queue concluded A was gone and made task-7 visible again, which let Worker B reclaim it legitimately. From the queue's point of view there is now exactly one valid owner (B), but A never learned it lost the lease, so A finishing later is an expected consequence of at-least-once delivery, not a surprise. Lease expiry is a recovery event, not a correctness defect by itself.

The correctness defect appears only if the completion path is not idempotent. Two successes are reported (A's late one and B's), and if completion simply applies the side effect each time, the work runs twice. So the fix is structural: completion state must live at the durable side-effect boundary, recorded atomically with the effect itself, keyed by the task's stable identity. In the chapter's example that is the completed set keyed by task ID, and finish_once returns whether this caller was the first to record it. The first reporter (whichever of A or B records first) wins and applies the effect; the second reporter sees the key already present and its completion becomes a harmless no-op. The dedupe record cannot live in a worker's local memory, because the two workers do not share memory; it has to live in the durable store next to the effect.

To reduce replay without slowing recovery, the lever is the visibility timeout relative to real handler time, plus heartbeats. A timeout that is too short relative to how long the handler actually takes will expire leases on healthy, still-working workers and cause needless reclaims; lengthening it globally just delays recovery when a worker truly dies. The better answer is heartbeat-based lease renewal: a worker that is still making progress periodically extends its lease, so a slow-but-alive worker keeps ownership while a dead worker's lease still expires quickly. That decouples "how long real work takes" from "how fast we recover from a crash."

The metric that tells you the lease duration is badly matched to handler time is the lease-expiry / redelivery rate, ideally read against the distribution of actual handler durations. A redelivery rate that climbs while almost no workers are actually crashing is the signature of a visibility timeout set below the p95 or p99 handler time: leases are expiring on workers that are simply slow, not dead. Task age (time from enqueue to terminal completion) is the companion signal, because excessive reclaims inflate it. Watch those two together and you can tune the timeout, or switch to heartbeats, with evidence instead of guesswork.

use std::collections::HashSet;

/// Durable completion record, keyed by the task's stable identity.
/// In production this lives next to the side effect (same DB transaction),
/// not in a single worker's memory, because the two workers share no memory.
struct Completions {
    done: HashSet<&'static str>,
}

impl Completions {
    /// Returns true only for the worker that records the task first.
    /// Worker A's late success and Worker B's success both call this;
    /// exactly one sees `true`, so the side effect is applied once.
    fn finish_once(&mut self, task_id: &'static str) -> bool {
        self.done.insert(task_id)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut completions = Completions { done: HashSet::new() };

    // Worker B reclaims after A's lease expired, then reports success first.
    let b_applied = completions.finish_once("task-7");
    // Worker A comes back from the dead and also reports success.
    let a_applied = completions.finish_once("task-7");

    println!("worker_b_applied = {b_applied}"); // true: first writer wins
    println!("worker_a_applied = {a_applied}"); // false: harmless duplicate
    println!("side_effects_applied = {}", completions.done.len()); // 1
}

Idempotent completion keyed by task ID: whichever worker records first wins, the other's success is a no-op.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The duplicate-execution path is explained concretely as the consequence of A's lease expiry and B's legitimate reclaim, with A unaware it lost the lease.
  • Completion/dedupe state is placed at the durable side-effect boundary, keyed by stable task identity, so only one success is applied.
  • Tuning and observability are addressed via visibility-timeout vs handler-time, heartbeat renewal, and the lease-expiry/redelivery rate plus task-age signals.
Exercise 3implementation

Build a lease-based worker with idempotent completion

The starter code has exactly two defects, and both are inversions of the intended condition. In requeue_if_timed_out, the guard reads if self.now < deadline, which requeues a task while its lease is still valid and drops it once the lease has expired, the precise opposite of what a visibility timeout means. A task should return to visibility only when the current time has reached or passed the deadline, so the condition must be if self.now >= deadline. With now = 6 and deadline = 5 the corrected guard fires and the task is redelivered.

In finish_once, the stub always returns false and never records anything, so completion is neither performed nor idempotent. The clean repair leans on the standard library: HashSet::insert returns true when the key was newly inserted and false when it was already present. Returning that value directly makes the method self-describing: the first completion of a given task ID returns true (this caller applied the effect), and every subsequent attempt returns false (a harmless duplicate). No extra flag, no second lookup, no branch. This is the "calmest duplicate signal" the hint points at.

Keeping all of this on one Queue struct, rather than scattering visible, completed, and now into globals, is what lets ownership do the bookkeeping. The methods take &mut self, so the borrow checker guarantees no two code paths mutate the queue's state concurrently through this owner, and the lifetime &'static str keys mean the completion set borrows nothing it could outlive. The struct is the durable boundary in miniature: redelivery state and completion state live together, the way they must when the real version is backed by a database row rather than a HashSet.

With both fixes the driver in main produces the lab's expected output: the task is claimed, time advances past the deadline, requeue_if_timed_out returns it to visibility, the redelivery is claimed again, the first finish_once records it, and the second returns false so !duplicate_apply prints true. completed.len() is 1 because the idempotent insert collapses the two completion attempts into one recorded effect.

use std::collections::{HashSet, VecDeque};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Task {
    id: &'static str,
}

struct Queue {
    visible: VecDeque<Task>,
    completed: HashSet<&'static str>,
    now: u64,
}

impl Queue {
    fn claim(&mut self) -> Option<Task> {
        self.visible.pop_front()
    }

    fn requeue_if_timed_out(&mut self, task: Task, deadline: u64) {
        // FIX 1: requeue only once the lease has actually expired.
        if self.now >= deadline {
            self.visible.push_back(task);
        }
    }

    fn finish_once(&mut self, task: &Task) -> bool {
        // FIX 2: `insert` returns true on first record, false on replay.
        // That return value IS the idempotency signal.
        self.completed.insert(task.id)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut queue = Queue {
        visible: VecDeque::new(),
        completed: HashSet::new(),
        now: 0,
    };

    queue.visible.push_back(Task { id: "task-1" });

    let first = queue.claim().unwrap();
    queue.now = 6;
    queue.requeue_if_timed_out(first.clone(), 5);

    let redelivery = queue.claim().unwrap();
    let _first_apply = queue.finish_once(&redelivery);
    let duplicate_apply = queue.finish_once(&redelivery);

    println!("redelivered = {}", redelivery.id);
    println!("completed = {}", queue.completed.len());
    println!("duplicate = {}", !duplicate_apply);
}

Two one-line repairs: invert the timeout guard, and return the HashSet insert result as the duplicate signal.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Timed-out work requeues correctly: the guard is now >= deadline, so the expired task returns to visibility.
  • Completion is idempotent: finish_once returns the HashSet::insert result, recording once and reporting later attempts as duplicates.
  • The lab prints redelivered = task-1, completed = 1, duplicate = true, matching the expected output.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Centralize distributed retries and poison-task policy

The defect is duplicated, divergent retry logic plus a missing terminal exit. Three handlers each carry their own retry loop with slightly different attempt limits, which means the system has three subtly different reliability behaviors and no single place to reason about or change them. Worse, every permanent validation error is requeued, so a malformed payload that can never succeed cycles forever, consuming a worker slot on each pass and inflating the redelivery rate. The chapter's state machine names the missing piece directly: there must be a one-way exit to DeadLetter, or the system will requeue a permanently broken task indefinitely.

The repair is to give retry one home: a shared RetryPolicy that owns four facts. First, max attempts, the visible attempt budget that bounds how many times any task may be re-tried. Second, the set of retryable failure classes, the classification that decides which failures even qualify for another attempt. Third, backoff, so retries are spaced (exponential with jitter) rather than hammering a struggling dependency. Fourth, terminal routing, the decision of where a failure goes when it is non-retryable or has exhausted its budget, namely the dead-letter queue. Centralizing these means all three handlers share one reliability behavior, and changing the policy is a one-line edit rather than three out-of-sync ones.

The failures that should be dead-lettered immediately are the permanent ones: validation errors, schema violations, deserialization failures, unknown-tenant or authorization rejections, anything where the same input will deterministically fail again. Retrying these wastes capacity and hides the real problem. Transient failures, such as a timeout against a throttled dependency, a connection reset, or a 503, are the only ones that earn a retry, and only until the attempt budget is spent; after that they too are dead-lettered so they stop circulating. This is exactly the chapter's discipline: classify before you retry, and separate transient retryable failure from permanent terminal failure.

The boundary between local in-process retry and queue-level requeue is the one teams blur most. Fast, in-handler retries (a couple of immediate attempts against a flaky local call, within one lease) are fine for sub-second transients and never touch the queue. But anything that needs real backoff, survives a worker crash, or counts against a durable attempt budget belongs at the queue level, because only the queue's redelivery and DLQ routing are durable across worker death. In-process bookkeeping ends where durability begins. Finally, the whole thing is testable without a broker: make the policy a pure function from a classified error and an attempt count to a RetryDecision (Retry { after }, DeadLetter, or Drop), and exercise it with a table-driven test plus assertions that terminal errors route to the DLQ. The transport stays mocked; the policy is just data in, decision out.

use std::time::Duration;

/// Classified failure kinds. Classification is the gate before any retry.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum FailureClass {
    /// Transient: worth another attempt after backoff.
    Transient,
    /// Permanent: same input will fail again; never retry.
    Permanent,
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum RetryDecision {
    Retry { after: Duration },
    DeadLetter,
}

/// One shared home for retry facts: budget, classification, backoff, routing.
struct RetryPolicy {
    max_attempts: u32,
    base_backoff: Duration,
}

impl RetryPolicy {
    /// Pure decision function: classified error + attempt count in,
    /// decision out. No broker required to test it.
    fn decide(&self, class: FailureClass, attempt: u32) -> RetryDecision {
        match class {
            // Permanent failures exit to the DLQ immediately.
            FailureClass::Permanent => RetryDecision::DeadLetter,
            // Transient failures retry until the visible budget is spent.
            FailureClass::Transient if attempt < self.max_attempts => {
                let after = self.base_backoff * 2u32.pow(attempt); // exp backoff
                RetryDecision::Retry { after }
            }
            FailureClass::Transient => RetryDecision::DeadLetter,
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn table_driven_classification() {
        let policy = RetryPolicy { max_attempts: 3, base_backoff: Duration::from_millis(100) };
        let cases = [
            (FailureClass::Permanent, 0, RetryDecision::DeadLetter),
            (FailureClass::Transient, 0, RetryDecision::Retry { after: Duration::from_millis(100) }),
            (FailureClass::Transient, 1, RetryDecision::Retry { after: Duration::from_millis(200) }),
            (FailureClass::Transient, 3, RetryDecision::DeadLetter), // budget exhausted
        ];
        for (class, attempt, expected) in cases {
            assert_eq!(policy.decide(class, attempt), expected);
        }
    }
}

One shared RetryPolicy as a pure decision function: permanent errors dead-letter immediately, transient ones retry within a budget.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Retry classification and the visible attempt budget are centralized in one RetryPolicy that owns max attempts, retryable classes, backoff, and terminal routing.
  • Transient retryable failures are separated from permanent terminal failures, with permanent ones dead-lettered immediately so poison tasks stop circulating.
  • A test strategy is named: a table-driven classification test plus DLQ-routing assertions against the pure decision function, with no live broker.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Trace a distributed task graph end to end

The defect is that the trace shows handler spans but is blind to everything between them, and across a queue "between them" is where most of the latency lives. The chapter's framing is the key: in one process a stack trace carries the causal chain for free, but across a queue there is no shared stack, so the causal chain has to be carried inside the message itself. A trace that only instruments the handler body silently assumes the in-process model and loses the queue wait, the fan-out lineage, and the fan-in join entirely. Each handler looks fast while the pipeline as a whole is slow, and nobody can attribute the slowness.

The fix begins with the task envelope. Every message must carry a stable set of IDs independent of its business payload: a trace_id shared by the whole graph, a span_id for this node, and a parent_span_id (or, for fan-in nodes, a set of parent IDs) recording lineage. It should also carry a stable task_id/message_id for idempotency and an enqueued_at timestamp. The trace_id ties the whole DAG together so you can query one pipeline run; the parent linkage is what reconstructs fetch -> parse -> { enrich, store } -> notify as a causal tree rather than a pile of unrelated spans.

Parent-child lineage has to be recorded at the structural nodes specifically. At a fan-out node (parse spawning both enrich and store), each child envelope inherits the parent's span as its parent_span_id, so the two branches are visibly siblings under parse. At a fan-in node (notify, which depends on enrich and store), the node records multiple parents, so the trace shows it as a true join and you can see which input arrived last. Without recording lineage at exactly these branch and join points, fan-out looks like duplication and fan-in looks like a node with a mysteriously late start.

Queue wait must be promoted to a first-class trace concept, not left implicit. Stamp enqueued_at when the task is published and claimed_at when a worker picks it up; the interval between them is a dedicated "queue wait" span (or at least a measured event) that sits before the handler span. That single addition is what turns a cheap-to-run, expensive-to-wait task from invisible into obvious, and it is the chapter's point that you separate queue wait from handler time before you optimize anything. Finally, the graph-specific signal that tells you the bottleneck is aggregation rather than worker execution is reducer lag, the time the fan-in node spends waiting for its slowest input after its other inputs are already done. High reducer lag with low per-handler time means the critical path runs through the join, not through any one worker; frontier size (how many nodes are ready but unscheduled) and end-to-end critical-path time round out the graph-level view that a flat per-handler profile cannot give you.

/// A production task envelope carries identity and lineage alongside payload.
/// These fields are what reconstruct the causal chain a stack trace would
/// give you for free inside one process.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Envelope {
    task_id: &'static str,        // stable identity for idempotency
    trace_id: &'static str,       // shared by the whole graph run
    span_id: &'static str,        // this node
    parent_span_ids: Vec<&'static str>, // 1 for linear, N for a fan-in join
    enqueued_at: u64,             // stamped at publish time
    payload: &'static str,
}

/// Queue wait recorded as a first-class span, distinct from handler work.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Timing {
    queue_wait: u64,   // claimed_at - enqueued_at
    handler_time: u64, // finished_at - claimed_at
}

fn measure(env: &Envelope, claimed_at: u64, finished_at: u64) -> Timing {
    Timing {
        queue_wait: claimed_at - env.enqueued_at,
        handler_time: finished_at - claimed_at,
    }
}

fn main() {
    // `notify` is a fan-in node: two parents (enrich, store) recorded as lineage.
    let notify = Envelope {
        task_id: "notify-1",
        trace_id: "trace-7",
        span_id: "span-notify",
        parent_span_ids: vec!["span-enrich", "span-store"],
        enqueued_at: 100,
        payload: "publish",
    };

    let t = measure(&notify, 140, 145);
    // Queue wait (40) dwarfs handler time (5): the cost is in waiting, and
    // a high wait on a fan-in node is the signature of reducer lag.
    println!("trace = {}", notify.trace_id);
    println!("parents = {:?}", notify.parent_span_ids);
    println!("queue_wait = {}", t.queue_wait);
    println!("handler_time = {}", t.handler_time);
}

Envelope carries trace_id and parent lineage; queue wait is measured as its own span, distinct from handler time.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The envelope carries a stable task/message ID plus trace lineage fields (trace_id, span_id, parent_span_ids), recorded at fan-out and fan-in nodes.
  • Queue wait is represented as a first-class trace/metric concept (enqueued_at to claimed_at), separate from handler time.
  • A graph-specific profiling signal is named: reducer lag at the join, with frontier size and critical-path time as companions, to locate aggregation bottlenecks.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose queue topology, aggregation, tracing, and profiling for a production task service

This is the full control plane for upload -> transcode variants -> scan -> persist metadata -> notify, and the design is driven by three asymmetries in the workload: uploads are bursty, transcode is a long-running GPU step, and operators demand replay and forensics. Each of those pushes a specific structural decision.

Queue topology: split by stage, and shard the expensive stage by resource. Give transcode its own queue (and its own worker pool bound to GPU hosts) separate from the CPU-bound scan, metadata, and notify stages. The reason is failure and resource isolation, the decoupling the chapter calls the whole point of a task queue: a GPU outage or a backlog of large transcodes must not block fast metadata writes or notifications, and bursty uploads should land in a buffer queue that absorbs the spike rather than overwhelming the GPU pool directly. Within transcode, fan out one queue message per variant (1080p, 720p, thumbnail) so variants run in parallel and a single failed variant retries independently instead of failing the whole transcode. That is the deliberate shard split: transcode-variants gets its own boundary because it is both the most expensive stage and the one with independent sub-units.

Leases for the long step: renew, do not lengthen. The GPU transcode is exactly the case the chapter calls out: a long-running specialist is a stronger argument for leasing discipline than for a longer global timeout. Lengthening the visibility timeout globally to cover the worst-case transcode would delay recovery for every other stage when a worker dies. Instead, transcode workers send heartbeats that renew the lease while the job is genuinely progressing (for example, advancing through encode frames), and the queue keeps a short base timeout so a crashed worker is still reclaimed quickly. A worker that stops heartbeating, crashed or hung, loses its lease and the variant is redelivered; a worker that is slow but alive keeps ownership. Pair this with idempotent persistence keyed by (upload_id, variant) so a reclaim-then-late-finish race writes each variant exactly once.

Aggregation and failure isolation: completion is a counting join, not a guess. The notify stage fires only when persist-metadata has recorded all required variants plus a clean scan result for one upload_id. Concretely, maintain a durable per-upload completion record (a set of finished variant keys); each variant's persist step idempotently inserts its key, and the coordinator checks "have all required variants plus scan landed?" after each insert. This is the chapter's ready-frontier idea applied to a join: the graph is complete when the fan-in node's dependency set is fully satisfied, recorded durably so the decision survives a coordinator restart. The failure-isolation rule: classify transcode failures, and route GPU-specific transient failures (OOM on a host, driver hiccup) to a dedicated retry lane with its own bounded concurrency and backoff, so a burst of slow GPU retries cannot consume the workers that healthy uploads need; permanent failures (corrupt input, unsupported codec) go straight to a DLQ for forensic inspection rather than recirculating.

Observability required before rollout: at least queue age per stage (time from enqueue to claim, which surfaces a starving GPU lane early), redelivery / lease-expiry rate per stage (a climbing transcode redelivery rate means the heartbeat or timeout is mistuned), reducer lag at the notify join (how long notify waits for its slowest input, distinguishing an aggregation bottleneck from slow workers), trace lineage carried in every envelope (trace_id plus parent spans so an incident reviewer can replay one upload's full DAG), and duplicate-suppression hits (how often idempotent completion absorbed a replay, which both proves the dedupe works and quantifies how much redelivery is actually happening). These are not nice-to-haves; the chapter's hardest-bug warning is that the failure is usually a silently wrong recovery model, and these are the signals that make the recovery model visible before the first incident rather than during it.

/// Sketch of the control-plane decisions, expressed as a config the
/// operator can review before rollout. Not a full system, just the shape.
struct StageConfig {
    name: &'static str,
    own_queue: bool,        // dedicated queue / shard boundary?
    sharded_by_unit: bool,  // fan out one message per sub-unit (variant)?
    base_visibility: u64,   // short base timeout in seconds
    heartbeat_renew: bool,  // renew lease on progress vs. lengthen globally?
    dlq: &'static str,      // terminal routing for permanent failures
}

fn pipeline() -> Vec<StageConfig> {
    vec![
        StageConfig { name: "upload",     own_queue: true,  sharded_by_unit: false, base_visibility: 30,  heartbeat_renew: false, dlq: "upload-dlq" },
        // Expensive GPU stage: own queue+pool, fan out per variant,
        // SHORT base timeout but renew-on-progress, isolated retry lane.
        StageConfig { name: "transcode",  own_queue: true,  sharded_by_unit: true,  base_visibility: 60,  heartbeat_renew: true,  dlq: "transcode-dlq" },
        StageConfig { name: "scan",       own_queue: true,  sharded_by_unit: false, base_visibility: 30,  heartbeat_renew: false, dlq: "scan-dlq" },
        StageConfig { name: "persist",    own_queue: true,  sharded_by_unit: false, base_visibility: 15,  heartbeat_renew: false, dlq: "persist-dlq" },
        StageConfig { name: "notify",     own_queue: true,  sharded_by_unit: false, base_visibility: 15,  heartbeat_renew: false, dlq: "notify-dlq" },
    ]
}

/// Required observability hooks, asserted present before rollout.
const REQUIRED_METRICS: &[&str] = &[
    "queue_age_per_stage",
    "redelivery_rate_per_stage",
    "reducer_lag_at_notify",
    "trace_lineage_coverage",
    "duplicate_suppression_hits",
];

fn main() {
    for stage in pipeline() {
        println!(
            "{:<10} queue={} sharded={} renew={} dlq={}",
            stage.name, stage.own_queue, stage.sharded_by_unit, stage.heartbeat_renew, stage.dlq
        );
    }
    println!("required metrics = {REQUIRED_METRICS:?}");
}

Per-stage control plane: transcode gets its own sharded queue with renew-on-progress leases; five observability hooks are required pre-rollout.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one deliberate queue/shard split is chosen: transcode gets its own queue and pool, fanned out per variant, isolated from CPU-bound stages.
  • A lease/renewal policy is defined for the long GPU step: short base timeout with heartbeat-based renew-on-progress rather than a longer global timeout.
  • One aggregation rule (durable per-upload completion set gating notify) and one failure-isolation rule (dedicated GPU retry lane plus DLQ for permanent failures) are described.
  • At least three observability hooks are named: queue age, redelivery rate, reducer lag, trace lineage, and duplicate-suppression hits.

Lab solution

The lab models a lease timeout followed by an idempotent completion, the same lifecycle as Example 1 reduced to its two essential mechanics. The driver pushes task-1, claims it (the first worker), then sets now = 6 to simulate the worker going quiet past a deadline of 5. The completed program fixes the two stubs in the starter: requeue_if_timed_out now guards on self.now >= deadline, so because 6 >= 5 the task returns to visibility, and finish_once now returns self.completed.insert(task.id) instead of a hardcoded false.

With the timeout guard corrected, the second claim succeeds and redelivery.id is task-1, printing redelivered = task-1. The first finish_once inserts task-1 into the completed set and returns true (recorded as _first_apply); the second finish_once on the same redelivery finds the key already present and returns false, so duplicate_apply is false and !duplicate_apply prints duplicate = true. Because the set insert is idempotent, the two completion attempts collapse to a single recorded effect, so completed.len() is 1 and the line prints completed = 1.

The design lesson is that the queue's recovery guarantee (lease expiry returns the task to visibility) and the application's correctness guarantee (idempotent completion) are separate and both required. Lease expiry alone would let the redelivered work run, but only the duplicate-safe finish_once keeps a second success from applying the effect twice. Both guarantees live on one Queue owner, so &mut self and the 'static keys let ownership enforce that the redelivery and completion state stay consistent.

Example 31-S. lease_idempotent_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::{HashSet, VecDeque};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Task {
    id: &'static str,
}

struct Queue {
    visible: VecDeque<Task>,
    completed: HashSet<&'static str>,
    now: u64,
}

impl Queue {
    fn claim(&mut self) -> Option<Task> {
        self.visible.pop_front()
    }

    fn requeue_if_timed_out(&mut self, task: Task, deadline: u64) {
        // Redelivery is correct only when the lease has actually expired:
        // the deadline is in the past relative to `now`.
        if self.now >= deadline {
            self.visible.push_back(task);
        }
    }

    fn finish_once(&mut self, task: &Task) -> bool {
        // `HashSet::insert` returns true when the key was newly added.
        // That return value is the idempotency signal: the first apply is
        // true, every replay is false, and no extra branching is needed.
        self.completed.insert(task.id)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut queue = Queue {
        visible: VecDeque::new(),
        completed: HashSet::new(),
        now: 0,
    };

    queue.visible.push_back(Task { id: "task-1" });

    let first = queue.claim().unwrap();
    queue.now = 6;
    queue.requeue_if_timed_out(first.clone(), 5);

    let redelivery = queue.claim().unwrap();
    let _first_apply = queue.finish_once(&redelivery);
    let duplicate_apply = queue.finish_once(&redelivery);

    println!("redelivered = {}", redelivery.id);
    println!("completed = {}", queue.completed.len());
    println!("duplicate = {}", !duplicate_apply);
}
Output
redelivered = task-1
completed = 1
duplicate = true

Review question answers

Why is at-least-once delivery the calm default assumption for distributed task systems?

Because durable queues cannot safely do otherwise: after a worker claims a task and then stops responding, the queue has no way to know whether the work finished, so the safe move is to redeliver. That choice guarantees the task is not silently lost, at the cost of occasionally delivering it more than once. At-most-once would risk dropping work whenever a worker dies mid-task, and true exactly-once delivery is not something transport can provide on its own; so at-least-once is the honest, durable default, and your code supplies idempotency to make replays harmless.

What is the practical difference between a lease expiry and a processing bug?

A lease expiry is a normal recovery event: the queue concluded a worker was unresponsive, so it reclaimed the task and made it visible again, which is exactly the mechanism that protects you from lost work when a machine dies. A processing bug is a defect in your handler or completion path. The two only intersect when the completion path is not idempotent: then the expected redelivery from a lease expiry causes a duplicate side effect, and what looks like a bug is really a missing idempotency guarantee, not a fault in the lease mechanism itself.

Why should retries and terminal failure paths be centralized instead of copied into each handler?

Copying retry loops into each handler produces several divergent reliability behaviors, with subtly different attempt limits, backoff, and failure classification that no one can reason about or change in one place. Centralizing them into one policy gives the system a single, testable home for max attempts, which failures are retryable, backoff, and terminal (dead-letter) routing. It also ensures permanent failures, such as validation errors, are dead-lettered immediately rather than requeued forever by an ad-hoc handler branch, and it lets you test the policy as a pure decision function without a live broker.

What makes queue wait time a first-class profiling signal?

Because a task can be cheap to run and expensive to wait for, and the in-process habit of profiling the handler body misses that entirely. In a distributed system, time spent sitting in the queue before a worker even starts is often the dominant latency, and it is invisible unless you measure it explicitly, for example by stamping enqueue and claim times and treating the interval as its own span. Separating queue wait from handler time is the first number to look at, because optimizing the hot function does nothing if the real cost is a starved or backlogged queue.

Why does a large task graph need explicit lineage and aggregation policy rather than one flat success counter?

A graph is a fan-out followed by a fan-in, and a single counter cannot express which nodes a join depends on or whether the right set has completed. You need explicit lineage (trace_id plus parent spans carried in each envelope) because there is no shared stack across queues to reconstruct the causal chain, and you need an aggregation policy that gates the join node on its full dependency set, recorded durably so the completion decision survives a restart. A flat counter could reach its target while the wrong tasks finished or a fan-in input was still missing, and it gives no way to locate a bottleneck at the reducer rather than at a worker.

Chapter 32 · MPI and High-Performance Computing

MPI and High-Performance Computing

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move from the highest-level decision in an MPI program down to the units a collective actually consumes. You start by choosing a partition and a collective shape from the algorithm, then learn to spot the layout mistake (Vec<Vec<T>>) that quietly makes every scatter and gather harder, then implement and test the balanced block-partition helper that every rank runs before it touches data. The later exercises shift from correctness to operations: converting row thinking into the cell counts and displacements a collective expects, building a measurement plan that separates compute from communication, and committing to a hybrid MPI-plus-threads deployment shape with an honest core budget.

The through-line is the chapter's central claim: an MPI program has two stacked boundaries with different rules. The outer boundary between ranks is full processes with separate address spaces, where nothing is shared and everything must be copied as a flat contiguous payload. The inner boundary inside a rank is ordinary Rust threading, where Arc<T> and Send/Sync still govern shared immutable state. Almost every hard MPI bug is one wrong boundary: the wrong layout, the wrong unit at a collective, one rank doing more work, or one node running too many local threads against too few cores.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose process partitioning and collective shape from the algorithm

Partition by rows first. The workload is described as a row-wise dense pass, which means each output row is computed from data that lives contiguously in a row-major buffer. A row partition makes each rank's share a single contiguous slice (start_row * cols .. end_row * cols), so the local kernel walks memory in the same order the algorithm reads it, and the eventual scatter or gather operates on one contiguous region per rank with no gather-list gymnastics. Column partitioning would force each rank to touch strided slices of every row, fighting the row-major layout and the cache. Tiling is a real option for two-dimensional stencils where a rank needs neighbors on all four sides, but it only pays for itself once the access pattern is genuinely 2D and halo exchange dominates; for a plain row-wise pass it adds boundary bookkeeping you do not need. The honest first move is the simplest layout that matches the access pattern, which here is balanced blocks of rows.

For the single global convergence scalar, the collective that fits depends entirely on who needs the answer. If only rank 0 needs the scalar (for example, to log it or decide termination centrally), MPI_Reduce is the honest fit: it combines one value per rank into a single result delivered to the root, and the non-root ranks contribute but do not receive. If every rank needs the scalar to drive its own next iteration, that is MPI_Allreduce: the same reduction, but the combined result is delivered to every rank. The third prompt is exactly this distinction made concrete. In an iterative solver where each rank decides locally whether to continue or to scale its next step using the global residual, allreduce is correct, because a reduce would leave every non-root rank without the number it needs, forcing an extra broadcast that allreduce already folds into one optimized collective. The right framing is not the API name but the data-flow shape: reduce is a funnel to one rank, allreduce is a funnel followed by a fan-out to all, and you pick based on the synchronization the next iteration actually requires.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Chooses row partitioning and justifies it from the row-major, row-wise access pattern rather than by preference.
  • Distinguishes reduce (result to root only) from allreduce (result to every rank) by who consumes the scalar.
  • Frames the choice in layout and synchronization terms: contiguous slices and funnel-versus-funnel-plus-fanout, not just API names.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the Vec<Vec<T>> mistake before the collective boundary

A Vec<Vec<f64>> for a dense matrix is the wrong default precisely at the collective boundary. The outer Vec holds rows pointers; each inner Vec is a separate heap allocation with its own length, capacity, and data pointer. So a dense R-by-C matrix becomes R+1 allocations instead of one, and reading element (r, c) is a double indirection: load the row pointer, then load the cell. The rows are not contiguous with one another, so the matrix has no single base pointer and no single length that describes the whole payload. That is the real problem, because an MPI send or a scatter is described by exactly those two things: a starting pointer and an element count over a contiguous region. With nested storage there is no contiguous region spanning multiple rows, so before you can scatter you must pack every row block into a temporary flat buffer, and after you gather you must unpack back into freshly allocated inner Vecs. The nested shape forces a copy on both sides of every collective, plus the per-row allocation churn, and it throws away cache locality during the local kernel as well.

One flat Vec<f64> of length rows * cols, indexed as matrix[row * cols + col], fixes all of this. The whole matrix is one allocation with one base pointer and one length, so a rank's row block start_row..end_row maps directly to the contiguous slice matrix[start_row * cols .. end_row * cols] that a scatter can hand out and a gather can write back with no packing step. You carry the shape separately as explicit row counts (and the cols multiplier), which is cheap and keeps the buffer itself a pure payload.
