This is the chapter's rule that flat buffers win in MPI: contiguous storage satisfies the caches, the local kernel, and the FFI boundary into the system MPI library all at once. The nested shape is still the honest choice when the data is genuinely ragged: rows of different lengths (a jagged adjacency list, variable-length records, a sparse structure where each row stores only its nonzeros). There, a flat buffer would need its own counts-and-offsets table to describe the ragged structure anyway, and per-row ownership accurately models data that really does have per-row lengths. The decision is dense versus ragged, not pretty syntax versus ugly syntax.

// Wrong default for a DENSE matrix: R+1 allocations, double indirection,
// no single contiguous region to scatter.
let nested: Vec<Vec<f64>> = vec![vec![0.0; cols]; rows];
// To scatter you must first pack rows into a temporary flat buffer,
// and after gather you must unpack again. Two copies per collective.

// Right default for a DENSE matrix: one allocation, one base pointer,
// one length. A rank's row block is already a contiguous slice.
let flat: Vec<f64> = vec![0.0; rows * cols];
let cell = |r: usize, c: usize| flat[r * cols + c];
let block = &flat[start_row * cols..end_row * cols]; // ready to scatter as-is

// Nested ownership stays honest only when rows are genuinely ragged:
let ragged: Vec<Vec<u32>> = vec![
    vec![1, 2],       // row 0 has 2 entries
    vec![3, 4, 5, 6], // row 1 has 4 entries
];

Dense data wants one flat buffer; nested Vec<Vec<T>> is only honest when rows are truly ragged.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains the dense cost precisely: R+1 allocations, double indirection, and no single contiguous region for a collective.
  • Recommends one flat Vec<f64> indexed as row * cols + col, tied to scatter/gather operating on a contiguous slice.
  • Names ragged data (jagged/sparse rows of differing lengths) as the case where nested per-row ownership is correct.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a balanced block partition for matrix rows

The helper must split rows as evenly as possible and hand any remainder rows to the lowest ranks, returning a half-open [start_row, end_row) range. The clean formula is the one from the chapter's first example. Let base = rows / ranks be the floor share every rank gets, and remainder = rows % ranks be the number of rows left over. Each of the first remainder ranks takes one extra row. A rank's length is therefore base + 1 if rank < remainder, else base, which Rust writes branch-free as base + usize::from(rank < remainder). The start offset must account for the extra rows already handed out to lower ranks: rank * base places the floor shares, and rank.min(remainder) adds exactly one for each earlier rank that received an extra row (capped at remainder, since once the remainder is exhausted no further extras exist). The end is start + len, kept exclusive so adjacent ranks meet without overlap and the union of all ranges is exactly 0..rows.

Using one formula for every rank, including rank 0, is the point of the exercise. Special-casing rank 0 and hoping the rest line up is how off-by-one gaps and overlaps appear: the invariant you want is that block_range(rows, ranks, r).end_row == block_range(rows, ranks, r + 1).start_row for every adjacent pair, which a single closed-form expression guarantees by construction. Verifying the rank-2 cell count for rows = 11, ranks = 4, cols = 5: base = 2, remainder = 3, so ranks 0, 1, 2 each get 3 rows and rank 3 gets 2, giving ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, 9..11. Rank 2 owns rows 6..9, which is 3 rows, and 3 * 5 = 15 cells. That is the value the lab prints.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Partition {
    start_row: usize,
    end_row: usize,
}

/// Balanced block distribution: every rank gets `rows / ranks` rows,
/// and the first `rows % ranks` ranks each absorb one extra row.
/// Ranges are half-open [start_row, end_row) and never overlap.
fn block_range(rows: usize, ranks: usize, rank: usize) -> Partition {
    let base = rows / ranks;
    let remainder = rows % ranks;
    let start = rank * base + rank.min(remainder);
    let len = base + usize::from(rank < remainder);

    Partition {
        start_row: start,
        end_row: start + len,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let (rows, ranks, cols) = (11usize, 4usize, 5usize);
    for rank in 0..ranks {
        let p = block_range(rows, ranks, rank);
        println!("rank {} = {}..{}", rank, p.start_row, p.end_row);
    }
    let p = block_range(rows, ranks, 2);
    println!("cells rank2 = {}", (p.end_row - p.start_row) * cols); // 15
}

One closed-form expression for all ranks; remainder rows go to the lowest ranks, ranges stay half-open and contiguous.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Remainder rows go to the lowest ranks via base + usize::from(rank < remainder), with start offset rank * base + rank.min(remainder).
  • Every range is half-open and adjacent ranges meet exactly, so the partition is non-overlapping and covers 0..rows.
  • Reproduces the lab output: ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, 9..11 and rank-2 cell count 3 * 5 = 15.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Choose flat counts and displacements for a collective

The defect is a unit mismatch at the collective boundary. The inherited code computes row counts correctly, but a scatter or gather over a row-major f64 buffer is described in elements (cells), not in rows. Passing row displacements where the collective expects element displacements means every rank after rank 0 reads or writes its slice cols-times too close to the buffer start, corrupting overlapping regions. The conversion from rows to cells must happen exactly once, at the point where you build the displacement and count tables the collective consumes, by multiplying the row quantities by cols. Keep two clearly named tables: the counts table stays in the unit the algorithm reasons in (rows) for the load-balancing logic, and a parallel send-counts/displacements pair is derived in cells right before the call. The chapter states the arithmetic as one rule: a cell's position is row * cols + col, so a row range maps to a cell range by multiplying both ends by cols.

Cumulative displacements follow from a single forward walk over the counts. The displacement of rank 0 is 0; the displacement of rank k is the sum of all earlier ranks' element counts, so you accumulate an offset as you go: out.push(offset); offset += rows_for_rank * cols. This is exactly displacements_in_cells from the chapter's second example. The invariant is that displacement[k] + send_count_in_cells[k] == displacement[k+1] for every k, and displacement[last] + send_count[last] == rows * cols, so the offsets tile the whole buffer with no gaps or overlaps. The test that catches this before a full cluster run is a tiny uneven matrix with hand-computed slices. Take rows = 5, cols = 2, ranks = 2: row_counts is [3, 2], so send counts in cells are [6, 4] and displacements in cells are [0, 6]. Assert those three vectors exactly, and assert that the reconstructed slices recover the original buffer. The unevenness is what makes the test sharp: a divisible shape can pass even with the rows-versus-cells bug masked, but an uneven shape with known offsets fails loudly the moment the units are wrong.

fn row_counts(rows: usize, ranks: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    let base = rows / ranks;
    let remainder = rows % ranks;
    (0..ranks).map(|r| base + usize::from(r < remainder)).collect()
}

/// Convert rows -> cells exactly once, where the collective is built.
fn send_counts_in_cells(counts: &[usize], cols: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    counts.iter().map(|&rows| rows * cols).collect()
}

/// Cumulative element offsets: one forward walk over the counts.
fn displacements_in_cells(counts: &[usize], cols: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(counts.len());
    let mut offset = 0usize;
    for &rows_for_rank in counts {
        out.push(offset);
        offset += rows_for_rank * cols;
    }
    out
}

#[test]
fn tiny_uneven_matrix_has_known_slices() {
    let (rows, cols, ranks) = (5usize, 2usize, 2usize);
    let counts = row_counts(rows, ranks);
    assert_eq!(counts, vec![3, 2]);
    assert_eq!(send_counts_in_cells(&counts, cols), vec![6, 4]);
    assert_eq!(displacements_in_cells(&counts, cols), vec![0, 6]);
}

Counts stay in rows for load logic; the rows-to-cells conversion happens once when building send counts and displacements.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Converts to the collective's unit (cells = rows * cols) exactly once, at the point the count/displacement tables are built.
  • States the cumulative rule: displacement[k] is the running sum of earlier ranks' cell counts via a single forward walk.
  • Proposes a focused test: a tiny uneven matrix (5x2 over 2 ranks) with hand-computed counts [6,4] and displacements [0,6].
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Profile communication-heavy HPC work conceptually before rewriting it

Resist the single-process instinct to profile the arithmetic kernel first. The kernel code path is unchanged and the mesh change is the only new variable, so the most likely cause is a shift in partition shape or communication pattern, not arithmetic intensity. The measurement plan separates time into three buckets per rank, every iteration: local compute time (the kernel between communication calls), halo-exchange time (the neighbor sends and receives), and collective time (the convergence allreduce or reduce). You place explicit timers around each region using a monotonic clock, accumulate per-region totals per rank, and crucially record them per rank rather than only on rank 0, because rank 0 is frequently not the bottleneck and any single-rank summary hides the slowest participant. The chapter's framing is the right question: who is waiting for whom, and where.

To distinguish load imbalance from too-frequent communication, look at two different signals. The rank-local signal is the spread of local compute time across ranks: compute the min, max, and the gap between the slowest and fastest rank's kernel time. A large spread means imbalance, which a mesh change easily causes by leaving one rank with more cells or more boundary work even though every rank runs identical code. The cross-rank signal is the time ranks spend blocked inside collectives: because a collective does not complete until the slowest rank arrives, time attributed to the allreduce is mostly wait time imposed by imbalance elsewhere, not the cost of the reduction itself. So a high collective-wait number with a wide compute spread points at imbalance; a high collective count with small per-call payloads and a narrow compute spread points at communication that is simply too frequent (for example, a barrier or allreduce inside a loop that could be hoisted or batched). Log per rank: local compute time, halo time, collective wait time, message counts and sizes, and the local cell or element count so imbalance is visible as a number rather than inferred. Only after that story is clear does kernel micro-optimization make sense; optimizing arithmetic while ranks are idle in an allreduce moves no real time.

use std::time::Instant;

#[derive(Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct RankTimers {
    compute: f64, // local kernel
    halo: f64,    // neighbor exchange
    collective: f64, // convergence reduce/allreduce (mostly wait time)
    local_cells: usize, // imbalance signal
}

fn iteration(t: &mut RankTimers, local_cells: usize) {
    t.local_cells = local_cells;

    let c = Instant::now();
    // ... local compute kernel ...
    t.compute += c.elapsed().as_secs_f64();

    let h = Instant::now();
    // ... halo_exchange() ...
    t.halo += h.elapsed().as_secs_f64();

    let r = Instant::now();
    // ... allreduce(residual) -- time here is mostly WAIT for the slowest rank
    t.collective += r.elapsed().as_secs_f64();
}

// Per rank, every rank logs its own line so rank 0 cannot hide the laggard:
//   rank=K compute=.. halo=.. collective=.. cells=..
// Imbalance  => wide spread in `compute` across ranks + high `collective` wait.
// Too-chatty => many small collectives, narrow `compute` spread.

Three per-rank timer buckets plus the local cell count make imbalance and chatty collectives distinguishable from kernel cost.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Separates compute, communication (halo), and collective wait time with explicit per-region timers.
  • Names a rank-local signal (spread of local compute time / local cell count) and a cross-rank signal (collective wait time).
  • Defers kernel micro-optimization until the communication and imbalance story is established.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose hybrid MPI plus threads and cluster deployment policy deliberately

I would deploy one rank per socket (or per NUMA domain) with a per-rank thread pool sized to the cores that rank owns, which is the chapter's dominant production layout, not one rank per core. The reasoning is economic and topological: crossing the network is the expensive boundary, so you want as few ranks as the topology allows while still keeping each rank's memory traffic inside one NUMA domain. CPU-heavy kernels parallelize well across cores within a socket using a Rayon or plain thread pool, and the single read-mostly lookup table per rank is loaded once per process and shared by all of that rank's threads, so more threads per rank amortizes both the table's memory footprint and the network cost. Pure one-rank-per-core would replicate the lookup table N times per socket and multiply the number of participants in every collective, inflating both memory and synchronization cost. A balanced mix only makes sense if a single socket spans multiple NUMA domains, in which case one rank per NUMA domain keeps each rank's allocations local.

Inside a rank, the boundaries map cleanly. The CPU-heavy kernel over the rank's row block is the intra-rank parallel work: a Rayon parallel iterator over the local rows, or a fixed thread pool, with no MPI calls inside the pool. The read-mostly lookup table is shared immutable state, so it lives behind an Arc<T> (Arc<LookupTable>) cloned into each worker; it is read concurrently, never mutated during compute, so Arc plus shared &T references satisfy Send and Sync without any lock. Arc and threads stay strictly inside the rank: Rust's thread rules govern that inner boundary, and an Arc never crosses a process boundary because it is a pointer into one address space that means nothing in another. MPI remains the only inter-rank boundary, carrying flat typed buffers: scatter the block in, allreduce the convergence scalar across ranks, and write the checkpoint. The load block -> local compute -> allreduce -> checkpoint pipeline therefore has exactly one shared-memory region (per rank) and one message-passing region (across ranks), and they never blur.

The core-budget tradeoff is the failure mode to police. A hybrid design is only good if ranks_per_node * threads_per_rank stays at or below the cores the scheduler granted per node; oversubscription makes threads contend for cores, and because a collective waits for the slowest rank, one oversubscribed node drags the entire job. Before rollout I would require at least these observability hooks: (1) CPU oversubscription per node (runnable threads versus allocated cores, e.g. load average against core count), (2) collective wait time per rank, which exposes imbalance hiding as communication cost, (3) per-rank throughput (cells per second) to surface a straggler rank, and (4) thread-pool queue depth inside each rank to detect intra-rank saturation. With those four, the tight cores-per-node policy is enforceable as numbers rather than as hope, and a misconfigured rank-by-thread fan-out shows up before it silently halves cluster throughput.

use std::sync::Arc;

struct LookupTable { /* read-mostly, loaded once per rank */ }

fn run_rank(
    rank: usize,
    size: usize,
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,
    table: Arc<LookupTable>, // shared immutable state, INTRA-rank only
) {
    // INTER-rank boundary: scatter the flat block in (MPI, flat typed buffer).
    let block: Vec<f64> = scatter_block(rank, size, rows, cols);

    // INTRA-rank boundary: thread pool over local rows; Arc clones are cheap
    // and the table is read concurrently with no lock (Send + Sync via &T).
    let local_residual: f64 = block
        .par_chunks(cols) // rayon: one row per task across this rank's cores
        .map(|row| kernel(row, &table))
        .sum();

    // INTER-rank boundary: every rank needs the global scalar => allreduce.
    let global_residual = allreduce_sum(local_residual);

    if rank == 0 {
        write_checkpoint(global_residual);
    }
    // Invariant: Arc/threads never cross the process boundary; MPI carries
    // only flat buffers. ranks_per_node * threads_per_rank <= cores_per_node.
}

One rank per socket; Arc-shared lookup table and a thread pool stay intra-rank; MPI carries only flat buffers across ranks.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Commits to one-rank-per-socket (or per-NUMA) hybrid with reasoning tied to network cost, NUMA locality, and CPU-heavy kernels.
  • Cleanly separates intra-rank shared immutable state (Arc<LookupTable>, thread pool) from the inter-rank MPI boundary carrying flat buffers.
  • Names at least three observability hooks: CPU oversubscription, collective wait time, per-rank throughput, and thread-pool queue depth.
  • Polices the core budget: ranks_per_node * threads_per_rank <= cores_per_node so one oversubscribed node cannot stall the collective.

Lab solution

The lab completes the starter by replacing the naive block_range (which used a single rows / ranks share and left the remainder stranded on a phantom range) with the balanced formula. With rows = 11 and ranks = 4, base = 11 / 4 = 2 and remainder = 11 % 4 = 3. Ranks 0, 1, and 2 are each below the remainder threshold, so they take base + 1 = 3 rows; rank 3 takes base = 2 rows. The start offset rank * base + rank.min(remainder) accounts for the extra rows already handed to lower ranks, producing the contiguous half-open ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, and 9..11.

Because every range is half-open and the start of each rank equals the end of the previous one, the four blocks tile 0..11 exactly with no overlap and no stranded rows, which is the property a real scatter relies on. The final line converts rank 2's row range into a cell count: rank 2 owns 3 rows, and at cols = 5 that is 3 * 5 = 15 cells, matching the chapter's rule that a row range maps to a cell range by multiplying by cols. The program uses only the standard library and prints the five expected lines.

Example 32-S. mpi_block_partition_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Partition {
    start_row: usize,
    end_row: usize,
}

// Balanced block distribution. Every rank gets `rows / ranks` rows; the
// first `rows % ranks` ranks each absorb one extra remainder row. The same
// closed-form expression serves every rank, so adjacent ranges meet exactly
// and the union is precisely 0..rows with no gaps or overlaps.
fn block_range(rows: usize, ranks: usize, rank: usize) -> Partition {
    let base = rows / ranks;
    let remainder = rows % ranks;
    // Earlier ranks that took an extra row push this start forward; capped at
    // `remainder` because once the remainder is spent there are no more extras.
    let start = rank * base + rank.min(remainder);
    // Branch-free "+1 if this rank is one of the first `remainder` ranks".
    let len = base + usize::from(rank < remainder);

    Partition {
        start_row: start,
        end_row: start + len, // half-open: end is exclusive
    }
}

fn main() {
    let rows = 11_usize;
    let ranks = 4_usize;
    let cols = 5_usize;

    for rank in 0..ranks {
        let part = block_range(rows, ranks, rank);
        println!("rank {} = {}..{}", rank, part.start_row, part.end_row);
    }

    // Rank 2 owns rows 6..9 (3 rows); 3 * 5 cols = 15 cells.
    let part = block_range(rows, ranks, 2);
    println!("cells rank2 = {}", (part.end_row - part.start_row) * cols);
}
Output
rank 0 = 0..3
rank 1 = 3..6
rank 2 = 6..9
rank 3 = 9..11
cells rank2 = 15

Review question answers

Why is MPI primarily a process model rather than a shared-memory model?

MPI runs each rank as a full operating-system process with its own private address space, typically spread across separate machines on a cluster, so there is no shared memory for ranks to read or write. Nothing is implicitly shared between ranks; every byte one rank needs from another must be copied explicitly as a message. This is the outer of the two boundaries in an MPI program, and it is exactly why partitioned data must be packed into flat contiguous buffers rather than shared through pointers. Shared-memory parallelism (threads, Arc, locks) still exists, but only inside a single rank, never across the rank boundary.

Why do flat contiguous buffers simplify collective operations so much?

A collective like scatter, gather, reduce, or allreduce describes its payload as a starting pointer plus an element count over a contiguous region, and the same is true of the caches and the FFI boundary into the system MPI library. A flat row-major Vec<f64> is one allocation with one base pointer and one length, so a rank's row block is already the contiguous slice the collective expects, with no packing or unpacking step. A nested Vec<Vec<f64>> has no single contiguous region spanning rows, so it forces a copy into a temporary flat buffer before every send and back again after every receive. Flat layout satisfies the kernel, the cache, and the collective simultaneously.

What is the practical difference between reduce and allreduce in an iterative solver?

Both combine one value per rank (a sum, max, and so on) into a single result, but they differ in who receives it. Reduce delivers the combined result only to the root rank, while allreduce delivers it to every rank. In an iterative solver where each rank needs the global convergence residual to decide whether to continue or how to scale its next step, allreduce is correct because every rank needs the number; using reduce would leave non-root ranks without it and force a separate broadcast that allreduce already folds into one optimized collective. Use reduce only when a single rank consumes the aggregate, for example to log it or make a central termination decision.

Why is a balanced partition helper worth testing as a first-class component?

Every rank runs the partition math before it touches any data, and its correctness underpins every subsequent scatter, gather, and slice index, so a single off-by-one there corrupts the whole run. The hard requirement is that ranges are half-open, non-overlapping, and cover 0..rows exactly even when the row count is not divisible by the rank count, which is precisely where ad hoc per-rank branching introduces gaps or overlaps. Because it is a small pure function of (rows, ranks, rank), it is cheap to unit-test with uneven shapes and known expected ranges. Testing it as a first-class component catches the most common distribution bug locally, before it manifests as silent data corruption on a full cluster.

What signals tell you an MPI program is communication-bound instead of compute-bound?

Time spent blocked inside collectives is the primary signal: a collective is a barrier that does not complete until the slowest rank arrives, so a profiler showing ranks idle in an allreduce usually indicates communication or imbalance cost, not arithmetic. A wide spread between the slowest and fastest rank's local compute time points to load imbalance (one rank doing more work), while a high count of small collectives with a narrow compute spread points to communication that is simply too frequent, such as a barrier or allreduce inside a hot loop. You separate these by placing per-region timers around compute, halo exchange, and collectives, recorded per rank rather than only on rank 0. If collective wait time and halo time dominate the kernel time, the program is communication-bound.

Why can hybrid MPI plus threads become slower if you ignore total core budgeting on the node?

In a hybrid layout each node runs ranks_per_node times threads_per_rank software threads; if that product exceeds the cores the scheduler allocated per node, the threads oversubscribe the cores and contend for CPU time instead of running in parallel. Because every collective waits for the slowest rank, a single oversubscribed node where threads are time-slicing drags the entire job's pace, not just its own. The speedup you expected from more threads is consumed by context-switching and scheduling overhead. Keeping ranks_per_node times threads_per_rank at or below cores_per_node, and monitoring CPU oversubscription per node, is what keeps the hybrid design honest.

Chapter 33 · Performance-Oriented Rust

Performance-Oriented Rust

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises turn performance work into a repeatable review process rather than a guessing game about inner loops. Each one rehearses a single discipline from the chapter: picking the measurement tool that matches the question, reading ownership choices for hidden heap traffic, designing fair comparisons, and choosing layouts and build settings deliberately. The throughline is that performance clarity and ownership clarity improve together, and that the most expensive mistake is descending to instruction-level work before the evidence points there.

Work through them in order. The warm-up and code-reading exercises build the vocabulary of the four costs worth tracking; the implementation and refactoring exercises make you commit to a measurable change; and the design scenario forces you to treat build mode, profile flags, and runtime observability as part of one decision instead of three separate afterthoughts. The lab at the end is the allocation-aware filter from the chapter, made concrete and runnable.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Separate benchmarking, profiling, tracing, and production observability

The four questions map to four distinct tools because each tool answers a different shape of question, and a confident answer from the wrong tool is how teams optimize code that was never on the critical path.

Comparing two parsing functions wants a benchmark. A benchmark runs the same logical workload under controlled input, in release mode, repeated enough times to be stable, so you can say version A is faster than version B for this input. The variable is the implementation; everything else is held fixed.

Explaining a latency regression inside one of those functions wants a profile. A profiler attributes time or allocations to lines and call frames, so it answers where inside this single execution the cost lives. The benchmark told you that one version is slower; the profile tells you which part of it is slower and why, for example that a per-item String allocation dominates.

Understanding where request time is spent across queueing and IO wants tracing. A trace shows the timeline and causality across boundaries: how long a request waited in the queue, how long it spent in the parser, how long it blocked on IO. A profile aggregated across many requests cannot show that a specific slow request spent its time waiting rather than computing, because the wait happens outside the function whose CPU time the profiler samples. That is the key distinction between profiling and tracing: profiling answers 'which code is expensive' by aggregating cost onto frames, while tracing answers 'where did this request's wall-clock time go' by following one request across thread and service boundaries, including time spent idle.

Confirming whether the regression matters in the live service wants production metrics and logs. A benchmark result is not a production diagnosis: a 30% improvement on a synthetic input means nothing if that code path is 2% of real traffic or if the real bottleneck is queue depth. Production signals such as p99 latency, error rate, and queue wait tell you whether the optimized build actually moved the number operators care about.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each question is mapped to a distinct tool with a workload reason: benchmark for controlled A/B comparison, profile for in-execution attribution, tracing for cross-boundary timeline, production metrics for live impact.
  • The answer states explicitly that a benchmark is not a complete production diagnosis because synthetic inputs and traffic share can make a real speedup irrelevant.
  • It explains that profiling aggregates cost onto code frames while tracing follows one request's wall-clock time across boundaries, including idle wait that a profiler does not see.
Exercise 2code reading

Find allocation pressure and hidden clones in a hot path

The described loop carries three separate costs, and naming them in the chapter's terms tells you exactly which repair each one needs.

First, the route strings are cloned into a temporary vector even though every downstream use only reads them. That clone is not semantically real; it papers over an API-shape problem. If the filter borrows from the input slice and returns Vec<&str> rather than building Vec<String>, the routes never touch the heap. This mirrors the chapter's borrowed-filter example: the return type is Vec<&str>, not Vec<String>, and the only allocation in the whole function is the result vector itself. The values that only needed borrowed access are exactly the route labels; the helper takes ownership only to read them, which is the signature of an accidental clone.

Second, the output buffer grows one record at a time. In a loop whose upper bound is the input length, that growth is avoidable: each reallocation copies the existing contents into a larger block, so an unbounded push pattern turns a bounded job into repeated allocator traffic. The repair is Vec::with_capacity(requests.len()) (or a tighter real bound if one is known), which sizes the result once and makes the capacity budget visible instead of relying on geometric growth.

Third, the per-item label formatting may be genuinely required output, in which case that allocation is semantically real and stays. The discipline is to separate the clone that exists only because of a poor signature from the allocation that produces a real result the caller consumes. Only the former should disappear.

After the refactor, confirm the change with workload evidence rather than intuition. Useful follow-up metrics are allocation count per request (the most direct measure of the change), bytes allocated per request, and p99 latency for the hot path under representative input. A drop in allocation count that does not move latency means the allocator was not on the critical path, which is itself a useful finding.

// Before: ownership taken only to read, plus unbounded growth.
fn hot_routes_slow(requests: &[(String, usize)], min_bytes: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    let owned: Vec<String> = requests.iter().map(|(r, _)| r.clone()).collect(); // clone #1
    let mut out = Vec::new(); // grows by reallocation
    for (i, (_, bytes)) in requests.iter().enumerate() {
        if *bytes >= min_bytes {
            out.push(owned[i].clone()); // clone #2, papers over the API shape
        }
    }
    out
}

// After: borrow-first, preallocated once from a real bound.
fn hot_routes<'a>(requests: &'a [(String, usize)], min_bytes: usize) -> Vec<&'a str> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(requests.len()); // one allocation, sized once
    for (route, bytes) in requests {
        if *bytes >= min_bytes {
            out.push(route.as_str()); // borrowed view, no heap copy
        }
    }
    out
}

The clones vanish once the signature returns borrowed views, and the single result allocation is sized from the input bound.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies the route clone as an unnecessary clone (ownership taken only to read) and the one-at-a-time push as an avoidable growth pattern in a bounded loop.
  • Proposes a borrowed read path (return Vec<&str>, borrow with as_str) and a preallocation repair (Vec::with_capacity from the input length).
  • Names concrete follow-up metrics: allocation count per request, bytes allocated per request, and p99 latency on the hot path.
Exercise 3implementation

Write a benchmark plan for an allocation-heavy function

A benchmark plan for the clone-heavy versus borrow-first log-enrichment function should make the input and the stop condition deliberately boring, so the only variable is the implementation.

Fix the input shape and size distribution up front. Use a single representative dataset, for example 10,000 log records with route strings drawn from a realistic length distribution (most short, a long tail of longer ones) and a fixed fraction that pass the enrichment predicate. Generate it once, outside the timed region, and feed byte-for-byte identical input to both implementations. If the input differs between variants, you are no longer comparing implementations.

State that the benchmark runs in release mode. Debug builds are for fast iteration and diagnostics, not trustworthy throughput numbers; a comparison built in debug mode can invert the real result. Either use a harness such as Criterion (which builds in release by default and handles warm-up and statistics) or run cargo build --release explicitly.

Define what you record. At minimum, wall-clock time per iteration for the A/B comparison. Because this function is allocation-heavy, also record allocations per iteration and bytes allocated, since the whole hypothesis is that the borrow-first version allocates less; latency alone could hide an allocation win that the allocator absorbed. Record the output count or a checksum of the result so you can confirm both variants did the same logical work.

Keep the compiler from optimizing the work away. If the result is unused, dead-code elimination can fake a win by deleting the function body. Consume the result with std::hint::black_box (or the harness's black_box) so the optimizer must compute it, and black_box the input where appropriate so it cannot constant-fold the whole call.

Finally, keep the plan honest about scope: this is a comparison step, not a diagnosis. The benchmark tells you which version is faster on this input; it does not tell you why, and it does not tell you whether the difference matters in production. The follow-up profiling step attributes the remaining cost to lines, and production metrics confirm relevance. Do not claim a speedup before the plan has actually run.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

fn bench<F: Fn(&[Record]) -> Vec<String>>(name: &str, input: &[Record], iters: u32, f: F) {
    // Warm-up so caches and the allocator reach steady state before timing.
    for _ in 0..16 {
        black_box(f(black_box(input)));
    }
    let start = Instant::now();
    let mut sink = 0usize;
    for _ in 0..iters {
        let out = f(black_box(input)); // black_box input: no constant folding
        sink ^= out.len();              // force the result to be computed
        black_box(out);                 // defeat dead-code elimination
    }
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    println!(
        "{name}: {:?}/iter over {} records (checksum {sink})",
        elapsed / iters,
        input.len()
    );
    // NOTE: also record allocations/bytes via a counting global allocator,
    // and run this binary built with --release (or under Criterion).
}

struct Record;

A minimal release-mode A/B harness; black_box on both input and output prevents the optimizer from faking a speedup.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Both variants run the same logical workload: one fixed dataset, identical byte-for-byte input, output count or checksum compared.
  • Names a release-build requirement (Criterion or cargo build --release) and measurement targets (wall-clock time plus allocations and bytes for an allocation-heavy function).
  • Distinguishes the later profiling step (attributes cost to lines) and production metrics (confirms relevance) from the benchmark step (A/B comparison only).
  • Refuses to claim a speedup before the plan runs, and uses black_box to stop dead-code elimination from faking one.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Refactor storage to improve locality

Replacing Vec<Vec<u64>> with one flat Vec<u64> plus rows and cols changes what the hardware sees while it walks the heatmap, which is the heart of the chapter's locality section.

The nested layout stores each row as a separate heap allocation, and the outer vector holds pointers to them. Walking every row therefore chases a pointer per row into an address the prefetcher cannot predict, and the rows may be scattered anywhere in the heap. A single flat Vec<u64> removes that indirection entirely: all rows-times-cols elements live in one contiguous block, so a full scan is a straight linear walk. The prefetcher can pull the next cache line before you ask for it, and you pay one allocation instead of rows-plus-one. This is not only about fewer allocations; it is about predictable traversal, which is what the access pattern (every row, every request) rewards.

The helper methods should expose rows as borrowed slices rather than reconstructing vectors. A row(i) accessor returns &self.data[i * cols .. (i + 1) * cols], and a rows() iterator yields self.data.chunks(cols). Both hand back &[u64] views into the flat buffer with no copying, exactly as the chapter's grid example carves rows out of one buffer with chunks(self.cols). Returning a freshly built Vec<u64> per row would reintroduce the allocation you just removed.

This also simplifies bounds-check reasoning in the inner loop. When you iterate a slice with a for or an iterator, the length is known to the compiler for the whole loop, so it can prove every access is in range and elide per-iteration bounds checks. Chunked iteration is even friendlier: chunks(cols) yields a slice whose length is a compile-visible constant relative to cols, giving the optimizer a clean proof story without ad hoc index arithmetic that it must re-verify on every access.

Measure before and after with a target tied to the hypothesis. Time the full row-scan over a realistically sized grid in release mode, and ideally collect cache-miss counts (for example via perf) since the claim is specifically about locality. Also record allocation count, which should drop from rows-plus-one to one. A latency improvement with a matching cache-miss reduction confirms the change worked for the stated reason.

struct Heatmap {
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<u64>, // one contiguous allocation, row-major
}

impl Heatmap {
    fn new(rows: usize, cols: usize) -> Self {
        Heatmap { rows, cols, data: vec![0; rows * cols] }
    }

    // Borrowed view into the flat buffer; no per-row allocation.
    fn row(&self, r: usize) -> &[u64] {
        &self.data[r * self.cols..(r + 1) * self.cols]
    }

    // Chunked iteration: length is known per chunk, so bounds checks elide
    // and the scan stays contiguous.
    fn row_sums(&self) -> Vec<u64> {
        self.data
            .chunks(self.cols)
            .map(|row| row.iter().copied().sum())
            .collect()
    }
}

One flat buffer plus chunked row views: contiguous traversal, one allocation, and a clean bounds-check proof for the inner loop.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Replaces nested ownership with a single flat Vec<u64> owner plus rows and cols for the dense case.
  • Explicitly ties the change to cache locality: one contiguous block lets the prefetcher work, where scattered per-row allocations defeat it.
  • Explains that slice and chunk views give the compiler a known length, so inner-loop bounds checks elide without ad hoc indexing.
  • Names before-and-after measurements: release-mode scan latency, cache-miss counts, and allocation count dropping from rows-plus-one to one.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Compare iterator and loop implementations responsibly

The folklore that iterator chains are slow and index loops are fast is, more often than not, backwards, and the chapter's point is that the style difference is a measurement question, not a religion. A responsible comparison isolates style as the only variable.

Keep the logical work identical. Both versions must consume the same slice, apply the same predicate and transform, and produce the same output value or side effect. The cleanest way to guarantee this is to have both functions return the same type and assert equal results on the benchmark input before timing anything. If the iterator version collects into a fresh Vec while the loop version writes into a caller-provided buffer, you are comparing allocation strategies, not iteration styles.

Watch for the unfair traps. The most common is exactly that hidden allocation: a .collect() in one variant and an in-place mutation in the other. Another is a changed branch structure, for example a filter that short-circuits differently, or an explicit index loop that introduces a data-dependent bounds check the iterator version avoids. Any difference in allocation, branch shape, or the work done per element makes the benchmark measure the wrong thing.

Before drawing conclusions from the benchmark number alone, inspect deeper. Look at the generated assembly (cargo asm or the compiler explorer) to confirm whether one variant vectorized or kept a bounds check the other dropped, or profile to see where the time actually went. The chapter's whole reason index loops can be slower is the data-dependent bounds check the optimizer cannot always remove; the generated code tells you whether that happened here.

Report the result as workload-specific. Say 'on this slice length and element type, in release mode, the iterator version was N% faster because it elided the bounds check the index loop kept,' not 'iterators are faster.' The same comparison on a different element type, length, or branch density can land the other way.

// Both consume the same slice and produce the same Vec<u64>.
// The ONLY difference is iteration style; verify equal output before timing.
fn sum_even_iter(xs: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    xs.iter().copied().filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).sum()
}

fn sum_even_loop(xs: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    let mut acc = 0;
    for &x in xs {        // iterate the slice directly: length known, no data-dependent index
        if x % 2 == 0 {
            acc += x;
        }
    }
    acc
}

// Fairness gate run before benchmarking:
// assert_eq!(sum_even_iter(input), sum_even_loop(input));
// Note the loop uses `for &x in xs`, not `for i in 0..xs.len() { xs[i] }`,
// so neither variant carries an extra bounds check the other lacks.

Same input, same output type, same branch shape; the for-over-slice form avoids the data-dependent index that would make the comparison unfair.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Both variants do identical logical work and identical output, verified with an equality assertion before timing.
  • Names at least one unfair trap: a hidden allocation (collect vs in-place) or a differing branch and bounds-check structure between variants.
  • Includes a follow-up inspection step beyond the benchmark: generated-code review or profiling to see whether a bounds check or vectorization differed.
  • Reports the outcome as workload-specific (this length, type, and build) rather than as a universal iterator-vs-loop rule.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose release settings and performance review policy for a service

The design point is that build mode, profile settings, and runtime observability are one decision, not three afterthoughts. Here is a concrete policy for this latency-sensitive binary with a hot parser, a CPU-heavy enrichment step, and an explicit-crash requirement.

Every performance run uses cargo build --release (or cargo bench, which builds in release). Debug builds are for iteration and diagnostics; their numbers are untrustworthy for throughput or latency, and the first repair for 'Rust is slow' is usually just --release. No measurement that informs a decision is taken from a debug binary.

Profile settings are workload tradeoffs, each justified, not collected as trophies. opt-level = 3 is the default for release and is the right baseline for a CPU-heavy enrichment step. lto = "thin" is worth enabling because it lets the optimizer inline and specialize across crate boundaries, which helps a hot parser split across modules; the tradeoff is longer link time and larger debug-info handling. codegen-units = 1 can squeeze out more cross-function optimization at the cost of slower compiles, reasonable for a release binary you build infrequently and run constantly. Each of these is a 'spend compile time to buy run time' decision; turn one on, measure, keep it only if it moves the hot-path number.

panic = "abort" is a binary contract choice, not a free speed flag. It removes landing pads and unwinding machinery, which trims binary size and can marginally help hot paths, but it changes program behavior: a panic terminates the process immediately instead of unwinding. It is acceptable, and even desirable, here precisely because the operator requires crash behavior to remain explicit: aborting on panic makes failure loud and unambiguous and avoids partially-unwound state. It would be the wrong contract for a library, or for a server that must catch_unwind at a request boundary to isolate one bad request from the rest of the process, because abort takes the whole process down.

Before trusting the optimized build in production, require live signals, since a clean benchmark is not a production diagnosis. At minimum: p99 (and p99.9) latency for the hot parser path, queue depth or wait time (a regression hid here in the chapter's opening scenario), allocation pressure or bytes-allocated per request, and error rate. A good performance review states what changed in both build behavior (flags, mode) and runtime behavior (these four signals), so a win in a benchmark is only accepted once production metrics confirm it.

# Cargo.toml — release profile for a latency-sensitive service binary.
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3        # default; right baseline for the CPU-heavy enrichment step
lto = "thin"         # cross-crate inlining for the hot parser; costs link time
codegen-units = 1    # more cross-function optimization; costs compile time
panic = "abort"      # explicit, loud crash contract per the operator requirement

# Every measurement run:
#   cargo build --release   (never benchmark a debug build)
# Required production signals before trusting the build:
#   p99/p99.9 latency, queue depth, bytes-allocated/request, error rate

A release profile whose every flag is a justified compile-time-for-run-time tradeoff, paired with the four live signals that gate acceptance.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names release mode explicitly (cargo build --release / cargo bench) as the only basis for measurement.
  • Justifies at least two profile settings with tradeoffs: lto = thin (cross-crate inlining vs link time) and codegen-units = 1 (more optimization vs compile time).
  • Frames panic = abort as a binary contract choice: acceptable here for an explicit loud crash, wrong for a library or a server needing catch_unwind at a request boundary.
  • Requires at least two production observability signals: p99 latency, queue depth, allocation pressure, and error rate.

Lab solution

The lab completes the starter by making two allocation-aware repairs to hot_routes. First, the result is built with Vec::with_capacity(requests.len()) instead of Vec::new(), so the vector is sized once from a real upper bound and never reallocates while the loop pushes. That makes the result budget visible at the call site instead of relying on repeated geometric growth. Second, the function returns Vec<&str> rather than Vec<String>: each pushed route is a borrowed &str view carved out of the input slice, so no route string is copied to the heap. The lifetime parameter 'a ties those views to the input, which is what lets the borrow check pass: the returned vector cannot outlive the requests it borrows from.

The predicate is request.bytes >= min_bytes with min_bytes = 512. Two requests qualify: /search at 900 bytes and /checkout at exactly 512 bytes (the starter's strict > would have wrongly excluded /checkout, yielding hot = 1). So hot.len() is 2, which prints hot = 2. The first qualifying route in input order is /search, so hot.first().copied().unwrap_or("none") prints first = /search.

The capacity line confirms the preallocation worked: because the vector was created with capacity equal to requests.len() (4) and capacity never shrinks on push, hot.capacity() is at least requests.len(), so hot.capacity() >= requests.len() is true and prints capacity ok = true.

Example 33-S. hot_routes_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Request<'a> {
    route: &'a str,
    bytes: usize,
}

// Borrow-first, preallocated hot-route filter.
// - The result is sized once from a real bound (`requests.len()`), so the
//   Vec never reallocates while pushing on the hot path.
// - Routes are returned as `&str` views borrowed out of the input slice; no
//   route string is ever cloned or copied onto the heap. The returned views
//   are tied by lifetime `'a` to the input, so they live exactly as long as
//   the slice they came from.
fn hot_routes<'a>(requests: &'a [Request<'a>], min_bytes: usize) -> Vec<&'a str> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(requests.len());

    for request in requests {
        if request.bytes >= min_bytes {
            out.push(request.route);
        }
    }

    out
}

fn main() {
    let requests = [
        Request {
            route: "/health",
            bytes: 128,
        },
        Request {
            route: "/search",
            bytes: 900,
        },
        Request {
            route: "/checkout",
            bytes: 512,
        },
        Request {
            route: "/metrics",
            bytes: 64,
        },
    ];

    let hot = hot_routes(&requests, 512);

    println!("hot = {}", hot.len());
    println!("first = {}", hot.first().copied().unwrap_or("none"));
    println!("capacity ok = {}", hot.capacity() >= requests.len());
}
Output
hot = 2
first = /search
capacity ok = true

Review question answers

Why is performance work usually clearer after ownership boundaries become honest?

When the borrow-versus-owned boundary is explicit instead of accidental, the places where data is actually copied become visible, and most allocation pressure comes from clones that exist only because a signature took ownership to read. An honest boundary tends to allocate less and read cleaner at the same time, so the cleanest API shape and the fastest one usually coincide. This is why the chapter says ownership clarity and performance clarity improve together: once you know where each value is owned, you can see which costs are real results and which are accidental heap traffic.

What is the practical difference between reducing allocations and reducing branch misses?

Reducing allocations attacks heap traffic: fewer calls to the allocator, fewer reallocations, and less cumulative cost from per-request Strings, clones, and growing vectors that put the allocator on the hot path. Reducing branch misses attacks control-flow cost: making the predictor's job easier so the CPU does not stall flushing a mispredicted pipeline, often by sorting or partitioning data so branches become predictable. They are different costs measured with different signals (bytes and allocation count versus cache-miss and branch-miss counters), and a fix for one does not address the other; you choose based on which cost the profile shows is actually on the critical path.

Why are slice-based and chunk-based loops often easier to optimize than index-heavy loops?

When you iterate a slice directly with a for loop or an iterator, the length is known to the compiler for the whole loop, so it can prove every access is in range and elide the per-iteration bounds check; chunk-based loops go further because each chunk's length is fixed relative to a known stride. A hand-written loop that indexes with a data-dependent index forces the compiler to insert a bounds check it usually cannot prove away, which is the real reason such loops can be slower than the equivalent iterator chain. Cleaner bounds reasoning also gives the optimizer a better proof story for vectorization, so the slice form frequently produces tighter code.

When is a clone economically justified even in performance-sensitive code?

A clone is justified when it produces a semantically real result the caller needs to own, or when it buys a structural simplification whose value exceeds its measured cost on a path that is not actually hot. If the clone is cheap relative to the work around it and removing it would force lifetime contortions or shared-ownership machinery that complicate the code without moving a production number, paying for the copy is the better engineering trade. The discipline is to distinguish that real, owned result from a clone that merely papers over a poor signature, and to confirm with measurement that the path even matters before bending the design to avoid it.

What does release mode change, and what questions does it still not answer by itself?

Release mode turns on optimizations (inlining, bounds-check elision, vectorization, and the profile's opt-level and LTO settings), which is why it is the only trustworthy basis for throughput or latency numbers and why --release is often the first repair for code that seems slow. But it only changes how fast a given workload runs; it does not tell you which code is on the critical path (that needs a profile), where a request's wall-clock time went across queueing and IO (that needs tracing), or whether a measured speedup matters under real traffic (that needs production metrics). A fast release build of the wrong code path is still wasted work.

Chapter 34 · Memory Profiling

Memory Profiling

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take memory profiling out of the realm of tool worship and put it on a fixed triage order: name the symptom precisely, measure allocation and retention together, correlate the memory curve with the workload curve, and only then commit to a diagnosis. The work moves from the cheapest possible instrument (a local clone or allocation counter) up through heap snapshots, reference-cycle inspection, and async backlog analysis, mirroring the chapter's claim that the most expensive optimization is the one made before the symptom is understood.

The through-line is that Rust's memory behavior is a consequence of ownership decisions you already control. A rising resident set can be allocation churn, retained heap, allocator fragmentation, a reference cycle, or an unbounded queue, and these have different fixes. The exercises train you to distinguish those cases with the smallest measurement that rules out the most wrong theories, then repair the design (borrow instead of clone, weaken a back-edge, bound a queue) rather than reaching for an allocator trick first.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Match the symptom to the measurement

Each symptom points at a different first measurement because each describes a different mechanism keeping bytes resident. The skill is to choose the measurement that fastest rules out the wrong theories, not to default to a full heap profiler.

Rising RSS after a burst that does not fall back down points first toward fragmentation or allocator retention. Before assuming a leak, measure the disagreement between live bytes (what your program logically holds, from a heap profiler or a global counter) and process RSS. If live bytes return to baseline while RSS stays high, the allocator is holding freed pages to satisfy the next request quickly. That is allocator behavior, not a leak; the right follow-up is allocator stats or an explicit trim, not a hunt for a missing drop.

Stable RSS but a rising task count points toward async backlog rather than a leak. Memory is flat, so nothing is being retained abnormally; the growing number is in-flight work. Measure task count and queue depth. This is an admission-control problem: producers outrun consumers, and the runtime accumulates tasks. The fix is a bound (semaphore or bounded channel), not allocator inspection.

Flat heap snapshots with a high allocation rate point toward churn rather than retained memory. Two successive snapshots show roughly the same live set, yet the allocator is busy. Measure allocation count and cloned bytes per request. Live data is not growing, so this is throughput cost from short-lived allocations (often deep clones), addressed by borrowing or reuse, not by leak hunting.

A graph of Rc nodes that never disappears points toward logical reachability and cycle inspection. Safe Rust never reads freed memory, but it does not promise that unneeded memory is freed. Inspect strong counts: if a subgraph's strong count never reaches zero after local work ends, a cycle still has owners. The repair is to make one back-edge non-owning (Weak) or to drop shared ownership entirely in favor of arena handles.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • A distinct first measurement is chosen per symptom: RSS-vs-live for retention, task/queue count for backlog, allocation count for churn, strong-count inspection for cycles.
  • Retained memory (cycles, fragmentation) is separated from allocation churn (flat snapshots, high rate) explicitly.
  • Each diagnosis is gated on evidence; none is called a leak before a measurement distinguishes it from churn, backlog, or allocator retention.
Exercise 2code reading

Find clone pressure in a sample workload

Read the path with one question in mind: which operations create a second owner of the same allocation, and which copy underlying bytes into fresh heap. In safe Rust the word clone covers both, and only the second one drives memory growth.

When the route filter clones owned strings into an output list with route.to_string() (the shape in the chapter's clone-pressure counter, where each surviving route does out.push(route.to_string())), that is a deep clone: it allocates a new buffer and copies the bytes. The later formatting step, building another owned label per selected item with format!(...), is a second deep clone for the same reason. By contrast, an Arc::clone or Rc::clone on a shared handle creates another owner of one allocation and copies no bytes; that is cheap and is not the source of growth. So the two .to_string()/format! sites are the deep clones; any Arc::clone in the path is not.

The helper that only needed borrowed access is the route filter itself. Choosing which routes survive requires reading the strings (route.starts_with("/api/")), not owning them. It can take &[&str] and return Vec<&str>, borrowing for the lifetime of the input slice. The deep clone is forced only if a downstream stage must outlive the input. If the queued work genuinely outlives the request buffer, that is where ownership should become explicit: clone once at that boundary with a comment naming why, rather than cloning eagerly inside the filter where the data is still borrowable.

Before reaching for a whole-process heap profiler, add a local counter on the hot path: count clone events and sum cloned bytes (using the borrowed source length before conversion). That single comparative number tells you whether a refactor doubled the duplicated bytes per request, which is usually enough to pick the next target without a full trace.

// Before: deep clones forced eagerly inside the filter, plus a per-item format.
fn select_and_label(routes: &[&str]) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for &route in routes {
        if route.starts_with("/api/") {
            out.push(route.to_string());            // deep clone #1: new buffer
        }
    }
    out.iter()
        .map(|r| format!("route={r}"))             // deep clone #2: new buffer per item
        .collect()
}

// After: borrow while choosing; clone (if at all) only at the boundary that outlives input.
fn select_api<'a>(routes: &[&'a str]) -> Vec<&'a str> {
    routes
        .iter()
        .copied()
        .filter(|r| r.starts_with("/api/"))        // borrowed access only
        .collect()
}

// Label lazily; the caller owns nothing extra unless it must outlive `routes`.
fn label<'a>(route: &'a str) -> std::fmt::Arguments<'a> {
    format_args!("route={route}")
}

The filter needs only borrowed access; defer ownership to the boundary that truly outlives the input.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one deep-clone site is identified correctly: route.to_string() and the per-item format! both allocate fresh buffers.
  • A borrowed-API repair is proposed: select_api returns Vec<&str> tied to the input lifetime instead of Vec<String>.
  • A local measurement is named: clone count and cloned-byte total computed from borrowed source lengths before conversion.
Exercise 3implementation

Instrument clone pressure on purpose

The goal is a narrow, comparative instrument that proves where deep-copy work happens, before committing to a heavier heap profiler. It follows the chapter's clone-pressure counter directly: filter, then clone, then count, with two separate numbers.

Keep clone events and cloned bytes as distinct counters. The count answers how many owned values this path produced; the byte total answers how heavy each one was. They describe different problems and can move independently: a refactor can hold the count flat while doubling the bytes, or fan out many tiny clones. Capture the byte size from the borrowed source length before conversion, so you are measuring the cost the path chose at the moment of choosing it.

Keep the instrumentation local to the hot path. A small &mut CloneStats threaded through one function is enough; do not promote it to a global allocator hook or a framework abstraction. The value is comparative, not absolute: you read it across a refactor or incident window to see what changed. The exact number on any single run matters far less than the delta between the suspect build and the baseline.

This is not a complete memory profile and is not meant to be one. It does not see allocations elsewhere, retention, or fragmentation; it answers exactly one question (how much deep-copy work did this path do) so it can point the next, heavier pass at the right subsystem. Delete it once the incident is resolved and the regression is confirmed fixed, because permanent micro-instrumentation accretes into noise; if the path is genuinely worth watching forever, graduate it to a real metric behind a feature flag rather than leaving the ad hoc counter in place.

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct CloneStats {
    clones: usize,
    cloned_bytes: usize,
}

fn select_api_routes(routes: &[&str], stats: &mut CloneStats) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(routes.len());

    for &route in routes {
        if route.starts_with("/api/") {
            // Measure the cost at the moment the path chooses to pay it.
            stats.clones += 1;
            stats.cloned_bytes += route.len(); // borrowed length, before conversion
            out.push(route.to_string());
        }
    }

    out
}

fn main() {
    let routes = ["/api/orders", "/health", "/api/users"];
    let mut stats = CloneStats::default();
    let selected = select_api_routes(&routes, &mut stats);

    println!("selected = {}", selected.len()); // outputs chosen, not clones
    println!("clones = {}", stats.clones);
    println!("cloned bytes = {}", stats.cloned_bytes);
}

Two separate counters, threaded locally; read the delta across a refactor, then delete.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Clone events and cloned bytes are counted explicitly as two separate fields on CloneStats.
  • The instrument stays local: a &mut CloneStats threaded through one hot-path function, not a global abstraction.
  • It is framed as comparative: a delta across a refactor window that guides the next profiling pass, not a whole-process trace.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Diagnose an Rc cycle leak

State the leak precisely in terms of strong ownership count, because the bug is not that Rust leaked; it is that the graph still has owners. Each Rc holds a strong count, and a value's destructor runs only when that count reaches zero. When the parent stores children as Rc<Node> and each child stores its parent as Rc<Node>, the two edges keep each other's strong count permanently above zero. After local work ends and the external handle drops, root's strong count does not fall to zero (the leaf still owns it), so neither node is freed. That is the logical leak: the memory is fully reachable by design and therefore never collected.

The key distinction is which edge owns lifetime and which edge only wants to look something up. The child-to-parent (back) edge is observational: a child needs to find its parent, but it should not keep its parent alive. The parent-to-child (forward) edge is owning: the tree's lifetime should follow the parent, and children should live as long as the parent holds them. So the forward edge stays Rc<Node> and the back-edge becomes Weak<Node>, exactly as in the chapter's rc-cycle example, where GoodNode stores parent: RefCell<Weak<GoodNode>> while keeping children as Rc.

With Weak, the back-edge no longer contributes to the strong count. To inspect the repair, print Rc::strong_count(&root) before and after dropping the external handle. In the strong-cycle build the count stays at two and the subgraph can never drop; in the Weak build it falls to zero when the last strong owner goes away, and the destructors run. Reading the parent goes through upgrade(), which returns None once the parent is gone, making the dangling case explicit instead of silently retained.

When shared ownership is not semantically real, the calmer design is arena handles: store nodes in a Vec or arena and represent edges as plain indices (NodeId). No reference counting, no cycle risk, no Weak upgrades; lifetime is the arena's, and a parent index is just data. That trades pointer-chasing convenience for an explicit ownership model and is usually the right call for tree- and graph-shaped data where no node truly owns another's lifetime.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

// Owning forward edge (Rc), observational back-edge (Weak): no cycle.
struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    parent: RefCell<Weak<Node>>,        // back-edge does NOT keep parent alive
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>,   // forward edge owns the children
}

fn main() {
    let root = Rc::new(Node {
        name: "root",
        parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()),
        children: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
    });
    let leaf = Rc::new(Node {
        name: "leaf",
        parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()),
        children: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
    });

    root.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(&leaf));
    *leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&root); // Weak, not Rc::clone

    println!("root strong before = {}", Rc::strong_count(&root)); // 1, not 2
    println!(
        "leaf sees parent = {}",
        leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade().map(|p| p.name).unwrap_or("none")
    );
    // Dropping `root` here lets the subgraph collect, because the back-edge is Weak.
}

// Alternative when shared ownership is not real: arena handles.
// struct Arena { nodes: Vec<ArenaNode> }
// struct ArenaNode { name: &'static str, parent: Option<usize>, children: Vec<usize> }

Weak on the back-edge keeps the strong count at 1; the subgraph collects when the last owner drops.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The leak is explained as strong-count retention: mutual Rc edges hold each other's count above zero, so destructors never run.
  • The parent back-edge is replaced with Weak<Node>, matching the chapter's GoodNode shape, while the forward edge stays Rc.
  • An alternative is named: arena handles (NodeId indices) when no node semantically owns another's lifetime.
  • strong_count before/after is named as the signal to inspect across the repair.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Profile async memory usage before calling it a leak

Async memory growth usually traces to a boundedness failure, not a leak, so collect all three signals first: queue depth, task count, and payload size, tracked together. A genuine leak moves one of them in isolation; an admission problem moves several at once, and that pattern is what tells them apart. The chapter's sketch groups the four fields into one struct precisely so you read them as a set.

This pipeline has two boundedness failures. The unbounded channel lets the queue absorb the gap whenever the consumer falls behind, and every queued message keeps its payload alive; queue depth and resident bytes rise together. The spawn-per-input-item has no cap, so task count climbs with input rate, and each in-flight task pins its large owned payload across the awaits it holds. Both keep memory alive while every object remains perfectly reachable by design.

The boundary that wants a cap is the producer-to-consumer channel: replace the unbounded channel with a bounded one so the producer experiences backpressure and stalls instead of buffering without limit. The spawn boundary wants a concurrency cap: gate it with a semaphore so only N tasks run concurrently, which bounds both the task count and the number of simultaneously pinned payloads. The reason is the same in both places: an unbounded admission point converts a throughput mismatch into unbounded memory.

The payload-shape repair is to shrink or borrow the data before it crosses the spawn boundary. A large owned payload that survives several awaits is held for the whole task lifetime; extract only the fields the task needs, or pass an Arc of the shared part so many tasks reference one allocation instead of each owning a copy. After bounding the channel, capping concurrency, and shrinking the payload, watch queue depth, task count, and resident bytes: if they plateau, it was admission, not a leak. You would still suspect a true leak if, with all three caps in place and the input drained, live bytes do not return to baseline; at that point inspect retention (reference cycles, a non-evicting cache, an arena that never resets) rather than backlog.

use std::sync::Arc;
use tokio::sync::{mpsc, Semaphore};

struct Payload {
    // large owned data; shared via Arc so spawned tasks don't each own a copy
    body: Vec<u8>,
}

async fn run(inputs: Vec<Arc<Payload>>) {
    // Bounded channel: producer feels backpressure instead of buffering without limit.
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Arc<Payload>>(64);
    // Concurrency cap: bounds in-flight task count and simultaneously pinned payloads.
    let limit = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(16));

    let producer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for item in inputs {
            // .send().await stalls when the queue is full -> backpressure.
            if tx.send(item).await.is_err() {
                break;
            }
        }
    });

    while let Some(item) = rx.recv().await {
        let permit = Arc::clone(&limit).acquire_owned().await.unwrap();
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            let _permit = permit;          // released on drop, freeing a concurrency slot
            let len = item.body.len();     // borrow what the task needs
            // ... work that crosses awaits, holding only `item` (Arc) ...
            let _ = len;
        }); // payload Arc drops here -> refcount falls -> memory reclaimed when last owner drops
    }

    producer.await.unwrap();
}

Bound the channel, cap concurrency with a semaphore, and share the payload via Arc; then watch the three signals plateau.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one boundedness failure is identified: the unbounded channel and the uncapped spawn-per-item.
  • A concrete cap is proposed with a reason: bounded mpsc for backpressure and a Semaphore to bound concurrent tasks/payloads.
  • A payload-shape repair (Arc-share or extract needed fields before the spawn boundary) plus a confirming metric (queue depth, task count, and resident bytes plateauing) are named.
  • A condition for still suspecting a true leak is given: live bytes not returning to baseline after all caps are in place and input drained.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Prepare a memory profiling checklist for a real service

The checklist's job is to force the team to rule out wrong theories quickly, in a fixed order, so it pairs allocator/heap signals with workload signals and ends in a concrete stop condition rather than a vibe. It mirrors the chapter's triage order: name the symptom, measure allocation and retention together, correlate with the workload curve, then diagnose.

First page of the investigation (collect together, not one at a time): process RSS; live bytes from a heap profiler or global counter; allocation count and rate; queue depth and queue age; task count; clone count and cloned bytes per request; cache size and hit rate. The point of putting them on one page is the correlation: RSS rising with live bytes flat means fragmentation or allocator retention; RSS flat with task count rising means backlog; live bytes rising with queue depth means an unbounded queue; high allocation rate with flat live bytes means churn. No single number diagnoses; the pattern across them does.

Named retention candidates to rule out explicitly: Rc or Arc cycles (inspect strong counts on the graph types; convert back-edges to Weak); unbounded queues or task floods (the async channel and spawn boundaries; add bounded channels and a semaphore); non-evicting caches (the read-mostly cache that only inserts; add a size or TTL bound); oversized or never-reset arenas (the parser's arena; confirm it resets per request and is sized to peak, not cumulative). Each candidate has a measurement that confirms or clears it before any code changes.

OS tools by platform, clustered by job (growth by callsite, resident-versus-logical disagreement, timeline correlation): on Linux, heaptrack or valgrind/massif for callsite growth, /proc/<pid>/status (VmRSS) plus jemalloc/tikv-jemalloc stats for resident-versus-logical, and perf or a metrics pipeline for the timeline. On macOS, Instruments (Allocations/Leaks) for callsites and the timeline, and vmmap/footprint for resident-versus-logical. On Windows, the VMMap and Heap tools (Sysinternals) or WPA/Windows Performance Recorder for callsites and timeline, and Task Manager/Performance Monitor working-set counters for resident. Pick the callsite tool for who allocated, the resident tool for fragmentation, and the timeline tool to align the memory curve with the workload curve.

Success condition (one concrete stop, not 'looks better'): after the fix and a repeat of the original burst, RSS returns to within an agreed margin of pre-burst baseline once the burst ends and the queue drains, and cloned bytes per request (or live bytes at steady state) are at or below the pre-regression number. Define it numerically before starting so a masked symptom (for example, RSS that merely grows slower) does not get mistaken for a resolved one.

// Memory profiling checklist (a service: parse -> arena -> queue -> async fan-out -> cache)
//
// 1. First-page numbers (collect TOGETHER; read the correlation, not any single line):
//      [ ] RSS (process resident set)
//      [ ] live bytes (heap profiler / global allocator counter)
//      [ ] allocation count + rate
//      [ ] queue depth + queue age
//      [ ] task count
//      [ ] clone count + cloned bytes / request
//      [ ] cache entries + hit rate
//
// 2. Retention candidates to rule out explicitly (each with its confirming measurement):
//      [ ] Rc/Arc cycles      -> inspect strong_count; Weak the back-edges
//      [ ] unbounded queue    -> bound the channel; add backpressure
//      [ ] task flood         -> Semaphore-cap concurrency
//      [ ] non-evicting cache -> add size/TTL bound; check it actually evicts
//      [ ] oversized arena    -> confirm per-request reset; size to peak, not cumulative
//
// 3. Platform tools (callsite growth | resident-vs-logical | timeline):
//      Linux:   heaptrack/massif | /proc/<pid>/status + jemalloc stats | perf/metrics
//      macOS:   Instruments       | vmmap/footprint                    | Instruments timeline
//      Windows: VMMap/WPR         | Task Mgr / PerfMon working set      | WPA timeline
//
// 4. STOP condition (define numerically BEFORE starting):
//      After repeating the original burst and draining the queue,
//      RSS returns to within X% of pre-burst baseline AND
//      cloned-bytes/request (or steady-state live bytes) <= pre-regression value.

A one-page checklist: correlated first-page numbers, named retention candidates, per-OS tools, and a numeric stop condition.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Allocator/heap signals (RSS, live bytes, allocation count) are paired with workload signals (queue depth, queue age, task count, clone count).
  • At least three retention sources are named explicitly: Rc/Arc cycles, unbounded queues, non-evicting caches, oversized arenas.
  • At least one tool per platform is chosen: Linux (heaptrack/massif, /proc, jemalloc), macOS (Instruments, vmmap), Windows (VMMap/WPR, PerfMon).
  • One concrete numeric success condition is defined: RSS back to within a margin of baseline after the burst drains, plus cloned/live bytes at or below the pre-regression value.

Lab solution

The starter code returned Vec<String>, cloning every selected route through track_clone, which incremented the atomic counter once per output element. Two routes start with "/api/", so the original path reported two clones for two selected items: the clone count tracked the selected count exactly because every survivor was deep-copied.

The fix is an API-shape change, not an allocator trick. Choosing which routes survive requires only borrowed access (route.starts_with("/api/")), so hot_routes can take &[&'a str] and return Vec<&'a str>, where the lifetime 'a ties the output references to the input slice. Each surviving &str is pushed by value as a borrow of the existing string literal; no new heap buffer is allocated and track_clone is never called. The borrow checker proves this is sound: selected may not outlive routes, which is exactly the constraint that makes avoiding the clone safe.

At runtime, two routes match so selected.len() is 2, and because nothing in hot_routes calls track_clone, the CLONES counter stays at the value set by CLONES.store(0, ...), printing 0. The program therefore prints "selected = 2" then "clones = 0", matching the expected output. The deep clone returns only if a later stage must outlive the input buffer, in which case you would clone once at that boundary with a comment, rather than eagerly inside the filter.

Example 34-S. clone_pressure_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};

static CLONES: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

// Kept only to show the contrast: the original path called this for every
// selected route, so `clones` counted one deep copy per output element.
#[allow(dead_code)]
fn track_clone(value: &str) -> String {
    CLONES.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    value.to_string()
}
