// The filter only needs to *read* the routes to decide which survive, so it
// borrows. Returning Vec<&str> tied to the input lifetime removes every deep
// clone: no fresh buffers are allocated, and `track_clone` is never called.
fn hot_routes<'a>(routes: &[&'a str]) -> Vec<&'a str> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(routes.len());

    for &route in routes {
        if route.starts_with("/api/") {
            out.push(route); // borrow the existing &str; no allocation, no clone
        }
    }

    out
}

fn main() {
    let routes = ["/api/orders", "/health", "/api/users"];
    CLONES.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);

    let selected = hot_routes(&routes);

    println!("selected = {}", selected.len());
    println!("clones = {}", CLONES.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
Output
selected = 2
clones = 0

Review question answers

Why is a local clone counter often a good first memory-profiling tool?

It is the cheapest instrument that distinguishes the most common cause of allocation churn in safe Rust, deep clones, from cheap reference-count clones, and it does so without a whole-process trace. Threaded as a small &mut counter through one hot path, it adds almost nothing and answers a single narrow question: how much deep-copy work did this path choose. Its value is comparative; reading the clone count and cloned-byte delta across a refactor or incident window proves whether one change doubled the duplicated bytes per request, which usually points at the next target directly. That lets you avoid rewriting the wrong subsystem before a heavier heap profiler is even warranted.

What is the practical difference between allocation churn and retained live data?

Allocation churn is how often and how many bytes the program asks the allocator for; retained live data is how much of what was allocated is still reachable and alive right now. Churn shows up as a high allocation rate with flat heap snapshots: the live set is roughly constant between snapshots even though the allocator is busy, which is a throughput cost usually fixed by borrowing or reuse. Retention shows up as live bytes that grow and do not return to baseline, which is a leak-shaped problem fixed by removing an owner (a cycle, an unbounded queue, a non-evicting cache). They are two separate numbers describing two different problems, and treating churn as a leak sends you hunting for a missing drop that does not exist.

Why can RSS stay high after the logical working set falls?

Because RSS measures the pages the operating system has given the process, not the bytes the program logically holds, and when you free memory the allocator does not necessarily return those pages to the OS. Allocators typically retain freed pages to satisfy the next request quickly, so the resident set can stay high while live bytes have already dropped back to baseline. This gap between logical and resident memory is fragmentation or allocator retention, not a leak; the way to confirm it is to compare live bytes against RSS, and if live bytes returned but RSS did not, the allocator is holding the difference. The remedy is allocator-level (tuning or an explicit trim), not a search for unreachable objects.

Why are unbounded queues and task floods often memory bugs even when no object is unreachable?

Because memory stays alive as long as something reachable owns it, and a growing backlog owns every item in it by design. When producers outrun consumers across an unbounded channel, the queue absorbs the difference and each queued message keeps its payload alive; when a service spawns a task per input without a cap, each in-flight task pins its payload across the awaits it holds. Nothing is unreachable, so a leak detector finds nothing, yet resident memory climbs with queue depth and task count. The fix is admission control, a bounded channel for backpressure and a semaphore to cap concurrency, not allocator inspection, and the tell is that several workload signals rise together rather than one in isolation.

What does Weak<T> repair that a strong Rc<T> or Arc<T> back-edge cannot?

Weak<T> lets an edge observe a value without owning its lifetime, which is exactly what a back-edge in a parent/child or graph structure needs. A strong Rc or Arc back-edge contributes to the strong count, so a parent and child that both hold strong references to each other keep each other's count permanently above zero; their destructors never run and the subgraph is logically leaked even though no unsafe code is involved. Replacing the back-edge with Weak removes its contribution to the strong count, so the value collects when its last strong owner drops, and reads go through upgrade(), which returns None once the target is gone. The forward, owning edge stays Rc/Arc; only the observational edge becomes Weak.

Chapter 35 · Performance Profiling

Performance Profiling

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises rehearse the one discipline the chapter is built around: before rewriting any function, split a slow request's wall time into the layers it actually spends time in, point at the widest layer, and only then confirm with a sampler or trace. Every problem here is a small, runnable version of that move. The data structures are deliberately tiny so the reduction stays visible, but the logic is the same one a flame graph performs for you visually.

You will start by matching profiling questions to the instrument that answers each with the least distortion, then implement the per-stage and per-layer reductions, isolate fixed per-crossing overhead at a WASM/FFI boundary, separate the two halves of lock cost, and finally write the decompose-first plan that settles a cross-team p99 dispute. The connecting thread is that a profiler narrows a judgment; it never removes one. Choosing the wrong build, the wrong workload, or the wrong metric still sends a senior team at the wrong fix.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Match the question to the instrument

The chapter's core rule is that the toolkit fans out from one decision: what kind of answer do you need? Walk the decision diagram from the question, not from the tool you happen to have open. Each of the three questions points at a different instrument, and reaching for the wrong one distorts the answer rather than failing loudly.

"Is version B actually faster than version A under a fixed workload?" is a comparison question, so the instrument is a benchmark, and Criterion is the ecosystem default. It runs the measured closure many times, discards warmup, and reports a distribution with confidence intervals rather than a single number, so it can tell you which alternative won and by how much without you eyeballing a stopwatch. A CPU sampler is the wrong first tool here because a sampler explains where compute concentrates inside one binary; it does not compare two implementations and will not tell you whether the difference between A and B is real or noise.

"Where is compute time concentrating in this running binary?" is a localization question, so the instrument is a sampling CPU profiler. It interrupts the running binary many times per second, records the call stack, and aggregates those samples into a statistical picture of where compute time concentrates, perturbing the program very little. A benchmark is the wrong tool here because it compares, it does not explain: it can tell you A is slower than B but not which stack inside A owns the time.

A CPU sampler is the wrong first instrument for an async task that takes 200ms of wall time but almost no CPU because a sampler only sees code that runs often enough to be caught between samples. The 200ms was spent enqueued, waiting on a semaphore permit, or parked on the blocking thread pool, and none of that is executing instructions the sampler can catch, so the profile comes back nearly empty and points at nothing. The right signal for a wall-time gap is tracing spans around each transition, which record where the task actually waits or blocks rather than where it burns cores.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names Criterion for the version-versus-version benchmark and a sampling CPU profiler for locating the hot compute path.
  • Explains that a sampler only captures code that runs often enough to be hit between samples, so it misses time spent enqueued, awaiting a permit, or parked.
  • States that an async wall-time gap is diagnosed with tracing spans around each transition, not with CPU samples.
  • Justifies each instrument by the question being asked rather than by whichever tool is already open.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the hottest-stage reduction

The function is hottest_stage(samples: &[StageSample]) -> (&'static str, u64, u64), and it performs two reductions over the same slice. The sample data is parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40.

The line let total: u64 = samples.iter().map(|sample| sample.micros).sum() borrows each StageSample, projects out its micros field, and folds the stream with addition. On the sample data this is 180 + 620 + 40 = 840 microseconds, the wall time spent across all stages.

The expression samples.iter().max_by_key(|sample| sample.micros) scans the slice and returns the StageSample with the largest micros value, wrapped in Some because the iterator yields elements. For this input that is serialize at 620. The .copied() turns the &StageSample into an owned StageSample, which is cheap because StageSample derives Copy, and .unwrap() is safe here because the slice is non-empty, so max_by_key cannot return None and unwrap cannot panic on this input.

The function returns the tuple (hottest.name, hottest.micros, total), which evaluates to ("serialize", 620, 840) in name, hottest-micros, total order. This max-over-stages reduction is the same question a flame graph answers visually: reducing a list of timings to one named winner is exactly what the flame graph does when it points you at the widest stack. The widest box owns the most aggregate sampled time, and serialize at 620 of 840 is the widest box in this data.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct StageSample {
    name: &'static str,
    micros: u64,
}

fn hottest_stage(samples: &[StageSample]) -> (&'static str, u64, u64) {
    // First reduction: sum of all stage micros -> the wall time.
    let total: u64 = samples.iter().map(|sample| sample.micros).sum();
    // Second reduction: the single stage that owns the most time.
    let hottest = samples
        .iter()
        .max_by_key(|sample| sample.micros)
        .copied() // StageSample: Copy, so this is cheap
        .unwrap(); // safe: non-empty slice => Some

    (hottest.name, hottest.micros, total)
}

fn main() {
    let samples = [
        StageSample { name: "parse", micros: 180 },
        StageSample { name: "serialize", micros: 620 },
        StageSample { name: "lock_wait", micros: 40 },
    ];
    // total = 180 + 620 + 40 = 840
    // hottest = serialize @ 620
    // returns ("serialize", 620, 840)
    assert_eq!(hottest_stage(&samples), ("serialize", 620, 840));
}

Hand-traced: the two reductions yield total 840 and hottest serialize at 620, returning ("serialize", 620, 840).

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The total is computed as 180 + 620 + 40 = 840 microseconds and identified as the sum of all stage micros.
  • max_by_key is identified as selecting the StageSample with the largest micros, returning serialize at 620.
  • The returned tuple is given as ("serialize", 620, 840) in name, hottest-micros, total order.
  • The answer connects reducing a list of timings to one named winner with the flame graph pointing at the widest stack.
Exercise 3implementation

Report each stage as a share of wall time

The goal is to turn the per-stage decomposition into a percentage breakdown so the widest layer is obvious before any tuning begins. The signature is fn share_of_total(samples: &[StageSample]) -> Vec<(&'static str, u64)>, taking a shared slice so the caller keeps ownership of its Vec and the function only needs read access.

Compute the total once with a single pass, then map each sample to (name, sample.micros * 100 / total). The order of operations matters: multiply by 100 before dividing by total so the fraction survives integer truncation. For parse=180 the correct path is 180 * 100 / 840 = 18000 / 840 = 21 (truncated); dividing first would compute 180 / 840 = 0 and then 0 * 100 = 0, collapsing every small stage to zero. With this ordering the result for parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40 is [("parse", 21), ("serialize", 73), ("lock_wait", 4)].

The empty-slice case must be handled before any division, because total would be zero and micros * 100 / 0 would panic. I return an empty Vec for an empty input: there are no stages to report a share of, so the natural answer is the empty breakdown. Guarding on samples.is_empty() (or, equivalently, on total == 0) keeps the divide-by-zero from ever executing. Everything else is integer arithmetic with no per-stage allocation beyond the result Vec itself.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct StageSample {
    name: &'static str,
    micros: u64,
}

fn share_of_total(samples: &[StageSample]) -> Vec<(&'static str, u64)> {
    // Documented choice: an empty input has no stages, so its breakdown is
    // the empty Vec. Guarding here also avoids dividing by a zero total.
    if samples.is_empty() {
        return Vec::new();
    }

    // One pass for the total.
    let total: u64 = samples.iter().map(|s| s.micros).sum();

    // Multiply before dividing so the fraction is not lost to truncation.
    samples
        .iter()
        .map(|s| (s.name, s.micros * 100 / total))
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let samples = [
        StageSample { name: "parse", micros: 180 },
        StageSample { name: "serialize", micros: 620 },
        StageSample { name: "lock_wait", micros: 40 },
    ];
    // 180*100/840=21, 620*100/840=73, 40*100/840=4
    assert_eq!(
        share_of_total(&samples),
        vec![("parse", 21), ("serialize", 73), ("lock_wait", 4)]
    );
    assert_eq!(share_of_total(&[]), Vec::new());
}

Two-pass integer reduction: sum once, then map each stage to micros * 100 / total, with an empty-slice guard.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The signature is exactly fn share_of_total(samples: &[StageSample]) -> Vec<(&'static str, u64)>.
  • For parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40 the result is [("parse", 21), ("serialize", 73), ("lock_wait", 4)].
  • Percentages use micros * 100 / total with multiplication before division, preserving the truncated fraction.
  • The empty-slice case returns an empty Vec, guarding before any division so total == 0 never divides.
Exercise 4implementation

Measure fixed per-crossing overhead

WASM and FFI share one failure mode: the cost is rarely in the Rust kernel and almost always in the crossing. The single highest-leverage experiment for both is to compare a noop call (tiny or empty payload) against the real call. The noop isolates the marshalling and call cost, so the difference between them is the fixed per-crossing overhead rather than the work of the callee or the kernel.

The signature is fn crossing_overhead(noop_ns: u64, real_ns: u64, calls: u64) -> (u64, u64), returning (per_call_overhead_ns, total_overhead_ns). Per-call overhead is real_ns minus noop_ns, but the subtraction must use saturating_sub. A noisy noop measurement can land above the real call, and unguarded u64 subtraction wraps on underflow, producing an absurd near-u64::MAX number; saturating_sub clamps that case to 0 instead. Total overhead is the per-call overhead multiplied by calls.

For noop_ns=30, real_ns=110, calls=1_000_000 the per-call overhead is 110 saturating_sub 30 = 80 ns, and the total is 80 * 1_000_000 = 80_000_000 ns. The reason this number drives an API decision is that a large per-crossing overhead is paid on every single call regardless of how fast the callee is. When the fixed cost dominates, a batched API that crosses the boundary once will beat any amount of tuning on the callee, because tuning the kernel cannot touch the part of the cost that lives in the crossing itself.

/// Returns (per_call_overhead_ns, total_overhead_ns).
///
/// A high per-crossing overhead favors crossing once with a batch over tuning
/// the callee, because the fixed cost is paid per call no matter how fast the
/// kernel is, and only batching reduces the number of crossings.
fn crossing_overhead(noop_ns: u64, real_ns: u64, calls: u64) -> (u64, u64) {
    // saturating_sub: a noisy noop above the real call yields 0, not a wrap.
    let per_call = real_ns.saturating_sub(noop_ns);
    let total = per_call * calls;
    (per_call, total)
}

fn main() {
    // 110 - 30 = 80 per call; 80 * 1_000_000 = 80_000_000 total.
    assert_eq!(crossing_overhead(30, 110, 1_000_000), (80, 80_000_000));
    // Noisy noop above the real call clamps to 0 rather than wrapping.
    assert_eq!(crossing_overhead(200, 110, 10), (0, 0));
}

noop subtracted from real call via saturating_sub isolates per-crossing overhead; scaled by call count for the total.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The signature is exactly fn crossing_overhead(noop_ns: u64, real_ns: u64, calls: u64) -> (u64, u64).
  • For noop_ns=30, real_ns=110, calls=1_000_000 it returns (80, 80_000_000).
  • The subtraction uses saturating_sub, so noop_ns greater than real_ns yields 0 rather than wrapping.
  • A comment states that high fixed overhead favors crossing once with a batch over tuning the callee.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix a lock metric that hides contention

The defect is that a single lock_cost_us conflates the two halves of lock cost the chapter insists on separating. The teammate's number is hold time only: the time a thread spends holding the guard and doing work. Wait time, the time other threads spend blocked waiting to acquire the lock, is never recorded. The two halves fail in opposite ways, so collapsing them into one averaged number erases exactly the signal needed to spot contention. The conclusion that a hot lock is fine because its number is small is therefore unjustified, because the small number is hold time and the missing number is wait time.

The fix is to replace the single field with a struct that stores hold_us and wait_us separately and reports both. classify(hold_us, wait_us) -> &'static str then returns "contention" when wait_us exceeds hold_us and "hold" otherwise. For (hold_us=5, wait_us=900) it returns "contention"; for (hold_us=900, wait_us=5) it returns "hold".

A lock held briefly but acquired constantly shows exactly this contention shape: low hold_us, high wait_us. Each critical section is short, so the guard is held only momentarily and hold_us stays small, but the lock is acquired so frequently that threads pile up waiting their turn, and that queue is where the wall time goes. A single averaged number would hide this because the brief hold time would dominate the average and make the lock look cheap.

Before reaching for lower-level lock-free structures, the chapter says to try the cheaper redesigns first, because a hot lock is often an ownership problem hiding underneath rather than only a synchronization one. Narrow the shared state so fewer threads contend for the same lock, shorten the critical section so the guard is held for less time, or give a subsystem its own owner so its state is not shared at all. Reach for lock-free structures last, after those redesigns have been tried.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct LockCost {
    /// Time the guard is held doing actual work.
    hold_us: u64,
    /// Time other threads spend blocked waiting to acquire the lock.
    wait_us: u64,
}

fn classify(hold_us: u64, wait_us: u64) -> &'static str {
    if wait_us > hold_us {
        "contention"
    } else {
        "hold"
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Brief hold, constant acquisition: short critical section, long queue.
    let hot = LockCost { hold_us: 5, wait_us: 900 };
    assert_eq!(classify(hot.hold_us, hot.wait_us), "contention");

    // Long critical section, little queueing: the cost is the work itself.
    let heavy = LockCost { hold_us: 900, wait_us: 5 };
    assert_eq!(classify(heavy.hold_us, heavy.wait_us), "hold");
}

hold_us and wait_us are stored separately; classify names the dominant half instead of averaging the two away.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Hold time and wait time are stored and reported as two separate fields rather than one combined number.
  • classify returns "contention" for (5, 900) and "hold" for (900, 5).
  • The explanation ties high wait_us with low hold_us to a frequently-acquired short critical section.
  • The answer names narrowing shared state, shortening critical sections, or giving a subsystem its own owner before going lock-free.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Resolve the p99 regression argument

The argument cannot be settled by any of the three signals on its own, because each engineer is reading one layer of a request that lives in several. The plan is to decompose one slow request's wall time into its layers before any function is rewritten, point at the widest layer, and only then confirm the call stack. Optimizing on sight is the failure mode this discipline exists to prevent.

The layers and their instruments are: CPU compute, measured with a sampling CPU profiler; queue wait, measured with tracing spans around the enqueue-to-dequeue transition; lock blocking, measured by recording hold time and wait time separately per lock; IO, measured with a trace that captures time queued before the IO begins, not CPU samples; serialization, measured by encode and decode time alongside allocations per message and bytes per message; and boundary-crossing overhead, measured by comparing a noop crossing against the real one. Each engineer's signal becomes one named layer with a budget rather than the whole story.

The order of operations is fixed: decompose the wall time into those layers first, point at the widest layer, then confirm the call stack with a sampler or trace. The widest stage is only the first suspect, not the verdict. The chief guard against blaming the first recognizable function is that a wide serialize stack is frequently the allocation and copy beneath it rather than the encoder's control flow, so tuning the serializer would barely move the number while cutting the copy would. The same guard applies to IO: a sampler shows the CPU busy inside a parser and the parser gets blamed, while a trace reveals the request spent most of its life queued before the parser ever ran. So the rule is to confirm what sits beneath the wide box before touching it.

The discipline I will hold the team to is one bounded question, one build, and one recorded workload. The question is scoped to a single thing such as "which layer owns the p99 wall-time increase since the release," not "make it faster." The build is one release build with symbols good enough for usable stacks, because a debug build profiles a different program. The workload is one recorded, representative input replayed identically, so that the engineer who later has to reproduce the regression measures the same thing the person who captured it did. One question, one build, one recorded workload keeps the profile an answer instead of a new argument.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The plan enumerates CPU compute, queue wait, lock blocking, IO, serialization, and boundary-crossing overhead, each paired with a fitting instrument.
  • The sequence is decompose first, point at the widest layer, then confirm the call stack with a sampler or trace, not optimize-on-sight.
  • The plan warns a wide serialize stack may be the allocation and copy beneath it, and an IO path's real cost is often queue time, not CPU samples.
  • Scope is fixed to one bounded question, one release build with usable symbols, and one recorded representative workload.

Lab solution

The lab decomposes a pipeline's wall time into four named layers and then names the layer that owns the most time, which is the core move of the whole chapter expressed in a few runnable lines. The layers function projects the PipelineStats fields into a fixed array of (name, micros) pairs, and wall_time folds that array with sum to get the total: 410 + 120 + 90 + 180 = 800 microseconds.

The only piece to fill in is dominant. It calls layers(stats).into_iter() to take the array by value (so each tuple is owned, not borrowed), then max_by_key(|(_, value)| *value) selects the pair with the largest micros, and unwrap is safe because the array always has four elements and can never be empty. For this data the largest is ("cpu", 410), so dominant returns that pair.

In main the share is computed as micros * 100 / wall = 410 * 100 / 800 = 41000 / 800 = 51 (integer truncation), multiplying before dividing so the fraction is not lost. The program therefore prints dominant = cpu, wall us = 800, and dominant share = 51, which matches the expected output exactly. The reduction from a list of timings to one named winner is the same question a flame graph answers by pointing at the widest stack.

Example 35-S. dominant_layer_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct PipelineStats {
    cpu_us: u64,
    io_wait_us: u64,
    lock_wait_us: u64,
    serialize_us: u64,
}

fn layers(stats: &PipelineStats) -> [(&'static str, u64); 4] {
    [
        ("cpu", stats.cpu_us),
        ("io", stats.io_wait_us),
        ("lock", stats.lock_wait_us),
        ("serialize", stats.serialize_us),
    ]
}

fn wall_time(stats: &PipelineStats) -> u64 {
    layers(stats).iter().map(|(_, value)| value).sum()
}

fn dominant(stats: &PipelineStats) -> (&'static str, u64) {
    layers(stats)
        .into_iter()
        .max_by_key(|(_, value)| *value)
        .unwrap()
}

fn main() {
    let stats = PipelineStats {
        cpu_us: 410,
        io_wait_us: 120,
        lock_wait_us: 90,
        serialize_us: 180,
    };

    let wall = wall_time(&stats);
    let (name, micros) = dominant(&stats);
    let share = micros * 100 / wall;

    println!("dominant = {}", name);
    println!("wall us = {}", wall);
    println!("dominant share = {}", share);
}
Output
dominant = cpu
wall us = 800
dominant share = 51

Review question answers

Why does choosing a profiling instrument start from the question you need answered rather than from the tool you already have open?

Because each instrument answers one kind of question and distorts the others: a benchmark compares two implementations but does not explain why one won, a sampler localizes hot compute but cannot compare versions, and a trace shows where time is spent waiting but is not a CPU picture. If you start from whatever tool is already open, you bend the question to fit the tool and get a confident answer to the wrong question. The chapter's rule is to walk the decision diagram from the question to the instrument that answers it with the least distortion.

What does the x-axis of a flame graph represent, and why is reading it as a timeline a mistake?

The x-axis is not chronological time; it groups boxes by the shape of the call stack, and the width of each box is the total sampled time attributed to that stack. The stack grows upward, so a wide box means that stack owned a lot of aggregate sampled time, not that it ran at a particular moment. Reading it left-to-right as a timeline leads you to infer an order of execution that the graph never encoded, and to miss that width, not horizontal position, is the signal that points at the widest stack.

What is the tradeoff between sampling and instrumentation, and when does each one mislead you?

Sampling watches from the outside at a fixed rate, so it perturbs the program very little but only sees code that runs often enough to be caught between samples; it misleads you by missing rare-but-expensive paths and time spent waiting, parked, or enqueued, which execute no instructions to catch. Instrumentation records explicit measurements at chosen points, so it is precise about exactly those points but adds overhead and can perturb the very thing it measures, especially in hot loops where the instrumentation cost rivals the work. The choice is overhead versus precision: use sampling to find where compute concentrates cheaply, and instrumentation when you need an exact number for a specific transition.

Why can a CPU profiler tell only part of the story for an async task that takes 200ms of wall time but almost no CPU?

A CPU profiler only sees instructions executing on a core, but most of those 200ms were spent enqueued, waiting on a semaphore permit, or parked on the blocking thread pool, where the task is not running any code to sample. The profile comes back nearly empty and points at nothing, because the wall-time gap lives in waiting, not in compute. The right signal is tracing spans around each transition, which record where the task actually waits or blocks; the fix usually lives in admission policy or queue wait, almost never in rewriting the executor.

What are the two halves of lock cost that must be measured separately, and how does each one fail differently?

The two halves are hold time, the time a thread spends holding the guard doing work, and wait time, the time other threads spend blocked waiting to acquire the lock. They fail in opposite ways: a lock held briefly but acquired constantly shows low hold time yet high wait time and is a contention problem, while a lock held for a long stretch shows high hold time and is a critical-section-length problem. Collapsing them into one averaged number erases exactly the signal you need, and because a hot lock is often an ownership problem underneath, the cheaper fixes are to narrow shared state, shorten critical sections, or give a subsystem its own owner before reaching for lock-free structures.

Chapter 36 · Distributed Tasks Profiling

Distributed Tasks Profiling

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move profiling out of a single process and into the spaces between processes. The recurring theme is that "slow" stops being one number once work travels through brokers, leases, worker pools, and reducers: the latency a user feels is the sum of queue wait, worker execution, retries, and fan-out, and each segment needs its own signal. The drills ask you to design that signal set deliberately, read an incident across logs, metrics, and traces, and compute the headline numbers an operator should see before the page fills with guesses.

The lab and the implementation exercise are the same shape as the chapter's first example: fold one profiling window down to worker saturation, retry rate, and an explicit storm flag. The later exercises push toward graph-aware profiling (critical path instead of stage-local averages) and capacity planning that includes replay traffic and drain time rather than only happy-path throughput. Throughout, the editorial rule is the same one the chapter states: handler CPU is usually not the system; queue age, retries, and fan-in often are.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Design metrics for worker saturation on purpose

The three pools answer different questions, so they need overlapping but distinct metric sets. The shared backbone is the same for all of them, and matches the chapter's three-shape rule: counters answer "how much happened," gauges answer "what is the level right now," and histograms answer "what is the distribution."

Counters (monotonic, per pool): tasks_admitted_total (admission), tasks_completed_total and tasks_failed_total (completion outcome), tasks_retried_total (replay load, not just failures), and dedupe_suppressed_total (duplicates dropped by idempotency). Admission minus completion over a window already hints at backlog; retried over claimed is the retry rate that the storm rule keys on.

Gauges (instantaneous level, per pool): queue_depth (visible backlog), in_flight (claimed-but-not-done work), and oldest_message_age_seconds. Oldest visible age is the one to watch hardest — it is a better operational target than average depth because a single stuck partition shows up there while the average still looks calm.

Histograms (distribution, per pool): queue_wait_seconds (time before claim), run_seconds (handler execution), and end_to_end_seconds (admission to durable completion). The split is what lets you separate worker saturation from queue saturation: worker saturation is busy_workers / total_workers near 1.0 with a healthy queue_wait; queue saturation is a rising queue_wait and oldest_message_age while run_seconds stays flat. The GPU pool will lean on run_seconds and in_flight; the reducer pool needs oldest_message_age and queue_depth most, because fan-in is where backlog hides.

Forbidden labels: never attach task_id or trace_id to a metric — those are unbounded and produce one time series per task, which is the classic cardinality explosion. Per-task identity belongs in logs and traces, where you can pivot on it; metrics should carry only low-cardinality dimensions such as pool name, queue name, and outcome.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Includes counters (admitted/completed/retried/dedupe), gauges (queue_depth, in_flight, oldest_message_age), and histograms (queue_wait, run, end_to_end), each with a stated reason.
  • Distinguishes worker saturation (busy/total near 1.0 with healthy queue wait) from queue saturation (rising queue wait and oldest age while run time is flat).
  • Names task_id and trace_id as forbidden labels because they are unbounded and explode cardinality.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace a tail-latency incident across logs, metrics, and traces

The dominant layer is not the handler. The trace splits the 970 ms of observed time into 900 ms before claim and 70 ms inside the handler, so roughly 93 percent of end-to-end time is queue wait, plus the replay overhead of two failed attempts before success. Handler p50 being flat is exactly the trap the chapter warns about: when end-to-end latency rises while run time stays flat, the time is being spent before the handler, not inside it. Optimizing handler CPU here would move p99 by tens of milliseconds against a 900 ms wait — it cannot fix the incident.

The metric that should have alerted earlier than handler p50 is queue wait (queue_wait p95) or, equivalently, oldest_message_age. Both rise as soon as work starts waiting for a free worker, minutes before any handler-time metric moves. A retry-rate counter would also have flagged the replay component early.

To make the retry path attributable to one task you need stable identity carried in the envelope and echoed into logs and trace events: task_id (the same value across all three attempts) and attempt (1, 2, 3, so you can separate the first try from the redeliveries), plus queue_name so multi-queue tail analysis is possible. With task_id you can collapse the three log lines into one story; with attempt you can confirm the first two were timeouts, not genuine handler failures.

The first mitigation to test targets the real bottleneck, which is queueing plus replay amplification — not handler CPU. Options, cheapest first: raise the worker budget for that pool (more concurrent claims drains the backlog), cap or back off retries so failed attempts stop adding to arrival rate, or split the slow class onto its own queue so it stops blocking fast work. Increasing the worker budget or capping retries is the change to try before touching handler code.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies queue wait (900 ms) plus replay, not handler CPU (70 ms), as the dominant layer.
  • Names queue_wait p95 / oldest_message_age as the earlier metric and task_id plus attempt as the identity fields that make the incident explainable.
  • Proposes a mitigation tied to the bottleneck (raise worker budget, cap retries, or split the queue) rather than optimizing the handler.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a retry-storm window summary

This is a metric-and-policy drill, not a transport drill, so the whole point is to keep the helpers side-effect free and make the threshold logic visible in code. Each helper is a pure reduction over one WindowStats sample.

Saturation is busy_workers / total_workers cast to f64, guarded against a zero pool so it returns 0.0 instead of NaN. Retry rate is retried / claimed, guarded the same way against an empty window. Both are simple ratios, which is the property that makes them reviewable and testable.

The storm rule is the part that must not hide in prose. Encode the two thresholds as named constants and make retry_storm a single boolean expression: saturation at or above the saturation threshold AND retry rate at or above the retry threshold. Requiring both is deliberate — high saturation alone can be healthy throughput, and a high retry rate on an idle pool is not yet a storm. It is the combination, the feedback loop of saturation causing timeouts causing retries causing more load, that the flag is meant to catch. With claimed=100, retried=40, busy=9, total=10 the sample yields saturation 0.90, retry rate 0.40, and storm true, because 0.90 >= 0.85 and 0.40 >= 0.30.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct WindowStats {
    claimed: u32,
    retried: u32,
    busy_workers: u32,
    total_workers: u32,
}

fn saturation(stats: &WindowStats) -> f64 {
    if stats.total_workers == 0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    stats.busy_workers as f64 / stats.total_workers as f64
}

fn retry_rate(stats: &WindowStats) -> f64 {
    if stats.claimed == 0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    stats.retried as f64 / stats.claimed as f64
}

// Policy lives in named constants so a reviewer can see and change it.
const SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD: f64 = 0.85;
const RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD: f64 = 0.30;

fn retry_storm(stats: &WindowStats) -> bool {
    saturation(stats) >= SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD
        && retry_rate(stats) >= RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD
}

Pure reductions over one window; the storm policy is two named thresholds combined with AND.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • saturation = busy/total and retry_rate = retried/claimed are computed correctly, with zero-guards to avoid division by zero.
  • The storm rule is an explicit boolean over two named threshold constants, not buried in prose.
  • On the sample it prints saturation 0.90, retry rate 0.40, storm true, matching the lab's expected output.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a profiling surface that hides queue latency

The defect is that the system instruments only the handler. Handler spans tell you run time, which is the one segment that already looks fine; the missing segment is everything before claim, so queue wait is invisible and backlog cannot be explained. The fix is to record the boundary timestamps and carry the correlation identity through the envelope.

Timestamps: stamp enqueued_at when the producer puts the task on the broker and claimed_at when a worker leases it. Queue wait is then claimed_at minus enqueued_at, and it can be computed without a dedicated span. The handler already gives you started_at and finished_at for run time. Carry these in the task envelope alongside the identity fields so the worker side has the producer-side timestamp available.

Log fields that must appear on both the enqueue side and the worker side: task_id and trace_id (stable across the whole trip and across retries), queue_name (without it, multi-queue tail analysis is nearly impossible), and attempt (separates first try from redeliveries). The enqueue-side log records the submission; the worker-side log records claim and completion; sharing task_id and trace_id is what stitches them into one record.

Model queue wait as derived time between two events (enqueued_at and claimed_at), not as a separate always-on span. The two events are cheap to stamp and the subtraction is free at query time, whereas a dedicated queue span adds an exporter write on every single task. For cost control on the hot path, keep aggregate metrics at full volume — a queue_wait histogram and oldest_message_age gauge are cheap and always-on — and attach full detailed traces only on a sampled fraction (plus always-sample on error or on tasks over a latency threshold). That gives you the population view from metrics and enough exemplars to explain one incident path without paying for a span per task.

/// Task envelope carrying the correlation identity and the boundary
/// timestamps that make queue wait derivable. Both producer and worker
/// read/write these fields.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct TaskEnvelope {
    task_id: u64,
    trace_id: u128,
    parent_task_id: Option<u64>,
    queue_name: &'static str,
    attempt: u32,
    enqueued_at_ms: u64,        // stamped by the producer
    claimed_at_ms: Option<u64>, // stamped by the worker on lease
}

impl TaskEnvelope {
    /// Queue wait is derived from two events, not a dedicated span.
    fn queue_wait_ms(&self) -> Option<u64> {
        self.claimed_at_ms.map(|c| c.saturating_sub(self.enqueued_at_ms))
    }
}

Derive queue wait from enqueued_at/claimed_at rather than a per-task span; carry task_id, trace_id, queue_name, attempt for correlation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Adds enqueue and claim visibility explicitly via enqueued_at and claimed_at, exposing queue wait that handler spans alone hide.
  • Includes stable correlation fields (task_id and trace_id) present on both the enqueue side and the worker side.
  • Names a cost-control tactic: full-volume aggregate metrics plus sampled (and error-triggered) detailed traces, with queue wait derived rather than spanned.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Profile a task graph by critical path instead of average stage time

The defect is treating end-to-end time as the sum of stage averages. In a DAG, parallel stages overlap, so summing their durations double-counts time the system never spent, and a per-stage average can look healthy while the graph is globally slow. The signal that actually predicts completion is the critical path: the longest dependency chain when each node's cost is its own queue wait plus run time added to the maximum finishing time among its parents. Add all three graph-aware signals — critical-path time as the headline, frontier (in-flight node) size to spot fan-out width blowing up the pool, and reducer backlog to spot fan-in stalls — but critical path is the first honest simplification.

Queue wait belongs inside the graph accounting, not outside it. Each node's contribution is queue_ms + run_ms, exactly as the chapter's Example 2 computes; if you fold queue time into a separate global number, a join that is slow purely because its inputs sat in a queue will be misattributed to the worker. Keeping wait per node is what makes the critical path honest.

To prove a join stage is the real bottleneck rather than one upstream worker, walk the critical path and check where the longest finishing time is realized. If the join's predecessors all finish early but the join's own queue_ms (it waited for a free reducer) or the max-over-parents term dominates, the bottleneck is fan-in, not a single upstream stage. The tail-stage name returned by the critical-path computation tells you which node sits at the end of the longest path; if it is consistently the join, that is your proof.

For attribution under fan-out and fan-in, carry parent_task_id (and the root trace_id) in every envelope so children can be reassembled into the parent graph, and sample whole traces by root rather than by individual span — otherwise a fan-out of width 200 gives you 200 disconnected fragments. Sampling by root keeps the graph story attributable: you either get the entire DAG for a sampled job or none of it.

type StageId = usize;

struct Stage {
    name: &'static str,
    deps: Vec<StageId>,
    queue_ms: u64, // wait stays per-node, inside the graph accounting
    run_ms: u64,
}

/// Longest-path completion: each node's cost is queue + run added to the
/// max finishing time among its parents. Returns (critical_path_ms, tail).
fn critical_path(stages: &[Stage]) -> (u64, &'static str) {
    let mut finish = vec![0_u64; stages.len()];
    let (mut best, mut tail) = (0_u64, "none");
    for (id, s) in stages.iter().enumerate() {
        let upstream = s.deps.iter().map(|&d| finish[d]).max().unwrap_or(0);
        finish[id] = upstream + s.queue_ms + s.run_ms;
        if finish[id] >= best {
            best = finish[id];
            tail = s.name;
        }
    }
    (best, tail)
}

Critical path with per-node queue+run cost; the returned tail names the stage at the end of the longest path.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Adds a graph-aware signal (critical-path time, plus frontier size and reducer backlog) beyond per-stage averages.
  • Keeps queue wait inside the graph by making each node's cost queue_ms + run_ms rather than a separate global number.
  • Proposes attribution via parent_task_id / root trace_id and sampling whole traces by root for fan-out and fan-in nodes.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Capacity-plan a distributed worker fleet with retries and slow-stage isolation

Design the pipeline ingest -> parse -> enrich -> store -> notify as separate stages with separate budgets, because a single global budget lets the one long-running stage starve everything else. The stage that deserves its own queue and worker pool is the long-running specialist (call it enrich). With one shared pool, slow enrich tasks hold workers while fast parse and notify tasks queue behind them; isolating it bounds head-of-line blocking and lets you scale it independently to meet the oldest-age budget.

Size each pool from arrival rate and service time, then inflate for replay. By Little's Law the in-flight work for a stage is arrival_rate x service_time, and the worker count needed is roughly arrival_rate x service_time targeted below the queueing cliff (do not plan a stage at 100 percent utilization — keep it around 70 to 80 percent so a small burst does not push oldest-age past 2 s). Retry traffic is not rare noise: it adds to arrival rate. If the failure profile is f (fraction of tasks that fail and redeliver), effective arrival is roughly arrival / (1 - f) for at-least-once delivery, so a 10 percent failure rate is about 11 percent more load, and a storm can be far worse. Plan the worker budget against the effective, replay-inflated arrival rate, not the submission rate of 180/s alone.

The metrics that warn the 2-second oldest-age budget is about to fail are, in order: oldest_message_age_seconds (the direct target), queue_wait p95, worker_saturation (busy/total approaching 1.0), and retry_rate. Watching oldest age plus saturation plus retry rate plus reducer/enrich backlog gives minutes of warning before the budget breaks, because those four move before the budget itself does.

Finally, put a drain target in the same plan: on shutdown or deploy, stop admitting new work and require the fleet to drain in-flight and queued tasks within a bounded window (for example, drain to oldest-age 0 within 30 seconds). Drain time is governed by backlog size divided by completion rate, so it is the same capacity arithmetic — a fleet sized only for steady-state throughput can have a drain time far longer than its lease timeout, which causes duplicate processing on restart.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Isolates the long-running specialist stage (enrich) onto its own queue and pool to prevent head-of-line blocking.
  • Includes retries in the budget by planning against replay-inflated effective arrival (arrival / (1 - failure_fraction)), not the raw 180/s.
  • Names at least three observability hooks: oldest_message_age, worker saturation, retry rate, and stage/reducer backlog.
  • Adds a drain/shutdown target (bounded drain within a window) alongside steady-state throughput, tied to the same capacity arithmetic.

Lab solution

Each helper is a pure reduction over one WindowStats window, which keeps the lab trivial to test: no I/O, no shared state, no transport. saturation divides busy_workers by total_workers, guarded against a zero pool so it returns 0.0 rather than NaN; retry_rate divides retried by claimed with the same guard. Both take &WindowStats by shared reference, so the caller keeps ownership and the same sample can be read by every helper without a clone.

The storm policy is deliberately not hidden in prose. Two named constants, SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD (0.85) and RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD (0.30), make the thresholds reviewable, and retry_storm is a single boolean expression requiring both to be met. The AND matters: high saturation alone can be healthy throughput, and a high retry rate on an idle pool is not yet a storm; it is the combination — the feedback loop of saturation causing timeouts causing retries causing more load — that the flag catches.

For the sample (claimed 100, retried 40, busy 9, total 10), saturation is 9/10 = 0.90, retry rate is 40/100 = 0.40, and the storm flag is true because 0.90 >= 0.85 and 0.40 >= 0.30. The {:.2} format specifier prints both ratios to two decimals, producing exactly the expected three lines.

Example 36-S. retry_storm_window_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct WindowStats {
    claimed: u32,
    retried: u32,
    busy_workers: u32,
    total_workers: u32,
}

// Worker saturation: how much of the pool is doing work right now.
// busy / total. A high value next to a rising queue age means overload.
fn saturation(stats: &WindowStats) -> f64 {
    if stats.total_workers == 0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    stats.busy_workers as f64 / stats.total_workers as f64
}

// Retry rate: fraction of claimed work that was a redelivery, not new work.
// retried / claimed. This is load amplification, not just error bookkeeping.
fn retry_rate(stats: &WindowStats) -> f64 {
    if stats.claimed == 0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    stats.retried as f64 / stats.claimed as f64
}

// Storm rule, stated explicitly so a reviewer can see and change the policy.
const SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD: f64 = 0.85;
const RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD: f64 = 0.30;

fn retry_storm(stats: &WindowStats) -> bool {
    saturation(stats) >= SATURATION_STORM_THRESHOLD
        && retry_rate(stats) >= RETRY_STORM_THRESHOLD
}

fn main() {
    let stats = WindowStats {
        claimed: 100,
        retried: 40,
        busy_workers: 9,
        total_workers: 10,
    };

    println!("saturation = {:.2}", saturation(&stats));
    println!("retry rate = {:.2}", retry_rate(&stats));
    println!("storm = {}", retry_storm(&stats));
}
Output
saturation = 0.90
retry rate = 0.40
storm = true

Review question answers

Why is queue latency often a better first incident signal than mean handler time?

End-to-end latency is the sum of queue wait, run time, and replay, and when work backs up the time accumulates before the handler ever runs. Mean handler time stays flat in exactly that situation, so it cannot page you, whereas queue wait (or oldest visible age) rises the instant work starts waiting for a free worker. The chapter's rule is that if end-to-end latency rises while run time is flat, the cost is before the handler, not inside it — so queue latency moves earlier and points at the real layer.

What makes a retry storm a load-amplification problem instead of only an error-rate problem?

A retry storm is a feedback loop: failures cause redeliveries, redeliveries add to the arrival rate, the higher arrival pushes workers past saturation, saturation causes more timeouts, and the timeouts produce still more retries. So retries are load, not just failure bookkeeping — every redelivery is another claim competing for the same workers. Treating it as only an error-rate problem misses that the system can be amplifying its own traffic until the queue and oldest-age signals climb out of control.

Why should task ID and trace ID stay out of metric labels but stay present in logs and traces?

Task ID and trace ID are effectively unbounded, so attaching them as metric labels creates one time series per task and explodes cardinality, which can overwhelm the metrics backend. Metrics should carry only low-cardinality dimensions like pool name, queue name, and outcome, which still aggregate cleanly. Logs and traces are where per-task identity belongs: there you pivot on a single task_id or trace_id to reconstruct one incident path, including separating the first attempt from its retries.

What does critical-path time explain that stage-local averages do not explain?

In a DAG, parallel stages overlap, so summing stage durations double-counts time the system never spent and a per-stage average can look healthy while the graph is globally slow. Critical-path time is the longest dependency chain, where each node's cost is its own queue wait plus run time added to the maximum finishing time among its parents — that is the number that actually predicts completion. It exposes reducer lag and join bottlenecks, because a fan-in node can sit on the longest path purely from waiting on its slowest input even when every stage's average is fine.

Why should capacity planning include drain time and retry traffic, not only steady-state throughput?

Retries inflate the effective arrival rate (roughly arrival / (1 - failure fraction) under at-least-once delivery), so planning on happy-path throughput underestimates the real worker budget and the pool tips over the queueing cliff sooner than expected. Drain time matters because on shutdown or deploy the fleet must clear in-flight and queued work within a bounded window; a fleet sized only for steady state can have a drain time longer than its lease timeout, which causes duplicate processing on restart. Both are the same Little's-Law arithmetic applied to replay-inflated load and to backlog over completion rate.

Chapter 37 · CUDA and GPU Acceleration

CUDA and GPU Acceleration

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises train one discipline: treat the GPU as a throughput device guarded by an expensive boundary, and prove that boundary pays for itself before any kernel ships. You start by choosing among CPU, Rayon, MPI, and CUDA from the shape of the workload, then count the bytes that actually cross the bus, then build the safe Rust wrapper that validates shape and launch configuration before one small unsafe launch. The later exercises move up the stack: repairing a tiny-kernel service that lost to the CPU, reading a profile to find the dominant cost category, and integrating a single device into an async and distributed service as a scarce shared worker.

The through-line is that almost every GPU failure in service code is a systems mistake wearing a performance costume. The kernel is rarely the problem. The trouble is too many small launches, too much copying, a borrowed buffer that outlived its request, or one shared device with no admission control. The answers below keep returning to arithmetic intensity, to transfer and launch amortization, and to the ownership story that lets Rust keep the host side of the boundary honest.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose CPU, Rayon, MPI, or CUDA from the workload

Map each workload to the execution model whose dominant cost it actually pays, not to whichever tool sounds most powerful. The single number that predicts a GPU win is arithmetic intensity: how much math you do per byte you move across the bus. Pair that with batch size and the level at which the real partition lives (host memory, one node, or many nodes), and each workload sorts cleanly.

The tiny request-local transform over one 4 KB buffer stays on the CPU. There is almost no arithmetic to do, the data is small, and a host-to-device copy plus a launch plus a synchronize plus a copy back would cost far more than running the transform inline. This is a low-intensity, low-volume job; the accelerator boundary would dominate the entire request.

The one-node dense batch score over host memory wants Rayon. The data already lives in one address space on one machine, the work is embarrassingly parallel across rows, and you can saturate the cores with a parallel iterator without ever leaving host memory or paying a transfer. There is no partition to ship across a network and no boundary to amortize, so the cheapest parallelism is the data-parallel CPU path.

The multi-node domain-decomposed solver wants MPI because the dominant partition is already process-level. The problem is split across machines by domain, the bottleneck is the halo exchange between ranks, and the natural unit of work is one process per subdomain communicating with its neighbors. Reaching for a GPU here would not address the real cost, which is inter-process communication, not single-node math throughput.

The dense batched tensor operation with high arithmetic intensity wants CUDA. Dense batched math does a large amount of computation per byte transferred, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the host-device copies behind it and the launch overhead is amortized across a big batch. This is the one case where the bus cost is paid back many times over by the arithmetic, which is the justification the GPU case actually requires.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • CPU for the 4 KB transform, Rayon for the one-node batch score, MPI for the domain-decomposed solver, CUDA for the dense batched tensor op covers all four targets.
  • The CUDA case is justified by the kernel running long enough to amortize transfer and launch, not by the word 'parallel'.
  • CPU-bound work (the math itself) is kept distinct from waiting-bound work (the inter-process halo exchange that drives the MPI choice).
Exercise 2code reading

Estimate transfer cost before discussing the kernel

Count the bytes on the bus before tuning any arithmetic; the transfer is a fixed cost that never appears in a kernel-only profile. One f32 matrix of 4096 by 4096 has 4096 * 4096 = 16,777,216 elements, and each f32 is 4 bytes, so one matrix occupies 16,777,216 * 4 = 67,108,864 bytes, which is 64 MiB.

The call transfers A and B to the device and copies C back once. That is three matrix-sized transfers in total: two host-to-device plus one device-to-host. Total traffic is 3 * 67,108,864 = 201,326,592 bytes, which is 192 MiB. The transfer_bytes helper in the chapter's transfer-budget sample computes exactly this shape: elements times the f32 size times the count of input plus output buffers.

This boundary is far less painful for GEMM than for a tiny vector add because of arithmetic intensity. A dense 4096-cubed matrix multiply does on the order of 2 * 4096^3, roughly 1.4e11 floating-point operations, against about 2e8 bytes moved. That is hundreds of FLOPs per byte, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the copies behind it and the 192 MiB transfer is paid back many times over. A vector add, by contrast, does one add per several bytes moved, is memory-bandwidth-limited, and is acutely transfer-sensitive, so the same boundary swamps the work.

Transfer is not the only fixed cost, though. Launch overhead and synchronization remain separate categories: every kernel launch costs a fixed amount regardless of size, and waiting for the device to finish before copying C back is its own stall. For a single large GEMM these are negligible relative to the math, but they are the costs that dominate when a service launches many tiny kernels, so they belong on the ledger as their own line items.

fn matrix_bytes_f32(rows: usize, cols: usize) -> usize {
    rows * cols * std::mem::size_of::<f32>()
}

fn gemm_traffic_bytes(n: usize) -> usize {
    // A and B go host-to-device, C comes device-to-host: 3 matrices total.
    3 * matrix_bytes_f32(n, n)
}

fn main() {
    let n = 4096;
    let one = matrix_bytes_f32(n, n);
    let total = gemm_traffic_bytes(n);

    println!("one matrix = {} bytes ({} MiB)", one, one / (1024 * 1024));
    println!("call traffic = {} bytes ({} MiB)", total, total / (1024 * 1024));
    // one matrix = 67108864 bytes (64 MiB)
    // call traffic = 201326592 bytes (192 MiB)
}

One matrix is 64 MiB; the full A,B in / C out round trip is 192 MiB on the bus.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The traffic total is computed as 201,326,592 bytes (192 MiB) from three 64 MiB matrices.
  • The amortization argument cites GEMM's hundreds of FLOPs per byte versus vector add's bandwidth-limited one-op-per-few-bytes.
  • Launch and synchronization overhead are named as separate cost categories from the copy traffic.
Exercise 3implementation

Sketch a safe Rust wrapper around a launch boundary

Put every invariant in the safe wrapper and shrink the unsafe region to the launch itself. This is the same wrapper discipline the book uses around FFI: the GPU boundary is not special, so the checks belong in ordinary safe Rust and the unsafe block does nothing but the call it cannot avoid.

validate_buffers rejects the two failure modes that would otherwise become silent device-side corruption. It returns Err for any zero-length buffer, because a zero-length launch is a launch with nothing to do, and it returns Err when the three lengths disagree, because mismatched shapes are the classic out-of-bounds the safe layer exists to prevent. It returns Result rather than a bare bool so the caller learns which invariant failed and can propagate it with the question mark operator, the same way the chapter's build_launch_config returns Err("empty input") and Err("threads_per_block must be > 0").

build_config computes the grid from the data, not from a hard-coded guess. Blocks is the ceiling division ((len + tpb - 1) / tpb) so the grid covers every element including a ragged final block, and it is zero when threads_per_block is zero, which the raw launch then refuses. That mirrors the chapter sample exactly: grid and block shape are derived and checked before the raw launch becomes even possible.

The unsafe region stays smaller than the validation around it. By the time control reaches the unsafe launch, lengths are equal and nonzero, the block and thread counts are nonzero, and the SAFETY comment can state those facts plainly so another engineer re-derives the invariants in a few seconds. The ownership story is the point: the host wrapper owns the device buffers, decides when they exist, and guarantees they outlive the launch, which is precisely the discipline that keeps a mismatched length from becoming undefined behavior.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct LaunchConfig {
    threads_per_block: u32,
    blocks: u32,
}

fn validate_buffers(a_len: usize, b_len: usize, out_len: usize) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    if a_len == 0 || b_len == 0 || out_len == 0 {
        return Err("zero-length buffer");
    }
    if a_len != b_len || a_len != out_len {
        return Err("buffer length mismatch");
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn build_config(len: usize, threads_per_block: u32) -> Result<LaunchConfig, &'static str> {
    if threads_per_block == 0 {
        return Err("threads_per_block must be > 0");
    }
    let blocks = ((len as u32) + threads_per_block - 1) / threads_per_block;
    Ok(LaunchConfig { threads_per_block, blocks })
}

unsafe fn raw_launch(_config: LaunchConfig, _len: usize) {
    // SAFETY: callers reach this only after validate_buffers confirmed equal,
    // nonzero lengths and build_config produced nonzero block/thread counts.
}

fn launch(len: usize, threads_per_block: u32) -> Result<LaunchConfig, &'static str> {
    validate_buffers(len, len, len)?;
    let config = build_config(len, threads_per_block)?;
    unsafe { raw_launch(config, len); }
    Ok(config)
}

fn main() {
    let config = launch(1_024, 128).unwrap();
    println!("blocks = {}", config.blocks);
    println!("threads = {}", config.threads_per_block);
    println!("launch ok = {}", true);
}

All shape and grid invariants are checked in safe code; the unsafe block only performs the launch.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • validate_buffers runs and must succeed before the unsafe call is reached.
  • build_config derives block count from len and threads_per_block with ceiling division.
  • The checked boundary returns Result<LaunchConfig, &'static str>, not a vague boolean.
  • The runnable lab prints blocks = 8, threads = 128, launch ok = true.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a tiny-kernel service path that lost to the CPU

Diagnose the path as launch-bound and transfer-bound, then fix it in the cheapest order. The service copies one small vector, launches one tiny kernel, synchronizes immediately, copies the result back, and repeats that whole cycle per request item. This is the fastest wrong architecture in the chapter: per-item it pays a full host-device round trip and a launch and a synchronize for an arithmetic payload too small to amortize any of them.

The first fix is batching, not kernel rewriting. Accumulate many request items into one large buffer and launch a single kernel over the batch, so one transfer and one launch and one synchronize cover thousands of items instead of one. Batching alone collapses both the launch count and the per-item copy overhead, which are the two costs actually dominating here. Fusing adjacent kernels is the natural second move once batching is in place, because it removes intermediate device-to-host round trips between stages; reusing persistent device buffers across batches is the third, since it stops re-allocating the same scratch on every call. Kernel-level tuning is last, because the kernel was never the bottleneck.

The signal that the path is launch-bound rather than kernel-bound is the relationship between launch count and kernel time. If a profile shows a high launch count with each kernel finishing in microseconds while wall time is dominated by queue wait and copy time, the device is spending its day on admission and transfer, not arithmetic. Concretely: kernel time is a small fraction of wall time, launches scale one-to-one with request items, and per-launch fixed overhead times the launch count approaches the total. That is launch-bound; shaving FLOPs would not move wall time.

The best repair is sometimes to not use the GPU at all for this route. If the per-item work stays small and cannot be batched, because items arrive one at a time with a tight latency budget and no opportunity to coalesce, the transfer and launch will always dominate and the CPU path will keep winning. The CPU fallback condition is exactly that: when arithmetic intensity is low and batch size cannot grow, run it inline on the host and reserve the device for routes that can fill a batch.

enum Repair {
    BatchThenLaunchOnce,
    FuseAdjacentKernels,
    ReuseDeviceBuffers,
    FallBackToCpu,
}

struct PathProfile {
    launch_count: u64,
    kernel_us: u64,
    wall_us: u64,
    batchable: bool,
}

fn diagnose(p: &PathProfile) -> Repair {
    let launch_bound = p.launch_count > 1 && p.kernel_us * 4 < p.wall_us;
    if launch_bound && p.batchable {
        Repair::BatchThenLaunchOnce
    } else if !p.batchable {
        // small, un-coalescable, latency-bound work: keep it on the CPU
        Repair::FallBackToCpu
    } else {
        Repair::ReuseDeviceBuffers
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = PathProfile { launch_count: 5_000, kernel_us: 2, wall_us: 24, batchable: true };
    let _ = (Repair::FuseAdjacentKernels, diagnose(&p));
}

Batch first when work is launch-bound and batchable; fall back to CPU when items cannot be coalesced.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Batching is named as the first repair and an un-batchable, low-intensity route is named as the CPU fallback condition.
  • The path is explained through transfer, launch, and synchronization overhead rather than 'GPU is faster'.
  • Launch count, queue wait, and per-launch kernel time are cited as the profiling signals that identify launch-bound behavior.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Profile a CUDA workload before rewriting the kernel

Break the 24 ms wall time into named stages and diagnose from the largest one, not from the kernel. The report gives kernel 2 ms, host-device copies 11 ms, queue wait 6 ms, and total 24 ms. Kernel math is only 2 of 24 ms, about 8 percent; copies are 11 ms and queue wait is 6 ms, which together are 17 ms, roughly 70 percent of the wall time. The remaining few milliseconds are launch and synchronization slack.

The dominant category is transfer and admission, not kernel arithmetic. Copies at 11 ms are the single largest stage and the queue wait at 6 ms says requests are also spending real time before the device even accepts them. The first diagnosis is that this batch scorer is transfer-bound with a secondary admission problem, and the kernel is comfortably the cheapest part of the round trip.

The premature rewrite is low-level kernel tuning. Optimizing instruction selection, occupancy, or shared-memory layout would attack the 2 ms stage and, even if it halved kernel time, would shave at most about 1 ms off a 24 ms wall time. That is the classic mistake the chapter warns against: a kernel-only profile cannot tell you whether you are transfer-bound, and here the rest of the report says plainly that you are. Kernel tuning is the wrong first target.

The next measurement is inside the transfer category. Split the 11 ms of copies into host-to-device and device-to-host, and check whether inputs are being re-sent each call when they could be resident on the device, and whether the copies overlap with compute or serialize against it. If inputs are static, cache them on the device and stream only the per-request payload; if copies serialize, move to pinned host memory and asynchronous copies so transfer and kernel overlap. In parallel, measure batch size against the queue to see whether the 6 ms wait is a batching or concurrency limit. The validation metric after the fix is wall time per request and the transfer share of it: success is the copy stage shrinking as a fraction of a falling wall time, with kernel time deliberately left untouched until it actually dominates.

struct Stages { kernel_ms: f64, copy_ms: f64, queue_ms: f64, wall_ms: f64 }

fn dominant(s: &Stages) -> &'static str {
    let admission = s.copy_ms + s.queue_ms;
    if admission > s.kernel_ms { "transfer/admission-bound" } else { "kernel-bound" }
}

fn main() {
    let s = Stages { kernel_ms: 2.0, copy_ms: 11.0, queue_ms: 6.0, wall_ms: 24.0 };
    println!("diagnosis = {}", dominant(&s));         // transfer/admission-bound
    println!("kernel share = {:.0}%", 100.0 * s.kernel_ms / s.wall_ms); // 8%
    // next: split copy_ms into HtoD/DtoH, cache static inputs, overlap copies.
}

Copies plus queue wait are ~70% of wall time; kernel math is ~8%, so kernel tuning is premature.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Transfer and admission cost (11 ms copies plus 6 ms queue) is identified as dominant over the 2 ms kernel.
  • Low-level kernel tuning is rejected as a premature optimization target given the profile.
  • The next measurement (split HtoD/DtoH, check resident inputs) and a validation metric (transfer share of a falling wall time) are both proposed.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Integrate a GPU worker into an async and distributed service

Treat the single device as a scarce shared worker behind one bounded queue, and make admission, ownership, retry, and replay policy explicit before the first incident. The pipeline is ingest -> parse -> score on GPU -> persist -> notify, traffic is bursty, there is one device per host, and duplicate replay must stay harmless after crash recovery.

The bounded GPU queue sits at the single admission point in front of the score stage, and it owns the device, the persistent device buffers, and the right to decide what runs next. There is exactly one consumer task draining this queue and driving the one device; async tasks upstream can generate work far faster than a single GPU can absorb it, so the queue is where backpressure lives. When it is full, ingest must slow, shed, or route to a CPU fallback rather than pile unbounded work onto a device that cannot keep up. Making this the one explicit choke point keeps the GPU from being treated as a free fan-out target.

The async side hands over owned data, not borrowed views, at the moment it enqueues. A request-local borrow cannot cross into the GPU worker, because the worker outlives the request task and may hold the payload across awaits and a multi-millisecond round trip; a borrowed buffer that outlives its request is exactly the dangling-reference failure the chapter flags. So parse produces an owned, Send payload (an owned Vec or boxed buffer) and moves it into the queue, transferring ownership to the worker. The worker copies it to the device, runs the kernel, and returns an owned result downstream.

Separate transient GPU retry from terminal failure with a typed error and a budget. Transient conditions (device busy, queue full, a recoverable launch error, a transfer hiccup) are retried a bounded number of times with backoff and may fall back to the CPU path when the retry budget is exhausted; terminal conditions (malformed input, a shape that can never be valid, a persistent device fault) fail the item outright and surface to the caller. Crucially, completion must be idempotent so replay after a crash or lease expiry is harmless: stamp each work item with a stable request id, make persist an upsert keyed by that id, and make notify deduplicate on it, so re-scoring a replayed item produces the same persisted record rather than a double write. Combined with a lease on the in-flight item, a crash mid-score simply lets the item time out and be re-admitted exactly once in effect.

Require observability before rollout, at least: queue age or wait time at the admission point, transfer bytes per request in each direction, launch count per second, and CPU-fallback rate. Add device utilization and per-stage latency so you can tell transfer-bound from launch-bound from genuinely kernel-bound under real load, which is the whole point of refusing to ship the boundary on faith.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

/// Owned payload moved across the async-to-GPU boundary; never a borrowed request view.
struct ScoreJob { request_id: u64, input: Vec<f32> }

enum GpuError { Transient, Terminal }

struct GpuQueue {
    capacity: usize,
    pending: VecDeque<ScoreJob>, // the one bounded admission point
}

impl GpuQueue {
    fn admit(&mut self, job: ScoreJob) -> Result<(), ScoreJob> {
        if self.pending.len() >= self.capacity {
            return Err(job); // full: caller sheds, backpressures, or routes to CPU
        }
        self.pending.push_back(job);
        Ok(())
    }
}

fn classify(err: &GpuError, retries_left: u32) -> &'static str {
    match err {
        GpuError::Transient if retries_left > 0 => "retry on GPU",
        GpuError::Transient => "fall back to CPU",
        GpuError::Terminal => "fail item",
    }
}

// persist is an upsert keyed by request_id, so replay after crash is idempotent.
fn persist_idempotent(request_id: u64, _result: f32) { let _ = request_id; }

One bounded queue owns the device; owned jobs cross the boundary; retry, fallback, and idempotent persist are explicit.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • A single bounded admission queue in front of the score stage owns the device and its buffers.
  • Owned, Send payloads are moved into the worker rather than borrowed request-local views.
  • Idempotent completion (stable request id, upsert persist, lease) makes crash and lease-expiry replay harmless.
  • At least three observability hooks are required: queue age, transfer bytes, launch count, and CPU-fallback rate.

Lab solution

This is the real thing: a CUDA C kernel (a string compiled to PTX at run time by NVRTC) launched through cudarc with one GPU thread per output element, measured against a cache-friendly i-k-j CPU baseline.

The kernel maps row/col from the 2-D block and grid indices, guards the N x N bounds, accumulates the dot product of A's row and B's column, and writes one C[row*N + col]. The host code copies A and B to the device, launches a 16x16-thread grid sized by div_ceil(N, 16), synchronizes, and copies C back. It times the GPU two ways: the kernel alone, and the end-to-end path including the host<->device copies.

Both numbers matter. The kernel speedup (~50x on an RTX 3080 at N=1024) is what the GPU is capable of; the end-to-end speedup (~9x) is what you actually get once the O(N^2) PCIe transfers are paid for around a single O(N^3) multiply. That gap is the chapter's transfer-budget lesson made concrete: GPU wins scale with compute done per byte moved, so larger matrices — or keeping data resident on the device across many kernels — widen the real-world win. The correctness check (max relative error below 1e-3) confirms the GPU and CPU agree to f32 precision.

Note

This lab depends on an external crate or toolchain (for example tokio, tracing, crossbeam, MPI, or a GPU SDK), so the listing below is a reference solution rather than a standalone rustc-only program.

Example 37-S. matmul_challenge.rs — Reference solution

//! Chapter 37 — real CUDA from Rust (SOLUTION).
//!
//! Multiplies two N x N f32 matrices on the GPU with a CUDA kernel (compiled at
//! run time by NVRTC, launched through cudarc), times it against a cache-friendly
//! CPU baseline, checks the two results agree, and prints the speedup.
//!
//! Run:  cargo run --release --bin matmul_solution [N]      (default N = 1024)

use cudarc::driver::{CudaDevice, LaunchAsync, LaunchConfig};
use cudarc::nvrtc::compile_ptx;
use std::time::Instant;

/// One CUDA thread computes one output element C[row][col].
const KERNEL: &str = r#"
extern "C" __global__ void matmul(const float* A, const float* B, float* C, int N) {
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (row < N && col < N) {
        float acc = 0.0f;
        for (int k = 0; k < N; ++k) {
            acc += A[row * N + k] * B[k * N + col];
        }
        C[row * N + col] = acc;
    }
}
"#;

/// CPU baseline in i-k-j order so the inner loop walks memory sequentially —
/// a fair fight, not a strawman.
fn cpu_matmul(a: &[f32], b: &[f32], n: usize) -> Vec<f32> {
    let mut c = vec![0.0f32; n * n];
    for i in 0..n {
        for k in 0..n {
            let aik = a[i * n + k];
            let brow = &b[k * n..k * n + n];
            let crow = &mut c[i * n..i * n + n];
            for j in 0..n {
                crow[j] += aik * brow[j];
            }
        }
    }
    c
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let n: usize = std::env::args().nth(1).and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(1024);
    let a: Vec<f32> = (0..n * n).map(|i| ((i % 13) as f32) * 0.5).collect();
    let b: Vec<f32> = (0..n * n).map(|i| ((i % 7) as f32) * 0.25).collect();

    // --- CPU ---
    let t = Instant::now();
    let c_cpu = cpu_matmul(&a, &b, n);
    let cpu_ms = t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3;

    // --- GPU setup: open the device, compile the kernel, fetch the function ---
    let dev = CudaDevice::new(0)?;
    dev.load_ptx(compile_ptx(KERNEL)?, "matmul_mod", &["matmul"])?;
    let func = dev.get_func("matmul_mod", "matmul").unwrap();

    let block = 16u32;
    let grid = (n as u32).div_ceil(block);
    let cfg = LaunchConfig {
        grid_dim: (grid, grid, 1),
        block_dim: (block, block, 1),
        shared_mem_bytes: 0,
    };

    // --- GPU run: time the end-to-end path and the kernel on its own ---
    let t_total = Instant::now();
    let a_d = dev.htod_copy(a)?;
