    let b_d = dev.htod_copy(b)?;
    let mut c_d = dev.alloc_zeros::<f32>(n * n)?;
    dev.synchronize()?;

    let t_kernel = Instant::now();
    unsafe { func.launch(cfg, (&a_d, &b_d, &mut c_d, n as i32))?; }
    dev.synchronize()?;
    let kernel_ms = t_kernel.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3;

    let c_gpu = dev.dtoh_sync_copy(&c_d)?;
    let total_ms = t_total.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3;

    // --- correctness: max relative difference between CPU and GPU results ---
    let (mut max_abs, mut max_val) = (0.0f32, 1.0f32);
    for (x, y) in c_cpu.iter().zip(c_gpu.iter()) {
        max_abs = max_abs.max((x - y).abs());
        max_val = max_val.max(x.abs());
    }
    let correct = (max_abs / max_val) < 1e-3;

    println!("device     = {}", dev.name()?);
    println!("matrix     = {n} x {n} (f32)");
    println!("cpu        = {cpu_ms:.1} ms");
    println!("gpu kernel = {kernel_ms:.2} ms");
    println!("gpu total  = {total_ms:.1} ms  (incl. host<->device copies)");
    println!("speedup    = {:.1}x kernel, {:.1}x end-to-end", cpu_ms / kernel_ms, cpu_ms / total_ms);
    println!("correct    = {correct}");
    Ok(())
}
Output
device     = NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Laptop GPU
matrix     = 1024 x 1024 (f32)
cpu        = 116.3 ms
gpu kernel = 2.35 ms
gpu total  = 12.7 ms  (incl. host<->device copies)
speedup    = 49.4x kernel, 9.1x end-to-end
correct    = true

Review question answers

What kinds of workloads actually amortize host-device transfer and launch cost well?

Workloads with high arithmetic intensity and a large enough batch: they do a great deal of computation per byte moved across the bus, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the host-to-device and device-to-host copies behind it, and the per-launch fixed cost is spread across many items. Dense, regular, batched math like a large GEMM or a batched tensor operation is the canonical fit. Small, low-intensity, bandwidth-limited work such as a vector add or a tiny per-request transform does not amortize the boundary and usually loses to the CPU, because the copy and launch dominate the trivial arithmetic.

Why is a safe Rust wrapper around a kernel launch mostly an ownership and invariant story?

Because the kernel call itself is one small unsafe operation, and everything dangerous around it is shape and lifetime: matching buffer lengths, nonzero grid and block counts, and device buffers that genuinely outlive the launch. The safe wrapper's job is to check those invariants in ordinary Rust and to own the device buffers so they cannot dangle, returning a Result that names any failure, leaving the unsafe block to do nothing but the launch. In C++ host code these invariants live in convention and review comments, where a mismatched length is silent corruption; Rust moves them into the type system and the wrapper, so the GPU boundary follows the same FFI discipline used elsewhere in the book.

What is the practical difference between host memory ownership and device memory ownership?

Host memory and device memory are two separate domains with separate allocators, and a pointer into one is meaningless in the other; a Vec<T> on the host is not addressable by the kernel, and a device buffer is not addressable by host code. So a device allocation needs its own owner whose Drop frees the device memory, distinct from any host Vec, and data only crosses between them through an explicit copy. The practical consequence is that the host wrapper must decide when device buffers exist and when they disappear, and must never let a kernel hold a pointer into host memory or into a device buffer that has already been freed.

Why are queue wait and launch count often more useful than one isolated kernel timing?

Because a kernel-only profile cannot tell you whether you are transfer-bound, launch-bound, queue-bound, or actually kernel-bound, and in service code the kernel is usually the cheapest stage. A high launch count with microsecond kernels signals a launch-bound path that wants batching or fusion, and a large queue wait signals an admission or concurrency limit in front of the device, neither of which a fast kernel time would reveal. Wall time should drive the first question; breaking it into named stages (queue, copy, launch, kernel, sync) tells you which cost to attack and keeps you from tuning arithmetic that was never the bottleneck.

When is CUDA the wrong choice even when a kernel itself is efficient?

When the surrounding system, not the kernel, dominates the cost: the work is too small to amortize the transfer and launch, the path launches too many tiny kernels, it copies too much across the bus, or one shared device has no admission control and becomes a contention point. An efficient kernel does not help if each request pays a full round trip and a synchronize for a trivial payload, which is the tiny-kernel service that loses to the CPU. In those cases the right answer is to batch, fuse, cache resident inputs, or keep the route on the CPU entirely, because the failure is a systems and ownership problem, not a kernel one.

Chapter 38 · Merkle Tree Games and Challenges

Merkle Tree Games and Challenges

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the chapter's central claim seriously: a Merkle tree is a commitment layer first and a navigation tree a distant second. The warm-ups force you to write down the policy that the hash itself never carries, the implementation work builds a flat owner that holds its levels directly, and the debugging work hunts the orientation and encoding disagreements that make two locally correct programs reject each other's proofs.

The through-line is ownership discipline. The commitment is an owned, immutable byte structure; the proof is a small bundle of copyable value types that crosses process boundaries cleanly; the parallel build stages work strictly level by level so the dependency graph stays vertical. By the end you should be able to defend leaf encoding, node domain separation, odd-leaf policy, sibling orientation, and the proof envelope as explicit protocol decisions rather than implementation accidents.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

State the commitment policy before you state the code

A Merkle root is 32 bytes (or in the chapter's demo, four) with no self-description. Two teams can each write a locally correct implementation and still produce different roots from the same file, because the root is a deterministic function of a policy that the hash never carries. The exercise is to make that policy explicit so another process can reproduce it.

Leaf encoding: at the leaf boundary you hash the raw chunk bytes with a leaf domain tag. The chapter's hash_leaf calls hash_bytes(0, text.as_bytes()) — the 0 is the domain separator. So the policy is "hash the exact chunk bytes, prefixed by tag 0," and you must also pin the chunk size, because where you cut the file determines which bytes land in which leaf.

Node encoding: internal nodes hash the concatenation of their two child hashes under a different domain tag. hash_node packs left and right as little-endian bytes and calls hash_bytes(1, ...). The tag 1 versus tag 0 is the domain separation that stops a leaf and an internal node from ever colliding — without it, an attacker could present an internal node's preimage as if it were a leaf (a second-preimage / type-confusion attack). The policy must also fix byte order (the chapter uses little-endian) and child order (left then right), because both feed into the hash.

Odd-leaf policy: when a level has an odd count, you must say what happens to the last unpaired hash. The chapter duplicates it — right = if pair.len() == 2 { pair[1] } else { pair[0] } — promoting a lone node by hashing it with itself. That is one defensible choice; promoting the node unchanged to the next level is another. The point is not which you pick but that you pick one and write it down, because the two choices yield different roots for the same odd-count input.

Proof envelope: a bare sibling list is not verifiable across processes. The contract must carry the leaf_index and leaf_count (so the verifier can reconstruct sibling orientation and the odd-leaf decisions at each level), the sibling hashes themselves, and policy identifiers — hash_alg and tree_version — so the receiver knows which rules produced the root. Drop any of these and the proof becomes ambiguous.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Leaf encoding (tag 0 over raw chunk bytes, plus chunk size) and node encoding (tag 1 over little-endian child concatenation) are defined separately.
  • Odd-leaf policy is chosen explicitly — duplicate the lone node — and justified against the alternative of promoting it unchanged.
  • The proof contract names leaf_index, leaf_count, and sibling orientation, plus hash_alg and tree_version for cross-process reproducibility.
Exercise 2code reading

Read a pointer tree and explain why flat levels are calmer

The Rc<Node> design models the tree as a pointer graph: each node owns reference-counted handles to its children (and perhaps its parent). That is the instinct a C++ or object-oriented background brings, and it is the wrong reflex here. A Merkle tree's two real operations — produce the root and produce or verify a sibling path — never require pointer navigation. They are linear folds over arrays.

Serialization: the flat Vec<Vec<Hash>> design serializes trivially because it is already plain owned data — nested vectors of fixed-size hashes with no aliasing. The Rc design cannot be serialized as-is; you must flatten it first, which means the pointer graph was incidental machinery you pay to build and then pay again to undo. Proof steps as value types (ProofStep { sibling, sibling_is_left }) are Copy and self-contained, so they cross a queue or a process boundary as bytes with no lifetime or reference-count baggage.

Parallelism: flat levels parallelize cleanly because each level is a contiguous slice you can split into independent pair-hashing jobs (the chapter's par_chunks(2) shape). The Rc graph fights this — Rc is not Send, so shared nodes cannot move across threads without switching to Arc, and even then the pointer-chasing access pattern is cache-hostile compared to scanning a flat array.

Copy-on-write snapshots: when one leaf changes, only the log2(n) nodes on its path to the root change. A flat representation makes a persistent snapshot by sharing the untouched level slices and rewriting just the affected path — the chapter's persistent-tree idea. A pointer tree can do structural sharing too, but it carries Rc's runtime reference counting on every node for a navigation capability the workload does not use.

The tradeoff: if a system later needs richer navigation — range queries, subtree iteration, mutable in-place updates with parent back-pointers — then an explicit node structure starts to earn its cost. But the chapter's framing is that Merkle trees are commitment layers first and navigation trees second, so the flat representation is the calm default and you reach for pointers only when a concrete navigation requirement appears.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that root computation and proof generation/verification are linear folds over arrays, so a pointer graph is unnecessary for this workload.
  • Identifies flat-level wins: trivial serialization of nested vectors and copyable value-type proof steps, plus clean slice-based parallelism (Rc is not Send).
  • Names the tradeoff: a pointer/node structure starts to pay off only if richer navigation — range queries, subtree iteration, in-place mutation — is later required.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a basic Merkle tree API

The owner is a MerkleTree holding levels: Vec<Vec<Hash>>. Level 0 is the leaf hashes; each subsequent level is built by folding the one below it in chunks of two; the root is the single element of the last level. There is no Rc, RefCell, or raw pointer anywhere — the tree owns its hashed levels directly, which keeps it both Send and trivially serializable.

from_leaves hashes every leaf with the leaf domain tag, then loops while the top level has more than one element. Each iteration walks the current level in chunks(2). The odd-leaf case is explicit in the build loop: when a chunk has length 1, the lone hash is duplicated (right = pair[0]) so it can still produce a parent. That single line is the odd-leaf policy from Exercise 1 made concrete.

proof(index) is sibling selection plus parent-index movement. At each level except the root, the sibling sits at index ^ 1 conceptually: if index is even the sibling is to the right at index + 1 (clamped to the last element to honor the duplicate-on-odd policy), and if index is odd the sibling is to the left at index - 1. Each step records the sibling hash and an orientation bit, sibling_is_left = sibling_index < index. Then index /= 2 moves to the parent for the next level. Because each ProofStep is a small Copy value, the returned Vec<ProofStep> moves across boundaries without borrowing into the tree — the proof outlives nothing in the owner.

This is the chapter's Example 1 structure. Verification (shown for the lab) reverses the fold: start from the leaf hash and, at each step, combine in the recorded order — hash_node(sibling, acc) when the sibling was on the left, hash_node(acc, sibling) when it was on the right — and compare the final accumulator to the expected root.

type Hash = u32;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct ProofStep {
    sibling: Hash,
    sibling_is_left: bool,
}

fn hash_bytes(tag: u8, bytes: &[u8]) -> Hash {
    let mut hash = 2_166_136_261_u32 ^ tag as u32;
    for &byte in bytes {
        hash ^= byte as u32;
        hash = hash.wrapping_mul(16_777_619);
    }
    hash
}

fn hash_leaf(text: &str) -> Hash {
    hash_bytes(0, text.as_bytes())
}

fn hash_node(left: Hash, right: Hash) -> Hash {
    let mut bytes = [0_u8; 8];
    bytes[..4].copy_from_slice(&left.to_le_bytes());
    bytes[4..].copy_from_slice(&right.to_le_bytes());
    hash_bytes(1, &bytes)
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MerkleTree {
    levels: Vec<Vec<Hash>>,
}

impl MerkleTree {
    fn from_leaves(leaves: &[&str]) -> Self {
        assert!(!leaves.is_empty(), "a Merkle tree needs at least one leaf");
        let mut levels = vec![leaves.iter().map(|l| hash_leaf(l)).collect::<Vec<_>>()];

        while levels.last().unwrap().len() > 1 {
            let current = levels.last().unwrap();
            let mut next = Vec::with_capacity((current.len() + 1) / 2);
            for pair in current.chunks(2) {
                let left = pair[0];
                // Odd-leaf policy: duplicate the lone hash so it still forms a parent.
                let right = if pair.len() == 2 { pair[1] } else { pair[0] };
                next.push(hash_node(left, right));
            }
            levels.push(next);
        }
        Self { levels }
    }

    fn root(&self) -> Hash {
        self.levels.last().unwrap()[0]
    }

    fn proof(&self, mut index: usize) -> Vec<ProofStep> {
        let mut proof = Vec::new();
        for level in &self.levels[..self.levels.len() - 1] {
            let sibling_index = if index % 2 == 0 {
                (index + 1).min(level.len() - 1)
            } else {
                index - 1
            };
            proof.push(ProofStep {
                sibling: level[sibling_index],
                sibling_is_left: sibling_index < index,
            });
            index /= 2;
        }
        proof
    }
}

fn verify_proof(leaf: &str, proof: &[ProofStep], expected_root: Hash) -> bool {
    let mut acc = hash_leaf(leaf);
    for step in proof {
        acc = if step.sibling_is_left {
            hash_node(step.sibling, acc)
        } else {
            hash_node(acc, step.sibling)
        };
    }
    acc == expected_root
}

fn main() {
    let leaves = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta"];
    let tree = MerkleTree::from_leaves(&leaves);
    let proof = tree.proof(2);
    println!("proof len = {}", proof.len());
    println!("verified = {}", verify_proof("gamma", &proof, tree.root()));
}

Flat Vec<Vec<Hash>> owner; from_leaves makes odd-leaf duplication explicit and proof returns copyable sibling steps.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The tree owns its hashed levels directly as Vec<Vec<Hash>> with no Rc, RefCell, or raw pointers.
  • Proof generation returns a deterministic sibling path with orientation, via sibling selection plus index /= 2 parent movement.
  • Flat owned vectors and Copy ProofStep values keep the design trivially serializable and movable.
  • Running main proves leaf 'gamma' (index 2): verified = true.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a proof verifier that forgot orientation

The defect is that the verifier combines its running hash with each sibling in one fixed order, ignoring whether the sibling sat on the left or the right of the current node. Hashing is not commutative: hash_node(a, b) is a different value from hash_node(b, a). So a verifier that always computes hash_node(acc, sibling) will reconstruct the wrong root for every leaf whose proof contains even one left-sibling step, and will reject a perfectly valid proof.

Sibling order is part of the proof contract because the orientation bit is exactly the information the verifier needs to reproduce the producer's folding order. The sibling hash alone tells you what to combine; it does not tell you in which slot. The chapter encodes this as ProofStep::sibling_is_left, derivable from the leaf index because a node's parity at each level decides whether its sibling is the left or right child.

The fix is a branch on that bit: when the sibling was on the left, compute hash_node(sibling, acc); when it was on the right, compute hash_node(acc, sibling). That is the orientation logic in verify_proof.

The test vector that catches this immediately is the smallest balanced tree, four leaves [alpha, beta, gamma, delta]. Prove gamma at index 2. Its first sibling is delta on the right (so hash_node(acc, delta)); its second sibling is the left subtree root hash_node(alpha, beta) on the left (so hash_node(left, acc)). A verifier with a fixed order gets the second step backwards and fails to match the root, while the corrected branch reproduces it exactly. This is the same family of bug as a canonical-serialization mismatch: if two sides disagree on child byte order, endianness, or which tag separates leaves from nodes, both compute locally consistent but mutually incompatible roots — the disagreement is in the policy, not the hash function.

// BUGGY: fixed order ignores which side the sibling was on.
fn verify_proof_buggy(leaf: &str, proof: &[ProofStep], expected_root: Hash) -> bool {
    let mut acc = hash_leaf(leaf);
    for step in proof {
        acc = hash_node(acc, step.sibling); // wrong for every left sibling
    }
    acc == expected_root
}

// FIXED: branch on the recorded orientation bit.
fn verify_proof(leaf: &str, proof: &[ProofStep], expected_root: Hash) -> bool {
    let mut acc = hash_leaf(leaf);
    for step in proof {
        acc = if step.sibling_is_left {
            hash_node(step.sibling, acc) // sibling || acc
        } else {
            hash_node(acc, step.sibling) // acc || sibling
        };
    }
    acc == expected_root
}

// Deterministic test that traps the bug: the four-leaf tree, proving gamma (index 2).
// proof = [ {delta, is_left=false}, {hash_node(alpha,beta), is_left=true} ]
// The second step is a LEFT sibling, so the buggy version produces the wrong root.

The orientation branch (sibling||acc vs acc||sibling) is the contract; the four-leaf gamma proof exposes the fixed-order bug.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names the bug concretely: hashing is non-commutative, so a fixed combine order rebuilds the wrong root whenever a sibling is on the left.
  • Repairs the verifier with an explicit left-or-right branch: hash_node(sibling, acc) versus hash_node(acc, sibling).
  • Cites the four-leaf tree proving gamma at index 2 as the minimal test, whose second (left-sibling) step the buggy version gets wrong.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Parallelize the wide levels, not the whole idea blindly

Merkle construction is a textbook fan-in, and its dependency graph is purely vertical: within one level every parent depends only on its own pair of children, on nothing else at that level, and level k+1 cannot begin until level k is complete. So the independent unit of work is the pair-hash inside a single level, and the synchronization point is the level boundary. You parallelize across the pairs of one wide level, then join, then advance. You never try to parallelize across levels — that would violate the vertical dependency.

The build keeps the same flat ownership model as the serial version. Each level is a contiguous &[Hash] slice; splitting it into independent ranges (the chapter's par_chunks(2) shape, or scoped threads dividing the slice) hands each worker an owned-by-borrow sub-slice that produces a Vec<Hash>, and the results collect back into the next level in order. Because the data is plain Hash values with no aliasing, the parallel reducer and the serial reducer are interchangeable — build_root(leaves, next_level) and build_root(leaves, next_level_parallel) must return the same root, which the chapter's Example 2 asserts.

The threshold matters because each round halves the level width. The bottom levels are wide and worth splitting; the top few levels have a handful of elements, where thread spawn and join cost dominates the work. So the parallel reducer should fall back to serial below a cutoff — the chapter uses if level.len() <= 2 — and a production version would set that cutoff higher (a few thousand pairs) and tune it per machine. Parallelizing tiny upper levels only adds scheduler cost.

The metric that confirms the win is end-to-end build latency for the target batch size, not microbenchmarks of one level. Compare wall-clock build time serial versus parallel across realistic leaf counts, and watch CPU utilization (the parallel path should keep cores busy on wide levels) and batch throughput (trees built per second). If latency does not drop at your real leaf counts, the parallelism is overhead and the cutoff should be raised — possibly to infinity, meaning serial is correct for that workload.

fn next_level(level: &[Hash]) -> Vec<Hash> {
    let mut next = Vec::with_capacity((level.len() + 1) / 2);
    for pair in level.chunks(2) {
        let left = pair[0];
        let right = if pair.len() == 2 { pair[1] } else { pair[0] };
        next.push(hash_node(left, right));
    }
    next
}

const SERIAL_CUTOFF: usize = 2; // raise in production; tune per machine

fn next_level_parallel(level: &[Hash]) -> Vec<Hash> {
    // Below the cutoff, thread spawn/join dominates the actual hashing.
    if level.len() <= SERIAL_CUTOFF {
        return next_level(level);
    }
    // Split this ONE level into independent pair ranges; never split across levels.
    let pair_count = (level.len() + 1) / 2;
    let split = (pair_count / 2 * 2).max(2).min(level.len());
    std::thread::scope(|scope| {
        let (left, right) = (&level[..split], &level[split..]);
        let lh = scope.spawn(move || next_level(left));
        let rh = scope.spawn(move || next_level(right));
        let mut out = lh.join().unwrap();
        out.extend(rh.join().unwrap());
        out // identical ordering to the serial reducer -> identical root
    })
}

Independent work is pair-hashing within a level; the cutoff falls back to serial once a level is small enough that scheduling dominates.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Parallelizes pair-hashing within a single level only, respecting the vertical dependency that level k+1 waits for level k.
  • Defines an explicit serial-fallback threshold (level.len() <= cutoff) for tiny upper levels.
  • Keeps the flat Vec<Hash> ownership model identical, so serial and parallel reducers are interchangeable and produce the same root.
  • Names a measurement — end-to-end build latency at target leaf counts, plus CPU utilization or batch throughput — to confirm the win.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose challenge tracks for content-addressed storage, game integrity, and distributed verification

The three tracks share the commitment-plus-proof core but pull on different trust problems, so each gets its own ownership boundary, durability rule, and execution budget. The discipline is to keep commitment policy, storage policy, and execution policy separate rather than collapsing all three into one slogan.

Content-addressed chunk store. The Merkle root becomes the address: a blob is named by its root, and a fetch is valid only if the recomputed root matches the name. Ownership boundary: the store owns immutable chunks keyed by leaf hash and immutable roots keyed by content; nothing is ever updated in place, which gives free deduplication (identical chunks share a hash) and free tamper-evidence (a corrupted byte changes the address). Durability: roots and chunk hashes must outlive any single process, persisted to durable storage so a client can re-verify a download months later. This is the system that most needs versioned proof envelopes across services — hash_alg and tree_version pinned per blob — because content stored under one policy must still verify after the producer upgrades. Observability: proof-failure rate on fetch, because a rising mismatch rate signals either corruption or a policy drift between producer and consumer.

Tamper-evident game checkpoint feed. The backend periodically commits the match state into a checkpoint root and publishes it; later, any disputed move can be checked against a snapshot root. Ownership boundary: the checkpoint log owns an append-only sequence of roots, each a commitment to the state at that tick; the live game state is mutable, but the published roots are immutable once emitted. Durability: snapshot roots must be durable enough for replay and dispute resolution — this is the system whose roots most need to survive, because the whole value is being able to reconstruct or contest history after the fact (the Chapter 31 replay/lineage idea applied to game state). Execution: publication is steady and modest, so no large worker pool is needed; what matters is a bounded, reliable emit path. Observability: checkpoint publication lag — how far behind real time the latest durable root is — because a stalled feed silently loses the very history it exists to protect.

Distributed verification service. Clients submit inclusion proofs; the service checks them before authorizing or downloading the full payload, so a bad proof is rejected cheaply. Ownership boundary: the verifier owns only the trusted root(s) and a bounded worker pool; it borrows each incoming proof, verifies it, and keeps no per-request state. This is the system that most wants batch verification and bounded worker pools — proofs arrive in bursts, verification is independent per proof, and a fixed pool with a bounded queue (the Chapter 37 budgeting discipline) keeps tail latency predictable. Budgets: bound the queue depth, set a per-proof timeout, and apply bounded retries only for transient transport failures, never for cryptographic rejections (a failed verification is a final answer, not a retry candidate). Observability: oldest-queue-age and proof-failure rate, so you can tell a backlog (raise workers) apart from an attack or a policy mismatch (a spike in rejections).

Across all three, the failure and observability signals required before rollout are: proof-failure rate (correctness and policy drift), oldest queue age or checkpoint publication lag (liveness), and an explicit alarm when a verifier's trusted-root set or tree_version no longer matches what producers are emitting.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Describes all three systems with distinct goals: content-addressed store, tamper-evident checkpoint feed, and proof-checking verifier service.
  • Gives each an ownership or durability boundary: immutable content-keyed chunks, append-only durable snapshot roots, and a stateless verifier owning only trusted roots and a worker pool.
  • Places batching/queue/retry budgets where justified: bounded worker pool and queue with retries only for transport (not cryptographic) failures in the verifier.
  • Includes observability hooks per system: proof-failure rate, checkpoint publication lag, and oldest-queue-age.

Lab solution

The lab builds a fixed four-leaf tree by hand so the proof is unambiguous. The leaves are the FNV-style demo hashes of "alpha", "beta", "gamma", and "delta". The two intermediate nodes are left = hash_node(alpha, beta) and right = hash_node(gamma, delta), and the root is hash_node(left, right). The proof for gamma (which sits at index 2, the left child of the right subtree) has two steps: first its sibling delta on the right, then the left subtree root left on the left.

The only code to fill in is verify_proof. It seeds an accumulator with hash_leaf(leaf) and folds up the tree, and the single decision that makes it correct is honoring each step's orientation. Step one combines as hash_node(acc, delta) because delta is the right sibling, reproducing the right subtree node. Step two combines as hash_node(left, acc) because left is the left sibling, reproducing the root. For the good case the accumulator therefore equals the expected root, so it prints verified good = true.

The bad case feeds the wrong leaf string "gxmxa". Its leaf hash differs from gamma's, so every step of the fold diverges and the final accumulator no longer matches the root, printing verified bad = false. The pair of lines demonstrates both halves of an inclusion proof: a valid leaf with the right siblings verifies, and any altered leaf is rejected — which is exactly the tamper-evidence the chapter's commitment property promises.

Example 38-S. merkle_proof_verify_lab.rs — Reference solution

type Hash = u32;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct ProofStep {
    sibling: Hash,
    sibling_is_left: bool,
}

fn hash_bytes(tag: u8, bytes: &[u8]) -> Hash {
    let mut hash = 2_166_136_261_u32 ^ tag as u32;

    for &byte in bytes {
        hash ^= byte as u32;
        hash = hash.wrapping_mul(16_777_619);
    }

    hash
}

fn hash_leaf(text: &str) -> Hash {
    hash_bytes(0, text.as_bytes())
}

fn hash_node(left: Hash, right: Hash) -> Hash {
    let mut bytes = [0_u8; 8];
    bytes[..4].copy_from_slice(&left.to_le_bytes());
    bytes[4..].copy_from_slice(&right.to_le_bytes());
    hash_bytes(1, &bytes)
}

// Fold from the leaf up to the root, combining with each sibling in the
// orientation the proof records. The order is load-bearing because hashing
// is not commutative: a left sibling hashes as (sibling || acc), a right
// sibling as (acc || sibling).
fn verify_proof(leaf: &str, proof: &[ProofStep], expected_root: Hash) -> bool {
    let mut acc = hash_leaf(leaf);

    for step in proof {
        acc = if step.sibling_is_left {
            hash_node(step.sibling, acc)
        } else {
            hash_node(acc, step.sibling)
        };
    }

    acc == expected_root
}

fn main() {
    let alpha = hash_leaf("alpha");
    let beta = hash_leaf("beta");
    let gamma = hash_leaf("gamma");
    let delta = hash_leaf("delta");

    let left = hash_node(alpha, beta);
    let right = hash_node(gamma, delta);
    let root = hash_node(left, right);

    let proof = vec![
        ProofStep {
            sibling: delta,
            sibling_is_left: false,
        },
        ProofStep {
            sibling: left,
            sibling_is_left: true,
        },
    ];

    println!("verified good = {}", verify_proof("gamma", &proof, root));
    println!("verified bad = {}", verify_proof("gxmxa", &proof, root));
}
Output
verified good = true
verified bad = false

Review question answers

Why is odd-leaf handling a protocol decision rather than a local helper detail?

Because the root is a deterministic function of every leaf and of the exact rules used to fold them, and odd-leaf handling changes the bytes that get hashed at a level with an odd count. If one implementation duplicates the lone node and another promotes it unchanged to the next level, the two produce different roots from the same input while each looks locally correct. So the policy has to be agreed upon and written into the contract — alongside leaf encoding and node domain separation — because it is part of what makes a root reproducible across processes, not an internal implementation choice.

Why are flat levels usually calmer than pointer trees for Merkle workloads?

The only operations a Merkle tree actually needs — computing the root and generating or verifying a sibling path — are linear folds over arrays, not graph navigation, so a pointer structure adds ownership machinery the workload never uses. Flat Vec<Vec<Hash>> levels serialize trivially because they are plain owned data with no aliasing, and they parallelize cleanly because each level is a contiguous slice that splits into independent pair-hashing jobs (whereas Rc is not Send). Persistent copy-on-write snapshots also fall out naturally by sharing untouched level slices and rewriting only the changed path. A pointer/node design earns its cost only if the system later needs richer navigation such as range queries or in-place mutation.

What makes sibling orientation part of the proof itself?

Hashing is not commutative: hash_node(a, b) differs from hash_node(b, a), so combining a running hash with a sibling in the wrong slot rebuilds a different root. The sibling value tells the verifier what to combine but not in which position, so the proof must also carry whether each sibling was on the left or the right. With that orientation bit the verifier computes hash_node(sibling, acc) for a left sibling and hash_node(acc, sibling) for a right one, reproducing the producer's exact folding order; without it, every proof containing a left sibling is rejected even when the leaf truly belongs under the root.

When is level-wise parallelism worth the overhead, and when should it stop?

It is worth it on the wide lower levels, where there are many independent pair-hashes and the dependency graph is already staged vertically: level k+1 cannot start until level k finishes, but within a level every pair is independent, so the level is a natural fan-in to split across workers. It should stop once a level becomes small, because each round halves the width and near the root thread spawn and join cost dominates the handful of remaining hashes. A practical build sets a serial-fallback cutoff (the chapter's level.len() <= 2, raised and tuned in production) and confirms the win by measuring end-to-end build latency at realistic leaf counts rather than microbenchmarking one level.

Why should a proof envelope carry more than only the sibling hashes?

A root is just opaque bytes with no self-description, so once a proof leaves the process that built the tree, the receiver has to reproduce the producer's exact rules, and those rules are not visible in the hash. The sibling list alone cannot tell the verifier the orientation at each level or how odd levels were handled, so the envelope must also carry leaf_index and leaf_count to reconstruct the path, plus hash_alg and tree_version to identify which policy produced the root. Drop any of these and the proof becomes ambiguous: two locally correct systems can quietly disagree on encoding or odd-leaf policy and reject each other's valid proofs.

Chapter 39 · Graph Search Games

Graph Search Games

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the four classic graph traversals and treat them the way the chapter does: as data-processing components whose hardest decision is made before any algorithm runs. The first decision is storage and identity. Once nodes live in one owning table and edges hold stable NodeId handles instead of borrowed references, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, and A* all become ordinary loops over indices, and the borrow checker stops fighting your search.

The set moves from classification and code reading toward a runnable BFS over an adjacency list, then into a recursion-to-explicit-stack refactor, and finally into two production-shaped designs: a dependency resolver that must explain failure, and a distributed frontier search that must bound work and stay observable. The recurring theme is that the calm Rust graph is one owner plus handles, not a web of objects each owning its neighbors.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose adjacency list, matrix, or stable-index arena from the workload

The decision order the chapter teaches is: ask whether the graph is sparse or dense first, then ask who owns the nodes and how long edges need to stay meaningful. Apply that to each case rather than reaching for a favorite representation.

The sparse service dependency graph wants an adjacency list. Real service graphs have a handful of dependencies per node out of hundreds of services, so the edge set is tiny relative to N squared, and every traversal iterates neighbors rather than testing arbitrary pairs. An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist and gives O(degree) neighbor iteration, which is exactly the access shape BFS, DFS, and topological sort need. A matrix here would waste memory quadratically and buy nothing.

The dense all-to-all 64-node connectivity matrix justifies an adjacency matrix. The graph is both dense and fixed-size, so the quadratic storage is bounded and cheap (64x64 fits in a few kilobytes), and the workload is dominated by O(1) 'does an edge exist between i and j' lookups rather than neighbor iteration. That is the one situation where the matrix's constant-time edge test earns its space.

The long-lived mutable route graph that is serialized and reloaded wants stable indices backed by one node table (an arena-style Vec<Node>). Because it mutates over time and must round-trip through serialization, you want a single owner of nodes and edges expressed as plain NodeId values, not many cross-references. Indices serialize trivially (they are just integers), survive vector growth, and keep mutation calm because there is exactly one owner to reason about. The grid maze with uniform step cost is better modeled as a graph over (row, col) coordinates: neighbors are computed from the coordinate (up, down, left, right) instead of stored as explicit edges, so you never materialize an edge list at all and the 'graph' is implicit in the grid.

In growth terms: the matrix grows as N squared regardless of how many edges exist, which is why it only pays off when density is high. In traversal terms: the adjacency list is shaped for iteration-dominated workloads because reading a node's neighbors touches only that node's edge vector.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Adjacency-list case (sparse service graph, iteration-dominated) and adjacency-matrix case (dense fixed 64-node, O(1) lookup) are each chosen with a concrete reason.
  • The mutable serialized route graph is assigned stable indices / arena-backed ownership as the calmer default, justified by single ownership and trivially serializable integer handles.
  • The matrix is explained by N-squared memory growth and the adjacency list by O(degree) iteration shape, so one representation is explained by memory and one by traversal.
Exercise 2code reading

Explain why stable indices beat borrowed neighbors in a growable graph

The Vec<Node>-plus-usize design is the one that survives growth and serialization honestly; the Vec<Node>-plus-long-lived-&Node design is the wrong contract. Both store nodes in the same owner, so the difference is entirely in what an edge holds.

A long-lived &Node into a growable owner table is wrong because the reference borrows from storage that is allowed to move. Pushing one more node can trigger a reallocation of the backing buffer, after which every previously stored &Node points at freed memory. Rust will not even let you write this in safe code: the borrow checker ties the lifetime of each &Node to an immutable borrow of the Vec, so as long as any edge holds a borrowed neighbor you cannot call the &mut self method that adds the next node. You are forced to choose between a frozen graph and unsafe pointers. That is the borrow checker correctly refusing a design where the edge's lifetime contract ('this neighbor exists as long as I do') cannot be honored by a container that reallocates.

The stable-index version stores a NodeId (a usize newtype) per edge. An index is not a borrow, so it does not constrain mutation: you can keep adding nodes and edges while old edges remain valid, because NodeId(3) still means 'slot 3 in the table' after the table grows. What you give up is automatic invalidation. The compiler no longer proves that an index points at a live, correct node, so a stale or deleted-and-reused slot is a logic bug rather than a compile error; you carry that discipline yourself (for example, with generational indices or tombstones if nodes can be removed). What you gain is substantial: mutation stays calm, indices are trivially queueable in a VecDeque or BinaryHeap, they are cheap Copy values you can log and trace, and they serialize as plain integers with no pointer fixups on reload. This is the same owner-plus-handle shape used by many ASTs and dependency graphs.

A truly shared-owner graph still justifies Rc or Arc when ownership is genuinely shared rather than centralized in one table: nodes that outlive any single container, that are created and dropped independently by multiple subsystems, or that are reference-counted because no one component can be named as the sole owner. If you reach for Rc only to dodge the borrow checker on a graph you actually own as a batch, you have imported another language's object web; reach for it when the sharing is semantically real, such as interned values shared across several independent graphs, or a node whose lifetime is decided by reference count rather than by a parent table.

// Wrong: borrowed neighbors into growable storage.
// This does not compile, and that is the point.
struct BadNode<'a> {
    name: &'static str,
    edges: Vec<&'a BadNode<'a>>, // borrows from the same Vec
}
// Pushing a new node needs &mut Vec, but outstanding &BadNode
// hold a shared borrow of it -> cannot grow after wiring edges.

// Right: stable handles. Edges are values, not borrows.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct NodeId(usize);

struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    edges: Vec<NodeId>, // just indices; immune to reallocation
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Graph {
    nodes: Vec<Node>,
}

impl Graph {
    fn add_node(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len());
        self.nodes.push(Node { name, edges: Vec::new() });
        id // handle stays valid across every future push
    }

    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.nodes[from.0].edges.push(to);
    }
}

Borrowed neighbors deadlock against growth; NodeId handles stay valid across reallocation and serialize as plain integers.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Explains that borrowed neighbors into a growable Vec are the wrong stability model because reallocation invalidates them and the borrow checker forbids growth while they exist.
  • Names operational wins for stable indices: mutation calm, cheap queueable Copy handles, and serialization as plain integers with no pointer fixups.
  • Identifies that Rc/Arc is semantically real when ownership is genuinely shared (independent lifetimes, interned values across graphs, reference-counted node lifetime) rather than centralized in one table.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement BFS over an adjacency list with stable indices

The implementation follows the chapter's Example 1 exactly: one owning Vec<Node>, edges stored as NodeId handles, and a VecDeque for the FIFO frontier. There are no Rc, RefCell, or raw pointers anywhere, because the only thing an edge needs to remember about a neighbor is which slot it lives in.

bfs_order does a standard breadth-first sweep. A visited bitmap (Vec<bool> indexed by NodeId.0) records which nodes have already been queued so each node is enqueued at most once. We mark start visited before pushing it, then repeatedly pop the front of the queue, append it to the order, and push any unvisited neighbor (marking it visited at enqueue time, not at dequeue time). Marking on enqueue is what prevents a node from being added twice when two predecessors in the same layer both point at it.

shortest_hops counts the minimum number of edges from start to goal. Instead of a boolean visited array it uses a distance vector initialized to usize::MAX (the 'not yet reached' sentinel). The first time a node is dequeued we check whether it is the goal and return its recorded distance; otherwise each freshly reached neighbor gets dist[neighbor] = dist[current] + 1 and is enqueued. Because the queue is FIFO, nodes leave it in non-decreasing distance order (layer by layer), so the first time a node is reached is along a shortest unweighted path. That is the core BFS invariant and the reason we never need to revisit or relax a node the way Dijkstra does. The traversal is deterministic because edges are iterated in insertion order and the queue is FIFO, so the visit order is fully reproducible from the construction order.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct NodeId(usize);

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    edges: Vec<NodeId>,
}

#[derive(Default, Debug)]
struct Graph {
    nodes: Vec<Node>,
}

impl Graph {
    fn add_node(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len());
        self.nodes.push(Node { name, edges: Vec::new() });
        id
    }

    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.nodes[from.0].edges.push(to);
    }

    fn names(&self, ids: &[NodeId]) -> Vec<&'static str> {
        ids.iter().map(|id| self.nodes[id.0].name).collect()
    }

    fn bfs_order(&self, start: NodeId) -> Vec<NodeId> {
        let mut visited = vec![false; self.nodes.len()];
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
        let mut order = Vec::new();

        visited[start.0] = true;
        queue.push_back(start);

        while let Some(id) = queue.pop_front() {
            order.push(id);
            for &next in &self.nodes[id.0].edges {
                if !visited[next.0] {
                    visited[next.0] = true;
                    queue.push_back(next);
                }
            }
        }
        order
    }

    fn shortest_hops(&self, start: NodeId, goal: NodeId) -> Option<usize> {
        let mut dist = vec![usize::MAX; self.nodes.len()];
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();

        dist[start.0] = 0;
        queue.push_back(start);

        while let Some(id) = queue.pop_front() {
            if id == goal {
                return Some(dist[id.0]);
            }
            for &next in &self.nodes[id.0].edges {
                if dist[next.0] == usize::MAX {
                    dist[next.0] = dist[id.0] + 1;
                    queue.push_back(next);
                }
            }
        }
        None
    }
}

BFS and shortest-hops over one owning Vec<Node>, edges as NodeId handles, VecDeque frontier, no Rc/RefCell/raw pointers.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The graph owner is a single Vec<Node>; add_node/add_edge mutate only that table.
  • Edges are stored as NodeId handles, and bfs_order/shortest_hops operate entirely on those indices.
  • BFS uses a FIFO VecDeque and marks on enqueue, so nodes are visited in deterministic layer order.
  • Wired into the lab's main, this prints visited = api,auth,billing,search and hops = 2 as expected.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a DFS or cycle-check implementation that over-relies on recursion

The exact defect is twofold. First, recursive DFS on user-supplied graphs ties traversal depth to the OS thread stack, so a deep or adversarial dependency chain can overflow the stack and abort the process rather than returning an error you can handle. Second, the cycle check is almost certainly using a single visited bit, which cannot tell 'a node I am currently still exploring' apart from 'a node I already finished exploring on a different branch.' Confusing those two states is what produces the 'confusing re-entry bugs': revisiting an already-finished node looks identical to closing a loop, so the check either reports false cycles or misses real ones.

The fix for the depth problem is an explicit stack. Move the frontier from the call stack into a Vec you own, so depth is bounded by heap memory rather than the (much smaller, fixed) thread stack, and you can instrument it directly: log or histogram stack.len() at its peak, and you can even cap it and fail gracefully instead of crashing. An explicit stack is also far easier to pause, resume, snapshot, and rate-limit than recursion.

The fix for the correctness problem is to stop using one bit and instead track three states per node, the standard white/gray/black coloring: White means not yet seen, Gray means currently on the active DFS path (entered but not finished), and Black means fully explored. A cycle exists exactly when you reach a Gray node, because that means you have found an edge back into the path you are still walking. A Black node is simply already done and must not be reported as a cycle. The cleanest way to express this with an explicit stack is to push frames that carry the node plus the index of the next child to visit, color a node Gray when first pushed, and color it Black when its frame is popped after all children are processed; encountering a Gray neighbor mid-walk is the cycle.

To report a concrete cycle witness rather than a bare boolean, keep the current path (the chain of Gray nodes) explicitly. When you hit a Gray neighbor v, the witness is the slice of the path from v's first appearance to the current node, plus v again to close the loop. Return that Vec<NodeId> (resolved to names) so operators can see the actual cycle, not just that one exists. For production diagnostics, emit the cycle witness path on failure, a depth histogram or peak-frontier-size metric so you can see graphs that drive unusual depth, and a per-node fan-out summary (max out-degree, total edges) so an operator can spot a pathologically wide or deep submitted graph before it becomes an incident.

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Color { White, Gray, Black }

/// Iterative DFS cycle detection with an explicit stack and a
/// returned cycle witness. No recursion, so depth is bounded by
/// heap memory and can be instrumented directly.
fn find_cycle(graph: &Graph) -> Option<Vec<NodeId>> {
    let n = graph.nodes.len();
    let mut color = vec![Color::White; n];
    // Each frame: (node, index of next child to explore).
    let mut stack: Vec<(NodeId, usize)> = Vec::new();
    let mut path: Vec<NodeId> = Vec::new(); // current Gray chain
    let mut peak_depth = 0usize;

    for s in (0..n).map(NodeId) {
        if color[s.0] != Color::White {
            continue;
        }
        stack.push((s, 0));
        color[s.0] = Color::Gray;
        path.push(s);

        while let Some(&(node, child_ix)) = stack.last() {
            peak_depth = peak_depth.max(stack.len());
            let edges = &graph.nodes[node.0].edges;
            if child_ix < edges.len() {
                stack.last_mut().unwrap().1 += 1;
                let next = edges[child_ix];
                match color[next.0] {
                    Color::Gray => {
                        // Back edge into the active path: cycle witness.
                        let start = path.iter().position(|&p| p == next).unwrap();
                        let mut witness = path[start..].to_vec();
                        witness.push(next); // close the loop
                        // (peak_depth available here for a depth metric)
                        let _ = peak_depth;
                        return Some(witness);
                    }
                    Color::White => {
                        color[next.0] = Color::Gray;
                        path.push(next);
                        stack.push((next, 0));
                    }
                    Color::Black => {} // already finished, not a cycle
                }
            } else {
                color[node.0] = Color::Black; // all children done
                stack.pop();
                path.pop();
            }
        }
    }
    None
}

Explicit-stack DFS with white/gray/black coloring; reports a concrete cycle path and tracks peak depth for instrumentation.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Clearly separates traversal depth (the explicit Vec stack) from cycle state (the white/gray/black color array).
  • Proposes an explicit stack as the repair, with the reason that depth becomes heap-bounded and directly instrumentable instead of crashing the thread stack.
  • Includes production diagnostics: a concrete cycle-witness path on failure, a peak-depth/depth histogram metric, and a node fan-out summary.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design a dependency resolver challenge

The resolver is a topological sort with an explicit failure path. The design commits to three concrete choices: graph direction, the algorithmic pieces, and stable identity.

Graph direction: store edges as dependency -> dependent (an edge from A to B means 'B depends on A, so A must be built first'). This is the calm direction for a scheduler because Kahn's algorithm becomes natural: a node is ready exactly when all of its dependencies are already built, which is when its indegree (count of incoming dependency edges) drops to zero. Seeding the ready frontier with the indegree-zero nodes and decrementing successors as you emit each unit produces the execution order directly. (The reverse direction is fine too, but then 'ready' is the out-degree-zero set and the mental model is muddier; pick one and document it.)

Algorithmic pieces and how they fit: use Kahn's indegree counting plus a ready frontier (a queue or, if you want deterministic output, a sorted/min-heap frontier keyed by stable label) as the primary path, and keep a separate DFS cycle witness for the failure path. They are complementary, not redundant: Kahn's algorithm gives you the valid ordering and also detects that a cycle exists (if you emit fewer nodes than the graph contains, the un-emitted set is exactly the part trapped in cycles). But Kahn alone does not hand you a readable loop; the gray-node DFS from Exercise 4 run over the leftover nodes produces a concrete cycle path to surface. So: Kahn for the success ordering and cycle existence, DFS over the remainder for the cycle witness.

Stable identity: every node carries a stable string label (for example the build-unit name like crate@semver or a content-addressed id) interned to a NodeId index at load time. The NodeId is the internal handle used in all the vectors and queues; the label is what appears in logs, error messages, and test fixtures. This separation matters because cycle reports and replay tests must be stable across runs and across machines: integer indices are fast internally but meaningless in a log, so you always resolve back to the label when reporting. Fixtures pin the label set, so a recorded failure replays identically.

Valid ordering path: load units, compute indegrees, seed the frontier with indegree-zero units (sorted by label for determinism), then repeatedly emit the smallest-label ready unit and decrement each dependent's indegree, pushing any that reach zero. The emitted sequence is the execution order. Cycle-reporting path: if the emitted count is less than the unit count, collect the un-emitted (still-indegree-positive) units, run gray/black DFS over just those, and surface the first cycle path by label, for example billing -> reports -> billing. Return Result<Vec<NodeId>, Cycle> so callers must handle failure explicitly.

Extension / scoring track: add version-conflict and optional-edge handling. Optional (soft) edges express 'prefer A before B but it is not required'; they participate in ordering only when they do not create a cycle, and are dropped (with a warning) when they would. Version conflicts are detected before the sort: if two units pin incompatible versions of the same dependency, fail fast with both pins named, rather than producing an order that cannot actually build. A scored challenge gives Bronze for a correct order on acyclic input, Silver for a precise cycle witness on cyclic input, and Gold for resolving optional edges and reporting version conflicts with actionable messages.

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct NodeId(usize);

struct Unit { label: String, deps: Vec<NodeId> } // edges: dependency -> dependent built via indegree

#[derive(Default)]
struct Resolver { units: Vec<Unit>, by_label: BTreeMap<String, NodeId> }

enum ResolveError { Cycle(Vec<NodeId>) }

impl Resolver {
    /// Kahn's algorithm; deterministic via a sorted ready frontier.
    fn order(&self) -> Result<Vec<NodeId>, ResolveError> {
        let n = self.units.len();
        let mut indegree = vec![0usize; n];
        let mut dependents: Vec<Vec<NodeId>> = vec![Vec::new(); n];
        for (i, u) in self.units.iter().enumerate() {
            for &d in &u.deps {
                indegree[i] += 1;        // i depends on d
                dependents[d.0].push(NodeId(i));
            }
        }
        // Seed with indegree-zero units, label-sorted for stable output.
        let mut ready: VecDeque<NodeId> = (0..n)
            .map(NodeId)
            .filter(|id| indegree[id.0] == 0)
            .collect();
        sort_by_label(self, ready.make_contiguous());
        let mut emitted = Vec::with_capacity(n);
        while let Some(id) = ready.pop_front() {
            emitted.push(id);
            for &dep in &dependents[id.0] {
                indegree[dep.0] -= 1;
                if indegree[dep.0] == 0 { ready.push_back(dep); }
            }
        }
        if emitted.len() == n {
            Ok(emitted)
        } else {
            // Leftover nodes are trapped in cycles; DFS them for a witness.
            Err(ResolveError::Cycle(cycle_witness(self, &indegree)))
        }
    }
}

fn sort_by_label(_r: &Resolver, _ids: &mut [NodeId]) { /* sort by self.units[id.0].label */ }
fn cycle_witness(_r: &Resolver, _indegree: &[usize]) -> Vec<NodeId> { Vec::new() /* gray/black DFS over indegree>0 set */ }

Kahn's topological sort over dependency->dependent edges, deterministic label-sorted frontier, with a cycle-witness failure path.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines one stable identity strategy: an interned string label per unit mapped to an internal NodeId, label used for logs and fixtures.
  • Describes a valid ordering path (Kahn indegree + ready frontier) and a cycle-reporting path (DFS witness over the un-emitted set), returned as Result.
  • Adds an extension/scoring track: optional (soft) edges and version-conflict detection, scored Bronze/Silver/Gold.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design a distributed graph-search challenge with bounded frontier workers

Distributed frontier search is half algorithm and half control plane. The design keeps BFS's layer structure and parallelizes only within a layer, then specifies the message boundaries, duplicate suppression, boundedness, observability, and scoring.

Owned frontier message boundary: the unit of work crossing a worker boundary is an owned frontier chunk, a Vec<NodeId> (plus the path-cost metadata needed to publish best-path-so-far). The coordinator splits the current level's frontier into chunks and hands each chunk to a worker as an owned message; the worker expands it into a private next-frontier buffer and returns that buffer as an owned message. Nothing is shared by reference across the boundary, which is what makes the workers independent and the design safe to move across threads or processes. Each level is a synchronization point: the coordinator collects all returned buffers before starting the next level.

Duplicate suppression: discoveries must be deduplicated against a visited set so the same node is not expanded twice, which is what would otherwise turn a graph with many converging paths into infinite replay or a retry storm. Two layers of suppression: workers dedupe locally within their chunk (cheap, no contention), and the coordinator dedupes globally during the merge step by checking and inserting into the authoritative visited set as it folds the returned buffers into the next frontier. A node enters the next frontier only on its first global discovery. The merge step owns the visited set so the membership test and insert are a single atomic action at the coordinator, avoiding the race where two workers both think they were first.

Boundedness: bound worker concurrency (a fixed worker-pool size or a semaphore) so the number of in-flight chunks cannot exceed capacity, and bound the queues that carry chunks (a bounded channel with capacity limits) so a fast producer cannot pile up unbounded work. If a queue is full, the producer blocks or sheds, which applies backpressure instead of exhausting memory. The visited set's growth is naturally bounded by the node count, but the in-flight frontier is not, so the chunk queue capacity is the key bound.

Observability hooks (at least two, here several): oldest-frontier-age (how long the oldest un-expanded chunk has waited) is usually the first metric to alert, because a stuck frontier shows up as rising age before CPU does; duplicate-hit-rate (fraction of discoveries already in visited) tells you whether suppression is working and whether the graph is highly convergent; merge-lag (time the coordinator spends folding buffers per level) reveals when the merge step has become the bottleneck; and current-frontier-size per level reveals exponential blow-up early. Frontier size and duplicate rate are more diagnostic than raw CPU at first.

Scoring tracks: Bronze is a single-process, level-synchronous frontier expansion with correct dedupe against a visited set. Silver adds a real worker pool, bounded chunk queues with backpressure, and the oldest-frontier-age and duplicate-hit-rate metrics. Gold makes it distributed across processes with trace lineage (each node carries the id of the chunk and worker that discovered it so a path can be replayed and audited), publishes best-path-so-far incrementally, and alerts on oldest-frontier-age crossing a threshold.

use std::collections::HashSet;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, std::hash::Hash)]
struct NodeId(usize);

/// One owned frontier chunk crosses the worker boundary.
struct Chunk { nodes: Vec<NodeId> }

/// Worker: expand a chunk into a PRIVATE next-frontier buffer.
/// Pure and owned, so it is trivially Send across threads/processes.
fn expand(chunk: Chunk, neighbors: &dyn Fn(NodeId) -> Vec<NodeId>) -> Vec<NodeId> {
    let mut local_seen = HashSet::new();
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for n in chunk.nodes {
        for nb in neighbors(n) {
            if local_seen.insert(nb) { out.push(nb); } // local dedupe
        }
    }
    out
}

/// Coordinator merge: the ONE place that owns `visited`. The
/// contains-then-insert here is the global duplicate-suppression rule.
fn merge(visited: &mut HashSet<NodeId>, buffers: Vec<Vec<NodeId>>) -> Vec<NodeId> {
    let mut next = Vec::new();
    for buf in buffers {
        for id in buf {
            if visited.insert(id) { next.push(id); } // first global discovery only
        }
    }
    next // becomes the next level's frontier; bound the chunk queue that carries it
}

Owned frontier chunks per worker, local dedupe, and a single coordinator-owned visited set as the global duplicate-suppression point.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines an owned queue boundary (owned Vec<NodeId> frontier chunks) and a duplicate-suppression rule (contains-then-insert into a single coordinator-owned visited set).
  • Includes boundedness rules: fixed worker-pool concurrency and a bounded chunk queue with backpressure.
  • Mentions multiple observability hooks: oldest-frontier-age, duplicate-hit-rate, merge-lag, and per-level frontier size.
  • Includes a Bronze/Silver/Gold scoring and extension track.

Lab solution

The two stub methods are the whole lab; everything around them (NodeId, Node, Graph, and main) is already wired. bfs_order runs a breadth-first sweep from api. It marks api visited, then pops it and visits its edges in insertion order (auth, then billing), enqueuing each. Popping auth enqueues search; popping billing finds search already visited and skips it; popping search has no outgoing edges. The resulting order is api, auth, billing, search, which names() resolves to the printed visited = api,auth,billing,search.

shortest_hops uses a distance vector instead of a bare visited bit. api gets distance 0; auth and billing are reached at distance 1; search is reached from auth at distance 2 and is not re-relaxed when billing also points at it, because BFS records each node the first time it is dequeued and that first time is along a shortest path. When search is dequeued, id == goal, so the function returns Some(2), and main prints hops = 2.

The design point the lab demonstrates is that one owning Vec<Node> plus NodeId handles makes both traversals plain index loops: edges are cheap Copy values, the frontier lives in a VecDeque, and nothing borrows from the node table while the search runs, so there is no Rc, RefCell, or raw pointer anywhere.

Example 39-S. graph_bfs_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::VecDeque;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct NodeId(usize);

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    edges: Vec<NodeId>,
}

#[derive(Default, Debug)]
struct Graph {
    nodes: Vec<Node>,
}

impl Graph {
    fn add_node(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len());
        self.nodes.push(Node {
            name,
            edges: Vec::new(),
        });
        id
    }

    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.nodes[from.0].edges.push(to);
    }

    fn names(&self, ids: &[NodeId]) -> Vec<&'static str> {
        ids.iter().map(|id| self.nodes[id.0].name).collect()
    }

    fn bfs_order(&self, start: NodeId) -> Vec<NodeId> {
        let mut visited = vec![false; self.nodes.len()];
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
        let mut order = Vec::new();

        visited[start.0] = true;
        queue.push_back(start);

        while let Some(id) = queue.pop_front() {
            order.push(id);

            for &next in &self.nodes[id.0].edges {
                if !visited[next.0] {
                    visited[next.0] = true;
                    queue.push_back(next);
                }
            }
        }

        order
    }

    fn shortest_hops(&self, start: NodeId, goal: NodeId) -> Option<usize> {
        let mut dist = vec![usize::MAX; self.nodes.len()];
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();

        dist[start.0] = 0;
        queue.push_back(start);

        while let Some(id) = queue.pop_front() {
            if id == goal {
                return Some(dist[id.0]);
            }

            for &next in &self.nodes[id.0].edges {
                if dist[next.0] == usize::MAX {
                    dist[next.0] = dist[id.0] + 1;
                    queue.push_back(next);
                }
            }
        }

        None
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut graph = Graph::default();

    let api = graph.add_node("api");
    let auth = graph.add_node("auth");
    let billing = graph.add_node("billing");
    let search = graph.add_node("search");

    graph.add_edge(api, auth);
    graph.add_edge(api, billing);
    graph.add_edge(auth, search);
    graph.add_edge(billing, search);

    let order = graph.bfs_order(api);
    let hops = graph.shortest_hops(api, search).unwrap_or(0);

    println!("visited = {}", graph.names(&order).join(","));
    println!("hops = {}", hops);
}
Output
visited = api,auth,billing,search
hops = 2

Review question answers

Why are stable indices usually calmer than borrowed references in graph owners that grow or serialize?

A borrowed &Node into a growable owner table is invalidated whenever the table reallocates, and the borrow checker forbids growing the table while any such reference is outstanding, so a reference-rich graph is effectively frozen or forced into unsafe code. A stable index (a NodeId newtype over usize) is just a value, so it survives reallocation, does not constrain mutation, and serializes as a plain integer with no pointer fixups on reload. Indices are also cheap Copy values you can queue, log, and trace, which is why the owner-plus-handle shape is the calm default for ASTs, dependency graphs, and route graphs.

When is BFS the correct answer even if Dijkstra or A* looks more advanced?

BFS is correct, and is the simplest correct option, whenever the graph is unweighted (every edge has uniform cost) and you want a shortest path in number of hops. Because BFS explores strictly layer by layer, the first time it reaches a node is along a minimum-hop path, so it needs no priority queue, no cost relaxation, and no heuristic. Reaching for Dijkstra or A* on an unweighted graph adds a heap and bookkeeping that buy nothing; the chapter's correction is to not use a general weighted search when the workload is unweighted.

What is the difference between an admissible and a consistent (monotone) heuristic for A*, and which one does the standard closed-set version need to avoid re-opening nodes?

An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost to the goal, which guarantees A* finds an optimal path. A consistent (monotone) heuristic is stronger: for every edge from u to v with cost c, h(u) <= c + h(v), so the estimate never decreases faster than real cost accrues; consistency implies admissibility but not vice versa. The standard closed-set version that marks a node final on first expansion and never re-opens it needs a consistent heuristic, because consistency guarantees the first time a node is popped it already has its optimal cost; with a merely admissible (but inconsistent) heuristic you can pop a node too early and must allow re-opening to stay optimal.

Why can frontier parallelism still fail if the visited-set or merge step is one hot lock?

Splitting a layer across workers parallelizes the neighbor expansion, but every discovered node must still be checked and inserted into the shared visited set, and if that check-and-insert is guarded by a single global lock, all workers serialize on it. The merge step then becomes the bottleneck, and worse, contention on one hot lock can make the parallel version slower than the sequential one once lock handoff and cache-line bouncing dominate. The fix is to keep expansion lock-free with private per-worker next-frontier buffers and dedupe only once at the coordinator's merge, or to shard the visited set so workers contend on different partitions rather than one lock.

What extra operational questions appear the moment graph search crosses process or queue boundaries?

Once the frontier travels over queues and processes, the problem becomes a control-plane problem: where the owned message boundary lives, how duplicate discoveries are suppressed so the system does not fall into infinite replay or a retry storm, which queues are bounded and how backpressure is applied when they fill, and how trace lineage is preserved so a discovered path can be replayed and audited. You also need observability that algorithm code never required, such as oldest-frontier-age, duplicate-hit-rate, and merge-lag, because a stuck or storming search shows up in those signals before it shows up in CPU usage.

Chapter 40 · Matrix Optimization Games

Matrix Optimization Games

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises drill the chapter's central claim: matrix performance is decided by a fixed order of decisions, and the order starts with storage layout and loop order, not with the loudest accelerator. The warm-up fixes that pipeline in your mind, the code-reading and implementation tasks make you walk memory by hand and rebuild the kernels that the order recommends, and the debugging and design tasks force you to defend a placement decision with evidence rather than enthusiasm.

Throughout, the recurring lens is ownership and contiguity. A matrix is a two-dimensional idea flattened into a one-dimensional Vec<f32> by the offset = row * cols + col rule, and every optimization in the chapter is really a question about which traversal that rule makes cheap. Get the layout and loop order honest first; SIMD, tiling, parallelism, and GPU offload only pay off once the local memory walk is already contiguous.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

State the optimization order and why it holds

The pipeline runs left to right, cheapest-to-get-right first: storage layout, then loop order, then SIMD, then blocking/tiling, then CPU parallelism, and only last GPU offload. Each stage is cheaper to verify and harder to get wrong than the one after it, and each later stage silently assumes the earlier ones are already settled.

The reason a clever SIMD kernel or a thread pool cannot rescue a bad layout or loop order is that those later levers multiply throughput on top of the memory traffic the earlier stages produce; they do not reduce that traffic. If the inner loop walks a column of a row-major right-hand matrix, every step strides across a fresh cache line, and vectorizing or parallelizing that loop just spreads the same cache-miss-bound work across more lanes or cores. SIMD needs data that is already contiguous to load a full register cheaply; parallel workers still each pay the per-element miss. You cannot vectorize your way out of a layout that defeats the cache, because the bottleneck is memory bandwidth and latency, not arithmetic units.

GPU offload is reached last and least often because the kernel runtime is only one term in the end-to-end cost: you also pay device wait, host-to-device copy, launch, and device-to-host copy. For most workloads a layout-and-loop-order fix on the host removes the bottleneck entirely, so the GPU stage is entered only after the layout question has been answered and the host path is genuinely saturated.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Order stated as storage layout and loop order, then SIMD, tiling, parallelism, and GPU offload last.
  • Explains later stages multiply throughput over the memory traffic earlier stages produce, so layout and loop order must be honest first.
  • Notes GPU offload is rarely needed and only entered after the host layout question is settled.
Exercise 2code reading

Trace the CSR frontier step

The input frontier is [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0], so only rows 0 and 2 are active; rows 1, 3, and 4 have frontier value 0.0 and hit the continue before doing any work.

Row 0 reads the slice indptr[0]..indptr[1] = 0..2, which selects indices[0..2] = [1, 2]. So row 0 reaches columns 1 and 2, and the loop sets next[1] = 1 and next[2] = 1 (data at those edges is 1.0, which is nonzero). Row 2 reads indptr[2]..indptr[3] = 3..5, which selects indices[3..5] = [3, 4]. So row 2 reaches columns 3 and 4, setting next[3] = 1 and next[4] = 1. Note the slice bound for row r is indptr[r]..indptr[r + 1]; the starter prompt's indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1] is the half-open range of edge slots owned by that row.

After both active rows, the next vector is [0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Column 0 is never reached by any active row, so next[0] stays 0. Inactive rows are skipped entirely because a zero frontier value means that vertex is not part of the current breadth-first wavefront, so its outgoing edges contribute nothing this step; skipping them is exactly what makes the sparse traversal touch only active edges instead of the whole matrix.

graph.nnz() returns data.len() = 6, the number of stored nonzero edges. graph.dense_bytes() returns rows * cols * size_of::<f32>() = 5 * 5 * 4 = 100 bytes, the cost of materializing this graph as a dense matrix. The contrast is the point of CSR: the structure pays a little metadata (the indptr and indices arrays) to store only the 6 real edges and to visit only active outgoing edges, instead of allocating and scanning 100 bytes of mostly-zero dense storage.

// Hand-trace of advance_frontier with frontier = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0].
// indptr = [0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 6], indices = [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4], data all 1.0.
//
// row 0: frontier[0] = 1.0 -> active. slice indptr[0]..indptr[1] = 0..2
//        indices[0..2] = [1, 2]  -> next[1] = 1, next[2] = 1
// row 1: frontier[1] = 0.0 -> continue (skipped)
// row 2: frontier[2] = 1.0 -> active. slice indptr[2]..indptr[3] = 3..5
//        indices[3..5] = [3, 4]  -> next[3] = 1, next[4] = 1
// row 3: frontier[3] = 0.0 -> continue (skipped)
// row 4: frontier[4] = 0.0 -> continue (skipped)
//
// next            = [0, 1, 1, 1, 1]
// graph.nnz()     = data.len() = 6
// graph.dense_bytes() = 5 * 5 * 4 = 100

Step-by-step trace of one CSR frontier expansion and the nnz vs dense-bytes contrast.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Row 0 expands over indptr[0]..indptr[2] reaching columns 1 and 2; row 2 over indptr[2]..indptr[4] reaching columns 3 and 4.
  • Resulting next frontier is 0,1,1,1,1 with rows 1, 3, 4 skipped because their frontier value is 0.0.
  • nnz is 6 (data length) and dense_bytes is 5*5*4 = 100, illustrating the metadata-versus-density tradeoff.
Exercise 3implementation

Reorder the multiply loops from i-j-k to i-k-j

The naive kernel nests i, then j, then k, accumulating a single dot product into a local acc before writing out[i, j] once. The arithmetic is a sum of products over k, and that sum is associative, so we are free to reorder the loops as long as every (i, j, k) product still lands in out[i, j]. Reordering to i-k-j gives up the single-write acc pattern in exchange for a contiguous inner walk.

The transformation has two parts. First, hoist a.get(i, k) into a local a_ik immediately inside the k loop, so each element of A is read once per (i, k) pair rather than once per (i, j, k) triple. Second, make the innermost loop iterate j and accumulate a_ik * b.get(k, j) into out[i, j] by reading the current value, adding, and storing. Because k is now an outer loop, each output cell receives partial contributions across successive k iterations, so out must start at zero (Matrix::zeros guarantees that) and is added to, never reset.

The payoff is the memory walk. With i-k-j the inner loop holds i and k fixed and sweeps j, so b.get(k, j) reads consecutive offsets k * b.cols + j along a single row of B in row-major storage, one element at a time with no stride. out.get(i, j) and out.set(i, j, ...) likewise sweep one contiguous row of the output. The naive i-j-k order instead strided b.get(k, j) down a column of B (offset jumps by b.cols each step), touching a new cache line per access. The result is bit-for-bit the same up to floating-point reassociation, which is why approx_eq, with its tolerance, reports the two kernels equal on the chapter's 3x3 inputs.

fn matmul_ikj(a: &Matrix, b: &Matrix) -> Matrix {
    assert_eq!(a.cols, b.rows);
    let mut out = Matrix::zeros(a.rows, b.cols);

    for i in 0..a.rows {
