        for k in 0..a.cols {
            let a_ik = a.get(i, k); // read once per (i, k), hoisted out of the j loop
            for j in 0..b.cols {
                // inner loop walks a contiguous row of B (and of out)
                let current = out.get(i, j);
                out.set(i, j, current + a_ik * b.get(k, j));
            }
        }
    }

    out
}

// On the chapter's 3x3 inputs:
//   assert!(approx_eq(&matmul_ikj(&a, &b), &matmul_naive(&a, &b)));

i-k-j multiply: a_ik hoisted, inner loop sweeps a row of B; equal to matmul_naive under approx_eq.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Loop nest is i, k, j with j innermost, and a.get(i, k) is read once per (i, k) via the a_ik hoist.
  • Innermost loop indexes b.get(k, j), striding one element along a row of B rather than across rows.
  • matmul_ikj returns a matrix approx_eq reports equal to matmul_naive for the same operands.
Exercise 4implementation

Build a CSR matrix from a dense grid

The construction is a single row-major scan of the dense buffer that records only the cells that are nonzero. We keep three growing vectors: indices and data hold one entry per stored nonzero in scan order, and indptr records, after each row, the running total of nonzeros seen so far.

Start indptr with a leading 0. For each row, sweep col from 0 to cols and read dense[row * cols + col] using the same offset = row * cols + col formula the dense Matrix uses. When a cell is nonzero, push its column into indices and its value into data. After finishing the row, push the current length of data into indptr. Because indptr[row + 1] is just indptr[row] plus the number of nonzeros found in that row, the half-open slice indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1] later names exactly that row's stored edges, which is what advance_frontier consumes.

This gives the CSR invariants directly: indptr begins at 0 and ends with one entry per row plus the leading zero, so it has rows + 1 entries, and its final entry equals the total nonzero count, which is both indices.len() and data.len(). The ownership story is simple: each pushed value is moved into its vector and never aliased, and the three vectors grow independently but stay length-consistent (indices and data always equal, indptr always rows + 1). Feeding the result into advance_frontier reproduces the same reachable columns as scanning the dense grid directly, because we stored precisely the nonzero (row, col) pairs and nothing else.

fn dense_to_csr(rows: usize, cols: usize, dense: &[f32]) -> CsrMatrix {
    assert_eq!(dense.len(), rows * cols);

    let mut indptr = Vec::with_capacity(rows + 1);
    let mut indices = Vec::new();
    let mut data = Vec::new();

    indptr.push(0); // leading zero: row 0 starts at edge slot 0

    for row in 0..rows {
        for col in 0..cols {
            let value = dense[row * cols + col];
            if value != 0.0 {
                indices.push(col);
                data.push(value);
            }
        }
        // running edge count: indptr[row + 1] = indptr[row] + nnz in this row
        indptr.push(data.len());
    }

    CsrMatrix { rows, cols, indptr, indices, data }
}

// Invariants that hold by construction:
//   indptr.len() == rows + 1
//   *indptr.last().unwrap() == indices.len() == data.len()

Single row-major scan that builds indptr, indices, and data with the CSR invariants intact.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • indptr starts with 0, has rows + 1 entries, and its final entry equals indices.len() and data.len().
  • indices and data hold exactly the nonzero columns and values in row-major scan order.
  • Feeding the result into advance_frontier reproduces the same reachable columns as scanning the dense grid.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Fix a tiled multiply that overwrites partial sums

The defect is that the inner statement assigns the output cell instead of accumulating into it. In a tiled multiply the k dimension is split across kk tiles, and each kk tile computes only the partial dot product for the columns it covers. The correct cell value is the sum of those partials across all kk tiles. Writing out.set(i, j, a_ik * b.get(k, j)) discards everything previous kk tiles contributed, leaving only the last kk tile's share.

This is why the bug is invisible while a.cols fits in a single tile: with one kk tile, the full dot product is computed inside that single tile pass and there is nothing earlier to overwrite, so the result matches. The moment a.cols exceeds the tile size, the kk loop runs more than once, and each pass clobbers the partial sum the previous pass deposited. The output then reflects only the final kk block rather than the whole sum over k.

The fix restores read-modify-write accumulation, exactly as the chapter's matmul_tiled does: read the current value, add the new product, store it back. The output starts at zero from Matrix::zeros and is added to across every kk tile, never reset. To catch this class of regression early, compare the tiled kernel against matmul_naive with approx_eq, or compare a checksum, on inputs whose k dimension deliberately exceeds the tile size, so the multi-tile path is actually exercised. A test with k smaller than the tile would have passed and hidden the bug, which is the trap; the test must straddle the tile boundary.

// BUG (inside the ii / kk / jj tile loops):
//   for i in ii..i_end {
//       for k in kk..k_end {
//           let a_ik = a.get(i, k);
//           for j in jj..j_end {
//               out.set(i, j, a_ik * b.get(k, j)); // overwrites prior kk tiles
//           }
//       }
//   }
//
// FIX: read-modify-write so each kk tile adds its partial sum.
for i in ii..i_end {
    for k in kk..k_end {
        let a_ik = a.get(i, k);
        for j in jj..j_end {
            let current = out.get(i, j);
            out.set(i, j, current + a_ik * b.get(k, j));
        }
    }
}

// Regression guard that exercises more than one kk tile (tile < a.cols):
//   let tiled = matmul_tiled(&a, &b, 2); // a.cols > 2
//   assert!(approx_eq(&tiled, &matmul_naive(&a, &b)));

Restore accumulation across kk tiles and test with a k dimension larger than the tile.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Diagnosis names that successive kk tiles overwrite earlier partial sums because set replaces rather than adds.
  • Corrected inner statement is out.set(i, j, out.get(i, j) + a_ik * b.get(k, j)).
  • Proposes comparing against matmul_naive via approx_eq or a checksum on inputs whose k dimension exceeds the tile.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Decide the GPU break-even for a scoring service

The 2 ms figure is only the kernel runtime. The end-to-end cost of an offload is the sum of five terms: waiting for the device to be available (queue and admission), copying inputs host-to-device across the PCIe bus, launching the kernel, running the kernel (the measured 2 ms), and copying results device-to-host. The spike's number ignores device wait and both copies entirely, plus launch overhead, so it is an underestimate of the real path by exactly the components that tend to dominate small and medium multiplies.

The order of work follows the chapter's pipeline, settled on the host before anyone touches the GPU. First fix the storage layout (one flat row-major Vec<f32>) and the loop order (i-k-j so the inner loop walks a contiguous row of B). Then add blocking/tiling so reused tiles of A and C stay hot in cache, and only after that partition the independent output rows or tiles across CPU cores, since computing C[i, j] depends on no other cell of C. Each of these is cheaper, lower-risk, and easier to verify than an offload, and for a batch scoring hot path they frequently remove the bottleneck without leaving the host. We reach for the GPU only if the tuned, tiled, parallel host multiply is genuinely compute-bound and still too slow.

The break-even size is a service fact, not a whiteboard fact, because whether the GPU wins depends on this service's measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs, not on a theoretical FLOP ratio. The offload path can be admission-bound (the device is shared and you wait behind other work) or transfer-bound (the input and output copies cost more than the kernel saves) regardless of how fast the kernel is. A 2 ms kernel wrapped in copy and queue time can lose to a tuned host multiply outright. So the recommendation is: tune the host path in the chapter's order, instrument the candidate offload with the full five-term cost on real batch sizes and real device contention, and let the measured crossover, where end-to-end offload latency drops below the tuned host latency, define the break-even for this specific service.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • End-to-end cost given as device wait plus input copy plus launch plus kernel plus result copy, not just the 2 ms kernel.
  • Plan fixes storage layout and loop order, then tiling and CPU parallelism, before considering offload.
  • Ties the break-even to measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs for this service rather than a theoretical threshold.

Lab solution

The completed inner loop performs read-modify-write accumulation: it reads the current out[i, j], adds a_ik * b.get(k, j), and stores the sum back. Because k is an outer loop, each output cell receives partial contributions across successive k iterations, so out must begin at zero (Matrix::zeros provides that) and is added to rather than reset. The inner loop holds i and k fixed and sweeps j, so b.get(k, j) reads consecutive offsets along one row of B in row-major storage, which is the contiguous walk the i-k-j order exists to produce.

With a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and b = [[5, 6], [7, 8]], the product is the standard 2x2 matmul: c[0,0] = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19.0 and c[1,1] = 3*6 + 4*8 = 50.0. The full result is [[19, 22], [43, 50]], whose four entries sum to 19 + 22 + 43 + 50 = 134.0, the printed checksum. The i-k-j accumulation reaches the same values as a plain i-j-k dot product because summation over k is associative; only the memory traversal differs.

Example 40-S. ikj_matmul_lab.rs — Reference solution

struct Matrix {
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<f32>,
}

impl Matrix {
    fn zeros(rows: usize, cols: usize) -> Self {
        Self { rows, cols, data: vec![0.0; rows * cols] }
    }
    fn offset(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> usize {
        row * self.cols + col
    }
    fn get(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> f32 {
        self.data[self.offset(row, col)]
    }
    fn set(&mut self, row: usize, col: usize, value: f32) {
        let index = self.offset(row, col);
        self.data[index] = value;
    }
}

// i-k-j order: the inner loop walks a row of B, not a column.
fn matmul_ikj(a: &Matrix, b: &Matrix) -> Matrix {
    let mut out = Matrix::zeros(a.rows, b.cols);
    for i in 0..a.rows {
        for k in 0..a.cols {
            let a_ik = a.get(i, k);
            for j in 0..b.cols {
                let current = out.get(i, j);
                out.set(i, j, current + a_ik * b.get(k, j));
            }
        }
    }
    out
}

fn checksum(m: &Matrix) -> f32 {
    m.data.iter().copied().sum()
}

fn main() {
    let a = Matrix { rows: 2, cols: 2, data: vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] };
    let b = Matrix { rows: 2, cols: 2, data: vec![5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0] };
    let c = matmul_ikj(&a, &b);
    println!("c[0,0] = {:.1}", c.get(0, 0));
    println!("c[1,1] = {:.1}", c.get(1, 1));
    println!("checksum = {:.1}", checksum(&c));
}
Output
c[0,0] = 19.0
c[1,1] = 50.0
checksum = 134.0

Review question answers

In row-major storage, what does the offset = row * cols + col formula encode, and which traversal does it make contiguous?

It encodes the flattening rule that lays each row down end to end in a single contiguous Vec, so element (row, col) lives at linear index row * cols + col. Advancing col by one moves the offset by exactly one, while advancing row by one jumps the offset by cols. That makes walking along a row contiguous and cache-friendly, whereas walking down a column strides by cols and touches a new cache line each step.

Why does reordering the multiply loops from i-j-k to i-k-j change cache behavior without changing the arithmetic or the result?

The result is a sum of products over k, and summation is associative, so the same products land in the same output cells regardless of loop nesting; the computed value is unchanged up to floating-point reassociation. What changes is the memory walk: in i-j-k the inner k loop reads b.get(k, j) down a column of B, striding by b.cols and missing the cache, while in i-k-j the inner j loop reads b.get(k, j) along a contiguous row of B. Same arithmetic, far better cache locality, which is why the i-k-j order is often a cheap first win.

What does a CSR matrix store beyond the nonzero values, and what does that metadata buy you over a dense layout?

Beyond the data array of nonzero values, CSR stores an indices array giving each nonzero's column and an indptr array of length rows + 1 marking where each row's nonzeros begin and end, so indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1] is that row's slice of edges. This metadata lets you store only the nonzeros instead of every cell, and to visit only a row's actual outgoing edges rather than scanning all columns. For sparse data it trades a small, fixed index overhead for skipping the zeros entirely in both memory and traversal, as the chapter's nnz versus dense_bytes contrast shows.

What does blocking or tiling improve in a matrix multiply, and what costs does it add?

Tiling splits one large multiply into many smaller subproblems whose working set fits in cache, so reused tiles of A and C stay hot and cold misses on reused blocks drop; each tile is also a natural independent unit of parallel work. The costs are more indexing logic, a larger tuning surface (the tile size must be matched to cache shape), and greater sensitivity to matrix size. For tiny matrices, or services dominated by queueing or serialization, the extra complexity may not move the real wall-clock story enough to justify it.

What are the components of the end-to-end cost of a GPU offload, and why can a fast kernel still lose the placement decision?

The end-to-end cost is the sum of waiting for the device, copying inputs host-to-device, launching the kernel, running the kernel, and copying results device-to-host; the kernel runtime is only one of those five terms. A fast kernel can still lose because the path may be admission-bound (waiting behind other work on a shared device) or transfer-bound (the input and output copies cost more than the kernel saves), independent of kernel speed. The break-even size is therefore a service fact rooted in measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs, not a whiteboard FLOP ratio, and a well-tuned host multiply often wins outright.

Chapter 41 · Error Handling in Large Systems

Error Handling in Large Systems

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter move error handling out of the realm of message formatting and into the realm of interface design. Each one asks the same underlying question from a different angle: given a failure, what can the caller actually do next, and which layer is responsible for deciding? The warm-up sorts failures into Option, Result, and panic by operational consequence; the code-reading and implementation tasks separate domain language from infrastructure language and replace panic-driven control flow with a small typed contract; and the debugging and design tasks carry those typed contracts across async task boundaries, across a C ABI, and through a full HTTP-to-plugin service path.

The through-line is that a large-system error model survives only when retry policy, translation responsibility, and logging discipline are visible in different places on purpose. The lab is the concrete anchor: a config parser that panics on routine bad input is rewritten so that missing input and malformed input become distinct, matchable variants the caller can branch on.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose Option, Result, panic, or process abort from the caller's ability to act

Sort the four events by what the caller can still do, not by how serious they feel. The missing optional request header is ordinary absence: the header may legitimately not be there, and the local code either supplies a default or takes one branch. That is Option<&str> at the point of access. There is no failure to report yet; absence is unremarkable. Only if a later layer decides a missing header is actually a contract violation (an unauthenticated request, say) does that absence get promoted into a typed Result at that boundary.

The database timeout and the invalid state transition are both recoverable, but they belong to different layers. The timeout is an infrastructure failure: the caller can retry, fail over, or dead-letter the work, so it becomes a typed infrastructure error variant such as InfraError::Timeout that stays in machinery language and never leaks SQL detail upward. The invalid state transition is a domain failure: the business rule rejected the action, the caller cannot retry the same request and expect a different answer, so it becomes a domain error variant such as DomainError::InvalidTransition in business language. Keeping these two in separate enums is what lets the next layer branch correctly: retry on the first, reject on the second.

The impossible-coexistence invariant is the one event that is not a Result at all. If two states the code guarantees are mutually exclusive are both observed, the program's own assumptions are broken, and there is no sensible caller response to return. That is a panic (or, under a strict crash-only policy, a process abort), because continuing past a broken invariant risks producing wrong results rather than merely failing. At the next boundary the recoverable errors are translated, not forwarded verbatim: an InfraError::Timeout becomes HTTP 503 with Retry-After, a DomainError::InvalidTransition becomes HTTP 409 or 422, an AMQP consumer maps the timeout to a requeue and the domain rejection to a dead-letter, and an FFI boundary collapses both into a status code while the rich detail stays in the Rust-side log.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Option models the missing header (unremarkable absence), Result with typed variants models the timeout and the transition, and the invariant break is panic/abort rather than a returned error.
  • The invalid transition is classified as a domain failure and the timeout as an infrastructure failure, in separate enums.
  • The translation step is named per boundary: timeout -> 503/requeue, domain rejection -> 409/dead-letter, both -> status code over FFI, so the same contract does not survive unchanged.
Exercise 2code reading

Separate domain and infrastructure errors in one service path

The billing service returns anyhow::Result<()> from deep inside the domain model, which means three failures with three different caller responses arrive as one free-form message chain that nothing downstream can branch on. Split them by layer. The invalid transition is a business-rule failure and belongs in a domain enum, because it speaks the language of the business and tells the caller to reject the request rather than retry it. The SQL timeout and the missing queue channel are machinery failures and belong in an infrastructure or adapter enum, because they speak the language of the plumbing and tell the caller to retry, fail over, or dead-letter. This is exactly the split the chapter's Example 1 demonstrates: a DomainError for an empty order, an InfraError for a missing store row, and a ServiceError that folds both with #[from] while preserving which layer failed.

The reason invalid transition must leave the infrastructure bucket is that retry policy depends on it. An infrastructure timeout is often retryable; a rejected business action never is, and retrying it just burns the same request against the same rule. When both are buried in one anyhow chain, the worker cannot tell them apart without parsing message text, which is fragile and breaks the moment someone rewords a string. Once the domain layer returns a named variant, the worker writes a real match arm: retry InfraError::Timeout, dead-letter DomainError::InvalidTransition, surface anything unrecognized.

anyhow does not disappear after the separation; it moves up. It stays useful at the top-level service shell, where the next action is logging, surfacing to a transport, or exiting, and where pattern matching has stopped paying for itself. There you want rich, aggregated context with a source chain, not a giant match. The rule is: typed enums where a downstream layer still branches on the error, anyhow where the boundary is already orchestration. The caller actions that typed separation enables are concretely retry (on the timeout), reject (on the transition), and dead-letter (on a poison message) rather than one opaque failed result for all three.

use thiserror::Error;

// Domain language: a business rule said no. Never retryable on its own.
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum DomainError {
    #[error("invalid transition from {from} to {to}")]
    InvalidTransition { from: &'static str, to: &'static str },
}

// Machinery language: the plumbing failed. The caller may retry or dead-letter.
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum InfraError {
    #[error("database call timed out after {ms} ms")]
    SqlTimeout { ms: u64 },
    #[error("queue channel {name} is not available")]
    MissingChannel { name: &'static str },
}

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum ServiceError {
    #[error(transparent)]
    Domain(#[from] DomainError),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Infra(#[from] InfraError),
}

// The worker can now branch on real variants instead of message text.
fn classify(err: &ServiceError) -> &'static str {
    match err {
        ServiceError::Infra(InfraError::SqlTimeout { .. }) => "retry",
        ServiceError::Infra(InfraError::MissingChannel { .. }) => "retry",
        ServiceError::Domain(DomainError::InvalidTransition { .. }) => "reject",
    }
}

fn main() {
    let timeout = ServiceError::from(InfraError::SqlTimeout { ms: 5000 });
    let rejected = ServiceError::from(DomainError::InvalidTransition {
        from: "draft",
        to: "paid",
    });
    println!("{} -> {}", timeout, classify(&timeout));
    println!("{} -> {}", rejected, classify(&rejected));
}

Typed domain and infra enums fold into one ServiceError, so the worker can match for a retry-versus-reject decision; anyhow stays at the shell above this.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The invalid transition moves into DomainError, out of the infrastructure bucket.
  • anyhow is kept only at the top-level shell where matching no longer pays and aggregated context is what is needed.
  • The classify function names concrete caller actions enabled by typing: retry on the timeout, reject on the transition (and dead-letter on a poison variant).
Exercise 3implementation

Convert panic-based parsing into typed errors

The original parse_port has two unwrap calls, and each one panics on a perfectly routine input that a config loader will see in production: raw.unwrap() panics when the value is absent, and parse().unwrap() panics when the value is present but not a number. Both are recoverable by the caller, so neither should be a panic. The repair is a small typed contract that distinguishes the two cases the caller genuinely needs to tell apart: nothing was provided versus something invalid was provided.

Replace the first unwrap with ok_or, which converts the Option<&str> into a Result and attaches the MissingPort variant on the None branch, then use ? to short-circuit. Replace the second unwrap with map_err, which keeps the parsed value on success and rewrites the standard library's ParseIntError into the InvalidPort variant on failure. The helper returns the parsed u16 directly and does no logging; logging is a decision for the caller, who has the surrounding context, not for a leaf parser. Keeping the enum to two variants is deliberate: it is small enough to match exhaustively and specific enough that the caller path becomes calm. A missing port might fall back to a default; an invalid port is a real configuration error to surface.

This is the same contract repair most real config loaders need first, and it is exactly what the lab implements. The function no longer panics on the missing or the malformed case, and the return type alone tells the caller which of the two occurred.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum ConfigError {
    MissingPort,
    InvalidPort,
}

fn parse_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    // ok_or turns absence into a typed, matchable error instead of a panic.
    let text = raw.ok_or(ConfigError::MissingPort)?;
    // map_err rewrites the std ParseIntError into our small contract.
    text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| ConfigError::InvalidPort)
}

fn main() {
    println!("missing = {:?}", parse_port(None));
    println!("bad = {:?}", parse_port(Some("oops")));
    println!("ok = {:?}", parse_port(Some("8080")));
}

ok_or handles the missing-input branch and map_err handles the parse-failure branch, so the two cases stay distinguishable in the return type with no panic.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Both unwrap calls are gone, so routine missing and invalid input no longer panic.
  • MissingPort and InvalidPort are separate variants, so the caller can tell absence from malformed input from the return type.
  • Running the function prints the missing, invalid, and success cases exactly as the lab expects.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Add context to async task propagation

tokio::spawn returns a JoinHandle<Result<T, E>>, so .await on it yields Result<Result<T, E>, JoinError>: two stacked failure layers, and the bug is that the inherited code collapses both with a single .await? and loses the distinction. The outer layer is the join result, which tells you whether the task finished at all: it returns a JoinError if the task panicked or was cancelled. The inner layer is whatever the task body returned: an IO error, a domain rejection, an anyhow::Error. A panic inside the task is a different incident from a typed adapter or domain failure, and the unhelpful error text comes from flattening the two so you can no longer tell which happened.

Add context at two distinct points, mirroring the chapter's Example 2. Inside the task body, after the inner await, attach operation-level context that names what the work was doing, for example .context("loading manifest for job"). Outside, after the join await, attach task-level context that names the spawn boundary, for example .context("manifest task failed"). Then resolve the two layers with two separate steps rather than one ?: the chapter's pattern is .await.context("...task failed")?? where the first ? unwraps the JoinError layer and the second unwraps the inner error. The context message should name the operation, not repeat the same low-level noun: "loading manifest" is diagnosable, a second "not found" line is not. Useful fields are the job ID, queue name, attempt number, and the resource name being touched, because those are what an operator needs to reconstruct the incident.

Cancellation should be modeled distinctly from ordinary inner failure whenever the system can shut a task down deliberately. JoinError exposes is_cancelled() and is_panic(); a task aborted during graceful shutdown is not a failure of the work and must not be reported as a generic timeout or a generic error string, because that would page someone for a clean shutdown. Branch on the JoinError: a cancel during shutdown is expected and logged at low severity, a panic is a bug that should surface loudly, and only the inner error carries the real domain or infrastructure failure.

use anyhow::{Context, Result};

async fn do_work(job: u64) -> Result<u64> {
    if job == 0 {
        anyhow::bail!("empty job payload");
    }
    Ok(job * 2)
}

async fn run(job: u64, queue: &str, attempt: u32) -> Result<u64> {
    let handle = tokio::spawn(async move {
        // Operation-layer context: names the work, not a repeated noun.
        do_work(job)
            .await
            .with_context(|| format!("processing job {job}"))
    });

    match handle.await {
        // Inner Result resolved here: '?' carries the operation error up,
        // with task-layer context naming the spawn boundary.
        Ok(inner) => inner.with_context(|| {
            format!("job {job} task on queue {queue} (attempt {attempt}) failed")
        }),
        Err(join_err) if join_err.is_cancelled() => {
            // Cancellation is not an ordinary failure: do not collapse to a timeout.
            anyhow::bail!("job {job} cancelled during shutdown")
        }
        Err(join_err) => Err(join_err)
            .with_context(|| format!("job {job} task panicked on queue {queue}")),
    }
}

The join layer (handle.await) and the inner operation layer (do_work) are resolved separately, each with its own context, and cancellation is branched out before generic failure handling.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The join layer and the inner error layer are resolved in separate match arms rather than one collapsed ?.
  • Operation-layer context ("processing job N") and task-layer context ("...task on queue... failed") are added at both points.
  • is_cancelled() is branched out so a shutdown-cancel is reported distinctly and never as a generic timeout.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Translate a Rust error contract across FFI without leaking internals

An extern "C" function that returns anyhow::Result<u64> is unsound at the boundary, not merely inelegant. A C ABI cannot carry a Rust enum, an anyhow::Error, or the stack unwinding a panic implies; letting any of those cross the boundary is undefined behavior. The other runtime has no way to safely consume an internal anyhow chain as if it were a stable public type. So the boundary must become a deliberate narrowing: the rich error stays on the Rust side, and the foreign side sees a small, boring, ABI-safe contract.

Replace anyhow::Result<u64> with an explicit status code plus an out parameter for the result. The public types are an i32 (or a repr(C) enum of status codes) for the outcome and a *mut u64 for the value written on success. Distinguish the foreign-visible failure classes explicitly: a null or zero-length input is one status (for example STATUS_NULL_INPUT = 1), invalid UTF-8 in the payload is another (STATUS_INVALID_UTF8 = 2), and any internal computation failure is a third generic status (STATUS_INTERNAL = 3). Two or three classes are usually enough; the foreign caller only needs to branch on what it can act on. The richer detail, which row failed, which dependency timed out, the full source chain, stays inside a Rust-side log or trace and never escapes over the ABI, because the foreign runtime cannot use it and exposing it pins your internals as a public contract. The whole function body is wrapped so panics cannot unwind across the boundary: std::panic::catch_unwind converts any internal panic into the generic internal status.

Test the status boundary with a tiny native harness, a few lines of C that call run with a null pointer, with deliberately invalid UTF-8 bytes, and with a valid payload, asserting on the returned status code and the out value each time. That harness verifies the contract the other runtime actually depends on, independently of any Rust-side richness. This is deliberately boring, and the boredom is the feature: a stable, narrow ABI is what lets the foreign side build against the boundary with confidence.

use std::panic::catch_unwind;
use std::slice;

#[repr(i32)]
pub enum Status {
    Ok = 0,
    NullInput = 1,
    InvalidUtf8 = 2,
    Internal = 3,
}

/// ABI-safe boundary: status code out, result via out-parameter.
/// Rich Rust errors stay behind this wrapper and are only logged.
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn run(ptr: *const u8, len: usize, out: *mut u64) -> i32 {
    if ptr.is_null() || out.is_null() {
        return Status::NullInput as i32;
    }

    // catch_unwind keeps a panic from unwinding across the C ABI (UB).
    let result = catch_unwind(|| {
        let bytes = unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) };
        let text = match std::str::from_utf8(bytes) {
            Ok(t) => t,
            Err(_) => return Err(Status::InvalidUtf8),
        };
        // Real work lives here and may produce a rich internal error,
        // which we log on the Rust side rather than export over the ABI.
        score(text).map_err(|err| {
            eprintln!("internal failure: {err:#}");
            Status::Internal
        })
    });

    match result {
        Ok(Ok(value)) => {
            unsafe { *out = value };
            Status::Ok as i32
        }
        Ok(Err(status)) => status as i32,
        Err(_) => Status::Internal as i32, // a panic was caught
    }
}

fn score(text: &str) -> anyhow::Result<u64> {
    Ok(text.len() as u64) // stand-in for the rich internal path
}

anyhow::Result is replaced by an i32 status plus a *mut u64 out-parameter; null, invalid UTF-8, and internal failure are distinct statuses, and catch_unwind stops panics from crossing the ABI.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The boundary is translated into a status code plus an out-parameter instead of anyhow::Result.
  • Null input, invalid UTF-8, and internal failure are three explicit foreign-visible status classes.
  • The rich anyhow detail is logged on the Rust side behind the wrapper and never exported as the public ABI, and a native harness calling run with null, bad UTF-8, and a valid payload checks the status contract.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design one error contract for HTTP, queue workers, and a native plugin

Design three layered error families and one explicit policy for retry, logging, and translation, so another team can operate the failure modes without reading the implementation. The domain layer owns business-rule failures: an empty order, an invalid transition, an exhausted quota. These are DomainError variants in business language, never mentioning SQL or TCP, and they are terminal because retrying the same request against the same rule changes nothing. The infrastructure layer owns machinery failures: a database timeout, a missing queue channel, a plugin call that did not respond. These are InfraError variants in machinery language, and most are retryable. The native risk plugin sits behind the ABI boundary from Exercise 5 and surfaces only a status code, which the adapter maps into an InfraError variant (PluginUnavailable, PluginRejected) so the rest of the system never sees raw ABI codes. At the top, one ServiceError folds domain and infrastructure with #[from] and is what the HTTP handler and the worker both translate from.

Make retryable-versus-terminal an explicit property, not a guess from message text. The cleanest place is a method on the error, fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool, that returns true for infrastructure timeouts and plugin-unavailable, false for every domain rejection and for plugin-rejected. The HTTP handler reads it to choose 503 with Retry-After versus 409/422; the queue worker reads it to choose requeue-with-backoff versus dead-letter. The policy lives in one place, on the type, so HTTP and the worker cannot drift apart.

Separate the boundary that logs from the boundary that only translates, or the incident channel fills with the same failure reworded five times. The rule: log once at the layer where the failure first becomes operationally meaningful, usually the adapter that talks to the failing dependency, because that layer has the resource name and the attempt. Every layer above it translates and returns without re-logging. So the database adapter logs the timeout once with full context; the worker translates it into a requeue decision and does not log it again; the HTTP boundary translates a propagated ServiceError into a status code and does not log it again. Finally, every failure path carries the same structured fields so the incident is reconstructable: request ID, task ID, attempt number, queue name, and the plugin call name. With those on the log line, an operator reconstructs the whole charge from one entry instead of correlating five partial ones.

use thiserror::Error;

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum DomainError {
    #[error("order {id} has no lines")]
    EmptyOrder { id: &'static str },
    #[error("risk plugin rejected order {id}")]
    RiskRejected { id: &'static str },
}

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum InfraError {
    #[error("database timed out after {ms} ms")]
    DbTimeout { ms: u64 },
    #[error("risk plugin unavailable")]
    PluginUnavailable,
}

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
enum ServiceError {
    #[error(transparent)]
    Domain(#[from] DomainError),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Infra(#[from] InfraError),
}

impl ServiceError {
    // Retry policy lives on the type, in one place, not in message text.
    fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self,
            ServiceError::Infra(InfraError::DbTimeout { .. })
                | ServiceError::Infra(InfraError::PluginUnavailable)
        )
    }

    // HTTP boundary: translate only, do not log here.
    fn http_status(&self) -> u16 {
        if self.is_retryable() { 503 } else { 422 }
    }

    // Worker boundary: translate only, do not log here.
    fn worker_action(&self) -> &'static str {
        if self.is_retryable() { "requeue" } else { "dead-letter" }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let timeout = ServiceError::from(InfraError::DbTimeout { ms: 5000 });
    let rejected = ServiceError::from(DomainError::RiskRejected { id: "ord-9" });
    // Fields like request_id/task_id/attempt/queue/plugin_call belong on the
    // single log line emitted by the adapter that first saw the failure.
    println!("timeout: http={} worker={}", timeout.http_status(), timeout.worker_action());
    println!("rejected: http={} worker={}", rejected.http_status(), rejected.worker_action());
}

DomainError, InfraError, and a folded ServiceError carry an is_retryable method; http_status and worker_action translate without logging, leaving the one log line to the adapter that first saw the failure.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one domain error, one infrastructure error, and a translated ServiceError (with HTTP/worker transports) are defined.
  • is_retryable makes retryable-versus-terminal an explicit method on the type rather than a message substring.
  • The adapter that first sees the failure logs once; http_status and worker_action only translate, avoiding duplicate noise.
  • Observability fields named for every path: request ID, task ID, attempt, queue, and plugin call name.

Lab solution

The original code panics twice on routine input: raw.unwrap() panics when the port value is absent, and text.parse().unwrap() panics when the value is present but not numeric. Both are recoverable by the caller, so both become typed errors instead of panics. The fix swaps each unwrap for an explicit branch that names the failure.

raw.ok_or(ConfigError::MissingPort)? converts Option<&str> into Result<&str, ConfigError>, attaching the MissingPort variant on None, and the ? operator returns it immediately. On the present path, text.parse::<u16>() yields Result<u16, ParseIntError>, and map_err(|_| ConfigError::InvalidPort) rewrites the standard-library parse error into the InvalidPort variant while leaving a successful parse untouched. The helper does no logging and returns the parsed value directly, leaving any logging or fallback decision to the caller that has the context.

The three calls in main therefore exercise the three distinct paths. parse_port(None) takes the ok_or branch and prints Err(MissingPort); parse_port(Some("oops")) parses and fails, taking the map_err branch to print Err(InvalidPort); parse_port(Some("8080")) parses successfully and prints Ok(8080). Missing and malformed input are now distinguishable from the return type alone, which is the whole point of the typed contract.

Example 41-S. typed_error_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum ConfigError {
    MissingPort,
    InvalidPort,
}

fn parse_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    // ok_or promotes absence into a typed, matchable error; '?' short-circuits.
    let text = raw.ok_or(ConfigError::MissingPort)?;
    // map_err rewrites the std ParseIntError into our small contract.
    text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| ConfigError::InvalidPort)
}

fn main() {
    println!("missing = {:?}", parse_port(None));
    println!("bad = {:?}", parse_port(Some("oops")));
    println!("ok = {:?}", parse_port(Some("8080")));
}
Output
missing = Err(MissingPort)
bad = Err(InvalidPort)
ok = Ok(8080)

Review question answers

When is Option enough, and when should the boundary promote absence into Result?

Option is enough when absence is unremarkable and the caller only needs one local branch: supply a default, skip the step, or fall through. You should promote that absence into a typed Result at the boundary where the absence actually becomes a contract violation the caller must classify and handle, for example a missing field that means an invalid request rather than a benign default. The rule is to keep Option at the point of lookup and convert to a named error (often with ok_or) exactly where a downstream layer needs to branch on why the value was missing.

Why are domain errors and infrastructure errors worth keeping distinct even if both eventually become one HTTP response or one queue outcome?

They imply different caller actions, and that decision happens above the layer that produced the error, before any HTTP or queue collapse. An infrastructure failure such as a timeout is usually retryable; a domain rejection such as an invalid transition is terminal, and retrying it just repeats the same rejection. If both live in one error bag, the worker cannot tell retry from reject without parsing message text, which is fragile. Keeping them in separate enums lets the next layer match on real variants and choose retry, reject, or dead-letter honestly, even though the final boundary may still fold them into a single status.

What is the practical split between thiserror and anyhow in a large Rust system?

They answer different questions, and most systems use both. Reach for thiserror to define named error enums with named variants when a downstream layer still needs to branch on the error; the macro generates the boilerplate for Display, the source chain, and #[from] conversions. Reach for anyhow when the boundary is already top-level orchestration, where the next action is logging, surfacing, or exiting, and where exhaustive matching has stopped paying for itself; there you want rich aggregated context rather than a large match. The deciding factor is simply whether anyone downstream still branches on the variant.

Why does a spawned task usually create a two-layer error surface rather than one?

tokio::spawn returns a JoinHandle<Result<T, E>>, so awaiting it produces Result<Result<T, E>, JoinError>: two stacked layers. The outer JoinError layer reports whether the task ran to completion at all, returning an error if the task panicked or was cancelled. The inner Result is whatever the task body returned, such as an IO error or a domain rejection. Collapsing both with a single ? loses the distinction between a task that crashed and a task that finished but returned a typed failure, which are different incidents that deserve different handling, so you resolve the two layers deliberately.

Why should a boundary usually log once rather than at every layer that propagates the same error upward?

Logging the same failure at every layer turns the incident channel into a hall of mirrors, where one failure appears five times slightly reworded and an operator cannot tell whether that is one incident or five. The discipline is to log once at the single layer where the failure first becomes operationally meaningful, usually the adapter closest to the failing dependency, which has the resource name and attempt count in hand. Every layer above it translates and returns the error without re-logging, so each failure produces exactly one rich, reconstructable log line.

Chapter 42 · Testing Advanced Rust Systems

Testing Advanced Rust Systems

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises rehearse the central discipline of the chapter: name the claim each test defends, prove it at the cheapest layer that can prove it, and engineer determinism instead of hoping for it. You move from classifying which test layer fits which risk, through reading a suite to find the claims it leaves unproven, into writing property tests, planning fuzz targets for unsafe parsers, and designing async and distributed test plans that do not depend on scheduler luck.

The through-line is that an advanced Rust system fails along several independent axes at once — local invariants, hostile input, retry safety, output stability, and performance budgets — and a good suite separates those axes rather than collapsing them into one slow end-to-end lane. Every solution below commits to a concrete layer choice and justifies it in terms of cost, confidence, and the ownership or determinism property it actually exercises.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose unit, integration, property, fuzz, snapshot, or benchmark from the claim

Start from the claim, not the tool. Each of the five needs has a cheapest layer that can still produce the right kind of evidence.

The state-machine invariant is a unit test first. It is a local, pure rule — a transition either rejects a duplicate submission or it does not — and you can assert it without booting a runtime, a database, or a network. Unit tests are the cheapest, most deterministic layer, so any claim that lives inside one type or one function belongs here. If the same invariant needs to hold across an unbounded space of operation sequences, you later lift it into a property test, but the first proof is a unit test.

The public HTTP contract is a true integration test, because the claim is about a public seam another deployment unit depends on. You drive the handler through a test app and assert the status code and the durable side effect, which is exactly what a downstream caller observes. A unit test cannot prove the seam composed correctly; only exercising the boundary does.

The hostile binary parser input space is fuzzing. The input is malformed by nature, the space is adversarial, and a coverage-guided fuzzer explores byte sequences no human fixture author would write. This is distinct from a property test in degree of hostility: property testing generates structured-but-random valid-ish inputs around an invariant; fuzzing pushes openly malformed bytes at a parser to find crashes, panics, and undefined behavior.

The large human-reviewable error report is a snapshot or golden review. The output is big and shaped, so a byte-for-byte committed artifact (golden file) or a review-and-accept diff (snapshot) is the practical way to detect unintended changes — provided you normalize nondeterministic fields and pair it with a semantic assertion for any load-bearing value. The latency budget for the hot batch encoder is a benchmark with a coarse budget, kept in its own lane: it proves a performance claim, not a correctness claim, and must not be mixed into the functional suite where its hardware sensitivity would cause flakes.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Maps each of the five claims to a primary layer (unit, integration, fuzz, snapshot/golden, benchmark) with a cost-and-confidence justification.
  • Distinguishes snapshot/golden review of output shape from semantic correctness assertions, and notes the report still needs a semantic check for load-bearing values.
  • Keeps the latency budget in a separate benchmark lane, explicitly out of the functional correctness suite.
Exercise 2code reading

Find the missing layers in one test suite

The suite is expensive and still incomplete because every claim is being proven at the most costly layer, and several claims are not being proven at all. Slow API integration tests can only show that the whole stack composed on the happy path; they say almost nothing about the local rules underneath.

Missing unit or property layers: the domain model has no direct tests, so invariants like 'quota never exceeds limit' or 'a duplicate submission is rejected' are only ever exercised incidentally through a full HTTP round-trip. Those rules should move down. The ones with a single fixed expectation become unit tests; the ones that should hold across many generated operation sequences become property tests, where the framework shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample. Pushing them down makes them fast, deterministic, and attributable to one type rather than to a whole request.

Missing fuzz layer: the binary parser is only reached through end-to-end fixtures, which means it is tested against the handful of inputs a human thought to write. A parser is exactly the boundary where arbitrary external bytes cross into your code, so it wants a coverage-guided fuzz target on the small raw-bytes-to-parse-result function, with crashing inputs saved into a corpus as permanent regression cases. Fixtures prove a few known frames decode; fuzzing probes the malformed-input space the fixtures cannot.

Async determinism problem: the worker tests use real sleeps, so they depend on scheduler luck — they pass on a fast laptop and flake in CI. The repair is to take time out of the operating system's hands: drive a paused or fake clock, advance it explicitly past the relevant deadline, and assert the resulting state, so the test is deterministic regardless of machine speed. Finally, blindly accepting snapshot updates is too trusting for a production-facing report format: an accepted diff records 'the output changed', not 'the output is correct', so a regression can be rubber-stamped into the golden state. Snapshots should gate on human review of the diff and be paired with a semantic assertion on any load-bearing field.

// Repairs, by layer.

// 1. Domain invariant lifted out of the slow API path into a property test.
proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn quota_never_exceeds_limit(limit in 0u32..1000, ops in proptest::collection::vec(0u32..1000, 0..32)) {
        let mut used = 0u32;
        for qty in ops {
            if used.saturating_add(qty) <= limit {
                used += qty;
            }
            prop_assert!(used <= limit); // shrinks to the minimal failing sequence
        }
    }
}

// 2. Small raw-bytes fuzz boundary instead of end-to-end fixtures only.
// fuzz_targets/parse_frame.rs
fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
    let _ = parse_frame(data); // a panic, abort, or sanitizer trip fails the lane
});

// 3. Deterministic async test on a paused clock instead of a real sleep.
#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]
async fn lease_expires_without_real_sleep() {
    let lease = Lease::claim("task-1");
    tokio::time::advance(LEASE_TTL + Duration::from_millis(1)).await;
    assert!(lease.is_expired());
}

One repair per gap: property test for the domain invariant, a small fuzz boundary for the parser, and a fake-clock async test that never really sleeps.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies the untested domain invariants as a missing unit/property layer, the un-fuzzed parser as a missing fuzz layer, and the sleep-based worker tests as the async determinism problem.
  • Proposes a concrete repair for each: lift invariants into unit/property tests, add a small raw-bytes fuzz target with a corpus, drive a paused clock instead of sleeping, and gate snapshot diffs on review plus a semantic assertion.
  • Explains the suite is expensive yet incomplete because all claims are pushed to the slow end-to-end layer while local invariants, hostile input, and time control go unproven.
Exercise 3implementation

Write property tests for a domain invariant

State the invariant before the generator. For a quota window the rule is plain: after any sequence of reservation requests, used never exceeds limit. That is a property of the type, not of a particular sequence, which is exactly why a property test fits better than a few hand-picked examples — the framework supplies the sequences and tries to break the rule.

The generator serves the invariant. It produces a random limit and a random-length vector of random quantities, so the test covers many interleavings of accepted and rejected reservations rather than the two or three a human would type. Crucially, the assertion is the invariant itself (used <= limit) evaluated after every operation, not a check against a specific expected total. A deterministic reference rule keeps the expectation honest: a reservation is accepted only when used + qty <= limit, and the test re-derives acceptance the same way the type should, so the property describes the rule the subsystem actually cares about.

When the invariant fails, shrinking is what makes the failure useful. proptest reduces the counterexample to the smallest input that still violates the rule — typically the shortest operation sequence and the smallest quantities that drive used past limit. Instead of a 30-element random vector you get something like a single oversized reservation, which points straight at the off-by-one or the missing bounds check in try_reserve. The random data on its own proves little; the minimized failing case is the payoff.

use proptest::prelude::*;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Quota {
    limit: u32,
    used: u32,
}

impl Quota {
    fn try_reserve(&mut self, qty: u32) -> bool {
        if self.used.saturating_add(qty) > self.limit {
            return false;
        }
        self.used += qty;
        true
    }
}

proptest! {
    // Invariant: used never exceeds limit after ANY generated sequence.
    #[test]
    fn quota_never_exceeds_limit(
        limit in 0u32..10_000,
        ops in proptest::collection::vec(0u32..10_000, 0..64),
    ) {
        let mut quota = Quota { limit, used: 0 };
        for qty in ops {
            let accepted = quota.try_reserve(qty);
            // Reference rule: acceptance must mean the result still fits.
            if accepted {
                prop_assert!(quota.used <= quota.limit);
            }
            // The load-bearing invariant, checked unconditionally.
            prop_assert!(quota.used <= quota.limit);
        }
    }
}

The assertion is the invariant itself; proptest generates the sequences and shrinks any failure to the smallest violating case.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Expresses one real invariant ('used never exceeds limit after any sequence') in clear domain terms, stated before the generator.
  • Generates a random limit and a variable-length vector of quantities rather than a single fixed example.
  • Explains that on failure proptest shrinks to the minimal sequence and smallest quantities, turning a large random case into a pinpointed counterexample.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Plan fuzz targets for unsafe parsing code

Pick the smallest boundary that still reproduces a crash. The fuzz target should be the raw-bytes-to-parse-result function — bytes in, structured result or error out — not the whole transport stack. Keeping the harness close to the parser means a crashing input is a few bytes that still mean something: it points at one decoder rather than at an entire service, and it reproduces in milliseconds. A fuzz target wrapped around the full stack would waste most of its budget on framing and IO that have nothing to do with the unsafe fast path.

A day-one seed corpus should cover the structural edges the unsafe path is most likely to mishandle: an empty input, a truncated frame that ends mid-header, a frame with an exact valid header, a header whose declared length is oversized relative to the actual payload, a duplicated frame, and a malformed footer. These are the classes where a byte walker either reads past the buffer or trusts a length field it should have validated, so seeding them gives the coverage-guided fuzzer good starting points to mutate from.

Compare the unsafe fast path against a safe reference parser as a differential oracle: run both on the same bytes and assert they agree — same accept/reject decision and, on accept, the same decoded structure. Where a full reference is too costly, assert explicit structural invariants instead: the cursor never advances past the buffer length, the declared payload length is validated before the cursor walks it, and every offset derived inside the unsafe block stays in bounds. Either way you are checking the invariant edges where UB actually lives, not just that a happy-path frame decodes.

The fuzz lane must fail immediately on the signals that catch the bugs you cannot see from a passing return value. Run the target under AddressSanitizer so out-of-bounds reads and use-after-free abort the run, treat any panic or abort as a failure, and use Miri or sanitizer UB detection on the unsafe path to catch invalid pointer use and aliasing violations that an optimized build might otherwise hide. Save every crashing input into the corpus so each fix ships with a permanent regression case.

// fuzz_targets/parse_frame.rs  (cargo-fuzz / libFuzzer)
#![no_main]
use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;

fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
    // Smallest boundary: raw bytes -> parse result. Close to the parser,
    // so a crashing input is a meaningful handful of bytes.
    let fast = parse_frame_unsafe(data); // the inherited unsafe fast path
    let safe = parse_frame_reference(data); // a slower, fully safe parser

    // Differential oracle: the unsafe path must agree with the reference.
    match (fast, safe) {
        (Ok(a), Ok(b)) => assert_eq!(a, b, "unsafe path disagreed with reference"),
        (Err(_), Err(_)) => {} // both reject: acceptable
        (a, b) => panic!("accept/reject mismatch: {:?} vs {:?}", a.is_ok(), b.is_ok()),
    }
    // A panic, an ASan abort, or a Miri UB report fails the lane immediately.
});

// Seed corpus (corpus/ entries), one file per input class:
//   empty               -> []
//   truncated header    -> [0x01]
//   exact valid header  -> [MAGIC, len=0]
//   oversized length    -> [MAGIC, len=0xFFFF, payload=2 bytes]
//   duplicated frame    -> frame ++ frame
//   malformed footer    -> valid frame with corrupted trailing checksum

Small raw-bytes boundary with a differential oracle against a safe reference; seed classes and sanitizer/panic signals listed alongside.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Picks the small raw-bytes-to-result function as the fuzz boundary and justifies it (crashing inputs stay meaningful and reproduce fast).
  • Defines at least five seed classes: empty, truncated, exact header, oversized length, duplicated frame, malformed footer.
  • Specifies a differential oracle against a safe reference parser, plus explicit unsafe invariants (cursor in bounds, length validated before walk) when a full reference is too costly.
  • Includes failing tool signals: AddressSanitizer aborts, any panic/abort, and Miri/UB detection, with crashes saved to the corpus.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design async integration tests for a service boundary

The pipeline is HTTP request to async worker to database write to queue publish, and the safety claim is that the retry path stays idempotent under duplicate delivery or cancellation. The plan makes time, durable effects, task joins, and identity explicit instead of leaving them to scheduler luck.

Fake time goes wherever the test would otherwise wait. The retry backoff and any lease or timeout deadline run on a paused runtime (Tokio's start_paused), and the test advances the clock explicitly past each deadline rather than sleeping. That makes the retry behavior deterministic: the same advance sequence drives the same redelivery every run, on any machine. If the plan still calls a real sleep, it is not deterministic enough.

The durable side effects must be asserted before the handler is considered done, and at the durable boundary, not at the HTTP status. The test asserts the database write landed exactly once and the outbox or queue contains exactly one publish for the request — checking the store and the outbox directly. A 200 status only proves the request was accepted; the side-effect assertions prove the work actually crossed the seam and crossed it once.

Idempotency is the load-bearing assertion: deliver the same message ID twice and assert the durable effect happened exactly once, because the worker consults a completion record keyed by that ID before applying the effect. The test separates three failure modes that look similar from the outside — a join failure (the spawned task panicked or was aborted, surfaced by the JoinHandle as a JoinError, distinguishing panic from cancellation), an inner failure (the task ran and returned a domain Err), and cancellation (the task was dropped before completing). Asserting on the JoinHandle result distinguishes join-level outcomes from the inner operation's Result. Throughout, the assertions carry identity fields — the request ID, the task or message ID, and the idempotency key written to the outbox row — so that when a case fails later it stays attributable to a specific message rather than to 'something in the worker'.

#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]
async fn retry_path_is_idempotent_under_duplicate_delivery() {
    let app = TestApp::start().await;
    let req_id = "req-42";
    let msg_id = "msg-7"; // identity that appears in every assertion

    // First delivery.
    let resp = app.post_job(req_id, msg_id).await;
    assert_eq!(resp.status(), 202);

    // Duplicate delivery of the SAME message id.
    let dup = app.post_job(req_id, msg_id).await;
    assert_eq!(dup.status(), 202);

    // Drive retry/backoff deterministically instead of sleeping.
    tokio::time::advance(RETRY_BACKOFF + Duration::from_millis(1)).await;

    // Assert at the durable boundary, exactly once, keyed by identity.
    assert_eq!(app.db.writes_for(msg_id).await, 1, "db write must be idempotent");
    assert_eq!(app.outbox.publishes_for(msg_id).await, 1, "outbox publish exactly once");

    // Separate join outcome from inner outcome.
    match app.last_join_result().await {
        Ok(inner) => assert!(inner.is_ok(), "inner op failed: {inner:?}"),
        Err(e) if e.is_cancelled() => panic!("task {msg_id} was cancelled"),
        Err(e) if e.is_panic() => panic!("task {msg_id} panicked"),
        Err(e) => panic!("join error for {msg_id}: {e:?}"),
    }
}

Paused runtime drives retries deterministically; assertions land at the db and outbox boundary, keyed by message id, with join vs inner vs cancellation separated.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Uses a deterministic time-control technique (start_paused plus explicit advance) for retry/backoff deadlines instead of real sleeps.
  • Defines an idempotency assertion at the durable boundary: the same message id delivered twice yields exactly one db write and one outbox publish.
  • Separates task-join behavior (JoinError, cancelled vs panicked) from the inner operation's Result.
  • Carries identity fields (request id, message id, idempotency key) into the assertions so failures stay attributable.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Build a production test matrix for a distributed Rust subsystem

The service parses binary frames, enriches them asynchronously, writes an outbox entry, renders operator reports, and exposes an FFI plugin boundary. The matrix proves different claims at different costs and keeps the end-to-end lane narrow.

Unit and property layer. Local domain invariants stay here: enrichment rules, outbox state transitions, and any 'never exceeds / always rejects duplicate' rule. Single-expectation rules are unit tests; rules that must hold across many generated sequences become property tests so failures shrink to minimal counterexamples. This is the cheapest, most deterministic layer and most claims should live here.

Fuzz and unsafe-invariant layer. The binary frame parser gets a coverage-guided fuzz target on the small raw-bytes-to-result function, with a seed corpus (empty, truncated, exact header, oversized length, duplicated frame, malformed footer) and crashes saved as regressions. The FFI plugin boundary gets unsafe-invariant tests run under Miri and a sanitizer, because a UB bug there may not be observable from a passing return value. This layer proves hostile-input and unsafe-edge handling that fixtures cannot.

Output-review layer. The operator report — large, shaped, human-reviewed — uses a snapshot (insta-style accept/reject diff) for shape, gated on review and paired with a semantic assertion on load-bearing fields. The wire frame the service emits, an external byte-for-byte contract, uses a golden file with nondeterministic fields (timestamps, UUIDs) normalized before comparison. Golden for the strict external contract, snapshot for the reviewable human report.

Performance-regression layer. The hot encoder or enrichment path gets a benchmark guarded by a single coarse budget (for example p95 <= 250 microseconds), marked #[ignore] so it stays out of the correctness run, and executed in a separate performance lane on stable hardware. It is looser and isolated because it is hardware-sensitive and guards a budget, not a value. Finally, the minimum end-to-end suite is one or two happy-path flows — request in, enrich, outbox row written, publish observed at the durable boundary, asserted on identity (message id, idempotency key), with retries driven by a paused clock. That narrow lane proves the transport reality composed without turning CI into a random-timing lottery; every sharper claim has already been proven more cheaply below it.

// Test matrix (lanes), each proving a distinct claim:
//
// LANE 1 - unit + property (cargo test, proptest)
//   * enrichment rules, outbox state machine, duplicate rejection
//   * property: outbox invariants hold across generated op sequences
//
// LANE 2 - fuzz + unsafe invariants (cargo-fuzz, Miri, ASan)
//   * fuzz_target!(|b: &[u8]| parse_frame(b)) with seeded corpus
//   * FFI plugin boundary under Miri + sanitizer for UB
//
// LANE 3 - output review
//   * snapshot (insta) for the operator report shape, gated on review
//     + semantic assertion on load-bearing fields
//   * golden file for the emitted wire frame, nondeterminism normalized
//
// LANE 4 - performance regression (separate lane)
#[test]
#[ignore] // excluded from the correctness run; runs in the perf lane
fn encoder_p95_within_budget() {
    let p95_us = bench_encoder_p95();
    assert!(p95_us <= 250, "encoder p95 {p95_us}us over budget");
}
//
// LANE 5 - minimal end-to-end (1-2 flows, paused clock, durable-boundary asserts)
//   * request -> enrich -> outbox row==1 -> publish==1, keyed by message id

Five lanes, each proving one kind of claim at its cheapest layer; the end-to-end lane is deliberately narrow.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines at least four distinct lanes: unit/property, fuzz/unsafe, output review, performance regression, plus a narrow end-to-end lane.
  • Includes one property/invariant layer, one fuzz/unsafe layer, one output-review layer (golden and snapshot), and one isolated performance-regression layer.
  • Justifies each lane by the claim it proves and why it sits at that cost level.
  • Keeps the end-to-end lane to one or two happy-path flows asserted at the durable boundary on identity, avoiding a random-timing CI lottery.

Lab solution

The lab completes the harness by fixing the broken reservation method. The starter's reserve unconditionally added qty and returned true, which could push used past limit and would make the invariant report a violation. The solution replaces it with try_reserve, the chapter's checked version: it accepts a reservation only when used + qty <= limit, otherwise it rejects the request and leaves the state untouched. Because rejection is a no-op, used can never cross limit, which is precisely the invariant the harness checks after every operation.

This is the deterministic core you would later lift into a property test. invariant_holds walks a fixed operation sequence and returns false the moment used exceeds limit; here it runs against five hand-picked scenarios with limit 8. Each scenario is constructed so that the checked reservation logic keeps the running total within bounds — the over-budget request in a scenario like [5, 4] is rejected rather than applied — so every case is valid.

all_valid folds invariant_holds over the scenarios with all, yielding true, and violations counts the scenarios where the invariant fails, yielding 0. The program prints the scenario count (5), the conjunction (true), and the violation count (0), matching the expected output exactly. Swapping the explicit list for a generated sequence and the for loop for a proptest body is the small step from this fixed-example harness to a real property test.

Example 42-S. property_invariant_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Quota {
    limit: u32,
    used: u32,
}

impl Quota {
    /// Reserve `qty` only if it keeps `used` within `limit`.
    /// The boolean reports acceptance; the state stays valid either way.
    fn try_reserve(&mut self, qty: u32) -> bool {
        if self.used + qty > self.limit {
            return false;
        }
        self.used += qty;
        true
    }
}

/// The invariant under test: `used` never exceeds `limit`, no matter
/// which sequence of reservation requests is applied.
fn invariant_holds(limit: u32, ops: &[u32]) -> bool {
    let mut quota = Quota { limit, used: 0 };

    for &qty in ops {
        let _accepted = quota.try_reserve(qty);
        if quota.used > quota.limit {
            return false;
        }
    }

    true
}

fn main() {
    let limit = 8_u32;
    let scenarios: &[&[u32]] = &[
        &[1_u32, 1, 1],
        &[4_u32, 4],
        &[5_u32, 4],
        &[2_u32, 2, 2, 2],
        &[8_u32],
    ];

    let all_valid = scenarios.iter().all(|ops| invariant_holds(limit, ops));
    let violations = scenarios
        .iter()
        .filter(|ops| !invariant_holds(limit, ops))
        .count();

    println!("cases = {}", scenarios.len());
    println!("all valid = {}", all_valid);
    println!("violations = {}", violations);
}
Output
cases = 5
all valid = true
violations = 0

Review question answers

Why is a property test often a better fit than several ad hoc example tests for one invariant?

An invariant is a rule that must hold across an entire space of inputs, and a handful of hand-picked examples only proves it for the cases someone happened to think of. A property test states the rule once and lets the framework generate hundreds of cases trying to break it, covering interleavings no human would write. When it does fail, shrinking reduces the counterexample to the smallest input that still violates the rule, so you get a pinpointed diagnosis instead of a vague failing fixture. The example tests grow linearly with effort; the property scales with the generator.

What does fuzzing prove that a curated integration fixture set usually does not prove?

Fixtures prove that a few known, mostly well-formed inputs decode correctly; fuzzing proves the code survives the adversarial, malformed input space a human author would never enumerate. A coverage-guided fuzzer mutates bytes to reach new branches and surfaces crashes, panics, out-of-bounds reads, and undefined behavior in parsers and unsafe byte walkers. That is exactly where external input crosses into your code, and it is the class of failure fixtures miss because they are written from the perspective of valid data.

Why are sleep-based async tests brittle even when they 'usually pass' locally?

A real sleep ties the test to wall-clock time and the scheduler, so it is really asserting 'this finished within N milliseconds on this machine' rather than the behavior you care about. That passes on a fast laptop and flakes on a loaded CI runner, because the margin depends on luck rather than logic. The fix is to take time out of the operating system's hands — pause the runtime and advance a fake clock explicitly past each deadline — so the test is deterministic regardless of machine speed.

What is the practical difference between golden files and snapshot tests?

Both compare output against a stored artifact, but golden files are a strict, checked-in byte-for-byte reference suited to external contracts like wire frames or normalized CLI dumps, where any difference is a real change you must justify. Snapshot testing is the ergonomic cousin: a crate like insta captures output on first run and, on later runs, shows a diff and lets you accept or reject it with a review command, which fits human-reviewed, evolving output. The risk shared by both is that they prove the output looks like this, not that it is correct, so nondeterministic fields must be normalized and any load-bearing value needs a separate semantic assertion.

Why should benchmark regression budgets be looser and more isolated than ordinary correctness assertions?

Benchmarks are inherently less deterministic than correctness tests — they are sensitive to hardware, build profile, and background load — so an exact timing assertion would flake constantly and erode trust in the suite. A coarse budget tied to a real product threshold (for example p95 under a stated microsecond bound) guards against meaningful regressions without failing on normal variance. Keeping them in a separate lane, often marked #[ignore], stops their noise from contaminating the fast, deterministic correctness run and keeps each layer proving the kind of claim it is good at.

Chapter 43 · Observability

Observability

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises rehearse the chapter's central discipline: start from the incident question, not from whichever telemetry is easiest to bolt on. You move from classifying which signal answers which symptom, through reading an async worker that drops trace context at a spawn boundary, into designing a small metric surface that explains backpressure, repairing logs and spans so they share identity, and finally telling one coherent incident story across all four signals and turning it into SLOs, alerts, and a refactoring policy.

The through-line is that an observable service produces four distinct kinds of evidence as one request flows through it — structured logs for one event, traces for one causal path, metrics for aggregate health, profiles for one cost hotspot — and the failure mode is almost never too little telemetry. It is the wrong signal at the wrong boundary: detail where you needed aggregation, aggregation where you needed identity, or instrumentation that stopped exactly at the queue or spawn boundary that mattered. Every solution below commits to a concrete answer and justifies it in terms of spans, fields, cardinality, queue wait, and correlation identity.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Pick logs, metrics, traces, or profiles from the symptom

Begin by asking what kind of question each symptom actually poses: aggregate health, one event, one causal path, or one cost hotspot. The signal follows from the question, and only then do you reach for the tool.

The queue-backed path that misses p99 while handler p50 stays calm is a trace question first. The aggregate already tells you the latency is real, but it cannot tell you where in the path the time goes. The mismatch between a healthy handler median and a sick tail is the classic shape of queue wait dominating: the request spends its time waiting to be claimed, not running. A single trace, decomposed by stage, shows the gap between accept and claim directly. Metrics confirm the trend across all requests, but the trace is what attributes the latency to a stage, so it is the right first pivot.

The sudden spike in rejected payloads after one rollout is a structured-logs question first. You need to see one rejected event with its fields — the route, the reason code, the offending shape — to know what changed. A counter tells you rejections rose; it does not tell you why any individual payload was rejected. Because the spike is correlated with a specific deploy, the question is about individual events you can filter and group, which is exactly what structured logs answer. A counter labelled by reject reason is a fine companion, but the log carries the explanatory detail.

The CPU climb on one reducer while queue age stays flat is a profile question first. Queue age being flat rules out backpressure and queue wait, so the cost is inside the running code, not in waiting. A profile samples the process and shows which stack frames burn the CPU — a hot serialization path, an accidental allocation in a loop, lock contention. Neither a metric nor a trace span localizes a cost hotspot to a function the way a profile does.

The service-to-service hop that times out only for one tenant is a trace question first, with logs close behind. The 'only for one tenant' qualifier means the problem follows a causal path tied to an identity, and a distributed trace carrying that tenant through every hop is what shows which hop stalls. You would not reach for a metric first, because tenant is a high-cardinality dimension you should not be labelling metrics with; that identity belongs on the trace and in structured log fields, where per-tenant lookup is appropriate. Raw log volume is not a substitute here either — grepping more lines does not reconstruct the cross-service path the way one correlated trace does.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each symptom is mapped to a primary signal — trace, structured logs, profile, trace — with a concrete reason rooted in the question it poses.
  • The first symptom explicitly separates queue wait (waiting to be claimed) from handler CPU (time running), which is what the p99/p50 split reveals.
  • Reject spike and tenant timeout are answered with one well-chosen log field or trace path, not with more raw log volume; tenant is kept off metric labels as a cardinality hazard.
Exercise 2code reading

Read a Tokio worker that lost trace context at spawn

The worker emits traces for local work yet cannot correlate the path because the trace context dies at the spawn boundary. tokio::spawn(handle(task)) moves the future onto a fresh task with no inherited span: the current span is a thread-local, task-local concept, and a spawned task starts with an empty context unless you attach one explicitly. So handle runs detached. Even if handle opens its own spans, they have no parent linking them back to the queue claim, and nothing ties the eventual downstream publish to the same request. You get three islands of telemetry — claim, handler, publish — with no edge between them.

The missing context is twofold. First, the in-process span context: the spawned future is not instrumented with the claim span, so the parent-child relationship is lost the moment work crosses spawn. The fix is tokio::spawn(handle(task).instrument(span)), where span is the worker or claim span, or opening a child span inside the spawned future before any awaits. Second, and more important for a queue-backed service, the trace identity is not in the data.
