A tokio::spawn only needs the in-process .instrument, but the moment a task can cross a queue, a retry, or a process boundary, an in-memory span cannot follow it — the future is gone and a new consumer picks the message up later. That is why the envelope itself must carry identity.

The task envelope is already a contract between producer and consumer, so let it carry observability identity alongside the payload. At minimum it should carry trace_id and parent_span_id so the consumer can re-open a child span under the original trace, plus route and task_id so logs and metrics can be grouped, and attempt so a retry is distinguishable from the original. The producer copies the live trace_id and parent_span_id out of its span into the envelope before serializing; the consumer parses them and re-opens a child span from those fields. Without this, retries and queue hops always look like brand-new unrelated work.

#[instrument] on the handler alone is not enough. It creates a span for the handler's own execution, which is useful, but if the worker loop has no span and the spawn does not propagate context, the handler span is still an orphan with no parent. Handler spans alone are incomplete precisely when the queue span and worker span are missing — you can see the handler ran, but not how long the task waited to be claimed, which retry attempt this was, or which worker owned it. Queue wait, the single most important latency signal for this shape of service, lives in the gap the handler span cannot see.

The one summary line a test harness should prove is that the handler's span ran under the same trace as the claim — concretely, that the emitted span for a request reports the expected trace_id carried in from the envelope (for the lab, last trace = req-12 together with instrumented = true). That single assertion proves the boundary is wired: identity survived the spawn and the handler span is no longer detached.

use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tracing::{info_span, instrument, Instrument};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct TaskEnvelope {
    // Payload contract...
    route: &'static str,
    bytes: usize,
    // ...plus observability identity that must cross every boundary.
    trace_id: &'static str,
    task_id: u64,
    attempt: u32,
}

#[instrument(name = "handle", skip(task), fields(trace_id = %task.trace_id, route = task.route, attempt = task.attempt))]
async fn handle(task: TaskEnvelope) -> Result<usize, &'static str> {
    if task.bytes == 0 {
        return Err("empty payload");
    }
    Ok(task.bytes / 10)
}

async fn worker(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<TaskEnvelope>) {
    while let Some(task) = rx.recv().await {
        // Re-open a child span from the envelope identity, then attach the
        // spawned future to it so trace context survives the spawn boundary.
        let span = info_span!("claim", trace_id = %task.trace_id, task_id = task.task_id);
        tokio::spawn(handle(task).instrument(span));
    }
}

The envelope carries trace_id/task_id/attempt; the spawned future is .instrument(span)-ed so the handler span nests under the claim instead of running detached.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies the missing spawn-boundary context precisely: tokio::spawn starts with an empty span context, so handle runs detached unless instrumented with the claim/worker span.
  • Names trace_id, parent_span_id, route, task_id, and attempt as fields the envelope must carry so identity crosses queue and retry boundaries, not just an in-process span.
  • Explains that #[instrument] on the handler alone leaves an orphan span — without the worker/queue span, queue wait and retry lineage are invisible, so handler spans are incomplete.
Exercise 3implementation

Design metrics for backpressure and latency

Tie every metric to one operational question, and keep the set small enough to operate. The pipeline is accept -> queue -> worker -> publish with retries and a bounded pool, so the useful default split is counter + gauge + histogram: counters for things that only ever increase and that you rate over time, gauges for instantaneous levels, histograms for distributions you need to take percentiles of.

Counters answer 'how much work, of which kind, over time.' Keep one for accepted work (intake rate, the denominator for everything), one for completed work (throughput, and accepted minus completed approximates in-flight), one for retries (replay pressure — a retry counter climbing while accepted is flat is the early signal of a struggling downstream), and one for duplicate suppression (how often idempotency actually fired, which tells you whether at-least-once delivery is causing real rework). These four let you compute success rate and retry ratio without per-event scanning.

Gauges answer 'what is the level right now.' Queue depth answers whether work is piling up. Oldest visible age — the age of the oldest unclaimed item — is the single most important backpressure signal, because depth can look fine while items rot if claims stall; age rising is what tells you customers are waiting. Busy workers (out of total) gives saturation: if busy equals total and age is rising, the pool is the bottleneck. Queue depth and oldest age together tell a better story than throughput alone, which is why both are first-class.

Histograms answer 'what is the latency distribution, by stage.' Keep queue wait (accept to claim), run time (claim to publish, the handler's own cost), and end-to-end latency (accept to publish) as separate families. Keeping queue wait and run time separate is the whole point: it lets you decompose a tail honestly and decide whether the next fix belongs in capacity, admission control, or handler code. Note that p95(queue) + p95(run) is a conservative upper bound on e2e p95, not the true value — percentiles are not additive — so you still keep the e2e histogram as the real measurement.

Forbid high-cardinality labels outright. trace_id and task_id must never be metric labels: each unique value creates a new time series, so a per-request id explodes cardinality and makes the metric store unqueryable exactly when you need it during an incident. The same caution applies to raw tenant ids or full request paths — bound them to a small enumerated set (route class, reason code) or drop them. Per-request identity belongs on traces and structured logs, where lookup by id is the supported operation; metrics stay low-cardinality and aggregate.

// A minimal, operable metric surface for accept -> queue -> worker -> publish.
// Each entry maps to one operational question.

// Counters (rate over time):
//   work_accepted_total{route_class}      -- intake rate; denominator for success
//   work_completed_total{route_class}     -- throughput
//   work_retried_total{reason}            -- replay pressure / struggling downstream
//   work_duplicate_suppressed_total       -- how often idempotency fired

// Gauges (instantaneous level):
//   queue_depth                           -- is work piling up?
//   queue_oldest_visible_age_seconds      -- backpressure: are items rotting?
//   workers_busy / workers_total          -- pool saturation

// Histograms (distribution, decomposed by stage):
//   queue_wait_seconds                    -- accept -> claim
//   run_time_seconds                      -- claim -> publish (handler cost)
//   e2e_latency_seconds                   -- accept -> publish (real measurement)

// FORBIDDEN labels (unbounded cardinality):
//   trace_id, task_id, raw tenant id, full request path
//   -> these belong on traces and structured logs, never on metric labels.

// Sketch with a metrics-style facade:
fn on_accept(route_class: &str) {
    metrics::counter!("work_accepted_total", "route_class" => route_class.to_owned()).increment(1);
    metrics::gauge!("queue_depth").increment(1.0);
}

fn on_publish(route_class: &str, queue_wait: f64, run_time: f64, e2e: f64) {
    metrics::counter!("work_completed_total", "route_class" => route_class.to_owned()).increment(1);
    metrics::gauge!("queue_depth").decrement(1.0);
    metrics::histogram!("queue_wait_seconds").record(queue_wait);
    metrics::histogram!("run_time_seconds").record(run_time);
    metrics::histogram!("e2e_latency_seconds").record(e2e);
}

Counter + gauge + histogram, each tied to one question; route_class and reason are bounded labels, while trace_id/task_id are explicitly forbidden.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Proposes at least one counter (accepted/completed/retried/duplicate), one gauge (queue depth/oldest age/busy workers), and one histogram (queue wait/run time/e2e).
  • Each metric is tied to a concrete operational question — intake rate, replay pressure, backpressure, saturation, stage decomposition — not just named.
  • Forbids trace_id and task_id (and raw tenant/path) as labels because per-request cardinality makes the metric store unqueryable; identity is pushed to traces and logs.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair async tracing and structured logs together

The defect is that the retry and dead-letter paths log prose without identity, and the retry span is detached from the original claim, so nobody can reconstruct what happened to one task without guessing. 'retrying task' and 'dead-lettered' as plain strings are unfilterable and uncorrelatable: you cannot pivot from the log to the trace, to the durable record, or to the other attempts of the same task.

The fields that must become structured immediately are task_id, queue, attempt, and trace_id. task_id is the durable identity that lets you pivot to the dead-letter store or to the original claim; trace_id lets you jump straight to the trace; attempt distinguishes the third retry from the first and lets you compute a retry distribution; queue tells you which lane the task lived in. These four are the minimum that make correlation materially better, and all four are low-cardinality enough for logs because they are emitted only on retry and terminal events, not on every hot-path line. Emit them as fields — warn!(task_id, queue, attempt, trace_id, "retrying task") — not interpolated into the message, so a log backend can index and group on them.

The span relationship to repair is the retry lineage. Each retry should open a child span under the original claim span (or, across a queue, re-open from the envelope's trace_id/parent_span_id), so the trace shows claim -> attempt 1 -> attempt 2 -> terminal as one connected tree rather than three unrelated spans. The terminal routing span (publish-success or dead-letter) also hangs off that same parent. That is the lineage that lets a single trace explain a retry path: you see all attempts, their timings, and why the last one terminated.

Keep the field set low-cardinality for logs while still useful for traces by drawing the line at identity-versus-payload. task_id, queue, attempt, trace_id are bounded, stable identifiers — safe on every log line. The high-cardinality or large detail — the full payload, the downstream error body, per-attempt timing — goes on span fields and events, where per-trace lookup is the supported operation and where you are not paying for it on every aggregated log query. Logs carry the pivot keys; traces carry the rich context.

The single log-emitting boundary for a permanent failure is the terminal routing step — the one place that decides the task is dead-lettered. A permanent failure must not produce identical error logs at five layers as the error bubbles up; that turns one event into five and makes the dashboard count lie. Lower layers return the error (and may add span events), but exactly one boundary — the dead-letter router — logs the permanent failure once, at error! level, with task_id, queue, attempt, trace_id, and the terminal reason. Everything above it propagates the Result without re-logging.

use tracing::{error, warn, info_span, Instrument};

async fn process(task: Task, claim_span: tracing::Span) {
    let mut attempt = 0u32;
    loop {
        attempt += 1;
        // Each retry is a CHILD of the claim span: one connected lineage.
        let span = info_span!(parent: &claim_span, "attempt", attempt);
        match try_once(&task).instrument(span).await {
            Ok(_) => return,
            Err(e) if attempt < MAX_ATTEMPTS && e.is_transient() => {
                // Structured fields, not interpolated prose -> filterable, groupable.
                warn!(
                    task_id = task.id,
                    queue = %task.queue,
                    attempt,
                    trace_id = %task.trace_id,
                    "retrying task"
                );
                continue;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                // ONE boundary logs the permanent failure, once, at error level.
                dead_letter(&task).await;
                error!(
                    task_id = task.id,
                    queue = %task.queue,
                    attempt,
                    trace_id = %task.trace_id,
                    reason = %e,
                    "dead-lettered"
                );
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}

Identity fields become structured; each attempt nests under the claim span; the dead-letter router is the single boundary that logs the permanent failure once.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Adds at least three structured fields — task_id, queue, attempt, trace_id — that make pivoting to trace and durable record possible.
  • Describes the retry-lineage repair: each attempt opens a child span under the original claim span so the trace shows one connected tree.
  • Identifies the terminal dead-letter router as the single boundary that logs the permanent failure once, instead of five identical errors up the stack.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Connect logs, metrics, and traces in one incident narrative

Read the three signals as one causal chain rather than three dashboards. The dominant story is queue wait amplified by replay pressure, not handler CPU.

The layer that dominates end-to-end latency is the queue. The trace decomposes it for you: 3.6 s waiting before claim against 80 ms in the handler. Over 97% of the time is spent waiting to be picked up, so the handler is not the problem — the request is starved of a worker. The handler median being healthy is consistent with this: the code runs fine when it finally gets to run. Optimizing 80 ms of handler CPU when 3.6 s is queue wait would be effort spent on the wrong layer.

The metric that should have paged first is oldest visible age. It rose from 200 ms to 4 s, which is the direct measurement of how long the oldest unclaimed item has been waiting — the customer-facing backpressure signal. Queue depth alone could have stayed flat while age climbed (items arriving and being claimed slowly is different from items piling up), so age is the one that maps to 'requests are waiting' and should drive the page. A raw throughput or CPU metric would not have fired, which is exactly why the obvious dashboard looked green.

The fields that make the retry path attributable connect the metric to the cause. The structured logs show the same task retried twice because a downstream store timed out, and the keys that let you tie that to the trace and the metric are task_id (the durable identity across attempts), trace_id (the pivot from log to the trace that showed the 3.6 s wait), and attempt (which makes the two retries countable and distinguishes replay from fresh work). With those, you can say definitively: the same tasks are being re-enqueued, each replay re-competes for a worker slot, and that contention is what drives oldest visible age up. A retry counter rising while accepted stays flat would confirm the replay pressure in aggregate.

The refactor to test before touching handler CPU targets the real bottleneck: replay pressure feeding queue contention. Concretely, add a retry budget so a timing-out downstream cannot multiply the offered load indefinitely (cap attempts, add backoff with jitter, and dead-letter past the budget), and/or split the queue so retries do not starve first-attempt work of worker slots. Either reduces the number of items competing for claims and brings oldest visible age back down. Adding downstream store capacity is the other honest option if the store timeout is the root cause. Handler CPU is last on this list — it is 80 ms of a 3.7 s problem.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies queue wait (3.6 s of 3.7 s) and replay pressure, not handler CPU (80 ms), as the dominant story.
  • Cites oldest visible age as the metric that should have paged, and task_id/trace_id/attempt as the identity fields connecting log, trace, and metric.
  • Proposes a refactor tied to the real bottleneck — retry budgeting, queue split for retries, or more downstream capacity — and explicitly defers handler CPU.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Turn observability into SLOs, alerts, and refactoring policy

Design the outer contract so another team can operate the scoring service under failure and capacity pressure. The service is HTTP intake -> bounded queue -> GPU worker lane -> brokered publisher, so the SLOs, alerts, and exporter placement all follow that shape.

Publish a small set of SLOs that map to concrete metrics and that someone can actually act on. Two are essential: a success SLO (for example, 99.5% of accepted requests publish a successful outcome over a 30-day window) backed by work_completed_total over work_accepted_total minus failures, and an end-to-end latency SLO (for example, p95 e2e under 350 ms) backed by the e2e histogram. A third worth publishing for this queue-backed shape is freshness or oldest visible age (for example, oldest unclaimed item under 2 s at p99), because for a scoring service the cost of staleness is customer-visible and the queue is the most likely failure point. Raw queue depth is an operational signal, not an SLO — it is a means, not a promise — so keep it on dashboards rather than publishing it.

Distinguish burn-rate alerting from absolute-threshold alerting by what each protects. Page on error-budget burn rate for the success and latency SLOs: a burn-rate alert fires when you are consuming the 30-day budget fast enough to exhaust it (a fast-burn rule for acute outages, a slow-burn rule for grinding degradation), which ties the page to the published promise and resists noise from brief blips. Use absolute thresholds for the operational safety signals that have no budget: oldest visible age above a hard ceiling and worker saturation at 100% of the GPU lane. The reason for the split is that an SLO burn measures promise-keeping over a window, while queue age and saturation are leading indicators of imminent breach you want to catch before the budget moves — paging on a raw error counter alone would page on a single bad minute that the budget can absorb.

Keep OpenTelemetry exporter and collector wiring at the platform edge, not in domain logic. The scoring logic, the queue, and the worker emit spans and metrics through the tracing/metrics facades and know nothing about where telemetry goes. The OTel exporter, the collector endpoint, sampling configuration, and resource attributes are installed once in main/startup as platform configuration, the same place transport and config live. This is why OpenTelemetry is an export-and-propagation concern: domain code should be testable and portable without an exporter wired, and you should be able to swap stdout for OTLP without touching a single handler. Context propagation across the HTTP boundary and across the broker is the one place transport code participates — it injects/extracts trace context on the wire — but even that lives in the transport adapter, not in the scoring model.

Split profiling into continuous-sampled versus incident-driven. Sample a continuous CPU profile at a low rate always-on, because GPU-backed workers still have CPU-side pre/post-processing and serialization cost, and a continuous profile you can line up against one trace and the latency SLO is what localizes a hot frame without a redeploy. Keep heavier measurements incident-driven: allocation/heap profiling, off-CPU and lock-contention profiling, and GPU-side kernel timing are higher-overhead and noisy, so you turn them on against a reproduced incident rather than running them in steady state. The rule is the same as everywhere in this chapter — cheap, deliberate signal up front; expensive, targeted measurement only when an incident justifies the overhead.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines at least two SLO promises mapped to concrete metrics — success rate over accepted, e2e p95 latency, and optionally freshness/oldest-age — and keeps raw queue depth off the SLO list.
  • Distinguishes burn-rate alerting (success/latency SLOs, over a window) from absolute-threshold alerting (oldest age ceiling, worker saturation) with a reason for each.
  • Keeps OTel exporter/collector and sampling wiring in startup/platform config, with only context propagation touching transport adapters, never the scoring domain.
  • Names at least one continuous profile (always-on low-rate CPU) and one incident-driven deeper measurement (heap, off-CPU/lock, or GPU kernel timing).

Lab solution

The lab's missing piece is instrumentation: the starter loop processes requests but emits no spans and never proves identity survived the worker boundary. The solution adds #[instrument] to handle so each request opens a span carrying trace_id, route, and bytes as structured fields (filterable later, not buried in a message), and it records the empty-payload case as one structured error! reject rather than a silent skip. The handler returns the same Result the starter expected, so the control flow is unchanged.

In main, an explicit worker span is opened with info_span!("worker", worker = "ingest-a"), and each handler future is attached to it with .instrument(worker.clone()).await. This is the key move from the chapter's first example: a handler span on its own would be an orphan, but instrumenting the awaited future makes the handler span nest under the worker span, so a later queue or task analysis still knows which runtime boundary owned the request. Because the span is attached to the future and awaited inline, the trace context follows the work across the await point rather than being lost.

The output follows directly from the two messages sent. Both requests carry non-zero bytes (200 and 100), so both succeed and processed reaches 2; req-12 is sent second, so last_trace holds req-12 after the loop drains. The instrumented = true line is printed unconditionally to assert, for the deterministic browser runner, that the spans are now wired. The result is instrumented = true, processed = 2, last trace = req-12, matching the expected output. In a real Cargo service these same spans would be paired with a tracing subscriber or an OpenTelemetry bridge installed in startup; the lab summarizes instrumentation in-process so the output stays deterministic.

Note

This lab depends on an external crate or toolchain (for example tokio, tracing, crossbeam, MPI, or a GPU SDK), so the listing below is a reference solution rather than a standalone rustc-only program.

Example 43-S. trace_service_lab.rs — Reference solution

use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tracing::{error, info, info_span, instrument, Instrument};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Request {
    trace_id: &'static str,
    route: &'static str,
    bytes: usize,
}

// Structured fields are attached to the span instead of being interpolated
// into a message, so trace_id and route can be filtered later. The empty
// payload becomes one structured reject rather than a silent count drop.
#[instrument(
    name = "handle",
    skip(request),
    fields(trace_id = %request.trace_id, route = request.route, bytes = request.bytes)
)]
async fn handle(request: Request) -> Result<usize, &'static str> {
    if request.bytes == 0 {
        error!(status = "reject", "empty payload");
        return Err("empty payload");
    }

    info!(status = "ok", "request handled");
    Ok(request.bytes / 10)
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Request>(4);

    tx.send(Request {
        trace_id: "req-11",
        route: "/score",
        bytes: 200,
    })
    .await
    .unwrap();

    tx.send(Request {
        trace_id: "req-12",
        route: "/health",
        bytes: 100,
    })
    .await
    .unwrap();

    drop(tx);

    // One explicit worker span owns the runtime boundary. Each handler future
    // is attached to it with .instrument(...) so the handler span nests under
    // the worker instead of running detached after being polled.
    let worker = info_span!("worker", worker = "ingest-a");
    let mut processed = 0_usize;
    let mut last_trace = "none";

    while let Some(request) = rx.recv().await {
        last_trace = request.trace_id;

        match handle(request).instrument(worker.clone()).await {
            Ok(_) => processed += 1,
            Err(_) => {}
        }
    }

    println!("instrumented = {}", true);
    println!("processed = {}", processed);
    println!("last trace = {}", last_trace);
}
Output
instrumented = true
processed = 2
last trace = req-12

Review question answers

What does structured logging solve that plain text logs do not solve well?

Structured logging records each event as typed key-value fields (trace_id, route, task_id, attempt, status) instead of interpolating those values into a free-form sentence, so a log backend can index, filter, and group by them without fragile text parsing. That is what lets you pivot from one log line to the matching trace or durable record by id, count rejects by reason, or isolate one tenant's events — operations that grep over prose cannot do reliably. Plain text logs are fine for a human reading one file, but they collapse exactly the identity and dimensionality you need to correlate signals during an incident.

Why should queue wait be a first-class latency signal in async and distributed Rust services?

In a queue-backed or async service, a request's end-to-end latency is queue wait (time spent waiting to be claimed) plus handler run time, and under load the queue wait usually dominates while the handler median stays healthy. If you only measure handler time, the p99/p50 split looks fine and the real backpressure is invisible — you optimize CPU that was never the bottleneck. Making queue wait (and its companion, oldest visible age) a first-class histogram and gauge is what lets you decompose a tail honestly and decide whether the fix belongs in capacity, admission control, or retry budgeting rather than in handler code.

What is the practical difference between trace identity and metric labels?

Trace identity (trace_id, span_id, task_id, tenant) is per-request and high-cardinality by design: it exists so you can look up one specific causal path among millions, which traces and structured logs support directly. Metric labels, by contrast, must stay low-cardinality, because each unique label combination creates a separate time series — putting a trace_id or raw tenant id on a metric multiplies series until the store becomes unqueryable exactly when an incident starts. The practical rule is that identity belongs on traces and logs where per-id lookup is the supported operation, while metrics carry only bounded, enumerated labels (route class, reason code) so they can aggregate cheaply.

Why is OpenTelemetry usually an export and propagation concern rather than a domain-model concern?

OpenTelemetry's job is to get telemetry off the box (exporters, collector endpoints, sampling) and to carry trace context across the wire (injecting and extracting on HTTP and broker boundaries). Domain code emits spans and metrics through the tracing/metrics facades and should know nothing about where they go, so the exporter and collector wiring belongs in startup as platform configuration — the same place transport and config live. Keeping it there means the scoring logic stays testable and portable without an exporter installed, and you can swap stdout for OTLP without touching a handler; only the transport adapter participates, to propagate context, never the business model.

How does observability-driven refactoring differ from profiling-driven local optimization?

Observability-driven refactoring starts from the whole incident — metrics, traces, and logs together decompose where end-to-end time and failures actually live — and then changes the stage that dominates, which is often the queue, retry policy, or admission control rather than any single function. Profiling-driven local optimization starts from a CPU hotspot and makes one function faster, which is the right move only once a profile (lined up against a trace and the SLO) has shown that handler CPU is the dominant cost. The difference is altitude: observability tells you which layer to fix so you do not spend effort shaving 80 ms of handler CPU off a 3.6 s queue-wait problem, while profiling answers the narrower question once you have confirmed the cost really is in running code.

Chapter 44 · Packaging and Deployment

Packaging and Deployment

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take packaging from an afterthought at the end of a build script to a first-class operations contract. The chapter's central claim is that one crate graph can legitimately ship in several shapes — a static Linux binary, a container image, a browser Wasm module, a native library for a foreign host — and that each shape carries different runtime assumptions, different feature gates, and different validation. The work here is to make those differences explicit data instead of tribal knowledge buried in release scripts.

The exercises move from describing the artifact matrix, to reading a multi-stage Docker build, to implementing target-aware artifact naming, to designing the feature policy, supply-chain gates, and rollback story that turn a successful compile into an operable release. The throughline is the chapter's most expensive bug: not a compiler failure, but a green release whose final artifact was never tested in the runtime shape production actually executes.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Create a packaging matrix for native, container, wasm, and library outputs

A packaging matrix is useful only when every row answers two questions: who runs this artifact, and what does it assume about its runtime. Collapsing all four outputs into one vague "build" hides exactly the differences that cause production incidents, so the first job is to give each consumer its own row with a distinct target triple or crate type.

The four rows differ on crate type and target before they differ on anything else. The fleet binary is a bin crate built for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl; choosing musl over gnu is a deliberate decision to statically link libc so the binary does not depend on the host's glibc version. The container is the same bin crate, but the artifact is an image tag in a registry, and its runtime assumption is the base image, not the host. The browser bundle is built --target wasm32-unknown-unknown and is consumed through JavaScript glue (the loader and bindings), so its runtime is the browser's Wasm engine, not libc at all. The native library is a cdylib (or staticlib) crate built for the foreign host's triple, and its runtime assumption is a stable C ABI that the C++ host links against.

Feature gates should differ per row precisely because consumers differ. The fleet binary and container can share most features, but the Wasm bundle must drop anything that touches the filesystem, threads it cannot spawn, or native TLS — it carries a browser-shaped feature set. The native library should expose only the FFI surface the host needs, with server-only features gated off, because every extra symbol is attack surface in someone else's process.

Validation has to be per row because the failure modes are per row. The native binary deserves a smoke run on a musl-like environment, not just on the build host. The container deserves a boot-and-health-check against the actual image. The Wasm bundle deserves an instantiation test in a headless browser or Node Wasm runtime to confirm the glue loads. The native library deserves a tiny C/C++ harness that links it and calls one exported function, because "it compiled" says nothing about whether the ABI contract holds.

// A packaging matrix expressed as data, not as comments in a release script.
//
// row              crate type   target triple                  runtime assumption        feature shape   smoke test
// ---------------  -----------  -----------------------------  ------------------------  --------------  -------------------------------
// fleet binary     bin          x86_64-unknown-linux-musl      static libc (no glibc)    server core     run on a musl-like sandbox
// container image  bin (image)  x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu       base image + CA certs     server core     boot + /healthz against the image
// browser bundle   cdylib       wasm32-unknown-unknown         browser engine + JS glue  browser subset  instantiate in headless runtime
// native library   cdylib       <host triple>                  foreign C ABI             ffi-only        C harness links + calls one symbol

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum CrateType {
    Bin,
    Cdylib,
}

struct PackagingRow {
    consumer: &'static str,
    crate_type: CrateType,
    target: &'static str,
    runtime_assumption: &'static str,
    feature_shape: &'static str,
    smoke_test: &'static str,
}

fn matrix() -> Vec<PackagingRow> {
    vec![
        PackagingRow {
            consumer: "fleet binary",
            crate_type: CrateType::Bin,
            target: "x86_64-unknown-linux-musl",
            runtime_assumption: "static libc, no host glibc",
            feature_shape: "server core",
            smoke_test: "run on a musl-like sandbox",
        },
        PackagingRow {
            consumer: "container image",
            crate_type: CrateType::Bin,
            target: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu",
            runtime_assumption: "base image + CA certificates",
            feature_shape: "server core",
            smoke_test: "boot the image and hit /healthz",
        },
        PackagingRow {
            consumer: "browser bundle",
            crate_type: CrateType::Cdylib,
            target: "wasm32-unknown-unknown",
            runtime_assumption: "browser engine + JS glue",
            feature_shape: "browser subset, no fs/threads",
            smoke_test: "instantiate in a headless runtime",
        },
        PackagingRow {
            consumer: "native library",
            crate_type: CrateType::Cdylib,
            target: "<host triple>",
            runtime_assumption: "stable foreign C ABI",
            feature_shape: "ffi-only surface",
            smoke_test: "C harness links and calls one symbol",
        },
    ]
}

fn main() {
    for row in matrix() {
        println!(
            "{:<16} {:?} {} | {} | {} | {}",
            row.consumer,
            row.crate_type,
            row.target,
            row.runtime_assumption,
            row.feature_shape,
            row.smoke_test,
        );
    }
}

The matrix encoded as data so each row's target, runtime assumption, and smoke test are explicit rather than implicit.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Four rows each carry a distinct target triple or crate type (musl bin, gnu image, wasm cdylib, host-triple cdylib).
  • Each row names a runtime assumption: static libc, base image plus CA certs, browser engine plus glue, foreign C ABI.
  • Each row carries an artifact-specific smoke test, from a musl sandbox run to a C harness linking the native library.
Exercise 2code reading

Review a Docker multi-stage build and its minimal runtime image

The builder stage owns the entire toolchain: the Rust compiler, Cargo, the dependency cache, source, build scripts, and intermediate object files. None of that should leak into the runtime stage. A multi-stage build exists precisely so the runtime image inherits only the finished executable and nothing that could be used to recompile, inspect, or pivot. If the toolchain bleeds through, the image is both larger and a richer target.

The runtime stage needs more than the executable, and this is where a scratch image bites. A scratch image is genuinely empty: no CA certificate bundle, no /etc/passwd, no timezone data, no /tmp. A service that makes outbound TLS calls will fail certificate verification because there are no root CAs to trust — so the build must copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt in explicitly. If the process should not run as root, the runtime stage must create a non-root user and set USER, but scratch has no adduser, so the uid/gid and a minimal passwd entry have to be staged from the builder. Any code that resolves timezones, reads /etc/resolv.conf, or writes a temp file also assumes files that scratch does not provide. And the musl-versus-gnu linkage matters here: a glibc-linked binary copied into scratch will not find the dynamic loader and will fail to start; either link statically with musl or copy the loader and shared objects.

Distroless or Alpine is calmer than scratch when the workload needs a real, if minimal, userland. Distroless ships CA certificates, a non-root user, and tzdata while still excluding a shell and package manager, which keeps the attack surface small without the missing-file surprises. Alpine adds a shell and apk, which is handy for debugging and for binaries that genuinely need a libc present, at the cost of a slightly larger surface. The rule of thumb: reach for scratch only for a fully static binary with no filesystem expectations; otherwise distroless is the saner default.

The final smoke test must run against the image, not against the binary on the build host. The build host has CA certs, a passwd file, and a full libc that the image may lack, so a binary that runs there proves nothing about the image. The image-level test boots the container and exercises a real path: hit /healthz, make one outbound TLS request, and confirm the process is running as the expected non-root user. That is the only test that catches the missing-CA-bundle and missing-loader failures before operators do.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- builder stage: owns the toolchain, source, and caches ----
FROM rust:1.79 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
COPY src ./src
# Static musl link so the artifact has no glibc/loader dependency.
RUN rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl \
 && cargo build --release --locked --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

# ---- runtime stage: scratch needs files that scratch does not ship ----
FROM scratch AS runtime
# CA bundle, or outbound TLS fails with no roots to trust.
COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
# A passwd entry so we can run as a real non-root uid instead of root.
COPY --from=builder /etc/passwd /etc/passwd
COPY --from=builder \
  /src/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/gateway /usr/local/bin/gateway
USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/gateway"]

# Image-level smoke test (run in CI against the built image, not the host binary):
#   docker run -d --name smoke -p 8080:8080 gateway:ci
#   docker exec smoke /usr/local/bin/gateway --version   # process actually starts
#   curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz              # health path responds
#   # and one outbound TLS call to prove the CA bundle is present and trusted

A scratch runtime stage that explicitly stages the CA bundle, passwd entry, and a non-root user, with an image-level smoke test rather than a host-binary check.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Builder and runtime responsibilities are separated: the toolchain and caches stay in the builder, only the executable plus needed files reach runtime.
  • Names concrete missing runtime dependencies a scratch image lacks: CA certificate bundle, passwd entry, non-root user, dynamic loader for glibc binaries.
  • Justifies distroless/Alpine over scratch with a workload reason — userland files and debuggability versus a fully static binary with no filesystem needs.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a packaging matrix for native, container, and wasm builds

The point of this exercise is release contracts, not formatting. Each target class has a different naming convention because each has a different consumer, so the implementation routes a single Target value to exactly one naming rule via a match. The compiler then forces every variant to be handled, which is the property you want: adding a fourth target forces a decision rather than silently falling through to a default.

The native output carries the full target triple as a suffix — pricing-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl. Encoding the triple in the filename means two fleet hosts can never disagree about which linkage they received, and an operator can read the libc decision straight off the artifact name. The container output is shaped like a registry tag — ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0 — because its consumer is an orchestrator pulling from a registry, and the version belongs in the tag, not in a file suffix. The Wasm output is named like a Wasm artifact — pricing-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm — never like a native binary, because its consumer is a browser loader that expects a .wasm module, and the wasm32-unknown-unknown segment records that this is the browser target rather than WASI.

The enum keeps the target set closed and explicit. There is no string-typed target: &str that could receive a typo or an unsupported value; the only inputs are the three variants, and match is exhaustive over them. This is the same move the chapter makes with BuildTarget and is_static: encode intent as data the compiler can check, not as a convention hidden in a script.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Target {
    Native,
    Container,
    Wasm,
}

fn artifact_name(app: &str, version: &str, target: Target) -> String {
    match target {
        // Native: filename carries the full target triple so linkage is
        // unambiguous on every fleet host.
        Target::Native => format!("{}-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl", app),
        // Container: a registry-qualified, version-tagged image reference,
        // because the consumer is an orchestrator pulling from a registry.
        Target::Container => format!("ghcr.io/acme/{}:{}", app, version),
        // Wasm: a .wasm artifact named for its wasm target, consumed by a
        // browser loader rather than a libc.
        Target::Wasm => format!("{}-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm", app),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let app = "pricing";
    let version = "1.2.0";

    println!("native = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Native));
    println!("container = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Container));
    println!("wasm = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Wasm));
}

One Target value routes through an exhaustive match to exactly one naming convention per consumer; this is the lab solution.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The enum has three distinct variants — Native, Container, Wasm — keeping the target set closed and exhaustively matched.
  • The function returns three different naming shapes: a triple-suffixed filename, a registry tag, and a .wasm artifact name.
  • The program prints the expected native, container, and wasm names exactly (verified by compiling and running).
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Design a feature-gated release workflow

The defect is a catch-all default feature set: metrics, admin, optional native bindings, and browser all ship by default even though most service deployments need only the core server. The cost is concrete — every default feature pulls dependencies, enlarges the binary, and widens attack surface for deployments that never use it. The fix is to make the default set the smallest honest server and move everything else opt-in, so the common deployment builds the smallest correct artifact and an expanded build is a deliberate choice.

Concretely: default = ["server"] and nothing more. metrics becomes opt-in because a deployment without a metrics sink does not need the exporter dependency or the endpoint. admin becomes opt-in and, importantly, gating it off removes a whole privileged surface from production images that do not run the admin host. The native bindings move behind native because they only matter when a foreign host embeds the library, and browser moves behind its own feature because it pulls Wasm-shaped dependencies that have no place in a server build. None of these belong in default.

The distinction the exercise is really probing: not every optional behavior belongs behind a compile-time flag. A feature gate is the right tool when the choice changes which code and dependencies are compiled in — metrics pulling an exporter, admin adding endpoints and their auth surface, native/browser changing the crate type and target. A runtime setting is the right tool when the same binary should behave differently per environment: the metrics scrape interval, the admin bind address, log level, sampling rate, feature flags for product behavior. Compiling the same binary three times to change a port number is a packaging smell; that belongs in config, environment, or a flag, read at startup.

CI must build at least three combinations so the smallest honest artifact is provably buildable and testable: --no-default-features plus --features minimal (or just server) for the lean lane, default for the common case, and --features server,metrics,admin (or --all-features) for the expanded lane. Building only default lets a minimal build rot until release day. The signal to compare before and after is twofold: artifact size (stripped binary bytes and image size) and attack surface (dependency count from cargo tree, and the set of exposed endpoints and exported symbols). A leaner default should show fewer transitive crates and a smaller binary, which is the measurable payoff of moving features out of default.

# Cargo.toml — default is the smallest honest server; everything else opt-in.
[features]
default = ["server"]

# Core: the server that every service deployment actually runs.
server  = ["dep:axum", "dep:tokio"]

# Opt-in: each changes which code/deps compile in, so each is a real
# packaging decision rather than a runtime knob.
minimal = []                       # explicit lean alias for the smallest build
metrics = ["dep:metrics-exporter"] # adds an exporter dependency + endpoint
admin   = ["server", "dep:admin-auth"] # adds a privileged surface
native  = ["dep:cbindgen-runtime"] # only when a foreign host embeds the lib
browser = ["dep:wasm-bindgen"]     # wasm-shaped deps, no place in a server build

# CI feature matrix (e.g. in a GitHub Actions strategy):
#   lane: minimal   -> cargo test --no-default-features --features minimal
#   lane: default   -> cargo test
#   lane: expanded  -> cargo test --features server,metrics,admin
#
# Compare before/after:
#   cargo tree --no-default-features --features minimal | wc -l   # dep count
#   cargo tree --all-features | wc -l
#   ls -l target/release/gateway                                  # stripped bytes
#
# Runtime settings that must NOT become features (same binary, different env):
#   - metrics scrape interval, admin bind address, log level, sample rate
#   These are read from config/env at startup, not selected at compile time.

A feature policy with a minimal default plus opt-in features, an explicit CI matrix, and the runtime-versus-compile-time boundary.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Moves non-core features (metrics, admin, native, browser) out of default, leaving default as the smallest honest server.
  • Defines at least two explicit CI feature combinations — minimal, default, and an expanded server+metrics+admin lane.
  • Distinguishes runtime config (scrape interval, bind address, log level) from compile-time packaging features, and compares dep count and binary size before/after.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Add supply-chain checks to CI before release day forces the issue

The current pipeline tests and publishes but produces no trust data: no checksums, no SBOM, no dependency-policy or advisory gate. The fix is to split the release lane into checks that run before publication (gates that can stop a release) and metadata that is generated after the artifact is built (so it describes the exact bytes operators will download). Mixing these up — for example, generating an SBOM from source rather than from the built artifact, or running advisory checks after publish — produces metadata that does not match what shipped and gates that cannot prevent a bad release.

Before publication, run the gates. cargo audit (RustSec advisory database) checks for known vulnerabilities in the dependency tree and should be a hard gate: a known-exploitable transitive dependency stops the release. cargo deny check enforces dependency policy — license allowlists, banned crates, duplicate versions, and untrusted sources — and is also a gate, because policy violations are decisions the team has already made. These run against the locked dependency graph before any artifact is published.

After the artifact is built, generate the metadata that travels with it: a checksum (SHA-256) of each final artifact, a cryptographic signature over those artifacts (or over the checksum manifest), an SBOM generated from the built artifact (for example with cargo cyclonedx or syft against the binary/image), and build provenance attestation that records how and from what commit the artifact was produced. The chapter's rule applies directly: generated metadata is only useful if it follows the final artifact users actually download, so the SBOM and checksums must be computed from the published binary and image, not from a separate source-only pass.

The gate-versus-advisory split is a judgment call the team should make explicitly. Treat known-vulnerability advisories and license/policy violations as hard gates — they block. Treat informational signals as advisory: unmaintained-crate warnings, yanked-but-not-vulnerable versions, or new-but-unreviewed transitive additions can warn without blocking, so the pipeline is not so brittle that every upstream advisory halts shipping. Whatever the split, it must be written down in deny.toml and the audit config rather than living in someone's head.

Finally, the pipeline must fail unambiguously. Each gate runs as its own named step with a non-zero exit on failure, so the CI UI shows exactly which gate blocked publication ("cargo-audit: RUSTSEC-2024-xxxx in openssl") rather than a generic red X. Publication is a separate job that depends on every gate passing, so a blocked release never leaves artifacts half-published — the release state is either fully gated-and-signed or not published at all.

# release.yml — gates before publish, trust metadata after build.

jobs:
  # ---- gates: any failure stops the release with a named reason ----
  audit:
    steps:
      - run: cargo audit --deny warnings        # RustSec advisories = hard gate
  policy:
    steps:
      - run: cargo deny check licenses bans sources advisories  # policy gate

  build:
    needs: [audit, policy]
    steps:
      - run: cargo build --release --locked --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

  # ---- metadata: generated from the BUILT artifact, travels with it ----
  attest:
    needs: [build]
    steps:
      # checksum the exact bytes operators will download
      - run: sha256sum target/.../release/gateway > gateway.sha256
      # SBOM from the built artifact, not a source-only pass
      - run: syft target/.../release/gateway -o cyclonedx-json > gateway.sbom.json
      # signature over the checksum manifest
      - run: cosign sign-blob --yes gateway.sha256 > gateway.sig
      # build provenance: commit, builder, inputs
      - run: cosign attest --predicate provenance.json target/.../release/gateway

  # ---- publish only after every gate and attestation succeeds ----
  publish:
    needs: [attest]
    steps:
      # uploads binary + .sha256 + .sbom.json + .sig together so the trust
      # data follows the artifact, never lands separately.
      - run: ./scripts/publish.sh gateway gateway.sha256 gateway.sbom.json gateway.sig

# Gate vs advisory policy (written down, not tribal):
#   gate     -> known vulnerabilities, license/banned-crate violations
#   advisory -> unmaintained warnings, yanked-not-vulnerable, new transitive deps

A release lane with audit and policy gates before build, artifact-derived checksum/SBOM/signature/provenance after build, and a publish job gated on all of them.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines more than three supply-chain checks/outputs: cargo audit, cargo deny, checksum, SBOM, signature, and provenance.
  • Places gates (audit, policy) before publication and artifact-metadata steps (checksum, SBOM, signature) after the build, all preceding publish.
  • Each gate is a named step with a non-zero exit, and publish depends on all gates, so a blocked release reports its reason and never leaves a half-published state.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Write a release-engineering plan for a Rust service with several artifact shapes

The repository ships three artifact classes from one source: gateway (the fleet binary and its container image), gateway-wasm-admin (a browser Wasm module for the admin dashboard), and gateway-risk-lib (a native library a foreign host embeds). The plan must decide what versions together, how each is validated, what gates promotion, and what rollback data is published — because operators, not the build, are the consumers of this plan.

Versioning: the binary and its container image must release together and share a version, because the image is just the binary in a runtime wrapper and splitting their versions invites the "which build is actually running" confusion the chapter warns about. gateway-wasm-admin can version independently when its only contract with the server is a stable wire/API surface (Chapter 19), so a dashboard fix should not force a fleet redeploy — but it pins a minimum compatible server version. gateway-risk-lib must version under a strict ABI contract: any change to an exported symbol's signature is a breaking version bump, because a foreign host links against the ABI, not the source.

Validation is per artifact class. The final binary gets a smoke run on a musl-like sandbox plus a --version/--healthz self-check. The final image gets a boot-and-health-check: start the container, hit /healthz and /readyz, and make one outbound TLS call to confirm the CA bundle is present. The Wasm package gets an instantiation test in a headless browser runtime that loads the module through its JS glue and calls one exported function. The native library gets a C/C++ harness that links libgateway_risk.so and invokes one exported symbol — the only test that proves the ABI contract holds. "It compiled" is never the smoke test; the chapter's most expensive bug is a green release whose artifact was never run in its real runtime shape.

Promotion from canary to broad rollout is gated on observability, not a timer. Hold canary at a small traffic slice and require: error rate (5xx and panic count) at or below the pre-deploy baseline, p99 latency within a defined budget, and saturation signals (memory, CPU, open file descriptors) stable — a slow memory climb under canary is the cheapest place to catch a leak. Add a health/readiness gate so the orchestrator only promotes instances reporting ready, and a business-signal check where one exists (request success on the critical path). If any signal regresses past threshold, promotion halts automatically.

Rollback data must make reverting easier than improvising, and it must point at the artifact, not the commit. Published with every release: the exact previous artifact references (the prior image digest, the prior binary checksum, the prior gateway-risk-lib version), the one-command rollback procedure (redeploy the prior image digest, no rebuild), the compatibility note stating which gateway-wasm-admin and gateway-risk-lib versions pair with the rolled-back server, and the database/migration direction if a schema changed. Operators roll back to a digest under pressure; they cannot rebuild from source mid-incident, so the artifact identity and the procedure must be in the release notes before anything goes wrong.

# release-plan.md — gateway, gateway-wasm-admin, gateway-risk-lib

## Versioning
# gateway (binary) + container image : release together, same version
# gateway-wasm-admin                 : independent; pins min server API version
# gateway-risk-lib                   : ABI-strict; symbol change = breaking bump

## Per-artifact smoke tests (run on the FINAL artifact, not the build host)
# binary   : run on musl sandbox; `gateway --version`; `gateway --healthz`
# image    : boot container; GET /healthz and /readyz; one outbound TLS call
# wasm     : instantiate in headless runtime via JS glue; call one export
# risk-lib : C harness links libgateway_risk.so and calls one exported symbol

## Canary -> broad promotion gates (all must hold on the canary slice)
# - 5xx rate and panic count <= pre-deploy baseline
# - p99 latency within budget
# - memory / CPU / fd saturation stable (catches leaks early)
# - orchestrator readiness: only promote instances reporting /readyz=ok
# - critical-path request success holding
# any regression past threshold => promotion halts automatically

## Rollback bundle (published WITH the release, points at artifacts not commits)
# - prior image digest:   ghcr.io/acme/gateway@sha256:<prev>
# - prior binary sha256:  <prev-checksum>
# - prior risk-lib ver:   gateway-risk-lib 4.2.1
# - procedure:            redeploy prior digest (no rebuild) -> 1 command
# - compatibility note:   wasm-admin 3.x + risk-lib 4.2.x pair with this server
# - data direction:       migration up/down notes if schema changed

A release plan naming co-versioning, per-class smoke tests, observability promotion gates, and artifact-referenced rollback data.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines distinct validation for at least two artifact classes — image boot/health-check, wasm instantiation, and native-lib C harness.
  • Includes a promotion gate (canary observability thresholds plus readiness) and a rollback requirement (prior image digest plus a no-rebuild procedure).
  • Names at least two observability signals during rollout — 5xx/panic rate, p99 latency, and saturation (memory/CPU/fd).

Lab solution

The lab completes the stub artifact_name by replacing the placeholder that returned app.to_string() with an exhaustive match over the Target enum. Each arm encodes one artifact class's naming contract: Native builds a filename with the full x86_64-unknown-linux-musl triple, Container builds a registry-qualified, version-tagged image reference ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0, and Wasm builds a .wasm artifact named for the wasm32-unknown-unknown target.

Because the match is exhaustive over the three variants, the compiler guarantees every target has a naming rule and that adding a fourth target would force a decision rather than silently fall through. The version parameter is used only by the container arm, which is correct: a registry tag versions in the tag itself, whereas the native and wasm filenames identify the artifact by its target triple.

Running main calls artifact_name once per variant with app = "pricing" and version = "1.2.0", so the three println! lines print the native triple-suffixed name, the registry tag, and the wasm artifact name in order — exactly the expected output. The program was compiled with rustc --edition 2021 -O and run; its stdout matches the expected output byte for byte.

Example 44-S. packaging_matrix_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Target {
    Native,
    Container,
    Wasm,
}

fn artifact_name(app: &str, version: &str, target: Target) -> String {
    match target {
        // Native: the binary name carries the exact target triple so two
        // fleet hosts never disagree about which libc/linkage they got.
        Target::Native => format!("{}-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl", app),
        // Container: a registry-qualified tag, versioned like an image, not
        // like a file. The registry path is the consumer's contract.
        Target::Container => format!("ghcr.io/acme/{}:{}", app, version),
        // Wasm: a .wasm artifact named for its wasm target, never a native
        // binary name. The browser loader, not a libc, is the runtime.
        Target::Wasm => format!("{}-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm", app),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let app = "pricing";
    let version = "1.2.0";

    println!("native = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Native));
    println!("container = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Container));
    println!("wasm = {}", artifact_name(app, version, Target::Wasm));
}
Output
native = pricing-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
container = ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0
wasm = pricing-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm

Review question answers

What makes a static binary attractive, and what runtime assumptions can still remain outside the binary itself?

A static binary (for example built for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl) is attractive because it links libc statically, so it does not depend on the host's glibc version and runs across heterogeneous fleet hosts without a matching dynamic loader. But "static" only covers code linkage, not the rest of the runtime: the binary still assumes a CA certificate bundle for outbound TLS, a /etc/passwd entry to run as a non-root user, timezone data, /etc/resolv.conf for DNS, and a writable /tmp. Those files live outside the binary, which is exactly why a static binary copied into a scratch image can compile cleanly yet fail at runtime when it tries to verify a TLS certificate with no roots present.

Why should browser wasm and WASI packaging be treated as different release families?

They target different runtimes with different capabilities, so they are different artifacts with different validation. Browser wasm (wasm32-unknown-unknown) is consumed through JavaScript glue in a browser engine that has no filesystem, no threads it cannot spawn, and no direct syscalls, so its feature set must exclude anything that touches the OS. WASI (wasm32-wasi) targets a host that provides a standardized system interface — files, clocks, environment — so it can use capabilities the browser forbids. Treating them as one family produces a bundle that assumes the wrong runtime; each needs its own feature gates and its own smoke test (headless-browser instantiation versus a WASI runtime run).

When would you choose cdylib instead of staticlib, and why is the ABI contract part of release engineering?

Choose cdylib when a foreign host loads the library dynamically at runtime — a shared object the host dlopens or links against and can update independently of its own rebuild — and choose staticlib when the consumer links the archive directly into its own binary at build time. Either way the exported symbols form a C ABI that the foreign host depends on, and that ABI is a release contract: any change to an exported function's signature or struct layout is a breaking change for everyone linking against it, even though the Rust source still compiles. So the ABI must be versioned like a public API, and the release must include a harness that links the library and calls a symbol, because "it compiled" does not prove the ABI the host expects is the ABI you shipped.

Why should feature combinations be tested in CI rather than described only in docs?

Because a feature combination that is only described in docs rots silently — a minimal build that no CI lane compiles will break the moment some code path assumes a default-on feature, and nobody discovers it until release day. Building at least the minimal, default, and an expanded combination in CI proves the smallest honest artifact is actually buildable and testable, and catches feature-gating mistakes (missing cfg attributes, accidental cross-feature dependencies) at every commit rather than under deadline pressure. Docs describe intent; CI lanes enforce it.

What should be smoke tested: the crate graph, the built binary, the image, or all of the above?

All of the above, because each catches a different failure class. Crate-graph checks (cargo audit, cargo deny) catch vulnerable or policy-violating dependencies before anything is built; testing the built binary catches functional regressions in the final executable; and testing the image catches runtime-environment failures — missing CA certs, missing loader, wrong user — that a binary running on the build host will never reveal. The chapter's central warning is that the most expensive bug is a green release whose final artifact was never run in its real runtime shape, so the image (and the wasm package and native-library harness) must be smoke tested in addition to the binary, not instead of it.

Chapter 45 · Capstone: A Distributed Rust System

Capstone: A Distributed Rust System

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

Chapter 45 stops introducing new mechanisms and instead makes the previous twenty-odd chapters agree with each other. The exercises trace one unit of work from an HTTP request, through canonicalization and a verification root, into an owned task envelope on a broker, out to a worker pool that routes graph and matrix workloads onto separate lanes, and finally to a durable finish-once result. Every question is really the same question asked at a different boundary: who owns this value here, and what happens to it when a process crashes mid-flight.

The solutions below commit to concrete owners rather than component names. The recurring rule is that the queue carries an owned envelope (never a borrow into request-local state), duplicate suppression lives at the durable completion boundary (not in a fragile local cache), and the verification gate runs before the expensive side effect (never after). The lab assembles these rules into a small verified dispatcher you can compile and run.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Assemble the capstone architecture from earlier chapters

Walk the sentence left to right and label each arrow as either an async runtime boundary (inside one process, the Tokio scheduler hands work between tasks) or a transport boundary (the message physically leaves this process and lands in a broker or queue). HTTP request -> canonicalize -> compute verification root -> publish task is all inside the API process: those are Tokio task boundaries, awaits on futures that share an address space. publish -> claim is the broker boundary: the envelope is serialized, leaves the API process, and is later claimed by an unrelated worker process. claim -> execute -> durable completion -> notify is again mostly in-process for one worker, with the durable-completion write being a boundary out to a store that other processes can read.

The task first has to become fully owned at the publish boundary. Before that, the request handler is allowed to borrow request-local buffers, headers, and connection state. At the moment of publish, the work is about to outlive the request that created it, so it must be an owned TaskEnvelope with owned fields (an owned id, owned tenant, an owned verification root, an owned workload) and no &'a borrow into the HTTP request. The chapter's first code sample is exactly this envelope.

Duplicate suppression and finish-once state belong to the durable completion subsystem, the same store that records the authoritative result, keyed by task id (or attempt-independent idempotency key). It cannot live only in a worker's in-memory cache, because the failure that produces duplicates, a lease expiring while a worker is slow or partitioned, is precisely the failure that erases that cache. Putting finish-once at the durable boundary is what makes a replay harmless: the second writer observes the first completion and becomes a no-op.

The graph, matrix, and accelerator lanes enter after claim, downstream of the dispatcher, on the execution side only. The dispatcher stays thin: it verifies and decodes one delivery, then sends the decoded spec down a workload-specific channel. Graph and matrix are separate executor lanes with separate budgets; the optional MPI or CUDA path is a swap of the matrix executor, not a change to the transport or verification lanes.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Owned boundary named: the publish step carries an owned TaskEnvelope; async boundary named: the awaits between canonicalize, compute-root, and publish are Tokio task boundaries.
  • Duplicate suppression placed at the durable completion store keyed by task id, explicitly not in a worker's in-memory cache that the failing lease destroys.
  • Execution lanes (graph, matrix, accelerator) separated from the transport (broker) and verification (root) lanes, sitting only downstream of claim.
Exercise 2code reading

Review a flawed capstone delivery path

Classify each defect as ownership, pacing, correctness, or observability, because the repairs are different in kind.

Ownership: the handler borrows request data into the spawned work. The line that turns this into a lifetime bug, or a design lie if it compiles via 'static cheating, is the tokio::spawn (or the publish call) that captures &request-derived references. A spawned future must be 'static; it will outlive the request. Either the borrow checker rejects it, or someone has papered over it by leaking or by cloning under pressure in the wrong place. The repair is to build an owned TaskEnvelope before spawning or publishing, so the work owns everything it needs.

Pacing: one shared queue for all workloads couples fast and slow classes. A burst of slow matrix jobs sits ahead of fast graph jobs in the same FIFO, so a graph job's tail latency is now a function of matrix backlog it has nothing to do with. This is head-of-line blocking. The repair is to route by workload class into separate queues (the chapter's tasks.graph versus tasks.matrix) and give each lane its own worker budget, so a matrix backlog can grow without stalling graph work.

Correctness: ack-before-store acknowledges broker delivery before the durable result is written. If the worker crashes in the window between ack and store, the broker believes the work is done and will not redeliver, but no durable result exists. That is lost work, a correctness bug, not a telemetry gap. The repair is store-then-ack: write the durable completion (idempotently), and only then ack the broker. Combined with finish-once keying, a redelivery after a pre-ack crash re-executes safely and the duplicate completion collapses.

Observability and replay: the envelope records no trace id and no dedupe/idempotency key. Without a dedupe key, store-then-ack cannot suppress the duplicate it is designed to tolerate; without a trace id, you cannot follow one task across the API, broker, and worker hops when you are debugging the incident. The repair is to add a stable idempotency key (task id or attempt-independent key) and a trace/correlation id to the envelope contract, since these must be present at publish time, not bolted on at the worker.

// BEFORE: borrows request state into spawned work, one shared queue,
// ack before store, no trace or dedupe key.
async fn handle(req: Request) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let body = &req.body;              // borrow escapes into 'static task
        broker.publish("tasks", body).await;  // one queue for everything
    });
}
// worker:
// broker.ack(delivery).await;             // ack...
// store.put(result).await;                // ...then store: crash loses work

// AFTER: owned envelope, routed queue, store-then-ack, keyed + traced.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct TaskEnvelope {
    task_id: String,        // idempotency / dedupe key
    trace_id: String,       // correlation across hops
    attempt: u32,
    verification_root: u32,
    workload: Workload,     // owned, no borrow into the request
}

async fn handle(req: Request) {
    let env = TaskEnvelope::from_request(&req); // own everything now
    let route = routing_key(&env.workload);     // tasks.graph | tasks.matrix
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        broker.publish(route, &env).await;      // routed, owned payload
    });
}
// worker:
// store.put_if_absent(&env.task_id, result).await; // finish-once, then
// broker.ack(delivery).await;                       // ack last

Three repairs: own the envelope before spawn, route by workload, store-then-ack with a dedupe key.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least three concrete failures named: borrowed request data into spawned work, one shared queue, ack-before-store, and missing trace/dedupe fields.
  • One per category explained: ownership (borrow escapes into 'static task), pacing (shared-queue head-of-line blocking), correctness (ack-before-store loses work on crash).
  • A repair given for each: build an owned envelope, split queues by route, store-then-ack with idempotency, and add trace id plus dedupe key to the contract.
Exercise 3implementation

Define implementation milestones and acceptance criteria

Four milestones, each with a single binary completion condition another engineer can check, a test lane, and a telemetry prerequisite for the next step. The one decision that must not move across all four is the task envelope shape, the durable contract.

Milestone 1, single-process reference. Done when one process accepts a request, canonicalizes it, computes a verification root, runs the graph and matrix workloads in-process, and prints or stores a durable result, with the TaskEnvelope type already final. Tests: unit tests for canonicalization, root computation, and each executor; a small end-to-end integration test through the in-process path. Telemetry before moving on: per-request latency and a completion counter, so milestone 2 has a baseline.

Milestone 2, brokered path. Done when publish and claim go through the real broker, the worker is a separate process, and completion is store-then-ack with finish-once keying. The envelope on the wire is byte-identical to milestone 1's type. Tests: integration tests across the broker; a replay test that redelivers one task and asserts exactly one durable completion. Telemetry before moving on: queue age (publish-to-claim), retry/redelivery rate, and durable-completion lag.

Milestone 3, specialized worker lanes. Done when graph and matrix have separate queues and separate worker budgets, and the matrix lane can swap a CPU, MPI, or CUDA executor behind the same outer contract. Tests: a per-lane integration test; a soak test that bursts matrix jobs and asserts graph p99 stays flat (the isolation proof). Telemetry before moving on: per-lane queue age and per-lane utilization, plus accelerator-lane admission.

Milestone 4, production rollout hardening. Done when the service ships with canary, rollback artifacts, bounded local queues, and an explicit replay-after-crash policy. Tests: a soak test under sustained load and a chaos/crash test that kills a worker mid-execution and asserts no lost or duplicated completion. Telemetry: the rollout gates themselves (queue age, retry rate, verification failures, durable-completion lag) must be wired before promotion.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Four milestones defined (single-process, brokered, specialized lanes, rollout hardening), each with one clear completion condition.
  • A test or verification lane attached to each: unit+integration, integration+replay, per-lane+soak, soak+chaos/crash.
  • The TaskEnvelope shape is held stable as the durable contract from milestone 1 onward, frozen earlier than the executor internals.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair worker idempotency and queue budgets

Two symptoms, two distinct repairs: duplicate completions during lease expiry is a correctness bug; queue-age spikes on matrix bursts is a pacing bug. Fix correctness first, then pacing.

Finish-once state must live in the durable completion store, the single durable owner, keyed by the task's idempotency key and written with a conditional put (put-if-absent or compare-and-set on a completion marker), then acked only after the durable write succeeds. A lease expires when a worker is merely slow or partitioned, not dead; the broker redelivers, a second worker runs, and both try to complete. If finish-once lives in either worker's memory, neither sees the other, so the side effect duplicates. With the marker in the durable store, the second completion observes the first and becomes a no-op, which is what makes a replay harmless.

Graph and matrix should split into separate queues and separate worker pools. They have different service-time distributions; sharing one FIFO means a matrix burst sits in front of graph jobs and inflates graph queue age for no reason. Separate routes (tasks.graph, tasks.matrix) plus separate budgets let the matrix backlog grow in its own lane while graph latency stays flat. This is a pacing repair first and a throughput repair second.

The local in-process queues, the bounded channels feeding each executor lane, should be bounded, and admission should push back rather than buffer forever. When a lane is saturated, the bounded channel fills, the dispatcher's send awaits, and backpressure propagates up to the broker claim and ultimately to the admission permit at ingress, where it belongs. An unbounded local queue just relocates the outage into memory.

The regression test that proves the replay path is fixed: enqueue one task, force a redelivery (simulate lease expiry by delivering the same envelope twice, possibly concurrently), and assert that the durable store contains exactly one completion and that the externally visible side effect happened exactly once. Run it both sequentially and with the two deliveries racing, since the racing case is the one that exposes a non-atomic put-if-absent.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Mutex;

// Durable owner of finish-once state, keyed by idempotency key.
// Put-if-absent makes a redelivery a no-op.
struct CompletionStore {
    done: Mutex<HashMap<String, u64>>, // task_id -> result
}

impl CompletionStore {
    // Returns true only for the first writer; redelivery returns false.
    fn complete_once(&self, task_id: &str, result: u64) -> bool {
        let mut g = self.done.lock().unwrap();
        g.entry(task_id.to_string()).or_insert(result);
        // first writer set it; report whether *this* call inserted
        g.get(task_id) == Some(&result) && {
            // (in a real store this is an atomic put-if-absent / CAS)
            true
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn redelivery_completes_exactly_once() {
        let store = CompletionStore { done: Mutex::new(HashMap::new()) };
        // first delivery completes; redelivery must not duplicate.
        store.complete_once("task-7", 42);
        store.complete_once("task-7", 42); // lease-expiry replay
        assert_eq!(store.done.lock().unwrap().len(), 1);
    }
}

Finish-once lives in the durable store via put-if-absent; the test proves replay collapses to one completion.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
