  • Idempotent completion placed in one durable owner (the completion store) via put-if-absent keyed by task id.
  • Slow matrix class isolated from fast graph class via separate queues and worker pools.
  • Bounded local channels named, with admission pushing back to ingress instead of buffering unboundedly.
  • A replay test defined: deliver the same envelope twice (sequentially and racing) and assert exactly one durable completion and one side effect.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Profile and refactor the capstone from evidence

Read the numbers before touching a kernel. Queue p95 is 800 ms while worker run time is 70 ms: the work spends roughly eleven times longer waiting in line than it does executing. The dominant bottleneck is queueing and accelerator admission, not local handler CPU. A 70 ms handler is not the first thing to optimize when items wait 800 ms to start.

The metric that should have paged first is queue age (publish-to-claim wait), not error rate and not handler CPU. The next trace to inspect is a single slow task's span timeline: the gap between enqueue and dequeue confirms the wait is in the queue, and per-lane breakdown shows whether the wait is concentrated in the saturated accelerator lane. The evidence already points there: one accelerator lane is saturated while CPU graph workers sit mostly idle, so capacity is mis-allocated across lanes.

The retry rate of 0.25 belongs in the capacity story, not only the error story. A quarter of work being retried is amplifying offered load by about 25 percent, which feeds the very queue that is already backed up. So before any graph or matrix kernel optimization, the refactor is to relieve the queueing pressure: split or rebalance the lanes so the saturated accelerator lane gets admission control and the idle CPU graph workers either take overflow (where the workload allows a CPU fallback) or are rebalanced, and classify retries so that non-retriable failures stop being re-enqueued. Kernel tuning would shave milliseconds off a 70 ms run while the 800 ms wait remains untouched.

Before-and-after signals that prove the repair moved the real bottleneck: queue p95 should fall toward the worker run time (a few times 70 ms, not 800 ms), and accelerator-lane utilization should drop out of saturation while CPU-graph utilization rises, showing the load rebalanced. A second confirming signal is retry rate falling after retry classification, and a third is that end-to-end p99 tracks queue age down rather than staying pinned, confirming queue wait, not execution, was the dominant term.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Queueing / accelerator admission identified as the dominant story (800 ms wait vs 70 ms run), not local handler CPU.
  • One metric (queue age) and one trace field (per-lane enqueue-to-dequeue span / lane utilization) chosen for the next diagnostic step.
  • One evidence-tied refactor proposed: lane split/rebalance with accelerator admission control plus retry classification, before any kernel work.
  • At least two validation signals named: queue p95 falling toward run time, accelerator utilization leaving saturation (plus retry rate and p99 as further confirmation).
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose rollout, acceleration, and failure isolation policy

Make the fallback boring and explicit. The stable fallback is the CPU-only execution path: it has no external toolchain dependency, no device to be unavailable, and the most predictable failure modes. The selection rule is to prefer a specialist lane (MPI or CUDA) only when it is healthy and the batch is dense enough to pay for it, and to fall back to CPU automatically when the specialist lane is saturated, unavailable, or failing its health check. Specialist acceleration is an optimization layered on top of a path that always works, never the only way to make progress.

During canary, the active lane must be visible, not inferred. Expose the build/version artifact id, the executor selection knobs (which lanes are enabled, the dense-batch threshold, the per-lane concurrency cap), and a per-task label recording which lane actually ran it. Operators need to read, from telemetry alone, which lane is active for the canary cohort without attaching a debugger.

Isolate retry storms by giving each specialist lane its own queue, its own worker pool, and its own retry budget. A CUDA driver hiccup that storms retries must stay confined to the CUDA lane: its bounded queue fills, admission pushes back into that lane only, and graph and CPU-matrix work continue. Without that split, one specialist's retry storm becomes a system-wide load amplifier. Classify failures so that non-retriable errors (verification drift, malformed input) dead-letter immediately instead of being retried into the storm.

Promotion gates, tied to concrete telemetry: queue age (per lane) must stay within budget, retry rate must stay below threshold, verification-failure rate must be at or near zero, and durable-completion lag must stay bounded; canary error and latency p99 must match or beat the incumbent. All four must hold for a sustained window before broad rollout. The rollback artifact is the previous immutable build/image plus its pinned configuration, kept ready so the operator action during an incident is a one-step pin-back to the known-good artifact, not a rebuild from memory. A feature flag that forces CPU-only execution is the fast in-place mitigation while the rollback completes.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Safe fallback defined (CPU-only path) and a specialist selection rule (use MPI/CUDA only when healthy and batch is dense; auto-fall-back otherwise).
  • A failure-isolation mechanism included: per-lane queue, worker-pool, and retry-budget split confining a specialist retry storm.
  • At least two rollout gates tied to telemetry: queue age, retry rate, verification failures, durable-completion lag (all named, with thresholds for a sustained window).
  • A pre-built rollback artifact named (previous immutable image plus pinned config) plus a force-CPU flag, so the incident action is a pin-back, not a rebuild from memory.

Review question answers

Where should the capstone first cross from borrowed request data into an owned durable envelope?

At the publish boundary, the moment work is about to leave the request that created it. Up to that point the handler may borrow request-local buffers and headers, but a published task can be claimed long after the HTTP request is gone, so it must be an owned TaskEnvelope with owned fields and no borrow into request state. Crossing into owned data here removes most async and retry lifetime confusion, because the spawned or published future no longer depends on anything tied to the request's lifetime.

Why should duplicate suppression live near durable completion rather than only in one in-memory worker cache?

Duplicates arise precisely when a lease expires because a worker is slow or partitioned, and the broker redelivers to a second worker; that same failure also destroys any state in the first worker's memory. A per-worker cache cannot see the other worker, so both complete and the side effect duplicates. Keeping finish-once state in the durable completion store, keyed by an idempotency key and written with put-if-absent, lets the second completion observe the first and collapse to a no-op, which is what makes a replay harmless.

What is the practical difference between profiling queue wait and profiling worker run time in this system?

Queue wait (publish-to-claim age) measures how long work sits before any worker touches it and is dominated by capacity, admission, and lane allocation; worker run time measures how long execution takes once started and is dominated by the kernel and the executor. They demand different fixes: high queue wait calls for queue splits, worker-budget changes, admission control, and retry classification, while high run time calls for kernel and executor optimization. Confusing them wastes effort, as tuning a 70 ms kernel does nothing for an 800 ms queue wait.

Why should specialist graph, matrix, MPI, or CUDA lanes still preserve one stable outer task contract?

The outer task envelope is the durable contract that the broker, the verification step, the completion store, and observability all depend on; the executor is an interior implementation detail. Keeping the envelope stable lets you swap a CPU executor for an MPI or CUDA one, split lanes, or rebalance budgets without rewriting transport, idempotency, or telemetry. If each specialist lane invented its own contract you would get contract drift, the exact failure mode where replay, acceleration, and observability stop agreeing with each other.

What makes an implementation milestone useful instead of decorative?

A milestone is useful when another engineer can tell unambiguously whether it is done, which means one concrete completion condition plus a verification lane (a test) and the telemetry needed to start the next milestone. Decorative milestones describe activity without a checkable end state, so progress becomes a matter of opinion. The capstone plan also keeps the durable contract, the task envelope shape, frozen early and stable across milestones, so later work changes the executor internals rather than the contract every other process relies on.

Chapter 46 · FastAPI-Style Web Apps, Swagger, and OpenAPI Codegen

FastAPI-Style Web Apps, Swagger, and OpenAPI Codegen

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises all circle one boundary: HTTP, the OpenAPI artifact, and the framework extractors live at the transport edge, and the domain service behind that edge stays free of them. The warm-up and code-reading exercises train your eye to see where transport types have leaked inward; the implementation exercise has you build the calm seam by hand; and the design and debugging exercises move from a single endpoint to the production concerns that dominate the second year of a service: workflow choice, drift prevention, versioning, pagination, idempotency, observability, and graceful shutdown.

The thread running through every answer is that the FastAPI-style feel you want in Rust is not a runtime feature. It comes from types and seams. A request flows in as bytes, decodes into a transport DTO, converts into exactly one application command or query, and only then reaches the service; the result flows back out the same way. When that one-way flow crosses the boundary exactly once, the service is testable as plain Rust, the contract is mechanically derivable, and a framework swap touches only the edge.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Map a FastAPI-style endpoint into Rust transport and service seams

Start from the handler signature you want a colleague to understand in ten seconds: create_invoice_handler(state: &ApiState, actor: AuthenticatedUser, request_id: &str, body: CreateInvoiceRequest) -> Result<CreatedInvoiceResponse, ApiError>. Reading that signature, you can already sort every value into transport-only versus business-relevant, which is the whole exercise.

Which values belong in transport DTOs and which belong in the command. The CreateInvoiceRequest body is a transport DTO: it carries only what a client can legitimately send, here customer_id and line_totals. It deliberately does not carry tenant, because the tenant is not something a client gets to assert. The application command, CreateInvoiceCommand, is the business-relevant shape: it carries customer_id, line_totals, and tenant, where the tenant is filled in from the authenticated caller rather than from the body. The split matters precisely because it closes a spoofing hole: if tenant lived in the request DTO, a client could write another tenant's data.

Which shared resources belong in typed app state. App state holds the things that outlive a single request and are shared across all of them: the connection pool, parsed configuration, the telemetry handle, and, for a create endpoint, the idempotency store. In this chapter's model, ApiState holds the InvoiceService and a service_name; in a real service it would also hold a PgPool, a metrics registry, and an idempotency-key store. The reason to make state typed rather than ambient is that the type tells you the handler's true dependencies, and the borrow checker enforces that a spawned task cannot keep borrowing request-local state after the request is gone.

Which checks belong in middleware or auth extraction versus the handler. A request ID and a tracing span must exist before anything else runs, so they belong in outer middleware. Authentication, turning a bearer token into an AuthenticatedUser, belongs in an extractor so that an invalid token is rejected before the handler body runs at all. The handler itself keeps only the checks that need the decoded body or the specific operation: the coarse permission gate (actor.can_create) and any edge validation of the body shape. Fine-grained authorization that depends on domain state stays in the service.

What the domain service must never learn. The service must never see the HTTP method, the path, status codes, headers, the request ID, or the framework's request type. It receives a CreateInvoiceCommand and returns a Result<Invoice, DomainError>. The reason is reuse and testability: a service that depends on framework request types can only be exercised through the framework, whereas one that takes a plain command can be driven from a unit test, a message-queue consumer, or a CLI without change.

// Transport DTO: only what a client may legitimately send.
struct CreateInvoiceRequest {
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

// Application command: business-relevant, tenant supplied by the caller context.
struct CreateInvoiceCommand {
    tenant: String,
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

// Typed app state: shared, long-lived dependencies. No HTTP types.
struct ApiState {
    invoices: InvoiceService,
    service_name: String,
    // In production: pool: PgPool, idempotency: IdempotencyStore, metrics: Registry
}

// One caller context, derived once by an auth extractor at the edge.
struct AuthenticatedUser {
    tenant: String,
    can_create: bool,
}

// The service signature the domain exposes: command in, domain result out.
// fn create_invoice(&self, cmd: CreateInvoiceCommand) -> Result<Invoice, DomainError>

The four seams: transport DTO, application command, typed state, and caller context, with the HTTP-free service signature noted.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Transport DTO (CreateInvoiceRequest: customer_id, line_totals) is kept distinct from the application command (CreateInvoiceCommand: adds tenant from the caller).
  • InvoiceService is placed in typed ApiState with a stated reason (shared, long-lived dependency the borrow checker can track), alongside named production additions like a pool and idempotency store.
  • Request ID, tracing span, and token-to-AuthenticatedUser authentication are assigned to middleware and the auth extractor rather than the domain service.
  • The domain service is shown to never see HTTP method, path, status, or the request type so it stays reusable from a queue or CLI and testable as plain Rust.
Exercise 2code reading

Spot transport leakage into the domain layer

The defect is stated in the starter prompt itself: BillingService::create_invoice accepts a CreateInvoiceRequest, returns Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode>, and has OpenAPI field-example comments sitting above the business-rule logic. Three different transport concerns have crossed into the service.

Which parameters and return types are transport concepts. The input CreateInvoiceRequest is an HTTP-facing DTO; it is the shape that decodes from a JSON body, not the shape the domain reasons about. The return Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode> is doubly transport-shaped: InvoiceDto is a wire representation, and StatusCode is literally an HTTP concept, 403 and 422 are not domain facts. The OpenAPI example comments are a documentation concern that belongs to the contract, not to the rule that sums line totals.

Which type the service should take instead. The service should take a CreateInvoiceCommand, the calmer boundary type. The handler is responsible for decoding CreateInvoiceRequest, attaching the caller's tenant from the AuthenticatedUser, and constructing that command. The service then depends on nothing HTTP.

Which type the service should return. The service should return Result<Invoice, DomainError>, a domain value and a domain error. Invoice is the real entity; DomainError enumerates business failures such as EmptyInvoice and Unauthorized. The handler maps DomainError to ApiError and then to an HTTP status on the way out. The service never names a status code.

Where documentation and status mapping should live. The OpenAPI field examples belong on the transport DTOs and the operation definition at the edge, next to the router, not interleaved with the summation logic. Status mapping belongs in the handler's map_err arm, where DomainError::EmptyInvoice becomes a 422-class ApiError::BadRequest and DomainError::Unauthorized becomes a Forbidden.

The concrete benefit of the repaired seam. Once the service takes a command and returns a Result<Invoice, DomainError>, you can unit-test the business rule with a plain struct and assert on a plain enum, no HTTP test harness, no router, no serialization. The diagnostic from the hint applies directly: if you could no longer call this service from a message-queue consumer or a CLI because it demands an HTTP DTO and emits a StatusCode, HTTP has leaked too far inward. The repair restores the ability to run the domain under any transport.

// BEFORE (transport leaked into the service):
impl BillingService {
    /// OpenAPI: customer_id example "cus_123", line_totals example [1200]
    fn create_invoice(&self, req: CreateInvoiceRequest)
        -> Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode>
    {
        if req.line_totals.is_empty() {
            return Err(StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY); // HTTP in the domain
        }
        // ... business rule mixed with doc examples and status codes ...
    }
}

// AFTER (calm service boundary):
impl BillingService {
    fn create_invoice(&self, cmd: CreateInvoiceCommand)
        -> Result<Invoice, DomainError>
    {
        if cmd.line_totals.is_empty() {
            return Err(DomainError::EmptyInvoice);
        }
        let total_cents = cmd.line_totals.iter().copied().sum();
        Ok(Invoice { id: format!("inv-{}", cmd.customer_id), tenant: cmd.tenant, total_cents })
    }
}

// Status mapping and doc examples move to the edge, in the handler:
// .map_err(|e| match e {
//     DomainError::EmptyInvoice => ApiError::BadRequest("invoice must contain at least one line"),
//     DomainError::Unauthorized => ApiError::Forbidden,
// })

The leaked service versus the repaired one; status mapping and OpenAPI examples relocate to the transport edge.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Identifies CreateInvoiceRequest as a transport-shaped input and Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode> (both InvoiceDto and StatusCode) as transport-shaped outputs that must leave the service.
  • Proposes CreateInvoiceCommand as the calmer input and Result<Invoice, DomainError> as the calmer output for the service boundary.
  • Relocates HTTP status mapping to the handler's map_err and the OpenAPI examples to the transport DTOs and operation definition.
  • States the concrete benefit: the business rule becomes unit-testable as plain Rust and reusable from a queue or CLI, which is impossible while it demands an HTTP DTO and emits a StatusCode.
Exercise 3implementation

Refactor a handler into a testable service boundary

A create handler should be boring in exactly four steps: authorize, map, call, translate. The implementation below mirrors the lab and the chapter's create_invoice_handler, and it keeps the service API free of any framework request wrapper.

Authorize. The handler takes an AuthenticatedUser produced by the auth extractor and performs one coarse edge check, if !actor.can_create { return Err(ApiError::Forbidden); }, before the service is touched. This is the authorization or edge validation that the acceptance criteria require, and it runs before any domain work, so an unauthorized caller never reaches the service.

Map. The handler converts the transport CreateInvoiceRequest into a CreateInvoiceCommand. The crucial move is that the command's tenant is filled from actor.tenant, the caller context, not from the body. The request DTO and the command are genuinely separate types, which is what keeps the service from ever seeing an HTTP-shaped input.

Call. The handler calls state.invoices.create_invoice(cmd) once. The service signature is fn create_invoice(&self, cmd: CreateInvoiceCommand) -> Result<Invoice, DomainError>. There is no Request, no StatusCode, no header map anywhere in that signature, so the service boundary does not accept HTTP request DTOs directly.

Translate. A single map_err arm turns each DomainError into one API-facing ApiError at the edge: EmptyInvoice becomes a BadRequest, Unauthorized becomes a Forbidden. On success the handler builds a CreatedInvoiceResponse carrying status = 201, the invoice ID, and the tenant, which is exactly what a deterministic test, or the lab, asserts on. Because the response is a plain struct of owned values, the test can compare fields directly without parsing HTTP.

The diagnostic from the hints holds: if the domain service still took the request DTO, the transport seam would not be finished. Here it takes a command, so the seam is complete, and the same service could be driven from a test, a queue consumer, or a CLI unchanged.

fn create_invoice_handler(
    state: &ApiState,
    actor: AuthenticatedUser,
    request_id: &str,
    body: CreateInvoiceRequest,
) -> Result<CreatedInvoiceResponse, ApiError> {
    // 1. Authorize at the edge, before any domain work.
    if !actor.can_create {
        return Err(ApiError::Forbidden);
    }

    // 2. Map the transport DTO into one command; tenant comes from the caller.
    let cmd = CreateInvoiceCommand {
        tenant: actor.tenant,
        customer_id: body.customer_id,
        line_totals: body.line_totals,
    };

    // 3. Call the service once. Its signature names no HTTP type.
    let created = state
        .invoices
        .create_invoice(cmd)
        .map_err(|err| match err {
            // 4. Translate one domain rejection into one API-facing error.
            DomainError::EmptyInvoice => ApiError::BadRequest("invoice must contain at least one line"),
            DomainError::Unauthorized => ApiError::Forbidden,
        })?;

    Ok(CreatedInvoiceResponse {
        status: 201,
        request_id: request_id.to_string(),
        invoice_id: created.id,
        tenant: created.tenant,
        total_cents: created.total_cents,
    })
}

The four-step create handler: authorize, map DTO to command, call the service, translate the domain error.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The handler constructs a separate CreateInvoiceCommand from the CreateInvoiceRequest rather than forwarding the DTO.
  • The service signature take CreateInvoiceCommand and returns Result<Invoice, DomainError>, so it never accepts an HTTP request DTO.
  • The handler runs the can_create authorization check before calling the service.
  • On success it returns status 201 with the invoice ID and tenant, matching the lab's deterministic expected output (status = 201, invoice = inv-7, tenant = acme).
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Choose code-first, spec-first, or mixed OpenAPI workflow honestly

Given one Rust server, one TypeScript client, and a partner team that wants the contract reviewed before implementation lands, the honest choice is a mixed workflow: Rust DTOs generate the spec, but the spec is checked in as its own artifact and gated in CI. The deciding question, as the chapter frames it, is which artifact is the source of truth, because docs, clients, and server are all downstream of it.

What makes code-first attractive here. The server is Rust and the team is comfortable there. Code-first makes the Rust DTOs authoritative and derives the spec from them, which keeps spec and server mechanically aligned, you cannot ship a handler whose types disagree with the emitted document, because the document is emitted from those types. There is no second source to drift.

What makes spec-first attractive here. The partner team wants to review the contract before implementation. Spec-first puts a human-readable, language-neutral document at the center that all parties can review and approve before anyone writes server code, which is exactly what a cross-team review boundary asks for. Its cost is that the spec and the Rust server can drift unless something forces them back together, and it front-loads design work that a small team might prefer to discover in code.

What the mixed workflow looks like. Rust DTOs still generate most of the spec via code-first emission, but the generated spec is committed to the repository as a reviewable file. CI regenerates the spec from the current code and fails the build if the committed file differs (a spec-diff gate). The partner team reviews changes to that checked-in file in a pull request, which gives them the spec-first review boundary, while the code-first emission guarantees the file always matches the server. The TypeScript client is generated from the same committed spec.

Which workflow makes generated clients least surprising. The mixed workflow, because the TypeScript client is always generated from a spec that is provably in sync with the Rust server and was reviewed before merge. There is no window where the client is cut from stale types.

The CI rule that keeps it honest: regenerate the spec in CI and fail if it differs from the committed file, so the spec can never silently fall behind the handlers. None of these styles is universally superior; the right one minimizes silent drift for the specific teams involved, and here that is the mixed approach because it satisfies both the mechanical-alignment need and the pre-implementation review need.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Chooses the mixed workflow as primary and justifies it from the team boundaries: Rust server (favors code-first alignment) plus a partner team needing pre-implementation review (favors a reviewable spec).
  • Names a tradeoff of each alternative: pure code-first gives no standalone artifact to review before code lands; pure spec-first risks server drift and front-loads design.
  • Includes the CI rule: regenerate the spec in CI and fail if it differs from the committed artifact (a spec-diff gate).
  • States explicitly that no style is universally superior; the goal is minimizing silent drift for these specific teams.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Prevent documentation drift and generated-code drift

The incident is the canonical drift bug: a handler input field changed, but the checked-in spec and generated client were not regenerated, unit tests passed because they exercised only the handler in isolation, and a downstream team broke. As the chapter puts it, the biggest documentation bug is not a missing description, it is a handler and an OpenAPI contract that silently stopped describing the same system, with no failing test to announce it. The fix is to make the contract part of the build, with at least two checks that have different jobs.

Which check should fail first. The spec-diff gate should fail first. CI regenerates the OpenAPI document from the current handlers and compares it to the committed spec; if a handler field changed and the spec was not regenerated, the regenerated document differs from the committed one and the build fails immediately, before a client release is ever cut. This is the cheapest, earliest signal. The generated-client compile and the contract-fixture test are the second line: if the spec did change, the client must regenerate and still compile, and recorded request/response fixtures must still validate against the schema. Different jobs: the spec-diff gate catches stale specs, the client-compile catches breaking shape changes, the fixture test catches semantic regressions.

Which artifacts are checked in versus generated only in CI. Check in the OpenAPI spec itself, because that is the artifact humans review in pull requests and the input from which clients are generated. Check in a small set of contract fixtures (recorded example requests and responses) as snapshots. The generated TypeScript client and server stubs are produced fresh in CI from the committed spec; checking the bulky generated client into the repo invites accidental hand-edits and merge noise.

How to review Swagger UI without treating it as the only proof. Swagger UI is a real user interface for the consuming teams and is worth reviewing for ergonomics, naming, and examples, but it is for humans. CI still needs machine-checkable evidence: the spec-diff gate and the contract-fixture test assert that the documented contract matches actual handler behavior. Use Swagger UI to judge clarity; use the fixtures and the diff gate to judge correctness.

Which fields and IDs to stabilize. Stabilize operation IDs and the error envelope. Operation IDs are the anchor for generated clients and docs review: if create_invoice silently becomes create_invoice_v2, every generated client method renames and every downstream diff becomes noise. A stable error envelope (a consistent error shape with a stable code field) means error-handling code in clients does not break when a new error case is added. With these stabilized, downstream diffs stay small and reviewable, which is the whole point: the most useful drift check is the one that fails before a client release is cut from stale types.

# CI: two checks with different jobs.

# Job 1 - spec-diff gate (fails first if the spec is stale):
cargo run --bin emit-openapi > openapi.generated.json
diff openapi.json openapi.generated.json   # nonzero exit fails the build

# Job 2 - generated-client compile + contract fixtures:
openapi-generator generate -i openapi.json -g typescript-fetch -o client/
( cd client && npm ci && npm run build )    # breaking shape change fails here
cargo test --test contract_fixtures         # recorded req/resp validate vs schema

# Stabilized anchors checked in the spec:
#   - operation_id: "create_invoice" (never renamed silently)
#   - error envelope: { "code": "...", "message": "..." } (stable shape)

Two CI jobs (spec-diff gate, then client-compile plus fixture tests) and the stabilized operation IDs and error envelope.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines two drift-prevention checks with different jobs: the spec-diff gate (stale spec) and the generated-client compile plus contract-fixture test (breaking and semantic changes).
  • Specifies a checked artifact and snapshot strategy (committed spec plus contract fixtures) and a generated-client validation strategy (regenerate and compile in CI).
  • Calls out stable operation IDs and a stable error envelope explicitly as the anchors that keep downstream diffs reviewable.
  • Explains that Swagger UI review is for humans and must be backed by machine-checkable contract assertions (the diff gate and fixtures) nearby.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design one production API surface with versioning, pagination, idempotency, tracing, metrics, and graceful shutdown

The billing API has create, list, and lookup endpoints, one async side-effect path, and an operator requirement that canary rollout and rollback stay safe under load. These are the concerns that do not appear in the first demo and dominate the second year, and each is a promise the contract makes to clients over time. The design below commits to one concrete rule per concern and keeps every rule tied to the transport and application boundaries rather than to framework knobs.

Versioning. Carry the version in the path prefix, /v1/invoices, and treat a version as a stability promise: within v1, an existing field's meaning never changes and required fields are never added to requests. Evolution within a version is additive only (new optional fields, new endpoints); anything that breaks an existing client's assumptions waits for /v2. The version boundary lives at the router, so the application services are version-agnostic and a v2 can map a different DTO onto the same command.

Pagination. The list route uses cursor pagination, not offset, so a large result set is delivered in stable, bounded pages even as rows are inserted. The edge validates limit against a hard cap (for example, reject anything above 100 and default to 50) and treats the opaque cursor as transport state the client must not interpret. Validating the bound at the edge keeps an unbounded scan from ever reaching the database.

Idempotency. The create route requires an Idempotency-Key header. The finish-once state lives in app state as an idempotency store keyed by (tenant, key): the first request records the in-progress key and, on success, stores the response; a retry with the same key returns the stored response instead of creating a second invoice. This is the rule that makes the async side-effect path safe to retry, the side effect fires once per key even if the client or a load balancer retries.

Trace and metric fields before rollout. Every request gets a request ID and a trace ID, both established in outer middleware before auth runs, and both attached to the tracing span and to log lines. Metrics include route label, status class, and request latency; for the async side-effect path, also publish queue age (how long a job waited) and publish latency (how long the side effect took). These give an operator the signal to judge a canary: if the canary's latency or queue age regresses, roll back. Request ID and trace ID are the minimum two observability hooks; queue age and publish latency cover the async path.

Graceful shutdown. On a shutdown signal the server first stops admitting new requests (close the listener / fail readiness so the load balancer drains it), then waits for in-flight handlers to finish within a bounded deadline, then flushes the async side-effect path so no enqueued job is dropped, and only then exits. The ordering is the point: admission stops before exit. If the service kept accepting requests or dropped queued side effects during deploy shutdown, it would produce duplicate or lost side effects, and the shutdown was not actually graceful. As the hint says, a production API design is an ownership and pacing design once traffic is real.

// Versioning: version at the router, services stay version-agnostic.
//   POST /v1/invoices, GET /v1/invoices, GET /v1/invoices/{id}

// Pagination: validate the bound at the edge before any query runs.
fn validate_page(limit: Option<u32>) -> Result<u32, ApiError> {
    match limit.unwrap_or(50) {
        n if n == 0 || n > 100 => Err(ApiError::BadRequest("limit must be 1..=100")),
        n => Ok(n),
    }
}

// Idempotency: finish-once state keyed by (tenant, key) in app state.
fn create_once(state: &ApiState, key: &str, cmd: CreateInvoiceCommand)
    -> Result<Invoice, DomainError>
{
    if let Some(prev) = state.idempotency.get(&cmd.tenant, key) {
        return Ok(prev);            // retry: return the stored result, no new side effect
    }
    let inv = state.invoices.create_invoice(cmd.clone())?;
    state.idempotency.put(&cmd.tenant, key, &inv);
    Ok(inv)
}

// Observability: fields that must exist before rollout.
//   request_id, trace_id (middleware), route, status_class, latency_ms,
//   queue_age_ms, publish_latency_ms (async side-effect path)

// Graceful shutdown: stop admission, drain, flush, then exit.
async fn shutdown(server: Server, side_effects: Worker) {
    server.stop_admitting().await;        // 1. close listener / fail readiness
    server.drain_in_flight(DEADLINE).await; // 2. let handlers finish, bounded
    side_effects.flush().await;           // 3. flush queued side effects
    // 4. exit
}

One concrete rule per production concern: path versioning, edge-validated cursor pagination, keyed idempotency, named telemetry fields, and an admission-stops-first shutdown.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • States one versioning rule (path-prefixed /v1, additive-only within a version), one pagination rule (cursor pagination with an edge-validated limit cap), and one idempotency rule (Idempotency-Key with finish-once state in app state).
  • Includes more than two observability hooks: request ID and trace ID, plus route, latency, queue age, and publish latency on the async path.
  • Describes a shutdown sequence that stops admission first, then drains in-flight handlers, then flushes the side-effect path, then exits.
  • Ties each rule to transport and application boundaries (router-level versioning, edge validation, idempotency store in typed state) rather than to framework settings alone.

Review question answers

What does it mean for a domain service to stay HTTP-free in a Rust web application?

It means the service's signatures name no transport concepts: it takes an application command or query and returns a domain value and a domain error (for example Result<Invoice, DomainError>), never a framework request type, a status code, or a wire DTO. HTTP DTOs, extractors, and the OpenAPI artifact live at the transport edge, and the handler is the only code that translates between that edge and the command. The practical test is that the same service could run unchanged behind a message-queue consumer or a CLI; if it could not, HTTP has leaked too far inward and the service is no longer testable as plain Rust.

Why are typed extractors and typed state a better long-term seam than passing one raw request object around?

Typed extractors decode exactly the parts a handler needs, the path, the body, the authenticated caller, into named types, so the handler signature documents its true dependencies and an invalid token or malformed body is rejected before the handler body runs. Typed state names the shared, long-lived dependencies (pool, config, telemetry, idempotency store) explicitly, and the borrow checker enforces that a spawned task cannot keep borrowing request-local state after the request is gone. A single raw request object hides all of this behind one opaque value, invites ambient assumptions about what is present, and makes the ownership model impossible for the compiler to verify.

When is code-first OpenAPI the calm default, and when does spec-first become more honest?

Code-first is the calm default when the Rust server is the source of truth and the team mostly needs the spec to stay mechanically aligned with the handlers, since deriving the spec from the DTOs means the two cannot disagree. Spec-first becomes more honest when a contract must be reviewed and approved by another team before implementation lands, because a language-neutral document is what a cross-team review boundary actually needs. In practice a mixed workflow is often the most honest: emit the spec from code, but check it in and gate it in CI so it is both mechanically aligned and reviewable, with the goal always being to minimize silent drift for the specific teams involved rather than to pick the theoretically purest style.

Why should generated clients stay in the transport layer rather than in the domain layer?

A generator encodes its own opinions about naming, optionality, and error shape, and those opinions will not match your domain's, so letting generated types reach into business logic couples the domain to a tool's conventions and to the wire format. Keeping generated clients and types at the transport boundary means the domain model stays expressed in its own terms, and a regenerated client (after a spec change) only forces edits at the edge, not throughout the core. This is the same boundary rule applied to the consuming side: transport code, generated or hand-written, translates into and out of domain commands and values but never becomes the domain.

What CI checks keep Swagger UI and generated SDKs from silently drifting away from handler behavior?

The first and cheapest is a spec-diff gate: regenerate the OpenAPI document from the current handlers in CI and fail the build if it differs from the committed spec, so a stale spec is caught before any client is cut from it. Backing that, regenerate the client SDK from the committed spec and require it to compile (catching breaking shape changes), and run contract-fixture tests where recorded requests and responses are validated against the schema (catching semantic regressions). Stabilizing operation IDs and the error envelope keeps downstream diffs small and reviewable, and because Swagger UI is for humans, these machine-checkable assertions, not the rendered docs, are what prove the contract still matches handler behavior.

Chapter 47 · gRPC Services with Protobuf and Service API Codegen

gRPC Services with Protobuf and Service API Codegen

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises practice the one habit the chapter keeps returning to: a gRPC service is two things at once — a protobuf contract shared across languages and a pile of generated Rust code — and the engineer's job is to keep them in their place. You will choose the right RPC shape from the data flow rather than from novelty, keep generated transport types from leaking into the domain model, build the small adapter seam that converts one generated request into one application command, and reason about deadlines, cancellation, backpressure, and status codes as parts of the API rather than as runtime accidents.

The lab and the implementation exercise both center on the same mapping seam, because that seam is where most real bugs hide and where unit testing pays off even when the live service runs on tonic. The debugging, evolution, and design exercises then widen the lens to the polyglot fleet: what counts as a breaking change to a contract that Go, C#, and C++ also generate from, what gates belong in CI, and what a production service lane needs before rollout. Throughout, the wire is rarely the surprise. The surprise is what each ecosystem used to do for you automatically that Rust now asks you to state explicitly.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose unary, server streaming, client streaming, or bidirectional streaming from the contract

Classify each endpoint by asking who sends once, who sends many times, and who controls the pace. The position of the stream keyword in the rpc line is the whole difference between the four shapes, so the question is which side fans out and which side fans in.

Create one invoice is a unary call: one request in, one response out. The client sends a single CreateInvoiceRequest, the server validates and persists it, and a single CreateInvoiceResponse (or a status) comes back. There is no accumulation and no open-ended pacing, so anything fancier than unary would add a lifecycle and buffer contract the workload does not need.

Watch invoice events over time wants server streaming: one request opens one subscription, and the server then fans out a sequence of event messages until the subscription ends or the client disconnects. The pacing implication is immediate — the server is now the producer and the client is the consumer, so you need a bounded buffer between event production and the network, and you must treat a client disconnect as a stop signal rather than keep producing into a dead channel.

Upload many invoices then get one summary wants client streaming: the client owns accumulation, sending many invoice messages, and the server replies with exactly one summary after the client signals end-of-stream. The buffering question here lives on the server's fan-in side — how much in-flight data it will hold while folding the stream into a running summary, and whether it bounds that to avoid a slow or hostile client pinning memory.

The long-lived sync conversation, where both peers keep sending updates with no fixed one-to-one ordering, is the only endpoint that truly wants bidirectional streaming. The backpressure question that appears immediately is: when one side produces faster than the other consumes, where does the slack go? You must decide on a bounded send queue per direction and a policy for what happens when it fills — block the producer, shed messages, or close the stream — because a bidirectional stream with no boundedness policy is still unfinished. The trap the exercise warns against is reaching for bidirectional streaming by default; three of the four endpoints are served by simpler, cheaper shapes.

// One contract, four rpc shapes. Read where `stream` sits.
//
// service Billing {
//   // unary: one request, one response
//   rpc CreateInvoice(CreateInvoiceRequest) returns (CreateInvoiceResponse);
//
//   // server streaming: one request opens one subscription
//   rpc WatchInvoiceEvents(WatchRequest) returns (stream InvoiceEvent);
//
//   // client streaming: many requests fold into one summary
//   rpc UploadInvoices(stream CreateInvoiceRequest) returns (UploadSummary);
//
//   // bidirectional: both peers send freely; needs per-direction backpressure
//   rpc Sync(stream SyncUpdate) returns (stream SyncUpdate);
// }

The same four endpoints expressed as protobuf rpc lines; the stream keyword's position is the classification.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Each workload is mapped to a shape with a transport reason: unary for create, server streaming for the subscription, client streaming for the upload-and-summarize, bidirectional for the sync conversation.
  • Pacing implications are named for the streaming cases: bounded buffer plus disconnect-as-stop for server streaming, bounded fan-in for client streaming, per-direction send-queue policy for bidirectional.
  • Bidirectional is reserved for the one endpoint whose data flow genuinely requires it; the other three use simpler shapes.
Exercise 2code reading

Read generated transport types without contaminating the domain model

The defect to spot is that the service method accepts a generated CreateInvoiceRequest and passes it unchanged into a domain aggregate constructor. A generated protobuf message is a transport type: it carries field tags, serialization rules, optional/default semantics from the wire format, and whatever shape the .proto happened to commit to for cross-language compatibility. Those are transport concerns, not domain concerns. The moment the aggregate constructor takes that type, the domain depends on the wire schema, and every additive protobuf change starts to look like domain churn.

Look at the request in Example 1 (grpc_transport_to_domain_mapping). The customer_id: String and line_totals: Vec<u64> are owned input that the transport already deserialized for you. Whether a string can be empty, whether a vector can be zero-length, the field numbering — those are properties of the deserialized message, not invariants the domain wants. The domain wants a non-empty customer and a non-empty invoice; the request type cannot guarantee either.

Tenant, caller identity, and other metadata-derived fields are the clearest tell. They do not live in the request body at all — they arrive in per-call gRPC metadata (the protobuf equivalent of HTTP headers) and are pulled out by an interceptor before the handler runs. They must be attached outside the generated message, at the adapter seam, precisely because the generated message has no field for them and should not grow one. In the chapter's code that is exactly the tenant parameter handed to into_command separately from the request.

The hand-written command type that makes the boundary calmer is CreateInvoiceCommand: tenant plus the validated, owned customer and line totals. It is the application service's contract, not the transport's. Once that mapping seam exists explicitly, three things get easier to test and refactor. Validation becomes a pure function you can unit test with no gRPC runtime, no tonic, and no metadata mocking. The domain stops recompiling when the .proto changes additively, because only the adapter touches the generated type. And the service signature reads in domain language, so a missing customer or empty invoice is rejected at the edge and never reaches InvoiceService::create.

// Transport concern (generated): field tags, wire defaults, no tenant slot.
struct CreateInvoiceRequest {
    customer_id: String,   // owned, but may be empty on the wire
    line_totals: Vec<u64>, // owned, but may be zero-length on the wire
}

// Domain/application concern (hand-written): tenant attached from metadata,
// fields already validated by the adapter before this type exists.
struct CreateInvoiceCommand {
    tenant: String,        // from per-call metadata, not from the request body
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

// The service speaks domain language and never sees the generated wrapper.
impl InvoiceService {
    fn create(&self, command: &CreateInvoiceCommand) -> String {
        format!("inv-{}", command.customer_id)
    }
}

The seam: generated request on the transport side, hand-written command on the domain side, tenant attached from metadata.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Generated DTOs (CreateInvoiceRequest, with field tags and wire defaults) are distinguished from the application command (CreateInvoiceCommand).
  • Tenant (and caller identity) are identified as metadata-derived fields attached at the adapter, outside the generated message code.
  • At least one benefit of the seam is named: pure-function testability of validation, and domain insulation from additive .proto changes.
Exercise 3implementation

Map a generated request into a domain command

Implement into_command as the entire transport boundary: it validates the generated request, moves its owned fields into a separate CreateInvoiceCommand, and returns a typed result. The validation is two explicit checks that mirror the domain's invariants — reject an empty customer id and reject an empty line set — and only on success does the function construct the command. This is the same seam you would unit test heavily even if the live service ran on tonic, which is why it is worth getting exactly right.

The ownership move is the point. CreateInvoiceRequest already owns its String and its Vec<u64>; the generated message deserialized them once. So the adapter moves them — request.customer_id and request.line_totals are moved field-by-field into the command, not cloned. Cloning here would allocate a second copy of data the transport is about to drop anyway. Data is owned once at the transport edge and moved into the application command exactly once, which is both cheaper and the idiomatic expression of "this value now belongs to the domain."

Keep the error type small and transport-facing. In the lab the result error is &'static str, which is fine for the runnable program; in the chapter's fuller Example 1 it is a TransportError enum (MissingCustomer, EmptyInvoice) so the adapter can map each shape problem to a distinct gRPC status later. Either way the error is the adapter's vocabulary, not the domain's — the downstream service never sees a Status, a Request wrapper, or a metadata API.

The returned command is deliberately a different type from the request. That is what lets the rest of the system depend on CreateInvoiceCommand without depending on gRPC. The lab then prints tenant, customer, and the summed total cents from the mapped command, proving the data crossed the seam intact.

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct CreateInvoiceRequest {
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct CreateInvoiceCommand {
    tenant: String,
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

fn into_command(
    request: CreateInvoiceRequest,
    tenant: &str,
) -> Result<CreateInvoiceCommand, &'static str> {
    if request.customer_id.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("missing customer id");
    }
    if request.line_totals.is_empty() {
        return Err("empty invoice");
    }

    // Move owned fields once; do not clone what the request is about to drop.
    Ok(CreateInvoiceCommand {
        tenant: tenant.to_string(),
        customer_id: request.customer_id,
        line_totals: request.line_totals,
    })
}

The adapter: validate two transport-shape problems, then move owned fields into a separate command type.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The mapping returns CreateInvoiceCommand, a distinct type from the generated CreateInvoiceRequest.
  • The adapter validates at least two transport-shape problems explicitly: empty customer id and empty line set.
  • The runnable lab prints tenant = acme, customer = cust-7, total cents = 4200 from the mapped command.
  • The error type and signature keep gRPC out of the downstream service: no Request wrapper, Status, or metadata API leaks past the seam.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Diagnose a deadline, cancellation, or streaming backpressure bug

There are two distinct defects, and both are the same underlying mistake: work keeps flowing after the caller or the stream has already said stop. Treat them separately because the repairs differ.

The unary handler keeps doing CPU-heavy work after the deadline has expired. The fix is to check the deadline at meaningful work boundaries, not once at entry. Read the remaining time before each expensive stage (and inside any loop over a large input), and as soon as elapsed exceeds the deadline, stop and return Status DeadlineExceeded rather than burning a core computing a result no one will read. In the chapter's Example 2 (grpc_status_deadline_retry) this is exactly what should_abort(deadline_ms, elapsed_ms, cancelled) expresses: abort when cancelled or when elapsed has reached the deadline. The principle is that a deadline is part of the API contract — the caller told you how long the answer is worth — so honoring it is correctness, not optimization.

The streaming handler keeps buffering items into a local channel after the client disconnects. This has two bugs layered on top of each other. The first is an ownership bug that exists even before cancellation: the buffer is unbounded, so a slow or absent consumer lets producers pin unbounded memory. Bound it — use a fixed-capacity channel — so that when the consumer falls behind, the producer feels backpressure (the send blocks or yields Err) instead of growing the queue forever. A disconnected client is a pacing signal, not a transport curiosity. The second bug is the missing cancellation check: when the send side reports the receiver is gone, or the stream's cancellation token fires, the producer must stop and drop its work, because continuing to produce into a dead stream is wasted CPU and a slow-leak of in-flight resources.

For status codes: surface DeadlineExceeded when the server gives up because the deadline passed, and Cancelled when the caller actively cancelled or disconnected. Importantly, Cancelled is not retryable — the caller chose to stop — whereas DeadlineExceeded on an idempotent call may be. To prove the repair helped, instrument the observable signals the API now exposes: the count of in-flight stream items (it should stop growing without bound), a cancelled-RPC counter, and a deadline-exceeded counter. A trace field recording deadline_remaining_ms at the point of abort, plus queue age or queue depth on the streaming buffer, lets you confirm that work actually stops near the limit rather than well past it.

use std::time::Instant;

// Unary: re-check the deadline at each work boundary, not once at entry.
fn handle_unary(deadline_ms: u64, started: Instant, cancelled: &dyn Fn() -> bool) -> Result<u64, &'static str> {
    let mut acc = 0u64;
    for stage in 0..expensive_stage_count() {
        let elapsed_ms = started.elapsed().as_millis() as u64;
        if cancelled() || elapsed_ms >= deadline_ms {
            // Map to Status::deadline_exceeded() / Status::cancelled() at the edge.
            return Err("deadline_exceeded_or_cancelled");
        }
        acc += run_stage(stage);
    }
    Ok(acc)
}

// Streaming: bound the channel so a stalled consumer creates backpressure,
// and stop producing the moment the receiver is gone (client disconnected).
fn produce_into_bounded(tx: &std::sync::mpsc::SyncSender<u64>, source: impl Iterator<Item = u64>) {
    for item in source {
        // try_send / blocking send on a *bounded* channel: full queue == backpressure.
        if tx.send(item).is_err() {
            // Receiver dropped: client disconnected. Stop; do not keep buffering.
            break;
        }
    }
}

// Bounded queue created up front, e.g. std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel(1024).
fn expensive_stage_count() -> u64 { 8 }
fn run_stage(_s: u64) -> u64 { 1 }

Deadline and cancellation checks at work boundaries, plus a bounded channel that turns a stalled consumer into backpressure.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • A deadline/cancellation check is placed at a real work boundary (per stage / per loop iteration), not only at handler entry.
  • The streaming buffer is bounded (sync_channel with fixed capacity) so a stalled or disconnected consumer produces backpressure instead of unbounded growth.
  • DeadlineExceeded vs Cancelled status codes are chosen correctly, and observability signals (in-flight items, cancelled-RPC count, deadline-exceeded count, queue age) are named to prove the repair.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Test generated APIs and prevent breaking protobuf changes

Classify the three changes first, because the CI gates follow from the classification. Adding one field with a new field number is additive and safe: old peers that do not know the field ignore it, and the wire identity of every existing field is untouched. Removing a field is breaking unless handled correctly — the danger is not that old code stops compiling, it is that the freed field number could later be reused for a different type and silently misread old data on the wire. Changing a method from unary to streaming is the largest break of the three: it changes the RPC shape, so every generated client and server signature for that method changes, and stale-generated peers will fail to talk to the new service. The rule of thumb is that protobuf evolution must be additive and boring; method-shape changes are neither.

The contract artifact to diff in CI is the .proto schema itself (or a descriptor set / FileDescriptorSet derived from it), checked in and compared against the previous version. A breaking-change linter such as buf is the standard tool: it flags field-number reuse, removed-without-reserved fields, type changes, and method-shape changes as build failures. This is the gate that matters most because it runs before a partner team regenerates from a stale or incompatible contract — schema drift becomes a build failure, not a post-rollout surprise. Treating broken codegen drift as merely "the Rust server still compiles locally" misses the point: it is still contract drift for everyone else.

Two kinds of transport test should run against generated code. First, a compile/contract test that simply regenerates client and server from the current .proto and builds them in CI — that catches the unary-to-streaming break immediately, because the trait and client signatures no longer match. Second, a round-trip test that constructs a generated message, serializes and deserializes it, and asserts the values survive, plus a small generated-client-to-generated-server test that exercises at least one method end to end. These are cheap and they fail loudly when the wire shape moves.

Finally, the policy must reserve removed field tags and names. After deleting a field, mark its number and its name reserved in the message (reserved 4; reserved "old_field";) so no future edit can recycle the tag for a new, incompatible type or recycle the name in a way that confuses readers. Reserving is the cheap insurance that turns a future foot-gun into a compile-time complaint.

// In the .proto, after removing a field, reserve its tag AND its name.
//
// message CreateInvoiceRequest {
//   string customer_id = 1;
//   repeated uint64 line_totals = 2;
//   string note = 3;            // ADDITIVE: new field, new number -> safe
//   reserved 4;                 // removed field's tag: never reuse
//   reserved "legacy_memo";     // removed field's name: never reuse
// }
//
// Changing a method shape is the big break:
//   rpc CreateInvoice(CreateInvoiceRequest) returns (CreateInvoiceResponse);          // before
//   rpc CreateInvoice(stream CreateInvoiceRequest) returns (CreateInvoiceResponse);   // after: BREAKING
//
// CI gates (conceptual):
//   buf lint                 # style + naming
//   buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'   # fails on field reuse, removed-not-reserved, method-shape change
//   cargo build              # regenerate + compile generated client/server (catches shape changes)
//   cargo test roundtrip     # serialize/deserialize a generated message and assert values survive

Additive vs breaking changes, reserved tags/names, and the CI gates that catch drift before partners regenerate.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one additive change (new field with new number) and one breaking change (removed field, or unary-to-streaming method) are classified correctly.
  • A schema-drift / breaking-change CI gate is defined (descriptor diff or a buf breaking check that fails the build).
  • A generated-client/server compile test and a serialize/deserialize round-trip test are named.
  • Removed field tags and names are explicitly reserved in the policy.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Design a polyglot gRPC service lane with auth, tracing, and retries

Design the billing service as a contract first and a Rust implementation second, because Go workers, a C# admin tool, and a C++ plugin all generate from the same .proto and consume the same operational guidance. Three artifacts are public: the .proto, the retry policy, and the metadata contract. Everything below is stated so another language team can adopt it without reading Rust.

Metadata on every call and stream session. Require an authorization token (a bearer credential in the authorization metadata key) and reject its absence with Unauthenticated before any handler runs — that rejection belongs in a server interceptor, the seam that reads metadata and either fails fast or inserts a typed caller context. Also require a tenant id and trace-propagation headers. For tracing, propagate W3C traceparent (and tracestate) on every call so a request that fans out across the Go worker, the Rust service, and the C++ plugin stitches into one trace; the interceptor reads the incoming traceparent, starts a server span as its child, and injects the propagated context onto any downstream call the handler makes. The caller-context rule and the trace-propagation rule together make the boundary observable and authorized before business logic begins.

Retry and idempotency classification. Use the chapter's classify(status, idempotent) discipline (Example 2, grpc_status_deadline_retry): Unavailable and DeadlineExceeded are retryable but only for idempotent methods, with exponential backoff and jitter; Cancelled is terminal because the caller chose to stop; InvalidArgument, FailedPrecondition, and the other caller-fault codes are terminal — retrying them just repeats the same rejection. The idempotency rule is the gate: CreateInvoice must carry a client-supplied idempotency key so a retried Unavailable cannot double-bill, and read-only methods are idempotent by construction and freely retryable. Publish this table alongside the .proto so every language's retry interceptor agrees.

Stream boundedness and concurrency. The streaming routes — WatchInvoiceEvents (server streaming) and any Sync (bidirectional) method — get explicit, per-route budgets: a bounded send queue per stream (so a slow consumer produces backpressure instead of unbounded memory growth), a cap on concurrent open streams per caller, and a maximum stream lifetime after which the server closes with a resumable cursor. A stream without a boundedness policy is under-specified for production, so this is a contract clause, not an implementation detail.

Telemetry before rollout. Ship at least: status-code-family counters (OK / caller-fault / server-fault, so you can see whether errors are 'their fault' or 'ours'); cancelled-RPC and deadline-exceeded counters; stream lifetime and in-flight-stream-item gauges per streaming route; and queue age / depth on the bounded send queues so a backpressure problem shows up as rising age before it shows up as an outage. With those four hooks, retries, cancellation, and stream pacing are observable from day one rather than diagnosed after the first incident.

// Public retry guidance, shared across Go/C#/C++/Rust (mirrors Example 2).
enum GrpcCode { Ok, InvalidArgument, FailedPrecondition, DeadlineExceeded, Unavailable, Cancelled, Unauthenticated }

fn retryable(code: GrpcCode, idempotent: bool) -> bool {
    match code {
        // Transient + safe to repeat only when the method is idempotent
        // (e.g. carries a client idempotency key, or is read-only).
        GrpcCode::Unavailable | GrpcCode::DeadlineExceeded => idempotent,
        // Caller chose to stop, or caller-fault: never retry the same request.
        GrpcCode::Cancelled
        | GrpcCode::InvalidArgument
        | GrpcCode::FailedPrecondition
        | GrpcCode::Unauthenticated => false,
        GrpcCode::Ok => false,
    }
}

// Server interceptor sketch (auth + trace) that runs before every handler:
//   1. read `authorization` metadata -> missing => Status::unauthenticated
//   2. read `tenant` metadata        -> attach typed CallerContext
//   3. read W3C `traceparent`        -> start child server span, inject downstream
// Streaming routes additionally declare: bounded send queue, max concurrent
// streams per caller, and a max stream lifetime with a resumable cursor.

Shared retry classification plus the interceptor and streaming-budget rules the polyglot contract must publish.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • An auth/caller-context rule (authorization token -> Unauthenticated, typed CallerContext) and a trace-propagation rule (W3C traceparent, child span) are both defined.
  • Retryable (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded under idempotency + key) vs terminal (Cancelled, InvalidArgument, FailedPrecondition) behavior is classified explicitly.
  • At least one boundedness/concurrency rule is included for a streaming path (bounded send queue, concurrent-stream cap, max lifetime).
  • At least three observability hooks are named: status-code-family counters, cancelled/deadline counters, stream lifetime, and queue age.

Lab solution

into_command is the entire transport boundary. It first runs two validation checks: a trimmed-empty customer id and an empty line set are both rejected before any command exists, so a malformed request never reaches the application layer. Only on success does it construct a CreateInvoiceCommand. The tenant arrives as a separate &str argument — standing in for a value an interceptor would pull from per-call metadata — and is owned by the command via tenant.to_string(), while the request's customer_id String and line_totals Vec are moved field-by-field rather than cloned, because the request owns them already and is about to be dropped.

main builds a request for cust-7 with line totals of 1200 and 3000 cents, maps it under tenant acme, and unwraps the Ok. It then sums the line totals with iter().copied().sum::<u64>(), giving 1200 + 3000 = 4200. The three println! lines read straight off the mapped command and its derived total, producing tenant = acme, customer = cust-7, and total cents = 4200.

The whole program compiles with only the standard library: it is the mapping seam in isolation, with no tonic, no protobuf runtime, and no async — which is exactly the point of the exercise, since this seam is unit-testable as a pure function regardless of what transport the live service uses.

Example 47-S. grpc_transport_mapping_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct CreateInvoiceRequest {
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct CreateInvoiceCommand {
    tenant: String,
    customer_id: String,
    line_totals: Vec<u64>,
}

fn into_command(
    request: CreateInvoiceRequest,
    tenant: &str,
) -> Result<CreateInvoiceCommand, &'static str> {
    // Validate transport-shape problems explicitly at the edge.
    if request.customer_id.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("missing customer id");
    }
    if request.line_totals.is_empty() {
        return Err("empty invoice");
    }

    // The request already owns its String and Vec; move them once into the
    // command. Tenant comes from metadata, not from the request body.
    Ok(CreateInvoiceCommand {
        tenant: tenant.to_string(),
        customer_id: request.customer_id,
        line_totals: request.line_totals,
    })
}

fn main() {
    let request = CreateInvoiceRequest {
        customer_id: String::from("cust-7"),
        line_totals: vec![1_200_u64, 3_000],
    };

    let command = into_command(request, "acme").unwrap();
    let total_cents: u64 = command.line_totals.iter().copied().sum();

    println!("tenant = {}", command.tenant);
    println!("customer = {}", command.customer_id);
    println!("total cents = {}", total_cents);
}
Output
tenant = acme
customer = cust-7
total cents = 4200

Review question answers

Why should generated protobuf types usually stop at the transport boundary instead of becoming the domain model?

Generated protobuf messages are transport types: they carry field tags, wire defaults, and a cross-language shape chosen for compatibility, none of which are domain invariants. If the domain depends on them directly, every additive .proto change looks like domain churn and the business logic recompiles for reasons that have nothing to do with the business. Keeping them at the boundary and mapping into a hand-written command lets validation become a pure, testable function and insulates the domain from schema evolution.

What makes field tags more durable than field names in protobuf evolution?

Field tags (the = 1, = 2 numbers) are what actually go on the wire; names are a source-level convenience that the encoder discards. You can rename a field freely and old serialized data still decodes, because decoding matches by number, but reusing or changing a number silently misreads existing data and breaks every peer that generated against the old schema. That is why the durable identity is the number, and why removed numbers must be reserved so they are never recycled.

Why are deadlines, cancellation, and backpressure part of the API design rather than only runtime behavior?

A deadline is the caller stating how long the answer is worth, cancellation is the caller withdrawing the request, and backpressure is the contract for what happens when a producer outpaces a consumer — all three are promises the two sides must agree on, not incidental runtime details. A streaming method with vague message rate, buffer size, and cancellation rules is an unfinished design, because an unbounded buffer is an ownership bug and ignored cancellation wastes work the caller no longer wants. Designing them in means choosing bounded queues, deadline checks at work boundaries, and explicit stop signals as part of the method's specification.

What is the practical difference between a retryable Unavailable and a non-retryable InvalidArgument?

Unavailable means 'I am temporarily unable; the same request might succeed later', so an idempotent call should retry it with backoff. InvalidArgument means 'your request is malformed; fix it and stop retrying', so retrying just repeats the same rejection and wastes capacity. The status code is chosen by what the caller should do next, not by the internal cause, which is what makes a shared retry policy possible across every language that generates from the contract.

Why should generated client and server artifacts be rebuilt or checked in CI whenever the .proto changes?

The .proto is a shared contract that Go, C#, C++, and Rust all regenerate from, so a change that compiles fine in the Rust server can still break partners who regenerate stale or incompatible code. Rebuilding generated client and server in CI, plus a breaking-change check (buf breaking) and a serialize/deserialize round-trip test, catches method-shape changes and field-number reuse before any partner regenerates. That turns schema drift into a build failure rather than a post-rollout incident, which is the cheapest place to catch it.

Chapter 48 · WebSockets and Long-Lived Connections

WebSockets and Long-Lived Connections

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move from picking the right long-lived transport to owning a single connection cleanly and then surviving the conditions that actually break WebSocket services in production: slow consumers, reconnect storms, protocol drift, and deploy-time shutdown. The through-line is the chapter's mental model, a connection as a small machine with one reader job, one writer job, and one application job in the middle, plus a set of explicit policies for what happens when something falls behind.

The payoff is a connection model you can reason about from the types alone. By the end you should be able to say, before a single client connects, who owns the read half, who owns the write half, what happens when a queue fills, how the protocol evolves under mixed clients, and what the server does during a drain. Every exercise here pins down one of those answers so it is a design decision rather than an emergency.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose WebSockets, SSE, polling, gRPC streaming, or a broker-backed edge fan-out

Start from direction, pace, and durability rather than from the transport you reach for by habit. The four products map cleanly once you ask what each one actually needs.

The browser dashboard that only receives updates wants Server-Sent Events. It is one-directional push from server to client, SSE rides plain HTTP, browsers reconnect automatically with a built-in Last-Event-ID cursor, and you avoid the entire upgrade-split-heartbeat-close lifecycle a WebSocket forces on you. The tradeoff is real but acceptable here: SSE is text-framed and one-way, so the moment the client needs to send commands you would be tunneling them over a separate channel.

The collaborative editor wants a WebSocket. Both sides send commands continuously, latency matters, and you want full bidirectional state over a single connection with ordered frames. This is the one case where the cost of the WebSocket lifecycle is justified by the requirement, not by familiarity.

The internal polyglot stream between services wants gRPC streaming. The clients are services, not browsers, so browser support is irrelevant, and what matters is a versioned protobuf contract with generated stubs across languages and HTTP/2 flow control underneath. You trade away browser reachability for schema tooling and typed contracts, which is the right trade when no browser is involved.

The durable event feed where clients reconnect after long offline gaps wants a broker-backed replay surface (Kafka, NATS JetStream, or a durable log) as the real durability boundary, with whatever edge transport delivering live tail. A raw socket fan-out has no memory: once a frame is sent it is gone, so a client offline for an hour cannot catch up. Making the broker the source of truth gives you replay by offset; the WebSocket or SSE becomes just the live edge. The tradeoff is operational weight, you now run and reason about a broker, but durability across long disconnects is exactly what a direct socket cannot provide.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least three of the four picks are deliberately not WebSockets: SSE for the dashboard, gRPC streaming for the service stream, and a broker for the durable feed.
  • Each choice is justified by pacing or durability (one-way push, long offline replay, typed cross-service contract), not by framework familiarity.
  • Tradeoffs named explicitly: SSE is one-way only, gRPC sacrifices browser support for schema tooling, and the broker adds operational weight in exchange for replay.
Exercise 2code reading

Review explicit read/write ownership in one connection loop

Read the two designs against the chapter's ownership boundary, the split into a read half and a write half after the upgrade, rather than against mutex overhead. The split design (one reader task, one application loop, one writer task) is the calm default, and the reasons line up with the chapter's three concerns: ordering, shutdown, and observability.

Frame ordering and close behavior are easier to reason about in the split design because exactly one task owns the send path. Every outbound frame, text, pong, and the final close, flows through one writer in the order it pulls from the outbound channel, so the close frame is necessarily the last thing written and nothing races past it. With Arc<Mutex<sink>> shared across many tasks, the order in which writers acquire the lock is whatever the scheduler decides; a task can grab the lock and write a frame after another task has already sent close, which is a protocol violation that is hard to even observe after the fact.

Cancellation and shutdown stage more easily in the split design because there is a single place to drain. You signal shutdown (the chapter uses a watch channel), the application loop stops accepting inbound work, and the writer drains its remaining outbound queue and then sends close. With a shared sink there is no single drain point: each task may still be mid-write when you tear down, so 'finish what is in flight, then close' has no natural seam.

Slow-consumer backpressure is easier to measure in the split design because the outbound channel is the one chokepoint. A bounded outbound channel gives you a single queue depth to watch and a single place where send() blocks or fails when the client falls behind. With a shared sink, backpressure is smeared across every task that holds the lock; there is no single number that says 'this connection is behind.'

A shared sink is still acceptable when writes are rare, unordered relative to each other, and not part of a strict close sequence, for example a low-frequency metrics or keepalive emitter where no two writes have an ordering relationship and the connection never needs a clean drained close. Even then it is a deliberate exception, not the default.

use tokio::sync::mpsc;

// The calm default: one writer task owns the send path. Other tasks ask it to
// send by pushing onto a bounded channel; they never touch the sink directly.
enum Outbound {
    Text(String),
    Pong(u64),
    Close,
}

async fn writer_task(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<Outbound>) {
    // One owner, one ordering, one place to measure depth and stage a drain.
    while let Some(frame) = rx.recv().await {
        match frame {
            Outbound::Text(_) | Outbound::Pong(_) => { /* sink.send(frame) */ }
            Outbound::Close => {
                /* sink.send(close); sink.close() */
