                break; // close is necessarily the last frame written
            }
        }
    }
}

// Contrast: Arc<Mutex<Sink>> shared across N tasks. Lock acquisition order is
// the scheduler's choice, so a stray Text can race past a Close, and there is
// no single queue depth to watch when one client falls behind.

One writer task owns frame ordering and the close seam; a shared sink scatters both.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names a concrete win of split ownership: a single writer guarantees close is the last frame and ordering is deterministic.
  • Names a concrete cost of the shared sink: scheduler-dependent lock order can let a frame race past close, and there is no single drain seam.
  • Ties the comparison to ordering (close sequencing), shutdown (single drain point), and observability (one bounded queue depth), not to syntax.
Exercise 3implementation

Implement a small message loop with explicit read/write ownership

Build the reader-app-writer pipeline the chapter's Example 1 demonstrates, but keep the focus on the ownership shape rather than on any particular WebSocket crate. Three tasks, two bounded channels, one shutdown signal.

The reader task is the only consumer of inbound frames from the transport boundary; it translates wire frames into an InboundFrame enum and pushes them onto the inbound channel. The application task is the only thing that interprets protocol, it reacts to Text, Ping, and Close distinctly, and it produces OutboundFrame values onto the outbound channel. The writer task is the only producer onto the transport; it drains the outbound channel in order. No task except the writer ever touches the send half, which is exactly the boundary that makes close ordering and backpressure tractable.

Keep the inbound and outbound enums separate. They are not the same alphabet: a Ping is inbound transport liveness and a Pong is the outbound reply; conflating them into one enum invites a task to construct a frame that only the other side should send. Two bounded channels (the chapter uses capacity 4) give you backpressure in both directions, if the application falls behind the reader, recv pressure builds on the inbound channel; if the client falls behind the writer, send pressure builds on the outbound channel.

Close is handled by signaling shutdown after the close frame is observed, not by abruptly dropping a task. When the application sees InboundFrame::Close it sends an OutboundFrame::Close so the writer can flush a clean close, then flips the watch channel to true. The writer, on seeing shutdown, drains any frames still queued and then exits. That ordering, observe close, emit close, drain, exit, is why the lifecycle is reviewable from the types alone.

On the borrowing prompt: do not move borrowed request-local data into a spawned task. Tokio's spawn requires 'static futures, so anything captured must be owned (a String, an Arc, an mpsc::Sender), not a reference into the handshake's stack frame. The connection will outlive that frame by hours, so a borrow there would be a use-after-free that the lifetime checker correctly rejects; owning the data, or sharing it behind Arc, is what makes the spawn legal and the lifecycle sound.

use tokio::sync::{mpsc, watch};

#[derive(Debug)]
enum InboundFrame {
    Text(String),
    Ping(u64),
    Close,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum OutboundFrame {
    Text(String),
    Pong(u64),
    Close,
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (inbound_tx, mut inbound_rx) = mpsc::channel::<InboundFrame>(4);
    let (outbound_tx, mut outbound_rx) = mpsc::channel::<OutboundFrame>(4);
    let (shutdown_tx, mut shutdown_rx) = watch::channel(false);

    // READER: only task that reads the transport boundary.
    let reader = tokio::spawn(async move {
        inbound_tx.send(InboundFrame::Text("ready".into())).await.unwrap();
        inbound_tx.send(InboundFrame::Ping(7)).await.unwrap();
        inbound_tx.send(InboundFrame::Close).await.unwrap();
    });

    // APP: only task that interprets protocol. Reacts to ping and close distinctly.
    let app = tokio::spawn(async move {
        while let Some(frame) = inbound_rx.recv().await {
            match frame {
                InboundFrame::Text(t) => {
                    outbound_tx.send(OutboundFrame::Text(format!("echo:{t}"))).await.unwrap();
                }
                InboundFrame::Ping(nonce) => {
                    outbound_tx.send(OutboundFrame::Pong(nonce)).await.unwrap();
                }
                InboundFrame::Close => {
                    let _ = outbound_tx.send(OutboundFrame::Close).await;
                    shutdown_tx.send(true).unwrap(); // signal, do not drop
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
    });

    // WRITER: only task that touches the send half. Drains, then exits on shutdown.
    let writer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        loop {
            tokio::select! {
                biased;
                Some(_frame) = outbound_rx.recv() => { /* sink.send(_frame) */ }
                _ = shutdown_rx.changed() => {
                    if *shutdown_rx.borrow() {
                        while let Ok(_frame) = outbound_rx.try_recv() { /* flush */ }
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    });

    reader.await.unwrap();
    app.await.unwrap();
    writer.await.unwrap();
}

Reader to app to writer over two bounded channels, with a watch signal staging the close.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Read and write ownership are explicit: only the reader reads the transport and only the writer touches the send half.
  • Application logic sits between IO; it owns all protocol reactions and never writes to the transport directly.
  • Ping and Close are matched as distinct arms: Ping produces a Pong, Close emits Close and signals shutdown.
  • Lifecycle is reviewable from types and channels alone: two bounded enums, two channels, one watch signal; spawned tasks capture owned data, not request-local borrows.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Replace unbounded broadcast with a bounded slow-consumer policy

The defect is named directly in the chapter: an unbounded per-client queue is not the absence of a slow-consumer policy, it is the policy 'grow memory until the process dies.' The room broadcaster pushes every event onto an unbounded VecDeque per client and only notices when RSS climbs, which means the failure is invisible until it is catastrophic and unattributable to a specific client.

The fix has two parts: a boundedness rule and a slow-consumer policy. For the boundedness rule, put the first bound per connection, because a single slow tab is the most common failure and a per-connection cap is the honest minimum. A per-room cap is a useful second bound (one runaway room should not be allowed to consume all server memory across its members), so 'both' is the mature answer, but if you only get one, make it per-connection.

For the policy, I would choose by message class rather than apply one rule everywhere, because there is no neutral slow-consumer policy and each choice changes product semantics. For a live state feed where only the newest value matters (cursor position, presence, a progress percentage), coalesce to one latest snapshot, the queue holds at most one entry and a slow client gets the freshest state, not a backlog of stale ones. For an ordered event log where every event matters (chat messages, audit events), you cannot silently drop, so the policy is bound the queue and disconnect the client at the limit, then let it reconnect and resume from a durable cursor. Dropping oldest events silently is the worst option for an event log because the client never learns it missed something. The lab makes the disconnect-at-limit policy concrete: a client already at max_pending is evicted on the next push rather than allowed to grow.

Metrics and tests close the loop. The metrics that should spike first are per-connection (and per-room) pending queue depth and queue age (how long the oldest unsent event has waited), plus an eviction or drop counter labeled by reason. Active connection count alone will not move when one client falls behind; queue depth and age will. The regression test asserts the policy mechanically: construct a hub with a small bound, seed one client at the limit, broadcast, and assert that client was evicted (or its queue was coalesced) and the bound was never exceeded, exactly the shape of the lab. The trap to avoid is replacing an unbounded VecDeque with a 'large' bounded one and calling it fixed; a bound of 100000 is still effectively unbounded for the failure you are defending against. The bound must be small enough that the policy actually fires under realistic slowness.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

// Boundedness rule: per-connection cap (the honest minimum).
// Policy by message class, chosen for product semantics.
enum Policy {
    CoalesceLatest, // live state feed: keep only the newest value
    DisconnectAtLimit, // ordered event log: never silently drop
}

struct Conn {
    pending: VecDeque<String>,
    max_pending: usize,
    policy: Policy,
    dropped: u64, // metric: spikes before RSS does
}

impl Conn {
    /// Returns false when the connection must be evicted by the caller.
    fn enqueue(&mut self, ev: String) -> bool {
        match self.policy {
            Policy::CoalesceLatest => {
                self.pending.clear(); // at most one entry, always freshest
                self.pending.push_back(ev);
                true
            }
            Policy::DisconnectAtLimit => {
                if self.pending.len() >= self.max_pending {
                    self.dropped += 1;
                    return false; // caller evicts; client reconnects + resumes
                }
                self.pending.push_back(ev);
                true
            }
        }
    }
}

#[test]
fn bound_is_enforced() {
    let mut c = Conn { pending: VecDeque::new(), max_pending: 2,
                       policy: Policy::DisconnectAtLimit, dropped: 0 };
    assert!(c.enqueue("a".into()));
    assert!(c.enqueue("b".into()));
    assert!(!c.enqueue("c".into())); // at limit -> eviction signaled
    assert!(c.pending.len() <= 2);   // bound never exceeded
    assert_eq!(c.dropped, 1);
}

Per-connection bound with a policy selected by message class, plus the regression test that proves it fires.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • One explicit boundedness rule stated: per-connection cap as the minimum, per-room as the second bound.
  • One slow-consumer policy chosen and justified by product semantics: coalesce-latest for state feeds, disconnect-at-limit for ordered event logs.
  • At least one metric (per-connection queue depth/age, eviction counter) and one regression test (bound-is-enforced) are named.
  • Explicitly rejects 'just make the bound huge' as leaving the queue unbounded under another name.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design a production WebSocket protocol with versioning, auth, and shutdown semantics

Make the envelope and lifecycle explicit before mixed clients force the decision in an incident. The chapter's framing is that a WebSocket protocol drifts the same way an HTTP API or broker envelope drifts, old clients and new servers coexist for as long as a tab stays open, so the contract belongs in the envelope, not implicit in code.

Envelope: every frame is a versioned, tagged envelope. Mandatory fields are protocol version (so a new server can detect and reject or downgrade an old client deterministically), a type tag (so the enum is a tagged union and new variants are additive), and a session ID (the stable identity that survives reconnects and ties logs together). Per-stream sequence numbers are mandatory for any ordered subscription because resume depends on them. A trace ID is strongly recommended on every message for cross-system correlation. Concretely, model it as Envelope<T> { version, type, session_id, seq, trace_id, payload: T } with #[serde(tag = "type")] on the payload enum so adding a variant never breaks old clients, which is exactly the serde shape the chapter sketches.

Layer separation: keep transport/control messages distinct from domain events. Transport-layer messages are Subscribe, Subscribed, Resume, Ack, Ping, Pong, Error, and the terminal GoingAway/Close. Domain-layer messages are the actual events the product carries (TaskProgress, Notification, and so on) wrapped in the same envelope. This separation lets the connection machinery handle liveness, resume, and shutdown without parsing domain payloads, and lets domain handlers ignore transport bookkeeping.

Reconnect and resume: the client persists the last applied (stream, seq). On reconnect it sends Resume { session_id, last_seq } per stream. If the server can still serve from that cursor (events retained in a bounded ring or a backing log), it replays from last_seq + 1; if the cursor is too old to honor, it responds with a Snapshot of current state plus a new baseline seq, and the client discards its stale assumptions. The rule the chapter insists on: this resume cursor is product liveness and is separate from ping/pong transport liveness, do not let one stand in for the other.

Shutdown: during a deploy drain the server first stops admitting new subscriptions, then sends an explicit terminal control frame, GoingAway { reason: "deploy", reconnect_after_ms, resume_supported: true }, before it closes the socket, so clients reconnect with jittered backoff and resume rather than hammering instantly. The terminal event is in the protocol from day one precisely because the server will eventually drain.

Authorization and origin: authenticate at the handshake where ordinary HTTP cookies and headers exist, validate the Origin header against an allowlist to refuse cross-site upgrades, and re-check authorization at subscribe time per tenant rather than trusting the handshake to settle authority for the connection's whole multi-hour life. Carry the tenant in the session and verify each Subscribe against it, because proving identity once does not prove continued authority to a given tenant's stream.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Envelope<T> {
    version: u16,        // mandatory: deterministic version negotiation
    session_id: String,  // mandatory: survives reconnects, ties logs together
    seq: u64,            // mandatory for ordered streams: resume cursor
    trace_id: String,    // recommended on every frame: correlation
    #[serde(flatten)]
    payload: T,
}

// Transport/control layer: handled by the connection machinery.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type")] // tagged union -> adding a variant is additive
enum Control {
    Subscribe { tenant: String, stream: String },
    Resume { stream: String, last_seq: u64 },
    Ack { stream: String, seq: u64 },
    Ping { nonce: u64 },
    Pong { nonce: u64 },
    // Terminal frame sent during drain, BEFORE the socket closes:
    GoingAway { reason: String, reconnect_after_ms: u64, resume_supported: bool },
    Error { code: u16, message: String },
}

// Domain layer: product events, wrapped in the same envelope.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type")]
enum DomainEvent {
    TaskProgress { task: String, percent: u8 },
    Notification { text: String },
    // On resume-too-old, server sends a fresh baseline instead of replay:
    Snapshot { stream: String, baseline_seq: u64 },
}

A versioned Envelope<T> with serde-tagged control and domain enums; control carries resume and the terminal GoingAway drain frame.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines one versioned envelope contract: Envelope<T> with mandatory version, session_id, seq, plus trace_id, and serde(tag) for additive evolution.
  • Transport/control messages (Subscribe, Resume, Ping/Pong, GoingAway) are separated from domain events (TaskProgress, Notification) explicitly.
  • States one resume rule (replay from last_seq, else Snapshot baseline) and one shutdown rule (stop admission, send GoingAway, then close).
  • Includes authorization/origin decisions: Origin allowlist at handshake plus per-tenant re-check at Subscribe time.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Test disconnect storms, reconnects, and long-lived shutdown behavior

Split the matrix into deterministic logic tests and metric-driven storm diagnosis, because storm handling is partly a test problem and partly an observability problem, and confirm both rather than relying on 'it reconnected once on my laptop.'

Deterministic tests cover the pure protocol logic where there is no excuse for flakiness: the protocol state machine (legal and illegal transitions), the resume rule (resume from a known cursor replays exactly the missing events; a too-old cursor yields a snapshot baseline), bounded queue enforcement (the lab's shape, a client at the limit is evicted and the bound is never exceeded), and graceful close ordering (admission stops, the terminal frame is emitted, then the socket closes). All of these are synchronous or controllable and should be plain unit and integration tests with asserted outcomes.

To simulate slow consumers and a drained shutdown in CI without wall-clock sleeps, drive time and IO explicitly. Model the slow consumer as a client whose receiver simply does not drain, then call broadcast and assert the queue hit the bound and the eviction fired, no sleeping, just a queue you control. For timing-dependent paths use a virtual clock (tokio's start_paused / advance, or an injected Clock trait) so a 30-second heartbeat timeout or a reconnect backoff is tested by advancing time programmatically, which is deterministic and instant. For the drain, trigger the shutdown signal directly and assert the sequence of emitted frames (admission rejected, GoingAway sent, close sent) rather than racing a real timer. This is how the plan avoids the timing lottery: time is an input, not a real-world wait.

The metrics that prove a disconnect storm is under control are reconnect rate (sustained spike means a flapping load balancer or a thundering reconnect), handshake error rate (auth or origin failures climbing during the storm), queue age and pending depth per connection and per tenant (the early warning that a consumer is behind), and per-tenant active connection count (so one tenant's storm is distinguishable from a global one). Together these are well over the three-hook minimum and they let you attribute a storm to a tenant or a path rather than just observing aggregate pain.

For attribution after the fact, every connection log and trace must carry stable IDs: session_id (survives reconnects so one client's whole reconnect history is one thread), tenant_id, and a trace_id per request/frame, plus the close reason on every disconnect. A single failed reconnect path is only debuggable later if those IDs were emitted at the time; without session_id you cannot even tell that ten log lines belong to one flapping client.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

// Deterministic bounded-queue test: no sleeps, the slow consumer is just a
// queue we never drain. Mirrors the lab's eviction rule.
#[test]
fn slow_consumer_is_evicted_at_bound() {
    let max = 2;
    let mut pending: VecDeque<String> = VecDeque::new();
    let mut evicted = false;
    for ev in ["a", "b", "c"] {
        if pending.len() >= max { evicted = true; break; }
        pending.push_back(ev.into());
    }
    assert!(evicted);
    assert!(pending.len() <= max); // bound never exceeded
}

// Drain test: assert the ORDER of control frames, no real timer involved.
#[derive(PartialEq, Debug)]
enum Frame { AdmissionRejected, GoingAway, Close }

fn drain_sequence() -> Vec<Frame> {
    // stop admission -> announce -> close (the only legal order)
    vec![Frame::AdmissionRejected, Frame::GoingAway, Frame::Close]
}

#[test]
fn graceful_shutdown_stops_admission_before_close() {
    let seq = drain_sequence();
    let admit = seq.iter().position(|f| *f == Frame::AdmissionRejected).unwrap();
    let close = seq.iter().position(|f| *f == Frame::Close).unwrap();
    assert!(admit < close); // admission halts before the socket closes
}

// For heartbeat/backoff timeouts, prefer tokio::time::pause + advance() so the
// clock is an input, not a wall-clock sleep that turns CI into a timing lottery.

Deterministic queue-bound and shutdown-ordering tests; timeouts use a paused virtual clock, never real sleeps.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Includes deterministic tests for both the bounded queue (eviction at limit) and shutdown ordering (admission halts before close).
  • Names well over three observability hooks: reconnect rate, handshake error rate, per-connection/per-tenant queue age and depth, per-tenant active connections.
  • Includes stable ID fields for logs/traces: session_id, tenant_id, trace_id, plus the close reason.
  • Explains avoiding timing-lottery sleeps via an undrained queue for slow consumers and a paused virtual clock for timeouts and backoff.

Lab solution

The lab converts the unbounded fan-out from the starter code into a bounded, slow-consumer-aware hub. The one change that matters is the capacity check inside broadcast: before pushing a payload onto a client's pending queue, it reads that queue's length and compares it against max_pending. A client already at the bound is treated as too slow for the current policy and evicted (removed from the map and recorded in evicted), rather than being allowed to grow its queue without limit. That is the chapter's point made mechanical: an unbounded queue is a policy that says 'grow memory until the process dies,' and replacing it with disconnect-at-limit makes the slow consumer visible the moment it falls behind.

Ids are collected into a sorted snapshot before iterating so that eviction order is deterministic; HashMap iteration order is unspecified, and the expected output names evicted clients in a fixed order (beta,gamma), so sorting is what makes the test reproducible. Trace the two broadcasts with max_pending = 2 and initial queue depths alpha=0, beta=2, gamma=1. On broadcast("first"), sorted order is alpha, beta, gamma: alpha (len 0) accepts and delivered becomes 1; beta (len 2) is at the limit and is evicted; gamma (len 1) accepts and delivered becomes 2, growing to len 2. On broadcast("second"), the surviving clients are alpha and gamma: alpha (len 1) accepts and delivered becomes 3; gamma (now len 2) is at the limit and is evicted.

After both broadcasts, only alpha remains, so active = 1; the eviction log is beta then gamma, so evicted = beta,gamma; and exactly three pushes succeeded, so delivered = 3. The program uses only std (HashMap, VecDeque, Vec, String) and prints precisely the expected three lines.

Example 48-S. bounded_fanout_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Client {
    pending: VecDeque<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Hub {
    clients: HashMap<&'static str, Client>,
    max_pending: usize,
    delivered: usize,
    evicted: Vec<&'static str>,
}

impl Hub {
    fn new(max_pending: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            clients: HashMap::new(),
            max_pending,
            delivered: 0,
            evicted: Vec::new(),
        }
    }

    fn add_client(&mut self, id: &'static str, pending: usize) {
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
        for _ in 0..pending {
            queue.push_back(String::from("old"));
        }

        self.clients.insert(id, Client { pending: queue });
    }

    fn broadcast(&mut self, payload: &str) {
        // Iterate over a stable, sorted snapshot of ids so eviction order is
        // deterministic regardless of HashMap iteration order.
        let mut ids: Vec<_> = self.clients.keys().copied().collect();
        ids.sort_unstable();

        for id in ids {
            // The capacity check happens BEFORE the push: a client already at
            // the bound is too slow for this policy and is evicted instead of
            // being allowed to grow memory further.
            let at_limit = self
                .clients
                .get(id)
                .map(|client| client.pending.len() >= self.max_pending)
                .unwrap_or(false);

            if at_limit {
                self.clients.remove(id);
                self.evicted.push(id);
                continue;
            }

            if let Some(client) = self.clients.get_mut(id) {
                client.pending.push_back(payload.to_string());
                self.delivered += 1;
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut hub = Hub::new(2);
    hub.add_client("alpha", 0);
    hub.add_client("beta", 2);
    hub.add_client("gamma", 1);

    hub.broadcast("first");
    hub.broadcast("second");

    println!("active = {}", hub.clients.len());
    println!(
        "evicted = {}",
        if hub.evicted.is_empty() {
            "none".to_string()
        } else {
            hub.evicted.join(",")
        }
    );
    println!("delivered = {}", hub.delivered);
}
Output
active = 1
evicted = beta,gamma
delivered = 3

Review question answers

Why is one writer task usually calmer than many tasks sharing the write half directly?

Because a single writer is the only thing that touches the send path, it imposes one deterministic order on outbound frames: text, pongs, and the final close all flow through it in the order pulled from the outbound channel, so close is necessarily last and nothing races past it. With many tasks sharing an Arc<Mutex<sink>>, the order in which they acquire the lock is the scheduler's choice, so a stray frame can be written after close, and there is no single seam at which to drain on shutdown. It also gives you one chokepoint, the bounded outbound channel, where backpressure and queue depth are measurable, instead of pressure smeared across every lock holder.

What makes queue age or pending depth more actionable than active connection count alone?

Active connection count does not move when a client falls behind, a slow consumer is still connected, so the number that should warn you stays flat while memory climbs. Queue age (how long the oldest unsent event has waited) and pending depth (how many events are backed up) rise immediately and point at the specific connection or tenant that is too slow for the current policy. They are leading indicators tied to the actual failure, whereas connection count is a lagging aggregate that only changes after you have already started disconnecting clients.

Why are reconnect and resume protocol decisions separate from ping or pong liveness?

Ping and pong are transport liveness, they only tell you the socket is still open and the peer is responsive at the TCP/WebSocket layer. Reconnect and resume are product liveness, they answer which application events a client has actually applied and which it still needs after a gap, using a durable sequence cursor or last-seen sequence number. A connection can be perfectly alive by ping/pong while the client is hours behind on events, and a client can be fully caught up by cursor while a single missed pong tears the socket down, so conflating the two lets one silently stand in for the other and hides real data loss behind a healthy heartbeat.

When is SSE a better answer than WebSockets even if the product still wants live updates?

When the direction is one-way: the client only ever listens and never needs to push commands back over the same connection. Server-Sent Events deliver server-to-client push over plain HTTP with automatic browser reconnection and a built-in Last-Event-ID resume cursor, so you avoid the entire WebSocket upgrade, split, heartbeat, and close lifecycle and the slow-consumer machinery that comes with owning a duplex connection. The tradeoff is that SSE is one-directional and text-framed, so the moment the client must send interactive commands, a WebSocket becomes the right tool again.

Why should graceful shutdown for long-lived sockets stop admission before closing active connections?

Because shutdown is an ordering problem, and the order is stop admitting new work, drain what is in flight, then cancel the rest with a deadline, the same sequence TCP services and brokers use. If you do not stop admission first, new connections and subscriptions keep arriving while you are trying to drain, so the in-flight set never settles and the drain never completes. And if you drop the runtime out from under active sockets instead of closing them in order, your close policy, the terminal GoingAway frame, reconnect advice, and clean close, never actually runs, so clients see abrupt resets and reconnect in a thundering herd rather than backing off with resume.

Chapter 49 · HTTPS, TLS, and Secure Service Boundaries

HTTPS, TLS, and Secure Service Boundaries

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

The exercises in this chapter all push toward one habit: treating a secure service boundary as a set of explicit, reviewable decisions rather than a single library call. You decide where public TLS terminates, which proxy headers you believe, which peers must prove their identity, how certificates rotate without downtime, and which HTTP defaults keep browsers honest. Each exercise isolates one of those decisions so it can be argued about in review and asserted against in CI.

The through-line is that almost everything here is policy you encode in plain Rust types, not behavior you hope a framework supplies. A typed ServiceEdge or HttpSecurityPolicy makes the termination owner, the forwarded-proto trust rule, the cookie flags, and the rotation window visible in one place. That visibility is the whole point: a boundary you can read and test is a boundary you can keep secure as the deployment changes underneath it.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Choose a TLS termination strategy from the real deployment boundary

The point of this exercise is to choose termination from the trust boundary in front of you, not from a default habit. Walk the four cases against three questions the chapter raised: who owns the public certificate, who trusts the proxy headers, and who needs the peer identity directly.

The browser-facing API behind a cloud load balancer naturally wants load-balancer termination. The load balancer already owns the public certificate (the cloud provider issues, renews, and serves it), so the Rust service never sees raw TLS for that hop. The consequence you must accept is that the service learns the original scheme only from a forwarded header, so forwarded-proto trust must be tied to the load balancer hop and stripped from anything arriving directly.

The internal admin tool on the same host as a reverse proxy fits reverse-proxy termination. The proxy and the app share a host, so the plaintext segment between them never leaves the machine, and the proxy can own the certificate and add the security headers in one place. This is the case where same-host reverse-proxy termination keeps the trust boundary smallest while still centralizing certificate handling.

The service-mesh deployment already has a sidecar trust boundary. TLS terminates in the sidecar, and the verified peer identity (the SPIFFE-style identity the mesh issues) is handed to the app out of band. You should model that identity handoff explicitly rather than assume "inside the mesh means trusted," because the whole value of the sidecar is that the peer identity becomes a policy input.

The dedicated edge appliance written in Rust most plausibly wants in-process TLS. It owns the full external edge, there is no upstream proxy to delegate to, and packaging the trust store and certificate lifecycle into the binary is the honest contract for an appliance. This is the case to justify with certificate ownership and packaging: the appliance ships and renews its own material, so it should terminate TLS itself. Across the four cases you have at least three distinct strategies, justified by trust-header policy (load balancer) and certificate ownership and packaging (the appliance), and none of them pretends one strategy fits every service.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Four cases produce three distinct strategies: load-balancer, same-host reverse-proxy, sidecar, and in-process.
  • Load-balancer choice is justified by forwarded-proto / trust-header policy; the appliance choice by certificate ownership and packaging.
  • The answer explicitly states that termination strategy depends on the boundary and that no single strategy is universally correct.
Exercise 2code reading

Identify insecure HTTP, cookie, and header settings in one API edge

Read each field as a policy statement and ask not "does the app still work" but "does the boundary stay safe under real browsers and proxies."

The settings that weaken transport or session safety directly are: cookie.secure = false lets the session cookie travel over plaintext HTTP, so any plaintext request leaks it; cookie.http_only = false exposes the cookie to JavaScript, turning any XSS into session theft; redirect_http = false leaves a plaintext entry point that a network attacker can sit on and downgrade; and hsts_max_age_secs = 0 means the browser never pins HTTPS, so the first request and any later typed URL can be intercepted before the redirect. Those four are unsafe on their own.

The combination problem is allowed_origin = "*" together with credentialed requests. A wildcard CORS origin is relatively harmless for anonymous public data, but the moment the API serves credentialed responses (cookies, Authorization headers) it becomes a path for arbitrary origins to read authenticated responses. same_site = "None" compounds this: it tells the browser to send the session cookie on cross-site requests, which is exactly what you do not want for an authenticated session, and SameSite=None is only valid alongside Secure, which is off here, so the pairing is both dangerous and inconsistent.

Everything here that a local demo tolerated should differ in production. A demo over http://localhost has no plaintext-network adversary and no cross-origin browser, so Secure=false, no redirect, no HSTS, and wildcard CORS feel harmless. In production those same values are the boundary's weak points. The secure replacements are: Secure=true and HttpOnly=true on the cookie, SameSite=Lax (or Strict for an admin session), redirect_http=true, a non-zero HSTS max-age (one to two years), and a single exact origin instead of *.

In CI, assert the policy and not just reachability. Concretely: assert that the Set-Cookie header carries Secure and HttpOnly and a non-None SameSite; assert that a plaintext request receives a redirect to HTTPS; assert that a successful HTTPS response carries a Strict-Transport-Security header with a non-zero max-age; and assert that the CORS response echoes only the configured origin, never *, on credentialed routes.

// Insecure config (the starting point) versus the secure replacement.
// The flags below are the exact fields CI should assert against.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct EdgeConfig {
    redirect_http: bool,
    allowed_origin: &'static str,
    cookie_secure: bool,
    cookie_http_only: bool,
    same_site: &'static str,
    hsts_max_age_secs: u64,
}

impl EdgeConfig {
    /// One predicate per CI assertion. A reviewer can read each line as the
    /// boundary rule it enforces.
    fn audit(&self) -> Vec<&'static str> {
        let mut problems = Vec::new();
        if !self.redirect_http {
            problems.push("plaintext entry point: enable HTTPS redirect");
        }
        if self.allowed_origin == "*" {
            problems.push("wildcard CORS: pin one exact origin");
        }
        if !self.cookie_secure {
            problems.push("cookie sent over plaintext: set Secure");
        }
        if !self.cookie_http_only {
            problems.push("cookie readable by JS: set HttpOnly");
        }
        if self.same_site == "None" {
            problems.push("cross-site cookie: use Lax or Strict");
        }
        if self.hsts_max_age_secs == 0 {
            problems.push("no HSTS: set a non-zero max-age");
        }
        problems
    }
}

fn main() {
    let insecure = EdgeConfig {
        redirect_http: false,
        allowed_origin: "*",
        cookie_secure: false,
        cookie_http_only: false,
        same_site: "None",
        hsts_max_age_secs: 0,
    };

    for problem in insecure.audit() {
        println!("FAIL: {}", problem);
    }
}

An audit predicate per field turns the insecure config into a list of CI-checkable boundary rules.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Names more than three concrete insecure settings: Secure=false, HttpOnly=false, redirect off, HSTS=0, and SameSite=None.
  • Proposes secure replacements for cookies (Secure/HttpOnly/Lax), redirects, exact-origin CORS, and non-zero HSTS, each with a stated risk.
  • Lists CI assertions for secure cookie flags, redirect-to-HTTPS behavior, HSTS presence, and exact-origin CORS.
Exercise 3implementation

Harden one API edge configuration deliberately

This is a boundary-policy exercise, not a framework exercise. The goal is to take the insecure defaults and express them as small typed Rust values whose secure shape is obvious to a reviewer and assertable by a test.

Keep the config as plain structs with one method per derived property, exactly as the chapter's https_tls_security_defaults example does. The hardening is four concrete moves. First, turn redirect_http on so there is no plaintext entry point. Second, harden the session cookie: secure = true so it never travels over plaintext, http_only = true so script cannot read it, and a same_site that is not "None" (Lax is the calm default for a browser session). Naming the cookie with the __Host- prefix is a small extra: that prefix is only honored when the cookie is Secure, has Path=/, and carries no Domain, so the name itself encodes part of the policy. Third, replace the wildcard origin with one exact origin so cors_mode() reports locked-down. Fourth, give HSTS a non-zero max-age so hsts_enabled() is true and reinforces the redirect.

The is_hardened() predicate captures why these belong together: a cookie is hardened only when Secure && HttpOnly && same_site != "None". Encoding that as one method means the next CI step asserts a single boolean instead of re-deriving the rule. Likewise hsts = redirect_http && hsts_max_age_secs > 0 insists that HSTS and the redirect reinforce each other; advertising HSTS while still serving plaintext would be contradictory, so the predicate ties them.

The summary then prints exactly the four lines the lab expects, each proving one value changed: redirect = true, cookie hardened = true, cors = locked-down, hsts = true. Because the values are explicit and typed, the diff in review is small and the assertions in CI are direct.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct SessionCookiePolicy {
    name: &'static str,
    secure: bool,
    http_only: bool,
    same_site: &'static str,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct HttpSecurityPolicy {
    redirect_http: bool,
    hsts_max_age_secs: u64,
    allowed_origin: &'static str,
}

impl SessionCookiePolicy {
    fn is_hardened(&self) -> bool {
        self.secure && self.http_only && self.same_site != "None"
    }
}

impl HttpSecurityPolicy {
    fn cors_mode(&self) -> &'static str {
        if self.allowed_origin == "*" {
            "wildcard"
        } else {
            "locked-down"
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // __Host- prefix is honored only with Secure + Path=/ + no Domain,
    // so the name encodes part of the policy.
    let cookie = SessionCookiePolicy {
        name: "__Host-session",
        secure: true,
        http_only: true,
        same_site: "Lax",
    };

    let policy = HttpSecurityPolicy {
        redirect_http: true,
        hsts_max_age_secs: 63_072_000, // two years
        allowed_origin: "https://app.example.com",
    };

    println!("redirect = {}", policy.redirect_http);
    println!("cookie hardened = {}", cookie.is_hardened());
    println!("cors = {}", policy.cors_mode());
    println!(
        "hsts = {}",
        policy.redirect_http && policy.hsts_max_age_secs > 0
    );
}

The hardened config: each field is an explicit policy statement a reviewer reads and a test asserts.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • redirect_http is true and a non-zero HSTS max-age makes the hsts predicate true, so redirect and HSTS reinforce each other.
  • The cookie sets Secure and HttpOnly (plus a non-None SameSite), so is_hardened() returns true.
  • allowed_origin is one exact host, so cors_mode() reports locked-down rather than wildcard.
  • main prints the four expected lines, proving each value changed.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Debug a TLS failure without weakening verification

Most TLS failures are evidence problems before they are code problems, so the repair path is a checklist that gathers evidence first and never ends with "turn verification off."

Start from the four questions the chapter mapped to the four ways a handshake fails. (1) Hostname / SNI: does the certificate's subject-alternative-name set actually cover the host the client asked for, and is the client sending the right SNI through the proxy? A name mismatch is the single most common cause, so check it first. (2) Full chain: did the server send its leaf plus any intermediates, or is it serving only the leaf so the client cannot build a path to a trusted root? A freshly rotated certificate that omits a new intermediate fails exactly this way. (3) Trust store: does the client trust the root that signed the chain, or did rotation move to a CA the staging trust store does not carry? (4) ALPN: did both sides agree on a protocol (for example h2 versus http/1.1), since a protocol mismatch can surface as a generic handshake failure.

Critically, the proxy is a prime suspect here precisely because two things changed at once: the certificate rotated and traffic moved to a different proxy layer. A proxy or termination change can look exactly like a certificate bug to the app. The proxy might present its own certificate for a hostname the client did not expect, might forward to a backend whose SNI no longer matches, or might terminate TLS and then forward over plaintext while sending a forwarded-proto header the app distrusts so the app believes the request was plaintext. So before blaming the leaf certificate, confirm which hop actually produced the error and whether the forwarded-scheme trust changed with the new proxy.

Reproduce with explicit trust material, never by skipping checks. Stand up a local CA you control, issue a leaf with the right SANs, and point the client at that trust bundle: this exercises the same chain assembly and hostname verification a real client performs, so a green local run is meaningful. In CI, run the same local-CA harness so the assertion lives in the pipeline. The one acceptable concession is scope: a global --insecure / skip-verify switch is fine for a single throwaway local probe to confirm the network route reaches the right box, but it is never an acceptable production workaround, because it removes exactly the guarantee TLS exists to provide. The production fix is to correct the chain, SANs, trust store, or proxy configuration, not to stop verifying.

// A diagnostic checklist as code: each step gathers evidence in order, and
// none of them is "disable verification." The local-CA path is the
// reproduction strategy, not a bypass.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum TlsEvidence {
    HostnameOrSni,   // does the cert's SAN cover the requested host / SNI?
    FullChain,       // is the server sending leaf + intermediates?
    TrustStore,      // does the client trust the signing root?
    Alpn,            // did both sides agree on h2 vs http/1.1?
    ProxyTrust,      // did termination / forwarded-proto move with the proxy?
}

fn diagnose_in_order() -> Vec<(TlsEvidence, &'static str)> {
    vec![
        (TlsEvidence::HostnameOrSni, "compare cert SANs to requested host"),
        (TlsEvidence::FullChain, "confirm intermediates are served after rotation"),
        (TlsEvidence::TrustStore, "check the new CA root is in the client store"),
        (TlsEvidence::Alpn, "confirm negotiated protocol matches expectation"),
        (TlsEvidence::ProxyTrust, "check the new proxy hop and forwarded-proto trust"),
    ]
}

fn reproduce_safely() -> &'static str {
    // Issue a leaf from a local CA with the real SANs and point the client at
    // that trust bundle. Same chain assembly and hostname check as production.
    "local-CA + explicit trust bundle (CI lane), never global skip-verify"
}

fn main() {
    for (i, (evidence, action)) in diagnose_in_order().into_iter().enumerate() {
        println!("{}. {:?}: {}", i + 1, evidence, action);
    }
    println!("reproduce: {}", reproduce_safely());
}

The checklist ordered by likelihood, with the local-CA reproduction in place of any skip-verify switch.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The checklist starts from hostname/SNI, then chain, trust store, ALPN, and proxy evidence, in likelihood order.
  • Disabling verification is explicitly ruled out as a production fix; only a single throwaway local probe is conceded.
  • Reproduction uses a local CA and explicit trust bundle in CI, exercising real chain and hostname verification.
  • Names concrete ways a proxy or termination change masquerades as a certificate bug: wrong presented cert, SNI mismatch, distrusted forwarded-proto after plaintext forwarding.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design certificate rotation and mTLS boundaries for a service fleet

Make renewal, reload, trust distribution, and peer-identity policy explicit now, before the first expiry or mixed rollout turns them into an incident.

Classify the hops by who needs to prove what. The public API needs server-authenticated TLS only: browsers and external callers verify the server, and the server does not generally hold a client certificate for each browser, so requiring client certs there would be wrong. The internal queue consumer talks to a broker; if the broker authenticates clients by certificate it is mTLS, but if the broker uses a token or network ACL and only the transport must be encrypted, server-auth TLS plus a separate credential is enough, so treat it as server-auth TLS unless the broker policy demands client certs. The service-to-service path that requires mTLS is the clear mTLS hop: both ends present certificates and each verifies the other. So at minimum the public API is server-auth-only and the service-to-service path is mTLS.

Decide where peer identity is enforced and own it deliberately. mTLS is worth nothing if the verified peer identity is not turned into a policy input somewhere explicit. In a mesh, the sidecar can verify the certificate, but the authorization decision ("is this peer allowed to call this route") should land in the service, because only the service knows which identities its routes permit. If you instead enforce at a reverse proxy, the proxy must forward the verified identity to the app in a header that the app trusts only from that proxy hop. The appropriate owner is the component that holds the route-to-identity policy; pushing the check there keeps the boundary reviewable.

Reload without downtime is the transition teams miss: renewing the material on disk and actually loading it into the running process are two separate events. With 30-day rotation and a zero-downtime requirement, renew well before expiry (a 14-day renew_before_days window, as in the chapter's rotate_now predicate), write the new material, and trigger a hot reload of the certificate resolver and trust bundle rather than a process restart. Distribute the new trust root before issuing leaves from it, so a peer that already trusts the new root accepts both old and new during the overlap. That overlap window is what makes a mixed rollout safe.

Watch the signals that warn before users do. At minimum track a certificate-expiry horizon (days remaining per certificate, alert before the renew window closes) and a reload-failure count (renewed on disk but the process never picked it up is the classic silent failure). Add an mTLS-rejection rate so a rollout that distributes a new root unevenly shows up as peers being rejected rather than as a vague latency spike. Those three together cover the failure modes that rotation introduces.

// Rotation as a small state machine plus the identity-and-trust decisions.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum PeerAuth { ServerAuthOnly, Mtls }

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Hop {
    name: &'static str,
    auth: PeerAuth,
    // Who turns a verified peer identity into an allow/deny decision.
    identity_enforced_at: &'static str,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct RotationPolicy {
    rotate_every_days: u16,
    renew_before_days: u16, // renew material on disk before this horizon
}

impl RotationPolicy {
    fn rotate_now(&self, days_left: u16) -> bool {
        days_left <= self.renew_before_days
    }
}

fn main() {
    let fleet = [
        Hop { name: "public-api", auth: PeerAuth::ServerAuthOnly, identity_enforced_at: "n/a" },
        Hop { name: "queue-consumer", auth: PeerAuth::ServerAuthOnly, identity_enforced_at: "broker-token" },
        Hop { name: "svc-to-svc", auth: PeerAuth::Mtls, identity_enforced_at: "in-process route policy" },
    ];

    let rotation = RotationPolicy { rotate_every_days: 30, renew_before_days: 14 };

    for hop in &fleet {
        println!("{}: {:?}, identity at {}", hop.name, hop.auth, hop.identity_enforced_at);
    }
    // Renew with two weeks of overlap; distribute the new root first, then hot-reload.
    println!("rotate now at 12 days left = {}", rotation.rotate_now(12));
    println!("signals: cert-expiry-horizon, reload-failure-count, mtls-rejection-rate");
}

Hops classified by peer-auth and identity owner, with rotation as a renew-before-horizon predicate.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Classifies the public API (and queue consumer) as server-auth-only and the service-to-service path as mTLS.
  • Locates peer-identity enforcement at the component holding route-to-identity policy and justifies that owner.
  • Gives a concrete rotation strategy: renew before a 14-day horizon, distribute new root first, hot-reload without restart.
  • Names at least two observability signals: cert-expiry horizon, reload-failure count, and mTLS-rejection rate.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Test HTTPS locally and in CI with realistic trust behavior

The whole point is to test the secure path itself, not a weakened stand-in, so the plan is built around a trusted local CA rather than any skip-verification bypass. CI should prove policy, not just reachability.

Local certificate coverage: issue leaves from a CA you control with SANs that match exactly the hostnames the tests use. For browser-facing tests cover the app host (for example app.localhost or app.test); for the service-to-service test cover the internal service name the client dials. Cover both the bare host and any aliases the harness uses, because a missing SAN is the most common reason a realistic local test fails. Wildcard SANs are acceptable only if production also uses them; otherwise mirror the production SAN shape so the chain and hostname check behave the same.

Trust material in CI: install the local CA root into the browser/client harness's trust store (or pass it as an explicit trust bundle to the test client), and have the servers present leaves issued by that CA. This is the safe substitute for --insecure: the client performs full chain assembly and hostname verification against material you provisioned, so a passing test means the real verification path works. Never set a global skip-verify flag in the harness, because then the tests stop testing the thing that matters.

Validate both mTLS directions explicitly. The acceptance test: a client presenting a valid leaf signed by the trusted client CA connects and is authorized. The rejection test, which is the one teams forget: a client presenting no certificate, or one signed by an untrusted CA, or one with the wrong identity, is rejected at the handshake or by the identity policy. Asserting the rejection path is what proves mTLS is actually enforced rather than merely offered.

The CI smoke test must assert transport policy beyond "the port opens over TLS." At least: a plaintext request returns a redirect to HTTPS; a successful HTTPS response carries Strict-Transport-Security with a non-zero max-age; the session Set-Cookie carries Secure and HttpOnly and a non-None SameSite; and a cross-origin request is answered with the one configured origin, never *, on credentialed routes. Because the same local CA and the same SAN shape are used in development and CI, the trust behavior the tests exercise stays close enough to production that a green pipeline is meaningful evidence and not a false comfort.

// A CI test plan expressed as assertions. The harness trusts a local CA's
// root; it never sets a global skip-verify flag.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct TlsTestPlan {
    local_ca_root_trusted: bool, // installed in the client/browser trust store
    leaf_sans: &'static [&'static str],
}

fn mtls_accept(client_cert_signed_by_trusted_ca: bool, identity_allowed: bool) -> bool {
    client_cert_signed_by_trusted_ca && identity_allowed
}

fn transport_assertions() -> Vec<&'static str> {
    vec![
        "plaintext request -> 301/308 redirect to https",
        "https response carries Strict-Transport-Security, max-age > 0",
        "Set-Cookie has Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite != None",
        "CORS echoes the one configured origin, never *",
    ]
}

fn main() {
    let plan = TlsTestPlan {
        local_ca_root_trusted: true,
        leaf_sans: &["app.test", "internal-svc.test"],
    };
    assert!(plan.local_ca_root_trusted, "CI must trust a local CA, not skip verify");

    // mTLS: one acceptance, one rejection.
    assert!(mtls_accept(true, true), "valid trusted client + allowed identity");
    assert!(!mtls_accept(false, true), "untrusted client cert must be rejected");

    for a in transport_assertions() {
        println!("assert: {}", a);
    }
    println!("sans covered: {:?}", plan.leaf_sans);
}

The CI plan as code: trusted local-CA root, matching SANs, mTLS accept/reject, and four transport-policy assertions.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Uses a local/CI CA root installed in the client trust store rather than a verification bypass.
  • Includes both an mTLS acceptance test and an mTLS rejection test (untrusted or missing client cert).
  • Asserts at least three transport-policy properties: HTTPS redirect, Secure cookie, HSTS, and exact-origin CORS.
  • Keeps local and CI trust behavior production-like by sharing the same local CA and SAN shape, so a green pipeline is meaningful.

Lab solution

The lab starts from the insecure defaults (redirect off, a cookie with Secure and HttpOnly false and SameSite "None", a wildcard CORS origin, and a zero HSTS max-age) and asks you to make four deliberate hardening moves so the four printed predicates flip to their secure values.

The cookie becomes hardened because is_hardened() returns secure && http_only && same_site != "None"; setting secure and http_only to true and SameSite to "Lax" satisfies all three terms, so the second line prints true. The transport policy sets redirect_http to true, which prints true on the first line directly. cors_mode() compares allowed_origin to "*"; because the origin is now the exact host "https://app.example.com", it returns "locked-down" and the third line prints that. The final line computes redirect_http && hsts_max_age_secs > 0; with the redirect on and a non-zero two-year max-age, both terms hold and it prints true, which also encodes the rule that HSTS and the redirect must reinforce each other rather than contradict.

The program uses only struct definitions, two impl blocks, and println!, so it compiles and runs with the standard library alone. Running it prints exactly the four expected lines.

Example 49-S. harden_edge_policy_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug)]
struct SessionCookiePolicy {
    name: &'static str,
    secure: bool,
    http_only: bool,
    same_site: &'static str,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct HttpSecurityPolicy {
    redirect_http: bool,
    hsts_max_age_secs: u64,
    allowed_origin: &'static str,
}

impl SessionCookiePolicy {
    fn is_hardened(&self) -> bool {
        self.secure && self.http_only && self.same_site != "None"
    }
}

impl HttpSecurityPolicy {
    fn cors_mode(&self) -> &'static str {
        if self.allowed_origin == "*" {
            "wildcard"
        } else {
            "locked-down"
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Hardened session cookie: Secure + HttpOnly, and SameSite is no longer
    // "None". The "__Host-" prefix is honored only when the cookie is Secure,
    // has Path=/, and carries no Domain, so the name encodes part of the policy.
    let cookie = SessionCookiePolicy {
        name: "__Host-session",
        secure: true,
        http_only: true,
        same_site: "Lax",
    };

    // Hardened transport policy: HTTP is redirected to HTTPS, a non-zero HSTS
    // max-age pins the browser to HTTPS, and the CORS origin is one exact host
    // instead of the wildcard "*".
    let policy = HttpSecurityPolicy {
        redirect_http: true,
        hsts_max_age_secs: 63_072_000, // two years
        allowed_origin: "https://app.example.com",
    };

    println!("redirect = {}", policy.redirect_http);
    println!("cookie hardened = {}", cookie.is_hardened());
    println!("cors = {}", policy.cors_mode());
    println!(
        "hsts = {}",
        policy.redirect_http && policy.hsts_max_age_secs > 0
    );
}
Output
redirect = true
cookie hardened = true
cors = locked-down
hsts = true

Review question answers

What is the practical difference between server-authenticated TLS and mTLS?

In server-authenticated TLS only the server presents a certificate, so the client verifies the server's identity but the server learns nothing cryptographic about who the client is; this is the right model for browser-facing and public APIs. In mTLS both ends present certificates and each verifies the other, so the server obtains a verified peer identity at the handshake. The practical payoff of mTLS is only realized if that verified identity is then turned into a policy input (an authorization decision) somewhere explicit; otherwise it is just extra ceremony. mTLS therefore fits internal service-to-service hops where you want to authenticate the caller, not just encrypt the bytes.

Why should proxy-header trust be tied to a known network boundary instead of accepted from arbitrary callers?

A header such as X-Forwarded-Proto is just bytes, and any client can set it to whatever it likes, so believing it unconditionally lets an attacker claim a plaintext request arrived over HTTPS. The value is trustworthy only when it was written by a proxy you operate and arrived through the specific hops you control, which is why forwarded-proto trust must be scoped to a known network boundary and stripped from anything arriving directly. Tying trust to the boundary means the app believes the forwarded scheme exactly when, and only when, a real termination point produced it. Without that scoping, forwarded-header trust becomes a way to forge the very security property the boundary exists to enforce.

When is HSTS a safe default, and when is it premature?

HSTS is a safe default once the site is reliably served over HTTPS on the host (and its subdomains, if includeSubDomains is set), because it instructs browsers to refuse plaintext and prevents downgrade on later visits. It is premature when any part of the host still legitimately needs plaintext, when HTTPS is not yet stable across every subdomain that would be covered, or when you would set a long max-age before you are confident, because a browser that has cached the policy will refuse to connect over HTTP and you cannot quickly undo that. The pragmatic path is to enable HTTPS and the redirect first, confirm stability, then turn on HSTS, and only later raise the max-age and consider preload. HSTS should reinforce an already-working redirect, never substitute for one.

Why are local CA and CI trust bundles safer than skip-verification flags for HTTPS testing?

A local CA plus an explicit trust bundle makes the client perform the same chain assembly and hostname verification it would in production, so a passing test is real evidence that the secure path works. A skip-verification flag removes exactly the checks TLS exists to provide, so the test proves only that a port answers, not that certificates, chains, or hostnames are correct. Skip-verify also teaches the team a shortcut that tends to leak from test harnesses into clients, where it silently disables protection. The local-CA approach keeps test trust behavior close to production while never normalizing an insecure bypass.

What makes certificate rotation a deployment problem as much as a cryptography problem?

The cryptography of issuing a new certificate is the easy part; the hard part is the lifecycle around it, because a certificate is a secret with an expiry date and renewing it on disk is a different event from loading it into the running process. Rotation therefore requires distributing the new trust root before issuing leaves from it, overlapping old and new material so a mixed rollout does not reject valid peers, and reloading the certificate and trust bundle without taking the service offline. Each of those is a deployment and orchestration concern, and the classic failure is renewing the file but never reloading it, which no cryptographic check catches. That is why rotation needs observability (expiry horizon, reload-failure count, rejection rate) and a reload strategy, not just a working key.

Chapter 50 · libp2p and Peer-to-Peer Rust Systems

libp2p and Peer-to-Peer Rust Systems

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises move from modelling a peer protocol as owned events to defending real connectivity and transport-selection decisions. The thread running through all of them is the chapter's central correction: a peer-to-peer node is calmest when one owner holds the protocol state and everything that crosses an async or channel boundary does so as an owned value, not as a shared reference to live transport. Get that ownership boundary right and the swarm loop becomes a plain state machine you can drive without a socket; get it wrong and you inherit duplicate-state bugs, shutdown races, and unbounded resource growth.

The later exercises broaden the lens from one node to a deployed mesh. Discovery has to survive hostile and noisy inputs, connectivity has to work for peers that cannot accept inbound dials, and the choice to use P2P at all has to be defended against brokers and service APIs that may fit the workload better. The recurring senior judgement is to treat NAT fallback, relay budgets, and convergence rules as product and operational concerns rather than networking trivia, and to reach for a hybrid transport split when topology and durability pull in different directions.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Model one tiny P2P protocol as events and state transitions

Split the protocol into two streams of owned values: local commands that your application issues downward, and network events that the transport delivers upward. The network edge produces events — ConnectionEstablished, Response, Gossip — because they are facts that already happened on the wire. Local application logic produces commands — Dial, SendRequest, Publish — because they are intentions you want the swarm to act on. Keeping these as separate enums is the whole design: the state machine has exactly two doors, on_command and on_event, and both take &mut self so there is one owner and no shared mutable transport handed around.

The identifiers that must thread through the machine are the PeerId and the request_id. The PeerId is the stable correlation field for connection and gossip events; the request_id is the stable correlation field for the request/response pair. Without the request_id you cannot match a Response back to the SendRequest that created it, and you cannot tell a duplicate or late response from a fresh one.

For pending work, the rule is simple: SendRequest adds a pending entry keyed by request_id, and the matching Response clears it. Dial and ConnectionEstablished move a peer toward the connected set but add no pending request; Publish and Gossip add no pending state at all because pub-sub is fire-and-forget news rather than a question that expects one answer. The transitions that add pending work are the ones that expect a reply; the transitions that clear it are the replies.

To make the sequence replayable in a deterministic test, record the ordered list of events and commands as plain values plus the resulting state snapshot (connected count, pending count, last log line). Because every input is an owned value rather than a live socket, another engineer can feed the same Vec of events into a fresh SwarmState and get byte-identical output — that reproducibility is the payoff of modelling the protocol as owned events instead of shared transport access.

// Two owned streams, one owner. Commands flow down, events flow up.
enum LocalCommand {
    Dial(PeerId),
    SendRequest { peer: PeerId, request_id: u64 },
    Publish { topic: &'static str, body: String },
}

enum NetworkEvent {
    ConnectionEstablished(PeerId),
    Response { peer: PeerId, request_id: u64, body: String },
    Gossip { peer: PeerId, topic: &'static str, body: String },
}

// SendRequest adds pending work; Response clears it; gossip adds none.
// request_id correlates the pair, PeerId correlates the connection.

Local commands and network events as separate owned enums, with the correlation fields called out.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Local commands (Dial, SendRequest, Publish) are a distinct enum from inbound network events (ConnectionEstablished, Response, Gossip).
  • SendRequest is identified as the transition that adds a pending-request entry, and ConnectionEstablished as the one that adds a connected peer.
  • request_id and PeerId are named as the stable correlation fields carried through the machine.
  • The replay argument turns on every input being a plain owned value rather than shared access to a live transport.
Exercise 2code reading

Identify ownership and async-task boundaries in a swarm loop

The swarm loop itself should own the swarm directly. In the libp2p shape from this chapter, the swarm is the outer machine that owns connections and does the polling, and exactly one task should drive it inside a select! whose two arms drain the two owned input streams: application commands coming down, and network events coming up. That task is the single writer of outbound transport effects. The broad shared lock in the inherited node is a symptom — it exists only because the design failed to pick one owner, so it papers over the missing ownership boundary by serialising every accessor instead.

Application state should have its own owner, separate from the swarm. The chapter is explicit that the swarm is not your business object and a behaviour is not your whole node: network orchestration and domain state belong in different places so tests can drive protocol state machines without real sockets. Practically, the swarm-driving task holds &mut node.state and is the only thing that mutates protocol maps and queues; the application reaches that state only by sending owned commands across a channel, never by grabbing a reference to the live connection.

The data that should cross boundaries as owned values is everything the unrelated tasks currently mutate in place: a task that wants to send a request should enqueue a SendRequest command rather than write to a transport handle, and a task that reacts to a response should receive a Response event rather than read shared connection state. Once one writer owns outbound effects, the outbound path becomes trivial to reason about — message ordering on the wire is just the order the single owner dequeues commands, and there is no interleaving of half-written frames from competing tasks.

The cancellation and shutdown bug that becomes far more likely with many partial owners is a double-free-style race on connection lifecycle: several tasks each believe they own the connection, so on shutdown one closes it while another is mid-write, or two tasks both try to dial-then-tear-down the same peer and the protocol state ends up describing a peer that is simultaneously connecting and disconnected. With one owner, cancellation is a single decision made in one place, and duplicate or contradictory state transitions cannot occur because only one &mut self ever applies them.

// Calmer shape: one task owns the swarm and the state; everyone else
// talks to it through owned commands on a channel.
async fn run(mut swarm: Swarm, mut commands: mpsc::Receiver<LocalCommand>) {
    let mut state = SwarmState::default();
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            Some(cmd) = commands.recv() => state.on_command(cmd, &mut swarm),
            event = swarm.next_event() => state.on_event(event),
            else => break, // single, unambiguous shutdown point
        }
    }
}
// No shared lock: on_command/on_event are the only mutators of state,
// and this task is the only writer of outbound transport effects.

One task owns both the swarm and the protocol state; other tasks reach it only through owned commands.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The swarm-driving task is named as the owner of the swarm, and SwarmState (domain state) is given a distinct owner so tests can run without sockets.
  • Outbound work is proposed as owned LocalCommand values sent over a channel rather than writes to shared transport handles.
  • The single-writer arrangement is tied to deterministic outbound ordering and to eliminating duplicate/contradictory state transitions.
  • The shutdown hazard is framed as a connection-lifecycle race among tasks that each think they own the connection, resolved by one owner with one shutdown point.
Exercise 3implementation

Build a small libp2p-style swarm loop over owned enums

Model the node as one plain struct, SwarmState, that owns three pieces of state: the set of connected peers, a map of pending requests keyed by request id, and a log queue for observability. There is no Rc, no RefCell, and no raw pointer in the main design — single ownership through &mut self is exactly what makes the loop testable, and it mirrors the ownership story many real libp2p nodes want internally.

The pending-request map is the honest core of the design. A SendRequest (or, in the lab's reduced vocabulary, a Request event) inserts an entry keyed by request_id whose value is the peer the request went to. The matching Response removes that entry. Because insertion and removal are keyed by the same id, the size of the map is always the count of genuinely in-flight requests; you cannot accidentally report a request as still pending after its response, and you cannot clear a request that was never issued. That keyed insert/remove pair is the simplest mechanism that keeps response handling truthful.

Connection events append to the connected collection, and every transition pushes a human-readable line onto the log queue. Reading the log back gives a deterministic trace of what the node did, which is what lets the runnable lab assert connected = 1, pending = 0, and a final log line of response peer-b state-v3 without any live transport. The whole point is that the same owned enums that would cross async or channel boundaries in a real node also drive this in-memory machine unchanged.

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct PeerId(&'static str);

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Event {
    Connected(PeerId),
    Request { peer: PeerId, id: u64 },
    Response { peer: PeerId, id: u64, body: String },
}

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct SwarmState {
    connected: Vec<PeerId>,
    pending: HashMap<u64, PeerId>,
    log: VecDeque<String>,
}

impl SwarmState {
    fn on_event(&mut self, event: Event) {
        match event {
            Event::Connected(peer) => self.connected.push(peer),
            Event::Request { peer, id } => {
                self.pending.insert(id, peer);
                self.log.push_back(format!("request {}", id));
            }
            Event::Response { peer, id, body } => {
                self.pending.remove(&id); // clear the in-flight entry
                self.log.push_back(format!("response {} {}", peer.0, body));
            }
        }
    }
}

One owner, one pending map keyed by request id, one log queue — the same shape a real libp2p node wants internally.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • SwarmState is the single central owner of connected peers, pending requests, and the log.
  • Request inserts a pending entry keyed by id and Response removes it, so pending count tracks genuinely in-flight work.
  • The log queue records each transition, letting the lab assert connected, pending, and the final line deterministically.
  • The design uses plain ownership with no Rc/RefCell/raw pointers, so it is testable without a live network.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair peer discovery with abuse controls and observability

The defect is that discovery is unbounded and unmeasured: it accepts every advertised peer, queues unlimited dials, and emits no telemetry, so it is both a correctness problem and a resource-exhaustion problem. Discovery treats hostile input as trusted input, which in a P2P system is exactly backwards — any peer can advertise any other peer.

Dedupe belongs in both places, against two distinct kinds of waste. A known-peer set prevents re-processing a peer you already know about and stops a flood of repeated advertisements from doing repeated work. A pending-dial set prevents queuing a second dial for a peer that already has one in flight, which is the dedupe that actually bounds the dial queue. They guard different failure modes — duplicate discovery versus duplicate dialing — so you want both.

Validation must run before any expensive work. Cheap rejection means checking the advertised record before you allocate a dial or touch the queue: reject malformed or non-routable multiaddrs, reject self-advertisements, reject peers already in the known set, and reject anything over the per-source advertisement budget. All of these are constant-time checks that cost nothing, and doing them first means a hostile peer cannot make you spend a dial slot or an allocation just by sending a record. The explicit budgets to make first-class are a maximum pending-dial queue depth, a per-peer dial-attempt cap with backoff, and a cap on accepted advertisements per source per interval.

For observability, instrument at minimum the dial-failure count (by reason), the relay-fallback usage rate, and the age of the oldest pending dial; duplicate-discovery rejections and current pending-dial depth are valuable additions. The oldest-pending-dial age is the early warning that the queue is backing up faster than it drains, and relay usage is the signal that the mesh is silently degrading. A good test or simulation case feeds a burst of thousands of advertisements for the same handful of peers plus a stream of unreachable addresses, and asserts that the pending-dial queue never exceeds its bound, that duplicate advertisements are rejected without new dials, and that dial-failure and relay-usage counters move as expected.

struct Discovery {
    known: HashSet<PeerId>,        // dedupe: already-discovered peers
    pending_dials: HashSet<PeerId>, // dedupe: dial already in flight
    queue: VecDeque<PeerId>,
    max_pending: usize,             // explicit queue budget
    metrics: Metrics,               // dial_failures, relay_used, oldest_pending
}

impl Discovery {
    fn on_advertised(&mut self, peer: PeerId, addr: &Multiaddr) {
        // Cheap validation BEFORE any dial/allocation work.
        if !addr.is_routable() || self.known.contains(&peer) {
            self.metrics.discovery_rejected += 1;
            return;
        }
        if self.pending_dials.contains(&peer) {
            return; // already dialing this peer
        }
        if self.queue.len() >= self.max_pending {
            self.metrics.dial_budget_dropped += 1;
            return; // explicit budget enforced
        }
        self.known.insert(peer);
        self.pending_dials.insert(peer);
        self.queue.push_back(peer);
    }
}

Two dedupe sets, an explicit pending-dial budget, cheap validation first, and metrics on every drop path.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Adds dedupe in both the known-peer set and the pending-dial set, plus an explicit max-pending-dial budget.
  • Routability/known/self checks run before any dial or allocation work, rejecting bad records cheaply.
  • Names at least three observability hooks: dial-failure count, relay-fallback usage, and oldest-pending-dial age.
  • Gives a simulation case: an advertisement flood plus unreachable addresses asserting bounded queue depth and correct counters.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Design NAT traversal, relay fallback, and connectivity telemetry

Every peer attempts the connectivity ladder in the same order, but the realistic outcome depends on where the peer sits. The default is direct dial first: a node tries the peer's advertised address directly. Cloud VMs with public routable addresses will usually accept this; laptops and branch-office devices behind NAT usually will not accept unsolicited inbound. When the direct dial fails, the node attempts hole punching (coordinated simultaneous dial using observed addresses) to establish a direct path through both NATs. Only when hole punching also fails does it fall back to a relay, where a third public peer forwards traffic. The relay is the escape hatch of last resort, not the first choice — it is exactly the dangerous silent default the chapter warns about.

The retry and lease policy for repeated direct-dial failures should be capped exponential backoff with a per-peer attempt budget, and relay circuits should be held on a short lease that is periodically re-challenged with a fresh direct-dial or hole-punch attempt. The reason to keep re-attempting direct connectivity even after a relay succeeds is that a relayed circuit consumes scarce relay capacity; without a lease that forces periodic upgrade attempts, peers settle permanently onto relays and the limited relay capacity becomes the bottleneck for the whole mesh. Connectivity budgets — how many simultaneous dials, how many relay circuits, how long a circuit may live before re-challenge — have to be settled before you ever reason about application throughput, because a peer that cannot connect cannot move data at all.

The telemetry has to make accidental relay dependence visible, since that is the failure that does not announce itself. Required dashboard fields before rollout: relay-usage rate (fraction of active connections currently relayed, the single most important number), hole-punch success rate, direct-dial failure rate broken down by reason, oldest queued outbound connection age, and relay-circuit capacity utilisation.
