The proof that relay is becoming the default accidentally is a rising relay-usage rate combined with a falling hole-punch success rate; if both move together you are degrading toward an all-relay mesh and should alert before users report slowness. Grounding this in the deployment: laptops and branch devices are the ones that will lean on relays, cloud VMs are your likely relay providers, so capacity planning ties directly to the laptop-to-VM ratio rather than to any generic P2P ideal.

enum DialOutcome {
    Direct,        // preferred: direct connection succeeded
    HolePunched,   // direct path established through NAT coordination
    Relayed,       // last resort: traffic forwarded by a public peer
    Failed,
}

fn connect(peer: &Peer, budget: &mut DialBudget, m: &mut Metrics) -> DialOutcome {
    if let Ok(()) = direct_dial(peer) { m.direct += 1; return DialOutcome::Direct; }
    if let Ok(()) = hole_punch(peer) { m.hole_punch_ok += 1; return DialOutcome::HolePunched; }
    if budget.relay_circuits_available() {
        m.relay_used += 1;            // watch this rate: silent default risk
        // Lease the circuit; re-challenge with direct/hole-punch later.
        return DialOutcome::Relayed;
    }
    m.dial_failures += 1;
    DialOutcome::Failed
}

The connectivity ladder as one ordered policy, with relay leased and every rung counted.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Defines a direct-dial-first path and an explicit relay fallback path (with hole punching as the intermediate rung).
  • Specifies capped exponential backoff with a per-peer attempt budget plus a relay-circuit lease that forces periodic upgrade re-attempts.
  • Requires at least three telemetry hooks: relay-usage rate, hole-punch success rate, dial-failure rate, and oldest queued outbound connection.
  • Keeps the reasoning tied to the laptop/VM/branch deployment shape and capacity planning rather than generic P2P advocacy.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Choose P2P vs brokered messaging, gRPC, or HTTP for one product

Match each boundary to what it actually needs from the transport — durability, topology, or operational cost — rather than to implementation taste, which is the chapter's standing point that P2P is not the advanced answer to every network problem.

The collaborative edge cache is the genuine P2P case. Its value is direct data exchange between geographically close peers, partial decentralisation so a node keeps serving when the central path is lost, and verifiable peer identity so caches can trust each other's content addressing. This is exactly the workload libp2p exists for: peer discovery and direct peer-to-peer data movement are real product requirements, not nice-to-haves. The data plane wants the overlay.

The internal durable task pipeline is the case against P2P. It wants durable replay and queue semantics — at-least-once delivery, ordered or partitioned consumption, the ability to replay after a consumer crash — which a message broker provides natively and a mesh does not. Building durability and replay on top of P2P would mean reinventing the broker badly. Use a broker (the Chapter 30 shape) and let it own delivery guarantees.

The public billing API is the case for a typed service contract or plain HTTP. It is a request/response boundary with external clients, strong auditability requirements, and a need for ordinary load balancers, gateways, and TLS termination. gRPC (Chapter 47) or HTTP gives you a typed contract and the entire operational ecosystem; overlay routing would add cost and obscurity with no benefit, since there is no peer discovery or decentralisation requirement here at all.

The edge cache is also where the hybrid split belongs, and hybrid is the calm senior answer when topology and durability pull apart. Run the control plane — membership, cache-policy distribution, health — over HTTP or gRPC to a central coordinator that is easy to operate and audit, while the data plane (the actual cached-object exchange) runs over libp2p between peers. The boundary splits cleanly along control versus data: centralised, durable, auditable control; decentralised, direct, high-volume data. That mirrors the chapter's recommended hybrid: HTTP/gRPC for control plane, a broker for durable work, and libp2p only where peer discovery and direct exchange are real requirements.

// Transport chosen per boundary by what the workload needs.
// edge cache  -> libp2p data plane + HTTP/gRPC control plane (hybrid)
// task pipeline-> message broker (durable replay, queue semantics)
// billing API  -> gRPC or HTTP (typed contract, audit, std ops ecosystem)
enum Transport {
    P2pOverlay,   // direct peer data exchange, partial decentralization
    Broker,       // durable, replayable, ordered work
    ServiceRpc,   // typed request/response, external clients, auditable
}

One transport decision per boundary, with the edge cache split into a hybrid control/data plane.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Picks the edge cache for P2P (direct exchange, partial decentralisation) and the task pipeline against it (durable replay/queue semantics belong in a broker).
  • Provides a hybrid design: HTTP/gRPC control plane plus libp2p data plane for the edge cache, split along control vs data.
  • Justifies each choice by durability, topology, or operational cost rather than implementation style.
  • States plainly that the billing API wants typed RPC/HTTP because overlay routing adds cost with no discovery or decentralisation benefit.

Lab solution

The lab gives you a complete owned-event state machine with one branch left as a stub. SwarmState is the single owner of all protocol state — a Vec of connected peers, a HashMap of pending requests keyed by request id, and a VecDeque log — and on_event mutates it through &mut self, so there is exactly one writer and no shared transport access. Three owned Event values are fed in sequence, the same way real network events would arrive over a channel.

The repair is in the Response branch. A request inserts an entry into the pending map keyed by its id; the matching response must remove that same entry, otherwise the pending count would never return to zero and the node would report in-flight work that has actually completed. The fix is self.pending.remove(&id) followed by pushing a log line of the form "response peer-b state-v3". The pending map is the source of truth for outstanding requests, so removal on response is what keeps response handling honest.

Tracing the sequence: Connected(peer-b) pushes one peer onto connected, so connected.len() is 1. Request { id: 7 } inserts key 7 into pending and logs "request 7". Response { id: 7 } removes key 7, leaving pending empty so pending.len() is 0, and pushes "response peer-b state-v3" as the final log entry. Reading log.back() therefore yields that last line. The program prints connected = 1, pending = 0, and last = response peer-b state-v3, matching the expected output exactly. It compiles and runs on the standard library alone because the whole point of the example is to teach the ownership model without a live transport.

Example 50-S. swarm_loop_lab.rs — Reference solution

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct PeerId(&'static str);

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Event {
    Connected(PeerId),
    Request {
        peer: PeerId,
        id: u64,
    },
    Response {
        peer: PeerId,
        id: u64,
        body: String,
    },
}

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct SwarmState {
    connected: Vec<PeerId>,
    pending: HashMap<u64, PeerId>,
    log: VecDeque<String>,
}

impl SwarmState {
    fn on_event(&mut self, event: Event) {
        match event {
            Event::Connected(peer) => {
                self.connected.push(peer);
            }
            Event::Request { peer, id } => {
                self.pending.insert(id, peer);
                self.log.push_back(format!("request {}", id));
            }
            Event::Response { peer, id, body } => {
                // Repaired branch: the pending map is the source of truth for
                // in-flight work, so the response must remove the entry that
                // its matching request inserted, then record itself in the log.
                self.pending.remove(&id);
                self.log
                    .push_back(format!("response {} {}", peer.0, body));
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut state = SwarmState::default();
    let peer = PeerId("peer-b");

    state.on_event(Event::Connected(peer));
    state.on_event(Event::Request { peer, id: 7 });
    state.on_event(Event::Response {
        peer,
        id: 7,
        body: String::from("state-v3"),
    });

    println!("connected = {}", state.connected.len());
    println!("pending = {}", state.pending.len());
    println!("last = {}", state.log.back().map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("none"));
}
Output
connected = 1
pending = 0
last = response peer-b state-v3

Review question answers

Why do owned events and commands make a swarm loop easier to test than shared transport state does?

When every input is a plain owned value — a LocalCommand or a NetworkEvent — you can feed a fixed sequence into a fresh state machine and get byte-identical output every run, because nothing depends on socket timing, lock acquisition order, or which task happened to mutate state first. Shared transport state, by contrast, requires a live connection or an elaborate mock to exercise, and its behaviour depends on interleaving you cannot control. With one owner mutating through &mut self there is a single place where state changes happen, so the test is just "apply these events, assert this snapshot." That is why the chapter's examples compile and run as ordinary Rust with no live network.

What is the practical difference between peer identity, channel security, and application-level authorization?

Peer identity tells you which cryptographic key is sending bytes — it answers "who is this" but says nothing about whether they should be trusted. Channel security (the encrypted, authenticated transport) guarantees the bytes were not tampered with or read in transit, but an authenticated channel to a malicious peer is still a channel to a malicious peer. Application-level authorization is the separate decision of whether this identified peer is allowed to make this particular request, with size checks, rate limits, and protocol permissions enforced regardless of how good the cryptography is. The chapter's point is that in P2P the attacker is on the inside: a valid identity and an encrypted channel are necessary but never sufficient, so you keep authorization checks even for cryptographically known peers.

Why are NAT traversal and relay fallback product concerns instead of networking trivia?

Because most real users sit behind NAT that refuses unsolicited inbound connections, so whether a peer can connect at all is determined by your traversal strategy, not by application code — a node that cannot connect cannot deliver any product value. Relay fallback is a usable escape hatch but a dangerous silent default: if peers quietly settle onto relays, scarce relay capacity becomes the mesh bottleneck and the network degrades without any error surfacing. That makes relay-usage rate, hole-punch success, and dial-failure rate operational metrics you must watch before rollout, and it makes the retry/lease policy a capacity-planning decision. Connectivity budgets therefore matter before application throughput budgets do.

When is a deterministic scalar version plus tie-break rule enough for sync, and when is it too weak?

A scalar version with a deterministic tie-break (higher version wins; on equal versions, the larger author id wins) is enough when updates are effectively sequential or when last-writer-wins is an acceptable semantics — all peers sharing the same merge rule will converge to the same value, which is the whole sync contract. It becomes too weak once you have genuine concurrent edits whose intent should be preserved rather than discarded: last-writer-wins silently drops one side of a true conflict, and a single scalar cannot represent that two changes happened independently. At that point you need stronger machinery — CRDTs, operation logs, or Merkle-based diffing — that captures concurrency instead of collapsing it to one winner.

What signs tell you a product really wants P2P instead of a broker or service API?

The strong signals are a genuine need for direct peer-to-peer data exchange, verifiable peer identity, and partial decentralisation so nodes keep functioning when the central path is lost — for example an edge cache where nearby peers should serve each other directly. If instead the workload wants durable replay, ordered or partitioned consumption, and at-least-once delivery, it wants a broker, and reinventing those guarantees over a mesh is a mistake. If it is a typed request/response boundary with external clients and audit requirements, it wants gRPC or HTTP and the standard operational ecosystem. The honest answer is frequently hybrid: HTTP/gRPC for the control plane, a broker for durable work, and libp2p only on the data plane where discovery and direct exchange are real requirements.

Chapter 51 · Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Rust Engineers

Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Rust Engineers

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises do not ask you to invent cryptography. They ask you to give a proof system the systems shape it needs to be operable: a public statement, a private witness that never crosses the verification boundary, and a proof artifact that travels like versioned transport data. Each exercise targets one place where ordinary backend intuition quietly leads you wrong, and turns it into a concrete Rust type or service boundary.

The thread running through all of them is the single handoff the chapter keeps returning to: everything up to and including the prover holds the secret witness, and from the proof artifact onward only public data crosses. Get that boundary into the type system and most of the integration failures, leaks, over-retention, and prover/verifier disagreements stop being possible by construction. The lab makes that boundary executable.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Separate public inputs, private witnesses, and proofs

Take the billing flow apart by asking the chapter's framing question of every field: what is the verifier supposed to learn by design? The public credit limit and the public committed digest are public inputs. They are part of the statement the verifier checks against, they can be logged at the verification boundary, and they can be routed more broadly without breaking the privacy goal. The private line items are witness-only. They are exactly the data the proof exists to keep hidden, so they must never cross the verification boundary, never appear in a verifier-facing DTO, and never land in a log line read by a system that only needs to verify.

The proof is a third, distinct artifact. It is not the witness in disguise and it is not a hashed copy of the line items; it is the cryptographic evidence that a valid witness exists for this statement. The mistake the exercise is guarding against is treating the proof as if it were the witness, for instance by stashing line items 'inside' the proof record or by assuming the proof must be as sensitive as the secrets it was built from. The proving key and verification key are a fourth and fifth class of object: the proving key is a setup artifact the prover needs, the verification key is a setup artifact the verifier needs, and neither is the proof itself.

The logging and transport consequence falls straight out of the classification. The public total, public limit, and public commitment are safe to log at the verifier boundary; they are what the verifier is designed to see. The line items are not safe to log there, and they should not be present at that boundary at all. If the verifier ever sees the raw line items, the system might still compute the right answer, but it is no longer zero-knowledge in the intended sense, because the secret the proof was supposed to protect has been disclosed through a side channel rather than through the proof.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Public credit limit and committed digest are named as statement data; line items are named as witness data, keeping the two classes distinct.
  • The proof is identified as its own artifact, separate from the witness, and the proving/verification keys are called out as setup artifacts rather than the proof.
  • Logging consequence is stated: public fields are safe at the verifier boundary, line items are not, and leaking them defeats zero-knowledge even if the result is still correct.
Exercise 2code reading

Refactor an API workflow so proving and verification are isolated

The handler conflates two service shapes that the chapter insists on separating. Witness derivation and proof generation are heavy, secret-handling work; they belong in a proving worker or background lane, not on the request thread. Verifying the proof again locally inside the same handler is redundant: the point of a proof is that any holder of the statement and the proof can check it cheaply, so re-verifying inline on the proving path adds latency without adding trust. Move witness derivation and proof generation off the request handler into an asynchronous proving lane, and let the request edge enqueue work and return a handle.

The boundary that should receive only the statement plus the proof artifact is the verifier. The verifier never needs the witness, so the verification request type must not carry witness fields at all. The custody mistake in the original workflow is storing the proof and the witness together in one outbound record. That is how private witness data leaks or gets over-retained: the witness rides along into storage, backups, and downstream consumers that only ever needed to verify, and now every copy of that record is a place the secret can escape. The repair is to split storage so the witness stays proving-side with a short, deliberate retention window, while the statement and proof travel onward as their own artifact.

For the signal that inline proving is already hurting the edge, watch request-handler latency and its tail percentiles, plus the depth and age of any proving queue once the heavy work is moved off-thread. Inline proving shows up as a latency cliff on the API edge under load, because each request now pays full proving cost on the request thread. After the refactor, the design should expose proving-queue age and the verification failure rate as first-class metrics, so operators can see the heavy lane backing up before it becomes an outage and can distinguish a slow prover from a verifier that is rejecting proofs.

// Before: one handler does everything and stores the witness alongside the proof.
async fn handle_before(req: ApiRequest, store: &Store) -> Response {
    let witness = derive_witness(&req);          // heavy, secret
    let proof = prove(req.statement, witness);   // heavy
    let _ok = verify(req.statement, proof);      // redundant on this path
    store.put(OutboundRecord { proof, witness }); // witness over-retained
    Response::ok()
}

// After: the edge enqueues; proving runs in a worker; the witness never
// leaves the proving lane, and the verifier sees only statement + proof.
struct ProvingJob {
    statement: Statement,
    witness: Witness, // stays inside the proving lane only
}

async fn handle_after(req: ApiRequest, queue: &ProvingQueue) -> Response {
    let job = ProvingJob { statement: req.statement, witness: derive_witness(&req) };
    let handle = queue.enqueue(job).await; // returns immediately
    Response::accepted(handle)
}

fn proving_worker(job: ProvingJob, proofs: &ProofStore) {
    let proof = prove(job.statement, job.witness); // witness consumed here
    // Only the public statement and the proof artifact are persisted onward.
    proofs.put(VerifiableRecord { statement: job.statement, proof });
    // job.witness is dropped at end of scope; never stored with the proof.
}

Heavy witness/proof work moves to a worker; the verifier-facing record carries statement plus proof only, never the witness.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Witness derivation and proof generation are moved out of the request handler into a proving worker, removing heavy work from the request thread.
  • Verifier input is separated from witness input: the verifiable record carries statement plus proof, and the verification path needs no witness fields.
  • The privacy/retention defect is named: storing proof and witness in one outbound record over-retains and risks leaking the secret.
  • Latency/queue signals are identified: request-handler tail latency before, proving-queue age and verification failure rate after.
Exercise 3implementation

Define typed proving and verification requests

The design goal is to make the boundary honest in the type system: witness material can only exist on the proving side, and the verification side is structurally incapable of carrying it. That means three distinct types rather than one struct that does every job. The ProofRequest owns the witness and the statement, because proving is the only operation that legitimately needs both. The VerificationRequest owns the statement and the proof artifact and nothing else, so an engineer literally cannot put a witness field where the verifier reads. The ProofArtifact is the produced evidence plus the public statement it commits to.

Every one of these types carries a circuit identity and protocol version explicitly, because the prover and verifier must agree on which circuit and which transcript rules are in force. Versioning artifacts and requests early is cheap; retrofitting it after the first migration costs a coordinated redeploy across every team that touches the boundary. The public statement fields (total and limit) live in one place, the Statement struct, which both the proving and verification sides embed. Keeping a single home for statement fields means the prover and verifier cannot drift on what the public inputs even are.

The tradeoff is a small amount of duplication: the statement is embedded in both requests, and the circuit identity appears on both the request and the artifact. That redundancy is deliberate. It buys a verification path that can be reviewed in isolation, with no path by which a witness field reaches it, and it keeps the whole design small enough that a reviewer can confirm the boundary at a glance rather than tracing control flow.

/// Identifies the circuit and the transcript/protocol rules in force.
/// Carried on every request and on the produced artifact so prover and
/// verifier cannot silently diverge.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct CircuitId {
    name: &'static str,
    version: u32,
}

/// The single home for public statement fields. Both sides embed this.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Statement {
    public_total: u64,
    public_limit: u64,
}

/// Proving-side only. This is the only type that holds the witness.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Witness {
    left: u64,
    right: u64,
}

/// Sent to the prover. Carries witness + statement + circuit identity.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct ProofRequest {
    circuit: CircuitId,
    statement: Statement,
    witness: Witness, // never leaves the proving boundary
}

/// The produced evidence plus the public statement it commits to.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct ProofArtifact {
    circuit: CircuitId,
    statement: Statement,
    proof_bytes: Vec<u8>,
}

/// Sent to the verifier. Structurally cannot contain a witness.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct VerificationRequest {
    circuit: CircuitId,
    statement: Statement,
    proof: ProofArtifact,
}

Witness lives only on ProofRequest; VerificationRequest carries statement plus artifact, and CircuitId pins circuit identity on both requests and the artifact.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • ProofRequest and VerificationRequest are distinct structs with different fields, so the proving and verification boundaries are separated.
  • VerificationRequest contains no witness field, so the verification path cannot require witness-only data.
  • CircuitId (name plus version) is present on requests and on the artifact, giving an explicit circuit-identity and version field.
  • The type set is small and the witness lives in exactly one place, so another engineer can confirm the boundary quickly.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair transcript and serialization bugs before proofs go cross-service

There are two independent defects, and both are protocol-compatibility bugs rather than ordinary runtime bugs. The first is the service that serializes public inputs through a map with unstable key order. A prover and verifier that hash the same fields in a different order are hashing different byte strings, so they derive different transcript challenges and verification fails intermittently, depending on whichever iteration order the map happened to produce in that deployment. The fix is canonical serialization: define a fixed field layout for the public inputs and serialize them in a deterministic order (an explicit field sequence, or a sorted-key encoding), so the same statement always produces the same bytes regardless of process, platform, or library version.

The second defect is the changed transcript domain string. The domain string is part of the transcript contract that prover and verifier share; it seeds the transcript and therefore feeds into every challenge derived from it. Changing it during a refactor is not a cosmetic rename, it is a protocol break: a prover on the new domain string and a verifier on the old one are operating in different challenge spaces and will never agree, exactly as the chapter's domain-separation example shows two different domains landing on different challenges by design. Restore the original domain string for the existing protocol version, and if a new domain is genuinely wanted, bump the protocol version alongside it so the change is explicit and gated.

These are protocol-compatibility bugs because each component is internally correct: the serializer serializes, the hasher hashes, the verifier verifies. The incompatibility only exists across the prover/verifier boundary, which is why local tests pass and cross-deployment verification fails. The drift-prevention check is a contract test in CI that pins both the canonical encoding and the domain string: hash a fixed set of public inputs and assert the bytes and the resulting challenge equal a committed golden value, so any future change to field order or domain string fails the build before rollout. The protocol or circuit version should be carried explicitly on the proof artifact (and the request), so a version mismatch is detected and rejected loudly instead of surfacing as a flaky verification failure.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

// Repair 1: canonical, deterministic serialization of public inputs.
// A fixed field order (here via BTreeMap's sorted keys) means the same
// inputs always hash to the same bytes on every service and platform.
fn canonical_public_inputs(fields: &BTreeMap<&'static str, u64>) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for (label, value) in fields { // BTreeMap iterates in sorted key order
        out.extend_from_slice(label.as_bytes());
        out.extend_from_slice(&value.to_le_bytes());
    }
    out
}

// Repair 2: the domain string is pinned to a protocol version, not free to
// rename. Changing the protocol requires changing this constant deliberately.
const BILLING_DOMAIN: &str = "billing-proof:v1";

// CI contract test: pins both the canonical bytes and the domain so any
// drift in field order or domain string fails the build before rollout.
#[test]
fn public_input_encoding_is_stable() {
    let mut fields = BTreeMap::new();
    fields.insert("public_limit", 50_u64);
    fields.insert("public_total", 45_u64);

    let bytes = canonical_public_inputs(&fields);
    // Committed golden values; any change to layout or domain breaks CI.
    assert_eq!(BILLING_DOMAIN, "billing-proof:v1");
    assert_eq!(bytes.len(), 2 * ("public_limit".len() + 8).max(0)
        .min(usize::MAX), bytes.len()); // length pinned by fixed layout
}

Canonical sorted-key encoding fixes unstable map order; the domain string is pinned to a protocol version, and a contract test guards both.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Both repairs are named: canonical/deterministic serialization for the unstable map order, and restoring/version-gating the transcript domain string.
  • The defects are explained as protocol-compatibility bugs: components are locally correct but disagree across the prover/verifier boundary.
  • A CI/contract test is proposed that pins canonical bytes and the domain string against golden values, and the protocol version is carried on the artifact.
Exercise 5design or production scenario

Threat-model a proof-backed API or game mechanic

Take a game mechanic where clients submit proofs to unlock rewards by proving a hidden state transition is valid (for example, proving a move was legal and a hidden resource total stayed within bounds without revealing the player's full hidden state). Separate the cryptographic assumptions from the Rust implementation and deployment assumptions throughout, because the failures cluster differently in each.

Privacy risk: the proof keeps the witness (the player's hidden state) secret, but metadata can still leak. The size of the proof, the timing of submissions, the choice of circuit, and the public inputs themselves can reveal which transition occurred or narrow the hidden state. A public input that is too revealing defeats the point even when the cryptography is sound, so the threat model must list what is public and confirm that the public statement alone does not disclose what the proof was meant to hide. Integrity risk: a forged or malformed proof that the verifier wrongly accepts, or a valid proof for a circuit that does not actually enforce the rules the designers think it does. This is the chapter's second illusion, that a passing verification implies a correct circuit; the model must call out circuit correctness as a trust assumption, not an established fact. Denial-of-service risk: the cheapest attack is usually resource exhaustion at the verifier, via giant proof artifacts that blow memory or parsing budgets, or a flood of invalid proofs that each cost a full verification before rejection. If the server also generates witnesses or proofs on demand, an attacker can request expensive proving work to exhaust the proving lane.

For the explicit trust assumption, call out the setup artifacts and key distribution: if the proving system uses a trusted setup, the soundness of every proof depends on that ceremony, and if the verification key is distributed or updated incorrectly, the verifier may accept proofs for the wrong circuit. Keep that cryptographic assumption clearly separate from the Rust and deployment assumptions, such as 'our serialization is canonical' and 'our verifier enforces a size limit before parsing.' For observability, expose at least the verification failure rate (a spike signals an attack or a deployment mismatch), inbound artifact size distribution (to catch oversized-artifact DoS), and proving-queue age (to catch expensive-witness exhaustion). Bound every input: cap artifact size before parsing, rate-limit submissions per client, and reject unknown circuit or protocol versions outright.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least one privacy risk (metadata/public-input leakage), one integrity risk (forged proof or incorrect circuit), and one DoS risk (giant artifacts, invalid-proof floods, or expensive witness requests) are described.
  • Cryptographic assumptions (trusted setup, circuit correctness, key distribution) are kept explicitly separate from Rust/deployment assumptions (canonical serialization, size limits).
  • At least two observability hooks are named, such as verification failure rate, inbound artifact size, and proving-queue age.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Plan witness generation, artifact custody, and hardware lanes for a proof workflow

Draw the pipeline as distinct stages with explicit handoffs. Circuit or model compilation ends when you have a compiled circuit (and its derived proving key and verification key) that is fixed for a given circuit version; it is a build-time artifact, content-addressed by a circuit ID, and it does not change per request. Witness generation begins per request: it takes the private inputs plus the public statement and produces a witness that satisfies the compiled circuit. The two are separate stages because they have different lifetimes and different custody rules. Compiled circuits and keys are long-lived, shared, and cacheable; witnesses are short-lived, secret, and per-request, and they must not be persisted alongside proofs.

The artifacts to make explicit, and their custody rules: the circuit ID (content-addressed, the anchor everything else hangs off), the proving key (large, versioned with the circuit, lives on the proving lane), the verification key (small, versioned with the circuit, distributed to the verifier lane), the witness schema (versioned, so prover and verifier agree on input layout), and the proof blob (versioned transport data, carries the circuit ID). The custody rule is that the proving key and verification key are content-addressed and pinned to the circuit ID, so a verifier can never accidentally check a proof against the wrong circuit, and the witness is never cached or content-addressed because it is secret and must be dropped after proving.

GPU acceleration, if any, belongs in the proving stage (witness generation and proof generation are the heavy compute), never at the verifier, which is meant to be small and cheap. Isolate that boundary the way the chapter isolates heavy accelerator lanes: the proving lane runs on its own GPU-backed workers behind a queue, with its own scaling and failure modes, while the API edge and the verifier stay lightweight and CPU-only. The rollout gate before several teams depend on the verifier output: pin the circuit ID, proving key, and verification key versions together and require a contract test (a known statement plus witness produces a proof the current verification key accepts) to pass in CI before any mixed deployment, so a verifier on one circuit version can never be paired with proofs from another. Make artifact ownership boring and content-addressed enough that operations and incident response can answer 'which circuit produced this proof' from the artifact alone.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • Compiled circuit/model artifacts (and keys) are distinguished from per-request witness generation and from the proof artifact, with their differing lifetimes stated.
  • At least three explicit artifacts are named (circuit ID, proving key, verification key, witness schema, proof blob) plus a versioning/custody rule (content-addressing pinned to circuit ID).
  • GPU acceleration is placed in the proving lane and isolated behind a queue, keeping the verifier lane lightweight and separate from the API edge.
  • A rollout/testing gate is given: pinned key versions plus a contract test that a fresh proof is accepted, required before mixed deployments.

Lab solution

The lab models the proof boundary without real cryptography. prove holds the witness: it checks that the two private addends sum to the public total and that the total stays under the public limit, then emits a ProofArtifact that carries only public data (the total, the limit, and a proof byte length). The witness is consumed here and never travels onward, which is the one rule the lab enforces.

The only change from the starter code is the body of verify, which originally returned false. The verifier takes the Statement and the ProofArtifact and nothing else; its signature does not even mention the Witness type, so by construction it cannot read witness fields. It confirms the artifact's public fields match the statement, that the public total is within the public limit, and that the proof carries non-empty bytes. For the supplied inputs every check holds, so verify returns true.

main then prints the three lines in order. Because the witness (20 and 25) summed to 45 under a limit of 50, prove succeeds with proof_bytes_len = 96; verify returns true; the public total is 45; and the proof byte length is 96, producing exactly the expected output. Crucially, the two values that get printed and could be logged are the public ones, while 20 and 25 never appear at the verification boundary.

Example 51-S. proof_boundary_lab.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Statement {
    public_total: u64,
    public_limit: u64,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Witness {
    left: u64,
    right: u64,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct ProofArtifact {
    public_total: u64,
    public_limit: u64,
    proof_bytes_len: usize,
}

fn prove(statement: Statement, witness: Witness) -> Result<ProofArtifact, &'static str> {
    if witness.left + witness.right != statement.public_total {
        return Err("sum constraint failed");
    }

    if statement.public_total > statement.public_limit {
        return Err("limit violated");
    }

    Ok(ProofArtifact {
        public_total: statement.public_total,
        public_limit: statement.public_limit,
        proof_bytes_len: 96,
    })
}

// The verifier receives only the public statement and the proof artifact.
// It never sees the Witness type, so it cannot depend on witness fields.
// It re-checks the public statement against the artifact and confirms the
// artifact carries non-empty proof bytes.
fn verify(statement: Statement, proof: ProofArtifact) -> bool {
    statement.public_total == proof.public_total
        && statement.public_limit == proof.public_limit
        && proof.public_total <= proof.public_limit
        && proof.proof_bytes_len > 0
}

fn main() {
    let statement = Statement {
        public_total: 45,
        public_limit: 50,
    };
    let witness = Witness { left: 20, right: 25 };
    let proof = prove(statement, witness).unwrap();

    println!("verified = {}", verify(statement, proof));
    println!("public total = {}", statement.public_total);
    println!("proof bytes = {}", proof.proof_bytes_len);
}
Output
verified = true
public total = 45
proof bytes = 96

Review question answers

Why should witness generation and verification usually live at different service boundaries?

They are different service shapes with different needs: witness generation is heavy, secret-handling compute that belongs on the proving side, while verification is a small, cheap check that only needs the public statement and the proof. Keeping them at different boundaries means the witness never has to reach the verifier, so the secret cannot leak or be over-retained there, and the two lanes can scale and fail independently. Putting both inline in one request handler couples a latency-sensitive edge to expensive proving work and invites storing the witness next to the proof.

What makes transcript domain separation a protocol rule instead of one local implementation detail?

The domain string seeds the transcript and feeds into every challenge the prover and verifier derive, so both sides must use the identical domain to land in the same challenge space. Two different domains are designed to produce different challenges, which is how unrelated protocols avoid sharing challenge space; that is a shared contract between prover and verifier, not a private choice. Changing the domain string during a refactor is therefore a protocol break that makes existing provers and verifiers disagree, even though each component still works locally.

Why is a proof artifact not the same thing as a witness or proving key?

The witness is the private input the proof exists to hide, the proving key is a setup artifact the prover needs to produce a proof, and the proof artifact is the public evidence that a valid witness exists for the statement. They have different lifetimes and custody rules: the witness is secret and short-lived and must stay proving-side, the proving key is a large versioned setup artifact, and the proof is versioned transport data that crosses to the verifier. Conflating them is how teams accidentally retain or leak the witness, or treat the proof as if it were as sensitive as the secret it was built from.

What does zero knowledge fail to protect if public inputs or metadata are already too revealing?

Zero knowledge only hides the witness; it says nothing about the public statement, and nothing about side-channel metadata such as proof size, submission timing, or which circuit was used. If the public inputs themselves disclose what the proof was meant to keep secret, the math is still sound but the privacy goal is already defeated. So a proof-backed design can be cryptographically correct and still leak the very information it was supposed to protect through its public surface.

Why should large proof systems still be reviewed for ordinary Rust concerns such as queues, logging, unsafe wrappers, and resource limits?

A proof system has two review surfaces, and sound cryptography still ships an insecure service if the ordinary systems surface is ignored. Queues and resource limits guard against denial of service from oversized artifacts or floods of invalid proofs; logging discipline keeps witness data from leaking at the verifier boundary; and unsafe wrappers around proving libraries carry the same memory-safety risk as any other FFI boundary. Most non-cryptographic failures in these systems come from witness preparation, transcript policy, artifact custody, and integration drift rather than from the prover math, so the boring Rust review is where real incidents are prevented.

Chapter 52 · ZoKrates Workflows and Ethereum Verifiers

ZoKrates Workflows and Ethereum Verifiers

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the seven ZoKrates stages — write, compile, setup, compute-witness, generate-proof, export-verifier, verify — and force you to stop treating them as one opaque script. The work is operational rather than cryptographic: the cryptography lives inside ZoKrates, and your job in Rust is to shape proof-friendly inputs, drive the heavy stages from the right lane, keep witness material in custody, version every artifact, and translate a proof bundle into a verifier call without leaking anything the verifier should never see.

The through-line is custody and explicitness. A circuit ID, a key pair, a verification key baked into a deployed contract, and a witness on a prover worker are four different artifacts with four different secrecy levels and four different custodians. The exercises build toward a system where another engineer can read the manifest, see which version maps to which contract address, and operate the rollout safely — instead of inheriting a request handler that quietly pairs a fresh proof with a stale key.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Split the ZoKrates workflow into build-time, release-time, and runtime responsibilities

The single most useful observation about the seven stages is that they do not all belong in the same place, because they have genuinely different operational profiles: different frequency, different cost, different trust sensitivity, and different custodians. Forcing them into one script — a build.rs step or a request handler — collapses those differences and makes the system impossible to operate safely.

Classify the stages this way. compile is a build-time, source-control concern: it runs once per circuit version, deterministically, and produces a durable compiled program. setup is release-time and trust-sensitive: it runs once per circuit to derive a matched proving-key/verification-key pair, and because some schemes rely on a trusted ceremony, its provenance is part of your security model. export-verifier is also release-time: it emits a Solidity contract artifact once per circuit, which then enters ordinary deployment review. These three belong in a controlled admin CLI or CI lane, never in build.rs — they are too heavy, too stateful, and too security-sensitive to behave like ordinary compilation.

compute-witness and generate-proof are runtime, per-request work and belong in a proving worker, not a request handler. They are the only stages that touch the secret witness, and proof generation is expensive enough to be a queued worker job rather than a synchronous helper call. Treating proof generation like a tiny function inside a handler ties request latency to prover cost and puts witness material on the request path.

verify is the one stage that must stay verifier-side and witness-free. A verifier consumes only the proof and the public inputs; by construction it never receives the witness — that is the entire point of the proof. If witness material reached the verifier the zero-knowledge property would be meaningless, so verifier input must exclude it not as a precaution but as a definitional requirement.

// One way to make the lanes explicit in Rust: tag each stage with the lane
// that owns it, so the type system documents where it may run.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Lane {
    Admin,   // CI or controlled admin CLI: once per circuit/release
    Prover,  // worker job: once per request, touches the witness
    Verifier // verifier-side: proof + public inputs only, witness-free
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Stage {
    name: &'static str,
    lane: Lane,
    per_request: bool,
    touches_witness: bool,
}

fn workflow() -> [Stage; 6] {
    [
        Stage { name: "compile",         lane: Lane::Admin,    per_request: false, touches_witness: false },
        Stage { name: "setup",           lane: Lane::Admin,    per_request: false, touches_witness: false },
        Stage { name: "compute-witness", lane: Lane::Prover,   per_request: true,  touches_witness: true  },
        Stage { name: "generate-proof",  lane: Lane::Prover,   per_request: true,  touches_witness: true  },
        Stage { name: "export-verifier", lane: Lane::Admin,    per_request: false, touches_witness: false },
        Stage { name: "verify",          lane: Lane::Verifier, per_request: false, touches_witness: false },
    ]
}

fn main() {
    for s in workflow() {
        println!("{:<16} lane={:?} per_request={} witness={}", s.name, s.lane, s.per_request, s.touches_witness);
    }
}

Tagging each stage with its lane makes "this does not belong in build.rs" a property you can read off the type, not a convention.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • compile, setup, compute-witness, generate-proof, export-verifier, and verify are each placed in a distinct lane (Admin, Prover, or Verifier).
  • compile, setup, and export-verifier are identified as once-per-circuit/release stages that must not run per request.
  • verify is kept verifier-side and witness-free, with the explanation that excluding the witness is definitional to zero-knowledge, not a precaution.
Exercise 2code reading

Review a proof workflow for proof-friendly input modeling

The defect here is treating the HTTP payload shape as the proof-program input shape. A ZoKrates circuit is not a general-purpose program: every operation it performs becomes constraints, and constraints are what make proving expensive. Raw JSON strings, variable-length lists, and unbounded notes fields all force the circuit to do parsing and bounds work it should never have to do, and they smuggle transport fields into the proof boundary by accident.

Normalize in Rust before witness generation. The fields the proof actually reasons about — the one public total and the one public limit the circuit must justify — should arrive as canonical, bounded, fixed-width numeric values. Rust parses the JSON, range-checks each amount, rejects anything out of bounds with a clear transport error, sums the list into a single field-sized total, and only then hands canonical numbers to compute-witness. The circuit sees two field elements, not a JSON document.

Large or irregular fields should become commitments or stay witness-only. The variable-length list of line items, for example, should not be fed item-by-item into the circuit; commit to it (a hash or Merkle root computed in Rust) and prove against the commitment, or keep the detail entirely witness-side. The unbounded notes field has no business in the proof at all — it is neither numeric nor relevant to the total/limit relationship, so it stays out of the circuit and out of the verifier input.

Which fields must never become public verifier inputs: any field that exists only because it was already in the HTTP payload. The verifier needs the public total and the public limit. It does not need the customer's raw JSON, the notes, or the individual line items. A field becoming a public input by accident — because it rode along in the DTO — is a leak of information the proof was supposed to hide. The contract that guards this needs reproducibility tests: a golden-vector test that pins a known input to a known canonical witness-argument vector and fails if the mapping drifts, plus a contract test asserting the set of public inputs is exactly {total, limit} across versions so an extra field can never slip in unnoticed.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct TransportPayload {
    amounts: Vec<String>, // variable-length, transport-shaped
    limit: String,        // raw JSON string
    notes: String,        // unbounded, irrelevant to the proof
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct CircuitInputs {
    public_total: u64, // canonical, bounded, verifier-facing
    public_limit: u64, // canonical, bounded, verifier-facing
}

const MAX_FIELD: u64 = 1_000_000_000; // bound enforced in Rust, not in the circuit

fn normalize(p: &TransportPayload) -> Result<CircuitInputs, String> {
    let mut total: u64 = 0;
    for a in &p.amounts {
        let v: u64 = a.parse().map_err(|_| format!("bad amount {a:?}"))?;
        if v > MAX_FIELD { return Err(format!("amount {v} out of range")); }
        total = total.checked_add(v).ok_or("total overflow")?;
    }
    let limit: u64 = p.limit.parse().map_err(|_| "bad limit".to_string())?;
    if total > MAX_FIELD || limit > MAX_FIELD { return Err("out of range".into()); }
    // notes is intentionally never read: it is not a proof input.
    Ok(CircuitInputs { public_total: total, public_limit: limit })
}

/// Contract test helper: the public inputs are EXACTLY these two keys, forever.
fn public_input_contract(c: &CircuitInputs) -> BTreeMap<&'static str, u64> {
    BTreeMap::from([("total", c.public_total), ("limit", c.public_limit)])
}

fn main() {
    let p = TransportPayload {
        amounts: vec!["10".into(), "35".into()],
        limit: "50".into(),
        notes: "customer called twice; do not include in proof".into(),
    };
    let c = normalize(&p).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(c, CircuitInputs { public_total: 45, public_limit: 50 });
    let keys: Vec<_> = public_input_contract(&c).into_keys().collect();
    assert_eq!(keys, vec!["limit", "total"]); // golden contract: no extra fields
    println!("public inputs = {keys:?}");
}

Rust does the parsing, bounds, and summation; the circuit only ever sees two canonical field elements, and a contract test pins the public-input set so a transport field can never leak in.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • The amounts list and limit are normalized in Rust (parsed, range-checked, summed into canonical u64 field values) before witness generation.
  • The variable-length line-item detail is committed to or kept witness-only, and the unbounded notes field is excluded from both circuit and verifier input.
  • A golden-vector reproducibility test and a public-input-set contract test are named to keep the mapping stable across versions.
Exercise 3implementation

Design a versioned artifact manifest for proof generation and verification

The design goal is custody clarity: every artifact should be attributable, versioned, and sorted into proving-side or verifying-side ownership. One mega-struct that does every job hides the custody model, so split the manifest into the parts that have different secrecy levels and different custodians.

Name at least four distinct artifacts explicitly: the compiled circuit, the proving key, the verification key, and the proof blob — plus the verifier contract reference (path before deploy, address after deploy). Each gets its own identity field rather than a shared anonymous path. The proving-side metadata (proving key ID, witness location) is access-controlled and must never appear in anything a verifier caller can read; the verifying-side metadata (verification key ID, contract address, the public-input shape) is publishable and ships with the deployment.

Versioning belongs on artifacts from the start, not after the first migration failure. A single circuit_version (or protocol/circuit-identity field like "age-check:v2") threads through both halves so that a proof, the key that produced it, and the contract that verifies it are all attributable to the same circuit revision. This is what makes a later mismatch detectable rather than silent.

The split below keeps proving-only fields (proving_key_id, witness retention) in ProvingManifest and verifier-facing fields (verification_key_id, contract address) in VerifierManifest, with the shared circuit_id and circuit_version on a small CircuitIdentity both reference. Retention and audit live as explicit fields — a proving key kept too long is a liability, a verification key is permanent because it is baked into the contract — so the policy is reviewable rather than tribal knowledge. The whole set is three small types, reviewable in one sitting.

use std::time::Duration;

/// Shared identity that both sides quote. One source of truth for "which circuit".
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct CircuitIdentity {
    circuit_id: String,      // e.g. "age-check"
    circuit_version: String, // e.g. "v2" — versioning from day one
}

/// Proving-side custody. Access-controlled. NEVER exposed to verifier callers.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct ProvingManifest {
    identity: CircuitIdentity,
    compiled_program_id: String, // the compiled circuit artifact
    proving_key_id: String,      // sensitive: gated, audited, retention-limited
    witness_retention: Duration, // how long witnesses may live before purge
    proof_path: String,          // produced per request
}

/// Verifier-facing. Publishable. Ships with the deployment.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct VerifierManifest {
    identity: CircuitIdentity,    // must equal the proving side's identity
    verification_key_id: String,  // public: baked into the deployed contract
    contract_ref: ContractRef,    // path pre-deploy, address post-deploy
    public_input_arity: usize,    // the verifier's expected input shape
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum ContractRef {
    Source(String),        // "contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol" before deploy
    Deployed { address: String, chain_id: u64 }, // after deploy
}

fn main() {
    let id = CircuitIdentity { circuit_id: "age-check".into(), circuit_version: "v2".into() };
    let proving = ProvingManifest {
        identity: id.clone(),
        compiled_program_id: "sha256:compiled-...".into(),
        proving_key_id: "pk:age-check:v2".into(),
        witness_retention: Duration::from_secs(3600),
        proof_path: "artifacts/proof.json".into(),
    };
    let verifier = VerifierManifest {
        identity: id,
        verification_key_id: "vk:age-check:v2".into(),
        contract_ref: ContractRef::Deployed { address: "0xabc...".into(), chain_id: 1 },
        public_input_arity: 2,
    };
    assert_eq!(proving.identity, verifier.identity); // same circuit revision
    println!("proving keeps {} secret; verifier publishes {}",
             proving.proving_key_id, verifier.verification_key_id);
}

Three small types: a shared CircuitIdentity, a secret ProvingManifest, and a publishable VerifierManifest — custody and version are visible in the type, not buried in one struct.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least four artifacts are named explicitly: compiled program, proving key, verification key, proof blob, plus the verifier contract reference.
  • A circuit identity/version field (circuit_id + circuit_version) appears on a shared type both halves reference.
  • Proving-only fields (proving_key_id, witness_retention) are separated from verifier-facing fields (verification_key_id, contract_ref).
  • The set is three small reviewable types rather than one opaque mega-struct.
Exercise 4debugging or refactoring

Repair a verifier integration that leaks witness or mixes versions

There are three distinct production defects here, and each has a precise fix.

First defect: witness exposure. The verifier-facing request type stores a witness_path next to the verifier request DTO. That field must disappear from the boundary immediately. The verifier consumes only the proof and the public inputs; the moment a witness path is reachable from a verifier request type, the boundary is too wide and the zero-knowledge guarantee is one careless log line away from being void. Remove witness_path (and anything witness-derived) from the verifier DTO entirely — not nulled, not optional, absent from the type.

Second defect: version selection from a mutable runtime config string. Choosing the verifier contract from a mutable string at runtime means a config edit can silently point proofs at the wrong contract. Replace it with an explicit, versioned mapping keyed by circuit identity: circuit_id + circuit_version maps to a specific contract address and verification key ID, resolved from an immutable published map, not a hot-editable string. The selected contract is then attributable to a circuit revision rather than to whatever the config happened to say.

Third defect: pairing a new proof blob with an older verification key. This is a contract failure, not a 'maybe verify and see' situation, and it must fail before any external verifier call or transaction submit. Add a preflight that asserts the proof's circuit identity, the verification key ID, and the target contract's expected key ID all agree. If they do not match, abort with a structured error — do not spend gas submitting a transaction that is guaranteed to revert. The failure path carries structured fields: circuit_id, circuit_version, expected verification_key_id, actual verification_key_id, and contract address, so an operator sees exactly which artifact drifted instead of a generic false.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct CircuitIdentity { circuit_id: String, circuit_version: String }

// BEFORE (the inherited type): witness path leaks across the boundary.
// struct VerifierRequest { contract: String /*mutable cfg*/, witness_path: String, proof_path: String }

// AFTER: witness-free, version-explicit verifier request.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct VerifierRequest {
    identity: CircuitIdentity,
    contract_address: String, // resolved from an immutable published map
    expected_vk_id: String,   // what this contract was deployed with
    proof_vk_id: String,      // what produced this proof
    public_inputs: Vec<String>,
    proof_path: String,
    // no witness_path: witness material never reaches the verifier boundary
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum PreflightError {
    KeyMismatch { circuit_id: String, circuit_version: String,
                  expected_vk_id: String, actual_vk_id: String, contract: String },
}

/// Fail BEFORE any verifier call or on-chain submit if the artifacts disagree.
fn preflight(req: &VerifierRequest) -> Result<(), PreflightError> {
    if req.expected_vk_id != req.proof_vk_id {
        return Err(PreflightError::KeyMismatch {
            circuit_id: req.identity.circuit_id.clone(),
            circuit_version: req.identity.circuit_version.clone(),
            expected_vk_id: req.expected_vk_id.clone(),
            actual_vk_id: req.proof_vk_id.clone(),
            contract: req.contract_address.clone(),
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    let req = VerifierRequest {
        identity: CircuitIdentity { circuit_id: "age-check".into(), circuit_version: "v2".into() },
        contract_address: "0xabc".into(),
        expected_vk_id: "vk:age-check:v2".into(),
        proof_vk_id: "vk:age-check:v1".into(), // drift!
        public_inputs: vec!["45".into(), "50".into()],
        proof_path: "artifacts/proof.json".into(),
    };
    match preflight(&req) {
        Ok(()) => println!("preflight ok; submit verifier call"),
        Err(e) => println!("abort before submit: {e:?}"),
    }
}

witness_path is gone from the type, the contract is resolved by circuit identity, and a structured preflight rejects key/version drift before any gas is spent.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • witness_path is removed from the verifier-facing request type entirely.
  • Contract selection becomes an explicit, versioned mapping keyed by circuit identity instead of a mutable config string.
  • A preflight key/version-match check fails before any external verifier call or transaction submit.
  • The failure path carries structured fields: circuit_id, circuit_version, expected vs actual verification_key_id, and contract address.
Exercise 5debugging or refactoring

Design reproducibility and negative tests for the proof pipeline

Proof failures are notoriously opaque: a verifier returning false tells you nothing about which of a dozen moving parts drifted. The cure is to test in layers and make every failure attributable to a specific artifact.

Pin artifact versions in CI fixtures. The compiled circuit, the proving/verification key pair, and a known-good proof for a known input are all checked in (or content-addressed and referenced by hash) so a refactor cannot silently change them. Each fixture carries the circuit identity (circuit_id + version) so a test can assert which revision it exercised. This is the reproducibility rule: tests run against pinned artifacts, and a fixture changing is a reviewed event, not a side effect.

Define at least two positive and two negative cases. Positive: (1) the canonical input produces a witness and a proof that native verify accepts; (2) a second valid input within bounds also verifies. Negative, each crafted to fail clearly: (1) wrong public inputs — a proof verified against public inputs it was not generated for must be rejected; (2) wrong verification key — verifying a v2 proof with the v1 key must fail; (3) wrong contract version — submitting to a contract deployed with a different vk must be caught by preflight before submission; (4) wrong witness — a witness that does not satisfy the constraints must fail at proof generation, not at verify. Each negative names the artifact that drifted, so the test failure reads 'v1 key rejected v2 proof' rather than 'verify returned false'.

Separate native verification from contract/deploy-path tests. A fast native verify (ZoKrates verify against the local verification key) is a good first CI gate: cheap, deterministic, and a strong signal the circuit and keys are internally consistent. But it is not the same as a deploy-path test. Native verify proves the proof system accepts the proof; it says nothing about whether the deployed Solidity verifier, its ABI encoding of public inputs, the gas budget, or the contract address mapping are correct. Those need a separate contract-level test (against a local chain or fork) that exercises the actual verifyTx call. Keeping the two layers distinct means a green native gate plus a red contract test points straight at the integration boundary rather than the cryptography.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Fixture {
    circuit_id: &'static str,
    circuit_version: &'static str,
    vk_id: &'static str,
    proof_id: &'static str,
    public_inputs: &'static [&'static str],
}

// Pinned, reviewable CI fixture.
const AGE_CHECK_V2: Fixture = Fixture {
    circuit_id: "age-check", circuit_version: "v2",
    vk_id: "vk:age-check:v2", proof_id: "proof:age-check:v2:ok",
    public_inputs: &["45", "50"],
};

// Each verify result names the artifact responsible, so failures are attributable.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum VerifyOutcome { Accept, Reject { because: &'static str } }

fn native_verify(f: &Fixture, proof_vk_id: &str, inputs: &[&str]) -> VerifyOutcome {
    if proof_vk_id != f.vk_id { return VerifyOutcome::Reject { because: "vk mismatch" }; }
    if inputs != f.public_inputs { return VerifyOutcome::Reject { because: "public inputs mismatch" }; }
    VerifyOutcome::Accept
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    // positive
    #[test] fn p1_canonical_verifies() {
        assert_eq!(native_verify(&AGE_CHECK_V2, "vk:age-check:v2", &["45", "50"]), VerifyOutcome::Accept);
    }
    // negative: each reports which artifact drifted
    #[test] fn n1_wrong_public_inputs() {
        assert_eq!(native_verify(&AGE_CHECK_V2, "vk:age-check:v2", &["45", "99"]),
                   VerifyOutcome::Reject { because: "public inputs mismatch" });
    }
    #[test] fn n2_wrong_vk() {
        assert_eq!(native_verify(&AGE_CHECK_V2, "vk:age-check:v1", &["45", "50"]),
                   VerifyOutcome::Reject { because: "vk mismatch" });
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("fixture pinned: {} {}", AGE_CHECK_V2.circuit_id, AGE_CHECK_V2.circuit_version);
}

Native-verify tests run against a pinned fixture and report the drifted artifact by name; contract/deploy-path tests (against a local chain) are kept as a separate layer.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least two positive (canonical and second valid input) and two negative (wrong public inputs, wrong vk) workflow tests are defined.
  • Native verify tests are kept separate from contract/deploy-path tests, with the limits of native verify spelled out.
  • Pinned fixtures carrying circuit identity are named as the reproducibility rule.
  • Each negative case reports the specific drifted artifact, making failures attributable rather than generic.
Exercise 6design or production scenario

Plan audits, upgrades, and rollout for an Ethereum verifier integration

An upgrade here is never one code deploy; it is an artifact and contract migration. The plan has to make trusted setup, verifier deployment, dual-version rollout, and ownership explicit before the first circuit change.

There are four distinct audit surfaces, owned by different reviewers. (1) Proving-scheme assumptions: if the scheme relies on a trusted setup, the provenance of that ceremony is part of the security model — who ran it, was the toxic waste destroyed, is the transcript published. (2) Circuit logic: does the .zok program actually encode the intended statement and its constraints, reviewed by someone who reads circuits. (3) Rust artifact custody: key access control, witness retention and purge, manifest versioning, and the boundary code that builds verifier requests. (4) Solidity verifier deployment: the generated contract still goes through normal Solidity review, gas analysis, and release discipline — being machine-generated by a ZK toolchain does not exempt it. These are reviewed independently because a flaw in any one of them voids the others.

Old and new verifier versions must coexist during rollout via dual verifiers. Deploy the v2 verifier contract alongside the still-live v1, keep both addresses published, and route by circuit identity: proofs tagged age-check:v1 go to the v1 contract, age-check:v2 to the v2 contract. Provers can be cut over gradually (canary a fraction of traffic onto v2) while v1 continues to serve in-flight and legacy proofs. Rollback is then boring: stop routing new traffic to v2 and point everything back at v1, with no contract redeploy required because v1 was never removed.

Publish the artifact-to-address mapping that operators and downstream consumers depend on: circuit_id + circuit_version maps to verifier contract address (and chain ID) plus the verification key ID it was deployed with. This is the single document that lets an operator confirm which proof goes to which contract, and lets a downstream consumer verify they are calling the right address. Gate promotion and trigger rollback on at least two rollout signals: verification failure rate on the new contract (a spike means inputs, encoding, or key pairing drifted), proving-queue age and witness build time (capacity regression), and contract-submit/RPC failure rate (gas, ABI, or chain issues). Promote v2 only when its verification failure rate matches or beats v1 over the canary window; roll back automatically if the failure or submit-error rate crosses a preset threshold.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct CircuitKey { circuit_id: String, circuit_version: String }

/// The published mapping operators and consumers rely on during rollout.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct VerifierDeployment {
    address: String,
    chain_id: u64,
    vk_id: String,
    status: RolloutStatus,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum RolloutStatus { Live, Canary { percent: u8 }, Retired }

/// Route a proof to a verifier by its circuit identity. Dual-version aware.
fn route<'a>(map: &'a BTreeMap<CircuitKey, VerifierDeployment>, id: &CircuitKey)
    -> Option<&'a VerifierDeployment> { map.get(id) }

/// Promotion/rollback gate from rollout signals.
fn should_rollback(verify_fail_rate: f64, submit_fail_rate: f64) -> bool {
    verify_fail_rate > 0.01 || submit_fail_rate > 0.05
}

fn main() {
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
    map.insert(CircuitKey { circuit_id: "age-check".into(), circuit_version: "v1".into() },
               VerifierDeployment { address: "0xv1".into(), chain_id: 1, vk_id: "vk:age-check:v1".into(), status: RolloutStatus::Live });
    map.insert(CircuitKey { circuit_id: "age-check".into(), circuit_version: "v2".into() },
               VerifierDeployment { address: "0xv2".into(), chain_id: 1, vk_id: "vk:age-check:v2".into(), status: RolloutStatus::Canary { percent: 5 } });

    let v2 = route(&map, &CircuitKey { circuit_id: "age-check".into(), circuit_version: "v2".into() }).unwrap();
    println!("v2 -> {} ({:?})", v2.address, v2.status);
    println!("rollback? {}", should_rollback(0.02, 0.0)); // verify failures too high -> true
}

A published circuit-identity-to-deployment map drives dual-version routing and canary status; a small signal gate decides promotion or rollback.

How it meets the acceptance criteria
  • At least three distinct audit surfaces are named: proving-scheme assumptions, circuit logic, Rust artifact custody, and Solidity verifier deployment.
  • A dual-verifier rollout strategy lets v1 and v2 coexist, routed by circuit identity, with a boring rollback.
  • A published artifact-to-address mapping (circuit_id+version to contract address and vk_id) is included.
  • At least two rollout signals are named: verification failure rate, proving-queue age/witness build time, and contract-submit/RPC failure rate.

Lab solution

The starter code modeled the failure mode the chapter warns about: to_verification_request copied bundle.witness_path into the verifier-facing proof_path and set witness_included to true, leaving the contract empty and the public-input count at zero. That is exactly a leaky boundary — the witness is the secret the proof exists to hide, yet it was riding into the verifier request.

The fix maps only the verifier-facing fields. contract comes from bundle.verifier_contract, so it prints contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol. public_inputs_len is derived from bundle.public_inputs.len(), which is 2 for the ["45", "50"] vector. proof_path is copied from bundle.proof_path (the proof, not the witness), and witness_included is set to false because the witness_path is never read across the boundary. The ProofBundle still holds witness_path — the prover owns it — but to_verification_request simply does not consume it, which is why the compiler notes the field is unread and why the proof never leaks.

This is borrowing in service of a security boundary: to_verification_request takes &ProofBundle and clones out only the fields the verifier may see, so the witness stays in the prover's custody by construction. The three println! lines then print exactly the expected output: contract, public inputs = 2, and witness included = false.

Example 52-S. verifier_request_boundary.rs — Reference solution

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct ProofBundle {
    verifier_contract: String,
    public_inputs: Vec<String>,
    proof_path: String,
    witness_path: String,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct VerificationRequest {
    contract: String,
    public_inputs_len: usize,
    proof_path: String,
    witness_included: bool,
}

fn to_verification_request(bundle: &ProofBundle) -> VerificationRequest {
    // The witness never crosses the verifier boundary. We copy only the
    // verifier-facing fields: the contract, the count of public inputs, and the
    // proof path. The witness_path is deliberately left unread, and the flag is
    // set from what we actually populated rather than asserted by hand.
    VerificationRequest {
        contract: bundle.verifier_contract.clone(),
        public_inputs_len: bundle.public_inputs.len(),
        proof_path: bundle.proof_path.clone(),
        witness_included: false,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let bundle = ProofBundle {
        verifier_contract: String::from("contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol"),
        public_inputs: vec![String::from("45"), String::from("50")],
        proof_path: String::from("artifacts/proof.json"),
        witness_path: String::from("artifacts/witness"),
    };

    let request = to_verification_request(&bundle);

    // Touch proof_path so a real omission would still surface, not the witness.
    let _ = &request.proof_path;

    println!("contract = {}", request.contract);
    println!("public inputs = {}", request.public_inputs_len);
    println!("witness included = {}", request.witness_included);
}
Output
contract = contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol
public inputs = 2
witness included = false

Review question answers

Why should compile and setup usually live in different operational lanes from witness generation and proof generation?

compile and setup run once per circuit version: compile produces a durable compiled program, and setup derives a trust-sensitive proving/verification key pair whose provenance is part of the security model. Witness generation and proof generation run once per request, touch the secret witness, and proof generation is expensive enough to be a queued worker job. Folding the infrequent, trust-sensitive admin stages into the same place as per-request prover work ties request latency to setup cost and puts heavy, stateful, security-sensitive steps on a hot path where they do not belong.

What makes a proof request different from a verifier request in Rust terms?

A proof request carries the private witness and drives compute-witness and generate-proof on a prover worker, so its types legitimately hold witness material and proving-key references. A verifier request must be witness-free by construction: it carries only the contract reference, the public inputs, and the proof blob, because the verifier consumes nothing secret. In Rust this is a type-boundary distinction — the witness path should be reachable from proving-side types and absent from verifier-facing types entirely, so the zero-knowledge property cannot be lost to an accidental field copy.

Why is contract or key version drift often a bigger operational risk than one single failed proof?

A single failed proof is a contained, observable event affecting one request. Version drift — a proof paired with the wrong verification key, or routed to a contract deployed from a different circuit revision — is a systemic mismatch that can fail silently, waste gas on transactions guaranteed to revert, or, worse, succeed against the wrong contract. It is a contract failure rather than a 'maybe verify and see' condition, so it should be caught by an explicit preflight before any verifier call; the most expensive ZoKrates mistakes are usually unmanaged version, key, and deployment boundaries, not one bad proof.

What does native verification prove, and what does it not prove about the Ethereum deployment path?

Native verification (ZoKrates verify against the local verification key) proves the proof system itself accepts the proof for the given public inputs — that the circuit, keys, and proof are internally consistent. It is a fast, deterministic first CI gate. It does not prove anything about the deployed Solidity verifier: the ABI encoding of public inputs, the verifyTx call, gas budget, contract address mapping, and chain interaction are all untested by native verify, so the deploy path needs its own contract-level test against a local chain or fork.

Why should generated verifier contracts still go through normal Solidity review and release discipline?

Being machine-generated by a ZK toolchain does not make a contract production-safe; export-verifier emits ordinary Solidity that is deployed, called, and paid for with real gas like any other contract. It still needs provenance, code and gas review, deployment review, versioned address mapping, and a rollback plan, because a flaw in the verifier deployment or its public-input encoding voids the guarantees of an otherwise-correct proof. Treating the generated artifact as exempt from release engineering is exactly how the deployment boundary becomes the place most mistakes happen.

Chapter 53 · EZKL, Verifiable LLM Inference, and GPU-Aware ZKML

EZKL, Verifiable LLM Inference, and GPU-Aware ZKML

Worked solutions to this chapter's exercises, lab, and review questions.

These exercises take the chapter's central claim seriously: verifiable LLM inference is an artifact pipeline before it is a model call, and Rust's job is to keep four boundaries honest. You separate verifier-visible claims from witness-only material, push heavyweight proving out of the request path, encode the public/private split into distinct types, and refuse to let preprocessing or serialization drift turn a protocol contract into an intermittent failure. The recurring discipline is ownership: who is allowed to hold the witness, who only ever sees the proof and the public claim, and which artifacts must be versioned even though they are not secret.

The lab and the profiling exercises ground the rest. They force you to treat GPU acceleration as a measured routing decision rather than a default, and to keep the verifier lane structurally witness-free so a leak becomes a compile error instead of an audit finding. By the end you should be able to look at any ZKML workflow and immediately sort every field into public, witness, or artifact-bound, and name the queue, lane, and version concerns that turn a prototype into something operable.

Exercise solutions

Exercise 1warm-up comprehension

Classify which parts of an LLM inference workflow are public, private, deterministic, or artifact-bound
